articles.text: Photo by Cara Yelland Dramatic photos of a bright orange sky over San Francisco were shared across the globe. September 9: Bay Area skies turned a dark, apocalyptic orange as an outbreak of wildfires continued to burn throughout California, making it the state’s worst wildfire season in history. The phenomenon – which was seen as far as Oregon – was a result of 16 different wildfire complexes burning in the region. The smoky conditions caused motorists to use their headlights as early as 8 a.m., and covered buildings, cars, and yards in ash. Residents noted that the sun was nearly invisible the entire day.
articles.title: An apocalyptic orange haze blankets San Francisco

articles.text: The Piedmont Post has named former mayor Bob McBain as its Man of the Year. After serving nearly nine years on the city council, the most recent three years as mayor. In his last official City Council meeting on December 7, McBain modestly pointed to city staff and councilmembers as the reason for successes under his tenure as mayor. McBain said that he was confident in the financial state of the city as outgoing mayor, the result of vigorous work for the duration of his 8-1/2 years on council. Many notable residents and former city staff poured in during public comment to offer their thanks to McBain, including former mayor Dean Barbieri, former City Administrator Paul Benoit, and former piedmont Beautification Foundation President Patty Siskind, among others. Even more wrote their thanks to McBain to the Post, which appeared as letters to the editor over the past few weeks. “Bob is one-in-a-million as mayor and man: kind, patient, and loyal,” wrote current Park Commission chair Patty Dunlap. “He is generous with tolerance, skimpy with judgment, and brimming with good will for all.” Former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain.
articles.title: Former Piedmont mayor Bob McBain

articles.text: Piedmont Post is naming University of California, San Francisco Epidemiologist, and Piedmont resident, George Rutherford as its Citizen of the Year. Dr. Rutherford became somewhat of a hero in town in much the same way that Dr. Anthony Fauci became a hero nationwide. Rutherford kept residents abreast of any and all medical advancements and responses to COVID-19 through multiple public forums. Some forums were more condensed and specific. Rutherford was called on by the League of Women Voters to offer his knowledge of the emerging pandemic early in its far-reaching impact. He also spoke during a UCSFhosted medical panel on the possibility of reopening schools. He has appeared several times at the school board meeting to offer advice on safe practices for reopening classes. Rutherford made himself available for Post interviews, even as many Bay Area stations contacted him for insights throughout the pandemic. He continues to be a leading expert and source for many Bay Area, and nationwide, news services. Piedmont resident, epidemiologist Dr. George Rutherford.
articles.title: UCSF Epidemiologist George Rutherford

articles.text: Editor: I am a parent to two PUSD students, as well as a spouse to a PUSD teacher. The COVID-19 pandemic has been incredibly difficult for our entire community, and the frustration everyone is feeling is natural and understandable. The recent anonymous letter to the editor advocating for donations to be withheld from the Piedmont Education Foundation, however, misplaces that frustration and is ultimately irresponsible and self-defeating. It’s important to point out that funds raised by the PEF allows PUSD to create the superior academic, emotional, creative, and social programs that help make PUSD such an awesome district, and these programs would likely not be as robust otherwise. When you factor in the inevitable budget cuts that are no doubt looming in the next couple of years from the economic impact of the pandemic, depriving the district of these additional funds will hurt only one constituency; our children. I have not always supported the decisions that have been made during this time, and I have thought that some stances taken by the district, by the teachers’ union, and by the parent community have been problematic and inconsistent. I will continue to give to PEF because when all of this is over, I want every tool available to those who have always taken great care in providing an exceptional educational environment. Regardless of my opposition to stances taken by the various communities connected to the district, I do believe that they have been operating with the intention of doing what is best for the children. Had the district opened early on, it is likely that we would have experienced the same chaos of intermittent openings and closings as has been the case with many other districts who have opened too soon or without proper planning. There is evidence now that children can safely go back to school, which is good news, and many of us support. Doing that, however, is complicated and not entirely up to the district, the teachers’ union, nor the parent community. We have to follow state and county mandates, as well as the best practices laid out by the various authorities who are doing their best to develop guidelines for constantly shifting circumstances. People should always give as their consciences and financial circumstances dictate, but I for one will be continuing to invest in our children through the institutions that have consistently supported them. –Spencer Perry
articles.title: Criticism of school donations seen as misplaced

articles.text: The year 2020 will end soon. Few will mourn its passing. It will be remembered as one of the most difficult years, if not the most difficult year, of our lives. Global pandemic. Racial injustice. Political turmoil. Economic uncertainty. The list is long. Thus, it was something of a relief, something of a small victory, to prepare the December 2020 preaching and worship schedule for our church newsletter. It was a sign that this hard year is drawing to a close. It was a signal that 2021 is on its way. None of us can know what 2021 will hold but if you are like me, you find yourself saying, “The odds are that it will be better than 2020.” As the year ends my wife, Karen, and I join our son, Aaron, and daughter-in-law, Teresa, in looking forward to the birth (due in early January) of a baby girl, their first daughter, our first granddaughter. The birth of every child needs to be greeted as a sign of God’s will that the world go on, as a sign of God’s promise to save and to bless. In this season we certainly receive this child with that understanding. Perhaps the best that can be said of 2020 is that it provided ample opportunity to learn and to grow. Zoom church. Distance learning. Virtual gathering. On-line medical appointments. Civic engagement from afar. Social distancing. Wearing a mask. Washing our hands. Facing difficulty. articles.text: I strongly disagree. In fact, it seems odd to me that the city would not extend the lease. The Center for the Arts has been a success, offering a rare space for visual artists, musicians and actors to show their work and perform. It also provides a wonderful – an exceptional – activity for people in the community and the East Bay, and right in our city. For example, we were treated to “The Sky’s the Limit,” an exhibition of dozens of artist Michael Stehr’s oil paintings, carefully organized so that it was Covid safe. It was great! As a realtor, I always mention the Center to buyers as one of the perks of living in Piedmont. As I understand it, the Center is run by a board of directors who are volunteers. I think they are doing an excellent job. They search and encourage local talent and use their connections to bring talent from faraway, balancing and curating usage by Piedmont talent – including the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the Piedmont Art fundraisers for the schools, youth rehearsals, youth recitals – and also some of the finest talent in the Bay Area and nationally. They have even hosted several international musicians. And before Covid-19 closed many public events, the calendar was full throughout the year. They also seem to do a great job of maintaining and operating the venue. The building has never looked better! And I understand their books are balanced and they are in good financial shape. With an operation that is so well run and serving a very useful public good, why wouldn’t the city extend their lease? In this time of Covid-19, we need the inspiration of artistic groups which are struggling to stay alive. I think now, more than ever, we need to support them. They provide beauty, humor and insights when times are tough. So, extend the PCA’s lease. It would be very sad – and I think a big mistake – to lose this exceptional part of our city. –Carol Brown
articles.title: LETTERS MAIN

articles.text: The following letter was sent to the City Council. Editor: I am writing to express my strong support for allowing the Piedmont Center for the Arts to continue to lease the space at 801 Magnolia Avenue. The Piedmont Center for the Arts provides invaluable local access to the arts for many young people and families in the area. My teenaged daughter, who has played violin since kindergarten, has participated in several studio performances and a master class at the Center, along with the other members of her Quartet. Having an inviting and centrally located venue that supports arts appreciation and performance is especially needed now for young people, for whom the arts provide a place of creativity, connection, and accomplishment during complex and challenging times. With the closure of the Montclair Women’s Art Center in 2015, the role of the Piedmont Center for the Arts in providing a community gathering place for the arts is especially important. It would be a great loss for families in the area if this community treasure were not to continue. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, –Jane Wellenkamp, Ph.D.
articles.title: Center for the Arts a nurturing venue for young artists

articles.text: What we won’t miss – from ‘Doomscrolling’ to ‘Blursday’ Commentary by Chris Honoré I recently read an article by New York Times reporter Tim Herrera which made the point that language is dynamic, perpetually responsive to our ever-trending pop culture and contemporary experiences. As a result, we have a vocabulary born of our health care and political crises. Find below a list of these words with definitions. Some I have used as springboards, others I’ve embellished with levity where appropriate, while a few are my own, gleaned from my sofa-bound travels. Let’s begin with Doomscrolling: unedited, online consuming of bad news and information known to be detrimental to one’s mental health and wellbeing. Quarantini: your go-to drink for lockdowns and beyond. The Messy Threshhold: how tidy, clean, put-away, vacuumed, dusted, organized does your now all too familiar digs have to be before it reaches a critical mass of good grief! intolerance. Ditto your Stay at Home Oufit: T-shirt scuzzy? Stand up, take off, turn inside out, put back on (try to get the label in back). You are now Zoom ready. And speaking of Zoom, the online, go-to remote, full-screen interaction and conferencing. No worries – frayed jeans/blown out sweat pants and flip-flops are de rigueur. Maskine: irritation and pimples developed from wearing a mask. Masks, those 4” x 11” piece of protective material, determined to be two-way safety gear, has gone totemic, its defiant absence has devolved into a political statement. As well, while wearing a mask, we’re all trying to say with our eyes and eyebrows what we once said with our grin, smile, and a flash of teeth. Behind the mask, shaving and flossing and fuzz removal are so yesterday. Remote learning, as if. Faceto-face teaching, finally acknowledged as an art, one requiring a trifecta of skill sets that not everyone possesses, long underrated and underpaid, and now suddenly viewed through a different prism. Just ask parents after two weeks of school closures and their attempts at being stand-ins for teachers. Pods: your designated group deemed safe to hang out with. Voter Fraud: non-existent, except in Trump world where unicorns have free range. Blursday: the unreliability of pandemic time, days steeped in déjà vu and all things groundhog-esque, often measured by the aging, brown-pocked bananas in a bowl in the kitchen. And then there’s Social Contact Tracing: trying to remember who you actually had a conversation with… was that this morning or yesterday? Flatten the Curve: not likely. For reasons that are inexplicable, millions of Americans traveled over Thanksgiving and Christmas (aka Superspreaders), refused to social distance or wear masks, which, in the aggregate, are, apparently, a bridge too far. Flattening the Curve proved to be eminently elusive hence, the graphs go vertical as Spikes or Surges. The term Superspreader was often used to characterize Trump’s ubiquitous rallies. It is now used to define holidays such as Thanksgiving and Christmas, when 85 million Americans were reported to have travelled over Christmas. Not exactly a lockdown. Edibles: Arizona, Montana, New Jersey, and South Dakota just legalized marijuana. Timing is everything. While some may reach for a comfort doobie, in the first six months of the pandemic some 19 million Americans bought guns. Feeling more relaxed? Streamers: Can you hear me now? A cohort of not camera shy denizens who sit for hours before a screen and over-share a spectrum of content, from baking to sleeping (really), apparently filling a niche. One streaming site is called “Twitch,” a perfect name for that tic likely to develop after dedicated watching. The last word is Unprecedented: a go-to descriptor that expresses our response not only to the novel coronavirus but the crashing-through-guard-rails presidency of Trump. It quickly became a utilitarian buzzword that grew so familiar it soon lost its ability to carry the weight of the moment. And what a moment it has been. Thus far.
articles.title: Say Goodbye, 2020

pages.text: Wednesday, December 30, 2020 3 Center for the Arts a nurturing venue for young artists The following letter was sent to the City Council. Editor: I am writing to express my strong support for allowing the Piedmont Center for the Arts to continue to lease the space at 801 Magnolia Avenue. The Piedmont Center for the Arts provides invaluable local access to the arts for many young people and families in the area. My teenaged daughter, who has played violin since kindergarten, has participated in several studio performances and a master class at the Center, along with the other members of her Quartet. Having an inviting and centrally located venue that supports arts appreciation and performance is especially needed now for young people, for whom the arts provide a place of creativity, connection, and accomplishment during complex and challenging times. With the closure of the Montclair Women’s Art Center in 2015, the role of the Piedmont Center for the Arts in providing a community gathering place for the arts is especially important. It would be a great loss for families in the area if this community treasure were not to continue. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, –Jane Wellenkamp, Ph.D. Extend the lease for Center for the Arts Editor: I think the city should extend the lease for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. I read an unsolicited email, as well as an opinion piece on the Piedmont Civic Association website, in which someone opposes extending the lease. LETTERS MAIN I strongly disagree. In fact, it seems odd to me that the city would not extend the lease. The Center for the Arts has been a success, offering a rare space for visual artists, musicians and actors to show their work and perform. It also provides a wonderful – an exceptional – activity for people in the community and the East Bay, and right in our city. For example, we were treated to “The Sky’s the Limit,” an exhibition of dozens of artist Michael Stehr’s oil paintings, carefully organized so that it was Covid safe. It was great! As a realtor, I always mention the Center to buyers as one of the perks of living in Piedmont. As I understand it, the Center is run by a board of directors who are volunteers. I think they are doing an excellent job. They search and encourage local talent and use their connections to bring talent from faraway, balancing and curating usage by Piedmont talent – including the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the Piedmont Art fundraisers for the schools, youth rehearsals, youth recitals – and also some of the finest talent in the Bay Area and nationally. They have even hosted several international musicians. And before Covid-19 closed many public events, the calendar was full throughout the year. They also seem to do a great job of maintaining and operating the venue. The building has never looked better! And I understand their books are balanced and they are in good financial shape. With an operation that is so well run and serving a very useful public good, why wouldn’t the city extend their lease? In this time of Covid-19, we need the inspiration of artistic groups which are struggling to stay alive. I think now, more than ever, we need to support them. They provide beauty, humor and insights when times are tough. So, extend the PCA’s lease. It would be very sad – and I think a big mistake – to lose this exceptional part of our city. –Carol Brown See More Letters on page 30 Commentary A year to forget Say Goodbye, 2020 What we won’t miss – from ‘Doomscrolling’ to ‘Blursday’ Commentary by Chris Honoré I recently read an article by New York Times reporter Tim Herrera which made the point that language is dynamic, perpetually responsive to our ever-trending pop culture and contemporary experiences. As a result, we have a vocabulary born of our health care and political crises. Find below a list of these words with definitions. Some I have used as springboards, others I’ve embellished with levity where appropriate, while a few are my own, gleaned from my sofa-bound travels. Let’s begin with Doomscrolling: unedited, online consuming of bad news and information known to be detrimental to one’s mental health and wellbeing. Quarantini: your go-to drink for lockdowns and beyond. The Messy Threshhold: how tidy, clean, put-away, vacuumed, dusted, organized does your now all too familiar digs have to be before it reaches a critical mass of good grief! intolerance. Ditto your Stay at Home Oufit: T-shirt scuzzy? Stand up, take off, turn inside out, put back on (try to get the label in back). You are now Zoom ready. And speaking of Zoom, the online, go-to remote, full-screen interaction and conferencing. No worries – frayed jeans/blown out sweat pants and flip-flops are de rigueur. Maskine: irritation and pimples developed from wearing a mask. Masks, those 4” x 11” piece of protective material, determined to be two-way safety gear, has gone totemic, its defiant absence has devolved into a political statement. As well, while wearing a mask, we’re all trying to say with our eyes and eyebrows what we once said with our grin, smile, and a flash of teeth. Behind the mask, shaving and flossing and fuzz removal are so yesterday. Remote learning, as if. Faceto-face teaching, finally acknowledged as an art, one requiring a trifecta of skill sets that not everyone possesses, long underrated and underpaid, and now suddenly viewed through a different prism. Just ask parents after two weeks of school closures and their attempts at being stand-ins for teachers. Pods: your designated group deemed safe to hang out with. Voter Fraud: non-existent, except in Trump world where unicorns have free range. Blursday: the unreliability of pandemic time, days steeped in déjà vu and all things groundhog-esque, often measured by the aging, brown-pocked bananas in a bowl in the kitchen. And then there’s Social Contact Tracing: trying to remember who you actually had a conversation with… was that this morning or yesterday? Flatten the Curve: not likely. For reasons that are inexplicable, millions of Americans traveled over Thanksgiving and Christmas (aka Superspreaders), refused to social distance or wear masks, which, in the aggregate, are, apparently, a bridge too far. Flattening the Curve proved to be eminently elusive hence, the graphs go vertical as Spikes or Surges. The term Superspreader was often used to characterize Trump’s ubiquitous rallies. It is now used to define holidays such as Thanksgiving and Christmas, when 85 million Americans were reported to have travelled over Christmas. Not exactly a lockdown. Edibles: Arizona, Montana, New Jersey, and South Dakota just legalized marijuana. Timing is everything. While some may reach for a comfort doobie, in the first six months of the pandemic some 19 million Americans bought guns. Feeling more relaxed? Streamers: Can you hear me now? A cohort of not camera shy denizens who sit for hours before a screen and over-share a spectrum of content, from baking to sleeping (really), apparently filling a niche. One streaming site is called “Twitch,” a perfect name for that tic likely to develop after dedicated watching. The last word is Unprecedented: a go-to descriptor that expresses our response not only to the novel coronavirus but the crashing-through-guard-rails presidency of Trump. It quickly became a utilitarian buzzword that grew so familiar it soon lost its ability to carry the weight of the moment. And what a moment it has been. Thus far. articles.text: As the Post celebrates its 23rd year of publication, it may bring a smile to the faces of our readers as they see a list of the top newspapers in the country. 1. The Wall Street Journal is read by the people who run the country. 2. The Washington Post is read by people who think they run the country. 3. The New York Times is read by people who think they should run the country and who are very good at crossword puzzles. 4. USA Today is read by people who think they ought to run the country but don’t really understand The New York Times. They do, however, like their statistics shown in pie charts. 5. 6. The Los Angeles Times is read by people who wouldn’t mind running the country if they could find the time, and if they didn’t have to leave Southern California to do it. The Boston Globe is read by people whose parents used to run the country and did a poor job of it, thank you very much. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. The New York Daily News is read by people who aren’t too sure who’s running the country and don’t really care as long as they can get a seat on the subway. The New York Post is read by people who don’t care who is running the country as long as they do something really scandalous, preferably while intoxicated. The Miami Herald is read by people who are running another country but need the baseball scores. The San Francisco Chronicle is read by people who aren’t sure if there is a country, or that anyone is running it; but If so, they oppose all that they stand for. There are occasional exceptions, such as if the leaders are handicapped minority feminist atheist dwarfs who also happen to be illegal aliens from any other country, or galaxy, provided, of course, that they are not Republicans. The National Enquirer is read by people trapped in line at the grocery store. The Piedmont Post is read by people who quietly run everything but the country, and prefer a smaller newspaper for Where In the World Are We photo ops when they travel. articles.text: At year-end, Piedmont had recorded 113 cases of COVID-19 As year ends, COVID-19 case load continues to grow in Alameda County and throughout the world. The global coronavirus pandemic was the defining issue of 2020 on a worldwide scale, and the ongoing calamity will likely be problem that shapes the next generation. The disease ravaged the world from Wuhan, China, where the disease was first identified in December 2019 according to the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention, to Piedmont, California. The unprecedented situation resulted in tragic deaths, overwhelmed hospitals, created economic lockdowns and several seasons of anxiety. The first California case of coronavirus was reported on February 26 in Solano County. On March 16, six Bay Area counties, including Alameda County, were the first in the United States to adopt an aggressive order requiring residents to stay at home for all but essential activities. Three days later, Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a statewide stay-at-home order. County Public Health Department reported that there were 10 confirmed cases of COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by coronavirus, amongst Piedmont residents – the county began providing a city-by-city breakdown of its data on April 8. Throughout May, three more cases were reported in Piedmont. County overtook Santa Clara County to become the Bay Area epicenter for the outbreak. Almost 4,000 cases were recorded as of June 1 countywide. Economic activity was largely limited to curbside and delivery retail. The spread of COVID-19 appeared to come under control in June, although cases began rising in July as restrictions were loosened. Alameda County paused reopening plans on June 29. the hardest hit state in the nation. Alameda County was placed on a COVID-19 “watchlist” by the state on July 12. In August, six cases were reported in Piedmont – with a population of less than 11,000 – in one week, bringing the total for the City to 29. At the end of August, the state placed Alameda County in the Purple Tier of its color-coded, four-tier Blueprint for a Safer Economy plan for reopening California’s economy. The Purple Tier is the most restrictive tier. In Alameda County, the cumulative case count surpassed the 20,000 threshold on September 14. On September 22, the state moved Alameda County into the Red Tier. The Red Tier is thirdmost restrictive tier and allows for indoor dining, gyms, museums and religious services with capacity limits. However, county officials took several weeks to monitor the situation and plan before announcing any changes to current health orders. At this point, Piedmont had recorded 33 total cases. On October 9, several more economic sectors and activities were reopened in Alameda County. Indoor museums, zoos, aquariums, and libraries reopened with capacity limits, and hotels were opened to tourists. Personal care services, such as skin care, waxing and tattoo parlors, were reopened with restrictions. County Public Health Department had recorded 41 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont. Alameda County was placed in the second-least restrictive Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, on October 13. Indoor dining with capacity restrictions was reintroduced to Alameda County on October 23 as the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county was 1.4 percent. This positivity rate stayed below 2 percent throughout October. Cases began spiking in Alameda County on October 28 and the year is ending with the pandemic being worse than ever. 53 cumulative cases of COVID- 19 reported in Piedmont. Alameda County enacted Purple Tier restrictions again for business and activities on November 18. Statewide, the number of cases crossed the 1 million threshold. Nine new cases were reported in Piedmont between November 10 and November 17, bringing the City’s total to 66. On December 1, the countywide cumulative COVID-19 case count was almost at 30,000 following huge spikes around Thanksgiving. Officials issued a new stayat-home order for the county that began Monday, December 7. Restaurants had to reduce operations to take-out and delivery only; outdoor and indoor dining were prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor playgrounds were also shuttered. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores were allowed to remain open with capacity restrictions. As the first doses of a COVID- 19 vaccine arrive in the San Francisco Bay Area, new cases of the disease are surging in Alameda County like never before. December 11 was the worst day for new cases in the county since the pandemic began, with 1,071 cases reported. Over 12,500 doses of a COVID-19 vaccine manufactured by Pfizer began being administered to hospital workers, firefighters and first responders on December 18. had recorded 80 cases of COVID- 19. On December 21, that number had been increased by 11 to 91 total. By December 28, the number of cases had swelled to 113 in the City. In Alameda County, 50,196 COVID-19 cases have been reported this year. The rolling seven-day positivity rate is 8.1 percent. On December 16, health officials from around the region announced that the availability of ICU beds fell below 15 percent in the Bay Area Region. Due to this, lockdown restrictions will continue until at least January 7 of 2021, but will likely be extended.

articles.text: History will remember 2020 as a year of devastating wildfires that burned around California and the western United States. An estimated 4 percent of California burned during the worst wildfire season in modern history. Even though Piedmont was spared from the fires, the City suffered through weeks of poor air quality and unearthly hazy conditions due to fire debris in the air hundreds of miles from the actual fires. The San Francisco Bay Area wildfire season took over national headlines in mid-August, when lightning sparked a trio of wildfires that ended up burning for weeks. Within days, two of the fires grew to historically large sizes. The CZU Lightning Complex burned between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties. The LNU Lightning Complex, the deadliest and most destructive of the three fires, burned in Napa and Sonoma counties. The SCU Lightning Complex burned in rural Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. In Piedmont, smoke from these fires severely impacted air quality. On August 19, 2020, the recorded air quality in the Bay Area was the worst in the world. The National Weather Service declared a Red Flag Warning, meaning high wildfire risk, for two days in Piedmont in late August, and again on September 7-9. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District declared a record-breaking 30 consecutive days of “Spare the Air” alerts from August 18 to September 17. These alerts mean that particulate pollution in the Bay Area is elevated, making air quality unhealthy. When an alert is declared, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves and outdoor fire pits is prohibited. The number of consecutive Spare the Air days in 2020 was over double the previous record of 14 days of Spare the Air alerts set in 2018. Another 24-hour Spare the Air Alert was declared on October 6, while another alert was issued October 10-12. more than 3.2 million acres had burned in California, and historic high for the U.S. Blazes also ravaged Oregon and Washington. Smoke from these fires caused terrible air quality in the Bay Area. The severe situation was strikingly evident on Wednesday, September 9, when Piedmont skies turned a dark orange color. Although the color dissipated, the unhealthy air conditions continued for days. Also in September, Piedmont firefighters joined others in battling the Creek Fire burning through the Sierra Nevada mountains near Fresno. On October 13, a Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills through October 16. On October 14, PG&E began notifying some Alameda County residents, including the Montclair neighborhood of Oakland, in October about a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to wildfire risk. More Red Flag Warnings were issued for the East Bay Hills from October 21 to October 23. The entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on October 25 as hurricane force gusts blew through the region. That day, the NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. In Mount Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The August Complex Fire, sparked by lightning in August, burned in and around the Mendocino National Forest. It was the largest wildfire in California history and became the state’s first “gigafire” in late October. A gigafire means a wildfire that burns over 1 million acres. In October, a fire in Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. No one was hurt but several people were displaced. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted by a scheduled PSPS on October 25. Several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power for several days. Cooler, wetter weather moved into the region in November, but wildfire risks continued. The August Complex Fire was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Risks continued even into December of 2020. A rare Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills by NWS from December 6 to December 7. There have been only two other December Red Flag Warnings in Bay Area history, both within the past decade – 2013 and 2017. At the height of drought conditions in California – in the 2010s – Red Flag Warnings were occasionally ordered in January. Meteorologists believe it is possible the region could see some Red Flag Warnings issued next month. As of yesterday, December 29, six of 12 Cal Fire units in Northern California had begun winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season is over.
articles.title: 2020 – worst wildfire year in California history

articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club, in conjunction with five other Bay Area garden clubs, is sponsoring a webinar that discusses the unique ecological system of the San Francisco Bay. The free webinar will be available on Wednesday, January 13, and will host four Bay Area professors who will discuss flooding, the importance of seaweed, restoration of marshlands, and the need to plant native plants. The event will begin at 9:30 a.m. with an opening slide show. The main program will run from 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. Titled “The Power of Plants Will Protect the Bay,” the webinar will describe how scientists are collaborating on ways to protect and restore the Bay shoreline by Boyer, professor of Biology and Wetlands Ecology; Josie Iselin, author of The Curious World of Seaweed; and Diana Benner and Laura Hanson, co-owners of The Watershed Nursery in Richmond. Co-sponsors include Piedmont Garden Club, Woodside-Atherton Garden Club, Marin Garden Club, Hillsborough Garden Club, Orinda Garden Club, and Carmel-By-the-Sea Garden Club. These six organizations are affiliates of the Garden Club of America, whose mission is to “restore, improve and protect the quality of the environment through educational programs and action in the fields of conservation and civic improvement.” Pre-registration for the event is required. Register at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/bay-visions-tickets-127648342629. Karina Nielsen, Director of Estuary and Ocean Science Center at San Francisco State University utilizing plants underwater, in the wetlands, and along the shores. articles.title: Piedmont Garden Club to co-sponsor Jan. 13 webinar on SF Bay ecological system

articles.text: The outfield grass at Hampton Park was closed for reseeding on December 23 and will remain closed until mid-February. Coaches Field, on Moraga Avenue, will also close for reseeding for two weeks beginning on January 4. The annual closure allows the City to aerate, reseed and patch worn and damaged areas. The artificial turf infield, tennis courts, and tot lot at Hampton Field will remain open for public use during field maintenance work. The public hours at Beach Playfield have been expanded to 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. through January 18.
articles.title: Hampton Park, Coaches Field to be reseeded

The webinar will feature speakers Karina Nielson, Director of the Estuary and Ocean Science Center, SF State; Dr. Katharyn 2020 – worst wildfire year in California history By Barry Eitel History will remember 2020 as a year of devastating wildfires that burned around California and the western United States. An estimated 4 percent of California burned during the worst wildfire season in modern history. Even though Piedmont was spared from the fires, the City suffered through weeks of poor air quality and unearthly hazy conditions due to fire debris in the air hundreds of miles from the actual fires. The San Francisco Bay Area wildfire season took over national headlines in mid-August, when lightning sparked a trio of wildfires that ended up burning for weeks. Within days, two of the fires grew to historically large sizes. The CZU Lightning Complex burned between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties. The LNU Lightning Complex, the deadliest and most destructive of the three fires, burned in Napa and Sonoma counties. The SCU Lightning Complex burned in rural Stanislaus and San Joaquin counties. In Piedmont, smoke from these fires severely impacted air quality. On August 19, 2020, the recorded air quality in the Bay Area was the worst in the world. The National Weather Service declared a Red Flag Warning, meaning high wildfire risk, for two days in Piedmont in late August, and again on September 7-9. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District declared a record-breaking 30 consecutive days of “Spare the Air” alerts from August 18 to September 17. These alerts mean that particulate pollution in the Bay Area is elevated, making air quality unhealthy. When an alert is declared, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves and outdoor fire pits is prohibited. The number of consecutive Spare the Air days in 2020 was over double the previous record of 14 days of Spare the Air alerts set in 2018. Another 24-hour Spare the Air Alert was declared on October 6, while another alert was issued October 10-12. By the middle of September, more than 3.2 million acres had burned in California, and historic high for the U.S. Blazes also ravaged Oregon and Washington. Smoke from these fires caused terrible air quality in the Bay Area. The severe situation was strikingly evident on Wednesday, September 9, when Piedmont skies turned a dark orange color. Although the color dissipated, the unhealthy air conditions continued for days. Also in September, Piedmont firefighters joined others in battling the Creek Fire burning through the Sierra Nevada mountains near Fresno. On October 13, a Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills through October 16. On October 14, PG&E began notifying some Alameda County residents, including the Montclair neighborhood of Oakland, in October about a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to wildfire risk. More Red Flag Warnings were issued for the East Bay Hills from October 21 to October 23. The entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on October 25 as hurricane force gusts blew through the region. That day, the NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. In Mount Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The August Complex Fire, sparked by lightning in August, burned in and around the Mendocino National Forest. It was the largest wildfire in California history and became the state’s first “gigafire” in late October. A gigafire means a wildfire that burns over 1 million acres. In October, a fire in Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. No one was hurt but several people were displaced. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted by a scheduled PSPS on October 25. Several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power for several days. Cooler, wetter weather moved into the region in November, but wildfire risks continued. The August Complex Fire was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Risks continued even into December of 2020. A rare Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills by NWS from December 6 to December 7. There have been only two other December Red Flag Warnings in Bay Area history, both within the past decade – 2013 and 2017. At the height of drought conditions in California – in the 2010s – Red Flag Warnings were occasionally ordered in January. Meteorologists believe it is possible the region could see some Red Flag Warnings issued next month. As of yesterday, December 29, six of 12 Cal Fire units in Northern California had begun winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season is over. Hampton Park, Coaches Field to be reseeded The outfield grass at Hampton Park was closed for reseeding on December 23 and will remain closed until mid-February. Coaches Field, on Moraga Avenue, will also close for reseeding for two weeks beginning on January 4. The annual closure allows the City to aerate, reseed and patch worn and damaged areas. The artificial turf infield, tennis courts, and tot lot at Hampton Field will remain open for public use during field maintenance work. The public hours at Beach Playfield have been expanded to 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. through January 18.

articles.text: Jazz band saxophonist. Rock band member. Composer. YouTube musician. Self-taught guitarist, drummer and pianist. As if that weren’t impressive enough for a 17-year-old, Piedmont High School senior Connor Stratman has yet another musical talent to list on his college applications: guitar teacher to local elementary students. “My favorite part is when I can find a song that they like or that I like, and they play it for the first time,” Stratman said. “It’s a really good feeling to see them excited. I remember that excitement. You finally get it down and it sounds like a song. It’s cool to see that on their faces. I’m reliving my experience of learning the guitar through them,” he added. Stratman taught himself to play guitar after finding one in his grandparents’ closet three years ago. Now he shares his skill each week with four beginning guitarists, meeting them PHS Senior Connor Stratman online or physically distanced in their backyards, even though it’s challenging to teach proper finger positioning or stances from a screen or six feet away. Nonetheless, it’s going well. “I like him a lot,” said one student, 10-year-old Ben McMurtry, who’s learning “Back in Black” by AC/ DC. “I like how he teaches me. It’s fun to play guitar with him.” The lessons come at an important time, when PUSD students are tired of distance learning from home, fourth graders are all playing recorders, and music education is optional for fifth graders. “I hope it’s fun for them to do a little bit something different,” said Stratman, who discovered a love of music when he was about his students’ ages. “I think it’s good to have a little bit of music going on for them in some way.” Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for all PUSD students. articles.text: January 22: $3.2 million was raised by Piedmont Education Fund for Piedmont schools through its annual Giving Campaign. The 17-week fundraiser set a record. January 24: Former Piedmont resident Linda Lei leads all 7th grade students through an intro lesson in Chinese brush paintings. February 6: Piedmont participates in state-wide rally “Fund Public Education Now!”, at the Community Hall. This public gathering of 75 people would be one of the last of the year. February 8: An all-girls Piedmont robotic team “Roses and Rivets” wins the Judges Award at the FIRST Tech Challenge Robotics Tournament in Napa. March 13: Piedmont’s School Board is the first in Alameda County to announce closure of its schools. MARCH 16: All Piedmont schools close due to COVID-19. Alameda County Department of Health initially orders schools closed for two weeks. Middle and High school students are still tasked with some school work via online work on Schedulicity. Limited, if any, screen time occurs between teachers and secondary students. Minimal work is assigned to elementary students. March 25: Alameda County Office of Education extends the closure of all schools in the county to May 1 to slow the spread of COVID-19. March 25: Supt. Randy Booker states that the California Department of Education will not require schools to comply with the requirement to have a minimum of 180 instructional days during the school year. He confirmes that the school district had made no plans to extend the school year into June to help make up for the lost days of instruction, nor did it have any plans to conduct summer school. Piedmont classes are scheduled to end on Friday, May 29, for summer vacation. March 27: Four Piedmont teens start Feedmont.org, a program to deliver groceries and other essentials to high-risk Piedmonters who want to avoid going into stores. The Feedmont Team is comprised of sophomore Atticus Lim and three seniors, his sisters Natalie and Diana Lim, and Amelia Costello. March 31: California State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond announces schools in California will not reopen before fall 2020. April 1: The school board declares the construction of the STEAM building is essential and amid a lockdown of much of the business community, construction continues. April 20: Class grading for the Spring semester is changed to Pass/No Pass. April 27: Led by incoming Senior Class President Audrey Edel, Piedmont High School students create a Virtual Mentor Program that connects high schoolers and elementary schoolers through crafts, tutoring, and reading. More than 70 high school volunteers sign up before the first day of mentoring. May 12: California State University (CSU), the largest public college system in the country with 23 campuses and 480,000 students, is the first college to announce all classes in fall will be online. May 13: The School Board decides to move forward with demolition of the 10’s building on the high school campus, to be replaced with the new Alan Harvey Theater. May 13: Sue Smegal, a former Piedmont Middle School teacher, School Board member and a longtime volunteer in the schools and community, is presented with the Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award by the School Board. May 14: State School Superintendent Tony Thurmond announces that the decision of when and how to reopen public schools will be left to each school district. May 19: PHS Senior Awards ceremony takes place online. The following seniors won multiple awards: Sophia Zalewski (4): Excellence in Mathematics Plaque, Outstanding Girl Athlete Trophy (Cross Country), Piedmont Certificate in Mandarin, Valedictorian Plaque. Anne Cheng (3): Dean Faberman Plaque (Mock Trial), Spanish for Excellence Trophy and English Trophy. Sophia Butler (2): Outstanding Senior in Drama Director’s Plaque and Susan Kawaichi Plaque Diversity Award. May 21: The University of California suspends the requirement of SAT scores for next year’s applicants, and discontinues the requirement of letter grades for academic classes taken in winter, spring and summer terms of 2020. May 25: The PHS Parents Club hosts a drive-thru for students to pick up their yearbooks and graduation caps and gowns. For many, this was the first in-person school function since March. May 28: Piedmont Middle School has online graduation ceremony through Youtube. May 29: PHS holds in-person, masked and distanced graduation ceremonies in groups of 50-60 students at Witter Field with each student allowed two guests from their household. No student speeches were given by class Valedictorian Sophia Zalewski or co-Salutatorians Diana Lim and Natalie Lim. June 4: School Reopening Task Force holds its first meeting with nearly 100 participants, including students, parents, classified employees, certificated educators, administrators, and two board members. June 9: The demolition of the administrative and classroom “10s building” begins. In its place will be a new $20 million theater building scheduled for completion Fall of 2021. It takes four Staff photo Piedmont High School’s 3-story classroom building was certified for occupancy by the State on October 16, 2020, two months after its scheduled opening. days to demolish the building. June 24: Governor Newsom announces Assembly Bill 77, which sets requirements for distance learning. Requirements are now in place for attendance, participation and daily teacher interaction with students. A portion of the bill limits distance learning only to certain at-risk students in the fall. “The idea of [full] distance learning is essentially pulled off the table for board consideration,” said Supt. Booker June 26: “Piedmont Partners” starts a petition to reopen schools in the fall. 740 parents, students and community members sign in the first four days. June 30: The School Board votes for a hybrid learning model for the 2020-21 school year during a nearly eight-hour meeting. The board approves in-person classes four or five days per week with face coverings and six foot spacing while breaking classes up into smaller cohorts when possible. July 8: Piedmont High School seniors Audrey Edel, Sadie Tschider, and Anthony Wong start “PiedmontMaskProject,” creating videos and social media posts to spread mask wearing awareness. July 13: The School Board directs the superintendent to start the school year online, citing increases in Bay Area COVID cases. July 17: Governor Newsom forbids public schools from opening if their county is on the COVID “watch-list,” (now equivalent to the purple tier). Alameda County has been on list since July 12. August 7: Five candidates vie for three seats on the School Board. Cory Smegal (incumbent), Hari Titan, Veronica Thigpen, Hilary Cooper, and Jason Kelley file applications to run. August 17: The opening of the STEAM building has been delayed. According to ongoing PUSD announcements, it had been on track to be completed by August 17, August 17: The first day of class begins with online classes, now requiring mandatory attendance and scheduled screen time. A chrome book is given to every student K-12. Parents and students give feedback that online learning has improved from spring. August 26: The school district reaches a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with school employees and (MOU) with teachers solely for Distance Learning. Teachers receive guarantee that in-person learning for TK-5th grade will not start until at least October 1. September 9: After months of deliberation and adapting to state and local policy changes, Piedmont teachers and PUSD strike a tentative agreement on an MOU for in-person learning. Teachers are given the right to dismiss any student not wearing a mask properly; cohort sizes are limited to 15. Exposure to someone with COVID-19 requires a 14-day quarantine and a return to distance learning. An unpaid administrative leave can be requested if a teacher is unable to return to in-person instruction because either they or someone in their household is at increased risk from COVID-19. Risk elements include being over 65 or having a BMI over 30. This agreement goes into effect if schools are allowed to open in the red tier. September 9: The School Board approves development of a Racial Equity policy, which creates an administrative position in the school district, a Director of Equity. A focus is placed on anti-racism policy; curriculum and hiring practices will also change. September 11: The high school student body leaders (ASB) hold a virtual Club Day during lunch. A record-high 39 clubs sign up. September 22: Alameda County moves to red tier. Alameda County schools would have the green light to open after two weeks in red tier, raising hopes that schools in town might finally be able to open. September 23: With a narrow 3-2 vote the School Board agrees to file a waiver with the county to allow TK-5th grade students back in school, regardless of COVID tier. The District will have to show it has testing, safety precautions and a reopening plan. Staying in the red tier looks like a more promising route to schools opening. The waiver program is later canceled by the County. October 6: The School Board approves a new school reopening plan. TK-2 students will return to class on November 3. Grades 3-5 plan to return November 10. October 9: Elementary school families are sent surveys to choose between in-person or distance learning. 75 percent choose in-person. October 12: Bradley Smet from San Luis Obispo is hired as the new high school Athletic Director. October 12: The District posts its reopening plan on the school district website, as part of the requirement to reopen. October 16: STEAM building receives Certificate of Occupancy 2 months after the projected open date. Teachers wait to be allowed in. October 16: Piedmont Makers donate 30 LEGO Mindstorms Robotics sets to Piedmont Middle School to create engineering and programming courses at PMS. The retail value is $18,000. October 23: Just 11 days before the scheduled reopening of schools, Supt. Booker announces a delay from November 3 to December 1 for the return to elementary school campuses due to the district’s inability to create a master school schedule. Teachers opting out of in-person teaching or still unsure leaves the district understaffed. November 3: Cory Smegal, Veronica Thigpen and Hilary Cooper are elected to school board. November 9: Alameda County allows secondary schools to reopen with protocols in place. Supt. Booker announces that the earliest time Piedmont secondary schools could open would be January 4.

articles.text: A parent called me the other day in a panic. “I’m worried that my son is falling behind in school because of Covid,” he said, in obvious distress. “Behind who?” I replied, giving him some time to consider my response. After a moment I added, “Every kid on the planet is in the same boat.” “Oh,” he said, with a little chuckle. “I see what you mean.” While there is nothing funny about the ways Covid is wreaking havoc on education, I believe that we are missing perhaps the only opportunity for optimism during this crisis by focusing on our children’s academic achievement rather than on their spiritual growth, of which there has been plenty in the past several months. Because of Covid, our kids are becoming Spiritual Warriors right before our eyes, and it’s an amazing thing to see. To me, Spiritual Warriors are those who effectively engage their mind, heart, and soul as they navigate the world. It’s a skill set, and Spiritual Warriors toggle among these aspects of themselves and recognize on a deep, perhaps subconscious level, that they must utilize all of these parts of themselves in order to thrive. For many of my students, Covid is the first situation in their lives where they, and their parents, have absolutely no control. They can’t problem-solve the pandemic way, or spend money (if they have it) to escape it. Covid is a hard stop. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s English Department has selected Naomi Klein’s book This Changes Everything: Capitalism vs. the Climate for its 11th annual community read project, known as Readmont. Klein argues that climate change should not be put on a shelf and studied but is a problem that requires fixing the economic system that she sees as already in trouble. A limited number of copies will be available for checkout at the PHS library when school reopens sometime in January. Interested readers can reserve a copy by contacting Librarian Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Books are available for purchase at A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair Village, where a 20% discount is being offered. Readmont teamed up with Piedmont Connect to host book discussions at the high school starting in February and continuing through April. For more information, contact Beth Black, PHS English Department Chair at bblack@piedmont. k12.ca.us.

articles.text: • • • • The Piedmont Recreation Department is offering new programs for the new year. Included in the new programs are: • Tag You’re IT, with the legendary Michael Murphy • Middle School Volleyball • Judo • Let’s Get Out and Play, with Mr. Wiz • Rugby (non-contact) • Hip Hop Fitness In addition to the new class offerings, the Winter Session includes ongoing programs, to include: Tennis, Tae Kwon Do, Fencing, Clay & Goodies, Multi Sports and Games with Ted Scherman, Skyhawks, One Village Sports, Cross Country and Move and Grove. Looking for a Stay-At-Home option? Try some of the Rec. Department’s Virtual Programs: • TikTok Dance Camp Dragonfly Designs Middle and High School Debate Public Speaking Tiny Techs View the class listing at w w w.register.com munit ypass.net. After-school programs The popular after-school programs Smart Start and Play Pods return as well. Operating outdoors at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood, Smart Start and Play Pods support families by giving kids a safe, fun environment in which to learn, play, and grow with their peers. In Camp Smart Start, trained Schoolmates staff assist children with their daily distance-learning assignments, while leading fun games and activities during lunch and breaks from class. Dates: January 4–January 22 Smart Start: 8:15 am–3:00 pm; Monday–Friday Play Pods: 2:30–5:30 pm; Monday–Friday For program details, contact Katrina Morris at kmorris@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

On January 3 pilots and airline workers threatened to join the strike and disrupt air travel. Macron ordered a break in the talks, and the next day, workers were back on the job. COVID-19 arrives in Europe The promise of 2020 as a year of disruption did not abate. In late February, Covid-19 broke out in Europe (a month before the U.S.) with a serious contagion concentrated in the town of Bergamo in Northern Italy. By March 1, France had 30 Covid-19 cases. Alarmed when new cases rapidly climbed to more than a thousand a day, Macron’s government laid out a nationwide lockdown of eight-weeks starting mid-March – the time when California and other states began implementing health restrictions. The lockdown required every resident to isolate at home, observe overnight curfew, and restrict movement to no further than a kilometer from home. The exceptions were for workers and businesses providing essential needs: food, medical, pharma, and for public safety and infrastructure workers. Employers were urged to send employees home to work wherever possible. Not much has changed all year with people still working from home. Museums, public venues, restaurants, theaters, sidewalk cafés, shops, and department stores were deemed non-essential and closed. Paris was a ghost town during the shutdown, with few cars lumbering through the streets. Winter days were gray and overcast, and people scurried to get a few essential groceries and go directly home. Not much was known about the highly contagious virus and fear weighed heavily. We donned facemasks, avoided eye contact, and hurried about outdoors. A month later, despite the lockdown, new cases reported a high of 4,200 a day, and deaths per day topped 1,400. However, at the eightweeks mark, France’s lockdown appeared to be working. Deconfinement, hurray Parisians emerged from confinement in triumph, as midMay showed great improvement with new Covid-19 cases having plateaued at 500 per day. Daily deaths from their April peak of 1,400 per day diminished to 100 deaths per day, and then less than 50 deaths per day during spring and summer months. pages.text: Wednesday, December 30, 2020 11 AMERICANS IN PARIS Covid-19 – the year 2020 in Paris By Patricia Forsyth We have lived our first end-toend year in Paris, and 2020 is sure to be a year of ambivalent memories as the world turned upside down. Flying home seemed a nonstarter during multiple months of changeable air travel restrictions. It was not a difficult decision, and Michael and I decided to stay put. Motoring through the French countryside to a romantic getaway didn’t feel right. We’ve adopted the catchphrase, an abundance of caution; albeit friends differ on degree. January 2020 began on foot in Week Six of France’s transportation workers’ strike, outlasting the holiday season and tiredly dragging on. These were stark, wintry days, yet we managed to hoof long distances without benefit of rail, metro, bus, taxi, and Uber, bound for Galleries Lafayette and the Left Bank’s Saint-Germain district. The Louvre’s galleries were gloriously ours, being only lightly attended. Generally, folks stayed close to home, shopped close to home, and were resolved to let the strike run its course. We innocently fell in with a Jaunes Gillets march going our way. Only later did Parisian friends warn us to steer clear as there could be terrorists. But in the moment, the protest seemed harmless. Ten minutes later at Les Halles, my nose wrinkled at an acrid odor. Michael said, “Tear gas, let’s get out of here.” Macron’s Pension Reform The transport-workers strike was punishing for employees getting to far-off job locations via rail and without a car. President Emmanuel Macron was the face of the national strike of transport union workers opposed to Macron messing with their pensions. Early Retirement for ground transport workers is a baked-in “perk” and unions fight tooth and nail to keep it. The unfavorable image of motorcar conductors retiring at age 42 has mostly resolved by job attrition. But taxpayer-outrage endures. Proponents of an improved economy and balanced budgets argue for “modernizing” union contracts, and taxpayers are on the hook. A steady flow of new Covid-19 cases has resulted in 300-600 deaths daily and 10,000 new cases, peeking at 21,000 cases on Christmas Eve. Compliance with safety protocols has slipped noticeably this time around. The French government indicated a third confinement may be necessary. articles.text: at the timeline of sports happenings; prep, collegiate, professional, and how the global pandemic has affected each. January The year started with both basketball and soccer programs plugging away for Piedmont High, little did we know it’d be the last semester of sports to finish its seasons. At this point last year, both girls’ and boys’ basketball were putting together their NCS profiles and competing in annual Holiday tournaments. Boys’ basketball guard Luke Harris came out of Piedmont High’s Winter Break hot as a junior, scoring a career high of 33 points against El Cerrito on January 2, helping lead the HighStaff Photo Photo by Paul Low Luke Harris opened 2020 with a career high of 33 points. He became an honorable mention for this year’s Post’s Athlete of the Year Award. With Extended hours to Fit Your Busy Schedule Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team won the Division 2 North Coast Section championship for the first time in school history on February 29, 2020. landers to an 11-1 record to start the year. The boys ended January 17-2 overall and 3-1 in the Western Alameda County Conference, its lone losses coming against Branson 50-47 on Dec. 7, and a heated double overtime 93-86 loss to rivals Bishop O’Dowd on January 15 in Binks Rawlings Gym. Sophomore JoJo Murphy, our 2020 Sophomore of the Year, scored 34 points including a dramatic fade away 3-pointer from the corner, where his shot appeared to come from behind the basket on the baseline. Murphy described having to “push it left” in order to make the shot. The girls’ basketball team, similarly, were starting the year 11-2 overall and on fire with a pair of standout freshmen Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill. They walked into 2020 after winning the McQueen Elite Tournament in Reno on Dec. 26-28—defeating three schools in the process; Nevada Union 62-34, Lowry 70-52, and McQueen 54-21 in the finals. Bryan Gardere’s bunch followed up with two wins at a twogame shoot-around hosted by Cardinal Newman, rolling over Windsor 62-21 and Justin Seina 53-14. They finished January 16-4 overall and 3-1 in the WACC. Boys’ soccer ended January 6-2-5 with Connor Curtis proving to be a Todd Sullivan’s new scorer in the midfield. Curtis, an honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year, finished as the team’s leading scorer. Girls’ soccer was 3-3-3 to end January, adjusting with freshman Emily Fitzgerald leading the attack and Ceci Brien converting to the midfield after three years at striker. On January 26, the sporting news which rocked the world was Kobe Bryant perishing in a tragic helicopter accident alongside his daughter Gianna and seven other passengers. The United States reported its first official COVID-19 case on January 20 February The San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs opened February with a thrilling Super Bowl LIV in Miami on February 2, where the Chiefs came back from a 20-10 deficit to score 21 points in the fourth quarter. This year is a far-cry from then, with SF 6-9 with a game left. Sorry for reminding you, Niners fans. The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inducted seven new members on February 10 at the Claremont Country Club, including Matt McGrath from the Class of 1988 (football, basketball, baseball), Heather Gibson from the Class of 1998 (cross country, track), Greg Lee of the Class of 1999 (tennis), Chazyn Morris Nunes of the Class of 2006 (basketball), Brendan Newland of the Class of 2007, Jeremy George of the Class of 2009 (football, soccer, baseball), and Arlyn Upshaw (swimming, water polo) of the Class of 2012. Back to Piedmont sports, it was the boys’ basketball team making history for the tiny school in the hills. They finished its regular season 21-5 to receive the No. 1 ranking in the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs, charging through No. 8 Eureka 87-63, No. 4 University 63-52, and battled with No. 3 St. Mary’s to a 77-67 Dr. Gutlaizer and Ellen and Liza Konnert Staff Photo Emily Fitzgerald (middle) scored the game-winning goal in Piedmont’s 2-1 win in the North Coast Section Soccer championships over No. 5 Urban on February 19. Ashley Nelson (No. 2) scored the winner in their 1-0 NCS Quarterfinals win over No. 4 Lick Wilmerding.

Emily Fitzgerald, a freshman at the time, scored the game winner against Urban in the second half, while senior captain Ashley Nelson had a nifty back-head flick to score the game-winner against Lick early on in the ninth minute—with freshman goalie Morgan Hunt making several big saves. The victory meant coach Dan Chubbock and co. qualified for its fourth straight NCS Semifinals. They lost to No. 1 Cardinal Newman 5-0. Boys’ soccer entered the D4 NCS with the No. 9 seed, defeating No. 8 Roseland Prep while on the road in Santa Rosa on February 18, but lost a nailbiter to No. 1 Cardinal Newman 1-0 on February 22. Cardinal scored the eventual winner in the ninth minute, parking the bus defensively to prevent the Highlanders from reeling off clear shooting opportunities. Girls’ basketball closed February in the NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 5 seed, losing to No. 4 Lick Wilmerding 69-45 on February 22. They opened the tournament with a 70-41 win over No. 12 Ygnacio Valley on February 19. The United States confirmed its first COVID-19 death in Seattle on February 29. The country’s total number of cases was 68. March March, the month where everything changed. Piedmont’s spring sports were getting started, while the boys’ basketball team felt robbed by the California Interscholastic Federation by getting ranked into Division 2 against the best schools in the state—a testament to Piedmont High’s rapid growth within the basketball community. They were awarded with the No. 13 seed in D2, pitted against No. 4 Weston Ranch in the opening round, battling them to a breathtaking 79-74 loss in overtime on March 3 in Stockton—a ridiculous matchup in regards to logical competition; a small school versus a perennial basketball powerhouse. Coach Ben Spencer, Weston Ranch coach Chris Teevan, BranPhoto by Todd Marshburn The boys’ lacrosse team was the last sport to play before the school shut down due to COVID after March 12. son coach Jonas Honick, and former PHS and new Berkeley coach Mike Hudson all expressed that coaches in Northern California expected lowly seeded Piedmont or Weston Ranch—which were surprised they weren’t ranked higher—to run the table. The Cougars were set to play in the D2 State Finals before the COVID-19 shutdown. Recollecting those early weeks of March are a lot to process. Spring sports were entering the fields, including baseball, softball, track, boys’ tennis, and boys’ and girls’ lacrosse looking to defend its D2 NCS championships. At the same time, California governor Gavin Newsom declared a State of Emergency on March 4. Soon after, the NBA postponed its season after an outbreak within the Utah Jazz—leading to other sports organizations also postponing its season. In fact, the boys’ lacrosse team perhaps played in one of the last interscholastic games in the country on March 12 against Redwood, a 12-3 loss. It was an eerie night to be in attendance where few minds were on the lacrosse match. Several players in the pre-game routines were calling it “Senior Night,” to the response of nervous laughter from teammates. We have not had any Piedmont sports since then. Girls’ lacrosse was 2-1 at the time of the stoppage of play with a roster set to continue challenging for an NCS title. The girls’ final match was March 5, a 13-10 win over D1 Redwood of Larkspur. Baseball was 3-2 when play ended with wins over St. Mary’s 3-2, St. Helena 3-2, and Luck Wilmerding 8-6. Softball, meanwhile, was debuting a team with 13 freshman and were 2-1-1 as of March 10 with a 7-1 win over St. Mary’s and 17-2 victory over Lick. April On Friday, April 3, the California Interscholastic Federation officially canceled the remainder of the Spring 2020 sports’ schedule shortly after the state announced that the remainder of the school year would be through online learning — an ongoing situation that still has little answers eight months later. For Piedmont High, Monday, November 9 marked the school’s first sign of sports since that Thursday, March 12 with the football program and other sports returning to conditioning at Witter Field, but everything is still up in the air, with no confirmation of permanent schedules.

With that, the Post has been stretching its legs and getting in shape, publishing more than 150 total miles of trails in parks throughout the Bay Area and Northern California, with a totel elvation gain of over 24,000 feet. This writer has been eternally grateful for the feedback received. We hope that “Hiking with Jon” has inspired some readers to hit the trails. Here are our favorite hikes from 2020. 1. Tafoni Trail & Rock Formation; El Corte de Madera Creek (December 2) Our trail to open December earns the top spot for its features at a fraction of the foot traffic It includes an estimated 30-million year old 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone and a nearby 1,800 year old redwood, the Methuselah Tree. The sandstone along the Tafoni Trail is a Tafoni rock formation, which is the giant boulder’s cavernous surface as a result of years of wind and rain creating its look. Continuing on the Tafoni Trail was an equal treat with stumps of old growth redwoods giving a glimpse of the Bay Area’s former logging days. The hike was 5-1/2 miles with a gain of 984 feet in elevation. 2. Five Lakes Trail; Tahoe National Forest (September 9) Five Lakes Trail in the Tahoe National Forest was our only published hike outside of the Bay Area. The SF Chronicle previously rated the destination as one of the best hikes in California with its collection of pristine landing zone. The hike was 6.38 miles with 1,347 feet in elevation gain. 4. Wildcat Peak, Nike Missile Site; Tilden Park (May 27) Wildcat Peak at Tilden Park is my favorite view in the entire East Bay, where you can spot a clear shot of the Bay Bridge, San Francisco, the Golden Gate, Richmond Bridge, Carquinez Strait, and the rolling hills of Orinda. Staying along the Nimitz Way Trail for two miles will take hikers to another prime viewing spot, the foundation of an old Nike Missile site similar to those found in the Marin Headlands. Our hike back in May totaled 9.44 miles with 1,210 feet in elevation gain. 5. Burma Road Trail; Mt Diablo State Park (July 1) We ranked Burma Road Trail in Mt. Diablo State Park No. 5 given that it is the most challenging trail on this entire list. The San Francisco Chronicle called Burma Road the most difficult in the entire Bay Area in December of last year, and part of me doubted that prior to taking it on myself. It was tough. In the middle of a heat wave in June, carrying camera equipment up some of the steepest gradients of Mt. Diablo was a task that brought pride in having accomplished it. The Burma Road Trail was a 6.2 mile hike, with a gain of 2,130 feet of elevation. Photo of the year: A great horned owl sits along the California Coastal Trail. alpine lakes. The hike was approximately 5 miles, gaining 1,111 feet in elevation to a high of 7.560 feet. But it is a popular destination. We passed 105 hikers along the way last fall. 3. Although a popular spot where you’ll run into a lot of people around Battery Townsley –we passed 112 people that day – the numbers thin out as you trek up the headlands to the peak of Hill 88, a former military radar and The Marin Headlands’ combination of scenic beauty, history, and art puts it in our top-five. Diablo’s State Park’s Burma Road Trail is mentioned as the Bay Area’s most difficult hike by the San Francisco Chronicle, and it is indeed a worthy challenge. articles.text: Phil Witte is an author and cartoonist. His cartoon “Flip” first appeared in the Piedmont Post in 2008 and now runs in every issue. His cartoons have appeared in dozens of publications in the U.S. and U.K., including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, Reader’s Digest, San Francisco Chronicle, New Statesman, and Private Eye, as well as in books and greeting cards. He co-writes the blog “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the Cartoon Collections website. His humor book, “What You Don’t Know About Turning 50” and the sequel on turning 60 have sold over 170,000 copies to date. Phil’s cartoons have been exhibited in group shows in San Francisco, Minneapolis, London, and Galway, Ireland. Original cartoons of his are owned by private collectors and a cartoon museum. He has been a cartoonist-in-residence at the Charles Schulz Museum and the San Francisco Cartoon Art Museum. He’s a member of the National Cartoonists Society. See www.philwitte.com. The cartoons shown below represent our favorite picks from 2020. “Excuse me, where did you get those sandals?” “You can’t believe everything the Russian bots tell you.” “He’s part-terrier, part-triceratops.” “I don’t want to live on the edge, but I wouldn’t mind visiting it.” “We’re the moles—you want the voles, two holes down.” “C’mon, get in!”

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is presenting A Midsummer Night’s Dream from January 21 through February 10. Choreographer George Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream is part of San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season and will be performed in Program 1. The ballet, one of the company’s most well-known, is a Shakespearean favorite making its triumphant return to San Francisco after a cut-too-short run in 2020. This 1962 ballet, set to the music of Felix Mendelssohn, was Balanchine’s first original full-length ballet, which quickly was hailed as a masterpiece. Balanchine loved the original play – he could recite large parts of it in Russian – so the ballet sticks close to its inspiration. It tells the story of four lost lovers in the woods, as well as of a royal fairy court made up of Queen Titania, King Oberon, and mischievous Puck. To obtain tickets to this digital event, visit https://www.sfballet. org/tickets/2021-season/.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Midsummer Night’s Dream begins streaming January 21

articles.text: SF Jazz will present saxophonist Maceo Parker in a special celebration on New Year’s Day, this Friday, January 1, at 5 p.m. Parker’s performances have been an SF Jazz tradition for several years, and this concert, recorded in January 2015, featured a potent version of his super-charged band with drummer Nikki Glaspie and P-Funk bassist Rodney “Skeet” Curtis. Parker made his mark in Jazz as an essential part of the powerhouse horn section backing James Brown. He then went on to contribute to albums and tours with the Red Hot Chili Peppers, Keith Saxophonist Maceo Parker Richards, Dave Matthews Band and most extensively, Prince. To watch this Friday’s previously-recorded event, visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/watch/#info-open.

articles.text: Musaics of the Bay will bring audiences a cross-continental celebration of the new year from Salzburg, Austria, one of the classical music capitals of the world. Musaics is partnering with musicians in Salzburg for a high-definition New Year’s performance, celebrating the music of fantasy and vision and a new world premiere for the established “Stay-at-Home Symposium.” The event will feature world-class musicians, including pianist Andrei Gologan, composer and violinist Luke Hsu, and cellist Simon Tetzlaff. The program will feature works by Beethoven, Kodaly, Schumann and the World Premiere of a new commission for the “Stay-at-Home Symposium” by Luke Hsu, titled “Piccolo Pezzo”. The composition was inspired by a painting titled “Homage to Edmundo” by Berkeley artist Darril Tighe. The concert can be viewed on Saturday, January 2, at 11 a.m. Reserve your spot at https:// www.groupmuse.com/events/ 11200-a-new-year-s-celebrationfrom-salzburg-fantasies-and-visions?source=shortlink-generic.
