Celebrate the New Year with Cal Performances and a special musical celebration tomorrow evening, Thursday, December 31, at 8 p.m. The event will star artists and musicians Yo-Yo Ma, Julia Bullock, Bria Skonberg, Leif Ove Andsnes, Matthew Whitaker, and others who have made the Fall 2020 Cal Performances at Home season possible. Guests will perform works by Darcy James Argue, Harold Arlen, Mozart, Kool & the Gang, Lil Hardin, Tessa Lark and more. Performances will include works by soloists, recitalists, jazz artists, and chamber ensembles, all featured in one online streaming event. Each performer has carefully chosen their program with the aim of sharing works that convey joy, hope, and warmth. Nathalie Joachim will host the event. The celebration will begin tomorrow with a premiere watch party at 8 p.m. The video will be available on demand beginning at 2 a.m. on December 31 and will be available through January 2 at 4 a.m. The pricing for all Cal Performances at Home events is on the honor system and is based on the number of people watching the performance. Visit https://calperformances.org/events/2020-21/ at-home/new-years-eve-musical-celebration/ for more information.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 30, 2020 17 Ring in the New Year with SF Chamber Orchestra By Allyson Aleksey The San Francisco Chamber Orchestra will celebrate the New Year with a special performance on Thursday, December 31, New Year’s Eve at 7:30 p.m. The concert is pre-recorded and will be a fun, family-friendly, and free performance. Join the Chamber Orchestra on New Year’s Eve from the comfort of your home for an uplifting program featuring young pianist Hilda Huang and more than 20 orchestra members. The program will include the music of Handel, Beethoven, and holiday fare with the orchestra and its all-star brass Pianist Hilda Huang ensemble. Visit https://www.thesfco.org/ events/nye-2020 to view the New Year’s Eve celebration. Musaics of the Bay celebrates New Year with concert from Salzburg By Allyson Aleksey Musaics of the Bay will bring audiences a cross-continental celebration of the new year from Salzburg, Austria, one of the classical music capitals of the world. Musaics is partnering with musicians in Salzburg for a high-definition New Year’s performance, celebrating the music of fantasy and vision and a new world premiere for the established “Stay-at-Home Symposium.” The event will feature world-class musicians, including pianist Andrei Gologan, composer and violinist Luke Hsu, and cellist Simon Tetzlaff. The program will feature works by Beethoven, Kodaly, Schumann and the World Premiere of a new commission for the “Stay-at-Home Symposium” by Luke Hsu, titled “Piccolo Pezzo”. The composition was inspired by a painting titled “Homage to Edmundo” by Berkeley artist Darril Tighe. The concert can be viewed on Saturday, January 2, at 11 a.m. Reserve your spot at https:// www.groupmuse.com/events/ 11200-a-new-year-s-celebrationfrom-salzburg-fantasies-and-visions?source=shortlink-generic. articles.text: Can a crisis evoke from us a one-shot pinnacle of creativity? In the case of two Austrian villagers some 200 years ago, the answer is an emphatic yes. It was in the small church of Oberndorf, Austria, near Salzburg, readying for the gala Christmas Eve service. The all-important pipe organ broke down, with no chance for repairs being done in time. To compensate for the crisis, the young priest Josef Mohr pulled out his poetic text now known as the sacred lullaby “Silent Night,” calming words for the Christ child in the manger, “Sleep in heavenly peace.” He passed these along to the village school-teacher Franz Gruber, who was suddenly the superfluous church organist. The very same day Gruber (1787-1863) produced the music to fit the voices— equally straight-forward, but uniquely memorable. He scored it for a pair of soloists, chorus and the best substitute instrument available, the guitar. Gruber called his effort “a simple composition.” The parishioners crowded in that night were treated to the 1818 world premiere of a work with singers who had barely had time to rehearse. Later the work was taken up by the Strasser Sisters singing group specializing in Tyrolean music, as well as the Rainers. It became a hit all over the touring itineraries, eventually attributed to the eminent composer Michael Haydn (brother of Franz Josef Haydn). Who, after all, would believe that two village nobodies could create great music? After 15 years it was finally published, and another six years later was already being heard in New York City. For decades uncertainty reigned about the carol’s creators. It took a court-room trial 26 years after the premiere to establish the truth, when Gruber’s son brought in a copy of the original manuscript to prove the true authorship before a governmental investigation committee. Case closed. Any thoughts that Gruber-Mohr could become the Austrian Rodgers and Hammerstein, or Lerner-Loewe, would be sheer fantasy. After 1818 they went their separate ways, given the usual moves and transfers, and never produced other significant works. It was sheer coincidence that the two were together at all; Mohr (1792-1848) had been sent to Oberndorf from his earlier posting because his delicate health could not cope with a harsh climate. Shortly before the Millennium, the sole manuscript regarding the carol’s origins was discovered, written in Mohr’s handwriting, dating back to 1820 or thereabouts. He attested that he had written the texts in 1816, with the music composed by Gruber in 1818. The lesson here is profound and invaluable: The Mozarts and Leonardos of our world could be brilliant every single day. As for the rest of us, however mediocre in the greater scale of things, we could still rise up once in full flower, like a century plant. We could create something uniquely masterful, provided we possess the will, the faith and the motivation. From adversity comes the flowering of inspiration. And a catalytic pairing doesn’t hurt, either. A Piedmont resident, Paul Hertelendy also writes on classical music in the arts journal www.artsSF.com.
articles.title: The Carol that rescued a failing Christmas

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco is presenting a digital exhibition entitled Meet Us Quickly: Painting for Justice from Prison on view until January 31 The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco, a Smithsonian affiliate, is presenting a digital exhibition entitled Meet Us Quickly: Painting for Justice from Prison, which will be on view until January 31. Meet Us Quickly is an exhibition of the work of 12 artists incarcerated at San Quentin State Prison. The twenty-one works in the exhibition include linocut prints, acrylic paintings, ink drawings on paper, and collage and are organized and curated by Prison Renaissance co-founder Rahsaan “New York” Thomas. Eclectic in influence, certain works in this exhibition nod to pointillism and neo-constructivism while others honor the importance of Aaron Douglas and the Harlem Renaissance. These artists maintain significant artistic practices spanning diverse techniques and subjects. The works are presented with accompanying statements written by each artist, allowing these incarcerated men to speak for themselves and share their vision and perspectives in their own words. The exhibition is made possible in part by a grant from The Creative Work Fund, a program of the Walter and Elise Haas Fund that also is supported by The William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. Eighty percent of proceeds from the auction go directly to artists based on the payment method of their choice. To view the artwork, visit https://www. prisonrenaissance.org/art-auction-2020.
articles.title: MoAD: Painting for Justice from Prison, a digital exhibition and online art auction

articles.text: Spirit of the American City (https://catherineburns.com/ spirit) is an online exhibit by Catherine Burns Fine Art that invites viewers to explore early 20th century prints through the perspective of period photography. See what the artists saw. Understand their inspiration. View them as a social time capsule while admiring the mastery of these revered printmakers. make hundred-year-old prints a momentary escape from the doom and gloom of the pandemic. A love letter to the artists and the cities that inspired them.” The show is online and free to the public at https://catherineburns.com/spirit. It is best enjoyed on a large screen. All of the featured prints are for sale. Catherine Burns has been a dealer in fine prints and drawings for more than 30 years and specializes in both American and European prints from the 19th and early 20th centuries. She launched her business after serving as the Curator of the art museums at University of Massachusetts, Amherst and Washington University in St. Louis. A founding member of the International Fine Print Dealers Association, Burns exhibits at national and international art fairs. To view her gallery and for more information, contact her at info@catherineburns.com, or call 510-654-7910. What makes this show special? This is the first time that original prints have been paired with related videos and historic photographs. From a private East Coast collection, these outstanding prints are by a wide range of well-known WPA period printmakers, including Edward Hopper, George Bellows, Charles Sheeler, Benton Spruance and Childe Hassam. Every print has been researched in detail and is accompanied by a mix of vintage photos, historic videos and news articles that give hints to what led the artists to capture that specific image in time. Not just for collectors This is a show for all to enjoy and is a breath of fresh air. articles.text: Led by House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of San Francisco, Congress passed legislation on December 22 providing much-needed shortterm financial relief for nonprofit arts and culture organizations throughout the U.S. It was part of the latest relief bill that both the House and Senate voted to approve The House Small Business Committee and San Francisco Arts Alliance were leading players in incorporating eligibility for arts and culture organizations. The effort was led by Pelosi and House Small Business Committee Chair Nydia Velazquez to include nonprofit arts organizations in the Save our Stages (SOS) bill and the Payroll Protection Program (PPP). Passage was secured with the partnership of Speaker Pelosi, Senate Minority Leader Sen. Charles Schumer of New York, Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, Rep. Velazquez of Brooklyn, and Sen. Marco Rubio of Florida and a broad bi-partisan support that secured the passage of this COVID-19 relief bill. “The arts and culture sector is an essential vehicle for healing and for driving the equitable and sustainable recovery and regeneration of communities across the nation,” said Deborah Cullinan, co-chair of the San Francisco Arts Alliance and CEO of Yerba Buena Center for the Arts. “As we evolve the ways we bring joy, inspiration, and healing into our hard-hit communities, it is only by working hand-in-hand with our elected officials and policymakers on the federal, state, and local level that we will be able to support our nation’s creative workforce in service of the health and wellbeing of our communities.” “As we move into 2021 and the roll-out of the vaccine, it is our fervent hope that arts and culture organizations will be able to reconnect communities through a return to cultural gatherings,” added Matthew Shilvock, General Director of San Francisco Opera and co-chair of the San Francisco Arts Alliance. “This relief bill supports the broad arts and culture sector in a number of important ways, both in sustaining our arts workers and organizations, and in ensuring greater equity of public access to digital artistic offerings through expanded broadband access. We are deeply grateful for this affirmative expression of support for the arts from Congress. It is critical to bringing back the arts and rebuilding our communities.” This relief package incorporates key components of the US Conference of Mayors Resolution sent to Congress in July 2020,. It reinforced federal policy recommendations advanced by more than 60 national arts organizations calling on Congress to ensure the recovery and survival of essential arts and culture organizational partners, including: ● Inclusion of the nonprofits arts and culture industry in specific relief efforts through the Save our Stages (SOS) federal grants for creative and cultural businesses. ● Extending the duration of unemployment insurance for artists, arts professionals, and self-employed workers whose income has been negatively impacted by COVID-19. ● Extending SBA and Paycheck Protection Program assistance for artists and arts professionals and providing additional forgivable SBA loans to nonprofit arts and culture organizations, self-employed workers, sole proprietors, small LLCs. ● Incentivizing increased contributed support for the arts and culture sector by extending through the 2021 tax year the universal charitable deduction for those that do not itemize their tax returns. ● Enabling equitable participation in artistic, educational, and cultural online activity through ensuring the most vulnerable populations have access to free or low-cost high-speed broadband program offerings. Contributing more than $877.8 billion to the nation’s economy in 2017, the arts and culture sector is an economic engine that directly employs more than 5 million workers nationwide. The current losses sustained by the arts and culture sector throughout the nation as a result of the COVID- 19 pandemic have reached a staggering $14.6 billion as of December 12, 2020. Included among the 26 mayors who introduced and co-signed the resolution to Congress in July 2020 were London Breed (San Francisco), Libby Schaaf (Oakland), Jesse Arreguin (Berkeley), and California mayors in Sacramento, Loa Angeles, San Diego, and San Jose.
articles.title: Congress passes relief bill for non-profit arts organizations

articles.text: The gardens of the Filoli House are lit up for the holidays. Filoli House and Gardens, located in Woodside, is dressed in festive lights for the holiday season through January 3. Take a walk through the gardens and enjoy the beauty of a winter garden adorned with lights and colorful décor. Visitors can cozy up next to a fire pit under twinkling lights while sipping on hot cider or mulled wine. Visit the gardens on a Monday night for “theme nights.” From a pajama party to solstice night, Filoli is making Monday nights merry and bright with jolly dress-up prompts; match the theme and receive a gift from Filoli. Daytime and evening admissions are available at different price points. Due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic and capacity limitations, all visitors must secure tickets beforehand. Face coverings must be worn at all times and social distancing will be observed. The Estate Trail will close at 4 p.m., and the house closes at 7 p.m. Restroom facilities are available onsite. To reserve tickets for holiday events at Filoli House and Gardens, visit https://filoli.org/ events/holidays/.
articles.title: Theme nights and festive lights at Woodside historic estate

The effort was led by Pelosi and House Small Business Committee Chair Nydia Velazquez to include nonprofit arts organizations in the Save our Stages (SOS) bill and the Payroll Protection Program (PPP). Passage was secured with the partnership of Speaker Pelosi, Senate Minority Leader Sen. Charles Schumer of New York, Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, Rep. Velazquez of Brooklyn, and Sen. Marco Rubio of Florida and a broad bi-partisan support that secured the passage of this COVID-19 relief bill. “The arts and culture sector is an essential vehicle for healing and for driving the equitable and sustainable recovery and regeneration of communities across the nation,” said Deborah Cullinan, co-chair of the San Francisco Arts Alliance and CEO of Yerba Buena Center for the Arts. “As we evolve the ways we bring joy, inspiration, and healing into our hard-hit communities, it is only by working hand-in-hand with our elected officials and policymakers on the federal, state, and local level that we will be able to support our nation’s creative workforce in service of the health and wellbeing of our communities.” “As we move into 2021 and the roll-out of the vaccine, it is our fervent hope that arts and culture organizations will be able to reconnect communities through a return to cultural gatherings,” added Matthew Shilvock, General Director of San Francisco Opera and co-chair of the San Francisco Arts Alliance. “This relief bill supports the broad arts and culture sector in a number of important ways, both in sustaining our arts workers and organizations, and in ensuring greater equity of public access to digital artistic offerings through expanded broadband access. We are deeply grateful for this affirmative expression of support for the arts from Congress. It is critical to bringing back the arts and rebuilding our communities.” This relief package incorporates key components of the US Conference of Mayors Resolution sent to Congress in July 2020,. It reinforced federal policy recommendations advanced by more than 60 national arts organizations calling on Congress to ensure the recovery and survival of essential arts and culture organizational partners, including: ● Inclusion of the nonprofits arts and culture industry in specific relief efforts through the Save our Stages (SOS) federal grants for creative and cultural businesses. ● Extending the duration of unemployment insurance for artists, arts professionals, and self-employed workers whose income has been negatively impacted by COVID-19. ● Extending SBA and Paycheck Protection Program assistance for artists and arts professionals and providing additional forgivable SBA loans to nonprofit arts and culture organizations, self-employed workers, sole proprietors, small LLCs. ● Incentivizing increased contributed support for the arts and culture sector by extending through the 2021 tax year the universal charitable deduction for those that do not itemize their tax returns. ● Enabling equitable participation in artistic, educational, and cultural online activity through ensuring the most vulnerable populations have access to free or low-cost high-speed broadband program offerings. Contributing more than $877.8 billion to the nation’s economy in 2017, the arts and culture sector is an economic engine that directly employs more than 5 million workers nationwide. The current losses sustained by the arts and culture sector throughout the nation as a result of the COVID- 19 pandemic have reached a staggering $14.6 billion as of December 12, 2020. Included among the 26 mayors who introduced and co-signed the resolution to Congress in July 2020 were London Breed (San Francisco), Libby Schaaf (Oakland), Jesse Arreguin (Berkeley), and California mayors in Sacramento, Loa Angeles, San Diego, and San Jose.

articles.text: Welcome to 2021. It’s a new year with some rays of optimism visible. What better time to clean up our Covid-weary language and return to the true meaning (and purpose) of words, phrases, especially idioms. The following list compiled by the Piedmomt Post staff includes the most over-used and over-valued expressions, rendering them superfluous. Let 2021 be a year when we learn to resist the temptations of repetition. Now more than ever The new normal All in this together Unprecedented Cohort From the safety of your home Flatten the curve Essential A safe distance Challenging times Social distancing Curfew Quarantine Purple tier 2nd Wave You’re on mute No fans in attendance Stimulus Hoax Fake news Stop the steal
articles.title: Words & phrases we won’t miss in 2021

articles.text: While fewer people walk around town at night, we all of course still experience the effects of exterior lighting most evenings from our cars and from transitional walks into buildings. And as noted below, we also see light fixtures themselves during the day. “Less is more” is a famous maxim attributed to the modernist architect Mies van der Rohe in 1947. It basically means that unadorned simplicity (less) results in a better design aesthetic (more). I think this maxim, while certainly not a universal truth, is especially applicable in the field of lighting, where we too often see projects over-illuminated. It seems to be that the best lighting designs go unnoticed – they just seem to naturally fit in place. This is because the focus of good lighting design is on what is being illuminated, not the illumination itself. Lighting is all about contrast, and subtle contrast is easier for the eye to adapt. Although starker contrast is useful for highlighting, in a small residential city like Piedmont, highlighting should be, and for the most part is, limited. Successful lighting designs often use different and multiple types of light sources (fixtures) for different illumination purposes. Using one tall, strong street light for example to also illuminate an entry will be be much less appealing and effective than using two separate fixtures, one to light the street, and another (or more) to light the entry. The issue of appropriate scale and character also enters into lighting design. The incredible lighting on the new east span of the Bay Bridge with its 65’ high poles is of course not appropriate even for a larger city the size of Oakland, and certainly not for a residential scaled city like Piedmont. Also important is the issue of “light trespass” from one type of light to another such as where residential and commercial uses abut. In my mind there are two main considerations relative to all light fixtures: the illumination they provide, and the aesthetic of the fixture itself, both lit up at night (on) and unlit during the day (off). The appearance of light fixtures In addition to providing exciting, dramatic and functional illumination, the design and placement of light fixtures themselves are very important. Both the more contemporary light fixtures of this beautiful Piedmont home (above) and the traditional style of this light fixture at Havens School (left) complement and enhance both the landscape architecture and architecture of which they are a part. correct can be noted and adjusted the following year. articles.text: Herdade do Mouchao, built in 1901, is one of the first wineries in the Alentejo region. [In January of 2020] I had an opportunity to visit a new wine region I had not previously explored. Along with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey, I set out to explore the wines of the Alentejo region of Portugal. While central Lisbon and the Algarve region in the south get the lion’s share of tourists, it is the region in between them that is of most interest to wine lovers. The Alentejo covers nearly onethird of Portugal and it consists of vast fields of grain and undulating hills, hosting forests of cork trees, sheep and pigs. And of course, vines. Miles and miles of vineyards producing wine that ranges from pedestrian to stunningly divine. Though the region boasts the UNESCO World Heritage city of Evora with its impressive 15th century architecture and an old Roman temple, it is mainly quiet and empty – Portugal’s least populated region. Even passing through towns and villages my fellow travelers would remark, “Where is everyone?” It made travel easy though, with excellent, nearly empty roads. pages.text: Wednesday, December 30, 2020 23 The Wine Corner When in Portugal, don’t forget the wines of the Alentejo Herdade do Mouchao, built in 1901, is one of the first wineries in the Alentejo region. By Pierre DuMont [In January of 2020] I had an opportunity to visit a new wine region I had not previously explored. Along with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey, I set out to explore the wines of the Alentejo region of Portugal. While central Lisbon and the Algarve region in the south get the lion’s share of tourists, it is the region in between them that is of most interest to wine lovers. The Alentejo covers nearly onethird of Portugal and it consists of vast fields of grain and undulating hills, hosting forests of cork trees, sheep and pigs. And of course, vines. Miles and miles of vineyards producing wine that ranges from pedestrian to stunningly divine. Though the region boasts the UNESCO World Heritage city of Evora with its impressive 15th century architecture and an old Roman temple, it is mainly quiet and empty – Portugal’s least populated region. Even passing through towns and villages my fellow travelers would remark, “Where is everyone?” It made travel easy though, with excellent, nearly empty roads. (In contrast, in Lisbon it appears everyone in Portugal has Mouchao Tinto is Pierre’s vote for Portugal’s best wine. The city of Evora, Portugal, is a UNESCO World Heritage site with a Roman temple. moved there. The other great thing about this region is the food. The native black, acorn-fed pigs produce succulent tasty pork served either grilled or sautéed with clams. The other star is the local soup called carrasquinas which consists of white beans, pork sausage and shoulder and thistle (artichoke) stems. Can’t get it out of my mind despite trying mightily to replicate it back home. The other culinary discovery was migas – day old bread mixed with olive oil and garlic and pan fried till it becomes the texture of polenta. Sounds gross, but it is anything but. • Mouchao This trip actually had its origin in a prior trip to northern Portugal where we stumbled upon a wine we grabbed off the shelf in a dusty wine shop in Oporto. The only thing the label said was “Mouchao”. It turned out to be one of the best wines of my life and I instantly fell in love with it. I knew someday I had to track it down. That search was aided by a big break. When I got back to the U.S. I discovered that the importer of this obscure wine was none other than my good friend Drake McCarthy with Golden State Wine Co. Drake was able to set up a visit with the sales manager of Mouchao, David Ferriera, and I began planning this trip. Though not well known in the U.S., Mouchao is the most well-respected and historic Alentejo winery. The structure built in 1901 is as traditional as a winery can be. Grapes are still crushed by foot in stone troughs called lagres. All picking is done Ernesto Botelho shows the clay amphoras at Rocim. with all the traditional methods and the wines have an earthy authenticity to them. The 2014 Quito do Mouro Tinto was just released at 6 years of age. Portuguese wines, like the Spanish Riojas, often are aged in their cellars and released only when ready to drink. The Quito do Mouro Tinto is a blend of Garnacha, Alicante Bouchet, Touriga National and Cabernet Sauvignon. It has an earthy Bordeaux-like nose with great structure and complex layers of flavor. They also make a second label, the Zagaloz Reserva, which is a blend of Trincadeira and Arogonez that has an intriguing nose or earth and berry fruit with excellent balance. Available on Wine.com. Winemaker Miguel Louro at Quinta do Mouro The Herdade do Rocim Alicante Bouchet proved to be the best value wine of the trip to Portugal. by hand and the wine is aged for years in large old chestnut casks. But what makes Mouchao special is the century-old vineyard of Alicante Bouchet grapes. This unpopular French varietal was planted here years ago and has truly found its finest home. One of the only red grapes that has red juice, it produces a profound, inky black wine with a beautiful flowery, berry fragrance. Mouchao has tannins that are soft enough to drink upon release, but also has the structure to improve in the cellar for three decades. I encourage you to seek out this truly outstanding wine which, though expensive at $60, is still a value compared to many Bordeaux’s or Napa Cabs. • Quinta do Mouro The other traditional winery that was recommended to us was Quinta do Mouro. We were hosted by Miguel Louro, whose father planted the first vines in 1989 and bottled their first vintage in 1994. Though not an old, historic winery, Mouro sticks • Herdade do Rocim In stunning contrast to the aforementioned wineries, Rocim is a striking modern jewel of a winery with sleek glass buildings and beautiful vast vineyards. Sales Manager Ernesto Botelho gave us a tour of the facilities, which included a look at two types of amphora that they use to ferment and age wine. It was kind of ironic that this most modern of wineries is reverting back to the oldest winemaking technique – the Roman amphora. The amphora wines were round and smooth like the shape of the vessels and had a livelier fruitiness to them than you would get from oak. The highlight wine for me was the 2017 Alicante Bouchet. It had a lovely perfumed nose with rich layers of soft plum and berry fruit with just the right touch of tannins on the finish. Delicious now, it will last for a decade. It is available for $18.99 on Wine.com and is a major bargain. Previously published in the Post on February 26, 2020

articles.text: Many of us probably felt that 2020 lasted a very long time. But now that 2021 is upon us, we can make a fresh start – and one way to do that is to make some New Year’s resolutions. Of course, you can make these resolutions for all parts of your life – physical, emotional, intellectual – but have you ever considered some financial Here are a few such resoluDon’t overreact to events. When the coronavirus pandemic hit in mid-February, the financial markets took a big hit. Many people, convinced that we were in for a prolonged slump, decided to take a “time out” and headed to the investment sidelines. But it didn’t take long for the markets to rally, rewarding those patient investors who stayed the course. Nothing is a certainty in the investment world, but the events of 2020 followed a familiar historical pattern: major crisis followed by market drop followed by strong recovery. The lesson for investors? Don’t overreact to today’s news – because tomorrow may look quite different. At the beginning of 2020, nobody was anticipating a worldwide pandemic and its terrible consequences, both to individuals’ health and to their economic well-being. None of us can foretell the future, either, but we can be prepared, and one way to do so is by building an emergency fund. Ideally, such a fund should be kept in liquid, low-risk vehicles and contain at least six months’ worth of living Focus on moves you can In response to pandemic-related economic pressures, some employers cut their matching contributions to 401(k) plans in 2020. Will some future event cause another such reduction? No one knows – and even if it happens, there’s probably nothing you can do about it. Instead of worrying about things you can’t control, focus on those you can. When it comes to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan, put in as much as you can afford this year, and if your salary goes up, increase your contribution. • Recognize your ability to build savings. During the pandemic, the personal savings rate shot up, hitting a record of 33% in April, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economy Analysis. It fell over the next several months, but still remained about twice as high as the rate of the past few years. Of course, much of this surge in Americans’ proclivity to save money was due to our lack of options for spending it, as the coronavirus caused either complete or partial shutdowns in physical retail establishments, as well as dining and entertainment venues. But if you did manage to boost your own personal savings when your spending was constrained, is it possible to remain a good saver when restrictions are lifted? Probably. And the greater your savings, the greater your financial freedoms – including the freedom to invest and freedom from excessive debt. When we reach a post-pandemic world, see if you can continue saving more than you did in previous years – and use your savings wisely. These aren’t the only financial resolutions you can make – but following them may help you develop habits that could benefit you in 2021 and beyond. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Marella Guigou, well-known for her daily walks at Witter Field in her crimson Stanford sweatshirt, passed away quietly on Thanksgiving morning, November 26, 2020, in Northbrook, Illinois, where she had been living since 2015. She was 89. Born Marella Rimbach on July 15, 1931, she was the daughter of Pearl and Francis Rimbach and grew up on a farm in Sterling, Massachusetts. After graduating from Cushing Academy in Ashburnham, she attended Clark University in Worcester where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree. After college she worked as a secretary at Harvard University and began teaching elementary school. She moved to San Francisco where she continued teaching, and where she married Charles (Charlie) Hubbard Guigou on October 19, 1963 at St. Mary the Virgin Episcopal Church. They moved to Piedmont in 1965 and raised a family of two daughters. She resumed her teaching career in 1984 after their older daughter attended Stanford, Charlie’s alma mater. For 10 years she was a reading resource teacher at Garfield Elementary School in Oakland. Throughout her adult life “she was absolutely passionate about education,” recalled Stephanie. After she retired from Oakland School District, she remained close to education and close to home, serving as a volunteer at Wildwood Elementary School, and Piedmont’s other two elementary schools. She had a wide circle of friends through her participation with the League of Women Voters, the Daughters of the American Revolution, Republican Women, Piedmont Community Church, and the many parents’ groups affiliated with the schools. She was a rabid Stanford fan, where her husband and elder daughter attended. She was a regular at Jazzercize classes in Piedmont, often completing the exercises in a room of women 20 years her junior. In addition to doing her daily laps walking the oval; track at Witter Field, she walked around the block every morning and brought her neighbors’ newspapers to their doorstep. Always well informed, she made sure the Piedmont Post was delivered on time each Wednesday. “When the phone rang at 6:05 p.m. on a Wednesday, we always knew it was Marella – politely informing us that she hadn’t received the paper,” recalled Post Editor Gray Cathrall. “She wanted to ‘make sure the paper boy was not sick or injured.’ We enjoyed those humorous conversations with her immensely,” he said. One of her favorite outings was having lunch regularly at Fenton’s Creamery. She became very attached to one of the waiters there who made sure she was well cared for. He later told Marella‘s daughter that the conversations with Marella inspired him to apply to and attend UC Berkeley. “He texted me a couple Marella Guigous passed away on November 26. She was 89. years ago to let me know he had graduated from Cal, and credits Marella with changing his life,” said Stephanie. She celebrated her 89th birthday in July at North Shore Place, a memory care home in Northbrook, Illinois. She maintained a happy life there and was adored by the staff. She told each of them every day how much she loved them. Marella is survived by a daughter, Stephanie Joseph and husband Christopher of Empire, Michigan. She was also the proud and playful grandmother of Logan (Catherine), Courtney and Erin Joseph. She is predeceased by her husband Charlie, who died in 2007, and her younger daughter Pamela, who died in 2017. Wearing their best Stanford colors, Marella and Charlie Guigous attended the Rose Bowl game in 2000, a lifetime highlight for both of them. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

Contra Costa County reports its first case of COVID-19, and Marin County declares a local emergency. March 4 California Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency after the first COVID-19 related death in California was announced. The fatality was a 71-year-old man from Placer County who was a passenger on the Grand Princess. The Grand Princess trip to Mexico is cancelled, and the ship has headed back to San Francisco. March 11 The World Health Organization declares that COVID-19 a pandemic. Trump orders a 30-day ban for parts of Europe. Alameda County announces a countywide ban of public gatherings of 1,000 or more people. March 15 Gov. Newsom orders all bars, nightclubs, wineries, and brewpubs to close. Adults aged 65 and above are asked to stay home, as are those with pre-existing health conditions. Restaurants may remain open but with reduced capacity. March 20 Piedmont tennis courts, playgrounds, and two of its sports fields – Beach Field and Coaches Field – were closed. Total coronavirus cases in the Bay Area surpass 50, local death toll reaches double digits, and the global death toll surpassed 10,000 The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the Treasury Department announced that the federal income tax filing due date has been extended from April 15 to July 15. March 26 The City of Piedmont closed another recreation area. On Thursday, March 26, Hampton Park was closed because people are “continuing to gather in violation of both the letter and the spirit of the shelter-in-place orders which have been issued by the county and state” the city wrote in a press release. Between March 20 and March 26 Piedmont police had to disperse groups from fields, parks and tennis courts at least 14 times, despite the closures, according to the police dispatch office. The Alameda County death toll due to COVID-19 reached four. More than half a million cases are reported worldwide. March 30 CDC Director Robert Redfield said that the agency is now reconsidering the data around mask use by the general public. Redfield made these statements in an interview with National Public Radio on Monday, March 30. “I can tell you that the data and this issue of whether it’s going to contribute [to prevention] is being aggressively reviewed as we speak,” Redfield told NPR. Shelter-in-place restrictions in Alameda County, which were to expire on March 30, were extended to May 1. March 31 In a letter to school leaders, California’s State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond wrote: “Due to the current safety concerns and needs for ongoing social distancing, it currently appears that our students will not be able to return to school campuses before the end of the school year.” April 1 The city closed Piedmont Park to prevent the spread of COVID- 19. The City estimated that the closure could last through May 3 during the shelter-in-place mandate from Alameda County. City Administrator Sara Lillevand ultimately made the decision to close all Piedmont parks after lengthy discussions with all of the City’s senior managers. Lillevand cited two main reasons for the closures. She stated that park closures support the letter and spirit of the shelter in place order, which aims to limit opportunities for community transmission and spread of the novel coronavirus. She added that police enforcement of the order is easier with full closures rather than partial closures. Photo by Jonathan Comeaux May 29: A protestor views a blaze on 7th street in downtown Oakland on a violent night of riots. An estimate of over 8,000 protesters were in the city. April 14 Gov. Newsom laid out a sixpoint framework to gradually lift shelter in place restrictions. April 23 It was the deadliest day for coronavirus so far in California. A total of 1,419 Californians have died from the virus and there are 37,339 confirmed cases of COVID. April 28 The U.S. confirmed it has exceeded 1 million confirmed cases of coronavirus, and 57,608 deaths, more than double the number of deaths of Spain. The U.S total is greater than the total of the next six highest reporting countries in the world. Spain reported 232,128 cases, Italy reported 201,505, France reported 166,036, the United Kingdom reported 162,350 cases, Germany has 159,239, and Turkey has reported 114,653 cases. China, the origin of the virus, reported 83,938 confirmed cases. May 11 Piedmont’s city staff hosted a virtual town hall meeting to answer residents’ questions on mandated lockdowns and restrictions. The Fourth of July parade committee decided to cancel this year’s parade, citing coronavirus concerns, and the inability to gather in large numbers. It was the first time the parade had been canceled and was the first cancellation of a major city event. May 13 Mayor Bob McBain offered an upbeat message to the community: “As we enter the ninth week of this shared experience, it’s important to reflect on these recent times. I was confident that our community would respond strongly and support steps taken to slow the spread of the virus. We are a conscientious and respectful community that understands the issues. Nonetheless, I was still amazed at the overwhelmingly considerate and respectful response of Piedmont residents.” May 19 The Piedmont Recreation Department announced that all originally planned summer camps and classes had been cancelled. The recommendation from the Alameda County Public Health Department for summer camps is to keep “stable groups” together for four weeks, and not have groups of students mix with each other. May 25 A black man in Minnesota, George Floyd, 46, is killed Monday, May 25 at the hands of a white police officer, Derek Chauvin. Floyd was detained, cuffed and brought to the ground after trying to pay with a counterfeit bill at a store. Video captured by pedestrians showed the white officer kneeling on Floyd’s neck for nearly 9 minutes, despite Floyd’s pleas that he couldn’t breathe. The officers involved ultimately were charged with murder, and the event sparked a national maelstrom. The California Department of Public Health announces that places of worship and in-store retail shopping may reopen statewide, subject to some limitations. Places of worship can hold religious services and funerals that limit attendance to 25 percent of a building’s capacity, subject to a maximum of 100 people. The vast majority of public gatherings is still prohibited under the state’s stay-at-home order. Events designed for political expression, such as protests, are allowed for up to 100 people. May 31 Residents of Piedmont organize a peaceful protest throughout the city and into Oakland. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers marched alongside protestors. “The organizers let [the Police Department] know that they expected a relatively small crowd, and that they would be in the area of Oakland Avenue and Highland Avenue,” Bowers explained. The May 31 event grew much larger than that, as protesters engaged in a march throughout Piedmont. Bowers said that the march was not anticipated, but that the primary focus for his officers was an emphasis on keeping protestors safe and facilitating traffic control. The City of Piedmont imposed a nightly curfew for the week, See Year in Review on page 29 Photo by Rob Yelland May 31: A protestor takes a knee during a march and peaceful protest that began in Piedmont and spilling over into neighboring Oakland.

articles.text: from 8 p.m. to 5 a.m. from June 1 through Saturday, June 6. The announcement follows a curfew for the entire county ordered by the Alameda County Sheriff’s office. During these hours, individuals are not allowed to be out in public anywhere in Alameda County with very limited exceptions. The majority of protests have been peaceful, but Oakland experiences extensive vandalism and looting through the weekend, prompting the curfew. Chief Bowers contacted Piedmont residents by wat of a “robocall” and advised people to stay home that night due to the possibility of violence. June 1 Oakland officials announced that at least 40 people were arrested on Monday night, June 1, for violating the new curfew order. The number represents a tiny fraction of the estimated 15,000 protesters who marched peacefully through Oakland during the day on Monday. June 13 A group of 20 Piedmont artists opened their home studios for Piedmont’s first Art Walk. Organized by Larraine Seiden and Jon Schleuning, community members were invited to follow a map with locations of each artist’s home and view art being displayed throughout the city. The event was spread out over Piedmont to avoid crowds and ensure social distancing. Visitors were asked to wear masks and maintain a six-foot distance from others, and to avoid touching displays. The spread of the novel coronavirus resulted in the cancellation of this year’s Spring fundraiser for the Art Fund. June 15 The City Council reviewed Piedmont police policies in the wake of nationwide civil unrest. Departments across the country were being asked to review their policies and use of force. In response, the Piedmont Police Department provided information on its policies in the context of nationwide discussions. “It is not enough to say, ‘what happened in Minneapolis could never happen here,” Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said. Protests in support of Black Lives Matter continued in Piedmont and have remained peaceful. Anne Callahan.

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a first reading of an ordinance which will require the electronic filing of campaign disclosure forms and statements of economic interests. California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a law in September of this year, which goes into effect on January 1, 2021, requiring all campaign filings to be posted on a City’s website within 72 hours of receipt. At the present time, filings are accepted on paper in Piedmont. The law allows local government agencies to require an elected and appointed official, candidate, or committee to file campaign statements, reports, and other documents online or electronically with a local filing officer. City Clerk John Tulloch explained that the proposal seeks to increase election transparency and save staff time. The city selected NetFile software to be the best solution for online filings in the future. The NetFile system is created specifically for cities responsible for administering campaign finance filings and Statements of Economic Interest and allows for electronic and paperless filing of campaign statements. The first reading was unanimously approved. The ordinance will be posted at City Hall after its second reading by the city council for at least 30 days and will become effective 30 days after the second reading.

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously approved a pilot program to install ‘speed cushions’ on Scenic Avenue and Greenbank Avenue at its December 21 meeting. The section of Scenic Avenue, from Blair Avenue to Alta Avenue, is a narrow street with no sidewalk and limited parking on both sides of the street. “It’s a very confusing and conflict-ridden street with respect to pedestrian safety, being that there are no sidewalks and visibility is compromised,” said recently retired Public Works Director Chester Nakahara. City staff was contacted by residents of Scenic Avenue in 2017 to address traffic concerns related to speed and pedestrian safety. One of their stated goals was to reduce the speed limit on the street from 15 miles per hour to 10 miles per hour. Due to the pandemic and city staff’s bandwidth, further meetings were delayed until October 20, when a virtual meeting was hosted by the city for all residents of the Scenic Avenue neighborhood. Three residents of this group joined in with Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Nakahara, City Engineer John Wanger, and traffic engineer Aaron Elias of Kittelson & Associates. They concluded that lowering the speed limit was not needed. Other options were explored and considered. In a discussion with Bowers and former Fire Chief Bret Black, speed cushions were determined to be the most viable solution. Speed cushions are vertical speed control elements placed in the roadway that are designed to manage traffic speeds. They are generally used on residential or slow-speed streets, where larger freight traffic is discouraged. They are different from speed humps, in that they include wheel cutouts that allow larger vehicles with wider tire spacing to pass through them at regular speeds while forcing passenger cars with narrower wheel spacing to reduce their speeds. A second location, the 200 block of Greenbank Avenue (between Oakland and Grand Avenues), was included in the plan to use speed cushions. The proposed placement of five speed cushions on Scenic are at 150, 210, 237, 266, and 288 Scenic Avenue. The proposed locations for two speed cushions on Greenbank are at roughly 211 and 231 Greenbank Avenue. “The pilot program is really an attempt to collect real-time data and feedback from residents, pedestrians, bicyclists, and allow our public safety vehicles to test the impact on their response time,” Nakahara explained. The cost of seven speed cushions is approximately $15,000, plus installation and required signage at $10,000, bringing the total to approximately $25,000, according to staff reports.
articles.title: Council OKs pilot program for ‘speed cushions’ on Scenic, Greenbank

articles.text: Leaves legacy of community events, improved relations with public After seven and a half years with the Piedmont Police Department, and a 22-year career in law enforcement, Sergeant Nicole Bolden has officially retired. Former Piedmont Police Chief Ricki Goede hired Bolden in 2013 and Bolden was promoted to the rank of Sergeant in January 2019. Bolden is not one to sit back and enjoy the ride. She pioneered the department’s community outreach program within Piedmont and in neighboring cities. The programs have gotten Piedmont officers involved with community members. “I have been most committed to community awareness, justice and giving people a forum or voice to speak,’ she said. “Nothing is ever black or white; we have to work together to make sure that everyone gets the justice that they deserve.” Bolden was born and raised in Richmond. Whenever law enforcement showed up, it was related to something negative, she recalls. In her time in Piedmont, Bolden worked for law enforcement to be a positive change in the community. “Sergeant Bolden brought her professional experience along with her personal experiences and passion to increase our Department’s connection with the public. I wish her all the best in the next chapter of her life and thoroughly enjoyed working with her,” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. Bolden was instrumental in bringing National Night Out to Piedmont. The nationwide event provides a chance for a casual and friendly mixing of residents with members of the police and fire departments. Residents are encouraged to organize block At her pinning ceremony in January 2019, Piedmont Police Officer Nicole received her Sergeant pin from her future husband, Jeffrey Jennings. parties and barbecues, and officers come to visit as many parties as possible. Bolden was also instrumental in starting Trunk or Treat, an event for Piedmont kids to decorate a patrol vehicle with Halloween decorations, pick up candy and take photos. Bolden expanded the Piedmont Police Department’s involvement to outside of the Piedmont community with “Shop with a Cop” in San Leandro. In this outreach program, Piedmont officers meet up with kids to help them shop at Walmart with donated gift cards. “Sgt. Bolden’s dedication and leadership have had a very positive effect on our community policing efforts. Our police-community relationships have improved based on her efforts,” said her immediate boss, Captain Chris Monahan. Bolden also initiated a partnership with Wednesday Walkers, a group of primarily seniors taking scheduled two-hour walks in town once a week. She saw it as an opportunity to promote public safety and awareness in the community, and led to the campaign. Bolden is also responsible for PPD’s involvement with Adopt a Family and for the partnership with Piedmont Fire Department in a gift-giving campaign called Three Wise Men. “With COVID there are a lot of limitations on any other opportunities. I thought that maybe I would be pursuing a second retirement in investigations, but I’m just going to take it for what it is, and enjoy the time I do have off,” Bolden said. Bolden lives in Sacramento, and recently was married to Jeffrey Jennings, the new Police Chief of the City of Emeryville. “I now have the time to enjoy my family members, who have been a great support and a driving point in my career. My son is in the Navy and my daughter works in the tech field for a San Francisco company,” she explained. “It’s great to leave this department on a high note and as a positive representative of the profession that I chose.” Bolden stated.
articles.title: Sgt. Nicole Bolden retires from police department

articles.text: The most recent Piedmont City Council meeting, on December 7, took an unorthodox turn when the council voted to split the position of the incoming vice mayor between councilmembers Tim Rood and Jen Cavenaugh. Instead of it being a traditional two-year term for one person, the council voted to have Rood, a six-year member of the council, assume the title for one year followed by Cavenaugh, a council member for four years, for one year. It was seen as a way to satisfy the traditional two-year vice mayorship that has been in place for 34 years. While there is no written precedent for the process of selecting a mayor and vice mayor, Piedmont has followed a tradition since 1986. According to City Clerk John Tulloch seniority would be the first qualifier, followed by the top vote getter. The position of vice mayor is chosen between councilmembers, and until recently, without any hiccups. Cavenaugh was the top vote-getter in 2016 and 2020, and Rood has seniority with six years on council. While it was ultimately decided by councilmembers that the vice mayorship would be “shared,” the decision was reached only after a lengthy discussion. The first formal nomination for vice mayor came from councilmember Betsy Andersen, who nominated Cavenaugh. “We don’t have [the selection] process on the agenda tonight, and I think it’s awkward to change the tradition when we’re in it,” Andersen offered. Tradition, she said, asserts that Cavenaugh would take the position. This was seconded by Cavenaugh. Mayor Teddy King, chairing

articles.text: Public Works Director Chester Nakahara will retire from his position on December 22 after a career of more than 23 years with the city. A licensed architect, he left his private practice to become the city’s principal building inspector and was promoted to the title of Director when Larry Rosenberg retied in 2010. As a resident of Piedmont, prior to joining the city staff he was a volunteer member of the Park Commission and the Main Park Renovation Task Force. Piedmont, with its steep hills, narrow, winding streets, and abundance of trees, can be subject to substantial wind and rain damage. Under Nakahara’s guidance, maintenance workers continued to keep ahead of the potential storm-related problems. “Chester is one of the most well organized, even-keeled people I know. articles.text: Total cases in Piedmont soars to 80 As the first doses of a COVID- 19 vaccine arrive in the San Francisco Bay Area, new cases of the disease are spiking in Alameda County like never before. The first doses of a COVID-19 vaccine manufactured by Pfizer will arrive in Alameda County in the next few days, health officials announced on Monday, December 14. The first people to be vaccinated will include hospital workers and 911 responders at highest risk of exposure. “While we are still in the early phases, this is a hopeful moment for Alameda County residents,” Alameda County Board of Supervisors President Richard Valle said in a statement. “A safe and effective vaccine will save lives and help residents and businesses return to some level of normalcy.” The county expects to receive 12,675 doses. More doses are anticipated to arrive in the coming weeks. “Acute care hospital health care workers and 911 first responders at highest risk for exposure to COVID-19 are our first line of defense in protecting our system of care from becoming overwhelmed and understaffed during this surge,” said Deputy Health Officer Dr. Kathleen Clanon. While it was not announced if any doses of the vaccine had been administered in Alameda County as of press time, several people were vaccinated at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital yesterday, Tuesday, December 15. The vaccine news comes as cases are surging to unprecedented levels in the region. On Friday, December 11, there were 1,063 new cases of COVID- 19 reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases in a single day ever and the first time more than a thousand cases were recorded in one day. There have been several days in the past two weeks with far more new cases than the surge in August, when daily new cases were previously at their highest levels. Nine new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters in the past week, a 23 percent increase since December 1. There have been 80 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 7.6 percent, the Alameda County Department of Public Health reported yesterday, Tuesday, December 15. The total caseload in Alameda County is now 38,971, an increase of over 5,200 cases from one week ago. Tragically, 33 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 558. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 13,338. In Hayward, 6,010 cases have been recorded. There are an additional seven cities in the county each with a caseload over 1,000. A new stay-at-home order for the county went into effect on Monday, December 7. The goal is to limit in-person interactions between people from different households. Restaurants must reduce operations to take-out and delivery only; outdoor and indoor dining are both prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor playgrounds are also now shuttered. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores can remain open with capacity restrictions. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The state order is activated when a regional group of counties, such as the Bay Area, announces that ICU capacity has dropped below 15 percent. While the Bay Area has not reached that threshold, health authorities from five Bay Area counties agreed to adopt the stricter stay-at-home restrictions as a precaution. The health orders in the Bay Area are scheduled to remain in place until January 4 but could be extended. Before the current surge, the worst day for the pandemic in Alameda County was August 13, when 417 cases were recorded. The rising case rate caused the state last month to put the entire county into the Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier. The Purple Tier is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system for reopening businesses and activities. As of this week, the county’s case rate is 19.8 cases per 100,000 people, a massive increase from one week ago. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. The state and county are urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes an alarming flood of cases throughout the United States even as the first COVID-19 vaccines are being administered. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 1,617,370 cases of COVID-19 in California. Cases have trended sharply upward since October 18. There have been 21,188 deaths Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver it to your doorstep every Wednesday.

articles.text: A program that lets California residents know if they have been exposed to COVID-19 was rolled out statewide last Thursday, December 10. The smartphone application, CA Notify, is available on all iPhones and Android devices. G ov. G av i n Ne w s o m announced the launch of CA Notify during a press conference last week when the application officially went live across the state. “Throughout this pandemic we have tapped California’s talent pool to fight this virus, and that includes working with tech innovators like Apple and Google,” said Gov. Newsom. “CA Notify will help slow the spread by alerting those who opt in to receive an alert if they’ve come into contact with someone who has tested positive. The process is private, anonymous and secure, and is one of the many tools in the state’s data-driven approach to help reduce the spread.” The program is voluntary and is not defined as contact tracing. It notifies users who have been in close contact with another user who has opted into the system and tested positive for the virus. When individuals voluntarily activate CA Notify, the tool uses Bluetooth technology to exchange random codes between phones without revealing the user’s identity or location. If a CA Notify user tests positive for COVID-19, they will receive a verification code to plug into the app, if they choose. Any other CA Notify users who have been within six feet for 15 minutes or more of the COVID-19 positive individual will get an anonymous notification of possible exposure. Users who have tested positive will get a text from the California Department of Public Health with a code, which they can enter into the CA Notify application, triggering an alert to phones of people who may have been exposed in the previous 14 days. Android users can download CA Notify through the application store. Apple iPhone users simply need to activate the built-in feature. It is accessible by enabling A new iPhone application alerts users of possible COVID-19 exposure. “exposure notifications” in the settings area of the device. “When combined with other actions like wearing masks and physical distancing, CA Notify can help curb the transmission of COVID-19,” said Dr. Mark Gahly, California Health and Human Services Secretary. “Every day that is saved in alerting others of a possible exposure, is a day that a possibly infectious person can begin self-quarantine and reduce the spread. This technology is another way for Californians to take proactive steps to keep themselves, their loved ones and their communities safe.” California launched a pilot of CA Notify in September for university students, staff and faculty at UC San Diego and UC San Francisco, and then later to other UC campuses in mid-November. The university system estimates that more than 250,000 people are now utilizing the application and technology. “Our pilot experience starting at UC San Diego and expanding to other UC campuses showed this technology was effective in identifying exposed individuals early for quarantine and testing, and helping keep our communities as safe as possible,” said Christopher Longhurst, MD, chief information officer of UC San Diego Health. “This free and reliable smartphone technology can help all Californians. As we enter a new, and hopefully final, surge in the pandemic, now more than ever is the time to put every possible tool to use to slow the spread of the virus.” For more information, see: CaNotify.ca.gov and Covid19. ca.gov. articles.text: Last week, a Red Flag Warning was issued for the East Bay Hills by the National Weather Service – a rare event for December. NWS issued the Red Flag Warning, meaning critical fire weather conditions are present, from Sunday, December 6 at 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. on Monday, December 7. The impacted area encompassed the East Bay Hills, including the Oakland Hills and Berkeley Hills, as well as all of the North Bay and the interior valleys. The warning also covered the Santa Cruz Mountains and the Pacific coastline along the San Francisco Peninsula. High, gusty winds moving from the Pacific Ocean over Sunday night paired with a warm, low-humidity Monday afternoon caused the NWS to order the Red Flag Warning. There have been only two other December Red Flag Warnings in Bay Area history, both within the past decade – 2013 and 2017. At the height of the drought in California in the 2010s, Red Flag Warnings were occasionally ordered in January. Meteorologists believe it is possible the region could see some Red Flag Warnings issued next month. Rain fell in the Bay Area on Sunday, December 13, but Cal Fire has not declared the 2020 wildfire season over just yet. While wildfire season traditionally ends around November 30, risks are continuing into winter. As of this week, Cal Fire has not ordered any of its 21 units throughout California to activate winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season for the year is done. The 2020 wildfire season will be remembered as one of the most devastating in history across California and the entire western United States. Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which burned in and around Mendocino National Forest, was the largest wildfire in California history and the state’s first “gigafire,” meaning a fire that burns over 1 million acres. Experts worry that global climate change is expanding California’s fire season into a year-round situation. Even when the 2020 wildfire season is declared over, the Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to stay vigilant and prepare for fire emergencies. Piedmonters can learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage on the City’s website and clicking on www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Request a Virtual or On-Site Quote

articles.text: Cooper, Thigpen sworn in as new board members Piedmont School Board Vice President Cory Smegal was elected at the December 15 school board meeting as its new president, taking over from Amal Smith. Smegal begins her second four-year term on the board. Megan Pillsbury was elected as the board’s new Vice President, and newly elected school board members Veronica Thigpen and Hilary Cooper were sworn into office for their first term “There is still work to be done and I am committed to that work,” said Smegal. “There is a light at the end of this dark tunnel, and we will get through this. I look forward to continuing to serve on the board of education.” “It is an honor to join the school board. I know many of the members already and have always admired and respected their public service. I am excited to be part of the board especially with Veronica. I think that we are going to work really well together,” Cooper said in an interview with the Post. “I am someone who will work with other board members, educators, and administrators to make sure each and every one of our students receives an excellent education and graduates ready for college and ready to pursue careers and ready to engage and take action on behalf of their communities,” said Thigpen after being sworn in. Looking at the newly convened board, Smegal said, “You know when someone joins the school board it is clearly not for monetary gain and it is clearly not for glory. There is not really any of that. It is because we want to serve. According to the Alameda County Registrar of Voter, the election results were certified as official on December 3. Cooper earned the third and last spot on the school board with 157 more votes than Jason Kelley. articles.text: Workshop is next step in updating 2014 Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan On Wednesday, December 9, the City held a lively community workshop via Zoom about how to improve traffic safety as part of the newly christened Piedmont Safer Streets project. About 25 people attended the virtual event. The feedback and discussion will go toward creating an upcoming Safer Streets plan, which will serve as an update to the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan adopted by City Council in 2014. The Safer Streets plan aims to “meaningfully advance” the 2014 plan “with an addition of a traffic safety component,” according to Gopika Nair, associate planner with the City. “The workshop reviewed the progress made since 2014 and included a lively community discussion on future directions,” Nair continued. The workshop last week was hosted by City staff along with Niko Letunic, a consultant tapped by Council to assist in updating the City’s Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan back in July. Nair noted that attendees discussed existing traffic conditions, potential traffic calming measures and street parking. Part of the workshop focused on improving the intersection at Fairview and Grand Avenues. articles.text: Anyone else ready to move on to a new year? As we finish another lap around the Sun, we’re closing out 2020 with a Virtual Balloon Drop New Year Celebration. You’re invited to join us virtually on Thursday, December 31 at 11 a.m. as we count down to the stroke of noon. Now more than ever, we can all come together for science… and a lot of fun! Balloon Drop has been a Chabot Space & Science Center tradition since 2000, creating a fun, day-time opportunity for families to celebrate the new year without staying up past their bedtime. This year, the party continues with STEM activities, a dance party, a family-friendly toast and the colorful live balloon drop spectacle. To keep the party fun and safe for learners of all ages, the Balloon Drop New Year’s Celebration will be hosted virtually this year. With so many celebrations put on hold during the COVID crisis, Chabot’s team was determined to create a magical moment for families at home this year. How do we know that Balloon Drop can still be fun at home? Well, we’ve already seen it. Back in 2018, a Chabot member was able to pull off an at-home Balloon Drop for her son. After her child came down with a stomach bug the day of the event, Chabot member Genie was able to create her own at-home party, pulling together a large bag of Happy Birthday balloons Kids celebrate the Chabot Space and Science Center annual New Year’s Eve Balloon Drop. and set herself up at the top of the stairs with the kids down below. Their family counted down and at the stroke of noon… they celebrated by releasing bouncing balloons down the staircase! And her son loved it, counting along and cheering with excitement! Right now, we’re finding more innovative ways than ever to come together. This year, our entire community has gotten creative as we celebrate milestones, holidays and more in new ways. We’ve seen drive-thru parades, live-streamed weddings and so many more new avenues of connection. While we’ll dearly miss the hundreds of smiling faces waiting eagerly for balloons to drop from our ceiling this year, our party will continue. Our community will still share a toast, a dance party, a countdown and, of course…a Balloon Drop! Together, we look forward to welcoming 2021 with excitement and optimism. During such a challenging year, we hope you’ll join us for a moment of joy and learning. Let’s say hello to a new year with one last party and a big ‘thank you’ to science! From all of us at Chabot Space & Science Center – Happy New Year! Be sure to join the Virtual Balloon Drop New Year Celebration by visiting: https://chabotspace.org/events/ events-listing/ Mary Catherine Frantz is Marketing & Communication Manager at Chabot Space and Science Center located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. Following the guidance from the CDC and local medical officials all in-person public programs and gatherings at the Center have been postponed or cancelled until further notice.
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom Chabot Science Center continues New Year Tradition

articles.text: For the Piedmont Pioneers, a middle school FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) robotics team, the COVID--19 restrictions this year have been challenging. The NORCAL FIRST organization had to overhaul the tournaments to be virtual. Even though we are mostly a rookie team, by leaning on our core values like teamwork and innovation, we have been able to make a robot we feel is successful. Despite the pandemic, and with six of seven members as newcomers, our team has been able to work well together. Early in the school year we were able to meet while wearing masks and remaining socially distanced as much as possible. Our coaches built us a large outdoor arena so Building the outdoor playfield. Piedmont Pioneers robotics team: (front) Caetano De Figueirido (left), Kaspar Jansson, Tiago DeFigueirido; (top) Nathaniel Welch, Vaughn Khouri, Lewy Seiden, and Cassandra Colby. that we could spend lots of time working on the robot outside. We split the practices into software and hardware meetings so that we could stay in smaller groups. During this time, we were busy raising $5000 for our season to cover robot parts, tournament fees, field equipment, and more. We have made a robot we feel is competitive with other teams, despite being a middle school team among mostly high school teams in Northern California. We have grown close by communicating over our Discord server, which lets us get together remotely. We like to play various video games “together,” especially Among Us, a whodunnit type of game. Recently, we helped lead a virtual Tech Social for the Piedmont Makers by hosting Among Us games for the social part of the event. We participated in a scrimmage in mid-November which helped test our robot. Then we made changes for our first NorCal qualifying tournament that started on December 6 and wrapped up with judges’ interviews on December 12. We started off strong the first day of the tournament with good scores on all of our recorded runs. We were ready to finish our other runs over the next week. But one day later, the tournament was cancelled due to the increased COVID lockdown restrictions. This was a major letdown. We took it in stride and used what we had learned to begin making improvements to our robot. Even though robotics has been challenging during COVID, I’m glad that our team has been able to make it work because it is such a unique learning experience. We are now looking forward to our next tournament in January. Lewy Seiden, an 8th grader, is captain of the Pioneers robotics team. Pioneers in a strategy session in September.
articles.title: Piedmont Pioneers robotics team update

articles.text: Four proposals for new courses to be offered at Piedmont High School were reviewed by the school board at a first reading on December 15. Courses include Financial Literacy, Physical Computing and Robotics, Field Science Electives, and Guitar Engineering. The proposals were submitted last year by PHS teachers. Social Studies teacher Gabby Kashani proposed a new semester-long course, Financial Literacy and Personal Finance, for grades 10-12 to start next Fall. The course would cover: Behavioral Finance, Checking, Saving, Budgeting, Paying for College, Types of Credit, Investing, Insurance, and even Taxes. Many high schools offer similar courses to help prepare students for real life. Computer Science teacher Irfan Ortak proposed a yearlong course, Physical Computing and Robotics, for grades 9 and 10. Computer Science courses concerned with software have become increasingly in demand at Piedmont but Ortak has noted, “We do not currently have any course that focuses on hardware and the physical part of computing.” The course is proposed to start next fall. Science teacher Andrew Willats proposed a series of four semester-long electives focusing on Field Science for grades 9-12. “Each one would emphasize data-driven research that will allow students to assess the changes occurring in our modern world, as well as field work in and around Piedmont,” Willats wrote. The courses include: Ornithology (focusing on bird identification), Entomology (insect study), Geology, and Marine Science. These courses would start in Fall 2021 and would present low-stress upper-division course alternatives. Science teacher Marna Chamberlain has proposed a Guitar Engineering course for students in 11th and 12th grades, to begin August 2021. “This course looks at the design elements, manufacturing and assembly of solid-body electric guitars. Students will construct their own electric guitar,” she said. Students will gain building skills and life skills in the shop while practicing soldering, making circuits and using a laser cutter. To view the agenda for the meeting with a description of each proposed course, see: www. agendaonline.net/public/Meeting. aspx?AgencyID=1241&MeetingID=81340&AgencyTypeID=0&IsArchived=False
articles.title: From Personal Finance to bird watching to guitar making
