articles.text: Children’s Fairyland’s famed puppeteer, Randal Metz, brought his Nutcracker puppet show to all the kids at Highlands’ Preschool in Piedmont last Friday, December 11. The school created an outdoor space for the puppet show, perhaps with fewer kids but the same love and magic that has distinguished it for decades. “[Randal] has come every year for over 20 years, and we were so sad at the thought of not being able to do it because of COVID. But he did it; he made it work. He set it up in our play yard and it was fantastic, just like always. We were so happy,” said Highlands Director Deanna Johnson. Beyond his work at Children’s Fairyland, Metz’s company, The Puppet Company, normally has 40 showings of the Nutcracker each year. But with Fairyland currently closed due to COVID, the Nutcracker puppet show was shown only once in person – at Highlands Preschool. “We were only able to do this by social distancing, with the kids on one end and me on the other, so everyone was safe about the whole thing, and I think it went really well,” Metz said. “The kids love it, just love it. Many of them have seen it year after year,” Metz added. The Nutcracker show battled through more than just a pandemic this year, as an unexpected rain threatened some the exquisitely crafted puppets. But just like real show business, the show went on with only a minor variance. “Our Chinese dragon did not breath fire like it was supposed to, it usually gives off a big smoke ring. Because it was partially raining that day, the rain foiled that. The kids asked me ‘how come the dragon did not do fire this year?’” Metz said. With or without fire the dragon impresses everyone as do so many of the characters in the performance. “There is a snow fairy that comes out in the beginning and she sprinkles iridescent snow all over where the kids are, like she is spreading it across the land. Then the little elephant comes out in The Lands of Sweets and shoots water out from his trunk. That’s definitely a fan favorite. The kids love that, it is so much fun,” Johnson recalled with a smile. Metz has been working with puppets at Children’s Fairyland in Oakland for 50 years. At the age of 10 Metz auditioned at Fairyland to be a child actor and earned the role of the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland; he began apprenticing as a puppeteer with Lewis Mahlmann, who created puppet shows at Fairyland for decades. “It is all about creating good memories for them. It was really nice to visit our friends. When the kids visit Fairyland they don’t hesitate to come up to me and say, ‘You came to our school!’” Metz said. Highlands Preschool hopes to have Metz back to perform Mei Lin and the Magic Brush for Chinese New Year in February. Fairyland had to close this month due to the pandemic, but aspires to reopen its puppet theater in January. “We are anxious to get the theater up and running. The Bay Area children would love to come back and see their puppet friends again,” Metz said. Randal Metz runs the longest ongoing professional puppet theater in the United States at Children’s Fairyland In November, Metz and The Puppet Company live-streamed the Nutcracker puppet performance with the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra playing highlights from Tchaikovsky’s The Nutcracker. You can view it at: www.thesfco.org/events/ nutcracker-sweet

articles.text: A Great Conjunction of 2020 in the heavens above Clearly we have been focused on this exigent and extraordinary year. It seems counterintuitive to look up to the night sky and try and put into perspective our place and purpose in the universe. But for a singular moment we are given a unique opportunity to look toward the heavens and witness an event the likes of which has not occurred since 1226, a time when Genghis Khan rode across Asia and the renaissance was still generations away. Next week, on December 21, at 6:40 P.M. PST, Jupiter and Saturn, the two largest planets in our solar system, now remarkably close together, will appear in the southwestern night sky, just after sunset. They will seem to brightly merge in the darkened sky, absent the sun’s nimbus of light. Astronomers are calling the event the Great Conjunction. Actually this orbital alignment of these two planets began at the beginning of this year. Keep in mind that Jupiter is half a billion miles from earth and the brighter of the two; Saturn is double that distance, hence, by degrees, will appear dimmer. You will not need a telescope or binoculars to witness the Great Conjunction. The naked eye will serve budding astronomers just fine. It has been referred to it as the Christmas star, though astronomers counsel that this event, coming at the end of a long arduous year has no other astrological meaning than its rare occurrence. If you have school age children looking for a project with extrapolation potential, check out the possibilities. It’s worth a Google search for some background information.

Oyster Bay Regional Shoreline Walking & Picnic Park 1600 Neptune Dr, San Leandro 888-327-2757, # 3, ext. 4548 www.ebparks.org/parks/oyster_bay Just south of the Oakland Airport is a preserved shoreline perfect for birdwatching and a beautiful day out of the house for a short walk. A variety of wildlife can be seen including marsh hawks, black-shouldered kites, and red-tailed hawks. Group picnic areas amongst tree berms await your family time out. The park has been undergoing renovation; enjoy the newly planted turf along the multipurpose trails. Interior trails lead to a view site with a sculpture called “Rising Wave.” The two-mile perimeter hiking and walking trail comes with majestic views and the salty breeze of the bay. Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve Hiking Trail 7227 Skyline Blvd. Oakland (510) 544-3111 www.ebparks.org/parks/huckleberry Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve remains open, including its parking lot. Take the 1.7-mile loop to get back in touch with the beauty of native plants both common and rare to the area. The 237-acre preserve has yearround blooming flowers to brighten your day. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: On a cold Christmas Eve in 1818, pastor Joseph Franz Mohr walked the three kilometers from his home in the Austrian village of Oberndorf bei Salzburg to visit his friend Franz Gruber in the neighboring town of Arnsdorf bei Laufen. Mohr brought with him a poem he had written two years earlier. He desperately needed a carol for his Christmas Eve midnight mass that evening. He hoped his friend Gruber, a school teacher who also served as the church’s choir master and organist, could set his poem to music. In a matter of a few hours, Franz Gruber composed the “Stille Nacht” melody for Mohr on that night of December 24, 1818. Flooding of the nearby Salzach River had put the church organ out of commission, so Gruber composed the music for guitar accompaniment. A few hours after Gruber finished the composition, he and Mohr stood before the altar at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf to perform the work. A local choir sang the new composition, breaking the silence of that “stille nacht.” Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth.
articles.title: Silent Night (Stille Nacht)

articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. The Twelve Days of Christmas – the Song On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me: A partridge in a pear tree. On the second day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Two turtle doves, and a partridge in a pear tree. On the third day of Christmas my true love gave to me Three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fourth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the fifth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the sixth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the seventh day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the eighth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the ninth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. On the tenth day of Christmas my true love gave to me: Ten lords a-leaping, nine ladies dancing, eight maids a-milking, seven swans a-swimming, six geese a-laying, five golden rings; four calling birds, three French hens, two turtle doves and a partridge in a pear tree. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, December 16, 2020 Piedmont Community Church Virtual Christmas Eve Services 400 Highland Ave., Piedmont 94611 PiedmontChurch.org L a k e s h o r e A v The Post wishes its readers the happiest of holidays Silent Night (Stille Nacht) On a cold Christmas Eve in 1818, pastor Joseph Franz Mohr walked the three kilometers from his home in the Austrian village of Oberndorf bei Salzburg to visit his friend Franz Gruber in the neighboring town of Arnsdorf bei Laufen. Mohr brought with him a poem he had written two years earlier. He desperately needed a carol for his Christmas Eve midnight mass that evening. He hoped his friend Gruber, a school teacher who also served as the church’s choir master and organist, could set his poem to music. In a matter of a few hours, Franz Gruber composed the “Stille Nacht” melody for Mohr on that night of December 24, 1818. Flooding of the nearby Salzach River had put the church organ out of commission, so Gruber composed the music for guitar accompaniment. A few hours after Gruber finished the composition, he and Mohr stood before the altar at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf to perform the work. A local choir sang the new composition, breaking the silence of that “stille nacht.” Silent Night, Holy Night By Franz X. Gruber and Joseph F. Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth. e n u B a p e t i s t C h u r c h The 12 Days of Christmas Background of the Song The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. From 1558 to 1829 Roman Catholics in England were not able to practice their faith openly, so they had to find other ways to pass on their beliefs. The song is an allegory. Each of the items in the song represents something of religious significance. The hidden meaning of each gift was designed to help young Christians learn their faith. ✝ In the song “On the first day of Christmas my true love gave to me” true love represents God, and “me” is the Christian. ✝ The “partridge in a pear tree” represents Jesus Christ who died on a tree. ✝ Two turtle doves represent the Old and New Testaments. ✝ Three French hens are faith, hope and love – the three gifts of the Spirit. ✝ Four calling birds are the four Gospels. ✝ Five golden rings are the first five books of the Bible, also known as the Books of Moses. ✝ Six geese a-laying are the six days of creation. ✝ Seven swans a-swimming are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Eight maids a milking are the eight beatitudes. ✝ Nine ladies dancing are the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit. ✝ Ten lords a-leaping are the Ten Commandments. ✝ Eleven pipers piping are the eleven faithful disciples. ✝ Twelve drummers drumming are the twelve points of the Apostles’ Creed. articles.text: ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!”

articles.text: It’s been months for Piedmont sports teams struggling to find field space and available pools, time to train, and sorting through updates from the leagues, the Sections and the California Interscholastic Federation, the governing body for all prep sports in the state. For tennis, Piedmont’s most successful sport for the past 20 years, it has meant coach Jim Landes continuing to keep player active and interested at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Vista and Bonita Avenue. “We’re doing clinics through the Recreation Department and all these kids are getting out on the court and practicing. They are looking good and we’ll have some good players,” said Landes. The clinics at the Piedmont courts are a common sight over the years. It is where Landes routinely determines his prospective roster. “Our girls from last year have gotten better and we’ll have some freshmen boys who could make an impact,” said Landes, reeling off his returners he expects to get some playing time. But this year is different. The State (CIF) initially pushed both girls’ and boys’ tennis together for practice in March and planned for their matches to be in April and May.. Now it seems there is some momentum to have the girls start in February and boys in late April. “We’re not playing any Shoreline Division teams, which I had suggested,” explained Landes. “It’ll be a short season but with eight tough matches with Alameda, Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, and Berkeley.” Landes has been working with league officials in the Western Alameda County Conference to Staff Photos Boys’ water polo coach John Savage talks about the challenges involved for his program. With the Piedmont Pool closed permanently, the high school does not have a local pool available for its water polo and swim teams. The school district does not have a pool. Piedmont High tennis players participating in coach Jim Landes’ clinics at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. create a functioning and realistic schedule. With the California Department of Public Health declaring that tennis can be played in Purple Tier counties, it certainly looks like girls’ tennis team could start earlier than originally planned by the CIF. “The schedule may change. The girls could start in February and the boys after that in lateApril or May. They were initially planned to start simultaneously on March 8,” said Landes. The varsity tennis team may begin workouts on Monday, January 18, but the plan for Junior Varsity tennis is still unclear. “We can’t start JV tryouts until March 8, which is quite a ways away. I know most of the players, because they are in my clinics.; he added. The future is not so rosy for boys and girls water polo, teams still in search of a pool for practices and competition. Coach John Savage confirmed that there is still considerable uncertainty with public pools still closed. “Unfortunately, I cannot provide a positive update in relation to the pools. If we were in Contra Costa County we could have in-pool workouts, but Alameda County has stricter guidelines. Laney College is likely our best bet, but they won’t let groups use their pool until students are allowed back onto campus,” he said. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) ruled Outdoor Water Polo as a high contact sport and would require Alameda County to enter the Orange Tier in order to play. With polo still set to be in the CIF’s first to start Season 1, Savage said, “I don’t think they’d push Water Polo (to Season 2) because of the overlapping of sports with the swim program, in addition to other sports. “If sports get shuffled around, I don’t see water polo being one of those,” said Savage. As for the possibility of playing in Contra Costa County, Savage confirmed that he has reached out to pools outside Alameda County. “At the moment, we’ve [contacted] some facilities and they are impacted as well. Everybody is looking for pool space for high school teams and club teams. Two facilities in Walnut Creek said we can have two hours on Sunday afternoons, and that was a month or two ago,” said Savage. Although the water polo teams are still searching for a pool, Savage said he is grateful the team has an opportunity to get together. “We have to wait for pools to open up. It doesn’t matter how many phone calls we put out if their response is the same. We’re grateful to be allowed to have workouts, I know some districts aren’t even allowing that. Our new A,D., Bradley Smet, has been very helpful. We’re workStaff Photos Audrey Edel is a senior on PHS girls’ tennis team. ing within the confines of a pandemic,” he added. On the track at Witter Field track, you can spot the water polo player working out to stay in shape for the time when they can finally get back int a pool – wherever it might be. “We’re currently working out at the field. We have anywhere between 15 and 20 kids showing up and our seniors are showing up as leaders. We’ve been doing a lot of individual challenges to set benchmarks, and we’re giving out awards to the highest number, fastest time, and most improved,” he said.
articles.title: PHS Tennis & Water Polo preparing the most they can

articles.text: Oregon, ASU, UCLA & Arizona sit outside the top-25 After a week, no Pac-12 teams are ranked in the Top 25 in men’s college basketball. Arizona State relinquished its No. 23 ranking after losing to San Diego State 80-68. With the win, the Aztecs jumped from No. 23 to 18. Right now, the Oregon Ducks (4-1) have 31 votes to enter the top-25, ASU (4-2) has 13, UCLA (5-1) nine, and Arizona (5-0) with five. Since our last writeup, the Ducks have done well with 87-66 and 74-71 victories over Florida A&M and Washington – their first conference game. They have two difficult games ahead of Christmas with the 5-3 San Francisco Dons tomorrow at 5:00 p.m. and UCLA on Wednesday, December 23. A loss vt the Sun Devils to the Aztecs shouldn’t be taken as cause for alarm, but they narrowly defeated unranked Grand Canyon 71-70 after trailing by a point at halftime. They should be expected to beat UTEP today at 6:00 p.m. and have a critical conference game against Utah on Tuesday, Dec. 22. The Bruins of UCLA, they did well to hold off a strong Marquette team, holding them to 26 points in the second half. They look ahead to a headline matchup on Saturday against former national champion Kentucky, which is just 1-4. The Bruins’ game on December 15 against Long Beach was postponed after LBSU had a COVID-19 outbreak. Arizona dispatched UTEP 69-61 and will play unanked California Baptist today at 4:00 p.m. Up next however is a game with Stanford on December 19. Also in the Pac-12, the Washington State Cougars are undefeated at 5-0 without playing any serious competition. They face Montana State on December 18, and Prairie on December 21. USC is also 4-1 overall and starts its conference schedule on Sunday against Oregon State (2-3). Colorado (3-1) should be the Trojans’ first challenge on New Years Eve. California (3-4)c is coming off an upset of University of San Francisco 72-70 on December 13. The Bears face Boston College (1-5) team on December 22, an Photo courtesy of OregonLive The Oregon basketball team is just outside the nation’s top-25 with 31 votes in the Associated Press poll. opportunity to lock down a win before visiting Oregon on New Years Eve. Stanford (3-2) defeated Ca State Northridge 82-71 on Tuesday but will be the underdog in a game on Saturday against Arizona. articles.text: Stanford at 3-2 opts out of bowl game, Cal season officially over A strange football season is almost over for the Pac-12 Conference. The Stanford Cardinal heads into its final game with a 3-2 record after defeating Oregon State 27-24. It is scheduled to visit UCLA on Saturday. The Cardinal at 3-2 would qualify for a post-season bowl berth, even if they were to lose to the Bruins. But the school announced that Stanford has opted out of a bowl game because the team has been off campus since December 1 as a result of Stay at Home orders prohibiting sports in Santa Clara County. “After being on the road since December 1, the Cardinal will decline postseason opportunities, the Stanford statement read. “On Monday, the program will relocate to Santa Barbara to prepare for Saturday’s game at UCLA. Stanford departed for the Seattle area on Tuesday, Dec. 1 to prepare for its road game at Washington on Dec. 5. Following that game, the program relocated on Sunday, Dec. 6 and spent the week in Corvallis, Ore. preparing for its game at Oregon State, a contest that was originally scheduled for Stanford Stadium,” wrote the school in a press release. Stanford is the first Pac-12 school to decline an invitation to the postseason. Earlier in the week, Boston College also announced it would not participate in any bowl games, as did Pittsburgh and Virginia. The Cardinal looks ahead to UCLA, which is coming off a dramatic 43-38 loss to No. 13 USC and look at Stanford as an opportunity to finish above .500, currently at 3-3. The A Stanford win will require more heroics from quarterback Davis Mills and running back Austin Jones. USC dialed up 47 pass attempts against UCLA, so you can bank on Mills getting a heavy workout. The California Golden Bears, however, had their final two games canceled after a player tested positive for COVID-19 and contact tracing protocols denied them of enough players for Washington State game last Saturday, December 12. Their game this Saturday, December 19, was officially canceled on Sunday because both Cal and the Arizona Wildcats are dealing with virus concerns. So, Cal’s tumultuous season mercifully comes to a conclusion. Its season-opener was canceled against Washington, and it got smashed 34-10 unexpectedly by UCLA. Then it relinquished the Stanford Axe back to Stanford on to a blocked PAT kick at the end of the game/ And now its final two games have been shut down. In spite of their 21-17 upset victory over Oregon on December 5, it was a season to forget. It may be worth mentioning that Cal passed up on former Piedmont High three-star football recruit Patrick Selna who signed with UCLA. Patch, we think you made the right call.

articles.text: Sunday’s rain was the heaviest in months for the Bay Area, which meant the Piedmont Post was out for another day of hiking. Walking to waterfalls is a joy during the winter season, and progressive rain should help the Bay Area recover from an extended drought. Last weekend we returned to Mt. Tamalpais in Marin County for a hike on the Cascade Falls and Carson Falls trails. Carson Falls is among the more popular destinations on Mt. Tam. The wet weather often deters others, creating some solitude for the lone, weather-resistant hiker. The weather allowed for opportune parking along Cascade Drive in Fairfax, which turns into the trailhead for Cascade Fire Road. The first landmark us about 0.7 mile away, Cascade Falls. The falls at this moment are more of a trickle due to the absence of rain for many months. Cascade Creek, however, is more of a treat with its bubbling brooks of running water from the falls. Walking back to the Cascade Fire Road is where our trek begins. 3.7 miles away is our second destination, the more popular and much more active Carson Falls. While the walk to Cascade Falls is level and easy, the hike to Carson Falls provides over 1,400 feet in elevation gain providing the chance for a good lower body workout. When totaling mile back to the car, you’re looking at around 2,100 feet in elevation gain in slightly less than nine miles. The trail goes along Cascade Creek on the way to Cascade Falls. A rocky road on the Cascade Falls Trail.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON Chasing waterfalls – Mt. Tam’s Cascade & Carson Falls

pages.text: 14 Wednesday, December 16, 2020 HIKING WITH JON Chasing waterfalls – Mt. Tam’s Cascade & Carson Falls By Jonathan Comeaux Sunday’s rain was the heaviest in months for the Bay Area, which meant the Piedmont Post was out for another day of hiking. Walking to waterfalls is a joy during the winter season, and progressive rain should help the Bay Area recover from an extended drought. Last weekend we returned to Mt. Tamalpais in Marin County for a hike on the Cascade Falls and Carson Falls trails. Carson Falls is among the more popular destinations on Mt. Tam. The wet weather often deters others, creating some solitude for the lone, weather-resistant hiker. The weather allowed for opportune parking along Cascade Drive in Fairfax, which turns into the trailhead for Cascade Fire Road. The first landmark us about 0.7 mile away, Cascade Falls. The falls at this moment are more of a trickle due to the absence of rain for many months. Cascade Creek, however, is more of a treat with its bubbling brooks of running water from the falls. Walking back to the Cascade Fire Road is where our trek begins. 3.7 miles away is our second destination, the more popular and much more active Carson Falls. While the walk to Cascade Falls is level and easy, the hike to Carson Falls provides over 1,400 feet in elevation gain providing the chance for a good lower body workout. When totaling mile back to the car, you’re looking at around 2,100 feet in elevation gain in slightly less than nine miles. The trail goes along Cascade Creek on the way to Cascade Falls. A rocky road on the Cascade Falls Trail. The hike along the Cascade Fire Road doesn’t provide much coverage, so remember proper attire if out in the rain. The fire road is a hard red dirt road, packed down from mountain bikers that usually roam the area. Merging with Pine Mountain Road, the road will be covered with loose rocks that could cause tired hikers to trip if they aren’t paying attention. Those hiking in wet weather will be wise to watch where they put their feet over each stone, but doing so will enable them to the shimmering colors of the rocks beneath them on Pine Mountain Road. Glistening in the water are batches of greenstone that has an unmistakable golden glitter. You’ll also see the state rock of California, the green serpentine. Turning onto the Oak Hill Fire Road will lead you to the Carson Falls Trail, going back under some trees for a brief time until reaching the top of the falls. The roar of water when approaching will provide some excitement after the strenuous hike. Following the Carson Falls Trail will bring you around the base of the Photos by Jonathan Comeaux Carson Falls is a popular destination on Mt. Tamalpais. creek as the water flows past you. The wet weather reduced the number of hikers. We saw only 19 people in the nine miles of hiking on a Sunday starting at 10:30 a.m. Nearly half of those were in the last couple of miles of when re-approaching the Cascade Falls Trailhead. Punch in “Cascade Canyon Open Space Preserve” to access this trailhead. There is also access to the trail off of the Fairfax-Bolinas Road for a quicker route to Carson Falls. A small amount of water creates Cascade Falls even now during a drought. The trail turns into a red dirt road along the Cascade Canyon Fire Road. The hike goes uphill with 2,100 feet in elevation gain throughout the day. Pine Mountain Road becomes a rocky gravel road. After stretches without tree cover, you’ll find some shade on the Carson Falls trail.

articles.text: I signed up for the Idioterod, I did. Now I wish I’d rode Idiot Airways instead. My huskies didn’t mush, but ran away. I wish I looked up the correct spelling. Iditarod is with and A, unlike any of my grades in cool weather self-preservation school. I suppose if I freeze I’ll be preserved well indeed. And to think, it’s just me. All the dogs ran home free, thankfully they are not stuck in this mound Of snow, sleet, ice, slush, powder and more snow. I must have been mentally sidetracked, and so went my sled. I headed off course, headed north, north, norse. But here come some funny looking deer and a warm coat of red held by little green men, so near. I may be losing my mind, but I think my saviors I did find. Go with the green men I shall; now we do fly. And I know not why but as I leave the snow With joy I yell out, “Ho! Ho! Ho!”
articles.title: Stranded Nick’s First Flight

articles.text: Show includes hundreds of paper puppets Cal Performances, as part of its Performances at Home series, will stream Manual Cinema’s Christmas Carol starting tomorrow until Saturday, December 19. The inventive company has created a new production tailored specifically for home viewing. The story follows “an avowed holiday skeptic,” Aunt Trudy, who has been tasked with presenting her family’s annual Christmas Carol puppet show from the isolation of her studio apartment – over a Zoom call while the family celebrates Christmas Eve under lockdown. But as Trudy becomes more absorbed in her own version of the story, the puppets take on a life of their own, and the famiA scene from Manuel Cinema’s Christmas Carol. ly’s holiday call transforms into a stunning cinematic adaptation of Dickens’ classic ghost story. Manual Cinema’s production features hundreds of paper puppets, miniatures, silhouettes, and an original music score performed live. Pricing for individual Cal Performances at Home is on an honor system. To purchase tickets, visit https://calperformances. org/events/2020-21/at-home/manual-cinema-a-christmas-carol/.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is presenting an archival performance of A Midsummer Night’s Dream available online from January 21 through February 10. Choreographer George Balanchine’s classic ballet, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, is part of San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season, and will be performed in Program 1. The ballet, one of the company’s most well-known, is a Shakespearean favorite making its triumphant return to San Francisco after its run in 2020 was cut short due to COVID. This 1962 work by Balanchine, to music by Felix Mendelssohn, was his first original full-length ballet and quickly was hailed as a masterpiece. Balanchine loved the original play – he could recite large parts of it in Russian – so the ballet sticks close to its inspiration, telling the story of four lost lovers in the woods, as well as of a royal fairy court made up of Queen Titania, King Oberon, and the mischievous Puck. To obtain tickets to this digital event, visit https://www.sfballet. org/tickets/2021-season/. articles.text: Join Musaics of the Bay for a cross-continental celebration of the New Year, filmed in Salzburg, Austria, one of the capitals of the world for classical music. The New Year’s celebration is part of Musaics of the Bay’s “Stay-at-Home Symposium,” a series of broadcasts featuring music premieres based on the creativity of community members. It is a collaboration among composers, performers, artists of all types, and community members near and far. To date, the series has featured artists from Wales, Greece, Holland, and now, Austria. Musaics is partnering with Salzburg artists, including pianist Andrei Gologan, composer and violinist Luke Hsu, and cellist Simon Tetzlaff. The program features works by Beethoven, Kodaly, Schumann, and Luke Hsu, whose Pianist Andrei Gologan new composition was inspired by “Homage to Edmundo” by painter Darril Tighe. The concert will be recorded in High Definition and will livestream on Saturday, January 2, at 11 a.m. PST. articles.text: World-renowned mezzo-soprano Susan Graham leads the cast of Opera San Jose’s first fully staged digital production. Three Decembers, based on playwright Terrence McNally’s unpublished play Some Christmas Letters, and written by Bay Area composer Jake Heggie, stars world-renowned mezzo soprano Susan Graham. It will be conducted by Christopher James Ray, and directed by Tara Branham. The opera was first presented under the working title “Last Acts” at its world premiere by the Houston Grand Opera. A 10-instrument chamber orchestra included two pianos played by Heggie and Patrick Summers, who also conducted the performance in Houston. The 90-minute chamber opera explores a family’s struggle to understand one another. The three parts of the opera are set in the month of December in the years 1986, 1996, and 2006. Three Decembers follows the story of a famous actress, Madeline Mitchell, in a role sung by Graham. Two adult children, Beatrice and Charlie, are portrayed by Opera San Jose Resident Artists Maya Kherani and Efrain Solis. Graham will be making her company debut at Opera San Jose as Madeline, reuniting with composer Heggie, who created the role of Sister Helen in Dead Man Walking specifically for her. Three Decembers began streaming on December 3 and will continue through the end of the month. It will feature a virtual post-show conversation with Graham, Heggie, and the full artistic team. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The New York Fashion industry. What comes to mind? Haute couture? Runways with tall, thin models draped in clothes that will never appear on any street, in any city, other than New York? Are creators of fashion involved in a headlong pursuit of the frivolous, far removed from life as most people live it? Or is fashion design as much an engine of creativity as any art form? After all, aren’t the ripples of its designs felt, however obliquely, in all of the clothes we choose to wear? A blouse by any other name – Prada, Gucci, Karan, Ford, Klein – is still a blouse. Right? Well, yes and no. But what is the connection between the industry and those sweatshops where people labor over sewing machines, stitching the garments that appear at shows and on the cover of major magazines? The documentary The September Issue, which is about fashion, does not address any of those questions. It does, however, offer an interesting glimpse behind the scenes of Vogue, the most influential fashion magazine being produced today. And the film draws an interesting portrait of its editor-in-chief, Anna Wintour, high priestess of fashion, examining how she marshals her large staff of designers, editors and photographers in a complex effort to produce the September issue, a signature fashion tome the size of a city phone book, weighing some four pounds. The September Issue is revelatory, but not as might be anticipated. It actually morphs into a character study of Wintour’s creative director, Grace Coddington, who has been with Wintour for more than 20 years. While Wintour is meticulously coiffed and dressed, Coddington, who walks the corridors of high fashion, is all but frumpy, her hair flaming-red, wild, her face deeply lined, her dresses shapeless, shod in practical sandals. She’s the antithesis of Vogue. She is also a strong woman with strong points of view and is fearless in her willingness to confront Wintour. Yet these two women have an alliance that is unwavering, sharing a mission to produce a stunningly beautiful magazine, Anna Wintour, Bee Shaffer and Karl Lagerfeld in The September Issue. Anna Wintour in The September Issue. Vera Wang and André Leon Talley in The September Issue. as rich in color and design as the styles that appear in its pages. The film is also a study of work. How people of far ranging abilities and egos and quirks manage to collaborate as the day of the magazine’s release draws ever nearer. The world of work is high fashion, Byzantine, intricate, the magazine unparalleled; yet the dynamics are essentially the same in any work place where people must co-exist in pursuit of a goal. The September Issue. Documentary. With Anna Wintour and Grace Coddington. Directed by R. J. Cutler. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG-13. Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: The city of Genova. on Italy’s northwestern coast, is a fabulously wealthy city. It was the birthplace of the explorer Christopher Columbus and violinist Niccolò Paganini. As you walk along Corso Garibaldi you can see some of those beautiful palaces. One of them is now Genoa’s City Hall. Its most famous piece of art is the Guarnerius violin of Paganini. Just down the street is an equally beautiful palace, but no one goes there. In its archives are the strings of Paganini‘s magic violin. The strings have a story to tell, one blessed by music and magic. Long ago in ancient Egypt, a music loving pharaoh had a harp made for him, but it was not just any old harp. This one was truly special – it was made of pure silver. The pharaoh made sure this particular harp was special and had it blessed by all of his priests. Some time later the great Jewish king, King David, obtained this special harp. And with it he sang his immortal songs. When the Romans put down the Jewish rebellion, they stole the harp and brought it to Rome. Emperor Nero became enamored with the harp. It was really this silver harp that he played and not that silly story of him fiddling on a violin while Rome burned. The harp remained in Italy and eventually became the instrument of the great operatic castrato FariPortait of young Niccolò Paganini nelli. Since Farinelli did not have any children, he gave the harp to a woman who was a brilliant noblewoman and socialite. She liked money more than she liked music and had the harp melted down and made into silver coins. After she died, her possessions were sold at auction. The most prominent Italian maker of violin strings went to the auction where he purchased a bag of silver coins. He used the silver to make some special violin strings for the great Paganini, and with these strings Paganini enchanted the world. After his death in 1840, Paganini requested that his violin be sent to Genoa. It is proudly displayed in the City Hall. The strings from that violin are in another palace down the street but are hidden from public view – silent once again. And now you know the entire story. Genoa City Hall

articles.text: Film directors Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht. No one at Camp Jened could’ve imagined that those summers in the woods together would be the beginnings of a revolution. Just down the road from Woodstock, Camp Jened was a camp for disabled teens. Directors Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht deliver a rousing film about a group of campers turned activists who shaped the future of the disability rights movement and changed accessibility legislation for everyone. Filled with the spirit, music, and humor of the era, Newnham and LeBrecht speak firsthand to the seeds of empowerment that were planted at Camp Jened. Footage from 1971 captures how the campers were finally seen beyond their disabilities. Milestones in the disability-rights movement intersect with LeBrecht’s personal story and the stories of several Camp Jened alums, including then-counselor Judy Heumann. She went on to play an indispensable role in historic protests leading to the Americans with Disabilities Act. Crip Camp shines a bright light on an overlooked civil-rights battle. Crip Camp acquires breadth and seriousness that neither its early scenes nor its playfully confrontational title suggest. As we follow campers into direct actions, occupations and unsparing encounters with government officials, the film’s approach remains anecdotal and emotional. Footage of a twenty-something Judy Heumann reproaching Eugene Eidenberg from the U.S. Department of Health is a master class in focused, righteous rage. Heumann went on to advise Presidents Clinton and Obama. Crip Camp opened the Sundance Film Festival and took home the Audience Award as Best Documentary. The film was produced by Barack and Michelle Obama under their production company Higher Ground. Join the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity film series on Zoom on January 7 from 5-6 p.m. with a screening and moderated discussion followed by a Q and A with co-directors LeBrecht and Newnham. For more information see the website www.diversityfilmseries. org for the January 7 event Zoom link. Or contact Julie at 510 599- 9227 (julie@diversityfilmseries. org). The Appreciating Film Series is co-sponsored by the Piedmont City Council, Piedmont Adult School, Piedmont Anti-Racism Diversity Committee, and the League of Women Voters Piedmont.

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Pom Poko. Movie review by Chris Honoré Pom Poko is a strange, convoluted film, perhaps best suited for teens and adults. And even then its audience may indeed be those who have find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that has, for decades, been the signature of Studio Ghibli. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poko is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. However, the weakness of Pom Poko resides not with its art, but in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine, thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog, with huge pouches. These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting wherein they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals. The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, on the outskirts of Tokyo, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes some 30 years later when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the war-like chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Pom Poko. tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous, often lack focus, and are, on occasion, leavened by slapstick and light-hearted fantasy. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and even kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. It’s a spectacle, a somewhat grim tale, leading to a dour denouement which sums up what proves to be a not family friendly fable framed by bizarre moments that can only be described as culturally curious. Pom Poko (1994), Animé from Studio Ghibli. Directed by Isao Takahata. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Spirit of the American City (https://catherineburns.com/ spirit) is an online exhibit by Catherine Burns Fine Art that invites viewers to explore early 20th century prints through the perspective of period photography. See what the artists saw. Understand their inspiration. View them as a social time capsule while admiring the mastery of these revered printmakers. What makes this show special? This is the first time that original prints have been paired with related videos and historic photographs. From a private East Coast collection, these outstanding prints are by a wide range of well-known WPA period printmakers, including Edward Hopper, George Bellows, Charles Sheeler, Benton Spruance and Childe Hassam. Every print has been researched in detail and is accompanied by a mix of vintage photos, historic videos and news articles that give hints to what led the artists to capture that specific image in time. Not just for collectors This is a show for all to enjoy and is a breath of fresh air. Launched on November 20 to a select group, the show has received rave reviews from leading print experts: “The feedback from the show has been extraordinary,” said Burns, a 35-year veteran in the art world. “The inspiration for the show was to find a way to make hundred-yearold prints a momentary escape from the doom and gloom of the pandemic. A love letter to the artists and the cities that inspired them.” The show is online and free to the public at https://catherineburns.com/spirit. It is best enjoyed on a large screen. All of the featured prints are for sale. Catherine Burns has been a dealer in fine prints and drawings for more than 30 years and specializes in both American and European prints from the 19th and early 20th centuries. She launched her business after serving as the Curator of the art museums at University of Massachusetts, Amherst and Washington University in St. Louis. A founding member of the International Fine Print Dealers Association, Burns exhibits at national and international art fairs. To view her gallery and for more information, contact her at info@catherineburns.com, or call 510-654-7910.

articles.text: Once a city has imaginative architects and designers working with receptive owners and skilled craftsmen, the result is often the creation of what I am referring to as design “punctuation points”. Walking around Piedmont it is easy to come across examples of punctuation that add so much interest and personality to all parts of our city. At the core of their work, all of the design professions balance the combination of functional requirements with an aesthetic concept. You may be familiar with the famous maxim, “Form follows function.” attributed to the influential Chicago architect Louis Sullivan in 1896. Because there are of course many different attitudes towards aesthetics and decoration (Form), this famous maxim has been interpreted, reinterpreted and argued over for generations. In the aesthetic half of the equation there are time-tested rules of order that make for appealing designs. But, as we have discussed in previous columns, there are also exceptions to every design norm, and often these exceptions are, well, exceptional! They can provide surprisingly wonderful results that, even though different and even sometimes contradictory, can punctuate the main design and contribute greatly to the spirit and visual character of our built environment. In my experience these punctuation points can be planned during the design phase, but also are sometimes created during construction, often necessitated by unforeseen construction complications requiring resolution, or the unavailability of a specified item, or even a sudden design inspiration. Sometimes they result from the suggestion of the owners, or the ingenuity of the craftsmen on the job. Hearst Castle is filled with what we are talking about: William Randolph Hearst coming across some incredible ceiling or artifact on his European travels, buying it and shipping it to California, and then letting his architect Julia Morgan incorporate it, in the field, into the design. The results of course are world famous. I also think the ideas for these Two examples of design punctuation are shown. One is a result of carefully studied resolution of complex roof connections, the other a creative and fun way of adding daylight with circular clerestory windows. Both are made into features on these beautiful homes. Also note the weather vane which enhances and completes the circular building form! articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on December 7, with 14 readers on the call to discuss Jane Austen’s classic novel, Pride and Prejudice. Some members of the group also read Longbourn by Jo Baker, which describes events in Pride and Prejudice from the perspectives of the house servants. Participating in the discussion were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Alicia Rivera, Jeri Lockhart, Margie Blodgett, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The group was also pleased to welcome first time participant Bill Blackwell. Pride and Prejudice, a romantic novel, was first published in 1813. Austen set the story at the turn of the 19th century, and it follows the main character, Elizabeth Bennet, as she deals with issues of manners, upbringing, morality, education, and marriage in the society of the landed gentry of Britain. articles.text: As the year draws to a close, it’s fair to say that we’ve all learned something about the social, political, physical and environmental forces that have affected everyone. In some ways our lives will be changed, perhaps permanently. But as an investor, what lessons can you learn from 2020? Here are some to consider: • Markets look ahead Here’s something many investors discovered in 2020: Investment prices don’t always move in the same direction as the overall economy. This might not have seemed apparent right after the COVID-19 pandemic struck in mid-February, as the overall economy and the stock market took big hits. But just about five weeks later, the markets began a rally that lasted several months. During this time, the economy also recovered somewhat, but still remains on weak footing. What can explain this discrepancy between the markets and economic activity? Essentially, economic numbers, such as the unemployment rate and gross domestic product (GDP), reflect what’s happening today, but the markets are always looking toward tomorrow, which means they are anticipating a stronger economic recovery and the results that come with it, such as greater corporate earnings in 2021. No one can say for sure what the future holds, but you can usually know the market’s opinion by its performance. • Opportunities will always exist for investors Although the coronavirus seems unprecedented, the equity markets have rebounded from many crises before it. From war to global financial meltdowns, the market has seen it all. But even at the height of these events, when the markets might be most affected, individual segments or industries can do well. For example, in the current environment, when many people have been forced to work and shop from home, and get their entertainment online, it’s probably not surprising that some parts of the technology sector have seen their economic activity grow, along with their stock prices. Here’s the key point: Investment opportunities always exist, especially in times of market stress – and smart investors will find them and incorporate them into their portfolios in a way that’s appropriate for their goals and risk tolerance. • Patience and discipline can pay dividends As mentioned above, the stock market dropped sharply in the weeks immediately following the pandemic, but then gained steadily for months afterward. Investors who tried to “cut losses” and exited the market likely did so at the wrong time and missed out on the beginning of the upturn. Unfortunately, this is not uncommon; investors who overreact to market declines often find themselves on the investment sidelines just when a new rally begins. Rather than being reactive in this way, you may be better off sticking with a longterm investment strategy, and buying and selling investments only when it makes sense for your situation, such as when you need to diversify your portfolio. For many reasons, it’s unlikely that we’ll see anything exactly like 2020 again. But some of the investment lessons we learned are applicable in every year – so keep them in mind for 2021 and beyond. May writes delicately of the struggles of life and the ways we may be able to prepare ourselves for such times.” —Emma Warren, Oblong Books & Music, Millerton, NY A Wealth of Pigeons: A Cartoon Collection by Steve Martin, Harry Bliss (Illus.), Celadon Books “Sharp wit, silly observations, clever art — Martin and Bliss offer up not just the perfect holiday gift, but perhaps the perfect antidote to 2020.” —Melissa Fox, Watermark Books & Café, Wichita, KS The Burning God (The Poppy War #3) by R.F. Kuang Harper Voyager “The ending ripped my heart from my chest, but I can’t imagine a more satisfying conclusion for this phenomenal trilogy. A perfect triad of books.” —Ava Tusek, Second Star to the Right, Denver, CO Before the Coffee Gets Cold by Toshikazu Kawaguchi Hanover Square Press “This was the most interesting and wholesome take on time travel I have ever read. There are some rules in order to time travel, but my favorite one? You can only stay in the past for as long as your coffee is warm.” —Lauren Suidgeest, Schuler Books, Grand Rapids, MI The Star-Crossed Sisters of Tuscany by Lori Nelson Spielman, Berkley “Three second-born daughters take a life-changing trip to Italy in hopes of breaking the family Wintering: The Power of Rest and Retreat in Difficult Times by Katherine May was selected as the number one pick by American independent booksellers for the month of December. curse dooming all second-born daughters in their family to never find love.” —Kathy Morrison, Newtown Bookshop, Newtown, PA Big Girl, Small Town by Michelle Gallen, Algonquin Books “You’ll most fall in love with Majella O’Neill, the narrator. She is unapologetically and completely herself, and unlike anyone I’ve met in fiction before. ” —Robert McDonald, The Book Stall, Winnetka, IL Oak Flat: A Fight for Sacred Land in the American West by Lauren Redniss, Random House “Vibrant illustrations and careful curation of competing voices convey the high stakes while honoring the dignity of the people on both sides, and the dignity of the natural world. This book is an astonishing achievement.” —Keith Mosman, Powell’s Books, Portland, OR Eartheater by Dolores Reyes, Julia Sanches (Transl.), HarperVia “The main character’s compulsion to eat earth felt visceral, the writing enigmatically lyrical. I couldn’t put it down, yet I had to force myself to absorb this book painfully slowly, so as to not let it pass me by.” —Tori-Lynn Bell, House of Books, Kent, CT

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Dear Abby: I’m not sure every family is like ours, but we love to sing at Christmas. I’m sending along a doggy carol that I thought your dog lovers might have fun singing to the neighbors as they carol on a dog walk. Doggy White Christmas I’m dreaming of a slow squirrel… One I could catch and make my toy… Or a lovely shoe That I could chew would add greatly to my joy. I’m dreaming of a dog biscuit... Tall as a house and twice as wide... Little toys that squeak And kids that shriek And huge bones make of rawhide. I’m dreaming of a long walkie… One where I choose where I will go... Greeting doggie friends Sniffing both ends Our tails wagging to and fro. I’m dreaming of a soft pillow… all to myself and end of day ... Where I snore the evening away Storing energy for doggie play. Dear Ariel and Peanut: We love to sing at Christmas, too. Maybe not on key, but we do try. Thanks for sending these yips and yaps. –Abby Dear Abby: We would really like to have a rescue dog but I’ve checked with all the dog shelters and they are, fortunately, overwhelmed by people adopting strays. Somehow we keep missing out. Would any of your readers happen to have a dog that needs a loving home? We have two cats, Mortimer and Nemo, and we both had a number of dogs growing up. I am a caregiver in Piedmont and my partner is a physical therapist working in an assisted living home in Berkeley. He grew up in Piedmont and we now live nearby and have a nice backyard. We would prefer a dog under 50 pounds, a female, but a male might work too. Bone-tired of life without a dog, –Eve and Jacob Dear Eve and Jacob: Oh Eve, we feel your pain. Calling all Piedmonters: Does anyone have a dog that needs a loving family? Here’s a wonderful couple that is ready to give some lucky dog a life changing opportunity. We know you and Jacob will make terrific dog parents, and the cats will certainly help with your training and welcoming new paws into your home. If anyone knows of a needy dog, please send a note to Eve at E.ratches@gmail.com. Keep your paws crossed! –Abby Dear Abby: Have you seen the new Happy Hanukkah video on Instagram? Hamilton star Daveed Digs sings
articles.title: A “Doggy” White Christmas

pages.text: Wednesday, December 16, 2020 25 Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets A “Doggy” White Christmas By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: I’m not sure every family is like ours, but we love to sing at Christmas. I’m sending along a doggy carol that I thought your dog lovers might have fun singing to the neighbors as they carol on a dog walk. Doggy White Christmas I’m dreaming of a slow squirrel… One I could catch and make my toy… Or a lovely shoe That I could chew would add greatly to my joy. I’m dreaming of a dog biscuit... Tall as a house and twice as wide... Little toys that squeak And kids that shriek And huge bones make of rawhide. I’m dreaming of a long walkie… One where I choose where I will go... Greeting doggie friends Sniffing both ends Our tails wagging to and fro. I’m dreaming of a soft pillow… all to myself and end of day ... Where I snore the evening away Storing energy for doggie play. Dear Ariel and Peanut: We love to sing at Christmas, too. Maybe not on key, but we do try. Thanks for sending these yips and yaps. –Abby Dear Abby: We would really like to have a rescue dog but I’ve checked with all the dog shelters and they are, fortunately, overwhelmed by people adopting strays. Somehow we keep missing out. Would any of your readers happen to have a dog that needs a loving home? We have two cats, Mortimer and Nemo, and we both had a number of dogs growing up. I am a caregiver in Piedmont and my partner is a physical therapist working in an assisted living home in Berkeley. He grew up in Piedmont and we now live nearby and have a nice backyard. We would prefer a dog under 50 pounds, a female, but a male might work too. Bone-tired of life without a dog, –Eve and Jacob Dear Eve and Jacob: Oh Eve, we feel your pain. Calling all Piedmonters: Does anyone have a dog that needs a loving family? Here’s a wonderful couple that is ready to give some lucky dog a life changing opportunity. We know you and Jacob will make terrific dog parents, and the cats will certainly help with your training and welcoming new paws into your home. If anyone knows of a needy dog, please send a note to Eve at E.ratches@gmail.com. Keep your paws crossed! –Abby Dear Abby: Have you seen the new Happy Hanukkah video on Instagram? Hamilton star Daveed Digs sings a new Hanukkah song - Puppy for Hanukkah. It’s pure puppy fun. You can also watch the funny video version on the Disney Channel every day until December 18, the last day of Hanukkah. Diggs reminds us of how we can win the Hanukkah lottery and celebrate the blessings of this sweet holiday of light with a super surprise. Kol ha’kavod Daveed! -Tina and Butch the Boxer Dear Tina and Butch: Wow, is that great! We have watched it several times. Daveed Digs’ voice is magical, and of course, we are crazy about puppies. You also reminded me to go back and watch him in the movie Blindspotting. Thanks for sending this total treat and taking us to a happy place. All respect to Daveed! Happy and yappy Hanukkah to all! L’Chaim to life. –Abby Dear Abby: What is the best diet to relieve diarrhea? Do I have to go the vet? I’m losing my appetite and my stomach is surly, –Bennet and Bernie the Old English Sheep Dog Dear Bennet and Bernie: Well, you can never go wrong visiting the vet. However, a diet of boiled chicken (preferably white meat) and rice, along with a little canned pumpkin swirled in, and a touch of chicken broth often seems to settle things down. But if the diarrhea persists, you definitely need to get checked and see if antibiotics are necessary. Sometimes we just eat the wrong things off the sidewalk. –Abby Send your dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at Melandogs@gmail.com. Nominations will Nominations are currently being accepted for the 28th annual Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame, honoring exceptional women who make a difference in their communities county-wide. Honorees will be celebrated in 2021 during an event co-hosted by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors and the Alameda County Commission on the Status of Women. The Women’s Hall of Fame is now accepting nominations in 13 categories: Business and Professions; Community Service; Culture and Art; Education; Emerging Leader; Environment; Health; Justice; Non-Traditional Careers; Philanthropy; Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics; Sports and Athletics; and Youth Services. You can nominate a community leader in be open year-round. The inductee should be established in her career or volunteerism with significant achievements that have benefited communities in Alameda County, should be successful in overcoming personal and professional obstacles, and is a role model for youth and women who strive to achieve their own success. More than 250 women have been inducted into the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame since its inception in 1993. In addition to honoring exceptional women leaders from Alameda County, the annual event raises funds for youth scholarships and supports local nonprofit community partners serving women, youth and families. “As we honor the remarkable 13 inductees, we also celebrate the 100th anniversary of the 19th Amendment [of the U.S. Constitution], guaranteeing and protecting women’s constitutional right to vote,” stated County Administrator Susan S. Muranishi. “In the past 100 years we have seen women become mayors, governors, Congresswomen, and now elected as Vice President of the United States of America. We commend the trailblazing women who came before us and make way for female pioneers to lead us through the next 100 years.” You can watch this year’s Hall of Fame ceremony and learn more about the honorees at: https:// www.classy.org/campaign/2020- alameda-county-womens-hall-offame/c298882. The date for the 2021 event will be determined after inductees are chosen early next year. articles.text: things mostly come quickly and intuitively – in order to enhance a certain design condition of a building, or to relieve the too regular rhythm of a landscape concept, or simply to satisfy the whimsey of the designer or craftsman. Certainly, this can be overdone. If there are many punctuation points, they are devalued and the design can end up chaotic – and labeled with the dreaded tag, “over-designed”. But a lack of punctuation on the other hand can result in what is all too common in much of new construction: a bland sameness, without interest or individuality. When done correctly, design punctuation points can be wonderful – a welcome addition to a building, landscape or street, with charm, texture, life, and character often the invaluable result. Next: Signage and lighting Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached at Will@MakingDesignSense.com The Arroyo Ave Ivy Arch! Fashioned on a utility and support pole, this whimsical landscape punctuation point is a delight, and who knows, may be a portal to another dimension? This very simple arrangement of carefully shaped perennial plants (topiary) is an incredibly beautiful and effective punctuation, enlivening the whole street.

Muranishi. “In the past 100 years we have seen women become mayors, governors, Congresswomen, and now elected as Vice President of the United States of America. articles.text: Serge Saxonov, the new owner of 121 Scenic Avenue received approval from the Piedmont Planning Commission to convert a tennis court to a 3300 square foot addition to the home. “We purchased the property because it can accommodate our four children, who range in age from newborn to 15 years old,” he told the commission. “We are excited to make 121 Scenic our home.” Saxonov will demolish an existing, detached garage at the northwest corner of the property, and remove a tennis court in the rear yard in order to construct a 3,357-square-foot, two-story rear addition. Architect Robert Pennell of Jarvis Architects noted that the privacy between neighbors will be maintained through landscaping, and that additions are all to the north of neighboring properties, so there “will be no view, light, or sunshine impacts.” Pennell added that there are options regarding the construction plan, scheduling, and demolition of the tennis court that will be done with minimal disturbance to the shared driveway. “The demolished concrete will be recycled on-site,” he said. The applicant also requested to make var ious inter ior changes, including the addition of four bedrooms and door and exterior lighting modifications throughout. The request included the addition of skylights, various site improvements in the rear yard including a sport court that also serves as a vehicle turnaround area, fence modifications, an arbor, terraced patios, retaining walls, and landscape areas. Com missioner Jonathan Levine said that some aspects of the design troubled him, including “adding an entirely new house where no house previously existed, on a lot which already [has] a house.” “I don’t think the applicants have done enough to address neighbors’ concerns, frankly,” he added. Commissioner Rani Batra said the design of the proposed additions were “lovely,” but she echoed Levine’s concerns. “[The proposal would] take valued privacy and buffered space away from neighbors on all sides, and needs to be scaled back,” she said. The design review passed 3-2, with additional modifications, with commissioners Batra and Levine dissenting. The project was approved with 24 conditions of approval. articles.text: her first city council meeting, then offered to nominate Rood. This was seconded by McCarthy. Because of the unique situation of two councilmembers being nominated for the position, City Attorney Michelle Kenyon, who was present, clarified that the council must first consider the nomination of Cavenaugh. If that motion did not pass, then the council would move to the second nomination of Rood, and then a motion and vote would be taken for that. A majority vote was needed to appoint a vice mayor. “This should not be a popularity contest. What I like about our tradition is that it is not a popularity contest among councilmembers, it’s the most votes,” Andersen reiterated. She added that her nomination for King as mayor followed that tradition. In response, McCarthy said that she would “absolutely welcome a conversation about the process,” but that she did not see a current one that was workable. Cavenaugh said that the meeting was supposed to be a “fairly straightforward session based on a long-established tradition,” and that the city did in fact have a clear process. “In the past, our vice mayor has always been the person next in line to be mayor, who is also the person with the greatest seniority at that time. When [there are] two people who have that, we look at the vote count,” she said. This would naturally leave a councilmember “out,” who would not have a chance to serve as mayor or vice mayor. “When we talk about vote count, what that really reflects is the will of the voters,” Cavenaugh added. McCarthy, in response to the tradition of top vote-getting, said that a “vote for council is not a vote for mayor.” She said that she did not want to move forward with the nomination of Cavenaugh with the information presented by her colleagues. The motion to nominate Cavenaugh failed, 2-2. McCarthy and King dissented. Discussion on the nomination of Rood, who was not present for the agenda item due to a work conflict, then transpired. Had Rood been there and voted for himself to take the position, the nomination would have passed 3-2 without conflict. Andersen acknowledged Rood’s qualifications but stayed firm in her stance on sticking to tradition. Cavenaugh suggested exploring one-year mayoral and vice mayoral terms in the future, but also stayed firm in her decision. King reiterated that she felt it was her responsibility to hear Rood’s stance, because he had explicitly expressed an interest in the position. “I want to let him have the chance to make his case, and from my perspective, [the council] owes him that,” she said. The motion to nominate Rood also failed, 2-2, with Andersen and Cavenaugh dissenting. Andersen then nominated a shared vice mayorship, “whereby Rood is vice mayor for one year, and we have Cavenaugh as vice mayor for the second year.” “This might be an elegant solution to the position we find ourselves in this evening,” she offered. McCarthy agreed, saying it was a good solution. King seconded Andersen’s motion, and the motion passed 3-1, with Cavenaugh opposing. Little discussion followed Andersen’s motion. The vote means that immediately following Rood’s one-year tenure as vice mayor, which starts this month, Cavenaugh would take over the position. The only written indication of a process in city code states that, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and ViceMayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” During the December 7 meeting, councilmember Andersen suggested making the process more concrete. If the newly configured city council decides to do so, it would be the first written guidelines in the city for selecting a vice mayor.

articles.text: The three orphaned Oakland Zoo mountain lions made it safely to their new home at the Columbus Zoo in Ohio on December 2. The three cubs, one male and two females, are at the Zoo’s Animal Health Center and are completing the standard, mandatory quarantine period for the next few weeks. The Columbus Zoo team has reported that all three are adjusting nicely. “The Columbus Zoo is proud Photo courtesy of Columbus Zoo to collaborate with Oakland Zoo and offer a home to these cubs, who will reside in the Zoo’s North America region. Oakland Zoo staff has provided the Columbus Zoo team with the opportunity to name the two female cubs, and the Columbus Zoo will announce the cubs’ names in the coming weeks,” the zoo said in a statement. The male cub was given the name Captain Cal by Oakland Zoo workers after it was rescued by firefighters in the August Complex fire in August.
articles.title: Once-orphaned Oakland Zoo mountain lion cubs arrive at Columbus Zoo

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, December 16, 2020 Tree Lot Continued from page 1 Council to sell out its supply of Christmas trees in the U.S. for six years. The sales went so fast that this week in the Scouting office, the phone has been ringing off the hook with people still looking to get a tree, according to Laural Fawcett, Registrar of the Council. A heart-warming tree lot tale comes from the Markopoulos family. “We weren’t planning on getting a tree this year due to the upside-down world, but Nikolas [my son] was super bummed and sent me and my husband photos of our last three trees that we got at the Scout Lot. He also said he wanted a bit of normalcy. His persuasion speech worked,” said Karen Marokolpouos. For first year tree lot supervisor Bill Murphy, this year was a resounding success. Volunteer and former Scout lot organizer David Ashton was instrumental in getting the tree lot operating this year. “It was hard for the Scouts to achieve approval to operate this year. It was a very difficult year to operate successfully. It was a high financial risk due to COVID, but we were successful,” said David Ashton, who orders the trees each year. “It’s my hope we brought some comfort to our community during the holidays, particularly in this time of great stress,” he said. The Markopoulos family’s beautiful Noble Fir purchased from the Piedmont Scout Lot, decorated by scouting sons Theo, 11th grade, Nikolas, 8th grade, and parents Kirk and Karen.
