articles.text: Bob McBain, Betsy Andersen, and Teddy Gray King Bob McBain termed out as Mayor of Piedmont at Monday night’s City Council meeting, December 7. He officially handed over the title to former Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King. McBain said that he was confident in the financial state of the city as outgoing mayor, the result of vigorous work for the duration of his 8-1/2 years on council. He also pointed to advanced public safety, city technology services set in place by his predecessor, and ongoing infrastructure projects as important elements of his time on the council. He commended city staff and councilmembers for having discussions that are focused on bringing the community together, and for it to be a more inclusive environment for everyone. “Staff and council recognize that a lot has changed in the community, and a lot continues to change. Our residents have different expectations and needs. That’s the challenge ahead – how to do that and retain the identity of a community that many of us have known for a long time. “I’m confident in the intelligence of staff, who will use that as a good challenge,” he said. In reflecting on his term as mayor, McBain sentimentally but humorously pointed to his daughter’s 5th grade yearbook at Havens Elementary School as a “benchmark.” The year was 2003. “I needed some kind of benchmark. [The yearbook is] courtesy of my daughter Liz, who gave this to me and said it’s a very good way to evaluate what you’ve done as mayor,” he said with a grin. – Former Piedmont Mayor Dean Barbieri Mayor McBain departs...........1 City tree lights on ..............1 Letters..............................2 COVID Report......................3 In praise of R. They included: ban homework, give a pet to each class, host monthly school carnival days, lower taxes, make houses cheaper, and make the town bigger. “It looks like it’s not going so well for me here,” McBain laughed. “I talked to [Public Works Director] Chester [Nakahara] a long time ago about moving our borders a little into Oakland every year. Over time, we’d have quite a bit of space, and they may not notice.” McBain thanked his colleagues whom he worked alongside during his tenure as mayor. He quoted Bill Gates in closing: “You may have the best plans, best strategies, but if you don’t have the right people, it just won’t happen.” “It all comes down to the people you work with,” McBain added. “Well, I think we have the right people – the right people on council, the right people on staff, and more importantly, in the community.”
articles.title: Bob McBain reflects on role as mayor at final City Council meeting

articles.text: The annual Piedmont Tree Lighting ceremony took place on the first Wednesday of December, as is its tradition dating back 56 years. But in the Year of Covid, it was changed from a live event to a virtual celebration. Residents were asked not to gather to watch the tree-lighting in person, but to watch it on KCOM (Channel 27), the city’s TV station. Speakers recorded their parts separately, which were then edited together for continuity. Speakers included Mayor Bob McBain, City Administrator Sara Lillevand, Piedmont Beautification Foundation president Gayle Lambert, and former foundation president Patty Siskind. Music was performed by the Piedmont High School Troubadours; The Troubadour vocalists also recorded their individual parts at home. “Given this last year, I doubt there are any years where it’s more important for us to celebrate our holiday season and to recognize and celebrate our traditions,” said McBain, who ends service as a member of City Council after eight and half years. McBain added that the ceremony would not be possible without the work of volunteers from many city organizations, including the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, which has helped organize and lead the ceremony for more than 50 years, and the Piedmont Garden Club. “Although I fully expect to come next year and watch it, this is the last time for me to preside [over the tree-lighting]. I want to say how grateful I am to the community for the support and the opportunity that they have given me to serve on the city council, and to serve as mayor for these past three years,” he said. “I have never been prouder to be mayor

articles.text: At a scheduled Piedmont City Council meeting on Monday, December 7, what was expected to be a purely ceremonial meeting thanking outgoing Mayor Bob McBain for his service to the city became quite unexpectedly – and suddenly – a protracted discussion over changing a longstanding unwritten agreement on who serves as vice mayor. Councilmembers initially approved former Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King as the city’s new mayor for two years but devolved into a heated discussion of the process used to select a vice mayor. Council members ultimately voted to have Tim Rood, now entering his sixth year on council, as vice mayor for the current year (2020-21), and council member Jen Cavanaugh as vice mayor for the following year, 2021-22. In Piedmont, the positions of mayor and vice mayor are chosen among city councilmembers. According to city code, “following each general municipal election, the City Council shall elect from among its member officers of the City who shall have the titles of Mayor and Vice-Mayor, each of whom shall serve at the pleasure of the Council.” King was chosen to be the mayor of Piedmont for the next two years, without objection. She accepted the nomination by her peers, and recognized the newest addition to council, Conna McCarthy, as well as the re-election of incumbent Cavenaugh. “Between the two of them, [McCarthy and Cavenaugh] they have so many years of dedicated volunteerism to the city of Piedmont,” King said. Rood was not present for the discussion of vice mayor apparently due to a work schedule conflict. Because of this, King, in her role as mayor, moved to choose a vice mayor at the next council meeting, December 21. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon confirmed that council could, by a consensus, choose to revisit the item at a later meeting. Cavenaugh, the top vote getter in 2016, said that her preference was to move forward with a nomination of vice mayor, so that the next meeting’s agenda could pertain strictly to business items. Andersen agreed, saying it would be “odd not to precede with the agenda item,” and that the tradition would be to nominate Cavenaugh to the role. New councilmember McCarthy favored delaying the decision. “I would prefer that we have opportunities for full discussion with all members when we’re talking about elevating someone to a leadership position,” she said. articles.text: Editor: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) leadership has made continued pleas to not suspend donations during the pandemic. Emily Harrold, a PEF board member, penned a thorough letter last week in the Post, but it was hollow on many points. We all agree that “Paying It Forward” is a notable concept. Supporting our schools is our #1 priority. However we paid it forward in the past, and now we are sorely disappointed in how the Piedmont Unified administration has been navigating through the pandemic – or should we call it fumbling through the pandemic? We “paid it forward” but we were burned. The only choice for many of us at this time is to suspend PEF donations until we see the PEF itself state it truly – that above all else it wants schools re-opened, even if such opening goes against the hard-to-reach requirements of the administration and teachers’ union. Is PEF willing to redirect or withhold some of its donations to the school district to positively impact a re-opening? The Foundation has this power and should exercise it. If PEF is more aligned with the teachers’ union and feels less adamant about re-opening schools, then say it. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 922-8711 • email: news@piedmontpost.org
articles.title: Time to suspend PEF donations?

articles.text: Editor: After spending nearly nine years on City Council and three years as mayor, we would like to congratulate and thank Bob McBain for his tireless and inspiring service to our beloved city. Piedmont community members are fortunate to have benefitted from Bob’s commitment and his leadership in many civic roles for nearly two decades. As a member of the Park Commission, it has been my pleasure to work with Bob over the last several years. As the Commission’s liaison, he was attentive to every issue we tackled, offering reasonable, thoughtful guidance and wisdom. Whether our meetings were 45 or 145 minutes, Bob was with us at every moment of every meeting. Bob is one-in-a-million as mayor and man: kind, patient, and loyal. From behind the glass door of a shuttered Illy café on Battery Street, the Italian manager waved at me, his hand in a blue disposable glove, with an apologetic smile. For days, his parents, quarantined in Florence over the coronavirus epidemic, had been imploring him to stay away from people. It seemed as if they got their wish granted. Boarding a bus in the strangely empty Salesforce Transbay Terminal, a couple of hand-sanitizers as a parting gift from my colleagues at the bank where I work – or worked? – as a contract writer, I took the first row of seats, to the right of the driver. I didn’t know when I’d be riding home from work again, and I wanted to get an unobstructed view of San Francisco Bay, obliviously magnificent on this spring day. The bridge traffic was light. It took us less than ten minutes to get down to the lower span, from where I could see the white Grand Princess cruise ship docked at an Oakland pier, a lonely helicopter hovering above it. “Princess death,” the driver muttered as we pulled off the bridge and began weaving our way toward the Oakland maze. My neighbor’s parents had been on that ship; they were now at Travis Air Force Base, awaiting the results of their testing. I spent the weekend oscillating between “this can’t be real” and asking myself myriad odd questions, such as whether to explain to the kids, at least to the sixteenyear-old, how to claim our life insurance. I raided the rapidly depleting grocery aisles, picking up things I never thought I’d need, like pinto beans or soap in a 12-pack, all the while feeling the futility of the effort.

Editor: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) leadership has made continued pleas to not suspend donations during the pandemic. Emily Harrold, a PEF board member, penned a thorough letter last week in the Post, but it was hollow on many points. “Fumbling through the pandemic. We paid it forward and were burned.” We all agree that “Paying It Forward” is a notable concept. Supporting our schools is our #1 priority. However we paid it forward in the past, and now we are sorely disappointed in how the Piedmont Unified administration has been navigating through the pandemic – or should we call it fumbling through the pandemic? We “paid it forward” but we were burned. The only choice for many of us at this time is to suspend PEF donations until we see the PEF itself state it truly – that above all else it wants schools re-opened, even if such opening goes against the hard-to-reach requirements of the administration and teachers’ union. Is PEF willing to redirect or withhold some of its donations to the school district to positively impact a re-opening? The Foundation has this power and should exercise it. If PEF is more aligned with the teachers’ union and feels less adamant about re-opening schools, then say it. Put conditions on the next wave of fundng. The bottom line is that student health is suffering. If you, PEF, want to pay it forward for the sake of the kids, demand that schools be re-opened. Emily Harrold asks us to separate the distance learning debate and our willingness to donate to PEF. This is not a reasonable request. Who donates to an organization if they disagree with its stance – a murky one in this case. Sorry, PEF. The one thing that’s worth stockpiling is decency, that silver lining of our lives back in the USSR, with its near-permanent state of national emergency. articles.text: Nominations are currently being accepted for the 28th annual Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame, honoring exceptional women who make a difference in their communities countywide. Honorees will be celebrated in 2021 during an event co-hosted by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors and the Alameda County Commission on the Status of Women. The Women’s Hall of Fame is now accepting nominations in 13 categories: Business and Professions; Community Service; Culture and Art; Education; Emerging Leader; Environment; Health; Justice; Non-Traditional Careers; Philanthropy; Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics; Sports and Athletics; and Youth Services. You can nominate a community leader in any of these categories by visiting http://www.acgov.org/whof/nominations.htm. Nominations will be open year-round. The inductee should be established in her career or volunteerism with significant achievements that have benefited communities in Alameda County, should be successful in overcoming personal and professional obstacles, and is a role model for youth and women who strive to achieve their own success. More than 250 women have been inducted into the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame since its inception in 1993. In addition to honoring exceptional women leaders from Alameda County, the annual event raises funds for youth scholarships and supports local nonprofit community partners serving women, youth and families. “As we honor the remarkable 13 inductees, we also celebrate the 100th anniversary of the 19th Amendment [of the U.S. Constitution], guaranteeing and protecting women’s constitutional right to vote,” stated County Administrator Susan S. Muranishi. “In the past 100 years we have seen women become mayors, governors, Congresswomen, and now elected as Vice President of the United States of America. We commend the trailblazing women who came before us and make way for female pioneers to lead us through the next 100 years.” You can watch this year’s Hall of Fame ceremony and learn more about the honorees at: https:// www.classy.org/campaign/2020- alameda-county-womens-hall-offame/c298882. The date for the 2021 event will be determined after inductees are chosen early next year. articles.text: I am writing to express my thanks to Former Mayor Bob McBain. The computer gods intervened to prevent the City Clerk from seeing my virtual raised hand at the Council Meeting on Monday night. I did want to praise Bob in person following his remarks culminating his tenure on the City Council. Bob made reference to his 30 years of residence; my time as a resident is more than twice that. During that period, I have seen at least 30 mayors finish their terms of office. One thing they all have in common is their peaceful surrender of office to their duly elected successors. Bob followed that tradition as well. In other respects, Mayor McBain’s tenure was unique. I don’t think any prior mayor has had such difficult circumstances with which to cope. And yet his performance has been outstanding. I truly regret we have term limits in our Charter, as I would love for Bob’s calm, competent and dedicated style of leadership to see us Piedmonters through to the conclusion of the pandemic. Bob took office at a time of financial and political turmoil in Piedmont. We had even made the national news in a most unfavorable light. Bob took the helm, and things began to improve. In surprisingly short time Bob ushered in an era of good will, financial stability and happy times. Had the pandemic not intervened, I believe the good times would have continued to the present. For evidence of Piedmonters’ contentment I cite the overwhelming support given the renewal of the City’s Parcel Tax. Critical appointments overseen by Bob will influence things in Piedmont for years to come. The appointment of Sara Lillevand to be City Administrator has shown huge dividends already as she copes with the pandemic and her duty to keep us all as safe as possible. Equally important was the appointment of Betsy Andersen to the City Council. Without Betsy and Bob’s leadership, we would not have passed a bond measure to build a community swimming complex. For years the pool issue has vexed one City Council after another. Now we have a first-class solution! The real need for leadership of a completely unscripted nature struck in March with the arrival of Covid 19. While Bob was already a constant fixture around City Hall, the demands on the shoulders of Bob, Sara and their team have been enormous – and have they ever risen to the task. Bob has laid a foundation for the new Council to follow, and he wished them well Monday night. Had Bob’s farewell taken place in the Council Chamber I would have called for all to give him a standing ovation. Bob McBain has been a Mayor for the Ages!
articles.title: In praise of Bob McBain – a mayor for the ages

In praise of Bob McBain – a mayor for the ages By Cameron Wolfe, Jr. I am writing to express my thanks to Former Mayor Bob McBain. The computer gods intervened to prevent the City Clerk from seeing my virtual raised hand at the Council Meeting on Monday night. I did want to praise Bob in person following his remarks culminating his tenure on the City Council. Bob made reference to his 30 years of residence; my time as a resident is more than twice that. During that period, I have seen at least 30 mayors finish their terms of office. One thing they all have in common is their peaceful surrender of office to their duly elected successors. Bob followed that tradition as well. In other respects, Mayor McBain’s tenure was unique. I don’t think any prior mayor has had such difficult circumstances with which to cope. And yet his performance has been outstanding. I truly regret we have term limits in our Charter, as I would love for Bob’s calm, competent and dedicated style of leadership to see us Piedmonters through to the conclusion of the pandemic. Bob took office at a time of financial and political turmoil in Piedmont. We had even made the national news in a most unfavorable light. Bob took the helm, and things began to improve. In surprisingly short time Bob ushered in an era of good will, financial stability and happy times. Had the pandemic not intervened, I believe the good times would have continued to the present. For evidence of Piedmonters’ contentment I cite the overwhelming support given the renewal of the City’s Parcel Tax. Critical appointments overseen by Bob will influence things in Piedmont for years to come. The appointment of Sara Lillevand to be City Administrator has shown huge dividends already as she copes with the pandemic and her duty to keep us all as safe as possible. Equally important was the appointment of Betsy Andersen to the City Council. Without Betsy and Bob’s leadership, we would not have passed a bond measure to build a community swimming complex. For years the pool issue has vexed one City Council after another. Now we have a first-class solution! The real need for leadership of a completely unscripted nature struck in March with the arrival of Covid 19. While Bob was already a constant fixture around City Hall, the demands on the shoulders of Bob, Sara and their team have been enormous – and have they ever risen to the task. Bob has laid a foundation for the new Council to follow, and he wished them well Monday night. Had Bob’s farewell taken place in the Council Chamber I would have called for all to give him a standing ovation. Bob McBain has been a Mayor for the Ages! THOMAS ROBINSON, College freshman Obviously the people aren’t seeing the trees, so that is different. This is my first year working here. I was a Scout last year here, so now I have more responsibilities. articles.text: Total cases in Piedmont rise to 71 Alameda County is currently undergoing the most severe of COVID-19 cases since the pandemic began. Officials issued a new stay-at-home order for the entire county, which includes Piedmont, that began Monday, December 7. On Friday, December 4, a total of 668 new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases in a single day. The worst day for the pandemic in Alameda County prior to this was August 13, when 417 cases were recorded. There have been several days in the past two weeks with far more new cases than the surge in August, when daily new cases were previously at their highest levels. Six new cases of COVID-19 were reported among Piedmonters since last week, bringing the city’s total to 71 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. The City has closed playgrounds in accordance with the Alameda County health orders, otherwise, Piedmont’s parks will remain open until further notice. “It is important that our entire community take action to stem the spread of this disease by limiting interactions with people outside their household,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said in a statement this week. “Our collective well-being is at stake and we owe it to each other to keep our community safe.” The new stay-at-home order is aimed at limiting in-person interactions between people from different households. Restaurants must reduce operations to take-out and delivery only, and outdoor and indoor dining are now prohibited. Museums, movie theatres, zoos and personal care businesses, like hair salons, must close. Outdoor children’s playgrounds are also now shuttered. Among the local venues to close temporarily are Oakland Zoo, Children’s Fairyland and Chabot Space & Science Center. Malls, shopping centers and retail stores can remain open with capacity restrictions. The county health order is connected to a supplemental state health order that went into effect this month due to coronavirus cases spiking across California. The state order is activated when a regional group of counties, such as the Bay Area, announces that ICU capacity has dropped below 15 percent. While the Bay Area has not reached that threshold, health authorities from five Bay Area counties agreed to adopt the stricter stay-at-home restrictions as a precaution. “Rising hospitalization rates across the region threaten not only our community members with severe COVID-19, but anyone who may need care because of a heart attack, stroke, accident or other critical health need,” Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss said in a statement last week. “By acting together now we will have the greatest impact on the surge and save more lives.” The health orders in the Bay Area are scheduled to remain in place until January 4 but could be extended. Overall in Alameda County, the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 5.9 percent, a metric that has swelled upward since the start of November. The total case load in the county is now 33,736, an increase of over 3,800 cases from one week ago, according to the Alameda County Department of Public Health yesterday, Tuesday, December 8. Tragically, 11 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 525. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 11,833. In Hayward, 5,145 cases have been recorded and there have been 2,670 reported in Fremont. San Leandro reported 1,929, Livermore reported 1,584, Union City reported 1,390 and Berkeley reported 1,328. The rising case rate caused the state last month to put the entire county into the Purple Tier, the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system for reopening businesses and activities. As of yesterday, Tuesday, December 8, the county’s case rate is 15.7 cases per 100,000 people, a massive increase from one week ago. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. Only four of 58 Californian counties are not in the Purple Tier. The state and county are urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes an alarming flood of cases throughout the United States even as several COVID-19 vaccine options appear to be on the horizon. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 1,389,707 cases of COVID-19 in California. Cases have trended upward since October 18. A total of 20,047 deaths have been recorded statewide.
articles.title: COVID-19 cases reaching all-time highs in Alameda County

articles.text: Police Officer Willie Wright was promoted to the rank of Sergeant on December 5 after 10 years with the City. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers appointed him to position in advance of the retirement later this month of Sgt. Nicole Bolden. As a Watch Commander Wright will be in charge of a group of officers in addition to a records clerk, dispatcher and animal control officer. He will continue to function as the department’s defensive tactics instructor and taser instructor. Prior to his promotion Wright served as a Patrol Officer, Field Training Officer and also was a Detective for four years. While in that role, he won the “Arrest of the Year” award four times due to his interview and interrogation skills. He has also been recognized four times for the Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) award. “The promotion is big to me, because right now law enforcement is going through a trying time,” said Wright. “I know as a sergeant I have the responsibility to not only take care of the officers assigned to my shift but also to make sure our department is shown in a good, positive light.” Wright holds a leadership role in the police union as President of the Piedmont Police Officers’ Association. Wright intends to shore up the image of the police department “by making sure that Piedmont’s Police patrolman and former detective Willie Wright was prompted to the rank of Sergeant on December 5. we do things correctly and hold each other accountable. We need to not only keep the citizens safe but also make sure we are doing things correctly in the public’s eye. If they don’t agree with what we are doing, we won’t have any legitimacy or trust with them. That is big in this day and time,” he said. As a sergeant, Wright believes he will have a better chance to make an impact, as he touched on why he initially wanted to serve in law enforcement. “Growing up in an under-privileged community, I had some real positive law-enforcement contacts. These were guys who cut me a break or gave me some wisdom, some insight.” “I continue to serve because I want to make a change like several officers I met in my past made a change for me,” he added. articles.text: Ashley Boren, Executive Director of Sustainable Conservation, was invited to speak at the most recent League of Women Voters of Piedmont forum. The event was held on Sunday, December 6, via teleconference application Zoom. League Program Committee Chair Jennifer Trainor introduced Boren and the non-profit organization she directs, and LWV co-president Lorrel Plimier moderated the discussion. The topic, “California’s New Normal: Drought and Deluge,” focused on “California’s pressing water issues,” Trainor explained. “For the past 23 years, Ashley has led the organization in bringing together industry, scientists, and environmental leaders in government, groups that often have divergent views. She’s helped make really tangible progress on important issues,” Trainor said. Boren described the mission of the non-profit Sustainable Conservation as “bringing Californians together to solve [the] state’s tough environmental challenges, with a current focus of helping California adapt to climate change and the more volperiods of drought. While California stores most of the rainfall for dry spells, the Los Angeles Times estimated that 80 percent of Southern California’s rainfall runs off and is wasted, Boren explained. “The amount of run-off from just one big storm in Los Angeles could supply the city’s entire population with water for an entire year,” she added. “That’s waste on a massive scale, and we need to fix that.” She pointed to the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, passed during a drought in 2014, as the state’s response to regulating run-off and waste. It was California’s first “water law” in over a century. “[The act] is probably California’s most important climate adaptation strategy, and we must continue to implement that law,” Boren said. An important first step, she added, is the Groundwater Sustainability plans that a group of water agencies submitted in January this year. articles.text: What better way to celebrate the end of 2020 than with a Virtual Instrumental Music Concert featuring the Piedmont Middle and High School Band and Orchestra Classes! The PMS/ PHS Virtual Winter Concert will be streamed from youtube on Wednesday, December 16 at 7 pm. A link to the event will be emailed to families prior to Wednesday, Dec 16th. The Virtual Concert will feature pieces by each of the following performing groups; the PMS Advanced Orchestra, 7th grade Band, 8th grade Band, PHS Orchestra, PHS Symphonic Band, PHS Jazz Band and PHS Jazz Combo. Small ensembles, as well as a selected number of solo and duets are also on the program. Band pieces on the program include Seasons of Love from the musical Rent, Arabian Nights from the Disney movie Aladdin, What a Wonderful World, made famous by Louis Armstrong, and the Liberty Bell March by John Phillip Sousa, among others. The acclaimed PHS Jazz Combo, given the highest rating awarded at the CMEA Bay Section Jazz Combo Festival in February 2020, will also perform. This quintet of advanced PHS Jazz students who practice weekly in an outdoor socially distanced setting, include seniors Liam Charron on keyboard, and Connor Stratman on alto saxophone; as well as juniors Will Davies on drums, Jason Machle on guitar, and Alex Tafapolsky on bass. Band teacher Andria Mullan and orchestra teacher Jessica Ivry have put in many hours of audio and photo editing to make this concert happen. Mullan especially thanks PHS band seniors Jackson Nooney and Liam Charron, who produced the high school Symphonic, Pep Band and Jazz Band audio tracks, and Thomas Yu and Connor Stratman, who produced the high school Band video tracks. A link to the concert will be emailed to all Band and Orchestra families prior to December 16. All families in Piedmont School District will also receive an email with the link. For more information contact Jan D’Annunzio at jd’annunzio@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Distance Learning may be the theme of 2020, but the PMS/ PHS performing ensembles are still making wonderful music together.
articles.title: Virtual school band, orchestra concert on Dec. 16

articles.text: Cori and Zach Kau with children Elena, Louis Hudson, and Sloane. Early each autumn, Cori and Zach Kau, parents of two children at Havens and one at PMS, make a generous contribution to the Giving Campaign. “We support the Giving Campaign every year, because it builds our community and ensures that our schools and children have the resources to excel. Piedmont has been a very special place to raise our children that is rooted in a sense of community and scholastic values,” said Cori. They immediately submit their gift receipt to Zach’s company so that the Giving Campaign can also benefit from a company match. Who doesn’t like free money? Piedmont Education Foundation is encouraging supporters to apply for a company match once they have made their donation. Many of the largest Bay Area companies, including Apple, Wells Fargo, PG&E, Disney/ Pixar, Google, and more have matching gift programs for their employees. Each company has its own system for processing matching gifts, but generally all that is needed is a donation tax receipt, which Giving Campaign donors receive by email. It’s not only big companies that do matching programs. PEF Executive Director Heather Frank encourages donors to ask their organizations about gift matching. “Many companies recognize what a benefit it is to match their employee contributions. Not only does it help with employee morale, the company receives tax benefits and additional, positive marketing from nonprofit recipients,” she said. Frank said that in prior years multiple donors have requested and received matches from companies including Apple, BlackRock, BNY Mellon, Charles Schwab, Chevron, Clif Bar, Disney, Genentech, Google, Lawrence Livermore, PG&E, Salesforce, Visa, and Wells Fargo. These matches, Frank adds, are not insignificant. “Last year, the PEF Giving Campaign received matching gifts from 71 different companies, totaling $327,000.” In January, PEF will publish the names of the donors for this year’s Giving Campaign. If you have not yet made a contribution, please visit PiedmontEdFoundation.org/donate, and remember to ask your company about their matching gift program.

articles.text: Piedmont School Board has changed its scheduled meeting of December 9 to Tuesday, December 15 at 7:00 p.m. Newly elected board members Hilary Cooper and Veronica Thigpen will be sworn in. It is expected that current Vice President Cory Smegal will take over as school board president. The official agenda for the meeting will be released on Saturday December 12 at: www.agendaonline.net/public/Agency. aspx?PublicAgencyID=1241 The meeting will include the swearing in of the two new board members and the certification of the November 3 election results. Returning board members include Amal Smith and Megan Pillsbury. Preliminary results will be released from a mental health screening of Piedmont secondary students. Initially this board meeting was scheduled for December 9 but has been moved to the 15th to allow for the new board members to attend after votes have been verified. The meeting Tuesday the 15th at 7:00 p.m. can be viewed on KCOM channel 27 or on the city’s website at www.piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/ kcom-tv/live_content_and_video_archive A date and time have not yet been set by the School District for a town hall-style meeting announced by School Superintendent Randy Booker in a notice to parents on November 30. The meeting would include the high school and middle school principals, one school board member and Booker. The subject of the meeting is on options for secondary school reopening.
articles.title: School Board meeting changed to December 15

articles.text: Oyster Bay Regional Shoreline Walking/ Picnic Park Just south of the Oakland Airport is a preserved shoreline perfect for birdwatching and a beautiful day out of the house for a short walk. A variety of wildlife can be seen including marsh hawks, black-shouldered kites, and red-tailed hawks. Group picnic areas amongst tree berms await your family time out. The park has been undergoing renovation; enjoy the newly planted turf along the multipurpose trails. Interior trails lead to a view site with a sculpture called “Rising Wave.” The two-mile perimeter hiking and walking trail comes with majestic views and the salty breeze of the bay. Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve Hiking Trail Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve remains open, as is the parking lot. Take the 1.7-mile loop to get back in touch with the beauty of native plants both common and rare to the area. The 237-acre preserve has year-round blooming flowers to brighten your day. Most East Bay Regional Parks remain open during the new shelter in place restrictions. To check the status of a park go to www. ebparks.org/news/covid_19_park_and_trail_updates.htm Lake Chabot Boat Rental Boating and Fishing - Open Lake Chabot’s boat rental service is a well-kept secret. Take a visit for a fun day on the water in any sort of vessel. Try your hand at boating while getting great exercise on row boats, kayaks (single and double), or pedal boats. Prefer a more leisurely time on the water? Electric motorboats are also available in four different sizes, four-person, 16’ with a Bimini top, electric pontoon patio boats and a 20 person-max tour boat. There’s a bait shop on the dock if you are an angler, or just enjoy a relaxing day at Lake Chabot. Museum of Children’s Arts (MOCHA) Daycare and Distance Learning Assistance MOCHA continues its “Equitable Pod” program at the museum for parents that need daycare and want their kids to be in a fun environment during distance learning. Staff members will assist kids in logging into their virtual classes and answering questions. Classes consist of 10-12 kids per stable pod aged 5-12, masks and social distancing are required throughout. An hour lunch time and two break times will let kids have a chance to run around and play games outside. The class runs from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. and additional after-care is available until 5:30 p.m. for $20 extra. articles.text: The Piedmont Makers successfully raised over $420,000 for the Engineering Lab in Piedmont High School’s new STEAM building. The funds will be used for computer-aided fabrication equipment such as a CNC router, laser cutter, 3D printers and more. It will also employ a dedicated lab staff member to help teachers shape course offerings. The school board will consider approval of the Engineering Lab gift at its meeting on December 15. Since the Engineering Lab was first discussed with the School Board in July, Makers has engaged with the school administration, teachers, and community to continue to shape the proposal. With a state-of-the-art engineering lab, teachers will work with the lab manager to take advantage of the new equipment to adapt current courses that teach Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) including engineering, as well as creating new courses. The engineering lab will be a workshop for design and prototyping, equipped with both manual and computer-controlled tools. It is a modern version of a wood or metal workshop and should allow PHS students to make almost anything: big or small; technical or artistic; serious or whimsical. The Piedmont Makers group was founded in 2014 to support and inspire S.T.E.A.M. education in Piedmont at all grade levels. Programs include events like the annual School Maker Faire and robotics. In the last four years, the Piedmont Makers robotics programs have grown from one team with 10 high school students to 34 teams and 220 students from kindergarten through 12th grade. The donation of $420,000 marks the largest capital campaign in the history of Piedmont Makers. Makers has also continued to support the district through other donations such as over 30 LEGO Mindstorms kits donated to Piedmont Middle School this fall and $10k in teacher grants that will be disbursed in early 2021. When the engineering lab is completed, the lab will function as the home base for the Piedmont Highlanders FRC (FIRST Robotics Competition) Team. FIRST Robotics Competition is the highest level of FIRST Robotics. The team will operate as a Piedmont High School team with a faculty advisor. The Engineering Lab is on the first floor of the STEAM building facing the interior of campus.
articles.title: PHS Engineering Lab funded by Makers up for School Board vote

articles.text: In its 52nd year of operation the Scout Tree Lot has gone digital with online ordering and contactless delivery or pickup at Coaches’ Field. Yet in spite of the shift away from the tradition of people coming to the tree lot at Coaches Field, and selecting their annual Christmas Tree, the Scouts have sold all Silver Tips and Douglas Firs. Noble Firs and wreaths and garlands were still available as of December 8. First-year Tree Lot Supervisor Bill Murphy has seen great support from the community, “I have already had several customers say, ‘I used to work here and I’m back because I want to support the council,” Murphy said. Piedmont’s Scouting Council, the smallest in the U.S., began back in 1910. To place an order, click on www.scouttreelot.org, select the size of the tree and make an appointment for the Scouts to tie it on your car. Pickup at Coaches’ Field is available by appointment from 3:00 - 8:15 p.m. weekdays and 9:00 a.m. - 8:15 p.m. on weekends. Deliveries are available weekdays at 3:00 or 5:00 p.m. and from 9 a.m.- 5:00 p.m. on weekends. For more information, call the Scout office at 547-4493. 8th grade scouts Peter Ichimaru (left) and Kevin McKillop, wrestle with twine as they tie a tree to the roof of a car at the Scout Tree Lot.
articles.title: Last chance to order a Christmas tree from the Scout Lot

articles.text: Paris, the City of Lights, is magical at Christmas, but while different, this year has many similar traditions. The lights turned up last week inside department stores and neighborhood shops. The store openings were widely heralded after Parisians endured the entire month of November on lockdown. Retailers were chomping at the bit for Christmastime buying to begin as they try to climb out of the disastrous sales in 2020. Street trees and store windows are dressed up in their best holiday goldware, twinkling seductively for shoppers to hurry in. The temperature is chilly with misty showers and sidewalks full of people and shopping bags, so it feels just like a normal Christmas. Starting December 4th Black Friday sales were everywhere, with featured goods up to 50% off as a way to bring in the hordes. We’re not sure people know what Black Friday is, but the concept, not unlike the United States, starts after Thanksgiving when merchants start to hope that the winding-down selling days for the year begin to move from red ink deficient to black ink and create prosperity. A Parisian symbol of the City of Lights and an oasis for shopping is Galleries Lafayette, which occupies the entire block of Boulevard Haussmann on the Right Bank. After a metro ride we exited at Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin, where we climbed out of the cavernous underground to the reveal of flashing, vividly hued window displays. Galleries was a luxury bazaar by design, and this is the 1912 Flagship store. It’s on everybody’s must-see list for its spectacular steel and glass dome, a department store inspired for the theater world and Paris Opera. The founders pioneered production of store-brand merchandise: high-fashion styles that were well-made and sold at budget prices. Still very much their marketing edge, this successful enterprise has expanded to 62 Galleries Lafayette locations worldwide. Each Christmas the largest tree imaginable is suspended from the dome. The holiday-decked main floor is wall-to-wall boutiques for cosmetics, perfumes, and accessories, amid hanging displays of color-rich cheer covering every wall and ceiling – or so it seems. It’s a good browse riding the escalators from floor to floor and strolling through beautifully designed displays in its departments. At the main store’s third floor, a glass footbridge allows visitors to cross Rue de la Chaussée D’Antin to Galleries pour Hommes. Across Boulevard Haussmann is Galleries Epicure. We left the Galleries before fulfilling our shoppers’ duty to buy and resisted the pastry kiosk craftily placed at the exit door. We will ourselves to leave and go home for dinner. Christmas Markets The much-loved Christmas Markets have arrived, and although several (Notre Dame Cathedral, Swedish, Alsace at Gare de L’Est) canceled their season due to Covid-19, the markets are spread throughout the Paris districts and located in Saint-Germain des Prés, Les Halles, Place Vendôme (The Ritz), and Hôtel de Ville. Many market shoppers are delighted with the rows of traditional wooden chalet booths with a variety of items for sale: ornaments, handmade craft items, arts and unique objects, holiday foods and produce; ideas for gifts, greenery, and so on. The Christmas Markets originating in Alsace and Germany have more recently been popularized as essential to the holiday season. https://www.parisdiscoveryguide. com/paris-events-december.html Concerts and other venues Standing concerts are scheduled tentatively for the Christmas season, but the exact regulations for capacity are yet being worked out. The same is true for clubs and nightclubs, which don’t yet have a resumption date. Movie theaters, museums, and theaters may be open again starting December 15; however the seating capacity is yet to be announced. Further, the curfew in Paris will remain from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m., which presents questions about event attendees out past curfew and the necessary retention of ticket stubs to avoid a curfew violation with a penalty of €135. That ticket is plenty lofty to ruin an otherwise pleasant evening out for a movie. Here’s a guide to the Paris Church concerts for the holiday season: https://www.parisdiscoveryguide.com/paris-church-concerts.html Shoppers wait to cross at a stoplight outside Galleries Lafayette main store. French News Restaurants and bars will be permitted to reopen in France but not until January 20. It’s been a long slog stuck on idle when typically the City hosts the biggest parties of the season. The Covid- 19 consequences are heartbreaking and breaking the bank of many businesses. As many as 30% of Paris bars and restaurants are expected to close for good. Covid-19 has infected 68 million people worldwide and the tally of deaths is approaching 1.6 million. Mask-wearing continues to be compulsory in France, and people are asked to maintain social distancing. France and U.S. share commonality in the Covid-19 epidemic, which is still not under control. France, too, has rebel merchants and individuals taking a stand against lockdown; but the French do not arm themselves or refuse to wear masks. Covid cases and deaths are rising at a fearful rate, and ICU beds in hospitals are nearing capacity. Continued on next page The Flagship Galleries Lafayette store on Boulevard Haussmann shows off this year’s six-story tall Christmas tree. An early 1900s illustration of Aux Galleries Lafayette shows the worldfamous department store. Holiday window at Galleries Lafayette is brightly lit and possibly garish with lots of swaying elements to fix young gazes. Black Friday stretched last weekend into four days of sales.

The Middle East brings the latest major news about the assassination of Iran’s top nuclear scientist, Mohsen Fakhrizadeh. It was done by a satellite-controlled machine gun mounted on a parked Nissan pickup along a highway outside Iran’s capital of Tehran guided by artificial intelligence. His wife, who sat 10 inches away, was not harmed. A security guard who jumped across in protection took four bullets and was also killed. On the Russia front, the U.S. withdrew from Open Skies Treaty, a 30-year treaty about trespassing borders in a country’s airspace. Biden has stated he wants to reinstate the pact. Europe is in strong opposition to Trump’s treaty withdrawal and leaders are critical about the President’s decision. EU allies had come to rely on the U.S. for its long-range surveillance; and they don’t have the technology. articles.text: Staff Photo Piedmont’s cross-country team has qualified for State Met for seven years, but the event was canceled this year due to COVID. Last week, the California Interscholastic Federation announced that it was canceling its both its Sectional and State championship meets. It also pushed official team workouts into January in response to a spike in COVID-19 spike throughout the state. The CIF decision to cancel North Coast Section playoffs affects all teams, but the termination of the state championship impacts only one program – cross country, Piedmont’s girls’ team has qualified for the State Championship in Woodward Park for seven years. At this time last year Sophia Zalewski just put the finishing touch of her high school career at the State Meet placing 11th in a crowded field of 212 runners. But this year, with COVID-19, a field of that magnitude was unrealistic to run, and the CIF canceled it entirely. “Given what is going around in the country and world, it makes sense for us not to have State this year. With all the people it takes to put on the state championship, it is completely understandable,” said PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund. The CIF decision mentioned that the cancelation of postseason competition gives an added opportunity for leagues like the Western Alameda County Conference to schedule more meets. “The state can change anything they put out, so the CIF and NCS don’t really give us announcements quickly. We wait for an official notice, then it gets pushed, then we wait again,” said Holmlund. For the WACC and its 12 member schools with cross country programs, there is some optimism that teams can schedule some sort of competition. Holmlund said that league officials are Staff Photo discussing possible options, but no plans have been announced. “What’s happening is our league is discussing possible options of what we could do to provide some kind of competition for our athletes in whatever sport, the WACC may develop an alternative plan to what the CIF and NCS lays out. We’re hopeful we’ll have one or two local competitions,” mentioned Holmlund. There has been some discussion about pushing Season 1 sports into the spring, which would merge Cross Country with Track and Field. Currently the CIF defines Season 1 sports as: football, water polo, girls’ volleyball, and cross country. The solace for Piedmont and its student-athletes is that their plans for working out in pods gained support from the school district. Kids are still eligible for some sporting structure in this uncertain time. “We’re still in the summer-conditioning realm until we become a season. Until we get official word, everything is conditioning and cross country is starting [Monday]. We’re working in Pictured is Adri McAuliffe (1256) at the State Meet a year ago. pods without equipment. We’ve been doing a lot of hill-work, now we have access to the track and we’ll be starting longer mileage workouts,” said Holmlund. “The school determined that the kids getting out to run and exercise was important for their mental health,” added the coach. Until this point, the cross country program was operating off-campus through the city’s Recreation Department, not the school district. That alone raises significant questions about the level of support being provided by PUSD and the high school. In the meantime colleges are eager to know how high school students are self-motivating without official sport activities. “This time takes a lot of mental toughness. We have some students who have really gotten into their running on their own. We definitely have those kids who have been persistent about getting out the door and running,” said Holmlund. Three months after the start of the school year, the cross country team will gain a bit more structure now that Witter Field is available to them. More information should be available on Season 1 sports on January 1, or in the days shortly afterward. The CIF’s initial start Staff Photo Piedmont senior Alex Weekes is captain of the boys’ team. of competition for Cross Country was January 27, but it’s likely to be changed to a later date. “The CIF does not expect the California Department of Public Health to issue any guidance allowing for schools to return to full practice and competition until after January 1, 2021 All full practice and competition start dates are officially on hold until updated guidance is issued,” the CIF stated last week. But this year, with COVID-19, a field of that magnitude was unrealistic to run, and the CIF canceled it entirely. “Given what is going around in the country and world, it makes sense for us not to have State this year. With all the people it takes to put on the state championship, it is completely understandable,” said PHS coach Jeanine Holmlund. The CIF decision mentioned that the cancelation of postseason competition gives an added opportunity for leagues like the Western Alameda County Conference to schedule more meets. “The state can change anything they put out, so the CIF and NCS don’t really give us announcements quickly. We wait for an official notice, then it gets pushed, then we wait again,” said Holmlund. For the WACC and its 12 member schools with cross country programs, there is some optimism that teams can schedule some sort of competition. Holmlund said that league officials are Staff Photo discussing possible options, but no plans have been announced. “What’s happening is our league is discussing possible options of what we could do to provide some kind of competition for our athletes in whatever sport, the WACC may develop an alternative plan to what the CIF and NCS lays out. We’re hopeful we’ll have one or two local competitions,” mentioned Holmlund. There has been some discussion about pushing Season 1 sports into the spring, which would merge Cross Country with Track and Field. Currently the CIF defines Season 1 sports as: football, water polo, girls’ volleyball, and cross country. The solace for Piedmont and its student-athletes is that their plans for working out in pods gained support from the school district. Kids are still eligible for some sporting structure in this uncertain time. “We’re still in the summer-conditioning realm until we become a season. Until we get official word, everything is conditioning and cross country is starting [Monday]. We’re working in Pictured is Adri McAuliffe (1256) at the State Meet a year ago. pods without equipment. We’ve been doing a lot of hill-work, now we have access to the track and we’ll be starting longer mileage workouts,” said Holmlund. “The school determined that the kids getting out to run and exercise was important for their mental health,” added the coach. Until this point, the cross country program was operating off-campus through the city’s Recreation Department, not the school district. That alone raises significant questions about the level of support being provided by PUSD and the high school. In the meantime colleges are eager to know how high school students are self-motivating without official sport activities. “This time takes a lot of mental toughness. We have some students who have really gotten into their running on their own. We definitely have those kids who have been persistent about getting out the door and running,” said Holmlund. Three months after the start of the school year, the cross country team will gain a bit more structure now that Witter Field is available to them. More information should be available on Season 1 sports on January 1, or in the days shortly afterward. The CIF’s initial start Staff Photo Piedmont senior Alex Weekes is captain of the boys’ team. of competition for Cross Country was January 27, but it’s likely to be changed to a later date. “The CIF does not expect the California Department of Public Health to issue any guidance allowing for schools to return to full practice and competition until after January 1, 2021 All full practice and competition start dates are officially on hold until updated guidance is issued,” the CIF stated last week. Staff Photo Ellie Black (1253) was named the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in June. Staff Photo Aya Troyer is a team-leader in her senior year. Photos by Michael Mabry Piedmont junior Seamus Chamberlain Carr (right) will be a leader on the boys’ XC team this year. A group photo at least year’s Capital Cross Challenge in Sacramento. articles.text: Photo courtesy of ArizonaSports.com Arizona State guard Remy Martin has the Sun Devils ranked No. 23 in the NCAA. Oregon is expected to have a top-25 ranking. Two weeks into the 2020-21 NCAA men’s basketball season, let’s loo at Pac-12 schools. The No. 23 Sun Devils of Arizona State are the only team in the conference currently in the top 25, holding a 3-1 overall record and 1-0 in the league after defeating Cal 70-62 on December 3. They have a team boasting returning starter G Remy Martin, who seems to be the leading candidate for the Conference Player of the Year honors. Marvin Bagley and Josh Christopher seem to be future NBA talents as well. Tomorrow, ASU plays its biggest game of the year against No. 24 San Diego State. Oregon received 26 votes to receive ranking in the top 25, currently at 2-1 with a season-opening 83-75 loss to Missouri. Currently just outside a ranking, wins against Florida A&M today, Washington on Saturday, and UCLA on Dec. 23 could be catapult their ranking. Washington State received three top-25 votes, and is 3-0 with three narrow victories to start their schedule. They will have winnable contests until facing ASU on December 31 to end 2020. Guard Isaac Bonton is their leading player. The UCLA Bruins were the preseason No. 1 by Pac-12 media polls; currently 3-1 as well, but lost to the SDSU Aztecs 73-58 to open the season on Nov. 25. The Arizona Wildcats, a usual NCAA basketball powerhouse, are 3-0 without their top six scorers from last season. But they bring back the nation’s No. 5 ranked recruiting class from last year. Arizona’s first test will be Stanford on December 19. The Cardinal is 2-2 after a healthy slate of early games, including a 4-point loss (67-63) to No. 16 North Carolina on Dec. 1. Senior forward Oscar da Silva leads a healthy returning cast, meaning Stanford will challenge the top teams in the conference despite not currently having a ranking. They face USC on Sunday, December 13 and Arizona the following Saturday. Over to the Trojans of Southern California, they are 4-1 and freshman forward Evan Mobley could be the newcomer of the year for the Pac-12. His brother, Isaiah Mobley, a fellow McDonalds All-American, make a tough combination to deal with. The Trojans play Stanford in their next contest, but also play the difficult San Francisco Dons, which are 4-2 and upset No. 18 Virginia 61-60 on Nov. 27. The Golden Bears of Berkeley will largely play upsetters this year. With a 2-3 overall record, the Bears gave the Sun Devils some fight in their 70-62 loss on Dec. 3, but will require large contributions out of an unproven roster, which includes former WACC star Monty Bowser from O’Dowd. Photo courtesy of the Seattle Times Washington State has a talented team this year and could end up in the top-25. Photo courtesy of OregonLive.com Photo courtesy of the LA Daily News UCLA is currently 3-1 outside of the top-25.

articles.text: The Las Vegas Raiders walked out of Week 13 with its heads held high after Derek Carr pulled off late-game heroics with a touchdown heave to Henry Ruggs, beating the Jets 31-28. The Niners weren’t as fortunate, losing to AFC East-leading Buffalo Bills 34-24. The Raiders got it done, but was not impressive against a winless New York Jets squad that is poised to get the No. 1 overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. Now improving its record to 7-5, Vegas is still in the AFC playoff hunt but still on the outside looking in and one game behind the Indianapolis Colts and Miami Dolphins, both teams on their remaining schedule. But the Raiders can control their destiny this week against the Colts, a difficult matchup with veteran quarterback Philip Rivers and a stout defense. Although Vegas has proven to show up for critical games, upsetting Indy will be tough. A defensive game will likely lean toward a Colts’ win, while Carr, head coach Jon Gruden, and Co. will have to force a high scoring game. Going with my gut, the Colts should win a one-possession ballgame. SF 49ers As for the 49ers, they took a predictable defeat to the Bills but are still in the NFC Wild Card hunt one game back of Vikings. Now scheduled to play this weekend in Arizona due to COVID complications, they will host Washington, a game that will reunite veteran quarterback Alex Smith with the franchise which drafted him back in 2005 out of Utah. Smith, hands down the NFL Comeback Player of the Year, famously recovered from life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis due to complications from leg surgery. Both teams are 5-7, while Washington is tied for the NFC East lead with its solid defense under recently hired head coach Ron Rivera, an All-American when playing for Cal. This is a more difficult game to predict, and SF would certainly be the hands-down favorite with a healthy roster. The 49ers’ offense will have the tools available to beat Washington with running back Raheem Mostert, and receivers Deebo Samuel, and Brandon Aiyuk. But they’ll have to use quick plays to avoid Washington’s Photo courtesy of Las Vegas Review-Journal Raiders’ rookie receiver Henry Ruggs scored the game-winner in Vegas’ 31-28 win over the Jets. Photo courtesy of CBS Sports Photo courtesy of Sportingnews.com Stephen Curry and the Golden State Warriors return for the 2021 season. The 49ers are favored against Washington, the home of former San Francisco QB Alex Smith. strong pass rush. It is hard to bet against Washington after it handed the Steelers their first loss of the season. Should the 49ers’ pass defense prove more useful early on, SF could win. If Washington is able to disrupt 49ers QB Nick Mullens, it could be a big day for the East Coast team. Golden State to start season The Warriors are back with Stephen Curry, Draymond Green, but not Klay Thompson due a second consecutive devastating season-ending injury. Their preseason starts this Saturday, December 12 against the Denver Nuggets. They move into 2021 with Curry, Green, first-round pick James Wiseman at center, Andrew Wiggins, and recently acquired forward Kelly Oubre. It’s hard to see the Warriors pulling off the same look as in recent years, where its triangle offense kept teams dizzy from its shooting options. Without Thompson, the Warriors’ offense could become pick-and-roll centric with Curry running the floor. With Wiseman, Green, Oubre, and Kevon Looney, Golden State has a large squad capable of being physical with any team in the league, which will be critical when facing defending champion LA Lakers. Premier League review Starting with the table, Tottenham (7-3-1, 24 points) continues in first place by goal differential over Liverpool (7-3-1), Chelsea (6-4-1, 22 points), and Leceister City (7-0-4, 21 points). The Spurs’ shutout Arsenal 2-0 in last week’s match of the week, the North London Derby. The intrigue coming out of England is, once again, the status of Manchester United manager Ole Gunnar Solskjær after the Red Devils’ early exit from Champions League. After losing 3-2 to Germany’s RB Leipzig, they were relegated to Europa League. In previous issues we’ve discussed United giving Solskjær the boot, and the “Ole Out” campaign continues in full force. But will it happen? Its loss to Leipzig seemed like the perfect storm. Superstar midfielder Paul Pogba’s agent dropped a bomb in a recent interview saying that his client was on the way out of Manchester. Ole took blame for the loss and refused to say whether the Pogba news was a distraction. With January 1 as the opening date of the transfer window, it could be now or never for Manchester United and likelihood of making a move shrinking by the day. Many around the club believe Solskjær just needs time with a predominantly young roster. Former Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino is the lead man for the job. Former Juventus manager Max Allegri is another solid gaffer, while Paris Saint Germain manager Thomas Tuchel is emerging as a name to watch.
articles.title: Tough tasks ahead for Raiders, 49ers; Warriors season to start; “Ole Out” in full force in the UK

articles.text: • • Califor nia State Parks announced on Friday, December 4, that campgrounds will be temporarily closed for regions within the Purple Tier of the state’s stay-at-home orders. Day use for parks will still be permitted. That includes all of Alameda County. “Yesterday, California took an important step to address the alarming pace of COVID-19 case rates that are threatening to overwhelm the health care delivery system,” said California State Parks Director Armando Quintero. “While the new Regional Stay at Home Order is asking Californians to stay home as much as possible and for campground sites in impacted regions to close, the state also recognizes that that outdoor activity is critical for mental health and physical health. We welcome you to recreate in the outdoors provided that you stay local, plan ahead to find out what is open, wear a face covering, practice physical distancing and avoid gatherings with people outside the immediate household. The California State Park systems issued several guidelines in response to the COVID-19 spike throughout the state, asking its day-use patrons to consider the following: • Stay Local – Stay close to home to slow the spread of COVID-19. Do not travel if you or someone in your household is sick. • Plan Ahead – Prior to leaving home, check the webpage of the park unit you plan to visit to find out if it is open, if parking is available, and what visitor guidelines are in effect. • Stay Safer at 6-feet – Maintain a physical distance of six feet or more. Visitors are being asked to leave if there are too many people to allow for the required physical distance. • Boating – Do not raft up to other boaters or pull up onto a beach next to other patrons. Keep Clean – Not all restrooms are open to the public. Bring soap/hand sanitizer. Please pack out all trash. Stay Covered – Individuals must have a face covering with them at all times. The state’s Regional Stay at Home Order has been implemented for areas with less than 15 percent of existing capacity in ICU units in hospitals. This includes, Northern California, Bay Area, Greater Sacramento, San Joaquin Valley and Southern California. State campground sites within these regions will be temporarily closed in accordance with the new order. Yosemite also limited to day-use Yosemite National Park also announced that they are have limited accress for day-use only starting December 7 in response to the Regional Stay at Home orders. The park will be closed from 5 p.m. to 8 a.m. “Hotels and campgrounds are closed. Wilderness permits are not available. While the wilderness (including big wall climbing) is open, overnight stays in wilderness (including on big walls) is prohibited… All visitors must leave the park by 5 p.m.,” a notice from the park stated. Yosemite added that it will continue working with Mariposa County to determine a timeline for a full park reopening. “Yosemite National Park is working closely with officials from Mariposa County Public Health and the California Department of Public Health to implement California’s regional Stay Home order. Consistent with the Governor’s order, these temporary restrictions will remain in effect until local conditions change,” it stated. For further details about lodging within Yosemite National Park, visit https://www.travelyosemite.com /aler ts/2020/ covid-19-guest-updates/ Photo courtesy of COVID19.ca.gov The current tier map for California’s Regional Stay at Home orders affecting California State Parks.

articles.text: Area reopened November 21 after wildfire closure Sunol Regional Wilderness of East Bay Regional Park District was reopened on November 21 after recovering from the SCU complex fires that raged for 44 days this fire season. Sunol Regional Wilderness is now open, so you can explore and enjoy all of the trails within the park boundary. The adjacent Ohlone Wilderness remains closed, however. The area is among the smaller of parks operated by East Bay Regional, but it is one of the more popular destinations due to Little Yosemite – a frequented water hole in the warmer months. The lack of rain this winter has reduced the creek to a trickle that feeds into the more active Alameda Creek area. Right now the trail is more of a beginners’ course in canyoning as you climb over boulders; keeping sharp eyes on where to put your feet, hands for secure landing spots. The walk from the Sunol Regional parking lot is a mellow 1.1 miles from the gate on Ohlone Road. Adjacent to the main trail is a more secluded path along the creek, eventually re-emerging with Ohlone Road on the way to Little Yosemite. The path down to the Little Yosemite area is narrow, and depending on the time of the day and year, you will likely be taking your time – especially during a time of COVID. pages.text: Wednesday, December 9, 2020 15 HIKING WITH JON Sunol Regional’s Little Yosemite and McCorkle Trail Area reopened November 21 after wildfire closure By Jonathan Comeaux Sunol Regional Wilderness of East Bay Regional Park District was reopened on November 21 after recovering from the SCU complex fires that raged for 44 days this fire season. Sunol Regional Wilderness is now open, so you can explore and enjoy all of the trails within the park boundary. The adjacent Ohlone Wilderness remains closed, however. The area is among the smaller of parks operated by East Bay Regional, but it is one of the more popular destinations due to Little Yosemite – a frequented water hole in the warmer months. The lack of rain this winter has reduced the creek to a trickle that feeds into the more active Alameda Creek area. Right now the trail is more of a beginners’ course in canyoning as you climb over boulders; keeping sharp eyes on where to put your feet, hands for secure landing spots. The walk from the Sunol Regional parking lot is a mellow 1.1 miles from the gate on Ohlone Road. Adjacent to the main trail is a more secluded path along the creek, eventually re-emerging with Ohlone Road on the way to Little Yosemite. The path down to the Little Yosemite area is narrow, and depending on the time of the day and year, you will likely be taking your time – especially during a time of COVID. Little Yosemite is a popular swimming hole, where giant boulders provide a beginner’s course in rock climbing and canyoning. Only a small trickle of water is at Little Yosemite now. During the warmer months, and with more water, the area is popular for hikers and swimmers. Photos by Jonathan Comeaux Alameda Creek runs along the Ohlone Road trail on the way to Sunol Regional Park’s Little Yosemite. Midway to ur destination, I had already passed 36 people, which would have undoubtedly doubled had we stayed on the main pathway for the entire walk. Don’t fret if you are COVID-conscious; the foot traffic thin out from there on. Another 1.1 miles away is the McCorkle trail, where we only passed four people, and then another four people on the remaining four miles miles on the way back to the car – a total of rounding 7 people per mile for the total hike. The four-mile McCorkle Trail was secluded and had only two couples passing by. The McCorkle loop starts your ascent. We topped out at 1,335 feet in elevation gain, but the medium slope means it is not over-challenging. The trails through the hills are shared with grazing cows, which means you may get uncomfortably close to them and be dodging cow-pies for a short distance. Although the cows seem to be accustomed to hikers, dog walkers should take notice. Following the McCorkle Trail back to the entrance gate on Ohlone Road will provide a sweeping view of Sunol Regional’s foothills, cows grazing through the winter-stripped grasslands, and the vibrant color of orange leaves throughout the area. The ascent up provides a glimpse of the Calaveras Reservoir. Punch in “Sunol Regional Wilderness” into your GPS device to access this park. The dry creek bed of Alameda Creek past Little Yosemite. The “W Tree” on the Ohlone Road trail. Cows share the foothills of Sunol Regional Park. The McCorkle trail goes directly up into the hills. A view of the foothills with its dry grasslands. The rolling hills provides a picturesque reward for the climb up the McCorkle trail.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre presents The Steadfast Tin Solider, written and directed by Mary Zimmerman, a noted playwright, available to stream until December 27. The play was produced by Looking Glass Theatre Company in Chicago. Zimmerman’s extravagant play is inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s story of the same title. The play features the unlikely adventure of a little tin solider that exudes a ton of bravery, and is infused with Zimmerman’s blend of storytelling through image and movement, accompanied by musicians. The Chicago Tribune called it a “treat for all ages. Barely more than an hour long, this major new work is one holiday experience you don’t want to miss.” Looking Glass Theatre Company’s The Steadfast Tin Solider. Tickets are available for one livestream performance plus access to video on demand. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/season/2021/steadfasttinsoldier.asp for purchasing information.

articles.text: San Francisco’s Cutting Ball Theatre has compiled quarantine stories from resident artists in a series entitled “Artists in Isolation.” The series features short, simple videos that showcase each artist’s strength. Indian film director Radhika Rao teaches improvisation comedy classes, actress Ella Ruth Francis offers a lesson in singing, and artists revisit playwright Richard Foreman’s wild writings to put their twist on some of his most iconic works. articles.text: Oakland Ballet Company is presenting its first ever drive-in movie theatre event, with five screenings of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker to be projected on the north wall of the historic Paramount Theatre. Although indoor theaters and performances remain closed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Oakland Ballet Company is continuing its annual tradition of bringing The Nutcracker to audiences from a safe distance. Screenings of the performance will take place Sunday through Thursday, December 20-24, at 6 p.m. each day. The parking lot located at 2100 Telegraph Avenue will open at 4:30 p.m. to ticket holders. This performance will mark the 49th year that the company will present a production of The Nutcracker. With a runtime of approximately 75 minutes, Lustig’s Nutcracker includes excerpts from the ballet’s 2019 producOakland Ballet Company will present The Nutcracker on outside wall of the Paramount Theatre. tion with original choreography. Since his appointment as Artistic Director in 2010, Lustig has revitalized the company, helping the organization reclaim its position as a leading arts institution in the Bay Area. He was trained at the Royal Ballet School in London, and has danced with the Dutch National Ballet and Birmingham Royal Ballet before joining the Oakland group. In addition to the Oakland Ballet Company’s professional ensemble, the production features more than 40 Bay Area dancers, ages 7 to 17, in the roles of snowballs, mice, soldiers and candies, with musical accompaniment from the Oakland Symphony and members of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Visit oaklandballet.org to secure tickets before the event. Tickets are limited. No on-site tickets will be available.
articles.title: Oakland Ballet to show The Nutcracker in drive-in screening at Paramount Dec. 20–24

articles.text: San Francisco Opera has found an intriguing way to bring the “stage” to audiences safely – by showing filmed productions of operas at the newly created drive-in theater at San Francisco’s Fort Mason. This weekend’s production is Tosca, an opera in three acts by Giacomo Puccini, with libretto by Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa, and based on the drama La Tosca by Victorien Sardou. It will run on Friday and Saturday this weekend, December 11 and 12, at 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. both days. The opera is sung in Italian with English subtitles and was performed at San Francisco Opera in 2009. It has a running time of two hours with no intermission. Tosca descends audiences into a portrait of Rome on the brink of war. A police state reigns over the city, and at its head is the merciless Baron Scarpia. Amid the tumult, love blossoms between two artists: the singer Floria Tosca and the painter Mario Cavaradossi. But Tosca has caught Scarpia’s eye. To claim the singer for himself, Scarpia concocts a plan to send her lover to the firing squad — and Tosca’s only hope to save him is to do the unspeakable. Pull into Fort Mason’s drive-in cinema experience to witness soprano Adrianne Pieczonka as Tosca and Georgian baritone Lado Ataneli as Scarpia in their company debuts. Reserve a parking spot for this weekend’s event by clicking on https://sfopera. com/opera-is-on/fort-masondrive-in-nov-dec-2020/tosca-ftmason/. Tickets are limited. Masks will be required by all attendees over the age of 2 when outside of the vehicle. Attendees are asked to remain in their vehicles when not using restroom facilities or purchasing items from the concession stand. articles.text: San Francisco Jazz (SFJAZZ) will share a live recording of Alex Shulman’s performance with bassist John Wittala and drummer James Gallagher on Christmas Eve, December 24, as part of its holiday online series. The holiday performances by pianist Shulman celebrating Bay Area jazz legend Vince Guaraldi and his soundtrack to Charles Schulz’s 1965 holiday classic, A Charlie Brown Christmas, are an SFJAZZ tradition. The program is one of the most beloved holiday albums of all time. The music was even voted into the Grammy Hall of Fame and Pianist Alex Shulman will perform A Charlie Brown Christmas on December 24 added to the Library of Congress’ National Recording Registry’s list of “culturally, historically, or aesthetically important” American recordings. Last December at SFJAZZ, Shulman performed his homage to Guaraldi by playing the classic music. The tradition will continue this year. To view the performance, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/.
articles.title: Adam Shulman to play Guaraldi’s A Charlie Brown Christmas on December 24
