articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré I am often reminded that people still love to be told a good story. And there is no medium that does this more powerfully than film. A fine example is the recently released The King’s Speech. It is extraordinary. A wonderful surprise. That it was ever made is remarkable. Imagine trying to pitch to a studio this very English film, set in the 1920s and 30s, about a shy man, Albert the Duke of York, albeit the future King of England, who possesses a stammer that has tormented him all of his life. Albert, aka Bertie (Colin Firth), has always been content (resigned, perhaps) to live his life in the shadow of his older brother, Edward (Guy Pearce), who is first in line to the throne held by their father, the overbearing and unsympathetic George V (Michael Gambon). For decades, Bertie has hidden from his family and the public ever fearful that in the midst of a mundane conversation his throat will close off, his words incarcerated by an uncontrollable stammer. The thought of standing before a microphone at a public speaking engagement sends him into a paroxysm of panic and harrowing silence. Wishing to overcome this affliction, he sees speech experts of questionable practices, one filling his mouth with ice cubes while insisting that they can cure him. Another encourages him to smoke, claiming that it relaxes the throat. He is deeply frustrated and constantly humiliated. Finally, his wife, the Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter), desperate, finds Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an eccentric speech therapist, who uses unorthodox methods and patiently explains to both the Duchess and the Duke that if they give him total control and their trust he can help Bertie do that which has eluded him all of his life: speech that is liberated and flows freely. And so begins the essence of the film: the creation of an improbable relationship between two men, Logue, the Australian expatriate and commoner, and the Albert, royalty, whose only wish is that he never have to assume Colin Firth portrayed Albert the Duke of York in The King’s Speech. the crown as the King of England. Their relationship, tentative and combative at first, filled with resistance and distrust, takes on a special importance when Bertie’s brother, Edward, is crowned King Edward VIII after the death of their father, George V. Edward, it turns out, scandalizing all of England, announces that he will abdicate the throne in order to marry Wallis Simpson (Eve Best), an American divorcee. That decision requires that Albert, next in succession, step forward and assume that singular role, the prospect of which has always terrified him. How can he ever speak to the people of England as their king when he can’t speak to his family or to Logue without a debilitating stutter? Adding to the exigencies of his position is the fact that England is on the cusp of war with Germany. Albert, who is soon to become King George VI, must reassure and inspire his countrymen during a period that will be characterized as their finest hour. And he must do this standing before a microphone. The relationship created between Logue and the Duke is touching, filled with humor and tension and scatological rants (Bertie never stammers when he’s angry and cussing). To watch the two men spar, teacher and pupil, is to observe two deeply gifted actors deliver the performances of their lives, while supported by the members of an astonishing ensemble – a dream cast. The King’s Speech is a brilliantly recreated moment in history that otherwise would have likely been just a footnote to those years leading up to World War II. Happily it isn’t. The King’s Speech. Starring Colin Firth, Helena Bonham Carter, Geoffrey Rush, Guy Pearce, Timothy Spall Derek Jacobi, Michael Gambon and Jennifer Ehle. Directed by Tom Hooper. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. Helena Bonham Carter, Colin Firth, and Geoffrey Rush in The King’s Speech.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The King’s Speech a touching film of a king who stuttered

articles.text: Helen Mirren and Ian McKellen stars in The Good Liar. Movie review by Chris Honoré The pleasure to be found in The Good Liar resides not in the story, though the first two acts are intriguing . It is in watching Helen Mirren and Ian McKellan, both knighted, portraying two attractive people, Betty and Roy, engaging in the initial drama of, well, not courtship exactly, but friendly companionship. Or so it seems. Initially we meet them seated across a posh restaurant table making introductions, smiling, having a drink. Both widowed, they’ve met online and this is their first opportunity to put a face to their correspondence. She is a retired Oxford professor, apparently affluent, lovely, and smart. He is… well, it’s a bit early. At first blush he seems to be a debonair, urbane oldster who runs a financial investment firm with a partner. Betty lives in the suburbs; Roy has a flat in London. They agree, given their age, that it’s hard to meet someone for the purpose of being simply good company. Soon, she discovers that Roy has a bad leg and struggles with the three flights of stairs to his apartment. Betty suggests that he use her guest room while his leg improves. This is against the advice of her grandson, Stephen (Russell Tovey) who is suspicious of Roy from the outset. Betty, however, is trusting and welcoming, though she makes it clear that their living arrangement is without benefits, so to speak. And it’s at this point that we begin to learn more about Roy, who still seems benign. They even take a trip to Berlin to tour and shop and reflect on WWII and their memories. The film title does frame the story and there are moments when you wonder if Betty is really the wealthy innocent, and Roy the shades of grey business guy who may see her as an invetment mark. She’s got a few million. But their rapport and connection seems consistently genuine. Until it isn’t. And that’s when act three betrays its enigmatic promise. Despite the best efforts of Mirren and McKellen, the film pretty much collapses. But watching them is witnessing a master class in acting and should be enjoyed for what it is: wonderful and a good enough reason to grab just under two hours and relish their individual gifts as they merge. The Good Liar. Directed by Bill Condon. Starring Helen Mirren, Ian McKellen and Russell Tovey. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R.
articles.title: The Good Liar an acting gem from the UK

Imagine trying to pitch to a studio this very English film, set in the 1920s and 30s, about a shy man, Albert the Duke of York, albeit the future King of England, who possesses a stammer that has tormented him all of his life. Albert, aka Bertie (Colin Firth), has always been content (resigned, perhaps) to live his life in the shadow of his older brother, Edward (Guy Pearce), who is first in line to the throne held by their father, the overbearing and unsympathetic George V (Michael Gambon). For decades, Bertie has hidden from his family and the public ever fearful that in the midst of a mundane conversation his throat will close off, his words incarcerated by an uncontrollable stammer. The thought of standing before a microphone at a public speaking engagement sends him into a paroxysm of panic and harrowing silence. Wishing to overcome this affliction, he sees speech experts of questionable practices, one filling his mouth with ice cubes while insisting that they can cure him. Another encourages him to smoke, claiming that it relaxes the throat. He is deeply frustrated and constantly humiliated. Finally, his wife, the Duchess of York (Helena Bonham Carter), desperate, finds Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), an eccentric speech therapist, who uses unorthodox methods and patiently explains to both the Duchess and the Duke that if they give him total control and their trust he can help Bertie do that which has eluded him all of his life: speech that is liberated and flows freely. And so begins the essence of the film: the creation of an improbable relationship between two men, Logue, the Australian expatriate and commoner, and the Albert, royalty, whose only wish is that he never have to assume Colin Firth portrayed Albert the Duke of York in The King’s Speech. the crown as the King of England. Their relationship, tentative and combative at first, filled with resistance and distrust, takes on a special importance when Bertie’s brother, Edward, is crowned King Edward VIII after the death of their father, George V. Edward, it turns out, scandalizing all of England, announces that he will abdicate the throne in order to marry Wallis Simpson (Eve Best), an American divorcee. That decision requires that Albert, next in succession, step forward and assume that singular role, the prospect of which has always terrified him. How can he ever speak to the people of England as their king when he can’t speak to his family or to Logue without a debilitating stutter? Adding to the exigencies of his position is the fact that England is on the cusp of war with Germany. Albert, who is soon to become King George VI, must reassure and inspire his countrymen during a period that will be characterized as their finest hour. And he must do this standing before a microphone. The relationship created between Logue and the Duke is touching, filled with humor and tension and scatological rants (Bertie never stammers when he’s angry and cussing). To watch the two men spar, teacher and pupil, is to observe two deeply gifted actors deliver the performances of their lives, while supported by the members of an astonishing ensemble – a dream cast. The King’s Speech is a brilliantly recreated moment in history that otherwise would have likely been just a footnote to those years leading up to World War II. Happily it isn’t. The King’s Speech. Starring Colin Firth, Helena Bonham Carter, Geoffrey Rush, Guy Pearce, Timothy Spall Derek Jacobi, Michael Gambon and Jennifer Ehle. Directed by Tom Hooper. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The character “Astro Boy” was created in 1951 by the celebrated animator of Japanese manga (comic books) and anime (movie and television animation), Osamu Tezuka. In the 1960s, Astro, originally known as Tetsuwan Atomu (Mighty Atom), appeared in a popular television show, viewed in more than 40 countries, and now Astro makes his debut in a feature film. For children today, Astro Boy will be new and fresh. Young moviegoers will be captivated by the story and the nonstop action. This first installment (others will likely follow) explains how a young boy, Toby (Freddy Highmore), is killed in an experiment conducted by his scientist father, Dr. Tenma (Nicolas Cage). Wracked with grief and guilt, Tenma creates an exact replica of his son, a small android, giving him all of Toby’s memories and a heart of “blue power” which makes the boy superhuman. He can fly, has machine guns in his butt, x-ray vision, amazing strength, and rockets in his shoes and hands. Astro, at first unaware he’s a robot, sets out to find his place in the world, meaning, Metro City, an urban island hovering above earth which has been turned into a dumpsite for outdated robots and broken machinery. After being rejected by his father, who cannot accept that he’s a robot, Astro goes to earth and meets a group of kids, orphans from Metro City, all his own age. These discarded kids have no families. They are, however, human and Astro is reluctant to disclose that he is not. And so the story goes. The kids long for Astro’s powers and he longs for their humanity. He also grieves for the loss of his father. There’s an evil Mayor of Metro City (Donald Sutherland) who covets Astro’s “blue power,” a duplicitous hustler named Hamegg (Nathan Lane) who wants only to use Astro, and, finally, a long journey back into the arms of his dad. While the story brings to mind Transformers and Pinocchio (likely not known to young filmgoers), kids will find Astro appealing and will immediately look forward to The Return of Astro Boy. Astro Boy. Animated. With the voices of Nicolas Cage, Freddie Highmore, Nathan Lane, Kristen Bell and Bill Nighy. Directed by David Bowers. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: Astro Boy comes to life for kids of all ages

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Tales From Earthsea was adapted from the Ursula Le Guin Earthsea fantasy novels and directed by the son of the iconic Ghibli animator and storyteller, Hayao Miyazaki. For years he had pondered whether it would be possible to capture the breadth and depth of Le Guin’s extraordinary work in one animated film. Reluctantly he agreed to allow his son, Goro Miyazaki, who was not an experienced filmmaker, to bring Tales to the screen. The father’s instincts proved correct, and while the film was in production, he kept his distance. The result is considered by many to be Studio Ghibli’s only release that has been described as a “train wreck.” While the film has the extraordinary animation expected from the Studio, it’s the storytelling that puzzles. Some critics have referred to it as boring, pretentious, and not suited for younger audiences (late tweens and teens, possibly). Though the film does have a familiar feminist point of view, one known to thread its way through many of Ghibli’s animated stories, and does possess a spectrum of themes, such as the imbalance of nature, it remains jarring if not indecipherable. Ditto the characters. The narrative opens with medieval flying dragons engaging in battle, followed by the protagonist, Prince Arren (Jeff Bennett), inexplicably killing his father, the kindly king of the Earthsea kingdom. Taking his father’s Excalibur sword, he flees, later to be rescued by a wizard, also called Sparrowhawk (Timothy Dalton), who becomes Arren’s mentor. The wizard takes the Prince to a farmhouse where he meets Tenar (Mariska Hagitay), and Therru (Adi Teshima), her young daughter. Tenar saves his life when he falls ill, Arren and Sparrowhawk stay at the farm where they labor and the Prince matures. But the world is still not in balance. They discover that the cause of this disharmony is the evil Lord Cob (Willem Dafoe) who strives for immortality with the help of his henchman, Hare (Cheech Marin), a man who kidnaps and sells into slavery people from the countryside. There is a final confrontation between Lord Cob, Arren and Sparrowhawk, one that takes place at Cob’s abandoned castle. And thus concludes Arren’s quest, a dark journey of self-discovery, which is, in the main, overshadowed by harshly rendered villains. Tales From Earthsea (2006), Directed by Goro Miyazaki. A Studio Ghibli animé. With the voices of Jeff Bennett, Willem Dafoe, Timothy Dalton, Mariska Hargitay and Cheech Marin. 1 hr., 55 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Goro Miyazaki’s Tales From Earthsea.
articles.title: Tales From Earthsea – a film for older teens

articles.text: Theme nights, festive lights, and Santa Saturdays all through December Filoli House and Gardens, located in Woodside, is dressed in festive lights for the holiday season through January 3. The lights were installed throughout the garden on November 21, making it the perfect socially-distanced activity to enjoy with family and friends of all ages. Take a walk through the gardens and enjoy the beauty of a winter garden adorned with lights and colorful décor. Visitors can cozy up next to a fire pit under twinkling lights while sipping on hot cider or mulled wine. Visit the gardens on a Monday night for “theme nights.” From a pajama party to solstice night, Filoli is making Monday nights merry and bright with jolly dress-up prompts; match the theme and receive a gift from Filoli. Santa Saturdays have also Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside. returned this year, with a twist: Santa will be outdoors in the Woodland Garden Court, where visitors are invited to take a socially distanced “selfie” with Santa Claus. Daytime and evening admissions are available at different price points. Due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic and capacity limitations, all visitors must secure tickets beforehand. Face coverings must be worn at all times and social distancing will be observed. The Estate Trail will close at 4 p.m., and the house closes at 7 p.m. Restroom facilities are available onsite. To reserve tickets for holiday events at Filoli House and Gardens, visit https://filoli.org/ events/holidays/.
articles.title: Holidays at Filoli House and Gardens

articles.text: For a change of pace try a breakfast of noodles and cottage cheese. Top with cinnamon sugar and any beverage you like. Are you tired of the everyday routine breakfast? Let’s look on the bright side. There are more holidays ahead. So, whether it’s Christmas, or Hanukkah, Kwanzaa or whatever, I offer the following as a present. This breakfast was a favorite of my father’s and you will enjoy it, too. moisten with broth and cap with the stem end of the pepper. Bake at 400° for about 40–60 minutes, until the peppers are soft. You can serve them as they come from the oven or make a sauce mixing the pan drippings with yogurt and paprika. I like to use hot paprika. Now you are prepared for next year’s Thanksgiving. All you need are four ingredients and literally no skill in the kitchen. Here is a festive breakfast of noodles and cottage cheese. 1. Boil any pasta you like. Flat noodles are best. 2. Add an equal amount of cottage cheese to the noodles. Ricotta cheese is OK. 3. Mix lightly. 4. Serve with a dusting of cinnamon sugar. That’s it. Any beverage will complement this one. Next week: The Musical Gourmet examines the good, the bad, and the ugly in music. Stuffed bell peppers Do you still have some leftover turkey? If not, any ground meat is good, or you can keep it vegetarian. Start with a bell pepper. A red pepper is preferred. The peppers with four bumps are the female peppers and those with three bumps are the male peppers. The four bumps peppers are sweeter. Cut off the stem end but don’t discard; you’ll need it for a cap. It will make a large opening. Clean out the interior of the pepper and add a little olive oil and salt. Meanwhile, dice some onion, celery, carrot and sauté lightly. You can also include some mushrooms. Let the vegetables cool briefly, then combine with your meat. Layer the peppers alternately with a grain like Farro or rice and your meat mixture. You can also use breadcrumbs or matzo meal instead of the grain. When you reach the top of the pepper, Begin your stuffed bell peppers with the peppers, a sharp knife, some leftover turkey or other meat, and olive oil. The finished product: stuffed bell peppers.

articles.text: California Revels returns to Oakland for its 35th season of one of the Bay Area’s premier holiday events. This year’s presentation is Unruly Magic: A Spirited Celebration of the Winter Solstice. Families, friends and holiday revelers are invited to watch wherever they may be, as this year’s production is entirely online, and can be viewed from December 12-20 at www.californiarevels.org. It will stream in High-Definition on Vimeo and YouTube, with live interactive components on Zoom. Audiences of all ages can celebrate the Winter Solstice with traditional music, dance, ritual, and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance.” The production features top musicians, actors, and featured performers. This year’s show includes Shay Black and Windborne Singers. Directed by Jeri Reed, newly filmed pieces are blended with archival footage to create a dynamic and moving feast for the eyes, ears, and spirit. The story of Unruly Magic Approaching the longest night of the year, a young Reveler turns to a magical staff to help her find a way through somber and troubled times. The staff, imbued Meara, from the 2019 Christmas Revels: A Solstice Journey Through Time. Meara is the main character of this year’s Christmas Revels: Unruly Magic. with ancient lore, takes her on an adventure that isn’t quite what she had in mind. Magic and mystery, spirits and song take the reins for this journey of the heart. The ancient traditions of bonfires, rituals, dances, and songs that have sustained generations through struggle and celebration are rekindled this Solstice, proving that tradition – and magic – live on. Dates and times of the seven performances are listed below. Saturday, December 12, 1:00 p.m. Sunday, December 13, 1:00 p.m. Friday, December 18, 7:00 p.m. Saturday, December 19, 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Sunday, December 20, 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Tickets are $20-$175 and are available online at www.CaliforniaRevels.org. For details and more information, call the box office at 650-534-6766 Monday to Friday from 11:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Unruly Magic is directed by Jeri Reed and Music Director Shira Kammen; Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director; and Marzena Jones is Children’s Music Director. California Revels Executive Director is Lisa Lowe.
articles.title: Full chorus, elaborate costumes, music, dance, and a dragon

articles.text: In this challenging era when the light of Christ is so deeply needed, the annual Christmas Concert at First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland will once again bring glorious musical performances and spiritual uplift to the community and beyond – thanks to its first-ever virtual concert, available online throughout December. Everyone is invited to tune in and listen to Christmas favorites and new arrangements performed by talented, well-known Bay Area musicians – sopranos Shawnette Sulker and Katy Stephan, tenor Darron Flagg, baritone Martin Bell, classical guitarist Richard Flores and organist Michael Moran and a rousing rendition of Handel’s Messiah. Stephan and Moran are the regular musicians for the church. The Sunday School Students will read the Bible account of the birth of Jesus. Beginning December 1st, a link to the concert will be available on the church website at: www. ChristianScienceOakland.org. For more information, call 510-832-2364, or visit the Christian Science Reading Room at 1000 Broadway in Oakland, open Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
articles.title: Christian Science Christmas Concert now online

articles.text: The editors of The Times Book Review recently selected their choice of best fiction and best nonfiction titles of this year. Having a great book to dive into can make staying at home not only possible, but preferable. For full descriptions, prices and links to buy go to: https:// www.nytimes.com/2020/11/23/ b o o k s / r e v i e w/ b e s t- b o o k s . html?searchResultPosition=3 A Children’s Bible W.W. Norton & Company With an unfailingly light touch, Millet delivers a wry fable about climate change, imbuing foundational myths with new meaning and, finally, hope. Deacon King Kong Riverhead Books McBride conducts his antic symphony with deep feeling, never losing sight of the suffering and inequity within the merriment. Hamnet Alfred A. Knopf This novel gives flesh and feeling to a historical mystery: how the death of Shakespeare’s 11-year-old son, Hamnet, in 1596, may have shaped his play Hamlet. Homeland Elegies Little, Brown & Company At once personal and political, Akhtar’s second novel can read like a collection of pitch-perfect essays that give shape to a prismatic identity. James McBride’s Deacon King Kong is one of three finalists for the 2021 Andrew Carnegie Medals for Excellence in Fiction, to be announced on February 4. The Vanishing Half Riverhead Books Beneath the polished surface and enthralling plotlines of Bennett’s second novel lies a provocative meditation on the possibilities and limits of self-definition. Shakespeare in a Divided America Penguin Press Shapiro takes two huge cultural hyper-objects — Shakespeare and America — and dissects the effects of their collision. Uncanny Valley MCD/Farrar, Straus & Giroux Wiener’s stylish memoir is an uncommonly literary chronicle of tech-world disillusionment. War Random House MacMillan argues that war – fighting and killing – is so intimately bound up with what it means to be human that viewing it as an aberration misses the point.
articles.title: New York Times – 10 Best Books of 2020

articles.text: For the scores of single 20 and 30 somethings of Piedmont, the nightlife scene has all but disappeared in the last few weeks due to the COVID- 19 induced curfew and stay at home order. Safety restrictions have been in place for almost nine months now, but it feels more like nine years. Staying up late and being out of the house, even if masked and alone, can give an illusion of a social life for us Millennials. (I prefer the label Gen Y). Beginning on November 21, California Governor Gavin Newsome enacted the curfew or “limited stay at-home order” that forbids non-essential work, movement and gathering between 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. When announced at the beginning of Thanksgiving week, the news decimated the collective of Piedmont’s hip, young, single crowd; goodbye Friendsgiving. Beginning December 7, outdoors and indoors dining is disallowed, hello Top Ramen. As of December 8, 54 of California’s 58 counties are in the purple tier, and 99.9 percent of the population. This status put the kibosh on Piedmont’s plan for the reopening of elementary schools at the start of December. Many parents may lament that today, December 9, is not the first week of school for their 5th graders. Within the ranks of Piedmont’s lively, unmarried population school may not be a concern but the curfew has grounded Piedmont’s night owls. Woe are we, Gen Y folk long for the days of hanging out front of Mulberry’s at 10:15 p.m. playing pickup sticks. It is just not as fun during the day. And whatever shall I do with all this nighttime bungee jumping gear I bought for the Oakland Ave. bridge? Should I bungee jump in the daytime in a glow in the dark suit? I think not. If you think the stock market stinks, the descent of the value of used bungee equipment will give you whiplash. I suppose no one trusts prestretched bungees or harnesses left out in the scorching Piedmont sun. With a curfew how can we head over the Piedmont border to pick up a late-night VHS at Silver Screen or a fancy new DVD at Video Room (still operating)? Did you know they disconnected the number for POPCORN (a machine that gave the precise time)? That number used to satiate the boredom of youth in the 90s. “At the tone, the time will be….too late to go out.” How about the paintball wars in Piedmont Park at night (with biodegradable paint of course), could a group activity be more socially distant? How can I howl at the moon from Scenic Ave. without leaving the house, a Zoom Howl? The portion of my stimulus check not used on bungee gear went into infrared night binoculars to document the behavior of nocturnal animals. How am I supposed to sleep with racoons, possums, skunks and owls skulking around unmonitored? They could be anywhere. Is nighttime street luging down Blair Ave. really a COVID risk? pages.text: Wednesday, December 9, 2020 21 New York Times – 10 Best Books of 2020 The editors of The Times Book Review recently selected their choice of best fiction and best nonfiction titles of this year. Having a great book to dive into can make staying at home not only possible, but preferable. For full descriptions, prices and links to buy go to: https:// www.nytimes.com/2020/11/23/ b o o k s / r e v i e w/ b e s t- b o o k s . html?searchResultPosition=3 FICTION A Children’s Bible W.W. Norton & Company By Lydia Millet With an unfailingly light touch, Millet delivers a wry fable about climate change, imbuing foundational myths with new meaning and, finally, hope. Deacon King Kong Riverhead Books By James McBride McBride conducts his antic symphony with deep feeling, never losing sight of the suffering and inequity within the merriment. Hamnet Alfred A. Knopf By Maggie O’Farrell This novel gives flesh and feeling to a historical mystery: how the death of Shakespeare’s 11-year-old son, Hamnet, in 1596, may have shaped his play Hamlet. HUMOR Piedmont nightlife crushed by curfew By Jay Russell For the scores of single 20 and 30 somethings of Piedmont, the nightlife scene has all but disappeared in the last few weeks due to the COVID- 19 induced curfew and stay at home order. Safety restrictions have been in place for almost nine months now, but it feels more like nine years. Staying up late and being out of the house, even if masked and alone, can give an illusion of a social life for us Millennials. (I prefer the label Gen Y). Beginning on November 21, California Governor Gavin Newsome enacted the curfew or “limited stay at-home order” that forbids non-essential work, movement and gathering between 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. When announced at the beginning of Thanksgiving week, the news decimated the collective of Piedmont’s hip, young, single crowd; goodbye Friendsgiving. Beginning December 7, outdoors and indoors dining is disallowed, hello Top Ramen. As of December 8, 54 of California’s 58 counties are in the purple tier, and 99.9 percent of the population. This status put the kibosh on Piedmont’s plan for the reopening of elementary schools at the start of December. Many parents may lament that today, December 9, is not the first week of school for their 5th graders. Within the ranks of Piedmont’s lively, unmarried population school may not be a concern but the curfew has grounded Piedmont’s night owls. Woe are we, Gen Y folk long for the days of hanging out front of Mulberry’s at 10:15 p.m. playing pickup sticks. It is just not as fun during the day. And whatever shall I do with all this nighttime bungee jumping gear I bought for the Oakland Ave. bridge? Should I bungee jump in the daytime in a glow in the dark suit? I think not. If you think the stock market stinks, the descent of the value of used bungee equipment will give you whiplash. I suppose no one trusts prestretched bungees or harnesses left out in the scorching Piedmont sun. With a curfew how can we head over the Piedmont border to pick up a late-night VHS at Silver Screen or a fancy new DVD at Video Room (still operating)? Did you know they disconnected the number for POPCORN (a machine that gave the precise time)? That number used to satiate the boredom of youth in the 90s. “At the tone, the time will be….too late to go out.” How about the paintball wars in Piedmont Park at night (with biodegradable paint of course), could a group activity be more socially distant? How can I howl at the moon from Scenic Ave. without leaving the house, a Zoom Howl? The portion of my stimulus check not used on bungee gear went into infrared night binoculars to document the behavior of nocturnal animals. How am I supposed to sleep with racoons, possums, skunks and owls skulking around unmonitored? They could be anywhere. Is nighttime street luging down Blair Ave. really a COVID risk? A curfew may be the best time to do so with fewer cars on the road. Oh well, it is all for the greater good, I suppose. After all, this virus stuff is no joke. Even the 20 and 30 somethings in Piedmont will have to sacrifice if we ever want to see an after-bedtime Roller Derby in Kiefer Court. On the palate it is medium bodied with a fleshy core of ripe fruit and some youthful chewy tannins that will melt away with bottle age. Charming and subtle, it has a long clean finish. • 2017 Jean-Ernest Descombes Morgon Cote du Py, $24 Morgon is one of the biggest bodied of the Beaujolais and can last surprisingly well in the cellar. This has a gorgeous, voluptuous bouquet with pure black 2017 Jean-Ernest Descombes Morgon Cote du Py While I know there are folks who have not yet discovered Beaujolais, I have yet to meet someone who dislikes it. It is a charming, fruity, refreshing, early drinking, easy-going wine that goes with tons of foods and is inexpensive. What’s not to like? In many ways it is the opposite of its closest neighbor Burgundy, whose wines are complex, scarce, require serious aging, and cost an arm and a leg. Burgundy was once planted with Pinot Noir and Gamay in roughly the same amounts. In 1395 the Duke of Burgundy decided he didn’t like Gamay and banished it from being planted in Burgundy. So, the Gamay grape migrated to an area just north of Burgundy near the town of Villefranche sur Saone, where it has flourished ever since. The Beaujolais area now produces hundreds of millions of bottles of wine a year and is also, with its green rolling hills, one of the most scenic wine areas to visit. Unlike Burgundy where you have to have an appointment at most places, the Beaujolais vintners have their doors open and welcome drop-in visitors. The two major wine producers in Beaujolais are Louis Jadot and Georges Duboeuf. They are “negociants” who work with hundreds of small farmers to blend and sell their wines. There are 10 villages that make up the heart of Beaujolais – Brouilly, Regnie, Chiroubles, Cote de Brouilly, Fleurie, Saint-Amour, Chenas, Julienas, Morgon, and Moulin-aVent. It is often these names rather than Beaujolais that you will see on the bottle and the name of the Village connotes a step up in quality than regular Beaujolais. As mentioned above, Beaujolais goes with a wide variety of foods and is the perfect picnic wine. It is very important to chill the bottle for a half hour in the fridge as its’ not as good at room temperature. I had the opportunity to taste some of the wines of the great Georges Duboeuf. From humble beginnings he has built an empire that sends 30 million bottles of wine all around the world each year. What is stunning about the Duboeuf wines is that even though they are mass produced he retains a very high level of quality. The following wines are ones chosen by Duboeuf from small grow-

articles.text: There are two major types of quality port – Vintage and Tawny. Vintage port is bottled early and left to mature in the bottles, something that takes a long time. If you buy a bottle of the current vintage port (2017) it may not be ready to drink for 10 years. For those of us who are getting up in years, this can be a problem. There is a solution however: tawny port. Tawny port is left in the barrels at the winery to age anywhere from 10 to 40 years. So, when it is released it is totally ready to drink with no further aging required. Its time in barrel turns the wine from dark purple to a tawny golden brown, hence the name. This beautiful wine starts slow and builds to a nice crescendo, with the acidity emerging to cut the fruit. This elegant wine has a semi-sweet finish to go with its vibrancy and energy. It’s a pretty picture overall with caramel, molasses and hints of chocolate on the finish. This wine cries out for a bowl of cashews, a nice pipe and a roaring fire. Originally published in the Piedmont Post on January 1, 2020. This has a gorgeous, voluptuous bouquet with pure black 2017 Chateau de Saint-Amour Saint-Amour cherries and cassis fruit that is very well-defined and harmonious. The palate is medium to full bodied with very smooth tannins. This is a suave Morgon that will be even better in a few years. • 2017 Chateau de SaintAmour Saint-Amour, $22 This is the northernmost Beaujolais Cru and the smallest and I have always found its wines especially charming. Aromas of raspSee Wine Corner on page 30 WINE OF THE MONTH Dow’s Tawny Porto 10 Years Old, $37 By Pierre DuMont There are two major types of quality port – Vintage and Tawny. Vintage port is bottled early and left to mature in the bottles, something that takes a long time. If you buy a bottle of the current vintage port (2017) it may not be ready to drink for 10 years. For those of us who are getting up in years, this can be a problem. There is a solution however: tawny port. Tawny port is left in the barrels at the winery to age anywhere from 10 to 40 years. So, when it is released it is totally ready to drink with no further aging required. Its time in barrel turns the wine from dark purple to a tawny golden brown, hence the name. This beautiful wine starts slow and builds to a nice crescendo, with the acidity emerging to cut the fruit. This elegant wine has a semi-sweet finish to go with its vibrancy 2017 Jean-Ernest Descombes Morgon Cote du Py By Pierre DuMont While I know there are folks who have not yet discovered Beaujolais, I have yet to meet someone who dislikes it. It is a charming, fruity, refreshing, early drinking, easy-going wine that goes with tons of foods and is inexpensive. What’s not to like? In many ways it is the opposite of its closest neighbor Burgundy, whose wines are complex, scarce, require serious aging, and cost an arm and a leg. Burgundy was once planted with Pinot Noir and Gamay in roughly the same amounts. In 1395 the Duke of Burgundy decided he didn’t like Gamay and banished it from being planted in Burgundy. So, the Gamay grape migrated to an area just north of Burgundy near the town of Villefranche sur Saone, where it has flourished ever since. The Beaujolais area now produces hundreds of millions of bottles of wine a year and is also, with its green rolling hills, one of the most scenic wine areas to visit. Unlike Burgundy where you have to have an appointment at most places, the Beaujolais vintners have their doors open and welcome drop-in visitors. The two major wine producers in Beaujolais are Louis Jadot and Georges Duboeuf. They are “negociants” who work with hundreds of small farmers to blend and sell their wines. There are 10 villages that make up the heart of Beaujolais – Brouilly, Regnie, Chiroubles, Cote de Brouilly, Fleurie, Saint-Amour, Chenas, Julienas, Morgon, and Moulin-aVent. It is often these names rather than Beaujolais that you will see on the bottle and the name of the Village connotes a step up in quality than regular Beaujolais. As mentioned above, Beaujolais goes with a wide variety of foods and is the perfect picnic wine. It is very important to chill the bottle for a half hour in the fridge as its’ not as good at room temperature. articles.text: Key volunteer with Turkey Trot, Center for the Arts, Chamber Music Festival Susan Freeman, a resident of Piedmont for 33 years, died on November 23, 2020 after battling cancer for five and a half years. She passed away surrounded by her loving family one week after her 70th birthday. Born on November 16, 1950 in Chicago, Illinois, she was the daughter of Peter and Rita Cotsirilos. She graduated from the University of Wisconsin, and received an MBA from Northwestern University in 1976, where she was one of few women to attend graduate business school. After college she took a job in the management training program at Harris Bank in Chicago, where she met her future husband, Peter. They were married in 1978 and moved to California that same year. Susan was a force of nature. Her energy filled the room and energized any task that she undertook. Susan was always quick to step in and offer help for new projects. She was a co-founder and leader for many years of the Piedmont Turkey Trot, which is now the city’s second largest public event. Her son Crosby was the overall winner several times, and he and his wife Jessica were the overall winners in 2019, the first couple to win the title. “Susan was instrumental in the revival and ultimate success of the Piedmont Turkey Trot,” said Marilyn Weber, current lead organizer. “Years ago, Susan called me when she learned that the leadership interest in managing and running the race was waning. She asked if we could work together to ensure that year’s race would happen. “This simple call started a many-year friendship. We both jumped in enthusiastically and developed a strong, collaborative and, most importantly, joyful friendship. Her ideas for improvements were never ending and her passion for this event and the community it served was endless,” she said. “What I will miss most about Susan was her deep care and affection for her family and friends. She was always there if you needed a good cheer or a good cry. She would be the friend you call if life’s obstacles were getting you down and she would always say, ‘Yes. What can I do to help?’” “We have lost a gem,” Weber added. Susan and her husband were active members of St. John’s Episcopal Church in Montclair, where she was an enthusiastic organizer of varied gala events. She was a key volunteer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, where she was a mainstay of the annual weeklong Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. “Susan was a cherished presence and a tireless volunteer who ran our box office during the first few summers of the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival,” said co-founder Wayne Lee, a PiedLongtime resident and Piedmont volunteer Susan Freeman died on November 23 after battling cancer for nearly six years. She was 70. mont native. “She gave us her complete support, her cheeky and cheerful feedback and led by example when she took it upon herself to bring our uneaten refreshments to the homeless. We miss her dearly,” said Wayne Lee, co-founder of the annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. “Susan Freeman not only handled the box office for theater productions at the Center for the Arts, she served as the unofficial den mother for the production team. She would see a need and without fanfare, would make things happen,’ said Sue Malick, president of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “Whether it was the Scottish National team lacrosse coach she brought from Scotland for the high school girls’ team, or college admission coaching for Piedmont students, or making sure that everyone had a seat for musical and theatrical productions at the Center, Susan made it work.” In her later years she was a college admissions coach and helped hundreds of high school students navigate through the challenge of college selection and applications. She sought the right fit and was justifiably proud that only two of her clients did not graduate from their original choices. Her children, Crosby and Libby, were products of the Piedmont schools from kindergarten through 12th grade. She was a talented cook who took great pleasure in hosting dinner parties. Through it all, Susan remained astoundingly hopeful and grateful for the life that had been given to her. She will be sorely missed. She is survived by Peter, her husband of 42 years, and by son Crosby and wife Jessica, and daughter Libby, all of Oakland. She is also survived by her mother Rita Cotsirilos, and siblings Steven, Patty, and Peter Jr. The family suggests that memorial donations in the name of Susan Freeman be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, c/o Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. Funds received will be used for a memorial tree which will be planted in the city in the future.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 9, 2020 25 Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Good suggestions for dogs bored with Covid By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: Well, the holidays are getting closer and I need some gift ideas for Pepper, our funny fur ball. She’s a terrific dog but she gets bored and seems to chew through treats in minutes that are supposed to last for hours, Then she starts yapping for more. Do you have any creative ideas? Frustrated, –Samantha and Pepper Pot the Mix Dear Samantha and Pepper Pot: Have you heard of the Furbo Treat Tosser? It’s on Amazon and it’s not exactly cheap. The price has just been cut to $129. You fill it with 100 treats and you can toss Pepper treats from anywhere, anytime so that you can wear her out. It also has an adjustable Barking Alert and 2-way audio so that you can adjust a barking sensor and stop the yapping. There’s also a live stream video camera that allows you to watch Pepper day or night with a 4x Zoom and a 160-degree angle lens. I’ve only heard amazing compliments about the Furbo. Besides, what dog doesn’t love a surprise treat to chase. To top it off, it looks like a sleek, modern sculpture. It’s worth a try to calm down your hot Pepper! –Abby Dear Abby: I’m concerned with all my SIPing that our bulldog Antonio is bored. After having given up chewing on our shoes for a year, he’s back at it and also enjoys digging up the garden. What can I do? I don’t take him with me on my errands as often because I’m trying to be more efficient with my time in public places because of Covid. Is Antonio bored or needs training? Or is he really becoming a bully dog? –Suzanna & Antonio the Bull Dog Dear Suzanna and Antonio: Sounds like Antonio is bored. I’m hearing a lot about this sort of behavior these days (see above). Good dogs getting into mischief, wreaking havoc in the garden, even being disinterested in their toys and now preferring your shoes. To stop destructive behavior by dogs, it’s usually easier to offer them constructive options. Often the dogs need physical and mental stimulation just like we do. Unfortunately, they can’t read a book. Try giving Antonio a frozen Kong to gnaw on—those weird thick plastic toys you put treats and peanut butter into and freeze. One tip: give Antonio the Kong at the same time every day...after a walk would be ideal. It may seem silly to us but to canines the Kong is quite a puzzle to work out. My guess is that he will be better on the walk and disinterested in your shoes as he waits for you to give him his daily Kong. Another fun idea is to teach Antonio to chase bubbles. Yeah, those same bubbles kids chase. Dogs definitely enjoy bubble blowing and aren’t bored. But unlike the frozen Kong, you have to be blowing those bubbles for him to chase so it’s not as easy when you need to do other things. Yet another easy and inexpensive trick is to go to the butcher and ask him to cut up a beef bone into ½-inch slices for Antonio. Tell the butcher that you need the bone for the dog, and it must be beef – no pork or chicken bones.) Before you give a slice to Antonio, you’ll have to boil the bone until it changes color. Let it cool and then let him go. Most dogs love to chew on them and to top it off, it’s a good way for teeth to be cleaned. The dog’s breath may still need some help, however. The best thing is to try to keep Antonio on a consistent schedule and have some new tricks ready when the stir-crazy activity starts. Small changes can make a big impact. Good luck with the Bonehead. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com. articles.text: As we finish up Thanksgiving leftovers and look forward to other food-centric holidays in December, food is on my mind. Turkeys, cookies, figgy pudding – food is an enduring part of the holiday season. Food is also an important issue in both the environmental and the humanitarian spheres. More than enough food is currently produced to feed everybody in the world, but 9 percent of the global population, or 670 million people, go hungry each year. A large amount is lost due to food waste, while a significant portion of grains go to biofuels and feeding livestock instead of people. There are numerous theories about how to feed the world, especially as our global population is projected to reach 10 billion by 2050. As we approach the goal of feeding everyone, we must also grapple with how to make food production less polluting. Environmentally, food is both an opportunity and a challenge. Our food system currently accounts for about 30 percent of global GHG emissions. This is larger than GHG emissions from either the transportation or energy sector. If we stopped all other emissions right now, emissions stemming from food would still stop us from meeting the goals outlined in the Paris Climate Accord. Meat, dairy, fish and eggs account for over half of food related emissions. Two-thirds of freshwater removal is for irrigation, while 43 percent of land is used for farming and livestock. As countries go through economic gains, more people want to eat red meat. This trend can be seen in places like China, where meat consumption has grown 15 times in the last 60 years. Raising enough livestock to feed more people is going to be difficult as we are simultaneously trying to reduce emissions. Fortunately, there are solutions. Relying on individual actions alone is unlikely to make a significant impact, but using policy to make change is one way to begin. The meat and dairy industries receive over $37 billion in federal subsidies annually. Using that money in other ways to encourage lower carbon diets could be a first step. Changing public health efforts to encourage less meat consumption could also make a difference. Meat isn’t the only issue. Changing how we farm can also make a big difference. Since the green revolution of the 1950’s, farmers have used fertilizers and mechanized systems to produce extraordinary yields. While the benefits of this style of farming seem obvious, there are drawbacks as well. Using fertilizers can lead to an insidious positive feedback loop, where more fertilizer needs to be used each year, requiring more resources annually. Relying on high yield practices can also mean more food waste. Examining farming techniques and consciously choosing lower carbon practices can both reduce emissions and costs, while keeping the farm land we all rely upon healthy for years to come. It is possible to both reduce emissions stemming from agriculture and feed everyone in a healthy way. The trick is determining how to do so, and quickly. Food is an important, and sometimes overlooked, aspect of climate change. Changing how individuals and countries eat food must be addressed now if we want to reduce emissions by a significant amount. In that vein, the City of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect are hosting a movie screening of Kiss That Ground on regenerative agriculture, which could be part of the solution we need. To sign up and take part in our free discussion visit this link: https://events. kissthegroundmovie.com/event/ piedmont-kiss-the-ground-community-discussion. Nate Redinbo is working in the Planning and Building Department for the next year as Piedmont’s Civic Spark fellow. He will be publishing a bi-monthly article on environmental topics that affect Piedmonters.
articles.title: Impact of food production on environment

articles.text: The invention of farming changed human history forever. Before farming, humans were primarily hunter-gatherers. As we have adopted new methods of planting and procuring food, the world we rely on for resources has changed as well. It is time to come to a reckoning about the methods that we use to farm, eat food, and what resources we use along the way. Climate change has been influenced by many different sectors, but one that is not often talked about is agriculture. Following the “Green Revolution” of the 1960’s and the increased yields brought about by advancements such as increased pesticide usage and the mechanization of equipment, farming radically changed both domestically and internationally. While many of the outcomes have been beneficial, there have been serious side effects, including environmental outcomes that must be addressed immediately if we want our food production to continue. These issues and more are addressed in the documentary Kiss the Ground, which released this year. Although “soil health” doesn’t sound thrilling, I promise that the revelations from this documentary are surprising and worthwhile. Caring for our shared environment involves all of us, from policy makers to consumers to farmers. With all this in mind, the City of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect have teamed up to bring you a free screening of the documentary film, Kiss the Ground. Kiss the Ground is available on Netflix if you have an account, but you can also watch it for free on Vimeo through the city’s link. The screening became available to viewers on December 8 and will be available through Thursday, December 10. We are encouraging registration through the link. This free registration will let you watch the movie for free, join our Q & A session with Jessica Handy, a member of the film’s production team. Your name will automatically be entered in a raffle for an EBCE gift card to reduce your energy bill. articles.text: At a meeting of the Piedmont Public Safety Committee on Thursday, December 3, the Piedmont Police Department discussed its participation in a new county program aimed at better serving people experiencing mental health crises In July the PPD began partnering with Community Assessment Transport Teams (CATT), a project launched by the Alameda County Emergency Medical Services Agency. Each two-person CATT team is comprised of a licensed clinician and a paramedic. They conduct evaluations of individuals possibly undergoing a mental health crisis and, if necessary, will transport the person to an appropriate facility or provide resources. A goal of the CATT project is “to provide better and more appropriate resources for people experiencing mental health crises or other issues when the police are frequently called to,” explained Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. ual when certain conditions are met. The person must be cooperative and not require restraints. Additionally, the person must not require emergency room care for an injury or medical complaint. The person must also be able to walk without assistance and maintain a steady gate. Since August, PPD has called for a CATT unit 10 times, and teams have responded in six of those cases. In the other four cases, CATT teams were unavailable due to demands on their time. The County pilot program began on July 20 with three teams and was expanded to five teams on October 11. Currently CATT teams are working throughout Alameda County from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. seven days a week. When a CATT unit is unavailable, officers will default to existing protocols. These include evaluating if the individual is a danger to themselves or others and assessing if the person is gravely disabled. Jerri Applegate Randrup, the Communications Director of Alameda County EMS, told the Post that the agency hopes to have a dozen teams serving the county by June next year. The pilot partnership, which includes several police departments across the county, has been declared successful so far, an appraisal that was echoed by Bowers at the committee meeting. ALCO EMS says that it hopes the program can receive additional funding to continue beyond the pilot program’s scheduled end in 2023. “Law enforcement has welcomed CATT staff who can take over care of the client to ensure they obtain the resources they need,” Randrup said. “The team arrives to meet with officers who are already on scene. Officers can transfer responsibility for the client to CATT who will perform an on-scene assessment and triage, freeing up the officer to respond to other law enforcement needs.” Bowers said that he is appreciative of the CATT pilot, but added “there needs to be even more capacity building in this space to meet the demands.” “At a time when we’re looking for different and better ways to respond to community issues, I was hopeful that this program could bring an enhanced response to our mental health responses which affect a cross section of our community,” said Bowers. “Communities throughout the country are involved in various efforts of reimagining response to mental health calls. Time will tell which efforts show themselves to be a best practice.” – Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers The pilot CATT program comes in the wake of nationwide protests regarding police brutality. Many researchers and advocates have noted that when a person is experiencing a mental health crisis in public, the police are usually dispatched. However, police officers are not the best trained professionals that could respond to such situations, and the presence of officers can sometimes exacerbate a person’s crisis. “A clinician has the ability to use clinical skills to address the situation,” explained Francesca Tenenbaum of the Mental Health Association of Alameda County. “They also have access to all the different resources in the system including contacting the person’s providers so they can truly make involuntary detention the last resort.” Piedmont Police members were trained in CATT procedures in July, and the department began calling in the specialized teams in August. articles.text: Funding signals go-ahead for playscape project at Linda-Beach The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) presented City Administrator Sara Lillevand with a check for $100,000 on December 2. The money will be used to help the Recreation Department move forward with its plans to redesign Linda-Beach Playfield, to include a playscape near the Oakland Avenue overpass. The check was presented to Lillevand by former PBF President Patty Siskind at the city’s virtual tree-lighting ceremony outside the Community Hall. The Linda Beach Master Plan conceptual design was adopted by City Council, and PBF helped make it a reality. In 2017, PBF began funding the design and installation of a new “playscape” at Linda Beach Playfield. The California Nature Playscape redesigns an area that is paved with asphalt into an outdoor recreation area for children. According to a brochure from the master plan, the all-new California Nature Playscape will “take full advantage of the topography of the site, connect to nature, and create climbing and play elements that allow for free-form exploration.” Once construction of the California Nature Playscape is completed, renovation of the Linda Beach tot lot will follow. The Tot Lot at Linda Beach is one of the most heavily used city recreation facilities and is long due for an upgrade. “$100,000 will go a long way to help us move forward with the Linda Beach master plan. The inspiration for the whole [project], was a wonderful community process, which several Piedmont Beautification Foundation members participated in,” Lillevand commented. “It will be an amazing addition to the city, and to an area between the Playfield and Oakland Avenue Bridge, which currently is not just underutilized, it’s unutilized.” Piedmont Beautification Foundation began working on the Linda Beach playscape project in 2017 following a master plan approved by council. Renderings are provided by PBF.

In fact, our artists have been so enamored with PCA that several have used the space for their own recording projects. Our series, Berkeley Symphony & Friends, has inspired other chamber groups and performing arts organizations to present their offerings in Piedmont. The ease of access and parking, and the overall warm atmosphere of the Center makes for an extremely pleasurable patron experience, one that keeps them coming over and over again. Our guests thoroughly enjoy the revolving art exhibits as well, and often purchase works on display after our concerts. The PCA Board and staff has consistently been extremely helpful and supportive. We cherish our relationship with PCA, and, as soon as possible, we so look forward to performing again in our favorite home away from home! –Rene Mandel Artistic Director, Berkeley Symphony Arts for another 10 years. I was one of the very first artists to show my work in the new space and have been able to show there 6 times total in the course of these 9 years. One reason I show at the PCA is that it is the only place I know that is affordable to rent and wont charge a 50 percent cut. For a beginning artist like me, a reasonably priced hometown venue to show art and gather as a community is a gift and a rarity. It’s impossible to find that in the Bay Area short of spending full days and full weekends at open studios. Also, as a Wildwood art teacher being able to invite parents, students, friends, neighbors, all a few blocks from their homes to socialize, share some snacks and see my work was important to me and so easy and fun for everyone. Piedmont shows its support of the arts – visual, musical, and theatre – by allowing the space to be used by so many local groups that would otherwise be without options. I’ve been able to attend student art shows there, music recitals, concerts, art shows, photography shows, plays, and lectures, all at the PCA. I love the arts that have come to our own town through the PCA. Reclaiming 801 Magnolia for more profitable and rental purposes would be misguided in my opinion and a huge loss to the core of our arts community. In fact, it’s the only visual arts venue for display in town and for many other arts uses. –Suzie Skugstad Artist, Art teacher

The City of Piedmont has accepted the official certificate of election results prepared by the Alameda County Registrar of Voters. The county Registrar certified the results on December 1. Locally, Piedmont had a total of 9,031 registered voters prior to November 3. A total of 8,123 Piedmont voters cast ballots, 7,687 by mail and 436 in person between Saturday and Tuesday, October 31 through November 3. Piedmont remained at the top of Alameda County’s list for voter turnout with 89.95 percent of its eligible voters. City Council Election Incumbent Jen Cavenaugh and Conna McCarthy comfortably took the two open seats for City Council. Cavenaugh received 5,771 votes, and McCarthy received 4,690 votes. Connie Herrick, in her first bid for council received 1,461 votes, School Board Election There was high interest in the Piedmont School Board this year, an initial pool of six candidates running for three open seats. Incumbent Cory Smegal was the top vote-getter with 5,140 votes. First-time candidate Veronica Anderson-Thigpen received 3,974 votes, and former Education Foundation board member Hilary Cooper received 3,026 votes. Jason Kelley barely missed being elected, falling 157 votes back of Cooper. Hari Titan, who twice before ran for school board, received 1,992 votes. James Crawford-Jakubiak withdrew from the race. Write-ins accounted for 53 total votes. Measure TT Measure TT, the proposed increase in the Real Estate Transfer Tax from $13 to $17 per $1000 of the value at the time of sale, failed to receive a 50.01-percent majority to pass. A total of 7,744 votes were cast, with the measure failing at 47.8 percent approval. The voter breakdown was 4,041 no votes and 3,703 yes. Measure UU In the city’s most widely publicized election item, Measure UU, a public bond proposing to rebuild the Community Pool for $19 million, was approved by voters at 68.5 percent. It needed a two-thirds majority to pass. A total of 5,336 residents voted yes and 2,451 voted no, More people voted for the two ballot measures than for public office candidates. articles.text: For so many years, Santa’s come to your town To meet you, and greet you, and see how you’ve grown. Hearing your stories, both naughty and nice, Have gladdened his heart like pearls beyond price. Most important to Santa is that you stay safe: Wear masks when you have to and shelter in place. So this special year I’ve a plan that can’t fail; Send all your wishes to Santa by mail. Santa loves to get letters and this special year Those letters can say what you want him to hear. A picture, of course, is a special addition To thoughts and wishes you may have written. And to ensure Christmas success, Please include a return address. A big mailbox near the big Christmas tree Will hold all the letters from you to me. And what we hope is even better, Santa will answer everyone’s letter. Come Christmas Eve, Santa visits each home With blessings and laughter and gifts for each one. So celebrate Christmas in joy without end, Staying happy and safe with family and friends. –Santa Claus, December 2020

articles.text: Everyone has had to transition this year – even Santa Claus. Santa Claus showed up at the virtual tree-lighting ceremony last Wednesday and urged kids to send well wishes and Christmas lists to him by mail this year. A brightly colored mailbox handcrafted by David Hopkins of Schoolmates fame has been placed on the patio outside the Community Hall and just below the 80-foot redwood that now sparkles with its Christmas lights. This is the first year that Piedmont will have a mailbox to Santa as part of its holiday celebrations. Traditionally, children line up inside the Community Hall to meet with Santa after the tree-lighting ceremony, but strict shelter-in-place guidelines due to the coronavirus scuttled that plan this year. The Piedmont Recreation Department has partnered with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the principal nonprofit organization behind the tree lighting, to execute this new addition. It was the Foundation’s idea to include a mailbox to the North Pole. Santa added that, to “ensure Christmas success,” all letters should include a return address. Kids who send letters with a return address can expect to receive a reply from Santa. Schoolmates Kindergarten students take a field trip to the Letters to Santa Mailbox in front of the Community Center on Monday, December 7. Pictured are Eloise Tunney-McDowell (left), Madeline Staley, Pierce Tunney-McDowell, Essie Bresovec, and Christian Guevara.

articles.text: About a dozen members of the Piedmont Garden Club and Beautification Foundation woke up early yesterday to string festive lights on the 80-foot tall redwood tree in front of the Community Hall. Public Works employees began installing strands of colored lights on the tree starting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, December 1, using a hydraulic boom lift. The Beautification Foundation took over the preparations for the ceremony more than 50 years ago, in the mid-1960s. The labor-intensive process begins with volunteers checking each bulb to ensure they are untangled and working. Unwound, the lights cover the entirety of the Community Hall floor, and are then carried strand by strand to the base of the tree, where they are raised to the top by a cherry picker. This year, volunteers observed social distancing and each person donned a mask. Traditionally, a large crowd gathers for a nighttime celebration when the lights are first turned on. A virtual tree lighting will be observed tonight, Wednesday, December 2, at 7 p.m. on KCOM, Piedmont Channel 27. A tree-lighting ceremony was taped last night, December 1, with speeches by Mayor Bob McBain, City Administrator Sara Lillevand, Piedmont Beautification Foundation president Gayle Lambert, and former foundation president Patty Siskind. Music will be performed by the Piedmont High School Troubadours. Residents are asked not to gather in person for this year’s tree-lighting. A youth representative from the Make-a-wish foundation, Ella Wade, a Piedmont resident, Volunteers from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Garden Club assist the Public Works Department in stringing festive lights onto the 80-foot-tall redwood tree in front of Community Hall. With the help of a cherry picker, Kent Donaghy and Jim Pichotto of Diamond Tree Service carefully string the lights before tonight’s ceremonial tree lighting. will assist with the tree-lighting ceremony. Santa Claus always makes an appearance for the event but will be sheltering-in-place this year. A special mailbox is fashioned next to the tree for notes destined for the North Pole. Piedmont Garden Club volunteers have ensured that all letters will be delivered to Santa.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is providing free flu shots to the public at Piedmont Community Hall today from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. while supplies last. Flu shots are free to anyone at no cost, with no insurance needed. The Center for Disease Control (CDC) recommends that everyone over the age of six months should get a flu vaccine every season, with some exceptions. “Getting a flu vaccine is more important than ever during 2020 and 2021, to protect yourself and the people around you from flu, and to help reduce the strain on healthcare system responding to the COVID-19 pandemic,” wrote the CDC in a press release. Today’s flu clinic in Piedmont is made possible by the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency and the Alameda County Public Health Department. Piedmont Community Hall is located at 711 Highland Avenue in the middle of Piedmont Main Park. articles.text: Editor: When Proposition 13 passed in 1978, California’s K-12 public schools lost $3 billion in funding overnight. In recent years, the California Budget and Policy Center found that California ranked: • 41st in K-12 spending per student • Last in the number of K-12 students per teacher • Last in the number of K-12 students per guidance counselor • Last in the number of K-12 students per librarian Proposition 15 on November’s ballot would have raised an estimated $6.5 to $11.5 billion annually in revenues for the State’s K-12 schools and community colleges, counties, cities, and special districts. Proposition 15 failed to pass. For the 2021-2022 school year, despite state and local funding including revenue from Measures G&H, the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) will have a shortfall of $1,930 per student. If the Piedmont Education Foundation did not exist, this would be the unfortunate financial reality for our schools and our students. For the last 45 years PEF has raised money from our generous community to help bridge the gap between state and local funding and what it costs to provide an excellent education to our students. The result is that PUSD has been able to lower class sizes, ensure crucial classroom aides and student support, offer AP courses, art, music, science and other vital curriculum to students, and have the resources to keep Piedmont schools as among the highest rated in the State. Regardless of the administration of PUSD, changes in approaches to K-12 education, fluctuations in student enrollment, economic recessions -- and even a global pandemic -- PEF remains steadfast in its mission. It is nonpartisan and focused. Its only mission is to fundraise and foster community engagement in support of Piedmont schools. Please separate any perspectives on how PUSD is navigating in-person or distance learning from the purpose of PEF’s Giving Campaign. The financial outlook for K-12 public schools in California has not changed under the COVID-19 pandemic. Some argue that without intervention, it will become worse. Withholding a Giving Campaign contribution today only sets the district back in its capacity to provide the highest level of education to our students during the next school year. Instead, let’s step up to support our schools and give them the resources they need to be ready for our students next fall, arguably after one of the most challenging academic years they will experience. Learn more about PEF’s Giving Campaign and make a contribution today at https://www. pied montedfou ndation.org / donate/. –Emily Harrold Member, Piedmont Education Foundation Board 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 922-8711 • email: news@piedmontpost.org REVIEWERS

The result is that PUSD has been able to lower class sizes, ensure crucial classroom aides and student support, offer AP courses, art, music, science and other vital curriculum to students, and have the resources to keep Piedmont schools as among the highest rated in the State. Regardless of the administration of PUSD, changes in approaches to K-12 education, fluctuations in student enrollment, economic recessions -- and even a global pandemic -- PEF remains steadfast in its mission. It is nonpartisan and focused. Its only mission is to fundraise and foster community engagement in support of Piedmont schools. Please separate any perspectives on how PUSD is navigating in-person or distance learning from the purpose of PEF’s Giving Campaign. The financial outlook for K-12 public schools in California has not changed under the COVID-19 pandemic. Some argue that without intervention, it will become worse. Withholding a Giving Campaign contribution today only sets the district back in its capacity to provide the highest level of education to our students during the next school year. Instead, let’s step up to support our schools and give them the resources they need to be ready for our students next fall, arguably after one of the most challenging academic years they will experience. Learn more about PEF’s Giving Campaign and make a contribution today at https://www. pied montedfou ndation.org / donate/. articles.text: November 23 was worst day in county history for pandemic On Monday, November 23, a total of 547 new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases added in a single day in the county. The pandemic is surging in recent weeks on a scale not seen since August, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The current spike is poised to be worse than this past summer. On Saturday, November 28, an additional 312 new cases were recorded in the county. Previously, the worst day for the county was 417 cases on August 13. The county’s case rate is now 9.1 cases per 100,000 people. The rising case rate caused the state to put the entire county, which includes Piedmont, into the Purple Tier this month. The Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier, is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. Overall in Alameda County, the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 3.7 percent, a metric that has swelled upward across the past week. The total caseload in Alameda County is now 29,865, an increase of over 2,000 cases from one week ago, the ACPHD reported yesterday, Tuesday, December 1. Tragically, 15 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 514. No new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters over the past seven days. There have been 65 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 10,777. In Hayward, 4,519 cases have been recorded and there have been 2,247 reported in Fremont. San Leandro reported 1,712, Livermore reported 1,365, Union City reported 1,215 and Berkeley reported 1,158. The county enacted Purple Tier restrictions for business and activities on Wednesday, November 18. Health officials across the Bay Area have hinted that new lockdown orders could be on the horizon as cases continue to rise. On Saturday, November 28, health officers from Alameda County and other counties issued a statement supporting a strict new order issued by Santa Clara County. The Santa Clara County order further restricts capacity for indoor retail as well as requiring people traveling into the county from more than 150 miles to quarantine for 14 days. Contact sports, from youth games to professional play, are prohibited. Especially with worries that there will be a surge of cases after Thanksgiving gatherings, officials believe similar restrictions could be ordered across the region. “What we see in the South Bay today we may soon see across the whole Bay Area,” Dr. Nicholas

articles.text: Wildwood Ave., Requa Rd., Hill Lane on city’s list The City of Piedmont expects to receive bids in January to repave several stretches of roadway next summer. On November 2, the City Council agreed to pay $122,570 for engineering proposals for the projects. The Public Works Department expects the work to primarily include roadway resurfacing and the replacement of certain curbs, gutters and sidewalks. Some 15 new pedestrian ramps will be added to City sidewalks. Two portions of Wildwood Avenue are slated to be repaved – a portion from Grand Avenue to Nova Road and then a longer span from Prospect Avenue to Highland Avenue. “Crossing modifications” to improve pedestrian safety will be added at the T-intersection of Wildwood and Highland Avenues, according to a report from Chester Nakahara, Director of Public Works. Nearly all of Requa Road, from Hazel Avenue to Wildwood Avenue, will be repaved. A portion of Grand Avenue between Wildwood Avenue to Fairview Drive will be repaved. Concrete bulb-outs, new pedestrian crossing signs and flashing beacons will be added to the crosswalk in front of Ace Hardware. All of these improvements were proposed as part of the City’s Pedestrian/Bicycle Master Plan. The span of Hampton Road between Glen Alpine Road and St. James Avenue will also be repaved, and new bike lanes will be installed. The City is still deciding on the nature of these bike lanes, which may necessitate the elimination of some on-street parking on Hampton Road. The City will be seeking input from residents, the Pedestrian & Bicycle Advisory Committee and Council on the issue. A full repaving of Hill Lane is being planned. It is an alley between Nova and Arbor Drive. Workers will have to bore through the roadway of Hill Lane for samples to determine the health of the underlying substrate. “This will help to determine the appropriate rehabilitation method that will be necessary,” Nakahara wrote in his report to council. Council last month approved a payment of $122,570 to Coastland Engineers for engineering services to plan the 2021 repaving projects. Coastland outlined a proposal in October. Money for Coastland Engineering’s work will come from Measure B funds. Nakahara said that construction drawings, specifications and bid documents will be completed in January of 2021. The project will go out to bid soon after Council approval of these documents. The City plans to start the repaving work in the middle of June, 2021. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Republican and former NFL player Burgess Owens defeated Democratic incumbent Rep. Ben McAdams in Utah allowing Republicans to regain control of all congressional seats in the conservative state. Owens will represent Utah’s fourth district, which covers the suburbs of Salt Lake City. The victory launches the political career of Owens, 69, a former University of Miami and NFL star who travels the country delivering a message of optimism, hope, and unity. The Republican campaigned to uphold conserFormer Oakland Raider Burgess Owens will represent Utah in Congress. vative values, vowing to protect American’s Second Amendment rights and secure the borders. During the Republican primary, Owens handily won in a crowded field by running to the right of his opponents. Owens’ message on race largely disregarded the notion that Black people or other minorities in modern America face discrimination or any special challenges because of the color of their skin. Instead, he emphasized values of self-reliance and the power of the American dream. He also regularly told the story of his great-great-grandfather, Silas Burgess, who came to the United States “in the belly of a slave ship” and was sold on an auction block at 8 years old but went on to become a successful entrepreneur. articles.text: The annual Toys for Tots campaign has begun, and Piedmont Fire Department has placed a donation bin by the front doors of City Hall. Residents are encouraged to drop off new, unwrapped gifts for children in the bin during daytime hours. Last year, the Marine Corps Reserve, which sponsors the nationwide campaign, had 109 donation sites in Alameda County and collected 25,000 toys for kids in the county. Firefighters will empty the bin at the end of each day. If residents wish to bring a large number of donations, call the Fire Department at 420-3030 to arrange for a firefighter to be there. The Toys for Tots drive will also be accepting monetary donations for the first time. Checks may be left with the Fire Department, but made payable to Toys for Tots. To donate directly to the campaign using a credit card, visit https://marinetoysfortots.salsalabs.org/localdonationform/index. html?fun_local_campaign_designation=CA-Alameda&scf_unit_ code_supporter=CA-Alameda.
