articles.text: For 36 years the Piedmont Scouts BSA has collected food and funds to help feed families in Alameda County. All food and funds are given to the Alameda County Food Bank. Piedmont residents were especially generous last year, donating 8,095 pounds of food and $6,215 in cash to the Food Bank. This year they have already exceeded the goal of raising $7,500. Instead of a one-day annual food collection drive, this year’s campaign has been extended for five weeks, from November 1 through December 6. In addition, every Tuesday is Giving Back Tuesday. “We hope that those who have so generously donated food in the past will give online this year to help us combat food insecurity,” said Katy Kobal, Piedmont’s Scouting for Food Chair. Every dollar donated allows the Food Bank to purchase $7 worth of food. “We estimate that our need has doubled in Alameda county,” said Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. “October was our biggest month in food distribution ever. We anticipated distributing five million pounds of food. That is record-breaking.” Pre-COVID, Alameda County had one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. Nearly 20 percent of residents in the county live below the poverty line. Of those receiving assistance from the Alameda County Food Bank, two-thirds are children and the elderly. Donate online today by going to https://tinyurl.com/scoutingforfood2020 and turn $1 into $7 of food. For details, contact Morgan Fjord at the Scout office at 510-844-4752.

Residents are encouraged to drop off new, unwrapped gifts for children in the bin during daytime hours. Last year, the Marine Corps Reserve, which sponsors the nationwide campaign, had 109 donation sites in Alameda County and collected 25,000 toys for kids in the county. Firefighters will empty the bin at the end of each day. If residents wish to bring a large number of donations, call the Fire Department at 420-3030 to arrange for a firefighter to be there. articles.text: understand. Developmentally, children begin to think more deeply about others’ thoughts and feelings at age 4-5, around the time when many children are entering the educational system. Prior to 4-5 years old, we as parents can introduce Theory of Mind through role play and pretend play, understanding character’s perspectives in storybooks, and creating imaginative narratives. After the age of 5, during the early school years, Theory of Mind continues to develop as kids move through school learning how to predict, infer as well as understand abstract language that requires Theory of Mind such as empathy, lying, sarcasm and humor. Increasingly abstract layers of Theory of Mind, which can be difficult into adulthood, include tuning into thoughts and feelings when others try to hide them. For example, people are often are feeling emotions which are different from the ones they display. Skills in the area of Theory of Mind should be highlighted and sharpened throughout the lifespan. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

articles.text: Superintendent Randy Booker sent out an email Monday evening announcing a town hall meeting will be held prior to Winter Break to address secondary school parents’ questions and give more information about school reopening. The meeting will be held through Zoom with Superintendent Booker, and secondary school principals. The school district has not confirmed the date and time, but it will likely take place the week of December 14. Demand for a public forum resulted largely from a survey sent out by Booker to parents of students in grades 6-12 asking for in-person or distance learning preference. With little previous public discussion, the survey asked parents that chose Distance Learning to sign off on a move to bring in an independent company, Edgenuity. What troubled many parents was that the Edgenuity Virtual Academy was only mentioned after starting the survey. Parents that only read the email and didn’t get deep into the survey would not know any detail about the Edgenuity online program. At least one school board member acknowledged that it was an error to spring the implementation of Edgenuity onto parents in the survey. The district will not use Edgenuity for 100 percent distance learning. If families and counselors want, on a case-bycase basis individual students can use the platform. Due to parents’ feedback, Booker closed the survey and now has called for a town hall-style public meeting prior to reissuing a new survey. In the initial survey it was revealed that distance learners would “receive the bulk of instruction in a variety of courses using an Edgenuity product “Courseware.’” For parents, one of the troubling portions of the survey included this description: “With a variety of course needs, the facilitation teacher may not be an expert in the course materials, so as an additional support, course specific live tutors are available on the platform.” “I was disheartened to see a move that put the quality of secondary student education in harm’s way without public debate by the school board,” said parent Hari Titan. “A major change to an online virtual academy typically is months in the making with an advisory board and multiple school board meetings. That did not happen this time. Instead, this major paradigm shift was buried deep in a survey given to secondary school parents.” The Edgenuity program is not planned to be discussed by administrators or board members in the Town Hall meeting. An e-mail on December 1 by Booker stated, “Distance learning students will receive instruction by a certified teacher.” The public meeting will address progress on “teachers and staff identifying various learning models, including piloting cameras to support a ‘concurrent classroom’ model for our program,” according to Booker. In-person classes could utilize filmed sessions live-streamed to students either in the other cohort, in quarantine or choosing distance learning. Other school districts have implemented or plan to use class filming, however, privacy issues must be addressed. As Alameda County currently is in the purple tier of COVID restrictions, in-person learning cannot begin until clearance is given by the Alameda County Public Health Department. Current restrictions require counties to move in the red tier before reopening schools. As of December 1, 52 of 58 of California’s counties are in the purple tier, including 99.2 percent of the state’s population. On November 19, a statement from Piedmont School District stated, “PUSD’s goal is to have secondary students return to a hybrid/in-person learning model at the beginning of the 2nd semester (January 20).” Since November 19, Alameda County’s COVID daily caseload has steadily increased.

articles.text: Today’s political and social climate requires us to understand biases and misconceptions, and to consider how our experiences relative to others’ experiences contribute to our beliefs. We are thinking about what unites us as opposed to what divides us. We are examining beliefs based on misinformation. We are discussing diversity and inclusion. All of this requires what educators call Theory of Mind – the ability to understand another person’s thinking. Theory of mind is the understanding that other people have their own thoughts and motivations and desires. Psychologists describe it as attributing mental states to others. Theory of mind is what allows us to understand that we do not all share the same point of view. Through Theory of Mind we can see how a person’s perspective affects how that person acts and feels, and we can adjust our behavior based on our knowledge of others’ perspectives. As children, we develop and integrate the important elements of Theory of Mind. First, one must understand wants/desires of oneself vs. others. Different people want different things, and to get what they want people act in different ways. This leads to the understanding of personal motivations and preferences. An additional element is understanding that other people have thoughts, and that those thoughts may be different than yours. This understanding is the basis for the knowledge that different people can have different beliefs about the same thing. A common test of this is “the bandaid test”. A child views a teacher emptying a band-aid box of its contents and filling it instead with chalk. When asked what the child’s mother, who is in the other room, will think is in the box, a child with Theory of Mind will answer “band-aids” because she understands false beliefs based on lack of different knowledge. The child without Theory of Mind will answer “chalk”. Another common example which many adults have experienced is speaking on the phone with a young child who does not have a fully developed Theory of Mind and asks the child what she is doing. articles.text: The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s digital 2020- 2021 concert season has begun. All digital performances are streamed on YouTube Premiere and will remain on PEBCC’s YouTube channel after broadcast for continued viewing. Don’t miss a performance by subscribing to PEBCC’s YouTube channel to receive concert notifications and reminders: www.youtube.com/PiedmontChoirs. Celebrate the start of a new year with the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir family. From the youngest Training Department musicians to the mature and seasoned performances of Concert Choir and Ensemble, this performance connects all of the ensembles in an inspiring showcase of the progressive musical growth and artistry of our singers. Winter Recital will be on Saturday, December 5 at 4 p.m. The YouTube premiere of the Candlelight Concert will be on Saturday, December 12 at 4 p.m. choir Vox Aurea from Finland alongside music from the Dominican Republic, England, Hungary, and Estonia. Because of the generosity of our patrons, PEBCC is able to offer its 2020-2021 Discovering Our Voices virtual concert season free to the public via YouTube Premiere. Your donation in any amount toward our normal ticket prices significantly offsets our production costs for our season and keeps the choir thriving during this time. articles.text: Berkeley parents have organized a rally starting at 10 a.m. this Saturday. December 5, calling for Berkeley public schools to reopen. The peaceful event starts at MLK Park between Allston and Center. Parents from Oakland and Piedmont are expected to join the rally. The first hour is dedicated for families to make posters. Speeches start at 11:00 a.m., UCSF’s Dr. Jeanne Noble will speak on the relative risks of COVID transmission in schools. At noon the group will march around the MLK Jr. Civic Center Park towards Berkeley City Hall. Parents are calling for more transparency in regards to the negotiations with teachers. The group wants to ensure schools are ready to open when the time comes. Piedmont and Berkeley were the first school districts in Alameda County to attempt phased reopenings, both of which were eventually thwarted when the county was placed in the purple tier of COVID restrictions. Parents in Oakland are planning a protest the following week December 12. To sign a petition and for more information, see: www. busdparents.com or contact rally organizer Lei Levi at lei. llevi@gmail.com
articles.title: Rally to reopen schools set for Saturday

articles.text: On November 20 the Oakland Zoo opened its gates to nighttime visitors for the brand new event “GLOWFARI-a wildly illuminating lantern festival.” GLOWFARI takes the place of Zoolights which has been a zoo tradition for two decades. GLOWFARI features larger light display lanterns, longer hours, and more available dates than Zoolights. Hundreds of larger than life animal lanterns illuminate the milelong stroll that is truly an event fun for all ages. The brilliantly-lit gondola will be open to provide access to the California Trail and its vast views of the bay. The trail atop the gondola has turned into the Land of the Lost, filled with huge dinosaur lanterns and life-like animatronic moving models of dinos like the T-rex, stegosaurus, and triceratops. “It was very important to offer something to people to get away and have an emotional break from the stress of this year’s daily challenges,” said the Zoo’s VP of Marketing and Communications Erin Harrison. Signs all through the park educate guests on animals’ status in the wild, what people can do to help, and the challenges each species face. Capacity is limited to around 1,500 and guests have been vigilantly abiding to the mask and social distancing requirements. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: A time of year to remember to shop locally Piedmont Avenue businesses that have struggled to stay in business will soon see relief with all stores being open during the holiday season. Due to the COVID epidemic, there won’t be a Holiday Stroll, or the traditional tree lighting ceremony at Key Route Plaza on Piedmont Avenue & 41st Street. “We are not doing the tree lighting this year,” confirmed retailer Philippa Roberts. “It takes a lot of time and money, neither of which is very abundant these days.” Businesses desperately need a strong holiday season this year. Most have had to be creative to save their businesses. Claudio Luporini, owner of Bella Ceramica and a personal friend of Kris Kringle, said that Santa will have to skip his annual trip to the Avenue due to the coronavirus health restrictions in place. However, Luporini as always, will provide egg nog, hot totties, hot cocoa, bubbly, and cookies for customers. Nathan Walden, owner of Nathan & Co. with locations on Piedmont Ave. and College Ave., has been busy adapting to the times. For Black Friday – the Friday after Thanksgiving – and the following week, if customers say they are friends of Oakland Tech High School or Claremont Middle School, 20 percent of the sale will go to the Teacher’s Association for that school. Nathan and Co. was quick to jump on a new platform called www.KeepOaklandAlive.com. The website has teamed up with the most popular stores in Oakland by offering free two-day delivery. The fabric of the community lies at stake this holiday season, local business have ramped up their online and curbside pickup options to do what they can to keep people engaged and safe. “Rest assured, Piedmont Avenue is open and ready for business,” said longtime Piedmont Ave. volunteer Ronile Lahti. “Our holiday shopping message is Shop Local, Shop Oakland, but Shop Piedmont Avenue first. If we don’t have it, we’ll do our best to find it for you.” – Ronile Lahti Piedmont Ave. volunteer “The whole year has been just a huge challenge. We are concentrating on PR and pushing our website. I have brought back a publicist to help drive traffic to the website to bring in some dollars, but business is still down 50 percent.” Walden has kept his commitments to the community however.

articles.text: The Noble and Douglas Firs come by way of Salem, Oregon and the Silvertip from near Quincy, CA. This year the lot has 1457 trees, around 25 percent fewer trees than normal, to reduce their financial risk in the dodgy days of 2020. “To say that our community is heavily stressed is an understatement. This is when character counts. It is a great opportunity to teach our youth to think beyond themselves and respond to the needs of their neighbors. A Scout takes an oath ‘to help other people at all times,’ and that doesn’t mean only during good times, but all times,” Ashton said. Tree Lot Supervisor Bill Murphy has the lot running smoothly this year despite a complete overhaul of the tree lot purchasing and operating processes. “We are trying to make it as customer friendly as possible. We realize that buying a christmas tree is a very personal decision,” Murphy said. “We have an ombudsman to handle customer service requests in terms of exchanging trees. We have only had a couple of exchanges. If there is a slightly taller tree or fuller tree in storage we have been able to accommodate everybody,” Murphy explained. Piedmont Scout tree lot at Coaches Field provides delivery or pickup for online sales. Sales began November 1 and the first pickups were made after Thanksgiving. Scouts from every troop in the council have volunteered and the trees are selling like hand sanitizer. “We anticipate like in years past, we will sell out by the December 13th weekend. We don’t want you to miss out!” Murphy advised. Go to www.scouttreelot.org to select your desired tree type and make an appointment for the scouts to affix it to your car for you. Pickups at Coaches’ Field are available by appointment from 3:00 p.m. - 8:15 p.m. weekLauren Ashton (left) and brother Bill, both Patrol Leaders in Troop 11, help at the Scout Tree lot with their dad, David, a 1983 Eagle Scout from Troop 1. articles.title: Tree sales going like hotcakes

pages.text: Wednesday, December 2, 2020 11 By Jay Russell The Scout Christmas Tree Lot in Piedmont could not be stopped this year by COVID- 19. In its 52nd year of operation the Tree Lot pivoted to online ordering and contactless pickup at Coaches’ Field or delivery. Although you can’t browse and painstakingly critique a cornucopia of trees, you can still get a beautiful tree while supporting Piedmont’s Scouting Council, the country’s smallest council, with roots going back to 1910. The Tree Lot first started in 1969 as a fundraiser for Piedmont Troop 6 out of Corpus Christi Church and the next year was taken over by the Piedmont Council and moved to its current location. The long tradition continues and so does the council’s biggest annual fundraiser, which netted over $100,000 last year. Treelot Committee Member David Ashton helps run the show at the Scout Lot. Having first worked in the lot in the mid-70s as a Scout, he also ran the lot with Warren Heffelfinger and Tom Crowley in mid to late 90’s. Ashton’s family has a timber farm in Oregon and now he has kids of his own to carry on the city and family tradition. Tree sales going like hotcakes The Noble and Douglas Firs come by way of Salem, Oregon and the Silvertip from near Quincy, CA. This year the lot has 1457 trees, around 25 percent fewer trees than normal, to reduce their financial risk in the dodgy days of 2020. “To say that our community is heavily stressed is an understatement. This is when character counts. It is a great opportunity to teach our youth to think beyond themselves and respond to the needs of their neighbors. A Scout takes an oath ‘to help other people at all times,’ and that doesn’t mean only during good times, but all times,” Ashton said. Tree Lot Supervisor Bill Murphy has the lot running smoothly this year despite a complete overhaul of the tree lot purchasing and operating processes. “We are trying to make it as customer friendly as possible. We realize that buying a christmas tree is a very personal decision,” Murphy said. “We have an ombudsman to handle customer service requests in terms of exchanging trees. We have only had a couple of exchanges. If there is a slightly taller tree or fuller tree in storage we have been able to accommodate everybody,” Murphy explained. Piedmont Scout tree lot at Coaches Field provides delivery or pickup for online sales. Sales began November 1 and the first pickups were made after Thanksgiving. Scouts from every troop in the council have volunteered and the trees are selling like hand sanitizer. “We anticipate like in years past, we will sell out by the December 13th weekend. We don’t want you to miss out!” Murphy advised. Go to www.scouttreelot.org to select your desired tree type and make an appointment for the scouts to affix it to your car for you. Baron Zhou gives this Christmas tree a fresh cut to keep it green throughout December. The Scout Tree Lot includes wreaths, garlands, wreaths with candles, and magnolia leaves. Pictured are Robbie Alazraqui and Anna Smegal. days and 9:00 a.m. - 8:15 p.m. on weekends. articles.text: The California Interscholastic Federation made two major announcements yesterday, Tuesday, December 1. In addition to postponing its official scheduled start of practice for winter sports on December 7, the CIF canceled regional and state playoffs for the year. Th sports affected are football, cross country, water polo, and boys volleyball. “The CIF State Office is removing all Regional and State Championship events from the Season 1 Sports calendar. By canceling Regional and State Championship events, more student-athletes will have the opportunity to participate in a longer season, rather than a truncated season with Regional and State post-season play for a limited number of schools,” wrote the federation in its press release. The CIF said it would not “issue any guidance” until after January 1 – at least – in response to the California Department of Public Health not issuing any updates on youth sports in its recent announcement. “Due to the continued surge in COVID-19 infections, the California Department of Public Health has postponed the issuance of its updated youth sports guidance. The CIF does not expect the CDPH will issue any guidance allowing for schools to return to full practice and competition until after January 1, 2021, at the earliest. Thus, all full practice and competition start dates are officially on hold until updated guidance is issued,” wrote the CIF. The head of the California Department of Public Health is the former Aameda County Public Health Director. Additionally, the CIF moved boys’ volleyball – which would have new at Piedmont High in the spring – to its Season 2 alongside the other chunk of sports like basketball, soccer, lacrosse, baseball, softball, track, swimming, golf, and badminton. The cancelation of the postseason means there will be no North Coast Section playoffs for football, cross country, or water polo, The Cross Country State Championship, the state’s oldest sports championship, has been called off. Photos courtesy of CIF The California Interscholastic Federation announced on Tuesday, December 1 that it is postponing the official start of high school practices and canceling its playoffs tournaments. North Coast Section playoffs have been abandoned for football, water polo, cross country, and girls’ volleyball. Cross-country may be the sport most affected by the change, as runners typically put in their fastest times at the NCS Meet of Champions in an effort to qualify for state. Without a regional postseason, this means that the Western Alameda County Conference could theoretically schedule more games for its 12-team conference. Piedmont football team was initially set to open its non-conference schedule on January 8 in a traditional game with Justin-Siena of Napa, with successive games each week until February’s league schedule in the WACC. “The CIF is confident this decision is a necessary and reasonable action for our member schools, student-athletes, and school communities in light of the current statewide crisis. This revision to the CIF State 2020-21 Season 1 Sports calendar offers our Sections and Leagues the flexibility and needed time to plan for the return to practice and competition once updated guidance is provided by the CDPH,” wrote the CIF.

articles.text: Western Alameda County Conference (WACC) commissioner Dave Kiesel voiced uncertainty around the California Interscholastic Federation’s sports schedule last week, saying his office has not yet received clarification from the CIF. “All they’ve said is that they’ll let you know when we know,” Kiesel said in an interview with the Mercury News. “I guess that’s the part that’s frustrating our athletic directors and our principals and our coaches in our schools – they don’t know when they’re going to know… So who knows what’s going to happen? It’s all a big question mark. All we know now is what we can’t do.” Staff Photos – League Commissioner Dave Kiesel Asked about whether schools are frustrated by the lack of clarification from the CIF, Kiesel said that WACC is “not ready” for the federation’s scheduled start of practice on December 7, given their lack of planning thus far. “There’s been frustration. Sixteen-year-olds don’t want to be told what they can’t do… The problem for them, and for coaches and athletic directors that represent them, is that there is frustration because everyone’s saying, ‘Well, you can’t do this, you can’t do that.’ That’s from school boards and school districts, or counties or the NCS, the CIF, or the State Department of Health,” he said. “They’re certainly aware of the seriousness of the virus, and they’re certainly not interested in doing stuff they shouldn’t be doing. But it’s just really difficult to plan if you don’t know how you’re going to plan, if you don’t Newly designated winter sports, including football, are scheduled to start practice on December 7. have a calendar for planning. I don’t think anyone believes we’re going to start practice on Dec. 7. I think that’s just not going to happen. We’re not ready for it, and no one wants to do it if it can’t be done in a safe manner, and (it’s) pretty evident now that it can’t be done in a safe manner.” Kiesel reiterated that he has “no idea” when he will receive an official plan or schedule information from CIF officials, who have repeatedly said they’ll advise the league when able to. “No idea. Again, all they’ve said is that they’ll let you know when we know. I guess that’s the part that’s frustrating our athletic directors and our principals and our coaches in our schools, is that they don’t know when they’re going to know,” said Kiesel. Piedmont High’s sports programs returned for its conditioning programs ahead of the 2021 schedule only a couple of days prior to Alameda County going back to the Purple Tier if CIVUD restrictions. Kiesel said each school district will dictate whether teams can continue practicing. “We’re all in Alameda County, and Alameda County has gone back to (the restrictive purple tier). That’s up to the individual districts to make that decision. But the kids are ready to participate in physical activity, whether they’re ready to participate in a game or not is really questionable because they haven’t done much for three months from a physical point of view. Everyone’s being cautious.” Although Kiesel added that he’s been impressed with the schools which are conditioning, like Piedmont, he is unsure of “how long that’s going to last” with the new restrictive measures. “I believe we have seven schools that are doing this now. I was really impressed by the safety precautions the various schools have put into effect in terms of the treatment of pods, the size of pods and the involvement of lots of school personnel to make sure the kids are doing what they’re supposed to be doing. I don’t know how long that’s going last,” he said. Kiesel added that he is unsure whether school football programs will be able to accomplish a 10-game season as planned. The WACC, which has 12 schools, still plans on merging with the eight-team Mission Valley Athletic League for the football season to form three divisions: Foothill, Shoreline, and Mission. Kiesel mentioned that the MVAL and WACC could work together on other sports because they are are close together geographically. Schools in the MVAL include Sourthern Alameda County high schools: American, Irvington, Kennedy, Mission, and Washington, Moreau, Newark Memorial and James Logan. Dave Kiesel mentioned that PHS is among seven schools that returned to non-sports specific training.

articles.text: Maradona passes away at age 60; Diop at 42 The International soccer world is mourning the loss of two of its most brilliant stars who passed away this week. Argentinian legend Diego Maradona passed away on November 25 due to a heart attack at age 60, while Senegalese star Papa Bouba Diop succumbed to ALS on November 29. He was only 42. Maradona’s illustrious career started at Argentinos Juniors and Boca Juniors from 1976-1982 before transferring to Barcelona on a world record free of $7.6 million until he requested a move in 1984 after a violent brawl with Athletic Bilbao, It resulted in his polarizing trade to Napoli for a record $10.48 million. Naples at the time was considered among the poorest cities in Italy, leading to assumptions that local mafia groups helped finance the purchase of Maradona’s contract. In the 1980s Maradonna’s arrival in Naples had a polarizing impact on the wealthier northern cities and the poorer residents of Italy’s southern peninsula. But from then on, Maradona became Naples’ favorite son. Local journalists called him a savior. They noted that the city lacked a “mayor, houses, schools, buses, employment and sanitation. None of this matters because we have Maradona.” He led Napoli to its only Serie A titles, in 1987 and 1990, while their UEFA Cup title in 1989 is its only major European championship. It took the organization 24 years to win another Coppa Italia after Maradona’s in ’87 and likewise for its Suppercoppa Italiana in 1990, not earning it again until 2014. For Argentina’s National Team, Maradona is popularly known for the “Hand of God” goal in their 2-1 win over England in the 1986 World Cup quarterfinals, where he controversially used his hand to score the winning goal – but referees, out of position without a clear view, allowed the score. Following the game, Maradona said the goal was “a little with the head, and a little with the hand of God.” It was voted the Goal of the Century by FIFA in 2002. Argentina went on to win the 1986 World Cup Finals 3-2 over West Germany. They lost in the 1990 Finals 1-0 in a rematch with West Germany. But one cannot mention Maradona and his death without also acknowledging his battles along the way. He suffered from drug addiction during his playing days Photo courtesy of CBS Sports Diego Maradona is shown in 1986 after Argentina won the World Cup. It is the last time Argentina won the acclaimed trophy. with Napoli and after his retirement. He was also diagnosed with hepatitis as a result of alcohol dependence later in life. He underwent emergency brain surgery on November 2 to treat subdural hematoma and was released 10 days later. Weeks later on November 25, Maradona suffered a fatal heart attack at his home in Argentina. Papa Bouba Diop, 42 Diop was an influential star for generations of African footballers. He is best known for his contributions to the Senegalese National Team where he made 63 total appearances at center back and central defense midfield. Diop, towering at 6 feet, 5 inches, was nicknamed “The Wardrobe” due to his ability to cover the midfield. The highlight of his career came in Senegal’s World Cup debut in 2002. He scored the game-winning goal in a 1-0 upset victory over defending champion France in the Group Stage, which ultimately eliminated Les Bleus from the tournament. In the Round of 16, Senegal upset Sweden with a 20-year old Zlatan Ibrahimovic in a classic 2-1 win in extra time. Senegal, The Lions of Teranga, danced on the field in celebration. Diop was also a mainstay throughout major European leagues. He made 47 appearances with France’s Ligue 1’s Lens from 2002-2004 before making his way to Fulham in England’s Premier League until 2007. After a stint in EPL club Portsmouth from 2007-2010, he eventually finished his career in AEK Athens of Greece for two seasons, returned to England’s West Ham United for 2011 and 2012, and Birmingham City until 2013. Diop died in Paris on November 29 of complications from the disease ALS (Lou Gehrig’s Disease). Photo courtesy of Sky Sports Papa Bouba Diop with the Senegal National Team.
articles.title: Remembering soccer legends Diego Maradona & Papa Bouba Diop

articles.text: One year ago seems like a world away right now. We’re stuck in the house with no sports under the lights at Witter Field or in Binks Rawlings Gym, and no coaches or athletes for this writer to corral for post-game interviews. CIF’s official start of practice next week on December 7 seems highly unlikely, given that Alameda county and much of California is in the Purple Tier of COVID restrictions. So to be productive, let’s all sit down, grab a drink, and reminisce over ye’ olden times, the year 2019. When looking back, The Post’s first issue in December reported on the conclusion of fall sports, and it seemed that an epic sports campaign was building for the Class of 2020. Sophia Zalewski, the Senior Class Valedictorian and the Posts’ Athlete of the Year, had just competed in the State cross country championships in Fresno. She finished 11th place in a time of 18-minutes, 17 seconds, shattering her own course record at Woodward Park by 16.3 seconds. She etched her name into the school’s record books by beating Jehan Sparks’ time of 18:58 set 17 years earlier at the State meet. The fall season turned out to be the last of Zalewski’s high school running career, as the track season was canceled entirely due to COVID-19. Prior to the State meet she was named the league cross-country MVP award for the second consecutive year. She became Piedmont’s first runner to break the 18-minute mark on a three-mile course with a time of 17:50.7 at the WACC Championship meet at Hayward High. Pictured are: Aya Troyer (left), Molly McWeeny, Maggie Black, Sophia Zalewski, Mara Lovric, Valerie Xiong, Ellie Black, and Adri McAuliffe. Piedmont’s girls’ cross country team won the North Coast Section Championship on November 23, 2019. Tennis The end of November 2019 marked the conclusion of the girls’ tennis season. Although the school had its 20-year streak of undefeated league championships come to an end, coach Jim Landes had a pair of seniors, Emily Becker and Audrey Call, bring In the fall of 2019, seniors Emily Becker (left) and Audrey Call won the North Coast Section Tennis Doubles Championship. Staff Photo Boys’ basketball coach Ben Spencer is shown in a 71-55 win over Alameda. Photo by Dennis Mockel Distance runner Sophia Zalewski was named the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2020. home the Div. 2 Doubles Title. It was the first time the two had played together since their sophomore seasons. Basketball The start of December typically has meant that Piedmont’s basketball programs were getting underway. At this time last year, the boys’ basketball team opened its schedule with a pair of wins, 76-27 over Ygnacio Valley, and 71-55 over league opponent Alameda. It was the start of the school’s run toward its first ever North Coast Section Championship. That team was the from Piedmont to compete, when al sports were postponed in March due to COVID-19. A sour taste was left in Piedmont after a controversial placement of the Div. 4 basketball team in Division 2 in the State Playoffs. It was a David vs. Goliath matchup. In conversations since last March, head coach Ben Spencer has consistently reiterated his players’ lack of closure brought by the CIF decision to have PHS play as a Fic. 2 school – historically designed for large enrollment schools. Seniors from that Class of 2020 program included Luke Barrett, David Kisieu, Paul Davies, DaRon Benson, Josh Eidam, Owen Colbert, Patrick Selna, Christian Hohener, and Jayden Lee.

Naples at the time was considered among the poorest cities in Italy, leading to assumptions that local mafia groups helped finance the purchase of Maradona’s contract. In the 1980s Maradonna’s arrival in Naples had a polarizing impact on the wealthier northern cities and the poorer residents of Italy’s southern peninsula. But from then on, Maradona became Naples’ favorite son. Local journalists called him a savior. They noted that the city lacked a “mayor, houses, schools, buses, employment and sanitation. None of this matters because we have Maradona.” He led Napoli to its only Serie A titles, in 1987 and 1990, while their UEFA Cup title in 1989 is its only major European championship. It took the organization 24 years to win another Coppa Italia after Maradona’s in ’87 and likewise for its Suppercoppa Italiana in 1990, not earning it again until 2014. For Argentina’s National Team, Maradona is popularly known for the “Hand of God” goal in their 2-1 win over England in the 1986 World Cup quarterfinals, where he controversially used his hand to score the winning goal – but referees, out of position without a clear view, allowed the score. Following the game, Maradona said the goal was “a little with the head, and a little with the hand of God.” It was voted the Goal of the Century by FIFA in 2002. Argentina went on to win the 1986 World Cup Finals 3-2 over West Germany. They lost in the 1990 Finals 1-0 in a rematch with West Germany. But one cannot mention Maradona and his death without also acknowledging his battles along the way. He suffered from drug addiction during his playing days Photo courtesy of CBS Sports Diego Maradona is shown in 1986 after Argentina won the World Cup. It is the last time Argentina won the acclaimed trophy. with Napoli and after his retirement. He was also diagnosed with hepatitis as a result of alcohol dependence later in life. He underwent emergency brain surgery on November 2 to treat subdural hematoma and was released 10 days later. Weeks later on November 25, Maradona suffered a fatal heart attack at his home in Argentina. Papa Bouba Diop, 42 Diop was an influential star for generations of African footballers. He is best known for his contributions to the Senegalese National Team where he made 63 total appearances at center back and central defense midfield. Diop, towering at 6 feet, 5 inches, was nicknamed “The Wardrobe” due to his ability to cover the midfield. The highlight of his career came in Senegal’s World Cup debut in 2002. He scored the game-winning goal in a 1-0 upset victory over defending champion France in the Group Stage, which ultimately eliminated Les Bleus from the tournament. In the Round of 16, Senegal upset Sweden with a 20-year old Zlatan Ibrahimovic in a classic 2-1 win in extra time. Senegal, The Lions of Teranga, danced on the field in celebration. Diop was also a mainstay throughout major European leagues. He made 47 appearances with France’s Ligue 1’s Lens from 2002-2004 before making his way to Fulham in England’s Premier League until 2007. After a stint in EPL club Portsmouth from 2007-2010, he eventually finished his career in AEK Athens of Greece for two seasons, returned to England’s West Ham United for 2011 and 2012, and Birmingham City until 2013. Diop died in Paris on November 29 of complications from the disease ALS (Lou Gehrig’s Disease). Photo courtesy of Sky Sports Papa Bouba Diop with the Senegal National Team.

articles.text: California’s woes came back to haunt them in a disastrous Big Game for the Golden Bears, allowing a blocked extra point attempt with the game at 24-23 with 58 seconds left. Cal was seemingly set to force overtime against the Stanford Cardinal, but Stanford won its 10th victory in 11 Big Games. Adding insult to injury, Cal’s sound system inadvertently played its fight song in anticipation of a converted field goal as Stanford celebrated its block. Like California playing their song after a tragedy, nothing has gone as expected this season. Cal sits at 0-3 with a roster full of upperclassmen and a string of COVID-19 infections; Stanford is now 1-2 after its program also had its run-in with the virus. Down 24-17 with 3:30 left in the game, the Golden Bears marched 90 yards to cap off a drive with Chris Brown Jr. to make it 24-23. But Cal’s special teams unit has shown in thre games that it struggles to handle the most basic of requirements. Cal, notably had a COVID run in with its offensive line and have had depleted numbers. In addition to the blocked PAT, it had a blocked 32-yard field goal attempt, and fumbled a punt return by Nikko Remigio. It also allowed a blocked punt in their 31-27 loss to Oregon State. Cal is set to face No. 23 Oregon this Saturday, and easily to go to an 0-4 record. The Cardinal wins the Axe in Big Game Stanford QB Davis Mills got the job done with 24 completions for 205 yards and a touchdown. Cardinal sophomore and former Bishop O’Dowd running back Austin Jones had a big day with 85 yards and two touchdowns on 21 attempts. It was his career-high. But it was defensive lineman Thomas Booker who increased his draft stock as a disruptive rusher with two blocked field goals against Cal. Stanford is set to face No. 22 Washington on Saturday and will be the underdogs. But because Stanford is in Santa Clara County, its team will not be able to practice in Palo Alto due to new COVID health restrictions. The team is considering staying in the Pacific Northwest after its game with the Huskies and preparing there for its season-finale against Oregon State on December 12. Photo courtesy of Sports radio service Stanford’s Austin Jones (20), a Bishop O’Dowd alum, ran for 85 yards and scored two touchdowns. Photo courtesy of AP Cal long snapper Slater Zellers sits in frustration after the field goal team allowed its PAT kick to be blocked.
articles.title: Stanford blocks Cal PAT kick to win Axe

articles.text: Area includes 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree & prehistoric Tafoni Rock Formation El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve in San Mateo County has some easily accessible features that many more popular destinations in the Bay Area don’t come close to offering. Located near Highway 35 (Skyline Boulevard) is a tree that predates the Europeans settling in America, the estimated 1,800- year old Methuselah Tree, It is the only old growth redwood tree in the Santa Cruz Mountains outside of Big Basin State Park. It is known by locals as the “Big Old Tree on Skyline.” The Peninsula Open Space Preserve describes that the Methuselah Tree sprouted in 217 AD, experienced Ohlone Native’s bark cultivation in 1,000 AD, was witness to European settlers and Mexico’s independence from Spain in 1821, while lumber mills in the 1870s’ California Gold Rush likely determined that its massive burl made Methuselah impossible to harvest. Although the gateway to the tree is closed due to dry conditions, the base is clearly visible from the road, making it an excellent starting point for a day of hiking. Across the road from the Methuselah Tree is the Sierra Morena Trail, the starting point for a 1.5 mile hike to another historic landmark, the Tafoni Rock Formation, a nearly 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone. It is estimated to be 30 million years old and progressively is deteriorating from wind and rain. A platform sits at its base with informative panels and a close view. The rock formation, Tafoni, is a name to describe the sandstone’s cavernous reaction from weather conditions. You can spot examples of Tafoni formations along the coast of the Pacific Ocean, with wind and waves eating away at shorelines. El Corte de Madera’s represents a prehistoric time, dating to the middle of the Cenozoic Era when the ocean covered San Mateo County. Continuing on the Fir Trail and a half-mile from the rock formation is another place of note, Vista Point. The overlook has a narrow view of the Pacific Ocean and a bench for relaxing. A memorial to an air wreckage in the 1950s sits at the point’s entrance. The Tafoni Rock Formation is a tall boulder made of sandstone. ista Point offers a view of the Pacific Ocean, and marks the mid-point of the 5.15-mile loop The Tafoni Trail past the rock formation is more secluded and is littered with stumps of old growth redwoods. The area is popular for mountain bikers, so hikers should be mindful of their surroundings. Bikers can find berms scattered around downhill portions. The flat surface makes it a pristine course.

Although the gateway to the tree is closed due to dry conditions, the base is clearly visible from the road, making it an excellent starting point for a day of hiking. Across the road from the Methuselah Tree is the Sierra Morena Trail, the starting point for a 1.5 mile hike to another historic landmark, the Tafoni Rock Formation, a nearly 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone. It is estimated to be 30 million years old and progressively is deteriorating from wind and rain. A platform sits at its base with informative panels and a close view. The rock formation, Tafoni, is a name to describe the sandstone’s cavernous reaction from weather conditions. You can spot examples of Tafoni formations along the coast of the Pacific Ocean, with wind and waves eating away at shorelines. El Corte de Madera’s represents a prehistoric time, dating to the middle of the Cenozoic Era when the ocean covered San Mateo County. Continuing on the Fir Trail and a half-mile from the rock formation is another place of note, Vista Point. The overlook has a narrow view of the Pacific Ocean and a bench for relaxing. A memorial to an air wreckage in the 1950s sits at the point’s entrance. Staff Photos The Methusela Tree is estimated to be 1,800 years old. It is near Highway 35 (Skyline Blvd). The Tafoni Rock Formation is a tall boulder made of sandstone. A closer view of the Tafoni Rock Formation’s cavernous shell from years of deterioration. ista Point offers a view of the Pacific Ocean, and marks the mid-point of the 5.15-mile loop The Tafoni Trail past the rock formation is more secluded and is littered with stumps of old growth redwoods. The area is popular for mountain bikers, so hikers should be mindful of their surroundings. Bikers can find berms scattered around downhill portions. The flat surface makes it a pristine course. The memorial was erected in 2006 to commemorate a British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines commercial airplane bound for Sydney, Australia which crashed in the park in October 1953. One can still find pieces of the wreckage on the park’s Resolution Trail. Continuing back to the parking lot rounds out an easy day of hiking at a mellow 3.6 miles. Continuing past the Tafoni Rock Formation on the Tafoni Trail you can turn right when leaving the pathway from the giant chunk of stone. The hike provides a 5.15- mile loop with less than 1,000 feet in elevation gain while you are surrounded by redwood trees and stumps from old giants. On the 5.15-mile hike on a Sunday morning, we counted 86 total passersby, an average of 17 people per mile. This loop certainly goes in the “hidden treasure” category in comparison to last week’s venture on Mt. Tam where we saw more than 80 people in 3.5 miles. The trails are a common place for mountain bikers zooming downhill and off berms, so hikers need to beware. No dogs are allowed in El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve. For directions to the area, punch in “Methuselah Tree, Redwood City” on your GPS device.

articles.text: Playwright Loy A. Webb’s The Light will be presented by Shotgun Players December 4-13. Berkeley-based Shotgun Players is presenting The Light live streamed December 4-13 on Youtube. The play follows real-life couple Leigh Rondon-Davis and Kenny Scott as they are forced to confront a devastating secret from the past, a surprise proposal gift that puts the future of their relationship at risk. The Light is a 70-minute, real-time comedy that deals with themes of romance, despair, and radical love. The couple will perform the play live in their own home. The Light is written by Loy A. Webb and directed by Nailah Harper-Malveaux. Shotgun Players will host two moderated post-show discussions for The Light to explore the themes of the play. The talks will take place immediately following the Sunday performances on December 6 and 13. They will be moderated by Amissa Miller and Lauren Spencer. To view the play, choose a preferred date. After you purchase a ticket, you will receive an email receipt, which includes a link to the performance’s private Youtube channel. A virtual waiting room will open 30 minutes prior to the show, and Shotgun Players strongly recommends that patrons arrive early so that staff can assist if any technical difficulties arise. Tickets are offered on a pay-what-you-can scale, and all proceeds go toward paying the artists, production team, and staff members. For tickets, see: https://shotgunplayers.org/Online/default. asp?BO param::WScontent:: loadArticle::permalink=the-light &BOparam::WScontent::load Article::context_id=

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Brian Copeland’s The Jewelry Box, available to stream through December 25. The comedy is a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show, Not a Genuine Black Man, and follows young protagonist Brian as he heads to the “mean streets” of Oakland to buy his mom a Christmas present. When he finds the perfect gift – a jewelry box in the White Front store – six-year-old Brian sets out to earn the required $11.97 by Christmas Eve. The play follows Brian’s adventures as he scours the “help wanted” ads, applies for jobs, and collects bottles, inching his way toward the perfect Christmas gift. Copeland debuted his first one-man play, Not a Genuine Black Man at The Marsh in San Francisco. The play explored his childhood experiences as a Brian Copeland will appear in a one-man show, The Jewelry Box, at San Francisco Playhouse. member of one of the only African American families living in a predominately white suburb of San Leandro, California. Not a Genuine Black Man went on to become the longest-running solo show in San Francisco theatrical history with over 800 performances. The show has been performed in over 30 cities, including a critically acclaimed run Off-Broadway in New York City. The play is currently in television series development. To stream The Jewelry Box, visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sf ph /2020-2021-season / the-jewelry-box.
articles.title: SF Playhouse to stream Brian Copeland’s The Jewelry Box through Christmas

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is presenting The Nutcracker online through December 31, just in time for the holidays. The performance will be encompassed in an interactive, virtual experience for family and friends from the comfort of homes. Watch San Francisco Ballet’s spectacular Nutcracker, streamed in high definition, and then join a virtual tour of the opera house. You can send holiday snapshots to friends and family, enjoy historical highlights of the Nutcracker, and learn steps from the choreography. The ballet company advises that this event is best experienced with a chrome browser on a computer, laptop, or iPad. The Nutcracker is one of America’s most celebrated ballets, and one of San Francisco Ballet’s most popular performances of the year. The story begins on a foggy Christmas Eve San Francisco Ballet returns with its popular ballet, The Nutcracker, this month. in 1915, with Drosselmeyer putting the finishing touches on a magical nutcracker doll. It’s his gift for the Stahlbaum family, who have invited him to join their holiday festivities. Customers drop by his shop for last-minute Christmas gifts and Drosselmeyer shows them toys and clocks. Later, outside the Stahlbaum house, as people hurry home to their Christmas revelries, Drosselmeyer arrives with his beautifully wrapped present. You can view a progression of the acts at https://www. sfballet.org/discover/backstage/ story-of-nutcracker/. The music is by Tchaikovsky and choreography by Helgi Tomasson. Tickets can be purchased at https://donate2.app/kbqBT1. Purchase allows grants audience members with 48-hour access.
articles.title: SF Ballet presents The Nutcracker online for the holidays

articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Kelley O’Connor will be featured in this year’s Napa Valley Festival, which will be virtual. Festival Napa Valley presents Songs of Gratitude in response to a year of unimaginable hardship for the local and global community. articles.text: Oakland Symphony honored Native Americans last week in a special episode of “rePAST,” a free, digital series of symphony archival concerts. Music Director Michael Morgan chose to highlight an excerpt from composer Jerod Impichchaachaaha’ Tate’s Lowak Shoppola (Fire and Light) performance. The excerpt was taken from a concert entitled VII Hymn. “For many of us, today is Thanksgiving. For Native Americans, it’s a day of mourning; mourning the genocide and loss of land they suffered,” Morgan said. “In this excerpt, we take a moment to remember their history and be thankful that there are Native Americans left to tell their story. At the Oakland Symphony we celebrate our Native American friends and neighbors.” You can listen to the performance excerpt at https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/repast/. articles.text: Thanksgiving, unlike the last election, is already a distant memory. Most Americans believe that Thanksgiving is an honest holiday. Just about everyone admits that the turkey is our desideratum - the Peoples’ choice. Last week’s column addressed the controversy of the turkey. This week we move on to turkey into the future, and some musical suggestions to accompany your banquets. Turkey adapts to almost any style of cooking, therefore when purchasing a turkey, buy a bigger bird than you think you need. There are so many ways to cook the turkey I hardly know where to start. Here are a few ideas to keep you well-fed and happy. 1. Soup Strip the meat from the carcass, include all bones and giblets, add a carrot, whole onion and celery. Allow to steep on a low flame for a long time. If you do it this way, your vegetables will remain firm. This will serve as a stock for all your other dishes. Many of the recipes are self-explanatory. I will give you some which I prepare with great regularity. Numbers 2,3,4, and 5 have the same basic ingredients. 2. Turkey paprikash Combine olive oil, crushed garlic clove, diced carrots, celery and onion and lightly sauté in a skillet. Add about 3 ounces of turkey stock and about 3 tablespoons of sour cream. Salt and pepper of course and lots of paprika. Slice the leftover turkey and serve it with a vegetable of your choice and either rice or noodles. 3. Improvised turkey pie Use the same basic recipe for #2, except do not add paprika. Add mushrooms and plenty of cream sherry. Put it in a prepared pie crust and top with polenta. This is an easy recipe. Slice the turkey and warm lightly with pesto sauce. Do not overheat the pesto. I roasted my own Anaheim peppers, but you can use a jar of roasted red peppers. I served it with red kidney beans, but I think that a grain like Farro would be better. The salad was a bright one and had some slices of Japanese persimmon. Improvised turkey pie using a commercial pie crust and polenta topping. Bake at 425° for about 45 minutes until the crust is firm and the turkey bubbles. 4. Turkey à la King Same recipe as #3, but serve over toast or rice. 5. Turkey pesto Lightly warm slices of turkey. Add pesto. Pesto should never be cooked. The best pesto I have found is Roland pesto. The list of turkey recipes is almost endless. Today I made turkey in a pesto sauce with roasted Anaheim peppers. You can use commercial roasted red peppers if you want. Serve this recipe with a grain like Farro or rice. Thanksgiving music? Music for Thanksgiving is not as plentiful as that for Christmas. But there are some very good pieces. When you sit down to a banquet see if you can find Tafelmusik by Telemann. This popular Baroque composer wrote Tafelmusik especially for banquet occasions. Nothing could be more appropriate. Handel was another great Baroque composer who was successful at writing music for any occasion. His water music will accompany your banquet just fine. The quixotic French composer Alkan wrote the exotic “Aesop’s Feast”. Let your mind run wild when you hear this one. For my religious readers I would suggest the beautiful song “Bless this house”. At the opposite end of the musical spectrum is “Spam,” the hilarious song by Monty Python. For dessert, treat yourself to one of the great candies in the world, Mozart Kugeln. And now a note to sports enthusiasts. If Mike Tyson can make a comeback at the age of 54, so can I at the age of 74. I was doing my road work and I heard in the distance one of the great operatic voices of the past. It was Maria Callas singing Rossini. I tell you without fear of contradiction that Piedmont is a fine place to live. The couple coming toward me were out for their evening constitutional and they were listening to Callas. And that, my dear readers, is enough turkey. Be well!
articles.title: All manner of turkeys

Everyone is invited to tune in and listen to Christmas favorites and new arrangements performed by talented, well-known Bay Area musicians – sopranos Shawnette Sulker and Katy Stephan, tenor Darron Flagg, baritone Martin Bell, classical guitarist Richard Flores and organist Michael Moran and a rousing rendition of Handel’s Messiah. Stephan and Moran are the regular musicians for the church. The Sunday School Students will read the Bible account of the birth of Jesus. Beginning December 1st, a link to the concert will be available on the church website at: www. ChristianScienceOakland.org. At what point is the human no longer the creative entity? Memorable images in this musical kaleidoscope included the ear-tingling delicate percussion sounds of Ellen Reid’s “Fear/ Release,” where for once drawn bows setting vibraphone blocks vibrating became far more effective than in the concert hall. Heightening the heterogeneity were the rap singing in Kev Choice’s “Movements,” in part filmed on a busy city street, and the subtle unaccompanied song-cum-contrabass solo by Esmeralda Spalding, playing barefoot in total tranquility. And Music Director EsaPekka Salonen, who was the coordinating engineer, was seen not so much leading on a podium as trekking through the wilds pensively. articles.text: California Revels will return to Oakland for its 35th season of one of the Bay Area’s premier holiday events. This year’s presentation is Unruly Magic: A Spirited Celebration of the Winter Solstice. Families, friends and holiday revelers are invited to watch wherever they may be, as this year’s production is entirely online, and can be viewed from December 12-20 at www.californiarevels.org. It will stream in High-Definition on Vimeo and YouTube, with live interactive components on Zoom Audiences of all ages can celebrate the Winter Solstice with traditional music, dance, ritual, and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance.” The production features top musicians, actors, and featured performers. This year’s show includes Shay Black and Windborne Singers. Directed by Jeri Reed, newly filmed pieces are blended with archival footage to create a dynamic and moving feast for the eyes, ears, and spirit. that have sustained generations through struggle and celebration are rekindled this Solstice, proving that tradition – and magic – live on. Dates and times of the seven performances are listed below. Saturday, December 12, 1:00 p.m. Sunday, December 13, 1:00 p.m. Friday, December 18, 7:00 p.m. Saturday, December 19, 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Sunday, December 20, 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Tickets are $20-$175 and are available online at www.CaliforniaRevels.org. For details and more information, call the box office at 650-534-6766 Monday to Friday from 11:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Unruly Magic is directed by Jeri Reed and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Marzena Jones is Children’s Music Director. California Revels Executive Director is Lisa Lowe. The story of Unruly Magic Approaching the longest night of the year, a young Reveler turns to a magical staff to help her find a way through somber and troubled times. The staff, imbued with ancient lore, takes her on an adventure that isn’t quite what she had in mind. Magic and mystery, spirits and song take the reins for this journey of the heart. The ancient traditions of bonfires, rituals, dances, and songs Meara, from the 2019 Christmas Revels: A Solstice Journey Through Time. Meara is the main character of this year’s Christmas Revels: Unruly Magic.

With the temporary closure, the museums will continue to offer opportunities to stay connected through digital platforms. Visitors can still view virtual events, museums newsletters, listen to podcasts, browse social media content, and more. San Francisco County has been placed in the most restrictive purple tier, which limits most nonessential indoor activities. If you have already purchased tickets to visit the museum in the coming weeks, you will be contacted regarding a refund. All virtual events will continue as planned. While the museum is temporarily closed, patrons can still access the Museum from Home platform and engage with art from a distance. Peruse a wide selection of digital experiences, including meditative art videos, virtual tours, at-home art activities, and more. articles.text: A scene from Avegners: Endgame featuring an all-star cast. Movie review by Chris Honoré Avengers: Endgame. So, this is how it ends… a rockin’ franchise of 22 connected installments, replete with superheroes and astonishingly crowded with imagination and let’er rip, stand alone narratives wherein the only way Marvel Studios can construct a spectrum brand is to call it the Marvel Comic Universe (MCU). Okay, grandiose perhaps, but somehow nicely comprehensive. Think of MCU as a panoply of cosmic players – beginning with Iron Man (Robert Downey), Captain America (Chris Evans), the Incredible Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd) – all outrageously brimming with skill sets, bionic bespoke gear/suits / weaponry, each displaying swagger with attitude, and, in the case of Endgame, buttressed by space (and time) travel that not only thrills but resonates. In the aggregate It’s extraordinary. Pedestrian and mysterious, perhaps, to some cinephiles, but nevertheless there it is. Blockbusters R-US. And fundamentally, it’s the word “resonates” that interests and compels. It’s not just a universe of art and stories displayed in panels of vibrant colors, text, and bubble dialogue, displayed with a delineated genius. These are mythic stories that have a certain power and are taken to the silver screen where each tale is adapted and then enhanced by CGI, which means that now, today, and going forward, if the writers, directors, and cinematographers can imagine it, the filmmakers can seamlessly create it. And that has made all the difference. The embedded question that Endgame asks, as does every superhero comic ever produced by Marvel or DC, dating back to the 1930s, is: How do we understand what there is about superhero archetypes that so compel. What causes this response, this need to construct a universe overlay of fandom, one that ensnares so completely that nearly a century of illustrated magazines (and now films) has morphed into this massive body of work, which defies the gravity of pop culture fickleness and instead has managed to follow an arc that continues to trend upward. It’s remarkable. To restate the plot of Endgame, heavy with predicates, it does connect directly to Infinity Wars, picking up where the latter left off. For those steeped in MCU culture are definitely up to speed and need no tutorial regarding who is who and where is where, including the why of it all – from the profoundly genocidal Thanos, to Captain America, to Thor, Hulk, Black Widow, Hawkeye, Rocket, and, of course, Ant-Man. Suffice it to say that they team up for an epic do-over/time travel journey, their mission to alter decisively what is referred to by some as Thanos’ “Snapture” wherein he vanishes half of all the inhabitants of the universe using “six infinity stones.” Any story involving time travel is tricky, a sort of Mobius strip script, so to speak. Problems will arise that often elude simple solutions – characters meet themselves and so on – but not only are such moments adequately resolved in Endgame, they offer some comedy relief (in one long scene, Captain America faces off against Captain America), as well as a running montage of best scenes from stories past. Avengers: Endgame is three hours long, amounting to a galactic Ben Hur without an intermission. But the story engages from the get-go and doesn’t let up. Of course, exposition has never been the dominant mode chosen to move any MCU plot along. The final question to be asked is this: is this symphony of a finale the end of the beginning, or the beginning of the end? Best bet: it’s not over until it’s over and the spirit of Stan Lee, et al. lives in the MCU. Avengers: Endgame. Directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo. Starring Robert Downey, Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson. 120 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Avegners: Endgame.

articles.text: Carey Mulligan stars in Suffragette. Movie review by Chris Honoré Though the film Suffragette takes place over 100 years ago (1912-1913), and though its core issue, that of a woman’s right to vote, has long ago been settled, the narrative in this 2015 British historical drama still feels contemporary and relevant. A century has indeed passed, yet we know that women today still struggle for equal pay and job opportunities and, of course, the ultimate control of their bodies. What has been dimmed by the passage of time are the harrowing risks women took as they did battle with an iron-fisted, often misogynistic patriarchy that was committed to preventing them from acquiring the right to vote. It is through the eyes of Maud Watts (Carey Mulligan), an English working class woman, who works 12-hour days in a large factory-like laundry, washing and ironing other people’s clothes, that the story is told. In act one, Maud, who leads an insulated, narrow life – she’s married and has a son – is terrified when she finds herself on a London street and is unexpectedly swept up in a demonstration by suffragettes who are insisting on the right to vote. Suddenly Maud finds herself surrounded by women who are prepared to confront the police, feel the pain of their clubs, and endure arrest and weeks of incarceration for a cause in which they passionately believe. These courageous women are a revelation to Maud. She has long felt oppressed and treated as if she were mere property to be used and then disposed of by men. Abruptly the scales fall from her eyes and her consciousness is raised. Against all of her instincts, against everything she has been told about her place in the world (repeatedly by her husband), she rebels and joins what soon becomes a rising tide of civil disobedience, including destruction of property. In one moving moment in the film, Maud sits in front of government officials and describes her work and life and finally says quietly, “There might be another way of living this life.” That other way becomes her new existence. But it comes at great cost and personal pain. She discovers that the government is capable of remorseless harm: the suffragettes are beaten, jailed, and force-fed. As well, their neighbors (and society at large), voice their disapprobation by shunning and ridiculing them. Maud didn’t know that she would be asked to sacrifice all that she once held dear; but that was the price. Suffragette tells a powerful story. And Carey Mulligan gives a nuanced, spot-on performance, every glance and gesture suffused with ambivalence, her face often riven with pain. If courage is defined as being gripped by fear and still summoning the will to act, then Mulligan crafts her portrayal of Maud perfectly. As she says to a police inspector (Brendan Gleeson), who is attempting to convince her to betray the cause, “We will win.” It is a line that is delivered with conviction and hope, leavened by fear and uncertainty. Mulligan is supported by a superb cast, to include Ben Whishaw as her rigid husband and Helena Bonham Carter as a pharmacist and one of the leaders of the movement. Recall that what women were attempting to change was not just a law. It was a spectrum of social attitudes during a time when the “rule of thumb” meant that a husband could not beat his wife with a staff any thicker than his thumb. The film makes that point and more. Suffragette. Directed by Sarah Gavron. Starring Carey Mulligan, Helena Bonham-Carter and Brendan Gleeson. 1 hr., 46 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Suffragette directed by Sarah Gavron.

Act two has chase scenes, slowed down with some barely relevant exposition, then foes miniature and back to normal, even reaching the height of 50 feet. Lots of action. Rinse and repeat. Of course, the skinny plot embellishments barely make any sense. But logical coherence is not required. There’s even a character called Ghost/Ava (Hannah JohnKamen) who appears and fades, then reappears. Who or why is never made clear, but has something to do with the energy from the Quantum Realm that will be needed if Ava is to survive. But plot comments aside, for kids to enjoy Wasp all they need do is embrace the gestalt of the film because its all about adventure: a rich imagined, sometimes breathtaking, CGI-laden adventure, adored by all those kids who are well versed in Marvel lore. They’re not kidding around. They barely need an invitation to step into this crowded comic book universe and feel the superhero burn. For now, however, Ant-Man and the Wasp will do just fine. Ant-Man and the Wasp. Starring Paul Rudd, Evangeline Lilly, Michael Douglas and Michelle Pfeiffer. Directed by Peyton Reed. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Porco Rosso. Movie review by Chris Honoré Porco Rosso (Crimson Pig) begins in a carefree, unselfconscious manner and for some 20 minutes there is not a hint that that the protagonist, Porco Rosso, is a pig wearing a trench coat, aviator goggles, and a discrete mustache. In other words, yes, according to writer/director Hayao Miyazaki, pigs can fly. In Porco’s case, it’s om a vintage airplane. Porco (Michael Keaton) was an ace Italian flyer during World War I, and was known then as Marco Pagot. For reasons never explained, he has been cursed to live the rest of his life as an anthropomorphized pig. There is, however, one flashback where Marco fights an air duel with Austro-Hungarian planes; however, it hardly qualifies as backstory. The time is now the 1930s, and the place is all that surrounds the Adriatic Sea. Porco is a mercenary- bounty hunter pilot, hired to fight the menacing air pirates (aka Mamma Aiuto) who roam the local skies. In a brief air battle, Porco’s plane is damaged and he finds his way to Milan for repairs. In Milan he meets a young girl, Flo (Kimberly Willia Paisley), who happens to be an airplane mechanic and engineer. Porco hires her to fix his plane. As it turns out, there is another girl, Madame Gina (Susan Egan), and despite Porco’s piggishness, she develops a crush on him. Meanwhile a pilot named Donald Curtis (Gary Ewles), a A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Porco Rosso. rival of Porco’s, is crazy about Gina. And so a competitive triangle is formed. Much of the interaction takes place in the Hotel Adriano where all the local flyers hang out, good guys and bad. The hotel is also where Gina sings. It all sounds a bit strange and convoluted, even eccentric, but it isn’t. In fact, the plot is spare, straight-forward, comedic and ideal for young audiences. Kids will enjoy immensely the premise of Porco and will find the handdrawn animation – skies filled with airplanes, floating among billowing porcelain clouds – truly breathtaking and poetic. Miyazaki has demonstrated repeatedly in his work a love of flight: airplanes soaring through cobalt blue skies, symbols of freedom. As Flo says in one scene, “These old planes are works of art.” And it’s those flying machines that border on the mythic encompassing excitement and fantasy and good-hearted fun. Porco Rosso (Crimson Pig). Studio Ghibli animé. 1992. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Michael Keaton, Susan Egan and David Ogden Stiers. 1 hr., 30 min. In other words, yes, according to writer/director Hayao Miyazaki, pigs can fly. In Porco’s case, it’s om a vintage airplane. Porco (Michael Keaton) was an ace Italian flyer during World War I, and was known then as Marco Pagot. For reasons never explained, he has been cursed to live the rest of his life as an anthropomorphized pig. There is, however, one flashback where Marco fights an air duel with Austro-Hungarian planes; however, it hardly qualifies as backstory. The time is now the 1930s, and the place is all that surrounds the Adriatic Sea. Porco is a mercenary- bounty hunter pilot, hired to fight the menacing air pirates (aka Mamma Aiuto) who roam the local skies. In a brief air battle, Porco’s plane is damaged and he finds his way to Milan for repairs. In Milan he meets a young girl, Flo (Kimberly Willia Paisley), who happens to be an airplane mechanic and engineer. Porco hires her to fix his plane. As it turns out, there is another girl, Madame Gina (Susan Egan), and despite Porco’s piggishness, she develops a crush on him. Meanwhile a pilot named Donald Curtis (Gary Ewles), a A scene from Hayao Miyazaki’s Porco Rosso. rival of Porco’s, is crazy about Gina. And so a competitive triangle is formed. Much of the interaction takes place in the Hotel Adriano where all the local flyers hang out, good guys and bad. The hotel is also where Gina sings. It all sounds a bit strange and convoluted, even eccentric, but it isn’t. In fact, the plot is spare, straight-forward, comedic and ideal for young audiences. Kids will enjoy immensely the premise of Porco and will find the handdrawn animation – skies filled with airplanes, floating among billowing porcelain clouds – truly breathtaking and poetic. Miyazaki has demonstrated repeatedly in his work a love of flight: airplanes soaring through cobalt blue skies, symbols of freedom. As Flo says in one scene, “These old planes are works of art.” And it’s those flying machines that border on the mythic encompassing excitement and fantasy and good-hearted fun. Porco Rosso (Crimson Pig). Studio Ghibli animé. 1992. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Michael Keaton, Susan Egan and David Ogden Stiers. 1 hr., 30 min. articles.text: Somewhere awhile back I read: If there is one building alone in a field, there is Architecture; if there are two buildings, we have urban design. I’ve always thought this a good summary definition or description of an essential discipline that makes up our built environment. In the design world it can often be simply stated as the arrangement of various buildings and the design of the spaces between them. It inevitably applies to all scales of development, from the highly urban downtown San Francisco’s new Transbay Terminal and garden neighborhood, to small residential cities like Piedmont. (A visit to this remarkable work of urban design at the Transbay Terminal and garden early on a Sunday is well worth it. Drive and park right outside on the street. It is not crowded, is staffed by the city, and is accessible and free.) Good Urban Design is the secret to what makes vital, real “places” instead of just a collection of buildings. It is my opinion that this important design consideration is not well understood and has been, at best, a disappointment throughout our country for many decades. Focus has been on individual buildings, but the public spaces that link them – the urban design – has too often been poorly designed or even completely neglected. In Piedmont there seems to be a strong awareness of this important concept. Although our urban design considerations are not as dramatic as large, dense urban areas, they are, like everywhere, essential in the creation of places that foster community. Our General Plan, Zoning Code, and Design Review Process are the tools with which we deal with the preservation and enhancement of the relationships between buildPiedmont’s iconic Exedra Plaza is an excellent example of meaningful Urban Design. Combining the disciplines of planning, architecture, and landscape architecture, it is wonderfully proportioned, placed to terminate the visual axis of Highland Ave and located to provide a landmark, a meeting place, a venue for various events and is as a result, a place that fosters community.
