articles.text: It’s hard to imagine how much wine is made in the Languedoc region of France. Curving along the Mediterranean from Provence to close to the Spanish border it is a vast, wild area covered with grape vines that were first planted by the Romans two thousand years ago. It is often combined with Roussillon, its neighbor to the south. Together they have 700,000 acres of vines, the biggest vineyard area in the world - producing more wine than the entire U.S. For many years, the wines were churned out by co-operatives and the emphasis was more on quantity than quality. Any grocery store in France will feature hundreds of bottles of Languedoc wine starting at 2 euros. But the exciting story in Languedoc is the emergence over the past two decades of many artisan winemakers who care deeply about the quality of their wines and whose finest examples can compete with any wine region in France. It’s good news for the consumer because the reputation has not quite caught up with the wines; they still represent remarkable bargains selling in the U.S. for between $10 and $20. This month we will explore my very favorite Languedoc producer. (The best way to find these wines is to use the Wine Searcher app.) Domaine La Tour Boisee I have twice had the opportunity to visit this charming winery located in the small village of Laure Minervois. The property includes part of a medieval stone wall and tower that gives the winery its name. We were greeted by Jean-Louis Poudou. the owner, and Florence Hallett, the gracious business manager who walked us through the lineup of about 13 wines. Winery Owner Jean-Louis Poudou. The 2017 Marie-Claude Chateau Tour Boisee Minervois. The flagship wine is the 2017 Minervois Cuvee Marie-Claude an inky monster that has a rich blueberry nose that leaps from the glass. In the mouth it is rich and full bursting with blackberry fruit and finishing with firm tannins. I brought this wine to a blind tasting recently and it killed wines four times more costly. Available for less than 15 Euros. it is a remarkable value. Another killer wine from Tour Boisee is the 2018 Carignan from 60-year-old vines. It is rich, complex, dark and opulent. It oozes dark berry fruit and has a smooth, soft finish. This has become my house wine. Everyone I have poured it for has ended up buying a case. Amazingly it is available on the internet for around $10 a bottle. A value like this does my French/Scottish heart good. The winery has come out with a new label since I first visited. The 2019 Un Historie de Famille is a blend of Grenache, Domaine La Tour Boisee in the village of Laure Minervois, France.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok This Pear-Cranberry Upside-Down Cake is an ideal treat for the holidays. The 2020 Holiday Season will be different for most of us – scaled back. Or way back in the case of our family. I usually bake volumes whilst we enjoy gatherings with friends and family. Sometimes my holiday baking projects are fancy but most of the time they are a simple presentation. This pear-cranberry upsidedown cake manages to be both stunning and simple. It is perfect for any time of day. Pear-Cranberry Upside-Down Cake Inspired by Alice Waters and adapted from David Lebovitz. Makes a 9-inch round cake INGREDIENTS: For the topping: • 4 tablespoons unsalted butter • 3/4 cup light brown sugar, lightly packed • 1 pear, ripe but firm • 1/2 - 3/4 cup whole cranberries, fresh or frozen For the cake batter: • 1/2 cup unsalted butter, room temperature/squishy-soft • 3/4 cup granulated sugar • 2 large eggs, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cups all-purpose flour • 1-1/2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/4 teaspoon salt • 1/2 cup whole milk, room temperature INSTRUCTIONS: Position an oven rack to the lower third of the oven and preheat the oven to 350°. Lightly butter the sides of a 9-inch round cake pan and dust with flour. Line the bottom with parchment paper. For the topping: Melt the butter and brown sugar in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring frequently until the mixture begins to bubble. Remove from heat and cool. Meanwhile cut the pear in half lengthwise and remove the core. Slice further into quarter-inch wedges. Arrange the pears and cranberries in a single layer in the bottom of the cake pan, atop the parchment paper. Pour the melted butter-sugar mix over the fruit and spread it out evenly. Use a small offset spatula or your fingers to spread, especially if the mixture has firmed up. Set aside. For the cake: In a small bowl combine the flour, baking powder and salt. In a 3-quart mixing bowl, use an electric mixer on medium-high speed to beat the 1/ 2 cup of softened butter and granulated sugar until very light and fluffy, about 3 – 5 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl frequently. Reduce the electric mixer to medium speed and add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well between each addition. Add the vanilla extract and continue mixing until blended. On low speed add half of the flour mixture, then the milk and finally the rest of the flour mixture. Take care to avoid over mixing. You can finish the mixing by hand with a spatula to make sure the flour is barely incorporated into the batter. Spread the batter evenly over the fruit. Bake for about 45 minutes. Test for doneness with a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake. It should come out clean, with maybe a crumb or two clinging on. Remove from the oven and cool on a wire rack for 10 minutes. Run a small knife around the edge of the pan. Place the serving plate over the cake pan and quickly flip it over so the bottom of the cake and all the caramelized fruit is on top. Note: Test the heat of the cake pan before picking it up and inverting it onto the serving place. If too hot for comfort, use a kitchen towel or potholders to protect your hands. Serve warm. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

Curving along the Mediterranean from Provence to close to the Spanish border it is a vast, wild area covered with grape vines that were first planted by the Romans two thousand years ago. (The best way to find these wines is to use the Wine Searcher app.) Domaine La Tour Boisee I have twice had the opportunity to visit this charming winery located in the small village of Laure Minervois. The property includes part of a medieval stone wall and tower that gives the winery its name. We were greeted by Jean-Louis Poudou. the owner, and Florence Hallett, the gracious business manager who walked us through the lineup of about 13 wines. Winery Owner Jean-Louis Poudou. The 2017 Marie-Claude Chateau Tour Boisee Minervois. The flagship wine is the 2017 Minervois Cuvee Marie-Claude an inky monster that has a rich blueberry nose that leaps from the glass. In the mouth it is rich and full bursting with blackberry fruit and finishing with firm tannins. I brought this wine to a blind tasting recently and it killed wines four times more costly. Available for less than 15 Euros. it is a remarkable value. Another killer wine from Tour Boisee is the 2018 Carignan from 60-year-old vines. It is rich, complex, dark and opulent. It oozes dark berry fruit and has a smooth, soft finish. This has become my house wine. Everyone I have poured it for has ended up buying a case. Amazingly it is available on the internet for around $10 a bottle. A value like this does my French/Scottish heart good. The winery has come out with a new label since I first visited. The 2019 Un Historie de Famille is a blend of Grenache, Domaine La Tour Boisee in the village of Laure Minervois, France. Syrah, Mourvedre and Carignan. It appears to be a sort of second label to the flagship Marie Claude and has similar aromas and tastes but is lighter in body and has a shorter finish. It is also an excellent value. Viognier is a notoriously temperamental wine to vintify, so I was delighted that the 2019 Viognier Bel Serrat came out so well. It is medium bodied with understated floral aromas, plus notes of white pepper, green apple and lime. Zesty on the palate, it picks up vibrant citrus notes on the brisk finish. Drink over the next few years. The 2019 Malbec/Alicante Bel Serrat is the lightest of Tour Boisee’s red wines. I have never seen these two grapes blended together but this combination of 80% Malbec and 20% Alicante Bouchet works quite well. It smells of cherries and plums and is light and supple in the mouth with a clean finish. This is a perfect picnic wine to accompany charcuterie and cheese. Saving the best for last I have saved my favorite for last – a wine that is history in a bottle. In 1905 a farmer in Miniervois Laure planted a vineyard with 23 different varietals of grapes. (Reading the list of the varietals on the info sheet I confess to not having heard of half of them.) Vineyard blends often give great complexity to a wine. The 2018 Plantation 1905 is a vineyard blend on steroids. It as a beautiful nose of blackberries and black currants followed by a complex palate of plums, cherries and a touch of earth and leather. It gains complexity as it sits in the glass and ends with a smooth satisfying finish. Can’t think of a better companion to roast duck or cassoulet. Brilliant. The Plantation 1905 from Boisee.

articles.text: One of the rewards of sitting at a table outside the Piedmont Avenue Library is seeing the variety of patrons and hearing, if you ask, their stories. Sometimes you might even learn something. For instance, Michael, who lives across the street and subscribes to the HOOT, the library’s newsletter, uses a number of the library’s services. He checks out books, but he also receives them on his I-pad. He gets some books on Libby and others on Hoopla, both library programs. He streams movies and can access older media. He says that in non-COVID times the staff librarians are helpful and knowledgeable and he thinks the current team, brought together from several branches, is doing a remarkable job during this difficult time. Cora, who walked over, makes her requests online and picks up the books when she gets a notice they’re on site. Her children, six and four, really miss being able to go inside to attend Storytime, and miss being able to browse through the books. Debora, a regular patron, joined us and couldn’t give enough praises about the regular staff and the current service. “They deserve five stars….no, at least seven. It’s amazing how they’re coping,” she said. In the midst of patrons coming and going, collecting and returning books, a van with the library logo on its side pulled up in the loading zone on the street. Todd, the driver, unloaded several bins full of books onto a dolly and pushed them to the back door of the library. Soon he returned with a bigger load of books from inside the library, hauled them to the van, then headed to the main library. Three of these vans and drivers provide this service to all the branches in the city. Sumona, with a tiny baby strapped to her chest, and a four-year-old at home, has been coming to the library for four years, She likes books on Kindle; and her husband prefers hard copy books. Keeping library services available for readers and listeners is a real challenge these days, but five days a week, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., Emily Odia and her crew are there, making sure patrons get the books they ordered. Children’s Library Oakland Public Library Children’s Services is excited to share their love of books and support early language development while Oakland Public Library indoor areas remain closed. Toddler Song videos are available for children 3 years and younger. Each week’s Toddler Song video will be shared on Facebook and Twitter (@oaklibrary) every other Saturday. To view the video and the rest of the Toddler Song video playlist, visit the Oakland Public Library’s YouTube Channel on Saturdays at 10:30 am. Subscription to the HOOT, the newsletter of Piedmont Avenue Library, is free and available online at http://fopl.org.

articles.text: The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held this Friday evening, December 4, but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,’ she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.

Sometimes you might even learn something. For instance, Michael, who lives across the street and subscribes to the HOOT, the library’s newsletter, uses a number of the library’s services. He checks out books, but he also receives them on his I-pad. He gets some books on Libby and others on Hoopla, both library programs. He streams movies and can access older media. He says that in non-COVID times the staff librarians are helpful and knowledgeable and he thinks the current team, brought together from several branches, is doing a remarkable job during this difficult time. Cora, who walked over, makes her requests online and picks up the books when she gets a notice they’re on site. Her children, six and four, really miss being able to go inside to attend Storytime, and miss being able to browse through the books. Debora, a regular patron, joined us and couldn’t give enough praises about the regular staff and the current service. “They deserve five stars….no, at least seven. It’s amazing how they’re coping,” she said. In the midst of patrons coming and going, collecting and returning books, a van with the library logo on its side pulled up in the loading zone on the street. Todd, the driver, unloaded several bins full of books onto a dolly and pushed them to the back door of the library. Soon he returned with a bigger load of books from inside the library, hauled them to the van, then headed to the main library. Three of these vans and drivers provide this service to all the branches in the city. Sumona, with a tiny baby strapped to her chest, and a four-year-old at home, has been coming to the library for four years, She likes books on Kindle; and her husband prefers hard copy books. Keeping library services available for readers and listeners is a real challenge these days, but five days a week, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., Emily Odia and her crew are there, making sure patrons get the books they ordered. Friday’s Cancer League Holly Ball to be virtual The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held this Friday evening, December 4, but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,’ she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.

articles.text: Pete LaChapelle, a former resident of Piedmont, died on November 3, 2020. He was 84. Born Peter Hall LaChapelle in Detroit, Michigan on February 23, 1936, he grew up in Webster Groves, Missouri and Denver, Colorado. He attended East High School in Denver and played on the school basketball and baseball teams. He played two years on the All-State basketball team and was inducted into the East High School Sports Hall of Fame. He attended Stanford University where played on both the basketball and baseball teams for the Indians. He joined the Beta Theta Pi fraternity and graduated with a B.A. in Economics. Pete went on to earn a law degree at Lincoln Law School in San Jose and spent a 30-year career working as a Deputy District Attorney for the Alameda County Counsel’s office. His true joy was spent on the baseball field as a coach. He coached a variety of teams of all ages for over 45 years, including Hyatt House in the Young America League in Oakland, the Highlanders in the Piedmont Pony league, and for many years as assistant coach for the Piedmont High School baseball team. Hundreds of kids knew him as Coach LaChapelle, the guy that remembered their birthdays, what position they played, their batting average or ERA, and usually a career highlight or two. After retiring from the County Counsel’s office, he continued to coach at Piedmont High, helping to mentor new generations of players. He loved watching the San Francisco Giants and was in attendance for some of the team’s most memorable moments: opening day at Candlestick Park, the last game played at Candlestick, Pete LaChapelle, Piedmont High School’s former assistant baseball coach for many years, died on November 3. He was 84. Barry Bonds’ record setting home run, opening day at Pac Bell Park, and the winning 2014 World Series game at AT&T park between the Giants and the KC Royals. He was an avid runner, running every day around Lake Merritt or on the trails in the Oakland hills. Pete spent a lifetime loving music. Whether singing at a party, playing his ukulele, harmonizing with friends and family, music was a constant source of joy. What started out as an opportunity to join the Kingston Trio became a personal hobby shared with family and friends over a lifetime. Pete was known for his dry wit and fantastic sense of humor. Never without a quick comeback, or a great practical joke, Pete always loved a good one-liner. Pete is survived by his loving wife of 43 years, Barbara LaChapelle, son Steve of Oakland; daughter Tracy, her life partner Sid Wagner, and her son, Michael Hageman of Cobb, Californial; son Tom, wife Alex and their daughters, Sadie and Josie of San Luis Obispo; and son Erik, wife, Mayra and their son, Oliver, of Alcala de Henares, Madrid, Spain. He is also survived by step-daughter Suzanne Heske and sons Alden, Benjamin, and Owen of Piedmont, and step-son Jeffrey Cathrall, wife Brenda and son Jake, of Rock Tavern, NY. There will be a private celebration of life with family. articles.text: Burch Fitzpatrick, a longtime resident of Piedmont died on November 3, 2020 of congestive heart failure. He was 82. Born Burch Henry Fitzpatrick, Jr., he was a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley and the Boalt School of Law where he was chosen for membership on the Law Review. He served in the U.S. Military as a Second Lieutenant before beginning his law career as a deputy attorney general for the State of California. From there he spent some twenty years with the real estate law firm of Miller, Starr and Regalia where he served as managing partner. During that time he distinguished himself by successfully defending property owners over rent control in the City of Davis and then again for the city of San Jose in a case that was eventually tried by the U.S. Supreme Court. He finished his career with the San Francisco law firm of Graham and James. As a co-founder of the Piedunconditional love. His oversight was an important factor in the life of his kin and will be sorely missed. He was known for his integrity, humor and his affectionate nature, which remained with him until his death. Burch is survived by Patsy, his wife of 53 years, and by son John Fitzpatrick, and daughter, Carey Fitzpatrick Galles. He is also survived by grandsons Brogan and Sullivan Fitzpatrick, and Reid and Rielly Galles. Additionally, he is survived by 10 nieces and nephews, including his esteemed niece Seinin, who, along with his children, assisted enormously in the waning days of his illness. In accordance with his wishes, no services will be held. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations be made to the children’s hospice, the George Mark Home, 2121 George Mark Lane, San Leandro, CA.94578 (www.georgemark.org). He bought up the adjoining land, creating a tract of 800 acres. In partnership with a dozen businessmen from San Francisco, they made plans to build a large hotel on 200 of those acres. The remaining acres would be available for sale as large villa lots. News of the mineral spring grew quickly. Before the hotel was built, Mark Twain visited the Piedmont Springs while on a lecture tour in Oakland in 1868. Photographer Eadweard Muybridge recorded this visit in front of the gazebo-covered spring. Twain is holding a cup of mineral water. The Piedmont Springs Hotel opened in 1871 and promptly became a popular destination as a resort. The hotel has been described in a previous column, but it bears repeating for anyone who may have missed it. The hotel had a wide veranda, 20-first class bedrooms and two suites, five dining rooms, telegraph service, and a Grand Saloon (for men only) with a mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove. The ladies’ entrance allowed women to enter the hotel, avoid the saloon and proceed directly to the main dining room with its crystal chandelier, linen tablecloths and fine china. Visitors came to the Piedmont Springs Hotel for a pleasant day or a week and enjoyed excellent meals prepared with fresh meat from the surrounding ranches, milk and butter from Blair’s Dairy, and fruit and vegetables from the hotel gardens. They strolled the meandering paths down to the mineral spring for the healthful waters. In 1878, the Piedmont Springs Hotel was described as the following: “One of the most pleasant resort … the chief attraction of the place was the Mineral Springs, the water of which contains sulphur, magnesia, iodine, and iron, and is said to possess great curative qualities. Upon the property is located a good hotel, with which the lines of the Western Union Telegraph Company connect, and the place is accessible by fine carriage-roads, or the Oakland and Piedmont Horse Railway.” Contemporar y accounts claimed the mineral waters to “have great curative properties for rheumatism, neuralgia, dyspepsia and kidney ailments.” Other accounts described the taste as “a mixture of gun-washings and rotten eggs.” One writer in 1874 smartly stated that the “chief ingredient in all springs is the fresh air, exercise and freedom from care and restraint.” After the Piedmont Springs Hotel burned in 1892, Frank C. Havens purchased the land and opened Piedmont Park in 1898 as a Victorian strolling park with its Piedmont Clubhouse. The mineral spring continued to attract the health-seeking or curious. Havens enhanced the mineral spring with a faux-stone grotto with a handy tin cup for visitors to “take the waters.” A second grotto was at the top of the park. Chicken wire supported a rough concrete grotto, shaped and stained to look like a giant boulder. articles.text: If it tastes bad, it must be good for you. That was the thinking in the mid-1800s when a mineral spring was discovered in the Piedmont hills. At that time loggers cut most of the trees in the East Bay hills for lumber to build the fast-growing San Francisco during the Gold Rush. Ten years later, several ranches filled the bare Oakland foothills, growing grain and raising livestock. Colonel John C. Hays built his “Fernwood” estate in the northern portion of today’s Montclair. Gerhardt Medau’s dairy ranch became the southern part of Montclair. The Beard ranch was in the Trestle Glen neighborhood, and the Reed ranch covered part of today’s Piedmont and the Crocker Highlands area. In the 1860s a man, whose name was never revealed in historical records, purchased the former Reed ranch land. While walking the property, he came across an old abandoned bathtub. Looking around, he “rediscovered” a mineral spring nearby. “Rediscovered,” because years prior a Mr. Holmes had discovered the mineral spring and purchased Frank Havens built this large faux-stone grotto of wire and concrete around the famous Piedmont Sulphur Spring in 1898. a portion of the Reed ranch. Mr. Holmes was a prominent member of Congress from South Carolina and knew from experience the value of soaking in mineral water to cure his rheumatism. After Mr. Holmes died, the few people who knew about the mineral spring forgot about it. The new discovery of a mineral spring in Piedmont was very exciting to this land speculator. The upper stone grotto, below today’s Community Hall, points the way to the Sulphur Springs.

The upper grotto is in the amphitheater just below the Piedmont Community Hall. The concrete pockets may have held gold fish and ferns too. (The barbeque to the right is a more recent addition.) The famous mineral spring is further down the lower path toward Witter Field. The lower grotto was built on the site of the original wood gazebo where Mark Twain was photographed. Chicken wire supported a rough concrete grotto, shaped and stained to look like a giant boulder. For decades Into the 1930s and 1940s mineral water continued to seep from the spring, and curious children playing the park could taste that awful smelling water. In the 1950s, residents complained of the sulphur fumes, and the city capped the spring. As part of the City’s Centennial celebration in 2007, the remains of the lower grotto were preserved within a new stone bench. A clever cut-out in the bench shows a porA new stone bench protects the faux-stone grotto for the mineral spring. A cut-out window gives a glimpse of the original cement grotto, stained to look like rock. tion of Havens’ original concrete grotto, stained to look like striated rock. You can find the location of this lower grotto on the History Trail sign posted in front of the Veterans’ Building. If you enjoy reading these biweekly columns on the history of Piedmont, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving its annual newsletter. More information on Piedmont’s history and membership is on the website: Piedmonthistorical.org, or contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@pacbell.net. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, December 2, 2020 Mayor McBain Continued from page 1 Jeff Wieler resigned. He officially took the seat that following year, November 2018. In 2012, he listed fiscal responsibility as one of his top priorities if elected to council. Eight-plus years later, he believes fiscal stability to be an accomplishment of his tenure, and credits city staff in helping him make that possible. Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King noted that McBain’s background in finance has proved beneficial to Piedmont. “Bob had a significant career in banking prior to serving in public life. His skills in the financial world have served the city of Piedmont well through many tough budget discussions,” she said. McBain said that the city’s ability to attract and retain high-quality professionals makes working in Piedmont city government an incredibly positive experience. “I’ve always made a big effort to listen to city staff as a whole. We’ve been fortunate over the years to have people who are very talented and honest,” he said. “There’s a tremendous amount of information, intelligence, and experience in this staff, and you have to take advantage of that, and I think I’ve tried to do that.” McBain has been active as a volunteer in Piedmont for 16 years. He served on the Recreation Commission for six years and was its Chair for two years. He also served on the Municipal Tax Review Committee in 2011, one year before his election to City Council. Bob McBain with City Administrator Sara Lillevand Mayor Bob McBain and family in last year’s July 4th parade. COVID-19 Continued from page 3 Moss, Alameda County Health Officers, said in a statement. “These actions will help slow the spread of COVID in Santa Clara County and beyond.” Currently, Purple Tier restrictions are in effect countywide. Indoor dining is prohibited. Retailers can operate only at 25 percent capacity. Indoor museums, fitness centers and religious services must close. On November 19, the state announced that Purple Tier counties must follow a “stay at home” order prohibiting non-essential work, movement and gatherings between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. The order is currently scheduled to end 5 a.m. on Monday, December 21, although it may be extended or revised. The new order allows restaurants to operate after 10 p.m. for takeout. People are free to go to the grocery store or pharmacy. People can also walk their dog in their neighborhood. The county is urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes a general uptick throughout the United States. Health officials nationwide have warned about potential spikes in COVID-19 due to Thanksgiving and other upcoming holidays. The vast majority of counties in California are in the Purple Tier. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 1,225,189 cases of COVID- 19 in California. Cases have trended upward since October 18 in the state. There have been 19,211 deaths due to the disease statewide. Bob McBain and his wife Pam held a modest election night event at his house for volunteers who helped in his re-election campaign in 2016. In addition to his years in elected office, McBain served as the Investment Chair for the Piedmont Educational Foundation, a past board member of the Piedmont Parents’ Club, and a deacon and leader at Piedmont Community Church, in addition to being a trip leader for three years on the church’s mission service project in Mexico during Spring Break. McBain will be succeeded by Vice Mayor King. “Working with Bob has been a dream,” King said. “Always the consummate professional, Bob shows nothing but respect, calm and humor as he tackles the significant issues facing our city. I’ve learned so much from him,” she said. Former City Administrator Paul Benoit, who worked with McBain throughout his five-year career in Piedmont, offered similar sentiments. “Over my 35 plus years in City government I have worked with well over a hundred different council members and many different mayors. Bob ranks among the very best – and in both categories. He has a special talent for focusing in on what matters most, and was always a calm and steadying influence - especially when a difficult issue had potential get heated and out-of-hand,” Benoit said. “Those qualities were bolstered by his intelligence and keen wit. As mayor, Bob was always supportive. He was someone I regularly turned to for sage advice – and when I needed a hearty laugh. Bob was among a number of Piedmonters who made my time with the City a highlight of my career.” Benoit’s successor, current City Administrator Sara Lillevand, said that she has benefited greatly from McBain’s guidance. “Bob took his job as Mayor quite seriously, but never took himself too seriously,” she said. “Bob is comfortable, confident and patient enough to let good ideas emerge through listening and dialogue without ever needing credit – even though he often has the good idea first. His leadership skills are outstanding and have particularly shined during COVID,” she said. Although McBain’s volunteer years in Piedmont have come to a close, there is still work to do over the next few years concerning the rebuilding of the Piedmont Community Pool. McBain has no obligation to continue working on plans for the facility, but said that he will be available when needed. “It’s going to be a wonderful project for the city to work forward to. I’m confident it will attract interest, funding, and donations to make it a really beautiful facility,” he said. It was unusual for the city to place a bond on the ballot. Measure UU, the bond that will generate funding to build a new pool, was the first public bond the city has ever put forward. “It was a great team that [councilmember] Betsy Andersen put together. We owed it to the community to put it on the ballot and let the people decide. Given a twothirds requirement to pass is a very high bar. But I thought if any community was going to pass this, it would be Piedmont,” he said. Andersen, a member of the City Council who has worked with McBain for three years, helped organized the Yes on Measure UU campaign. She confirmed that McBain has served as a mentor to her during her time on Council. “It has truly been an honor to serve with Bob for the last three years of his nearly nine-year tenure on City Council. He has been a gracious mentor, considerate colleague, and an inspirational leader,” Andersen said. Burgess Owens Continued from page 5 ing her district’s red House seat. Spartz grew up in the Socialist Republic of Ukraine, living under socialism for 42 years, prior to earning her U.S. citizenship. Owens said the group is geared toward forwarding commonsense conservative principles while opposing the radical agenda of The ‘Squad’. “It’s interesting because we have a group of people who came in, we are very diverse and different races. We share in common the love for our country... a group of people who believe in God and family; a respect for women and authority -- and the other side that hates everything I mentioned. This group will be ... giving a contrast to the hard left.” Owens said of his new freshmen colleagues. Owens was born in Columbus, Ohio, where his father had moved to obtain a graduate degree he couldn’t get in Texas because of Jim Crow laws at the time. The family later moved to Tallahassee, Florida, where his father was a college professor. Owens was one of the first black players to represent the University of Miami football team as an All-American defensive back, where he majored in biology and chemistry. During his college career, he was inducted to the Hall of Fame of Outstanding College Athletes of America (one of 40 selected from all athletes in America) and later to the University of Miami’s Hall of Fame. Following college, Owens was a first round draft pick of the New York Jets in 1973. Later that year, he was selected as the Jets “Rookie of the Year” and to the NFL’s All-Rookie team. He played with the New York Jets for ten years where he served as Defensive Team Captain his last three seasons. After being traded to the Oakland Raiders, Owens led the defensive squad in tackles during their championship season, Super Bowl XV in 1981. In 1982, his final season, he led the Raiders in interceptions. Since retiring from the NFL, Owens has devoted his time to mentoring and improving the lives of our next generation of leaders. He is the author of a number of books including Why I Stand: From Freedom to the Killing Fields of Socialism, which is the foundation of his political platform. He is currently the Executive Director for the Utah Chapter of The One Heart Project, whose mission is: “To rescue, restore, and rehabilitate youthful offenders, and provide them with a true second chance to experience the American Dream.” He is a frequent guest contributor on Fox News.

articles.text: A pedestrian stop was conducted by Piedmont police officers on two men walking in the middle of the roadway on Moraga Avenue and Red Rock Road at 4:04 a.m. on Thursday, November 26. A records check revealed that Rahim Kenjoni, 41, from San Ramon, had an outstanding bench warrant out of Foster City with a $25,000 bail. Kenjoni also was on probation in Alameda County for False Impersonation. A search resulted in finding 19 grams of suspected methamphetamine and a driver’s license belonging to another person. The second person, Robert Gallardo, 42, from Newark, was on parole for Assault with a Deadly Weapon and Felony Theft. Gallardo was also on probation from Alameda County for Possession of Burglary Tools, Narcotics possession, and Petty Theft. A search revealed he was in possession of under a gram of methamphetamine, in addition to shaved keys and saw blades used for car thefts. Both men were arrested and transported to Santa Rita jail.

articles.text: A Thanksgiving message from John Cleese (Monty Python) In light of your failure to nominate competent candidates for President of the USA and thus to govern yourselves, we hereby give notice of the revocation of your independence, effective immediately. Her Sovereign Majesty Queen Elizabeth II will resume monarchical duties over all states, commonwealths, and territories (except Arkansas, which she does not fancy). Your new prime minister, Boris Johnson, will appoint a governor for America without the need for further elections. Congress and the Senate will be disbanded. A questionnaire may be circulated next year to determine whether any of you noticed. To aid in the transition to a British Crown Dependency, the following rules are introduced with immediate effect: You should look up “revocation” in the Oxford English Dictionary. 1. Then look up aluminium and check the pronunciation guide. You will be amazed at just how wrongly you have been pronouncing it. 2. The letter ‘U’ will be reinstated in words such as ‘favour’ and ‘neighbour.’ Likewise, you will learn to spell ‘doughnut’ without skipping half the letters, and the suffix -ize will be replaced by the suffix -ise. Generally, you will be expected to raise your vocabulary to acceptable levels. (look up ‘vocabulary’). 3. Using the same 27 words interspersed with filler noises such as “like” and “you know” is an unacceptable and inefficient form of communication. There is no such thing as US English. We will let Microsoft know on your behalf. The Microsoft spell- checker will be adjusted to take account of the reinstated letter ‘u’ and the elimination of -ize. You will relearn your original national anthem, God Save The Queen. 4. July 4th will no longer be celebrated as a holiday. 5. You will learn to resolve personal issues without using guns, lawyers, or therapists. The fact that you need so many lawyers and therapists shows that you’re not adult enough to be independent. Guns should only be handled by adults. If you’re not adult enough to sort things out without suing someone or speaking to a therapist, then you’re not grown up enough to handle a gun. 6. Therefore, you will no longer be allowed to own or carry anything more dangerous than a vegetable peeler. A permit will be required if you wish to carry a vegetable peeler in public. 7. All American cars are hereby banned. They are crap and this is for your own good. When we show you German cars, you will understand what we mean. 8. All intersections will be replaced with roundabouts, and you will start driving on the left with immediate effect. At the same time, you will go metric with immediate effect and without the benefit of conversion tables. Both roundabouts and metrification will help you understand the British sense of humour. 9. The Former USA will adopt UK prices on petrol (which you have been calling gasoline)-roughly $10/US gallon. Get used to it. 10. You will learn to make real chips. Those things you call French fries are not real chips, and those things you insist on calling potato chips are properly called crisps. Real chips are thick cut, fried in animal fat, and dressed not with catsup but with vinegar. 11. The cold tasteless stuff you insist on calling beer is not actually beer at all. Henceforth, only proper British Bitter will be referred to as beer, and European brews of known and accepted provenance will be referred to as Lager. South African beer is also acceptable as they are pound for pound the greatest sporting Nation on earth and it can only be due to the beer. They are also part of British Commonwealth - see what it did for them. 12. Hollywood will be required occasionally to cast English actors as good guys. Hollywood will also be required to cast English actors to play English characters. Watching Andie Macdowell attempt English dialogue in Four Weddings and a Funeral was an experience akin to having one’s ears removed with a cheese grater. 13. You will cease playing American football. There is only one kind of proper football; you call it soccer. Those of you brave enough will, in time, be allowed to play rugby (which has some similarities to American football, but does not involve stopping for a rest every twenty seconds or wearing full kevlar body armour like a bunch of nancies). Don’t try Rugby - the South Africans and Kiwis will thrash you, like they regularly thrash us. No more Orange Bowl, Rose Bowl, Cereal Bowl or Super Bowl. From now on..... get used to the World Cup. 14. Further, you will stop playing baseball. It is not reasonable to host an event called the World Series for a game which is not played outside of America. Since only 2.1% of you are aware that there is a world beyond your borders, your error is understandable. You will learn cricket, and we will let you face the South Africans first to take the sting out of their deliveries. 15. You must tell us who killed JFK. It’s been driving us mad. 16. An internal revenue agent (i.e. tax collector) from Her Majesty’s Government will be with you shortly to ensure the acquisition of all monies due (backdated to 1776). 17. Daily Tea Time begins promptly at 4 pm with proper cups, never mugs, with high quality biscuits (cookies) and cakes; strawberries in season. articles.text: Dress Best for Less, the nonprofit retail store that contributes money to Piedmont schools, generated $3,466 in sales during its annual one-day Ski Sale, The event usually draws a larger number of buyers, but the absence of snow in the mountains and the impact of coronavirus combined to limit sales to about one-half of normal. Despite this, Dress Best for Less Vice President Linda Smith Munyan said that they were satisfied with the total, given the overall plunge in retail sales nationwide due to COVID-19. “People had to wait in line to get in,” she added. There were many logistical changes made this year in order to comply with public health regulations. In prior years Dress Best for Less accepted cash only during its one-day ski sale. This year, they made the change to contactless payment after discussing their plans with the City of Piedmont. “We submitted a full-site plan to the city and event layout and traffic flow that had to be approved before we could proceed with the sale,” Smith Munyan said. Other changes in 2020 included common sanitary fixtures seen in most retail establishments during the COVID-19 pandemic. Staff had to limit the number of people allowed inside, and masks were required. One entry and a separate exit point was made to allow for easy social distancing, and a plexiglass shield was installed at the cash register. DBFL still has lots of great ski and snowboarding gear available for sale at its retail store on Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery. You can still donate new and gently used ski and snowboarding gear, but donations are made by appointment on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. Schedule a time by clicking on: https://bit.ly/DBFL-Donations. Photos by Julie Reichle A long line of people waited to purchase items at the annual Dress Best for Less Ski Sale on November 15. A plexiglass shield was installed at the cash register as a health precaution.

pages.text: 30 Wednesday, December 2, 2020 HUMOR To the citizens of the United States of America A Thanksgiving message from John Cleese (Monty Python) In light of your failure to nominate competent candidates for President of the USA and thus to govern yourselves, we hereby give notice of the revocation of your independence, effective immediately. Her Sovereign Majesty Queen Elizabeth II will resume monarchical duties over all states, commonwealths, and territories (except Arkansas, which she does not fancy). Your new prime minister, Boris Johnson, will appoint a governor for America without the need for further elections. Congress and the Senate will be disbanded. A questionnaire may be circulated next year to determine whether any of you noticed. To aid in the transition to a British Crown Dependency, the following rules are introduced with immediate effect: You should look up “revocation” in the Oxford English Dictionary. 1. Then look up aluminium and check the pronunciation guide. You will be amazed at just how wrongly you have been pronouncing it. 2. The letter ‘U’ will be reinstated in words such as ‘favour’ and ‘neighbour.’ Likewise, you will learn to spell ‘doughnut’ without skipping half the letters, and the suffix -ize will be replaced by the suffix -ise. Generally, you will be expected to raise your vocabulary to acceptable levels. (look up ‘vocabulary’). 3. Using the same 27 words interspersed with filler noises such as “like” and “you know” is an unacceptable and inefficient form of communication. There is no such thing as US English. We will let Microsoft know on your behalf. The Microsoft spell- checker will be adjusted to take account of the reinstated letter ‘u’ and the elimination of -ize. You will relearn your original national anthem, God Save The Queen. 4. July 4th will no longer be celebrated as a holiday. 5. You will learn to resolve personal issues without using guns, lawyers, or therapists. The fact that you need so many lawyers and therapists shows that you’re not adult enough to be independent. Guns should only be handled by adults. If you’re not adult enough to sort things out without suing someone or speaking to a therapist, then you’re not grown up enough to handle a gun. 6. Therefore, you will no longer be allowed to own or carry anything more dangerous than a vegetable peeler. A permit will be required if you wish to carry a vegetable peeler in public. 7. All American cars are hereby banned. They are crap and this is for your own good. When we show you German cars, you will understand what we mean. 8. All intersections will be replaced with roundabouts, and you will start driving on the left with immediate effect. At the same time, you will go metric with immediate effect and without the benefit of conversion tables. Both roundabouts and metrification will help you understand the British sense of humour. 9. The Former USA will adopt UK prices on petrol (which you have been calling gasoline)-roughly $10/US gallon. Get used to it. 10. You will learn to make real chips. Those things you call French fries are not real chips, and those things you insist on calling potato chips are properly called crisps. Real chips are thick cut, fried in animal fat, and dressed not with catsup but with vinegar. 11. The cold tasteless stuff you insist on calling beer is not actually beer at all. Henceforth, only proper British Bitter will be referred to as beer, and European brews of known and accepted provenance will be referred to as Lager. South African beer is also acceptable as they are pound for pound the greatest sporting Nation on earth and it can only be due to the beer. They are also part of British Commonwealth - see what it did for them. 12. Hollywood will be required occasionally to cast English actors as good guys. Hollywood will also be required to cast English actors to play English characters. Watching Andie Macdowell attempt English dialogue in Four Weddings and a Funeral was an experience akin to having one’s ears removed with a cheese grater. 13. You will cease playing American football. There is only one kind of proper football; you call it soccer. Those of you brave enough will, in time, be allowed to play rugby (which has some similarities to American football, but does not involve stopping for a rest every twenty seconds or wearing full kevlar body armour like a bunch of nancies). Don’t try Rugby - the South Africans and Kiwis will thrash you, like they regularly thrash us. No more Orange Bowl, Rose Bowl, Cereal Bowl or Super Bowl. From now on..... get used to the World Cup. 14. Further, you will stop playing baseball. It is not reasonable to host an event called the World Series for a game which is not played outside of America. Since only 2.1% of you are aware that there is a world beyond your borders, your error is understandable. You will learn cricket, and we will let you face the South Africans first to take the sting out of their deliveries. 15. You must tell us who killed JFK. It’s been driving us mad. 16. articles.text: Sarah Pearson was the top vote getter when she was first elected to the Piedmont School Board in 2012. Andrea Swenson and Sarah Pearson concluded their tenures on the Piedmont School Board after nearly nine years of service. Pearson and Swenson received accolades and thanks from colleagues, friends and fans during their final school board meeting on November 10. Mayor Bob McBain made initial comments. “I can speak on behalf of the entire city council and the whole city staff in saying how much we have valued and benefitted from your roles on the school board, and more broadly speaking, your roles in the community for the last few years,” he said. McBain, whose 8-1/2 year tenure on the city council also ends in December, hinted at the need for a city proclamation honoring the two board members. Swenson and Pearson have been part of many initiatives by the school district since 2012, none bigger than the $66 million H1 bond. The fruits of that labor came into fruition in the form of the new three-story, state-of-theart STEAM high school classroom building, with a second building to be constructed next to it for the new Alan Harvey Theater. While COVID-19 prevented a ribbon cutting ceremony, the new school environment with unrivaled views and technology will be a pleasant reward for students when they are allowed to return to campus. In sharing her vision of the future, Pearson said, “My hope is that every student in our district finds joy and becomes an engaged learner. It inspires me to see our students become leaders for change who think critically for themselves and for the benefit of all.” The portion of the board meeting honoring the two civic servants was filled with admiration and respect, often overflowing into tears from callers and board members alike. Physics teacher Marna Chamberlain, head of the Science Department, called in to the zoom meeting to comment on the work and character of Swenson. After the acknowledgments Swenson noted, “I told myself I wouldn’t cry, but Marna undid me.” Chamberlain credited Swenson as instrumental in helping to build Chamberlain’s personal confidence and composure, especially in public speaking. In 2015 Swenson, Chamberlain, Cathy Glazier and much of the community helped fundraise and put together a memorial garden, outdoor classroom and bench area in honor of PHS science teacher Eileen Rohmer. Rohmer, Chamberlain’s best friend, passed away in 2012 and the garden carries on Rohmer’s legacy. “You showed up and you were digging in the dirt with me, putting in herbs, and that’s what we need,” Chamberlain said of Swenson. Swenson and Pearson’s last year on the board was not a victory lap, but an unexpected marathon with a blindfold due to COVID-19. The school board members were thrust into the spotlight with the towering tasks of a school closure due to the COVID pandemic. It required a brand-new model of teaching from a distance and searching for the best way and time for schools to reopen. Special school board meetings became as common as scheduled ones, and some labored on, over Zoom, for almost seven

Pearson, Swenson feted for service to School Board By Jay Russell Andrea Swenson and Sarah Pearson concluded their tenures on the Piedmont School Board after nearly nine years of service. Pearson and Swenson received accolades and thanks from colleagues, friends and fans during their final school board meeting on November 10. Mayor Bob McBain made initial comments. “I can speak on behalf of the entire city council and the whole city staff in saying how much we have valued and benefitted from your roles on the school board, and more broadly speaking, your roles in the community for the last few years,” he said. McBain, whose 8-1/2 year tenure on the city council also ends in December, hinted at the need for a city proclamation honoring the two board members. Swenson and Pearson have been part of many initiatives by the school district since 2012, none bigger than the $66 million H1 bond. The fruits of that labor came into fruition in the form of the new three-story, state-of-theart STEAM high school classroom building, with a second building to be constructed next to it for the new Alan Harvey Theater. While COVID-19 prevented a ribbon cutting ceremony, the new school environment with unrivaled views and technology will be a pleasant reward for students when they are allowed to return to campus. In sharing her vision of the future, Pearson said, “My hope is that every student in our district finds joy and becomes an engaged learner. It inspires me to see our students become leaders for change who think critically for themselves and for the benefit of all.” The portion of the board meeting honoring the two civic servants was filled with admiration and respect, often overflowing into tears from callers and board members alike. The Oakland Zoo introduces a new festival at night of larger than life glowing animal lanterns. “GLOWFARI” has been in the works for a year and a half, and takes the place of Zoo Lights. Hundreds of intricate, beautiful lanterns spaced throughout the zoo promise to create a wonderland of escape so desperately needed. Music, gorgeous views of the bay and animatronic dinosaur models make GLOWFARI an event for people of all ages. See story and more photos on page 11. articles.text: Editor: During this season of gratitude, we want to express our heartfelt thanks to everyone in the Piedmont community who has supported or who is planning to support the Giving Campaign this year. To date, we have raised $2.3 million [of a goal of $3 million] from more than 850 families for this year’s campaign to create stronger schools together. We need your support. The news this week about our county and most of the state falling back into the purple tier, and about our schools not reopening as planned, is sad and frustrating. The pandemic’s impact on our schools feels acutely painful. We are tired of distance learning. We all want our kids to have a better educational and social-emotional experience. Despite the challenges of the 2020-21 school year, we remain 100% committed to fundraising for our schools. Why give now? We are taking a long-term view; we deeply value having strong schools for our kids in our local community. When there is a widespread vaccination and kids [can] return to full-day school in person, we want our kids to be able to return to the robust, excellent educational experience we have always had in Piedmont. The dollars we are raising for the Giving Campaign are essential for the ‘21-22 school year. We understand that many people would like to have their voices heard and withholding Giving Campaign dollars, on the surface, may seem like a logical way to take a stand. However, lack of funding hurts Piedmont students more than anyone else. If we don’t raise our targeted funding, we will need to cut the school budget in June by increasing class sizes and cutting programs. The only way we can have strong schools for our kids to return to is by raising these dollars. It has always been, and still is, up to us. We know that fundraising can’t solve all of the macro health and safety challenges ahead of us, but if we do our part now, we can put our schools in a position to thrive once again when this pandemic is behind us. Please pledge or donate today at www.piedmontedfoundation. org/donate. -Amelie Kappes, Colleen Allan, and Teebie Saunders Giving Campaign co-chairs For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: Before entering the ministry, I spent nearly 20 years owning and operating a construction business in Boston, Massachusetts. Some of my contracts were for new construction but a fair amount of my business involved renovation. As a result, I have always seen demolition as part of the process of creating something better. For me, the dust, the piles of debris and the disruption of life don’t bother me because I know it can lead to a better future. As the pandemic rages on with yet another wave of destruction, there are also dangerous riptides of division tearing at the fabric of our country. Being so divided as we are, it seems almost impossible to imagine a future where we, as a society, actually live up to our name, The United States of America. But there is also the very real question of whether we have ever lived up to that name. The threat many feel of becoming a disenfranchised voter is nothing new. For instance, how could our ancestors ever describe our country as The United States of America while black and female citizens were denied a vote?

articles.text: Alameda County named Dr. Nicolas Moss as its permanent Public Health Director on November 17. He served in an interim role since July after Dr. Erica Pan was elevated to be California’s lead epidemiologist. Moss served as the Director of the HIV/STD section of the Alameda County Health Department for 7 years, from April 2013 to July 2020, until he took over as Interim Health Officer. Prior to that, he served as the Director of Clinical Prevention of the HIV Prevention Section at the San Francisco Department of Public Health for two years. Moss trained as an infectious disease medicine specialist and medical epidemiologist for the majority of his career, and is credited with overseeing the county’s response to the COVID- 19 emergency. “Dr. Moss brings extensive knowledge in communicable disease and nearly 10 years of experience in leadership roles,” said County Health Care Services Agency Director Colleen Chawla. “His appointment provides deep knowledge of, and ongoing continuity in, our response to the COVID-19 pandemic.” Moss received a degree from the University of California at Berkeley, and his medical degree from the University of California at Irvine. He trained in internal medicine, infectious diseases and public health at the University of Washington in Seattle. “My number one priority is Dr. Nicolas Moss to protect and improve health by achieving equity through partnership, fostering safe and healthy communities, and promoting fair and inclusive opportunities for all residents,” Moss said.
articles.title: Dr. Nicolas Moss named permanent County Public Health Director

articles.text: Dry spell forecast in Northern California for next few weeks While a bit of wet weather has moved in across Northern California, state officials are not yet declaring that the historically destructive 2020 wildfire season is over. Wildfire season often ends around November 30, but global warming has already changed fire trends in the state. As of yesterday, Tuesday, November 24, Cal Fire has not ordered any of its 21 units throughout California to activate winter preparations, traditionally a signal that the wildfire season for the year is done. Representatives from the National Weather Service and Cal Fire met this month and suggested that Northern California’s wildfire season appears to be in its closing stages, but nothing was officially announced. In fact, meteorologists are concerned that the next few weeks will be unseasonably dry. “Although temperatures have been slightly on the cool side of average for the past couple of weeks, along with some modest Northern California precipitation – it’s quite clear that fire season (locally mitigated though it may be) is not going out without a fight,” climate scientist Daniel Swain wrote in a report this week. Dry conditions are expected statewide through the first week of December, and there are concerns that strong winds in Southern California will significantly increase wildfire risks in the lower third of the state. The 2020 wildfire season will be remembered as one of the most devastating in history across California and the entire western United States. In Piedmont, skies turned a ghastly orange hue in September due to an outpouring of smoke from several fires blazing in the region. Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which burned in and around Mendocino National Forest, was the largest wildfire in California history and the state’s first “gigafire,” meaning a fire that burns over 1 million acres. The fire, sparked by lightning in August, was declared 100 percent contained by Cal Fire on November 12 after burning a total of 1,032,648 acres. Even when the 2020 wildfire season is declared over, the Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to stay vigilant and prepare for fire emergencies. Piedmonters can learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.title: Wildfire season continues as November comes to close

articles.text: The annual Toys for Tots campaign has begun, and Piedmont Fire Department has placed a donation box by the front doors of City Hall. Residents are encouraged to drop off new, unwrapped gifts for children in the bin during daytime hours seven days a week. Last year, the Marine Corps Reserve, which sponsors the nationwide campaign, had 109 donation sites in Alameda County and collected 25,000 toys to kids in the county. “With the help of Piedmont residents, we’re hoping that we can see that number go higher this year,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. Firefighters will empty the bin at the end of each day. If residents wish to bring a large number of donations, call the Fire Department at 420-3030 to arrange for a firefighter to be there. Checks may be left with the Fire Department, but made payable to Toys for Tots, 2144 Clement Avenue, Alameda, CA, 94501. articles.text: As Piedmont and Clayton engage in a friendly competition called the Census Challenge, Piedmont is still leading the state in 2020 census response rates with 90 percent of residents. Of that pool, 84.5 percent of residents responded online. As of press time, Clayton’s self-response is 88.9 percent, and 80.2 percent did so online. The two cities, which are about 23 miles apart, have nearly identical demographics. Both cities are comparable in population; Clayton, with 4,006 households, is slightly larger than Piedmont with 3801 households. In a front-page story in the Clayton Pioneer, the city’s weekly publication, Mayor Julie Pierce expressed readiness for a little friendly competition. “We’re determined to post the highest response rate in the state for the 2020 decennial,” Pierce told the Pioneer. “Clayton residents have a proud history of civic engagement and participation. We’re going to show Piedmont, and the rest of the state, just how engaged we are.” Pierce added that the stakes are very high for California this time around. “We could lose a congressperson. It’s essential that everyone be counted,” she said. Clayton resident and Census Bureau media specialist Pamela Michael explained the importance of responding to this year’s census. “The apportionment of legislators is based on census data. Each state is allotted two senators regardless of population, but your congressperson as well as state legislators is determined by the number of people in your given geography. It’s critical that everyone is counted in order for everyone to be represented,” Michael said. Residents had until July 31 to voluntarily respond to the census. On August 11, census takers began knocking on doors of households that have not responded, and the deadline to complete the census ended on October 15 this year. “This competition is a great way to engage our communities in an effort that is important to both our cities,” said Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain. “We need to reach out to all our residents to ensure that they have the chance to participate in the census. If a little competition can step up the effort, then we will have some fun and support a very good goal.” Mayor Pierce has promised a gift basket of Clayton-produced honey and other offerings should the town not come in first by the August 11 deadline. Piedmont’s prize has not yet been determined. California’s self-response rate is 69.6 percent, more than the national average. Alameda County had one of the highest response rates by county in the state, with 75.8 percent responding to the census, and 67 percent of that pool doing so online. Self-response data is available for viewing by county, city, and state, at https://2020census.gov/ en/response-rates.html.
articles.title: Piedmont still leads the state in Census response

articles.text: We’ve all been there: there’s no milk in the fridge and you need to go grocery shopping. Even though the store is only half a mile away, you jump into the car to make the drive instead of walking. It’s faster, convenient, and doesn’t matter that much in the grand scheme of things, right? Although it might feel that way, driving is hugely impactful in emitting carbon emissions. Transportation is California’s largest source of carbon emissions – about 41 percent of the total – and has been the largest since at least 2000. This is due to California’s infamous car culture. In a state of 39.5 million people, Californians have over 27 million drivers’ licenses. From 2000 to 2016, vehicle miles traveled in the state increased by 11 percent, even as emissions have decreased. This is largely due to SB 32 and subsequent updates, which helped make vehicle fuel standards more rigorous. As California is the fifth-largest economy in the world, laws that are passed here typically influence manufacturing decisions. Despite vehicles consistently becoming more fuelefficient, Californians are driving more, meaning that the percentage of emissions stemming from transit remains stagnant. Beyond California, transportation is a large source of emissions nationwide. In 2016, the transportation sector passed energy production as the largest source of carbon emissions nationally. Almost 60 percent of transit emissions stem from light duty vehicles like SUV’s, pickup trucks, and cars. Another 23 percent come from trucking. There are about 275 million vehicles in the United States alone. Although car emissions are an urgent climate issue, it’s tough to change the behavior of that many individual drivers. For that reason, states and the federal government are finding cleaner alternatives to the energy grid – another large source of emissions in the U.S. While many states have been working on this for two decades, changing how millions of drivers get around is more of an uphill battle. Changing how we produce energy from a few hundred power plants is an easier legislative task than taking a few hundred million cars off the road. That’s not to say that transportation solutions don’t exist. Throughout the country and especially in California there has been a push towards electric vehicles, or EVs. In 2019, almost 700,000 EV’s were sold in California alone. This push is designed to take advantage of the energy grid, which is becoming “cleaner,” to help solve the transportation problem, which is still “dirty.” Many of these issues don’t have a clear solution. Transportation is one of the top three highest emitting activities in Piedmont, which is why the City is encouraging drivers to switch to electric vehicles and cut usage of gas-powered cars. Public transportation, walking, biking, or even carpooling all emit fewer GHG’s than driving a traditional car. Reexamining activities that we take for granted can help make a difference. When it comes to a shared problem like climate change, solutions stem from actions we can all take. If you would like to learn about other ways to reduce your carbon footprint, sign up for the Piedmont Climate Challenge at: www. piedmontclimatechallenge.org. Nate Redinbo is with the Piedmont Planning and Building Department for one year as Piedmont’s Civic Spark fellow. Reach out to him at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov with any opinions and questions on reach codes, jogging, or bread baking. He is publishing a monthly article on environmental topics that affect Piedmonters.

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved updating the Pedestrian Bicycle Master Plan adopted in 2014. This update, called Piedmont Safer Streets (PSS), is intended to improve the conditions on our streets while including an additional focus on traffic safety. This plan will detail specific steps to make streets safer for the growing number of people who are walking and bicycling in town. To assist with the plan, a Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC), which has met in October and November, will advise staff and consultants with the development of the Safer Streets plan. The City believes that public participation is essential not only to ensure that workable decisions are made, but also to show trust in the planning process. With the goal of keeping the planning going through this pandemic, there are three opportunities for the public to provide input on safety needs and concerns. • Digital Community Workshop A zoom workshop is scheduled for Wednesday, December 9 starting at 6 p.m. The workshop will review progress made since 2014 and will include a community discussion on future directions. • Online survey A brief survey has been created to hear Piedmonters’ opinions on key questions concerning walking, biking, and traffic safety. Everyone who responds will be eligible to win a gift card at Mulberry’s Market. • Pinnable Map page Residents can post location-specific comments about walking, biking, and traffic safety, or even post your cool ideas and suggestions for improving street conditions. It’s another opportunity to win a gift card. For more information, contact Associate Planner Gopika Nair at gnair@piedmont.ca.gov. or details and to learn more about the Safer Streets project, visit Piedmont Safer Streets project website (https://www.piedmontsaferstreets.org/).
articles.title: City seeks input on pedestrian & bike safety

articles.text: For 36 years the Piedmont Scouts BSA has collected food and funds to help feed families in Alameda County. All food and funds are given to the Alameda County Food Bank. Piedmont residents were generous last year, with the donation of 8,095 pounds of food and $6,215 in cash to the Food Bank. The the Scouting for Food Campaign had to be moved to a virtual drive, this year residents have been even more generous. Last week the Scouts surpassed their goal of raising $7500 by several thousand dollars, and all obline. But the need is great year. The Piedmont Scout Food Drive will continue to December 6. “We hope that those who have so generously donated food in the past will give online this year to help us combat food insecurity,” said Katy Kobal, Scouting for Food Chair. Every dollar donated allows the Food Bank to purchase $7 worth of food. Alameda County has one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. Nearly 20 percent of residents in the county live below the poverty line. Of those receiving assistance from the Alameda County Food Bank, two-thirds are children and the elderly. Donate online today by going to https://tinyurl.com/scoutingforfood2020 and turn $1 into $7 of food. For more information contact Morgan Fjord at the Scout office at 510-844-4752. About Piedmont Council BSA The Piedmont Council has proudly served our community since 1910 when the first troop overnight event was held in Redwood Canyon in Oakland. The council was chartered eleven years later, in 1921. Although it is one of the smallest councils in the nation, it is widely recognized for its excellence and traditions of service and quality programs. Year after year more than 50% of the eligible youth in Piedmont participate in the council’s many programs. Currently more than 1000 young people and 300 adult volunteers actively participate in Scouting in Piedont. THIS FALL FOR YOUR SHOPPING CONVENIENCE Fine Papers Crafts Urban Art Journals

articles.text: We appreciate that every family celebrates the holidays differently, and we support everyone’s choice of festive foods. There’s a classic nationwide debate coming up around the Thanksgiving table… and it has nothing to do with politics. When serving up the holiday turkey, everyone has opinions on white meat or dark meat. So, what’s the difference? And which does science say is better? The difference in dark meat and white meat is rooted in the areas that the bird uses most during its lifetime. You’ll find dark meat in more highly used areas like the legs and thighs. White meat is found in less exercised areas like the breasts and wings. Every day is leg day when you’re a turkey Turkeys are rarely found in the air, preferring to get around by walking instead of flying. They have powerful legs and thick thighs that are better for locomotion than their wings. In fact, they can run up to 25 mph! Because they use their legs so often, turkeys build up muscles in their thighs and calves. As the muscles enlarge with usage, more capillaries, connective tissue and protein filaments develop, creating a tougher texture in dark meat. Dark meat is filled with myoglobin, which carries oxygen to the muscles and is more prevalent in more used areas. Myoglobin contains iron that oxidizes and creates richer color and flavor in dark meat. So, what’s the deal with white meat? Oppositely, white meat areas of turkey are used less often, like A turkey the way we’re used to seeing it on the roads of Piedmont. With fewer it is the holidays so don’t feel capillaries and myoglobin, the guilty over a few extra calories. meat has less color and flavor. However, white meat areas don’t need as much collagen to hold the meat fibers together, resulting in a more tender texture. Plus, white meat areas are usually lower in calories and fat. The Great Debate In conclusion, there are pros and cons to both varieties of turkey meat. Whatever your preference, here’s a cheat sheet to prepare you to defend your favorite type this holiday season. Dark Meat More used parts of the turkey, including legs and thighs Pros: more vitamins and minerals (higher in iron, zinc, folate, and vitamins B6 and B12), more intense flavor, darker color Cons: higher in fat and calories, tougher meat White Meat Less used parts of the turkey, including breast and wings Pros: lower calories and fat, more tender Cons: less color, less flavor Mary Catherine Frantz is Marketing and Communication Manager at Chabot Space and Science Center, 10000 Skyline Blvd. in Oakland.
