articles.text: “Calvin, life could be a lot worse…” – Calvin’s mom “Ya, but it could be a lot better too…” – Calvin –Bill Watterson, “Calvin and Hobbes” If 2020 was a logic problem, it would be something like this: “You are going down the river at 2 mph and your canoe loses a wheel, how much pancake mix is needed to reshingle your roof?” That just about sums up the year so far. Not a lot of it makes any sense. It has been single-handedly the slowest yet fastest year I have ever experienced. Throughout this year we have had a lot of sadness thrust upon us, but even through the sadness, we have seen some happiness. Like most of the Earth’s population, I watched many of my plans put on hold or completely canceled. I was supposed to go on tour with my choir to Canada, and on a vacation to Hawaii with my family for the first time in three years. Since March, we have been barred from going to school, with no end in sight. I rehearse Finnish songs on Zoom (that’s real fun) with a bunch of other lonely kids. The most entertainment I had during the fall was checking air quality on my battered phone my mom refuses to replace because she lost her job and is being frugal. Things are much worse for people who lost a loved one to Covid-19, or to police brutality, or in one of the many wildfires we experienced this summer and fall. Everyone has lost a piece of themselves. And now we as a human race are forced to put our heads together to figure out how to save ourselves from all of the problems that have been put on our shoulders. No one can carry all this weight by themselves, so we all need to support one another; that is how we will accomplish more. It may seem like there is too much chaos and confusion for there to be any good, but that’s not so. On November 3, 159 million Americans voted— the highest turnout since 1908. It looks like people were so fed up with our current head of power they decided to take matters into their own hands. On Saturday November 7, after four nail-biting days of waiting, America – and a large part of the world – rejoiced as Joe Biden was elected to be the 46th president. This comes after four years of waking up and being scared to look at the news headlines. Now, multiple agencies have announced they are close to developing a vaccine against coronavirus, and possibly ready by the end of the year. Maybe that means in the spring we will go back to school. We are about to have a holiday where you get to stuff your face with an immense amount of tasty food. Christmas is right around the corner (and my birthday is also soon). I guess one thing you could be celebrating is that your favorite columnist, who has given you quality content all through this year, managed to get through 2020. Let’s talk gratitude. There are always things that people should be grateful for. Even if it’s just finding the airpods you lost in the beginning of the year. Or maybe being grateful for not getting sick with The Rona. I am grateful for going from a D- in French to a B+, and for getting a 90 on my test in math. I’m grateful for a chance to jump into a hotel pool in my clothes, because my parents allowed me I know that it’s not the New Year yet, so why am I doing a flashback? This is Thanksgiving, and we’re supposed to reflect back on the things that happened. Here’s one: 2020 feels like whoever the greater power is, he just fell asleep on the job, or maybe, he got bored, and instead of spreading these events over the next 10 years, just typed in: “Put everything in one year.”
articles.title: What are you thankful for?

The house at 801 Magnolia Avenue had several occupants after Frank Havens. On October 19, 1910, the Oakland Tribune advertised a two-bedroom, two-bath furnished bungalow for lease at the location. Ads in 1912 listed “woman wanted” for cooking, laundry and sewing. In 1920, the census recorded that a woman named Lenora K DePuali lived at 801 Magnolia Avenue with her teenaged son, married daughter, husband, nephew, and servant. Gail Lombardi, co-chair of the Piedmont Historical Society, said that the house must have grown in size during that time. The DePauli family members lived in the house from at least 1920 to 1926. The 1930 census showed six people living in the building: Granville and Florence Abbott, Eugene and Ruth Ebey, their daughter Florence Ebey, and a servant. The Abbotts moved there in 1933, and the Ebeys left in 1934. Architect Noble Newsom, of the Newsom Brothers firm, occupied the residence briefly, from 1935 to 1937. Despite his architectural profession, Newsom did not remodel the property. “Until the Piedmont Historical Society acquired the church history, I had always assumed that Newsom had remodeled the house. However, the attached photo is dated 1928 in the church history,” Lombardi confirmed. Photo of the building at 801 Magnoiia Avenue in 1928 when it was a residence. The First Church of Christ, Scientist recorded the building’s history from there. They purchased the building at 801 Magnolia Avenue in 1928 as a temporary building while they continued to search in the city for a permanent location. After several years, church members decided that the property would be satisfactory as a permanent church. They hired architects Morton Williams and Ralph Wastell to remodel the house. The church built a separate structure in the 1960s as a Sunday School. The city purchased the property from the church in 2003, but it was sparingly used because of structural and maintenance problems. In those years, it had fallen into disrepair. A small group of residents proposed to the city council in 2011 that under the name Piedmont Center for the Arts they would operate as a non-profit with the goal of creating a cultural arts center for the entire city. It was the first such endeavor since the early 1900s with some arts and music being offered in what is now Piedmont Park. Next: Birth of a performing arts center

articles.text: Nikka Piterman, a former Piedmont resident and Piedmont High School graduate in 2012, was selected by the Republican Party as its candidate to challenge Barbara Lee for California’s 13th Congressional District in this year’s general election. The race ended with the likely winner, Lee, taking the seat; but the process of running a campaign was, for Piterman, an “overall positive experience.“ In order to get on the ballot in California, a candidate must meet a variety of state-specific filing requirements and deadlines. An individual can seek the nomination of a state-recognized political party, as an independent, or as a write-in-candidate. To gain the backing of the Republican party, Piterman met with local party leaders. “Typically you get a number of signatures from people in the party. It was about three or four months before we started collecting signatures [from the public] then I met with the local GOP, and they welcomed me with open arms and encouraged me to run,” he said. He added that he was surprised to find out that two years ago there were approximately 40 districts in California with no Republican representation. Democratic incumbents and candidates ran largely unopposed, or against write-in candidates. The process then began with gathering signatures. To run for California’s 13th Congressional District required obtaining 2,000 signatures by the filing deadline U.S. state. Piterman would like to see a referendum in Puerto Rico to ensure voluntary admission, and then upon admission, grant Puerto Rico with two senators and four representatives. He also sought to allocate five percent of the defense budget to the U.S. Space Force, and reclassify marijuana as a Schedule V substance. Piterman’s political aspirations began in high school in Piedmont. His involvement with the PHS debate club, the Junior Statesmen of America, was formative. In his final years of high school he served as Debate Club president and oversaw its growth from five members to nearly 40. Piterman confirms that he wasn’t expecting the race to come close, especially to political powerhouse Lee, now in her 12th congressional term. “I’m proud to say that we didn’t spend more than $10,000. It was comprised of all grassroots donations,” he said. In contrast, Lee’s campaign raised $1,643,177 and spent nearly all of that. Her largest campaign contributors were the University of California, Kaiser Permanente, Wells Fargo, Quadric Group, and Bernstein and Lipsett, a D.C.- based law firm that represents federal employees seeking overtime pay and liquidated damages under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Piterman questioned whether such well funded campaigns like this have a place in politics. “I’m not saying that people’s votes can necessarily be bought, but [politics] should be a conveyance of ideas,” he said. Nikka Piterman of December 6, 2019. “I didn’t mind going out to BART stations, collecting signatures, asking friends and family. I thought, why not? The last election was just a victory lap for [incumbent] Barbara Lee, so I wanted to offer some opposition,” he said. Piterman ran under the fairly conservative platform that called for tax cuts for all American citizens. Some unorthodox policy ideas did catch the attention of passerby during his bid for signatures, though. “I would like to see the United States implement the metric system, starting with the Department of Education. That was a controversial one,” he said. “Some people said ‘that’s enough, you have my vote,’ while others said, ‘why would you ever want to do that?” Piterman also cited Puerto Rican statehood as one of his most sought-after causes. The Piedmont Historical Society has maintained a record of the various occupants from the 1870s to the current day. The first records of occupancy begin with real estate developer Jesse Wetmore. In 1878, he and his wife Matilda built a summer retreat in the Piedmont hills at 342 Bonita Avenue, at the corner of Bonita Avenue and Vista Avenue. The Historical Society noted that it had a wide veranda on three sides that caught summer breezes, a welcome relief from the dust and noise of downtown Oakland. Wetmore then built a slightly smaller summer home next door (now 801 Magnolia) for his daughter, Blanche Sherman. Blanche and her children traveled to Piedmont to spend the summers in the hills. She moved to the residence permanently after her husband died unexpectedly in 1881. In 1898, Blanche sold her cottage to Frank C. Havens. The race ended with the likely winner, Lee, taking the seat; but the process of running a campaign was, for Piterman, an “overall positive experience.“ In order to get on the ballot in California, a candidate must meet a variety of state-specific filing requirements and deadlines. An individual can seek the nomination of a state-recognized political party, as an independent, or as a write-in-candidate. To gain the backing of the Republican party, Piterman met with local party leaders. “Typically you get a number of signatures from people in the party. It was about three or four months before we started collecting signatures [from the public] then I met with the local GOP, and they welcomed me with open arms and encouraged me to run,” he said. He added that he was surprised to find out that two years ago there were approximately 40 districts in California with no Republican representation. Democratic incumbents and candidates ran largely unopposed, or against write-in candidates. The process then began with gathering signatures. To run for California’s 13th Congressional District required obtaining 2,000 signatures by the filing deadline Piedmont grad challenges Barbara Lee for congressional seat U.S. state. Piterman would like to see a referendum in Puerto Rico to ensure voluntary admission, and then upon admission, grant Puerto Rico with two senators and four representatives. He also sought to allocate five percent of the defense budget to the U.S. Space Force, and reclassify marijuana as a Schedule V substance. Piterman’s political aspirations began in high school in Piedmont. His involvement with the PHS debate club, the Junior Statesmen of America, was formative. In his final years of high school he served as Debate Club president and oversaw its growth from five members to nearly 40. Piterman confirms that he wasn’t expecting the race to come close, especially to political powerhouse Lee, now in her 12th congressional term. “I’m proud to say that we didn’t spend more than $10,000. It was comprised of all grassroots donations,” he said. In contrast, Lee’s campaign raised $1,643,177 and spent nearly all of that. Her largest campaign contributors were the University of California, Kaiser Permanente, Wells Fargo, Quadric Group, and Bernstein and Lipsett, a D.C.- based law firm that represents federal employees seeking overtime pay and liquidated damages under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Piterman questioned whether such well funded campaigns like this have a place in politics. “I’m not saying that people’s votes can necessarily be bought, but [politics] should be a conveyance of ideas,” he said. The last election was just a victory lap for [incumbent] Barbara Lee, so I wanted to offer some opposition,” he said. Piterman ran under the fairly conservative platform that called for tax cuts for all American citizens. Some unorthodox policy ideas did catch the attention of passerby during his bid for signatures, though. “I would like to see the United States implement the metric system, starting with the Department of Education. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

Predominantly rural “reds” and predominantly urban “blues” were predicted well before the election started. Court cases are being filed pell-mell and rejected in rapid succession. We get to read the most troubling tweets in the national news emanating from our President. Respected law firms withdrew from Trump lawsuits leaving Rudy Giuliani as the lead attorney to fight alleged ballot fraud. His badly out-of-date lawyering skills were widely bemoaned. The media’s reporting about certain United States Senators caught in attempts to prop up a Trump fantasy victory in battleground states are playing out poorly, with no thought to consequences for the nation. Foreign leaders speaking out say that Trump’s actions are “irresponsible” and especially during a pandemic where Covid- 19 deaths in the world are reaching toward 1.4 million. Real dread has hung over the nation, but now, the president-elect’s transition appears to be moving forward. pages.text: Wednesday, November 25, 2020 11 your Oakland Zoo introduces Glowfari, a new nighttime lantern festival By Jay Russell On November 20 the Oakland Zoo opened its gates to nighttime visitors for the brand new event “GLOWFARI – a wildly illuminating lantern festival.” GLOWFARI takes the place of Zoolights which has been a zoo tradition for two decades. GLOWFARI features larger light display lanterns, longer hours, and more available dates than Zoolights. Hundreds of larger than life animal lanterns illuminate the mile-long stroll that is truly an event fun for all ages. The brilliantly-lit gondola will be open to provide access to the California Trail and its unrivaled views of the bay. The traill atop the gondola has turned into the Land of the Lost, filled with huge dinosaur lanterns and life-like animatronic moving models of dinos like the T-rex, stegosaurus, and triceratops. “Kids have been just flipping out The color-changing Cherry Blossom display near the Children’s zoo is not to be missed. The Oakland Zoo starts a new tradition this year, Glowfari. over the dinosaurs even just in the daytime,” said the Zoo’s VP of Marketing and Communications Erin Harrison. The zoo has been planning the transition to GLOWFARI for the last year and a half. The experience of walking through the beautiful lanterns transported this reporter to memories of Disnyland’s Main Street Electric Parade. Zoo staff are very encouraged by the overwhelmingly positive response they have received in the first few nights. “It was very important to offer something to people to get away and have an emotional break from the stress of this year’s daily challenges,” Harrison said. The winter wonderland aspires to offer more than just pretty light and lanterns, Zoo staff have worked hard to give the experience a deeper meaning. Signs all through the park educate guests on animals’ status in the wild, Immerse yourself in aquarium style lantern tunnels. what people can do to help, and the challenges each species face. Capacity is limited to around 1,500 (from a normal maximum of 5,000), and guests have been vigilantly abiding to the mask and social distancing requirements. GLOWFAR I r uns from 5:30 p.m. - 10:00 p.m., November 20, 2020 - January 17, 2021. 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland, (510) 632-9525 Advanced t icket i ng is required, GLOWFAIR will not take walkups. Visit: www.oaklandzoo.org The Blue Planet area at Glowfari gives this meadow a carnival atmosphere. A 20-foot wide crab lantern is most impressive. Watch out for the moving claws. Walk through the T-Rex’s jaws if you dare. The gondola ride offers breathtaking views of the entire SF Bay. A scorpion gets the attention of zoo guest Estrella Espinoza. The animatronic penguins walk and waddle in unison. Make sure to read the new signs around the park to learn about each species and animal conservation.

articles.text: The Oakland Strokes finished its second regatta of the fall season, the Tail of the Turkey, on Saturday, November 21 at the Oakland Estuary. This year is unique due to COVID-19, and has required extensive changes in order to conduct the sport. But because the sport is outside, thye’ve been ab;e continue competing, albeit on one-an boats rather than the traditional 9-man boats. “It has been a great way to get the kids some racing time, so we’ve had an internal scrimmage type of setting. It was good,” said varsity coach and Piedmont resident, Allison Ray. Last June marked the first time in over 20 years that the Post could not report on the Strokes racing in the Youth National Championships due to the ongoing virus. Operations were shut down in February. The Head of Oak novice regatta on October 17 marked the team’s first action since last spring. “March 16 was our last day. We went through a number of months of just engaging kids online. We went up to the San Pablo Reservoir to see what it would be like,” added Ray, describing the rigorous cleaning, social distancing, and protocols involved. articles.text: Cameron Smith (right), 27, was the first golfer to shot all four rounds under 70 at The Masters. He is pictured with his caddy, Matthew Tritton. Golf’s Masters Tournament knows no competition. Since 1934 it is the year’s most anticipated tournament, providing players and fans with four days of utter solace. Augusta National is the name of the course, possibly the most exclusive course in the world. Every hole looks like an edenistic garden. This year’s tournament was played to empty galleries from November 12-15. My grandfather once asked a friend if he could get onto the course. The golf pal from Georgia said maybe. Some years later his friend called back, “Hey I got you tickets to go watch The Masters Tournament.” My grandpop replied, “Huhn, I don’t want to watch the tournament, I want to play the course.” To wh ich h is f r ie nd replied, “What! Play it? That’s impossible!” As a members only country club, Augusta frequently has been in the spotlight for being overly exclusive. This year, the tournament directors stepped up their celebration of diversity. The first Black man to play on the course, Lee Elder, was honored throughout the tournament, in person and on the telecast. The tribute added a welcome touch to remind people that golf is played by young and old, man and women, and people of all identity. The tournament was easily won by Long Ball Dustin Johnson, who led the final day and set a course record with a score of -20 through the four days. After messing up a little to start Sunday, Johnson recovered and it really wasn’t close for the last four hours The lack of pressure at Augusta felt unnatural, unholy for the world’s biggest tournament. Usually the crowds go crazy and half the players totally cave to the pressure towards the end. But that was not the case due to a very limited capacity of fans which made it feel like a walk in the park. As it happens more times than not, the players I’m rooting against end up winning. I’m just grateful the tournament happened. Johnson, already ranked #1 in the world, probably would have slogged his caveman frame around oblivious to the happenings even if there was a crowd. The feel good stories which kept me watching came from two young golfers, Cameron Smith and Sung-jae Im who tied for second. Smith, an Australian, wears a scraggly imposter mustache that looks like it’s glued on, and his caddy looks more like a guy from a fishing boat that is slowly sinking into a swamp. Smith played valiantly, like a haggard wizard would, but Johnson had too great of a lead. Im, a 22-yearold from South Korea, had style and composure. He possibly has the coolest hat in all pro sports, it looks like a trucker hat from some made up company. Im’s perfect form and unflappability earned him just over $1 million for four days work. So The Masters happened, a storied event with more than a slice of history. The food and drink concessions remain at old school prices, and were just recently raised to $1.50 or $3.00 for a sandwich. Beer prices remain cheaper than at Whole Foods, all the more shame a large crowd couldn’t get rowdy in their khakis and visors. The Masters can be best understood by noting the expulsion of one of golf’s most colorful and popular TV commentators Gary McCord. While reporting at Augusta National the announcer with a curved mustache audaciously said, “There are some body bags down there, if that keeps going,” when a ball was rolling back off a green and toward Rae’s Creek. He also joked that “bikini wax” was being used to make Augusta National’s greens too slick for abal to stick. That resulted in McCord, then reporting for CBS, being banned from the course for life. That was in 1994. The ban has not been lifted. They’re serious at The Masters.
articles.title: A trucker, caveman and angler at The Masters

It is a threemile course that passes under six historic bridges along the river. Thousands of spectators typically line the bridges for clear views. The Boys varsity 8 boat won a silver medal with Rohan Saha on board. Annika Heuser helped the girls eight to a fourth place finish before heading off to MIT. took home another Silver for the boys varsity 8, while the girls won 4th place. articles.text: Jimmy G’s future?; Raiders fall short; Premier League update; sad new for Warriors The Raiders nearly pulled off its second upset of the Kansas City Chiefs, but lost 35-31 after Patrick Mahomes led KC back with 1:44 remaining. Meanwhile, the 49ers come out of the bye week and look ahead to the Los Starting with the 49ers, you’d be hard-pressed to predict an SF upset over the Rams regardless if players come back from injury this week. Instead, we’ll examine the future of quarterback Jimmy 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said last week that he “expects” Garoppolo to be the team’s starter in 2021. Meanwhile, Jimmy G has a no-trade clause in his contract until March 2022, so SF couldn’t deal him without his agreement. Reading between the lines, the 49ers are equally unlikely to find a team willing accept Garoppolo’s $25 million salary, find a partner which would trade them a first- or second-round pick, or have the quarterback waive his clause. Shanahan’s declaration of continuity makes sense from a Photo courtesy of NBC Sports What is the future of 49ers’ quarterback Jimmy Garoppolo? Cutting Garoppolo creates $24.1 million in cap space, but they’d receive a third-round 2021 compensatory pick at best if he signed with another team on the open market. Considering Garoppolo would be the top QB in the 2021 free-agent pool if released, SF wouldn’t move on from him unless they already had an option ready to roll for the season-opener. Given all those circumstances, the 2021 NFL Draft and Garoppolo restructuring his contract is the 49ers’ best bet. Flat out, if Shanahan sees an opportunity to improve at the position, he will take it. Currently projected at No. 12 in the next draft, SF could drop into the top- 10 and acquire a top-quarterback prospect while hoping Garoppolo gets his act together. If this season proved anything for Shanahan and the 49ers’ front office: the next-man-up is just as vital as the starter. Las Vegas Raiders The Raiders nearly proved us wrong a second time as we predicted the Chiefs to win another shootout on Sunday night. But now, the end of the season certainly favors Vegas with a matchup against the lowly Falcons in Week 12 and some easier games ahead. With Week 12’s game against Atlanta, stopping the passing attack is first and foremost. It has the potential to be another high scoring game if the Raiders’ defense doesn’t show up—but we’re going Vegas by over 14. The Spurs defeated Manchester City 2-0 in last week’s game of the week, and turn around to another critical match with Chelsea (5-3-1, 3rd) this Sunday, November 29 at 8:30 a.m. Liverpool (6-2-1, 2nd) will be watching closely after its Saturday match with Brighton (2-3-4, 16th). With an expected win over Brighton, the Reds will move to first with a Tottenham draw or loss. Warriors draft same day as Klay Thompson disaster Bay Area sports fans were shell-shocked last week on 2020 NBA Draft day just hours prior to what should’ve been a joyous time. The Golden State Warriors drafted 7 foot, 1 big-man James Wiseman out of Memphis, but their celebration was doused due to the newss that allstar Klay Thompson sustained a season-ending torn Achilles in a practice game. This comes after Thompson tragically tore his ACL in the 2019 NBA Finals. But the Dubs power on with Stephen Curry, Andrew Wiggins, Draymond Green, Wiseman, and recent acquisition Kelly Oubre as the presumptive starting-five. Oubre, 24, comes from Pheonix after averaging 34.5 minutes last season, 18.7 points per game with a 45.2 field goal percentage and 35.2 percent from beyond the arch.

articles.text: Cal v. Stanford: 123rd Big Game is this Friday Photo courtesy of California Golden Blogs The Golden Bears look to retain The Axe in Friday’s 123rd Big Game between California and Stanford. Here we are, the Wednesday before the 123rd Big Game between the California Golden Bears and Stanford Cardinal on Friday, November 27 at 1:30 p.m. Both teams limp into the game with 0-2 records and are looking mighty vulnerable. Of the two sides, the opening games have arguably left California the most devastated after getting bashed by UCLA 34-10 in Week 1 and upset last week by Oregon State, 31-27. The Bears held a 20-14 lead at halftime and were looking productive with 317 total yards at halftime. However, they could only amass 34 yards in the third and 88 in the fourth. Garbers struggled with accuracy you wouldn’t expect from a third-year starter, going 28 of 42 for 315 yards, three touchdowns, and two interceptions. Cal struggled mightily, showing that the lack of an offseason program has hit them harder than most programs. They had a pair of Nikko Remigio kick returns brought back due to penalties, each of which would have been touchdowns of 89 and 94 yards. Additionally, a blocked punt and a 24-yard shanked punt helped create Oregon State touchdowns. The Cardinal enter the Big Game with extra rest after its game with Washington State was canceled last week after a COVID outbreak within the Cougars meant they couldn’t field enough players. Cal has been rattled on defense after relying on a strong defense over the last few years under head coach Justin Wilcox. This could mean that Stanford will lean on quarterback Davis Mills, who went 31 of 56 for 327 yards and a touchdown against Colorado, though they lost 35-32. For NFL Draft enthusiasts, a notable matchup will be Bears cornerback Camryn Bynum squaring up with the Cardinal’s Simi Fehoko and other receivers. Given Garbers’ struggles to hit receivers, coupled with Cal’s COVID woes for its offensive line, it seems that Stanford could dial up a healthy dose of blitzes to keep the Golden Bears’ offense off balanced. For both programs at 0-2 and virtually out of the Pac-12 Conference championship and Bowl game appearances after its canceled games and losses, the Big Game becomes-essentially—each team’s biggest game of the season. “It certainly is different because of the unique nature of this season. But it doesn’t minimize the impact of the Big Game to our team, our fans - we know how much it means to us and everybody out there. We appreciate it for all that it is, regardless of these circumstances,” said Cal’s head coach, Wilcox. Photo courtesy of the Mercury News California struggled in its 31-27 loss to Oregon State. Photo courtesy of CollegeFootballNews.com Stanford and coach David Shaw look ahead to the Big Game after last week’s game with Washington State was canceled.

This could mean that Stanford will lean on quarterback Davis Mills, who went 31 of 56 for 327 yards and a touchdown against Colorado, though they lost 35-32. For NFL Draft enthusiasts, a notable matchup will be Bears cornerback Camryn Bynum squaring up with the Cardinal’s Simi Fehoko and other receivers. Given Garbers’ struggles to hit receivers, coupled with Cal’s COVID woes for its offensive line, it seems that Stanford could dial up a healthy dose of blitzes to keep the Golden Bears’ offense off balanced. For both programs at 0-2 and virtually out of the Pac-12 Conference championship and Bowl game appearances after its canceled games and losses, the Big Game becomes-essentially—each team’s biggest game of the season. “It certainly is different because of the unique nature of this season. But it doesn’t minimize the impact of the Big Game to our team, our fans - we know how much it means to us and everybody out there. We appreciate it for all that it is, regardless of these circumstances,” said Cal’s head coach, Wilcox. Photo courtesy of the Mercury News California struggled in its 31-27 loss to Oregon State. Photo courtesy of CollegeFootballNews.com Stanford and coach David Shaw look ahead to the Big Game after last week’s game with Washington State was canceled.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 25, 2020 15 HIKING WITH JON Mt. Tamalpais’ Dawn Falls to Barbara Springs trails By Jonathan Comeaux Mt. Tamalpais has well over 100 miles of hiking trails; from the steep and strenuous, to the relaxed and nature focused. For this week’s outing we walked 1.5 miles on the Dawn Falls Trail to the Southern Marin Line Fire Roud until reaching the Barbara Springs Trail and back to the car, making an easy but stunning 3.5- mile hike. Its Dawn Falls Trail is a short and popular 1.4-mile walk with over 510 feet in elevation gain to its main attraction, Dawn Falls. Although the “Falls” is more of a trickle given its only active during or after a heavy rain, the walk shows you what makes Mt. Tam so magnificent. At times, you will pass through narrow corridors of redwood trees that look like something out of a fairytale with the steam of cold air during these cold months. Starting at the Dawn Falls Trailhead on Madrone Avenue in Larkspur, the trail along the inactive Larkspur Creek is a palette of vibrant fall colors from maple leaves; redwoods tower over in every direction, while lush green moss covers every tree, stone, and branch. It is worth mentioning that the Dawn Falls Trail is a mostly slim passage, less than three feet wide, meaning you will have to be patient when passing by hikers and runners on weekends. Our 10 a.m. walk up to the falls passed a staggering 49 people in the 1.5 miles, passing another 34 people on the remaining two miles back to the car. For those conscious of personal space, continue on the Southern Marin Line Fire Road; a dirt road which is wide enough for two lanes of cars. Otherwise, you can continue up the Hoo Koo E Koo Trail and Blithedale Ridge trails, which will more than double your elevation gain to provide a workout of near 1,200 feet until re-intersecting with the fire road. You’ll get glimpses of Mt. Tam’s eastern peak from the fire road, a location we last visited over the summer. The 0.5 mile walk down the Barbara Springs Trail back to the car is a very steep 500 foot descent back with tree roots shooting out in every direction, so be wary. You’ll likely have to use your hands at point if you don’t have hiking sticks. Moss is a mean feature of this trail. Each stone, log, and tree is covered in lush moss The fall colors are everywhere on Mt. Tamalpais. Photos by Jonathan Comeaux A narrow corridor of redwood trees along the Dawn Falls Trail of Mt. Tamalpais. Be mindful that the trail is typically under 3-feet wide. Redwoods towering overhead in every direction. The Southern Marin Line Fire Road is aptly wide to keep your distance. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet company will present its wellloved The Nutcracker during the holidays, but online. The timeless fairy tale, with music by Tchaikovsky and choreography by Helgi Tomasson, will be available for viewing online from November 27 through December 31. The showing will be encompassed in an interactive, virtual experience for family and friends from the comfort of your home. Watch San Francisco Ballet’s spectacular Nutcracker, streamed in high definition, and then take a backstage tour of the opera house. You can send holiday snapshots to friends and family, enjoy historical highlights of the Nutcracker, and learn steps from the choreography. The ballet company advises that this event is best experienced on Chrome browser on a computer, laptop, or iPad. The Nutcracker is one of America’s most celebrated ballets. It begins on a foggy Christmas Eve in 1915, with Drosselmeyer putting the finishing touches on a magical nutcracker doll. It’s his gift for the Stahlbaum family, who have invited him to join their holiday festivities. Customers drop by his shop for last-minute Christmas gifts and Drosselmeyer shows them toys and clocks. Later, outside the Stahlbaum house, as people hurry home to their Christmas revelries, Drosselmeyer arrives with his beautifully wrapped present. You can view a progression of the acts at https://www. sfballet.org/discover/backstage/ story-of-nutcracker/. Tickets went on sale November 17 and can be purchased at https://donate2.app/kbqBT1.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Nutcracker goes online for the holidays

articles.text: The Youth Art Exchange, a shared creative practice between professional artists and Bay Area youth, is hosting its 10th annual San Francisco Youth Arts Summit. The event will take place from Monday through Friday, November 30 to December 4. The Summit, titled Arts is Essential, is a celebration of young artists and their vibrant contributions to the creative and cultural fabric of San Francisco and the greater Bay Area. The event will pivot online this year in light of the current public health crisis. It will be a week-long virtual arts summit with various workshops, panels, and professional development opportunities throughout the week. The Summit will culminate with the main event, the Youth Arts Celebration on Friday, December 4, from 4 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. Art is Essential kicks off with a series of professional development opportunities, panel conversations and workshops. The Summit features a variety of workshop offerings, some geared towards youth, some geared towards teaching artists and arts education professionals, and some are designed to be intergenerational. Workshops will be presented by Youth Art Exchange’s Faculty Artists; Youth Art Exchange’s Youth Advisory Board; RYSE Youth Center; de Young Museum; California College of the Arts; SFMoMA; Teaching Artist Guild; Arts Education Alliance of the Bay Area; San Francisco Art Institute; BAVC; CULK and more. For a full schedule of events, visit https://www.youthartexchange.org/events/2020/11/30/sfyas. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Brian Copeland’s The Jewelry Box, available to stream this Saturday, November 28 through December 25. The comedy is a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show, Not a Genuine Black Man, and follows young protagonist Brian as he heads to the “mean streets” of Oakland to buy his mom a Christmas present. When he finds the perfect gift – a jewelry box in the White Front store – six-year-old Brian sets out to earn the required $11.97 by Christmas Eve. The play follows Brian’s adventures as he scours the “help wanted” ads, applies for jobs, and collects bottles, inching his way Brian Copeland in the San Francisco Playhouse production of The Jewelry Box, streaming November 28 to December 25. toward the perfect Christmas gift. Copeland debuted his first one-man play, Not a Genuine Black Man at the Marsh in San Francisco. The play explored his childhood experiences as a member of one of the only African American families living in a predominately white suburb of San Leandro, California. Not a Genuine Black Man went on to become the longest-running solo show in San Francisco theatrical history with over 800 performances. The show has been performed in over 30 cities, including a critically acclaimed run Off-Broadway. The play is currently in television series development. To stream The Jewelry Box, visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sf ph /2020-2021-season / the-jewelry-box/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse’s The Jewelry Box premieres this Saturday

articles.text: California Revels will return to Oakland for its 35th season of one of the Bay Area’s premier holiday events. This year’s presentation is Unruly Magic: A Spirited Celebration of the Winter Solstice. Families, friends and holiday revelers are invited to watch wherever they may be, as this year’s production is entirely online, and can be viewed from December 12-20 at www.californiarevels.org. It will stream in High-Definition on Vimeo and YouTube, with live interactive components on Zoom Audiences of all ages can celebrate the Winter Solstice with traditional music, dance, ritual, and folk plays, including the mesmerizing “Antler Dance.” The production features top musicians, actors, and featured performers. This year’s show includes Shay Black and Windborne Singers. Directed by Jeri Reed, newly filmed pieces are blended with archival footage to create a dynamic and moving feast for the eyes, ears, and spirit. The story of Unruly Magic Approaching the longest night of the year, a young Reveler turns to a magical staff to help her find a way through somber and troubled times. The staff, imbued with ancient lore, takes her on an adventure that isn’t quite what she had in mind. Magic and mystery, spirits and song take the reins for this journey of the heart. The ancient traditions of bonfires, rituals, dances, and songs that have sustained generations through struggle and celebration are rekindled this Solstice, proving that tradition – and magic – live on. Dates and times of the seven performances are listed below. Saturday, December 12, 1:00 p.m. Sunday, December 13, 1:00 p.m. Friday, December 18, 7:00 p.m. Saturday, December 19, 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Sunday, December 20, 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Tickets are $20-$175 and are available online at www.CaliforniaRevels.org. For details and more information, call the box office at 650-534-6766 Monday to Friday from 11:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Unruly Magic is directed by Jeri Reed and Music Director Shira Kammen. Anne Bingham Goess is Associate Music Director. Marzena Jones is Children’s Music Director. California Revels Executive Director is Lisa Lowe.

articles.text: Cal Performances at Home project streams at 7 p.m. Cal Performances, based at University of California, Berkeley will host an evening with world-renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma and English pianist Kathryn Stott this Friday, November 27. The event is part of the Cal Performances at Home project that brings the arts into your home. Ma has performed as a soloist with orchestras around the world. He has recorded more than 90 albums and received 18 Grammy Awards. In addition to recordings of the standard classical repertoire, he has recorded a wide variety of folk music such as American bluegrass music, traditional Chinese melodies, the tangos of Argentinian composer Astor Piazzolla, and Brazilian music. Ma will be joined by acclaimed British classic pianist Kathryn Stott, who performs as a concerto soloist, recitalist and chamber musician. Her specialties include the English and French classical repertoire, contemporary classical music, and the tango. Yo-Yo Ma and Kathryn Stott will perform a concert this Friday hosted by Cal Performances. Stott and Ma have joined forces for a diverse concert recorded in mid-November at Taiwan’s National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts Concert Hall. Their Songs of Comfort and Hope, the program that will be featured this Friday, combines a wide range of selections from the piano and cello repertoire, with traditional and new takes on favorites. The program will be available to stream on demand through December 12. A pre-concert conversation will take place before the event, at 6:30 p.m. The streaming premiere will begin at 7 p.m. Cal Performances Executive and Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen will introduce Ma and Stott and will join them in conversation. To reserve a spot for the event, visit https://calperformances. org /events/2020 -21/recit al / an-evening-with-yo-yo-ma/. GET UP TO
articles.title: Kathryn Stott joins Yo-Yo Ma in a concert on Friday

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect will co-host a free screening of Kiss the Ground, a documentary that focuses on real solutions to climate change. Narrated and featuring Woody Harrelson, the film reveals the first viable solution to the climate crisis. Kiss the Ground asserts that, by generating the world’s soils, the global population can completely and rapidly stabilize Earth’s climate, restore lost ecosystems and create abundant food supplies. The documentary uses compelling graphics and visuals, along with NASA footage to show how this can be done. The documentary is currently available on Netflix, but the City and Piedmont Connect will offer free digital screenings from Friday to Sunday, December 4-6. Movie poster for Kiss the Ground After watching the film, join city staff on Thursday, December 10, at 7:30 p.m. for a one-hour virtual forum and discussion about the film. For more information, visit https://kisstheground.com/. Kiss the Ground, the latest documentary by husband-and-wife team of Josh Tickell and Rebecca Harrell Tickell, will be screened for free on December 4-6.

articles.text: A Scene from Jurassic Park: Fallen Kingdom. Movie review by Chris Honoré It’s been some 25 years since the first Jurassic Park was released, directed by Steven Spielberg and based on the Michael Crichton book. The central idea was that cretaceous creatures, most especially the high-rise dinosaurs with those signature reptilian eyes, could be reproduced using engineered DNA. It was a massive hit that combined all the ingredients of horror and action filmmaking for a breathtaking experience. As well, there is a through line from, say, a film like Jaws to the Jurassic series where a predator is loose and humans, no matter how resilient or well-defended, are ultimately helpless. A sense of overwhelming vulnerability represents the genius of these stories. After all, teeth-filled jaws come in all sizes and the image of a person’s torso dangling part way out of a raptor’s mouth will cause viewers to pay attention. Each of the movies that have followed, in the aggregate, have created what has been a durable franchise, while giving audiences a rush of adrenalin as computer generated raptors, scarily smart, manage to get free and overcome all best efforts to contain them. Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom is the second in what will be a trilogy that began with Jurassic World. The setup is fairly straight forward: Isla Nublar was devastated when once again the dinos got loose. What made World riveting was that the island was now a popular amusement park, all revolving around the reptiles. Of course, the dinos, now free, devastate the park and the tourists, who run for their lives. Finally, the island is abandoned to the animals. What has occurred in Fallen Kingdom is that a once dormant volcano is on the cusp of erupting. Claire (Bryce Dallas Howard) and Owen (Chris Pratt) are recruited by a long ago benefactor, Benjamin Lockwood (James Cromwell), to rescue the remaining dinos and transport them to another island habitat absent tourists and rides. But, as is explained, the plan is born of avarice and orchestrated by a nefarious Lockwood assistant, unbeknownst to Lockwood. The hidden plan is to put the captured dinos on the market to the highest bidder. So, instead of a pristine island, Claire and Owen are sent to the Lockwood compound, a massive, 19th century manor house. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, November 25, 2020 Piedmont Connect co-hosts screening of Kiss the Ground December 4–6 By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Connect will co-host a free screening of Kiss the Ground, a documentary that focuses on real solutions to climate change. Narrated and featuring Woody Harrelson, the film reveals the first viable solution to the climate crisis. Kiss the Ground asserts that, by generating the world’s soils, the global population can completely and rapidly stabilize Earth’s climate, restore lost ecosystems and create abundant food supplies. The documentary uses compelling graphics and visuals, along with NASA footage to show how this can be done. The documentary is currently available on Netflix, but the City and Piedmont Connect will offer free digital screenings from Friday to Sunday, December 4-6. articles.text: A Scene from Yoshifumi Kondo’s Whisper of the Heart. Movie review by Chris Honoré Whisper of the Heart is the first and only film by director Yoshifumi Kondo, protégé of Hayao Miyazaki. The narrative is based on the manga story of the same name, written by Hiragi Aoi. It is an engaging and sensitive tale, meant to carry on the Studio Ghibli tradition. Sadly, however, Kondo died unexpectedly in 1998 and Miyazaki returned to the Studio from an all too brief retirement. The film’s protagonist is Shizuku (Brittany Snow), a self-conscious, often shy 14-yearold girl, as well as the characters that surround her, all created with an aura that is often dreamlike. Shizuku lives in the Tama New Town suburb of Tokyo. A voracious reader, always curious, she studies the check-out cards in three of her borrowed library books and discovers, to her surprise, that they each had been read by an unknown boy named Seiji (David Gallagher). “Who is he?” she wonders. “What is he like?” she asks herself. And so, with her imagination in a whirl, her curiosity peaked, she begins to search for him instead of studying for her final exams and preparing to graduate from her junior high school with her best friend Kuko (Ashley Tisdale). One day she follows a strange cat to an antique shop. It’s a wondrous place, she discovers, owned by an old man named Nishi, who turns out to be the grandfather of Seiji, the boy she’s been obsessively looking for. Of course, the two meet and become friends. Shizuki soon learns that Seiji nurtures a dream of becoming a world-class maker of violins; however, he explains, in order to fulfill his dream he must travel to Italy and serve an apprenticeship. Shizuki is inspired by Seiji’s commitment to his goal, and comes to realize that more than anything she wants to write stories. Amazing stories. And so, she too begins to research, sitting at a table, hunched over a sheet of paper, worrying whether she has the right stuff to tell a compelling story. Meanwhile, her parents worry that her grades might suffer as they watch their daughter devote herself relentlessly to her task. Whisper of the Heart, a coming-of-age whisper, sweetly and slowly told. It examines first crushes, unrequited love, and the search for one’s true talent. The story is also held together by a supportive and romantic connection between Shizuki and Seiji, unexpressed until it almost misses making an interesting ending. Whisper of the Heart. Directed by Yoshifumi Kondo. Animé from Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Brittany Snow, David Gallagher and Ashley Tisdale. 1 hr., 51 min. Rated G. articles.text: A Scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 3. Movie review by Chris Honoré For all of its CGI-animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creator of the Toy Story franchise, has never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple, inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a day care center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat-of-your-pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a comingof-age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes. Toy Story 3 turns out to be the sweetest and best-told story in the series thus far. Toy Story 3. Starring the voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack and Don Rickles. Pixar Animation Studios. Directed by Lee Unkrich. Rated PG. Curbside pick up is always available. Just order and pick up! Or shop online H FREE DELIVERY TO PIEDMONT H 3982 Piedmont Ave. (510) 601-7938 www.bellaceramica.com

articles.text: The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir raised $119,000 in their first virtual fundraising concert, Discovering Our Voices, on Saturday, November 14. The event featured Choir performances from the advanced Ancora and Ensemble choirs, including a performance of “Autumn Time” presented by 36 Choir alumni from around the country. Funds raised during the event, aided by a silent auction, will support expanded financial assistance. The funds ensure that all children and youth who want to sing with the Choirs can participate. Discovering Our Voices was planned and executed by Development Consultant Lillian Archer of the Archer Group, and by the Choir’s Benefit Auxiliary Committee headed by Roshmi Mukherji. Technical production was supported by Galas at Home. Wine was donated to the event by Lin Jia Asian Kitchen. “Without the physical limitations of a venue or specific extended time for the event, the virtual format expanded access and allowed us to show up together as an inclusive community,” said new Executive Director Keri Butkevich. “Our team did amazing work and the performances went beyond Discovering our Voices to lifting our spirits, while we raised critical funding to ensure every child can connect and grow in the Choirs as part of our East Bay musical family.” Artistic Director Eric Tuan commented that the virtual event did have newly positive effects. Choir family Ann Kim, Kailamae, Koa, and Stuart. “Although we missed seeing each other in person, holding the event virtually meant we could welcome Choir friends both old and new scattered all around the world,” he said. “It was particularly moving to hear alums raising their voices together in “Autumn Time” alongside the beautiful virtual choir performances by Ancora and Ensemble. The love and passion for the Choir was palpable throughout the entire evening - from the amazing support shown in the Fund-A-Need, to the deeply impactful testimonials from our singers, to seeing all the Choir memories being shared in the chat. It was a once-in-a-lifetime event and a memory I will always treasure.” Viewers can enjoy the performance on the Choir’s Youtube channel at https:// w w w.yout ube.com /chan nel / UCZADkdlvhc4Mjie9hhTcm_g. Participating from the comfort of their home are Kiran Beattie, Aparna Rao, Joshua Beattie, Amba Beattie.
articles.title: Piedmont Children’s Choir raises $119,000 in virtual benefit concert

articles.text: We have just received fabulous news from our friend the brilliant guitarist in Barcelona, Jaume Torrent, with whom Debbie and I have performed many concerts. He recently was elected to the Academy of Arts in Catalonia. This is similar to being knighted in England or getting elected to the Legion of Honor in France. His letter announcing this distinction follows: Dear Joe and Debbie: I am writing to tell you that last week I was appointed Academician of the Royal Catalan Academy of Fine Arts of St. George. It is one of the greatest distinctions that can be given to an artist in Catalonia [Barcelona], and has so far been awarded to musicians such as Eduard Toldrà, Frederic Mompou, Xavier Montsalvatge and Carlos Guinovart. It’s such an honor for me and it makes me very happy. Yolanda is also very excited. I’ve never thought about having a recognition of this level, and I still find it hard to believe I’ve been given it. Guitarist Jaume Torrent of Barcelona, Spain, a frequent performer at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, has been given highest honors for his years of contribution to music and music education. Due to the pandemic, the act of public appointment will not be until April or May next year. I’ll have to give a speech, and I’ll also play something to exemplize the analysis of my work. I know you’ll share my joy. –Jaume
articles.title: Jaume Torrent named to Academy of Arts in Catalonia

articles.text: There was a big argument, and It did involve a turkey, But it wasn’t in Washington. However, some things never change. The combatants were Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, and Benjamin Franklin as they battled for how fledgling America would choose its national bird. Tempers f lared. Jefferson wanted the dove, Adams the eagle, and Franklin the turkey. Franklin‘s reasoning was the best, but he lost – and so did his turkey. Thanksgiving is tomorrow… But don’t get ahead of me. I want to give you a tasty recipe for fried fish. Like Ben Franklin, I believe my reasoning is very sound. You see, the first Thanksgiving did not star the turkey. It featured mostly fish and wild game – but not turkey. So here is an easy and tasty fried fish recipe: You need a flat fish like petrale sole fillets. Moisten them with a little milk or buttermilk. Put 2 tablespoons of packaged pancake mix in a plastic bag and shake the fish in it – just to dust the fish. Then fry the fish fillets to a golden brown. How easy is that? A big potato is a good side dish or you can be fancy and serve potatoes au gratin. White wine, of course. I like baked apples for dessert, and sometimes chilled poached pears in red wine sauce. Enjoy your Thanksgiving… but probably with the “traditional“ turkey. Bon appetite.
articles.title: Wherefor the turkey

articles.text: Theme nights, festive lights, and Santa Saturdays at Filoli Gardens in Woodside Filoli House and Gardens, located in Woodside, will be dressed in festive lights for the holiday season through January 3. The lights were installed throughout the garden on November 21, making it the perfect socially-distanced activity to enjoy with family members and friends of all ages. Take a walk through the gardens and enjoy the beauty of a winter garden adorned with lights and colorful décor. Visitors can cozy up next to a fire pit under twinkling lights while sipping on hot cider or mulled wine. Visit the gardens on a Monday night for “theme nights.” From a pajama party to solstice night, Filoli is making Monday nights merry and bright with jolly dress-up gatherings. Santa Saturdays will return in December, with a twist: Santa will be outdoors in the Woodland Garden Court, where visitors are invited to take a socially distanced “selfie” with Santa. Daytime and evening admissions are available. Due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic and capacity limitations, all visitors must secure tickets in advance. Face coverings must be worn at all times and social distancing will be observed. The Estate Trail will close at 4 p.m., and the house closes at 7 p.m. To reserve tickets for holiday events at Filoli House and Gardens, visit https://filoli.org/ events/holidays/. Filoli House and Gardens
articles.title: Filoli lights up the holidays

articles.text: The California Society of Printmakers’ 106th annual exhibition, currently at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, is postponed due to Alameda County being moved into the most restrictive “purple tier” and a current spike in coronavirus cases in the county. The purple tier calls for the closure of many non-essential indoor business operations, including museums and galleries. The exhibition will resume when county restrictions are lifted. When the exhibition returns, gallery viewings will be available by reservation only. Masks will be required, and social distancing will be observed. For updates, visit http://www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org/.
articles.title: Printmakers exhibit put on hold due to spike in COVID cases

articles.text: Part 11 in a series In the history of Piedmont, two saloons have quenched the thirst of residents and visitors. One saloon was in a respected hotel. The other was fraught with problems. The Piedmont Springs Hotel was built to serve visitors to the Piedmont hills and the mineral springs in Piedmont’s Bushy Dell Creek. Built in 1871 as a first class resort, the hotel had 20 rooms and a main dining room with a crystal chandelier and velvet drapes. The Grand Saloon (for gentlemen only) had a long mahogany bar, billiard table, spittoons and a pot-bellied stove in the corner. The Grand Saloon gained brief notoriety in 1891 when the wives of some of Piedmont’s more prominent businessmen petitioned the county to rescind the hotel’s liquor license. The women objected to their husbands stopping for a drink on their way home. The license was never rescinded, and the Piedmont Springs Hotel continued to serve liquor for another year before it burned to the ground in 1892. A Mon Chateau Piedmont’s other saloon was A Mon Chateau. As far back as the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran through a very pleasant valley – sunny, free of wind, rolling hills, scattered trees – that extended from Lake Merritt into the Piedmont hills. It was the route that many early Oakland residents took from downtown Oakland to picnic in the Piedmont hills. Today, that road is Grand Avenue until it crosses the city line near Rose Avenue. It continues as Pleasant Valley Road in Oakland until it crosses Broadway and becomes 51st Street. In 1892, Axel R. Gruggel built a restaurant at the southwest corner of today’s Grand and Linda Avenues and served refreshments to these travelers into the Piedmont countryside. He called it “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) and advertised it as a family resort and French restaurant. Taking advantage of the mild weather, he built a beer garden on the Linda Avenue side of the restaurant. During its first years, A Mon Chateau was a quiet, slow-paced retreat, but that changed with the 1906 earthquake. With the influx of San Francisco refugees to the East Bay, the surrounding land began to fill with new houses and residents. From 1903 on, A Mon Chateau had a series of owners with a series of troubles. Gruggel sold the restaurant to George Atcheson in 1903. He ran A Mon Chateau for a few years but encountered problems with his employees stealing liquor. In 1907, three bachelors began operating the restaurant. Thomas P. Fenton, George P. Mahoney and John F. Jennings lived on the second floor of the building and advertised it as “A pleasant place in Pleasant Valley [to eat dinner]. Dinner prepared by Emil Lotz, former chef of Poodle Dog, San Francisco.” Dinners were $1.00. Patrons were advised to take the Oakland Avenue streetcar, get off at Sunnyside Avenue and take a short walk to Pleasant Valley. The bachelor owners also advertised A Mon Chateau as a saloon and sold wine, liquor and cigars besides serving dinners. Soon, neighbors began objecting to what was becoming a boisterous saloon. When the new City of Piedmont (1907) passed its liquor licensing regulations, A Mon Chateau’s application for a liquor license was denied. Nonetheless, the three owners continued to sell liquor at A Mon Chateau without a liquor license. The following year in March 1908, all three were arrested and their liquor confiscated. Three months later in June of 1908, A Mon Chateau opened under new management and continued to advertise itself as a “First Class Restaurant and Family Resort.” New owners Seeger & Thomas continued to operate it as a restaurant, but without a liquor license the number of diners dwindled. In 1911, Rudolph Kohn took over the business. He sought a new way to attract more patrons. He called the former restaurant “The Piedmont Casino” and opened two rooms upstairs for those who enjoyed playing poker and faro. However, gambling was also illegal. The casino was raided in 1912, and nine card-playing patrons were arrested and fined $55 each. The casino closed shortly thereafter. Chateau had become the Grand Avenue Grocery Company, and business thrived. It may not have been a good location for a saloon, but it was an excellent spot for a grocery. Residents in the rapidly growing residential neighborhood could walk to the market at the corner of Grand and Linda Avenues. Proprietors changed, and the grocery business grew. By 1922, the grocery had become the Del Monte Market, run by Jack Ruedy and William VanLoo, who lived upstairs with their wives. The market sold meats, vegetables and delicatessen items. Ruedy and VanLoo added a new storefront, a drug store (Raymond’s Drugs), and built a bakery in the former beer garden to offer freshly baked breads to their customers. In 1930, George W. Leisz and his son Jacob H. Leisz were running the grocery store. The grocery store thrived until 1937 when new supermarkets began pushing out neighborhood grocery stores. Piggly Wiggly opened a supermarket at the other end of the block at Sunnyside and Grand This early photo of A Mon Chateau shows a horse trough in front, Pleasant Valley Road before it was paved, and open rolling hills beyond. “A Mon Chateau” is painted on the gable, and the sign announces “Family Resort.”

articles.text: David Perez was always that man you wanted to sit next to at an event because you knew he’d make it fun simply being in his company. He could make anyone feel comfortable, special, and appreciated. He had the unique ability to magically connect with people from all walks of life. But first and foremost, David was the most dedicated husband and father. His life’s journey ended all too soon as he fell victim to complications from the COVID-19 virus and passed away on October 14, 2020 surrounded by his family. He was 68. Born and raised in Oakland by parents Jesus and Connie Perez, Dave was constantly surrounded by family and his siblings Jessie, Becky, Josephine, and Rick. From the scrappy streets of West Oakland to the famed house on Spruce Street, Dave grew up to be a marvelous man with strong family roots, impressive streetcred, and above all, integrity. Seemingly larger than life, he lived every day to the fullest. He knew that the key to a fulfilling life was to make the people around him happy. Dave was a gregarious, fun-loving and genuLuna Beau Perez Kalafate.

He had a unique ability to relate, connect and share his uplifting contagious demeanor with anyone he met. It simply felt good to be in his presence. Dave was a wonderful friend and neighbor, always thoughtful of others and really fun to be around,” said Patty White. “He had a funny quip at his fingertips for every occasion and was so much fun to be around. He was a very kind, honest, and smart man.” Dave loved to travel and explore the world, and always with his wife Angie by his side. As a genuinely loving husband, the two of them made an extraordinary couple. Their sincere love for each other was one of envy and a prime example of what a lifelong relationship should be. “Dave made everyone feel like he was their best friend. He was full of joy. He was a man of substance and truly made the world a better place,” said Brooke Zimmerman. Dave also loved tennis – from the Piedmont Recreation courts to the Claremont Tennis Club, he always brought his A game and a good attitude. Every year, he and Angie would venture south to Palm Desert for the Indian Wells Tennis tournament. It later evolved into a highly anticipated annual family outing with kids and grandkids in tow. “I was friends with Dave for over 30 years, and my wife went to high school with him. Dave was absolutely an individual who was bigger than life. He was not only honest in his personal life but in business too,” said tennis coach Neil Rothenberg, a neighbor. “He had an infectious laugh that was sometimes comical when his glasses would tilt and he would give off that gleam in his eye and give a double take look like he was pulling your leg. I called him “El Grande” and he will be truly missed. Our hearts go out to Angie and the family.” Additionally, Dave was a fan of all kinds of music – soul, pop, classic rock but especially Latin, He never turned down an opportunity to dance and liven up a party, or just privately twirl Angie around the kitchen. He and Angie were an exceptionally devoted couple on and off the Dave and Angie Perez on vacation in the Dominican Republic in 2020 with grandchildren Mikey Beau and dance floor. Dave would always joke that Quality Body & Fender was his first child. The family-run business he poured his heart into started in1979 with the support of his father, Jesus. He believed in treating all clients, employees and partners equally and with the utmost respect. He spent his entire life serving the communities of Oakland, Piedmont, and Berkeley, establishing deep relationships and growing Quality into one of the best auto body shops in town. Proof of his selfmade enterprise was the recognition he earned from California’s Hispanic Chamber of Commerce honoring his dedication and services to the Hispanic community as a renowned Latino business owner. After a funeral service watched by over 250 people on Zoom, a 25-car procession went down Oakland’s Auto Row on Broadway driving by long-time business partners Toyota, Subaru, and Honda. More than 100 people stood outside with signs paying their respect, while the Honda dealer set off every single car alarm on the Sales Lot in Dave’s memory, The procession stopped at Quality Body & Fender where current and past employees stood in front with Oakland and Piedmont city officials and business colleagues for a coordinated release of white balloons. Such was the measure of the man. articles.text: The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held on December 4 but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,’ she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.
articles.title: Cancer League Holly Ball to be virtual on December 4

articles.text: Every weekday morning, Piedmont resident Kelly Brezovec and her five-year-old daughter, Esther, mount the family’s electric cargo bike and ride uphill from their home near Beach School to Esther’s transitional-kindergarten class at Havens Elementary School. The trip takes less than 10 minutes, with no parking problems or waiting in a line of cars to drop off or pick up students. “Riding the electric bike is such easy exercise,” said Brezovec, a dedicated bicyclist and e-biker. “We can spend more time outdoors. It shows my daughter that biking is just normal transportation, and I don’t need to fool with car seat challenges.” “The hills are hardly an issue,” she added. P r e - COV I D shut dow n , Brezovec commuted by e-bike to her job with East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) in Oakland’s Uptown neighborhood. She notes her e-bike is not only emission free, it uses no natural gas, thanks to Piedmont’s choice of 100 % wind and solar energy from EBCE. Brezovec and her husband, Steve, own a car, but rarely use it. They much prefer using their e-bike for grocery and other shopping (it can carry up to 220 lbs.), as well as for fun. The electric motor powers the bike up to 20 miles per hour, and the battery charge, depending on usage and Piedmont residents Esther Brezovec, age 5, and her mother, Kelly Brezovec, on the family’s electric bike. flat or hilly terrain, can last for up to three days. Kelly and Steve are both experienced bicyclists, having navigated San Francisco and Oakland streets on road bikes before moving to Piedmont, and are well aware of traffic and safety concerns. “Riding an electric bike has a learning curve, like buying a new car,” Kelly noted. “My bike weighs 60 lbs., and I had to get used to stopping and starting it. But it has fatter tires and built-in lights, It is easier to change lanes in traffic than on a non-electric bike.” Brezovec purchased her Yuba Boda Boda e-bike at Westside Joe’s in Alameda. She also recommends Blue Heron Bike Shop (https://www.blueheronbikesberkeley.com) in Berkeley, where owner Rob Allen has been selling bikes since 1972. “Buying an electric bike is not cheap. E-bikes cost from $1,500 to $10,000, with an average of about $2,500,” said Allen. “But if you think of the e-bike as a vehicle, it is far cheaper to buy and operate than a car. And with a cargo bike, you have both a back seat and a trunk. The cost is in the purchase, but the reward is in owning and the joy in riding it.” The choices of makes and models of electric bikes are almost as numerous as that of electric cars. Cargo bikes can be front loaders that hold passengers or cargo low in front of the seat, or “mid or long-tailed” that can carry loads and passengers behind the seat. There are folding e-bikes for transit commuters and electric pedal-assist bikes that are lightweight and less expensive than cargo bikes. “The pedal-assist bikes flatten the hills and are perfect for Piedmont,” said Allen. • • The annual Piedmont Climate Challenge is coming to the end of its first month. In an effort to get more households involved in the Piedmont Climate Challenge, the City is partnering with community groups and businesses to offer a raffle, which will take place from December 1 to December 21. The Climate Challenge is a website that helps Piedmont residents keep track of climate actions and how they can make a difference. Make an account and learn more at www.PiedmontClimateChallenge.org. In order to secure an entry into the raffle, residents can: Create a profile at the website (worth one raffle entry) Post about their progress using the hashtag #PiedmontClimateChallenge on Facebook or Instagram (This is worth an additional one entry) You can get a raffle entry for referring a friend. If the friend mentions that you referred them in the Instagram post or in the email, you will receive one more raffle entry. • Existing Piedmont Challenge users from last year will already be entered in the raffle, so no need to create a new profile. The Prize: Mulberry’s Market is offering a sampling of wines for the holidays, a $50 gift card to buy your favorite treats with, and a gourmet cheese platter to bring home for a festive holiday dinner. One winner will be chosen from the raffle entrants and notified the week of December 21. For any questions about the raffle, please contact nredinbo@ piedmont.ca.gov. The Climate Challenge is sponsored by the City of Piedmont, Piedmont Connect, Piedmont High School Green Club, and Mulberry’s Market. •

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, November 25, 2020 Features Electric bikes flatten Piedmont hills By Marjorie Blackwell Every weekday morning, Piedmont resident Kelly Brezovec and her five-year-old daughter, Esther, mount the family’s electric cargo bike and ride uphill from their home near Beach School to Esther’s transitional-kindergarten class at Havens Elementary School. The trip takes less than 10 minutes, with no parking problems or waiting in a line of cars to drop off or pick up students. “Riding the electric bike is such easy exercise,” said Brezovec, a dedicated bicyclist and e-biker. “We can spend more time outdoors. It shows my daughter that biking is just normal transportation, and I don’t need to fool with car seat challenges.” “The hills are hardly an issue,” she added. P r e - COV I D shut dow n , Brezovec commuted by e-bike to her job with East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) in Oakland’s Uptown neighborhood. She notes her e-bike is not only emission free, it uses no natural gas, thanks to Piedmont’s choice of 100 % wind and solar energy from EBCE. Brezovec and her husband, Steve, own a car, but rarely use it. They much prefer using their e-bike for grocery and other shopping (it can carry up to 220 lbs.), as well as for fun. The electric motor powers the bike up to 20 miles per hour, and the battery charge, depending on usage and Cancer League Holly Ball to be virtual on December 4 The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held on December 4 but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,’ she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.
