Kelly and Steve are both experienced bicyclists, having navigated San Francisco and Oakland streets on road bikes before moving to Piedmont, and are well aware of traffic and safety concerns. “Riding an electric bike has a learning curve, like buying a new car,” Kelly noted. “My bike weighs 60 lbs., and I had to get used to stopping and starting it. But it has fatter tires and built-in lights, It is easier to change lanes in traffic than on a non-electric bike.” Brezovec purchased her Yuba Boda Boda e-bike at Westside Joe’s in Alameda. She also recommends Blue Heron Bike Shop (https://www.blueheronbikesberkeley.com) in Berkeley, where owner Rob Allen has been selling bikes since 1972. “Buying an electric bike is not cheap. E-bikes cost from $1,500 to $10,000, with an average of about $2,500,” said Allen. “But if you think of the e-bike as a vehicle, it is far cheaper to buy and operate than a car. And with a cargo bike, you have both a back seat and a trunk. The cost is in the purchase, but the reward is in owning and the joy in riding it.” The choices of makes and models of electric bikes are almost as numerous as that of electric cars. Cargo bikes can be front loaders that hold passengers or cargo low in front of the seat, or “mid or long-tailed” that can carry loads and passengers behind the seat. There are folding e-bikes for transit commuters and electric pedal-assist bikes that are lightweight and less expensive than cargo bikes. “The pedal-assist bikes flatten the hills and are perfect for Piedmont,” said Allen. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: 2020 has been a difficult year for most of us to absorb. The pandemic, financial issues, the election- there have been a lot of anxiety-producing issues recently. Interestingly, this has spilled over into the field of residential structural repair. I wanted to discuss thoughts on what I have been observing in the field and what you should or should not do about the conditions you are seeing in your older homes. Most of the things you are seeing are not new People are spending a lot of time at home, which means they are paying a lot more attention to their home’s imperfections. About half of the calls I have received this year have been from homeowners concerned about “recent” changes they are observing. However, it is clear to me based upon the size, location, condition and severity of their issues that a lot of these are older problems which have developed over time. These are mostly cracks in stucco, interior walls and ceilings, walkways, stairs and porches, settled or sloping floors, water intrusion, etc. Deferred home repairs are moving to the forefront of people’s thinking. Given that for most of us our homes are our biggest asset and our safe haven, these observations can be very disconcerting, especially since their significance is not readily apparent to the untrained eye. There are a few simple things which may help you think about what might be developing, and whether it needs to be addressed. What is actually occurring? The most important thing to understand is that minor settlement issues, which make up a majority of these observations, are normal and expected in our area. The typical home was built in the 1920’s, and at 100 years old is experiencing multiple signs of aging. Some degree of cracking, sloping floors, and moisture infiltration is common, and is often more substantial on sloped properties. Foundations from this era are often shallow and of inadequate dimensions, usually lacking reinforcement (rebar) and the concrete is sometimes in average condition at best. pages.text: Wednesday, November 25, 2020 25 Having a pandemic of home repair problems? By Jim Gardner 2020 has been a difficult year for most of us to absorb. The pandemic, financial issues, the election- there have been a lot of anxiety-producing issues recently. Interestingly, this has spilled over into the field of residential structural repair. I wanted to discuss thoughts on what I have been observing in the field and what you should or should not do about the conditions you are seeing in your older homes. Most of the things you are seeing are not new People are spending a lot of time at home, which means they are paying a lot more attention to their home’s imperfections. About half of the calls I have received this year have been from homeowners concerned about “recent” changes they are observing. However, it is clear to me based upon the size, location, condition and severity of their issues that a lot of these are older problems which have developed over time. These are mostly cracks in stucco, interior walls and ceilings, walkways, stairs and porches, settled or sloping floors, water intrusion, etc. Deferred home repairs are moving to the forefront of people’s thinking. Given that for most of us our homes are our biggest asset and our safe haven, these observations can be very disconcerting, especially since their significance is not readily apparent to the untrained eye. There are a few simple things which may help you think about what might be developing, and whether it needs to be addressed. What is actually occurring? The most important thing to understand is that minor settlement issues, which make up a majority of these observations, are normal and expected in our area. The typical home was built in the 1920’s, and at 100 years old is experiencing multiple signs of aging. Some degree of cracking, sloping floors, and moisture infiltration is common, and is often more substantial on sloped properties. Foundations from this era are often shallow and of inadequate dimensions, usually lacking reinforcement (rebar) and the concrete is sometimes in average condition at best. Original foundation drainage is either non-existent or not functional unless it has been upgraded. Seismic improvements may be marginal or not present. The most common cause of many of these problems is the lack of downspout drainage. Rainwater dumping up against your house can be a major contributor to settlement issues. In spite of all of these inadequacies, most of our homes are quite hardy, and their design and construction keep them standing except in extreme circumstances. When should I be concerned? A majority of settlement issues occur due to inadequate drainage. If you do nothing else, make sure your downspouts drain away from your home. If you don’t have a downspout drainage system, at least attach some flexible black pipe (see Ace Hardware) to direct the water away from your house until the drainage is permanently addressed. Hairline or small cracks in walls, ceilings, concrete slabs and stucco, if not abundant, are normal and not a big concern. But if they become larger or increase dramatically in size or number, particularly in a short time frame, that may be indicative of a more urgent problem. More obvious problems such as substantial water in crawlspaces and basements, retaining walls that are leaning significantly, or concrete that is clearly in poor condition (i.e. chunks are coming loose or look badly deteriorated) should be addressed. If there are significant cracks or movement with porches and stairs, they should be checked underneath to make sure their structures are intact. Now is the time to become an expert Given that we are all spending more time in our homes, this is the perfect opportunity for us to learn more about how they work. It is not rocket science. Most home improvement problems are fairly straightforward. Our website at jimgardnerconstruction. com has a lot of useful information and photos on these subjects. Many homeowners are terrified to go under their houses, but after crawling around under thousands of them, I have never been bit by a spider or found a wild animal or anything scary to report. Our basements and crawlspaces will reflect what you are observing in your living spaces above. If they are damp, with poor concrete or have structural problems, these are often fairly obvious. Take pictures and notes on what you see under your home, and inside as well. If you have cracks and settlement create a logbook with photos and measurements of their location for future reference. The majority of people I meet are vague about when their issues developed, and it is the observation of problems over time that are important, since most of them are slow developing. This is even more important with newer homeowners as they have no history in their homes. If you do your homework, detailing conditions over time, you will have a better sense of what your house is trying to tell you and when you may need to address it with a professional. This article was written by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. A long-time Piedmont resident, he has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. articles.text: Piedmont High alum Renzo Downey (class of 2015), headed to the Sunshine State after college to become a news reporter covering state government for FloridaPolitics.com. In addition to the global pandemic and an economic downturn, Florida is rife with contention over the topic of civil rights vs. law and order. All of this occurring in a critical battleground state for the presidential election makes Downey’s job well worth the stifling humidity and sunburns. Downey attended Northwestern University and graduated from its acclaimed Medill School of Journalism. As his collegiate tenure culminated Downey took part in Northwestern’s journalism residency in Austin, Texas to cover that state’s 140-day legislative session. After that he looked for an opportunity to cover politics in a state capitol, particularly eyeing California, Texas, Florida and Washington, D.C. – Renzo Downey He landed in Florida’s capitol, Tallahassee, as a part of a small news team of about 10 reporters throughout the state. Even before COVID he worked from home using a second bedroom as his office. “Most folks are joining our lifestyle now. The Orlando Sentinel and Miami Herald got rid of their newsrooms, not because they wanted to, but because of the cost,” Downey explained. It seems that about every four years Florida finds its way into the national spotlight as a hotly sought-after swing state in the presidential election. This year proved to be no different. “In the last three weeks of the campaign, right after Trump recovered from COVID, he came down here six or seven times. Multiple times a week we were covering the presidential race coming directly to our backyard,” Downey explained. Florida Politics, his employer, Piedmont alum and Florida political reporter Renzo Downey, pictured at the Tallahassee airport covering a speech by current V.P. Mike Pence. has its reporters aim for balanced coverage. “On the editorial side I would say we are more on the left, but in terms of the day to day news stuff, we try to be down the center.” Downey covered a memorable Mike Pence visit to Tallahassee prior to the election. “It was at the airport here, in one of the private hangars on a back runway. He just pulled in on Air Force 2, and literally ran from the plane to the podium. It was a little weird. It was the same day that they announced his own chief of staff had COVID. And there he [Pence] was, running in the light rain from the plane to the podium.” This year Florida was not at the center of a recount vote controversy, and though the state voted predominately Republican, there have been no “stop the steal” protests. “Those folks that would have been protesting are happy how Florida turned out, the GOP seems to be pretty proud of the work they put in, especially in south Florida by making up ground in MiamiDade county.” Downey has a bit of a respite heading into the holidays, but the news will ramp up in January. “They are doing pre-session committee hearings early this year, in January. That’s going to be every week basically up until the session starts in earnest in March, and then it’s 60 days of a true legislative session.” Downey anticipates a fiercely contested legislative session this year as bills are being introduced. “There will be a law enforcement protection bill, a kind of an anti-violent protest bill. It will call for things like increased jail time for certain violent activities during a protest. It is all a part of that law and order message,” Downey predicted. session starts, Downey will be loaded with controversial storylines to unravel. “A shocking, attention grabbing thing in that bill, is if a local government defunds the police specifically – not an across the board slashing – then the state can withhold grants and funding to the local government. It’s a defund the defund-ers type of thing.” Also anticipated in Florida is a bill where if you are in a car and start getting mobbed, if you then hurt somebody with your vehicle trying to escape, there is some level of immunity. “That’s definitely going to be one flash point. It’s got the Democrats fired up of course,” Downey said. “I have really enjoyed the work, it’s never boring here covering politics in Florida. That’s exactly why I wanted to be here,” Downey said with a smile. All Florida Politics articles are pushed out via Twitter, you can follow Downey @RenzoDowney. You can also subscribe to one of Florida Politics’ newsletters like the morning Sunburn, and evening Last Call. Downey is heavily featured in every Takeaways from Tallahassee every Saturday. Florida Politics produces news stories daily, Downey’s archive can be seen at: www.floridapolitics.com/archives/author/renzo.

That’s going to be every week basically up until the session starts in earnest in March, and then it’s 60 days of a true legislative session.” Downey anticipates a fiercely contested legislative session this year as bills are being introduced. “There will be a law enforcement protection bill, a kind of an anti-violent protest bill. It will call for things like increased jail time for certain violent activities during a protest. It is all a part of that law and order message,” Downey predicted. By March, when the Florida session starts, Downey will be loaded with controversial storylines to unravel. “A shocking, attention grabbing thing in that bill, is if a local government defunds the police specifically – not an across the board slashing – then the state can withhold grants and funding to the local government. It’s a defund the defund-ers type of thing.” Also anticipated in Florida is a bill where if you are in a car and start getting mobbed, if you then hurt somebody with your vehicle trying to escape, there is some level of immunity. “That’s definitely going to be one flash point. It’s got the Democrats fired up of course,” Downey said. “I have really enjoyed the work, it’s never boring here covering politics in Florida. That’s exactly why I wanted to be here,” Downey said with a smile. All Florida Politics articles are pushed out via Twitter, you can follow Downey @RenzoDowney. articles.text: Photo by Tim Johnson. Staff members of The Lake Merritt Independent Seniors Community display a variety of masks they wear during a time of COVID. Pictured are: Stephanie Cox, Krasuandra Hunter, Ryan Wilcox, Ernestine Epperson, and Candi Zamora. The other day I was chatting with Judy, one of the residents at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Community. She was wearing a light blue mask with peaches on it. I said to her, “I don’t think I have ever seen that mask before. It’s very nice!” Her eyes lit up and she said, “It’s new. I now have six double-sided masks. That means I now have twelve different looks to select from!” Last week another resident, Faye, walked by. She was wearing a black mask with white polka dots, a white blouse with black polka dots, a black cardigan sweater and black slacks. Her black and white earrings matched her necklace and set off the outfit perfectly - pure class. I told her so. Her response was, “A fashionable lady knows how to color coordinate.” The U.S. Center for Disease Control (CDC) regularly updates its website with ways to help prevent COVID-19. While it has long been suggested that mask-wearing primarily protects the “other person,” in the CDC’s scientific brief updated on November 10, the agency cites studies that demonstrate that cloth mask materials can also reduce the wearers’ exposure to infectious droplets through filtration, including filtration of fine droplets. It’s common knowledge that nobody likes or really wants to wear a mask all the time, but the science is clear: Mask wearing helps save lives. Since it is likely we will be wearing masks for some time to come, why not look at some fashionable masks that show your personality? That is exactly what the staff at The Lake Merritt decided to do. As it turns out, it’s fun. As a pet lover, Stephanie was happy to find a line of masks that pay tribute to our furry friends. The fact that the paw print is made from rhinestones makes it all the better. Who doesn’t like a little bling? Krasaundra said, “Wearing a more fashionable mask made me feel good. After the residents started complimenting me, the idea became fun. It challenged me to up my game!” She has several different masks, but one of her favorites is the elegant black mask trimmed with pearls shown in the photo. Ryan likes his cat mask because he enjoys “just the right amount of zany on my face.” He likes things that are fun. We asked Ernestine why the sparkles? She wears masks that glitter and sparkle because they match her personality. Candi is wearing an “Alice in Wonderland” mask that she designed and made herself. She saw the need for masks early on and began making them for friends and family. Residents noticed her beautiful creations and have been asking Candi to make masks for them as well. Fashion has always had a way of taking our wardrobe essentials and turning them into statement pieces. It’s no surprise that the protective face coverings we’ve been advised to wear to curb the spread of the coronavirus have quickly been embraced and beautified by the fashion world. Since we’re going to wear one anyway, why not join with the residents and staff of The Lake Merritt and consider something with a bit of pizzazz? You’ll have fun doing it. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For information call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: Any kind of caregiving is going to require coordinating with other people and entities, such as doctors, therapists, insurance, maybe other family members or non-medical caregivers. “The challenges individuals face in navigating the health care and Long-Term Services and Supports systems are often amplified for their caregivers, who are acting on their behalf,” the AARP states in their “Caregiving in the U.S. 2020” report. “Among those who coordinate care, a greater proportion of caregivers report having at least some difficulty in coordinating care among their care recipients’ providers.” This report found that the percentage of family caregivers who find coordinating care difficult is increasing, up from 18% in 2015 who said it was “somewhat difficult” to 24% in 2020; and up to 6% who said it was “very difficult” in 2020. At the same time, those who described coordinating care as “somewhat easy” or “very easy” actually decreased. It seems the challenges of care coordination go across all genders, ages, and types of care, based on those surveyed for this report. If you are a family caregiver, chances are that you experienced some frustrations in trying to work with anyone from a volunteer organization to a specialist at the local hospital. For those caring for someone with emotional or mental health concerns, or memory impairments, the AARP report found an even greater difficulty with care coordination, as did those caring for someone who is over age 65. In order to coordinate the care needs of an individual, sometimes safety protocols within HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) can create hurdles to sharing the information between parties. In order to facilitate improved coordination, find out who is available. Does the insurance provider have a designated care coordinator? Does the hospital have someone in this role? Is there someone at the home care agency who can facilitate this need? Can you hire someone such as a care manager just for this “quarterbacking” for all parties? Once you are able to decide who is at the hub of the wheel, then the care can be coordinated and adjusted as needs change. In the Christian Scriptures the Apostle Paul refers to believers as “co-creators with God.” The troubles we face should not be signs of failure alone, but also as opportunities for growth. If a structure excludes others from the advantages we have enjoyed, perhaps it’s time to rip out a wall or two and expand our vision to include all. Perhaps it’s another time in our history to see opportunity in the chaos and blessing in the struggle. As we approach Thanksgiving, let us be cautious about what we are thankful for. I suppose it’s only human practice what I call “comparative gratitude”, that is, being thankful for things we have that others do not. But Jesus actually defined blessings as challenges. In his most famous sermon on the mount, he said, “Blessed are the hungry, blessed are those who mourn, and blessed are those who are persecuted...” One could argue that it is a very un-Christian thing to define a blessing as something we have that others do not. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. welcome addition, which lets you know who is tracking you), Apple Maps (finally almost as good as Google maps), and Mail. Renewable energies, whether wind or solar, are not dispatch-able: a BART train scheduled for a 6 a.m. departure would have to wait for the Sun to rise to be dispatched if all energy came from solar panels and wind turbines. Today the California base load that fills the gap is mainly supplied by natural gas power plants. The California energy mix in 2019 was 43% natural gas, 8% nuclear, and 17% hydroelectric. These plants, due to Carnot, resistive and electrostatic transmission loss and other factors, have an energy efficiency in converting gas to electricity of about 33% (as per a 2017 report by the California Public Utility Commission), and 79-95% of plants run at 29% efficiency. Therefore, an electric range can use as much as three times more gas in cooking a meal than a natural gas range. This situation may change in the long term when technology to store renewable energy is integrated into the grid. But there is currently no feasible storage technology at the scale needed, apart possibly from pumping water up and “turbine-ing” it down as done in Switzerland, a technology that requires building new reservoirs. The scheduled closing in 2024-25 of the two Diablo nuclear power units will only delay further the State’s decarbonization goal.

articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 8. Editor: In August of 2011, I had the pleasure of playing in a trio of French horns for the dedication of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Piedmont was then poised to enjoy the cultural and educational benefits of an arts performance and exhibition space in the center of town, something rather unique to communities of our size. My expectations were fulfilled. I watched and listened to the PCA’s offerings over the following years and was not disappointed. As President of the Berkeley Symphony, I was proud to see a chamber music series, Berkeley Symphony and Friends, take root at the Center. As a horn player, I was delighted to participate in the organization and performances of the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, which is based at the Center. I am now troubled to read the words of those would replace the Center with such things as a commercial health club, arguing that the PCA was merely an ‘’interim solution.” Since when have the arts been an ‘’interim solution’’? I cannot think of a better long-term investment than an arts center in the middle of our town. A look at the 2019 calendar of the PCA shows that the Center has remained true to its mission to promote artistic endeavors within Piedmont. On that calendar I see a wide range of events involving performing and visual arts, some presented by visiting artists and some by members of the Piedmont community, involving persons of all ages. I see, among others, the Piedmont Choirs, Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, PHS Drama, student recitals, and recitals by established chamber music groups. I see frequent art exhibits. I have been in discussion with the Piedmont Recreation Department about the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra becoming an offering of the Recreation Department. However, the Recreation Department likely does not have the expertise or time necessary to maintain the PCA’s unique blend of professional arts offerings together with space and time for local artistic talent and artistic instruction. In short, we have a unique institution in our midst that has enriched and will continue to enrich the cultural life of our community. The PCA is not an interim solution to anything, but rather it is an institution of enduring value of which we all should be proud. –Tom Reicher me who my real friends are, it showed me that there is still hope for the United States. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont City Council on November 5. Editor: The Piedmont Center for the Arts has been one of the best things to happen to Piedmont during my 43 years as a Piedmont resident. My wife and I have enjoyed dozens of world-class musical performances in this intimate and accessible venue, a jewel in the center of town within walking distance of one’s home. The many top-notch jazz and classical concerts at the PCA have enriched the community immeasurably. The Berkeley Symphony and Friends series and the annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival are highlights. As a retired professional musician (principal French horn in both the Oakland and Berkeley symphonies), I participated in inaugural performances during the PCA’s opening. But more recently, I have been part of a local group responsible for launching and running the fledgling Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, whose performances in the Center have thrilled capacity houses. The existence of the Center itself made the very idea of the orchestra possible, and, without the Center as its rehearsal and performance venue, this superb (if I may say so myself) ensemble would struggle to survive. The orchestra has been a great ambassador for the community. The orchestra is comprised of both professional and advanced amateurs, many of them Piedmont residents, and our audiences have come from throughout the Bay Area. There is an amazing reservoir of musical talent in our community that the orchestra has been able to tap, thanks to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. With great appreciation. –Stuart Gronningen
articles.title: Piedmonters show appreciation for PCA

articles.text: Editor: Councilmember Betsy Andersen is quoted in last week’s story on the PCA lease as saying “the city had many years in which to initiate its own programming in the space but didn’t”. Technically correct but wrong when taken out of context. The City acquired the 801 building in 2003 in a condition that prohibited the city from using it; principally, 801 was not ADA compliant. The City conducted several structural assessments of the facility and included 801 in the annual Capital Improvements program. However, by 2009, the $2M cost overrun of the Piedmont Hills Undergrounding district and tax revenue decline due to the recession prohibited the City from making the necessary upgrades to the building. Now that the City has $5M+ in the Facilities Maintenance Fund it would be appropriate for the City to upgrade both wings of the building, making 801 a more usable and profitable space. –Garrett Keating

We want what’s best for our Editor: It’s time to give thanks and it’s time to give to the annual Giving Campaign in support of our schools. I have been involved with the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) and the Giving Campaign since Ben and I moved to Piedmont several years ago. We moved for the strong schools and wonderful community. Our three children, grades 9th, 6th and 3rd, have each benefitted from an excellent education at Piedmont Schools. We recognize that this is in large part due to the additional funds raised each year kids and our community, and we know how important the funds raised are to our district. Our contributions make a huge difference, and it’s what makes Piedmont special. PUSD has only ever had a positive impact on our city. That is why Ben and I moved here, and that is why we are committed to ensuring our schools are fully funded every year. Our schools are what keep Piedmont flourishing. The growing challenges facing the schools in our state have become impossible to ignore. Even before the pandemic, our budget was challenged by reductions in state funding. Although we have some cushion from a successful Giving Campaign last year, plus the increased revenue from Measure H, we are still facing uncertainty. Funding our schools is still up to us. We donate to the Giving Campaign because doing so is essential to keeping our schools (and our community!) strong. For this reason, I passionately support the Giving Campaign and commit myself to fundraising on behalf of PEF. The dollars we are raising this year are essential for next year’s school year. We want our children to return to the robust, excellent educational experience we have always had in Piedmont. I urge you to make your donation today. Together, our commitment to our community and our schools are what make Piedmont extraordinary. Thank you, Piedmont, for keeping our schools strong. Cortney Allen is Vice-chair of the PEF Board. articles.text: Last year’s Turkey Trot was plagued with strong winds and cold temperatures, but that didn’t deter nearly 2,200 runners from showing up early Thanksgiving morning for everyone’s favorite 5K run on the streets of Winds knocked over the inflated black and white arch at thermometer registered a brisk 42 degrees. Neighbors still waved and cheered for the large flock of Turkey Runners began on Highland Avenue near the front of the police station, then wound their way through the city to the finish line in front of the Exedra. Many spectators watching from the sidelines commented on the cold weather, but most runners donned shorts and t-shirts as they sped through the course. In a historic first, Crosby Freeman and Jessica Huffman, his wife of one month, became the first husband and wife to win the men’s and women’s divisions at the same time. Four years earlier each of them won the race. Freeman joked that the double-win set a gold standard for the future of their marriage. “It sets a high bar,” he said with a smile. “We’re only one month into our marriage and we’ve already won Huffman said that the win meant a lot to both of them; they Jessica Huffman and Crosby Freeman, recently married, were crowned the winners of the 2019 Turkey Trot, the first couple to win the title. were married right around the corner from the finish line at the Community Hall. She also said that running is a huge part of the couple’s relationship. Freeman topped the male category with a time on 5K course of 16:47. Huffman won the woman’s division with a time of 20:12. The winners in each division received a turkey from Village Market, a pumpkin pie from Piedmont Grocery, flowers from J. Miller Flowers, a gift certificate from Transport running shoes, and 2019 race caps. Prior to the start of the race, five symphony French horn musicians gathered in heavy coats to play several fanfares on antique French hunting horns, or trompes de chasse, giving the event an authentic 15th century feel. The Trot has a long history that started with Piedmont High School running teams. It began in 2002 with PHS cross-country coach Doyle O’Regan. With just a few hundred participants in the event’s infancy, the original race didn’t even require blocking off the streets. But by 2013, over 2,000 participants were running in the race each year. Last year’s Trot had about 2,200 participants, despite cold weather.

articles.text: In this challenging era when the light of Christ is so deeply needed, the annual Christmas Concert at First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland will once again bring glorious musical performances and spiritual uplift to the community and beyond – thanks to its first-ever virtual concert, available online throughout December. Everyone is invited to tune in and listen to Christmas favorites and new arrangements performed by talented, well-known Bay Area musicians – sopranos Shawnette Sulker and Katy Stephan, tenor Darron Flagg, baritone Martin Bell, classical guitarist Richard Flores and organist Michael Moran and a rousing rendition of Handel’s Messiah. Stephan and Moran are the regular musicians for the Church. The Sunday School Students will read the Bible account of the birth of Jesus. Beginning December 1st, a link to the concert will be available on the Church website at: www.ChristianScienceOakland. org. For more information, call 510- 832-2364, or visit the Christian Science Reading Room at 1000 Broadway in Oakland, open Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
articles.title: Christian Science Church hosts Christmas Concert

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department received a report of a fall victim on Moraga Avenue on Thursday morning, November 19 at 8:24 a.m. Resident Patsie Kao was walking her dog on Moraga Avenue when two German Shepherds escaped from a yard and tried to attack her dog, a corgi. Kao fell to the ground in the act of protecting her dog. During the melee she suffered a dog bite puncture wound to her hand. Two witnesses responded to the scene quickly, upon hearing cries for help, and called the police and then the paramedics. Kao was treated by the paramedics and was taken to a hospital for emergency treatment for the bite wound. The corgi remains in high spirits, thanks to the quick action of Kao. The owner of the two dogs was notified of the incident, and the dogs have been placed on a 10-day quarantine at the house. The report of the incident has been forwarded to Animal Control Services.
articles.title: Dog walker attacked by 2 German Shepherds

articles.text: Piedmont’s plans to open elementary schools in December have been canceled. On Monday, November 16 Alameda County moved back into the most restrictive purple tier of COVID restrictions along with 40 other counties in California due to increased cases since the start of November. “It is our current understanding that Alameda County’s movement into the purple tier specifically eliminates the Piedmont Unified School District’s Reopening Plan’s goal of returning K-5 elementary students to a hybrid/in-person learning environment for December 1st and December 8th,” Superintendent Randy Booker announced in a press release. The tier system is a part of California’s “Blueprint for a Safer Economy,” current county status can easily be seen at https://dig. abclocal.go.com/kabc/covid-tiertracker/index.html The metric that Alameda County is failing is the per capita new daily cases. The 7-day average daily case rates for Alameda County went from 3.8 (per 100K residents) on November 8 to 7.0 on November 15. The cutoff for the purple tier is 7.0. Data has a seven-day lag time to allow for number adjustments and the most recent case numbers in the last week (not yet factored into the tier assignment) have continued to increase. The sudden move to purple was not possible a week ago, but Governor Newson has implemented an “emergency brake” by allowing counties to jump two tiers at once. Now, counties can move after only one week of data that would push them into a more restrictive tier. Previously, the state waited two weeks to analyze data to avoid quick movements between tiers. Last week Alameda was still in the orange tier and a move only to the red was anticipated. More changes to the tier sys-

articles.text: At its meeting on November 16, the Piedmont City Council approved, with a 3-2 vote, a first reading of an amended lease for the 9-1/2 year old non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts to continue its occupancy of the city-owned building at 801 Magnolia Avenue. City Administrator Sara Lillevand introduced the agenda item at Monday night’s meeting, which drew a lengthy two hourlong discussion. Approximately 13 residents spoke during the public comment portion of the discussion. The city entered into a lease agreement with the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) in May 2011. The building, former Christian Science Church, had been purchased by the City, but lay unused for six years. The center agreed to raise money to renovate the building in exchange for a 10-year lease. Its stated purpose was to create a cultural arts center for music, art, theater, author readings and similar special events. It operated from the outset as a group of volunteers providing the city with its first arts programming to the community. Lillevand added that significant improvements were made to the facility at the center’s expense, and “it was transformed from a mostly vacant, underutilized space to a thriving arts space.” The center is a tax-exempt, charitable organization. PCA board members have long stated their interest in renewing the 10-year lease. At the request of Lillevand, Public Works Director Chester Nakahara estimated that it would have cost the city approximately $200,000 to complete all the repairs and improvements that have been made to the property over the 10-year lease. “The important question to consider, is whether and to what degree do we value a community arts space in Piedmont,” Lillevand said. Council member Jennifer Cavenuagh said that it was clear from community feedback that the arts are important to Piedmont. “That is not in dispute in my mind. The question is what does
articles.title: Council approves first reading for renewed PCA lease

articles.text: The city formally welcomed Michael Despain to serve as Interim Fire Chief in Piedmont at a November 16 city council meeting. Despain will continue oversight of the critical operations of the fire department until April 18, 2021, or when a permanent chief is hired, whichever is sooner. Despain is a retired Fire Chief who is currently completing an interim appointment with the Lincoln Fire Department in Nebraska. He has served as Interim Fire Chief or Fire Chief for the cities of Fresno, Clovis, Rocklin, and Lincoln, where he currently resides. articles.text: Calif. tops 1 million reported cases; Piedmont total now 57 Due to an ongoing spike in COVID-19 cases for more than two weeks, Alameda County enacted purple tier restrictions for business and activities starting today, Wednesday, November 18. The state placed the entire county, which includes Piedmont, into the purple tier, a more restrictive category, on Monday, November 16. The purple tier is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system. The state moved Alameda County into the second-least restrictive orange tier, or moderate tier, on October 13. This week, the county skipped the red tier, or substantial tier, and was moved directly into the most restrictive category. The California Department of Public Health said that local and statewide increases in new cases caused the change in tier. According to the state, counties are placed in the purple tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. “We need Alameda County residents and businesses to, once again, rise to the challenge and help flatten the curve,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Health Officer, in a statement. Four more cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont during the past seven days, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department released yesterday, Tuesday, November 17. The total caseload for Piedmont since the pandemic began in March is now 57. New cases have been rising steadily in recent days in Alameda County. On Monday, 206 new cases were reported, compared to 35 reported on October 15. On August 13, the worst day yet for the county, 419 cases were recorded. COVID cases up; Alameda County downgraded to more restrictive Purple Tier Calif. tops 1 million reported cases; Piedmont total now 57 By Barry Eitel Due to an ongoing spike in COVID-19 cases for more than two weeks, Alameda County enacted purple tier restrictions for business and activities starting today, Wednesday, November 18. The state placed the entire county, which includes Piedmont, into the purple tier, a more restrictive category, on Monday, November 16. The purple tier is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system. The state moved Alameda County into the second-least restrictive orange tier, or moderate tier, on October 13. This week, the county skipped the red tier, or substantial tier, and was moved directly into the most restrictive category. The California Department of Public Health said that local and statewide increases in new cases caused the change in tier. According to the state, counties are placed in the purple tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. “We need Alameda County residents and businesses to, once again, rise to the challenge and help flatten the curve,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Health Officer, in a statement. Four more cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont during the past seven days, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department released yesterday, Tuesday, November 17. The total caseload for Piedmont since the pandemic began in March is now 57. New cases have been rising steadily in recent days in Alameda County. On Monday, 206 new cases were reported, compared to 35 reported on October 15. On August 13, the worst day yet for the county, 419 cases were recorded. articles.text: City hopes to replace retaining walls on San Carlos Ave. On Monday, November 16, City Council directed the Public Works Department to come up with a plan to replace retaining walls on San Carlos Avenue and a portion of Oakland Ave. near Sunnyside, both of which are deteriorating and leaning. The City hopes to complete the work by next spring, 2021. “This is a long-time public project that we’ve been working on,” noted Director of Public Works Chester Nakahara, who retires in December. He added that the project had been derailed by the coronavirus pandemic this year. The leaning wall on Oakland Avenue runs between Sunnyside and Olive Avenues. The wall on San Carlos Avenue runs on the lower roadway of that split-level street. Both walls have large cracks and are leaning significantly. If the retaining walls were to fail, it would impact the sidewalks, roadways and potentially private property. “These walls are aging, and have been leaning outwards towards the street,” Nakahara wrote in a staff report. The walls were initially cast in place, where concrete is poured to create the wall at the site. The council agreed with City staff’s recommendation that the new walls be created in this “castin-place” method, which could match the existing appearance of the walls as well as allow for some ornamentation. In replacing the existing retaining walls this way, the City could create an Oakland Avenue “bioswale,” a planted channel that removes water pollution. Other options presented to Council by civil engineer John Wanger included the “big blocks” method, where pre-cast blocks are stacked to create a new wall, and the tie-back “shotcrete” method where a natural-looking concrete wall is fastened to some of the existing wall and adjacent soil. Council also considered the “concrete masonry unit” method, where a new wall is built in front of the old and would require relocating the sidewalk, gutter and curb. Nakahara said that early cost estimates suggest cast-in-place for both walls would cost $387,000, making it the second least expensive method. articles.text: State measure passes with 56% majority Alastair Mactaggart A Piedmont couple, Celine and Alastair Mactaggart, can be credited with sponsoring the California Privacy Rights Act, seen on this year’s ballot as Proposition 24. The latest count shows that Prop. 24 is passing with a majority of 56 percent. The Privacy Rights Act will reinforce and redefine parts of the California Consumer Privacy Act, a 2019 law that gave state residents new rights as to how companies collect and use their personal information. Supporters of the proposition say that the new law will make it easier for people to opt out of having their 24 has as a central provision that no future amendments that harm consumer privacy would be permitted. Any other amendments, for example to help consumer privacy, are permitted with a simple majority vote of the Legislature, but anything that harmed consumer privacy would require another initiative.” This would eliminate the efforts of special interest groups in the legislature who may try to weaken the law. “Nearly one million voters signed a petition to put Proposition 24 on the ballot,” she added. The new law is designed to place power back into the hands of consumers. “I’ve worked very hard on this issue for six years, and we actually think privacy is the wrong word. This is really about power. Large companies buy and sell our personal information and data over and over again, every day without our knowledge or consent,” she explained. “Prop. 24 puts strong guardrails on that, so this is really about giving people a choice about their own personal information, like that of their race, ethnicity, or health, and letting them decide who gets to use it, or not.” The law will also triple fines for abuses of kids’ data. It will now require opt-in consent for the sale of personal information from consumers under the age of 16. “It will set a strong floor whereby future amendments to the law can only be made in furtherance of protecting privacy, creating a one-way switch for future protection,” Celine Mactaggart said. The proposition was endorsed by many notable industry leaders in the state, including former presidential candidate Andrew Yang, Congressman Ro Khanna, privacy expert and author Shoshana Zuboff. However, when they saw an allout assault by big tech in 2019 to weaken the law in the legislature, the Mactaggarts and supporters decided a ballot initiative was needed to protect the core princi- “We decided to put this on the ballot to give voters a choice about further protecting their and their family’s personal data,” Celine Mactaggart said. “Prop. Celine Mactaggart sumer Watchdog, California Firefighters, the state’s NAACP chapter, and several other state leaders and advocates. Celine Mactaggart said that because the initial polling was strong, she and her team felt confident in its passage but conceded that she never could have foreseen that she and her husband, as parents of three young children, would be running a campaign of this magnitude from home. “We are very fortunate. We had an absolutely wonderful team,” she said, and added that she feels honored that her team was led by women. Mactaggart credits much of the campaign’s success to campaign manager Robin Swanson, a strategist and communications expert with more than 20 years of political experience in Washington D.C. and Sacramento.

articles.text: Just after 4 a.m. EST on Friday, November 6, three days after America’s contentious presidential election, Georgia was not yet on everyone’s mind. Every major news network still colored the state with 16 electoral votes pink for a slight lead for Donald Trump. However, a local independent reporter, Robin Kemp from Georgia’s Clayton County, was able to break the news of Biden overtaking Trump in Georgia as it happened. The few hundred people following the updates on her Twitter account got the news first, while the rest of country sat in the dark. The now famous reporter, Robin Kemp, recently set up the first nonprofit news site in Clayton County, Georgia. She created The Clayton Crescent after the local county paper laid her off due to COVID-19. Even without a paycheck, Kemp kept reporting election results as they trickled in. She arrived at the Registrar’s office in Clayton County at 9:00 a.m. Thursday and didn’t leave until 5:09 a.m. Friday when the count was finished. As the vote tallies in Georgia came down to the end, Clayton County still had a few thousand mail-in ballots and the county just south of Atlanta hit the global spotlight. After 3:00 a.m. Friday, November 6, at least one major news network mistakenly announced Georgia’s Clayton County (which was voting 87 percent for Biden) had stopped counting and reporting numbers for the night. Kemp, originally from New Orleans, has been a reporter in Georgia for some years. She describes herself as “A spicy Popeyes sandwich out here Local, independent journalist Robin Kemp covered the breaking news ahead of the major networks, as Georgia flipped to blue in the presidential election on November 3 for the first time since 1992. in a Chick-Fil-A world.” Her dedicated exclusive coverage included interviews with GOP observers, and photos in the Registrar’s office of ballots being delivered, verified for signatures, stacked, counted and zip tied when done. She fielded questions from anxious followers on her Twitter and gave live video updates with the latest number of ballots outstanding, happenings in the office and presidential votes. Some news crews rushed to the Registrar’s office towards the end of Friday night, but Kemp was the only one there the entire day. Kemp gave the world updates from the ground and referred people to the county website to see that Biden had taken the lead by 917 votes just after 4 a.m. of Friday. She found herself suddenly with a touch of fame, being interviewed by reporters as far away as England. Someone dredged up an old GoFundMe for www. claytoncrescent.com and her new “Sleeping here at night is OK, but not walking around my carpet in your golf shoes.”

articles.text: The annual Toys for Tots campaign has begun, and Piedmont Fire Department has placed a donation box by the front doors of City Hall. Residents are encouraged to drop off new, unwrapped gifts for children in the bin during daytime hours seven days a week. Last year, the Marine Corps Reserve, which sponsors the nationwide campaign, had 109 donation sites in Alameda County and collected 25,000 toys to kids in the county. “With the help of Piedmont residents, we’re hoping that we can see that number go higher this year,” said Fire Chief Bret Black. Firefighters will empty the bin at the end of each day. If residents wish to bring a large number of donations, call the Fire Department at 420-3030 to arrange for a firefighter to be there. The Toys for Tots drive will also be accepting monetary donations for the first time. Checks may be left with the Fire Department, but made payable to Toys for Tots, 2144 Clement Avenue, Alameda, CA, 94501. To donate directly to the campaign using a credit card, visit https://marinetoysfortots.salsalabs.org/localdonationform/index. html?fun_local_campaign_designation=CA-Alameda&scf_ unit_code_supporter=CA-Alameda.

articles.text: Thanks to our eagle-eyed readers, two corrections are needed for the election coverage contained in the November 11 edition. And article titled “2020 General election outcome vaults Biden and Harris to White House,” stated “it took approximately four days for Electoral College results to become final.” The electoral college has not met yet, and the results of the president-elect are projections by popular vote. On December 8, 2020 Determination of Controversy as to Appointment of Electors is scheduled to take place. The electoral results should be final in mid-December. Also in an article titled “Piedmont Pool bond passes with 68 percent margin,” the headline should have stated that Measure UU won with 58% of the vote and a margin of 41 percentage points. articles.text: Trees are real – trees are sustainable Staff photo Oakland’s famous Tap Dancing Christmas Trees on opening day of the Piedmont Scout Tree Lot in 2018. Purchasing a real Christmas tree for the holidays is an environmentally friendly way to celebrate the season. Trees spend roughly eight years being grown before being harvested. They convert CO2 into oxygen, providing a habitat for wildlife and keeping large spaces of green across North America. Unlike artificial trees, they are 100% recyclable and 100% biodegradable. In our bold, new world, online sales are a lifeline for many; and during a time of COVID, the Piedmont Scout Council is taking a giant leap and offering tree sales online. For over 50 years, the Scouts have cheerfully procured, sold, trimmed and delivered everyone’s favorite conifers from Silver Tip to Noble and Douglas Firs. Online sale began November 1 and continue until all trees are sold, typically by about December 15. Sales are online at www. young participants. Last year the Scouts sold over 1,700 trees, raising $100,000 for Scout programs in Cub Scouts, Scouts, Explorers, Sea Scouts and coed Venturing programs. online sales and contactless pick-up and delivery, the Scouts allow customers to plan early for the Holidays, relaxing in the spirit of family and home. Piedmont Scout Tree Lot Online: it’s easy; it’s sustainable; it’s tradition; it’s relaxing; and it’s community. For more information contact Genevieve Bandrowski at the Scout office at 510-547-4493 or at bsa42trees@gmail.com. scouttreelot.org. A limited option to purchase by phone will be available for customers who do not have online access. Trees and wreaths will be available for pickup or delivery after Thanksgiving. Home deliveries will be to customers’ front door. Operated entriely by Piedmont Scouts and community volunteers, the Tree Lot also serves as a major fundraiser to support the local Piedmont Scout Council, a youth program with over 1,000

articles.text: Transitional Kindergarteners had their first day of school yesterday at Beach School on Tuesday, November 17. It may have been the second rainy day of the season, but the opening could not have come at a more fortuitous time. Alameda County was moved back into the purple tier of COVID restrictions this week, and only schools already in session are allowed to continue. If the TK class started one day later, it would have been a different story. A press release from Alameda County’s Department of Public Health states, “Any school that currently has students attending classes in person may continue to do so. Effective November 18 no additional schools may open for in-person instruction.” Piedmont School District’s painstaking and protracted plans to open in-person K-2 classes on December 1 and grades 3-5 on December 8 have been cancelled. California implemented Transitional Kindergarten in the fall of 2012. It is available only for students that turn five years old between September 2 and December 2. For the first week of class, parents are allowed to go onto campus with their TK students to help their transition to real school. After that, visitors on campus will be highly restricted. Students had an orientation on Monday, November 16, to see their new classroom and go over spacing and other COVID protocols. On Tuesday, Principal Michael Corritone personally welcomed parents and Piedmont’s youngest students. Most of the young scholars brought a small potted plant for their new teacher, Alexandra de Martini. TK students will have half-day classes Tuesday through Friday from 12:00 to 2:15 p.m., with distance learning on Mondays. Proud parents were on hand for their TK students’ first day of school. Beach School Principal Michael Corritone welcomes parents and students on the first day of school. Monday’s orientation for TK students helped the students understand distancing and other COVID protocols.

articles.text: MHS Art teacher Louisa Cheung teaches students about their next assignment and hands out art supplies for students to complete their Vanguard art projects at home. Millennium High School welcomed its freshmen back to campus on Friday, November 13, for 2 1/2 hours of advisory, tech support and supported study hall for the first time since March. Even with a surprise fire alarm and a quick trip outside, the return to campus was an overwhelming success. Students completed a health screener before arrival, wore masks, used hand sanitizer and sat in marked seats six feet apart with all the windows and doors open. With new safety precautions in place, students were still able to share stories with one another, joke and receive support from the staff on hand. “It was great to be here today,” exclaimed student Orla Cohen. Paraeducator Alisa Foster added, “I am so happy to be a part of this.” Students drew graphic representations of their identity and what was important to them as they introduced themselves to classmates they had met only on their computer screens. “Millennium is a small, tightknit community so it was really special to be able to welcome our new students to our campus,” said Principal Shannon Fierro. “I am so grateful to the staff and families and students for making this a safe, smooth and positive return,” she added. Additional small cohorts of MHS students, divided by grade, will be invited to campus over the next few weeks. One cohort of students will come to campus from 9:00 a.m.- 11:30 a.m. each Wednesday and Friday, through December 18. Students will have an hour of advisory and 75 minutes of supported study hall and instructional support. Each day of school in-person will have just one cohort on campus. Millennium will have 11 freshmen, 13 sophomores, 11 juniors and the 22 seniors (in two cohorts of 11). Students will leave campus at 11:30 a.m. and return home to complete the remainder of the school day (12:30 p.m. - 3:10 p.m.) remotely. Students on campus will be supervised by Principal Fierro with paraeducator support. Other teachers and support staff are invited and permitted to come and support but are not required to attend, student attendance is also optional. Prior to the return of Millennium students, only two small groups of Special Education students have been learning in-person. Separately, Piedmont schools welcomed back nine TK students yesterday at Beach School. Since Millennium was already in session prior to Alameda County moving into the purple tier, they are eligible to continue instruction. articles.text: Here are some sensory tips and tricks If and when school returns masks will be required at all times on school grounds. As a parent, the thought of getting a young child to wear a mask brings up memories of my efforts to keep hats on my children in order to prevent sunburn. Strategies I tried included distracting them, finding hats with ties making it harder to pull off or I let them pick out their favorite team’s hat with its logo. It was a struggle, nevertheless. Similarly, wearing masks and/ or keeping them on for a prolonged period (over two hours) is sure to be challenging for most children. Here are some sensory-based tips and tricks for helping the resistive child. To begin, talk with your child. Be certain that they understand why they must wear a mask. There are many social stories for young children that address mask wearing. Next, acknowledge that wearing a mask is not easy and ask why they do not like wearing a mask. You will be surprised by their ability to pinpoint what is bothersome for them. With that, you can begin to find solutions to make mask wearing more tolerable. The most likely reason that children resist wearing a mask is that there are one or more sensory aspects that are bothersome. Think of a mask as a piece of clothing. We all know that fit and comfort can make or break your wearing a certain garment. How many of you are wearing fitted jeans as you work remotely? Some common reasons for mask avoidance include: • It feels rough or scratchy. • It tickles (too loose) or is too tight. • It smells inside. • It’s too hot and sweaty. • It hurts their ears. • It’s hard to breathe. Once you have a better understanding of which sensations make wearing a mask difficult, you are ready to find a more sensory-friendly mask for your child. First, consider the following. • Material – soft cotton, polyester/spandex • Shape - square or diamond • Strap style design - ear loops, single band with adjustable tug cord After you have settled on a mask that fits your child’s sensory needs, begin building their tolerance to wearing the mask. Have them wear the mask for short periods at home while engaged in fun activities. Gradually increase the time worn daily. As the wearing time lengthens, you may encounter new sensory obstacles such as ear pain, moisture issues or smells. Here are a few tricks for these issues: • Be sensitive to laundry detergent smells. Scent free or scented? • Consider a silicone mask bracket insert to reduce moisture and fogging glasses. • Button headbands for ear loop masks - no more tugging at ears. • Ear savers allow a mask to be attached behind the head instead of around the ears. • Disposable for lightweight choice. • Brush teeth prior to donning a mask. • Suck on a mint or hard candy. • Let your child pick out the mask with their favorite characters or color. Sometimes that is motivation enough. • Provide fidgets to keep hands busy to reduce the urge to touch or remove masks. Armed with these sensory tips and tricks, here’s to a successful transition back to in-person learning for our youngest students while wearing their sensory-friendly masks. Kimberly Bonacum, MS, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist with Piedmont School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, contact mindfulfidgets@gmail.com. experience College Prep first-hand.
articles.title: Is your child an unwilling mask wearer?

articles.text: On a bright and chilly Sunday morning, November 8, car after car pulled up to deliver sweet treats through a backyard gate in central Piedmont. Behind the gate, a table held a delectable array of cakes, cookies, and tarts with a Halloween theme. The delicious dishes were made by students participating in the Top Chef Junior Piedmont competition, a student-led fundraiser for the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign. The fundraiser was created by Beach School 5th grader Luka Stevanovic. It was co-founded by 6th grader Preston Kwei, with organizing help from Piedmont High senior Bella Kjellen. The event raised $1,725 for the Giving Campaign and created a day of socially-distanced fun for young bakers and chefs across Piedmont. The Giving Campaign is a family affair for Stevanovic. “Part of why I did this is because of my aunt, Teebie Saunders. She is the head of the Giving Campaign,” he said. “I thought that this would be a way for people to raise money for the schools while having fun doing it.” Co-founder Preston Kwei had a similar motivation. “My parents have always supported the Giving Campaign, so I thought I should help in my own way too,” he added. The Kwei family hosted the socially-distanced judging portion of the competition in their backyard. The all-star panel of judges included chef Omri Aflalo of upcoming Oakland restaurant Town Revival; 4th grader Asher Dolid and his mother, Havens principal Anne Dolid; Beach teacher Claire Stephens; and middle school students Esme Krumins (6th grade), and Grace Rego (8th grade). Creating a cooking competition amid a global pandemic wasn’t easy, explained Rego. “The most challenging part was putting it together in a COVID world,” she said. “We made sure we were keeping safe distances and that the contestants were wearing masks when they dropped off their food.” On the morning of the event students met virtually via Zoom to review the rules, then began Luka Stevanovic (left), Preston Kwei, Esme Krummins, Grace Rego, and Bella Kjellen were the principal organizers of the successful Top Chef Junior event that raised over $1700 for the Giving Campaign. mixing, cooking, and baking in their own kitchens. At 12:30 p.m. they began delivering their creations for the judging. A total of 23 local students from 3rd to 8th grade participated. Krumins said the judging panel enjoyed their job. Reviewing all the entries turned out to be an arduous task. “I really liked tasting all the desserts! All of them were great,” she said. “At the end, we started to get really full. We had 23 things to taste, so I had to take very small bites.” The baking and cooking talent on display during the competition was impressive. Third grader Jane Weisner made pumpkin patch cake pops, painstakingly forming them with chopsticks. “I really like baking,” she said when dropping off her creation for the judges to sample. “The most fun was making the frosting!” Other creations included a cauldron filled with leaves and “Wild Mummy” jalapeño poppers wrapped in puff pastry created by 5th grader Cassidy Carter, and a massive “Apple Jack” cake shaped like a life-sized pumpkin, baked by Sophia and Callie Harris and Emma Sloan. The grand prize-winner was a chocolate cake baked by 3rd grader Elizabeth Payne with intricate fondant decorations. Judge and professional chef Aflalo was particularly impressed by the fondant bats attached to wires that appeared to float above the cake. Tied for second place were 5th grader Bailey Ramillosa (vegan chocolate cupcakes with cookie tombstones), and 3rd grader Ariana Bennett (gluten-free black-bottom pumpkin cupcakes with ghost cream cheese frosting and chocolate spider webs). Honorable mention awards went to 5th grader Lucy Dorsey (pumpkin-spice doughnuts encased in a chocolate shell), and 4th grader Annabelle Allessio (meatloaf zombie head emerging from a pool of tomato sauce “blood” with claws of pizza crust). Stevanovic and Kwei said they were very pleased with the results of their hard work. “We are so proud of our amazing turnout. We can’t wait to do another round,” said Stevanovic. Student judge Asher Dolid hopes to see the Piedmont Top Chef Junior competition become an annual event for the Giving Campaign. “I want people to know that this event is helping the Piedmont schools,” he said. “It’s supporting other people in a way that builds the community.”
articles.title: Students raise $1,725 with Top Chef Jr. Competition

She is the head of the Giving Campaign,” he said. “I thought that this would be a way for people to raise money for the schools while having fun doing it.” Co-founder Preston Kwei had a similar motivation. “My parents have always supported the Giving Campaign, so I thought I should help in my own way too,” he added. The Kwei family hosted the socially-distanced judging portion of the competition in their backyard. The all-star panel of judges included chef Omri Aflalo of upcoming Oakland restaurant Town Revival; 4th grader Asher Dolid and his mother, Havens principal Anne Dolid; Beach teacher Claire Stephens; and middle school students Esme Krumins (6th grade), and Grace Rego (8th grade). Creating a cooking competition amid a global pandemic wasn’t easy, explained Rego. “The most challenging part was putting it together in a COVID world,” she said. “We made sure we were keeping safe distances and that the contestants were wearing masks when they dropped off their food.” On the morning of the event students met virtually via Zoom to review the rules, then began Luka Stevanovic (left), Preston Kwei, Esme Krummins, Grace Rego, and Bella Kjellen were the principal organizers of the successful Top Chef Junior event that raised over $1700 for the Giving Campaign. mixing, cooking, and baking in their own kitchens. At 12:30 p.m. they began delivering their creations for the judging. A total of 23 local students from 3rd to 8th grade participated. Krumins said the judging panel enjoyed their job. Reviewing all the entries turned out to be an arduous task. “I really liked tasting all the desserts! All of them were great,” she said. “At the end, we started to get really full. We had 23 things to taste, so I had to take very small bites.” The baking and cooking talent on display during the competition was impressive. Third grader Jane Weisner made pumpkin patch cake pops, painstakingly forming them with chopsticks. “I really like baking,” she said when dropping off her creation for the judges to sample. “The most fun was making the frosting!” Other creations included a cauldron filled with leaves and “Wild Mummy” jalapeño poppers wrapped in puff pastry created by 5th grader Cassidy Carter, and a massive “Apple Jack” cake shaped like a life-sized pumpkin, baked by Sophia and Callie Harris and Emma Sloan. The grand prize-winner was a chocolate cake baked by 3rd grader Elizabeth Payne with intricate fondant decorations. Judge and professional chef Aflalo was particularly impressed by the fondant bats attached to wires that appeared to float above the cake. Tied for second place were 5th grader Bailey Ramillosa (vegan chocolate cupcakes with cookie tombstones), and 3rd grader Ariana Bennett (gluten-free black-bottom pumpkin cupcakes with ghost cream cheese frosting and chocolate spider webs). Honorable mention awards went to 5th grader Lucy Dorsey (pumpkin-spice doughnuts encased in a chocolate shell), and 4th grader Annabelle Allessio (meatloaf zombie head emerging from a pool of tomato sauce “blood” with claws of pizza crust). Stevanovic and Kwei said they were very pleased with the results of their hard work. “We are so proud of our amazing turnout. We can’t wait to do another round,” said Stevanovic. Student judge Asher Dolid hopes to see the Piedmont Top Chef Junior competition become an annual event for the Giving Campaign. “I want people to know that this event is helping the Piedmont schools,” he said. “It’s supporting other people in a way that builds the community.” Is your child an unwilling mask wearer? Here are some sensory tips and tricks By Kimberly Bonacum If and when school returns masks will be required at all times on school grounds. As a parent, the thought of getting a young child to wear a mask brings up memories of my efforts to keep hats on my children in order to prevent sunburn. Strategies I tried included distracting them, finding hats with ties making it harder to pull off or I let them pick out their favorite team’s hat with its logo. It was a struggle, nevertheless. Similarly, wearing masks and/ or keeping them on for a prolonged period (over two hours) is sure to be challenging for most children. Here are some sensory-based tips and tricks for helping the resistive child. To begin, talk with your child. Be certain that they understand why they must wear a mask. There are many social stories for young children that address mask wearing. Next, acknowledge that wearing a mask is not easy and ask why they do not like wearing a mask. You will be surprised by their ability to pinpoint what is bothersome for them. With that, you can begin to find solutions to make mask wearing more tolerable. The most likely reason that children resist wearing a mask is that there are one or more sensory aspects that are bothersome. Think of a mask as a piece of clothing. We all know that fit and comfort can make or break your wearing a certain garment. How many of you are wearing fitted jeans as you work remotely? Some common reasons for mask avoidance include: • It feels rough or scratchy. • It tickles (too loose) or is too tight. • It smells inside. • It’s too hot and sweaty. • It hurts their ears. • It’s hard to breathe. Once you have a better understanding of which sensations make wearing a mask difficult, you are ready to find a more sensory-friendly mask for your child. First, consider the following. • Material – soft cotton, polyester/spandex • Shape - square or diamond • Strap style design - ear loops, single band with adjustable tug cord After you have settled on a mask that fits your child’s sensory needs, begin building their tolerance to wearing the mask. Have them wear the mask for short periods at home while engaged in fun activities. Gradually increase the time worn daily. As the wearing time lengthens, you may encounter new sensory obstacles such as ear pain, moisture issues or smells. Here are a few tricks for these issues: • Be sensitive to laundry detergent smells. Scent free or scented? • Consider a silicone mask bracket insert to reduce moisture and fogging glasses. • Button headbands for ear loop masks - no more tugging at ears. • Ear savers allow a mask to be attached behind the head instead of around the ears. • Disposable for lightweight choice. • Brush teeth prior to donning a mask. • Suck on a mint or hard candy. • Let your child pick out the mask with their favorite characters or color. Sometimes that is motivation enough. • Provide fidgets to keep hands busy to reduce the urge to touch or remove masks. Armed with these sensory tips and tricks, here’s to a successful transition back to in-person learning for our youngest students while wearing their sensory-friendly masks. Kimberly Bonacum, MS, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist with Piedmont School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, contact mindfulfidgets@gmail.com. articles.text: Children’s Discovery Museum of San Jose Now Open Fri.-Sun. 180 Woz Way, San Jose (408) 298-5437 • www.cdm.org The Children’s Discovery Museum opened its outdoor space at 25 percent capacity. The 1/2 acre Bill’s Backyard will be home for a full day of educational fun in a safe physical environment. Kids can scale the Tree Climber, scurry through the tunnel to the LookOut Tower, and scoop gravel, sand, and dirt in the Dig Pit. At the Dry Creek, large smooth rocks can be stacked, carried, and re-arranged. In the Garden, help prepare soil, plant seeds, water and see plants grow and gain understanding about where food comes from. The Jr. Ranger Station has a new honeycomb viewing exhibit, to watch the tireless work of our bumbling bee friends. The space is constantly sanitized and well marked for proper distancing. The zoo was shut down from March- July and was the last to reopen in the state. Take the kids for a safe day at the zoo with limited capacity and universal mask wearing. Hayward Regional Shoreline consists of 1,841 acres of salt, fresh, and brackish water marshes, seasonal wetlands, and public trails. Activities at the shoreline include hiking, bicycling, jogging, birdwatching, picnicking and fishing. Fishing is allowed from the levees, except in the marsh areas. Picnicking is permitted and benches are located along the trail. Dogs are not allowed south of Winton Avenue to protect nesting and feeding wildlife.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. articles.text: A time of year to remember to shop locally Piedmont Avenue businesses that have struggled to stay in business will soon see relief with all stores being open during the holiday season. Due to the COVID epidemic, there won’t be a Holiday Stroll, or the traditional tree lighting ceremony at Key Route Plaza on Piedmont Avenue & 41st Street. “We are not doing the tree lighting this year,” confirmed retailer Philippa Roberts. “It takes a lot of time and money, neither of which is very abundant these days.” Businesses desperately need a strong holiday season this year. Most have had to be creative to save their businesses. Claudio Luporini, owner of Bella Ceramica and a personal friend of Kris Kringle, said that Santa will have to skip his annual trip to the Avenue due to the coronavirus health restrictions in place. However, Luporini as always, will provide egg nog, hot totties, hot cocoa, bubbly, and cookies for customers. Nathan Walden, owner of Nathan & Co. with locations on Piedmont Ave. and College Ave., has been busy adapting to the times. For Black Friday – the Friday after Thanksgiving – and the following week, if customers say they are friends of Oakland Tech High School or Claremont Middle School, 20 percent of the sale will go to the Teacher’s Association for that school. Nathan and Co. was quick to jump on a new platform called www.KeepOaklandAlive.com. The website has teamed up with the most popular stores in Oakland by offering free two-day delivery. The fabric of the community lies at stake this holiday season, local business have ramped up their online and curbside pickup options to do what they can to keep people engaged and safe. “Rest assured, Piedmont Avenue is open and ready for business,” said longtime Piedmont Ave. volunteer Ronile Lahti. “Our holiday shopping message is Shop Local, Shop Oakland, but Shop Piedmont Avenue first. If we don’t have it, we’ll do our best to find it for you.” – Ronile Lahti Piedmont Ave. volunteer “The whole year has been just a huge challenge. We are concentrating on PR and pushing our website. I have brought back a publicist to help drive traffic to the website to bring in some dollars, but business is still down 50 percent.” Walden has kept his commitments to the community however.
articles.title: Piedmont Avenue shops – Open and ready for holidays
