The season was canceled in March this year. “We have started conditioning three days a week, just getting the girls back in shape. We have about 14 students on average so far, I’m just happy we are getting the girls back on the field,” said Chan. It’s a time where team leaders are identifying themselves. For girls’ LAX, Chan mentioned that members of the 2019 championship squad are in place as leaders. “Our captain this year is Sadie Tschider; Caroline Devine is proving to be a leader as well and very likely will be a team captain. They are doing a wonderful job helping during conditioning and welcoming the new freshmen,” he added. The defending North Coast Section boys’ basketball team us unable to train inside the gym due to COVID-19 protocols but are using the Witter Field track for increased conditioning. Their official practice is set for March, with game scheduled to start in April. “We started conditioning this week,” said boys’ basketball coach Ben Spencer. “We go every Football started its official practices last week. As reported last week, Piedmont High’s football program is not the only sport at the school getting its offseason conditioning programs underway. From 3 pm through 9:30 p.m. athletes of multiple sports can be spotted with conditioning programs. Returning to Witter Field for training last week were the football team, water polo team for dry land conditioning, cross-country teams, volleyball team, boys’ and girls’ lacrosse teams, boys’ basketball and baseball teams, and the girls’ softball team. “This week has been very busy, but everyone is excited. We’ve got a bunch of teams starting this week,” said new athletic director Bradley Smet. “Football started [last week], water polo is working outside of the pool, boys’ basketball, volleyball, softball, and the baseball are starting this week. Just being at school is a terrific change for these student-athletes. You can tell the kids and coaches are ecstatic to see each other,” he said. However, the California Interscholastic Federation, the governing body for high school sports, announced this Monday, November 16 that competition between schools is still not allowed “until new guidance is provided,” meaning the state must still pass through health measures before allowing interscholastic matches. “In today’s COVID-19 press Staff Photos briefing, Governor Newsom and Dr. Mark Ghaly from the California Department of Public Health disclosed that the release of updated youth sports guidance has been postponed. Therefore, the current guidance remains in effect, and CIF competitions are not allowed until new guidance is provided,” wrote the CIF in a media release. Locally, Piedmont’s football team got the action started last week with its return, although in non-contact measures without equipment, which every team is following. “Everyone must remain in their own pods with social distancing and no-contact between each person,” explained coach Jerome Johnson at the team’s first practice. So what does practicing for sports mean without the gear required to play the sport? In short, a whole bunch of running. “We’re getting in shape. We’re running routes, and a lot of sprints. It’s the winter time; it’s important to get our bodies warmed up,” said Johnson. “We are all doing well and excited to be together. We’re a little out of shape, but not too bad, as I’m sure all the students are,” added girls’ lacrosse coach CarlGirls lacrosse, the defending North Coast Section champions, returned to Witter Field for conditioning. Monday and Wednesday from 6:45 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. We don’t have access to the gym; so we’re just working out on the track with lots of running.” Although conditioning continues, Monday’s announcement of Alameda County returning to the Purple Tier in the COVID ranking of restrictions doesn’t bode well for progressing past the no-contact phase in football and eventually playing interscholastic matches in January. The CIF master schedule has football as the first sport to return, with games to begin on January 6. The league football Boys basketball, the defending NCS Champions, has also returned. schedule begins on February 11. Piedmont will have non-league games in January and February with Justin-Siena, Miramonte, Salesian, and Kennedy. Johnson admits that schools and leagues will require some flexibility in regards to rescheduling games. “We haven’t had to reschedule anything yet; so far, so good. There will have to be some flexibility,” explained Johnson. Girls’ and boys’ water polo teams are still in the dark without the Piedmont Community Pool, recently closed due to repair and structural problems. Right now, both teams are doing dry land training. Water polo games are scheduled to start the week of January 20. In the meantime, the players, their families, and coaches are looking to the school district to find a pool for Piedmont for practices and games for the duration of the season. “We’re still working on that. We don’t have a pool. I don’t believe Alameda County is allowing pool work. We have to follow youth sports guidelines and school guidelines from Alameda County,” said Smet. next page.

articles.text: Photos by Ken DeCrosta Ceci Brien highlights the Piedmont High soccer team’s four-year run in the North Coast section semifinals. She is now a freshman at UC Santa Barbara. With the U.S. national soccer teams finishing up recent international friendlies, we take a look at the Piedmont High girls’ soccer program’s four-year postseason run. From 2017 to 2020, they reached the North Coast Section semifinals each year, and, seedd No. 2, they got to the finals in 2018 against No. 1 Branson. The four years are highlighted by Ceci Brien’s role on the team as a starter and team captain, eventually becoming the school’s all-time leading goal scorer. She’s now a freshman at UC Santa Barbara. The 2016-2017 team was led by senior Leah Kochendoerfer, who scored 18 goals with eight assists. Brien was second on the team that year with 13 goals and six assists. She was the starting striker as a freshman. The team finished 14-3-5 that season, and Brien was named Freshman of the Year by the Post. In the NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seed, they lost 2-1 after relinquishing the go-ahead goal in the second period. Piedmont had multiple shots ring off the crossbar. The Highlanders rode that success into the 2017-2018 season, its best year of the batch. They finished 15-2-4 that season and 7-2-1 in league to win the school’s first Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Championship. The Highlanders were the No. 2 seed in the North Coast Section post-seaosn playoffs, and traveled to Ross for the finals with No. 1 Branson. After two overtime periods, the match went to a shootout with gale force winds blowing at their faces. Branson netted just two of five penalty kicks to win it. Laila Adarkar scored Piedmont’s only PK. “It was definitely one of those games were we didn’t go away with any regrets. Branson is a great team; we defended well when we needed to. They were Staff Photo The 2018 PHS girls’ soccer team celebrates after winning the WACC Foothill Championship able to take control in the second half and had some remarkable work from their goalie in the shootout. It was really a great game,” said coach Dan Chubbock after the game in February 2018. As Chubbock iterated, Branson’s goalie Athena Manthouli was lights out in the shootout with three diving saves, shutting down Brien, Ellie Coleman, and Fiona Hunter. Piedmont received eight AllLeague selections that season. Brien scored 24 goals as a sophomore to lead the team, along with six assists. The following year in 2018- 2019, Piedmont went 13-1-6 overall with nine All-Leaguers but failed to repeat with the league title, struggling to a 3-1-4 finish in the Foothill conference. They went into NCS with the No. 4 seed and rolled over No. 13 St. Patrick 6-0, then beat No. 5 Head-Royce 2-0. But playing a strong Cardinal Newman squad the No. 1 seed, they were rtounced 5-1. Brien led the team in scoring that season with 17 goals and 13 assists. Last winter in the 2019-2020 season – notably the last completed prep sports season since COVID-19 – the Highlanders limped to a 6-4-8 record and went winless in league. They qualified for NCS as an underdog, the No. 12 seed, but they rose to the occasion and pllayed th role of spoiler. PHS upset No. 5 Urban 2-1 in the opening round, and followed up with a 1-0 win over another San Francisco school, No. 4 Lick-Wilmerding. In the semis. In the semifinals they faced No. 1 Cardinal Newman again, and lost 5-0. The season marked a debut for several of PHS coach Dan Chubbock’s next crop of athletes, including goalie Morgan Hunt and sttriker Emily Fitzgerald, who enabled Brien to move back into a midfield role as she prepared for UC Santa Barbara. Brien finished the year with 17 goals, finishing with 77 goals in her 4-year career. She goes down as the girls’ program’s All-Time leading scorer, and the school’ overall No. 2 soccer goal scorer behind Nikolai Littleton. Photo by Ken DeCrosta Ashley Nelson, Class of 2020, scored on a bicycle kick in the 2018 NCS Finals. Staff Photo Emily Fitzgerald was the soccer team’s starting striker last year as a freshman.

articles.text: Consistent with public health orders issued by Alameda County that are intended to slow the spread of Covid-19, Piedmont Unified School District’s Witter Field is open for community use during specified hours. Piedmont High School athletics recently resumed on a limited basis, and Witter Field is reserved for these programs each weekday from 3:00 to 9:00 pm. The track and synthetic turf field are open for community use outside these hours and on weekends. Individuals can enter Witter Field from the Wildwood Avenue steps, “PE Hill below the middle school, or the El Cerrito Ave. pedestrian gate. The Windsor Avenue gate, Wildwood Elementary School playground, baseball and softball fields, batting cages, and Witter Field House restrooms remain closed. Individuals must wear face coverings, maintain at least sixfoot social distancing from others who are not part of the same household or living unit, and avoid all social interaction when sick with a fever, cough, or other COVID-19 symptoms. The District previously closed Witter Field due to widespread and persistent lack of compliance with the Alameda County order at the Field. Witter Field is an important community resource and the decision to reopen the facility was made based on supportive public input. The Field will remain open as long as users comply with the public health orders issued by Alameda County. For questions, contact Director of Facilities Pete Palmer at ppalmer@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

A Look Back: PHS girls’ soccer teams of 2017-2020 Four straight NCS semifinals, then in finals in 2018 Photos by Ken DeCrosta Ceci Brien highlights the Piedmont High soccer team’s four-year run in the North Coast section semifinals. She is now a freshman at UC Santa Barbara. By Jonathan Comeaux With the U.S. national soccer teams finishing up recent international friendlies, we take a look at the Piedmont High girls’ soccer program’s four-year postseason run. From 2017 to 2020, they reached the North Coast Section semifinals each year, and, seedd No. 2, they got to the finals in 2018 against No. 1 Branson. The four years are highlighted by Ceci Brien’s role on the team as a starter and team captain, eventually becoming the school’s all-time leading goal scorer. She’s now a freshman at UC Santa Barbara. The 2016-2017 team was led by senior Leah Kochendoerfer, who scored 18 goals with eight assists. Brien was second on the team that year with 13 goals and six assists. She was the starting striker as a freshman. The team finished 14-3-5 that season, and Brien was named Freshman of the Year by the Post. In the NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seed, they lost 2-1 after relinquishing the go-ahead goal in the second period. Piedmont had multiple shots ring off the crossbar. The Highlanders rode that success into the 2017-2018 season, its best year of the batch. They finished 15-2-4 that season and 7-2-1 in league to win the school’s first Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Championship. The Highlanders were the No. 2 seed in the North Coast Section post-seaosn playoffs, and traveled to Ross for the finals with No. 1 Branson. After two overtime periods, the match went to a shootout with gale force winds blowing at their faces. Branson netted just two of five penalty kicks to win it. Laila Adarkar scored Piedmont’s only PK. “It was definitely one of those games were we didn’t go away with any regrets. Branson is a great team; we defended well when we needed to. They were Staff Photo The 2018 PHS girls’ soccer team celebrates after winning the WACC Foothill Championship able to take control in the second half and had some remarkable work from their goalie in the shootout. It was really a great game,” said coach Dan Chubbock after the game in February 2018. As Chubbock iterated, Branson’s goalie Athena Manthouli was lights out in the shootout with three diving saves, shutting down Brien, Ellie Coleman, and Fiona Hunter. Piedmont received eight AllLeague selections that season. Brien scored 24 goals as a sophomore to lead the team, along with six assists. The following year in 2018- 2019, Piedmont went 13-1-6 overall with nine All-Leaguers but failed to repeat with the league title, struggling to a 3-1-4 finish in the Foothill conference. They went into NCS with the No. 4 seed and rolled over No. 13 St. Patrick 6-0, then beat No. 5 Head-Royce 2-0. But playing a strong Cardinal Newman squad the No. 1 seed, they were rtounced 5-1. Brien led the team in scoring that season with 17 goals and 13 assists. Last winter in the 2019-2020 season – notably the last completed prep sports season since COVID-19 – the Highlanders limped to a 6-4-8 record and went winless in league. They qualified for NCS as an underdog, the No. 12 seed, but they rose to the occasion and pllayed th role of spoiler. PHS upset No. 5 Urban 2-1 in the opening round, and followed up with a 1-0 win over another San Francisco school, No. 4 Lick-Wilmerding. In the semis. In the semifinals they faced No. 1 Cardinal Newman again, and lost 5-0. The season marked a debut for several of PHS coach Dan Chubbock’s next crop of athletes, including goalie Morgan Hunt and sttriker Emily Fitzgerald, who enabled Brien to move back into a midfield role as she prepared for UC Santa Barbara. Brien finished the year with 17 goals, finishing with 77 goals in her 4-year career. She goes down as the girls’ program’s All-Time leading scorer, and the school’ overall No. 2 soccer goal scorer behind Nikolai Littleton. articles.text: Cal steamrolled in opener vs. UCLA; Stanford fails by 3 to Colorado Photos courtesy of Mercury News Cal struggled in its short-notice season-opener against UCLA in a 34-10 loss. The University of California Golden Bears finally got their season started, but it didn’t go their way in a devastating 34-10 loss to the UCLA Bruins on Sunday morning, November 15. Stanford, meanwhile, fell short of a fourth quarter comeback in a nail-biting 35-32 loss to Colorado on Saturday. The Bears’ game against UCLA came on short notice after originally scheduling a game with with Arizona State. However, the Sun Devils’ program has had an outbreak of COVID-19, including head coach Herm Edwards, and had to cancel. Cal’s season opener against Washington on November 7 was wiped out due to COVID protocols that ravaged the Bears’ defensive line. On Friday, the Pac 12 announced that California agreed to play UCLA on 9 a.m. on Sunday after the Bruins’ game against Utah was canceled after a Utes’ virus outbreak as well. Are you following this so far? This is the new normal. Cal’s lack of training showed, notably on the lack of tackling by the defense. The Golden Bears missed a plethora of tackles in Sunday’s game, many of which led to first downs and big breaks. The offense, meanwhile, showed the same inconsistencies which plagued them in previous years. Quarterback Chase Garbers was everywhere with the ball, going 18 of 33 for 122 yards and an interception. His offensive line didn’t do Cal any favors, allowing five sacks and nine tackles for loss. “We haven’t played a football game in about a year. We haven’t played anyone but ourselves in a real, live game scenario, live tempo, tackling, everything, in about a year. So there are obviously going to be some hurdles there,” Garbers said, via the Associated Press. “On both sides of the ball, we didn’t play to what we expected to and first game in a COVID season, some of those hurdles are expected.” Cal looks ahead to Oregon State this Saturday, November 21. Oregon State is 0-2 after losing 38-28 to Washington State in Week 1 and nearly pulling off an upset in a loss to Washington, 27-21. The Beavers just held the Huskies to 141 passing yards, and given Cal’s struggles against the Bruins, it’s conceivable that the Bears will try to get the running game going early with Christopher Brown. Stanford Stanford fell short of a comeback victory after trailing the Buffs 35-16 in the fourth quarter. Quarterback Davis Mills was a standout in his first appearance this season, going 31 of 56 for 327 yards with one passing and rushing touchdown. The Cardinal forced three punts in the final quarter, scoring their final touchdown with 2:34 remaining but retaining the ball for the last possession with just 10 seconds on the clock. Stanford plays Washington State this weekend, and it could be an offensive battle given that the Cougars are allowing 516 yards per game but are averaging 430 offensive yards. Mills is liekly to be the focus again, especially when factoring in the struggles of the Cardinal running game, which is averaging only 3.3 yards per carry. Look for Mills and the passing attack to open early, then begin to mix the attack with runs. It will be an interesting game to watch for both Cal and stanforrd, which wil meet one another in the histroic Big Game on Friday, November 27, the day afer Thanksgiving. articles.text: 6-2 win over Panama; 0-0 draw with Wales Join the bandwagon now before 2022 and the inevitable U.S. soccer craze in 2026. The United State Men’s National Team is putting its roster together for the 2022 World Cup, and doing so with a collective average age of 21 in the two recent friendlies with Wales on Thursday, November 12, and Panama on Monday, November 16. They drew 0-0 with the Welsh and dominated 6-2 over the Panamanians. Impressively, Nov. 12 was the team’s first match since February. The team had a roster with 22 of the 23 players from foreign clubs. Prior to the match, manager Gregg Berhalter said he’s hoping to show fans signs of hope for the future. It’s fair to say he’s doing just that. To put into context, Berhalter featured players who –theoretically – could appear on the men’s team for the next 10 years. The squad showed a swagger that is unalike the U.S. men’s program. They featured overlapping runs, balls over the top from the back, and symmetry one wouldn’t expect from a team that, largely, was playing together for the very first time. When realizing that they’ve had limited training together due to COVID-19, their two friendlies were that more impressive. Although the boys conceded a goal against Panama in the eighth minute, they resoundingly responded with the equalizer by 18-year old Gio Reyna after the young star from Dortmund smashed in a free kick from a yard above the penalty area. It was Reyna’s first USMNT goal and second appearance for Photo courtesy of The Guardian The United States Men’s National team dominated Panama 6-2 on November 16, playing in Austria. 18-year old Gio Reyna (right) scored once, and Nicholas Gioacchini (left) scored twice. Photo courtesy of NBC Sports 19-year old Sergino Dest was instrumental in the U.S. attack, moving the ball with superior technical ability. the team. He’s starting in the 10-role, Central Attacking Midfield, and schematically rotated to both sides of the pitch at times. Soon after, 20-year old Nicholas Gioacchini rebounded home his first goal for the U.S. team in the 18th after Uly Llanez, 19-years old, shot a hard ball on net that skipped off the keeper and conveniently to Gioacchini’s feet. Photo courtesy of MLS.com 17-year old Yunus Musah became the first U.S. Men’s National Team player under age 18 to start two matches. Four minutes later, Giocchini scored again, heading in perhaps the most beautifully worked USMNT goal in recent years. It started with a Tyler Adams (21- years old), sending a ball in to Weston McKennie, who lobbed a pass off the touchline to center back Matt Miazga, heading a pass to Giochinni for the goal. But Panama drew closer at 3-2 when Jose Fajardo scored his second in the 79th, but USMNT responded with quickness once again. A pair of 20-year olds from clubs in the Netherlands, Sebastian Soto headed home a perfect cross from Richie Ledezma—both were making their first U.S. appearances, for a 4-2 lead in the 83rd. Sebastian Lletget, the only MLS player on the roster, scored the fifth with another nice header on a pass fullback Reggie Cannon in 87th. Ledezma got his second assist on a long cross to Soto in the 91st. Scorelsss vs. Wales As for their 0-0 draw with the Welsh, it was somewhat a victory for U.S. fans and pundits from the standpoint of sheer potential . Sergino Dest was dynamic. The 19-year old Barcelona rising star danced on the ball with the grace one would expect from a Barca fullback. Meanwhile, 17-year old Yunus Musah of Velencia became the first player under 18-years old to start in two U.S. matches. Of the current 23-man roster, Tim Ream is the oldest at 33, and starting centerback John Brooks is next oldest at 27. The roster currently includes six players still in their teens The United States has no matches scheduled for the remainder of the year. The next International break for European clubs is for March 27, which coincides with CONCACAF’s World Cup qualifying matches.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 18, 2020 15 HIKING WITH JON The Post’s 10 best hikes and trails By Jonathan Comeaux Since 2017, we’ve developed the only weekly newspaper-published outdoors series for Bay Area and California hiking trails, which responsibly guides readers to new areas for them to consider. We’ve taken you to over boulders up mountain peaks, all the way down to sandy shores and low marshlands. Here is a list of our 10 favorite trails: 1. Five Lakes Trail, Tahoe National Forest Five Lakes Trail in the Tahoe National Forest is rated as one of the best hikes in California with its collection of pristine alpine lakes. It is a short five-mile outand-back hike, but at 7,560 feet of max elevation, the 1,100 foot ascent to the top can be difficult for some. This trail gets our top spot due to the picturesque views of KT-22 and Squaw Mountain peaks on the right, and pine-treed strewed mountains of Scott Peak and a mosaic of jagged rock cliff faces toward Ward Peak on your left. 2. Cataract Falls Trail, Mt. Tamalpais On the north end of Mt. Tamalpais is one of its most popular trails, Cataract Falls Trail. Although only less than fourmiles, you’ll gain over 1,000 feet in elevation over steep steps and tree roots. But your prize is the views along Cataract Creek with Staff Photos 1. Five Lakes Trail in the Tahoe National Forest gets our top vote for its unique group of five alpine mountain-top lakes. 2. Cataract Falls is at the end of a picturesque trail on Mt. Tamalpais with cascades along Cataract Creek. 3. Alamere Falls at Point Reyes is a local favorite, but current fire restrictions have altered the starting point. 4. The Marin Headlands is a treasure trove for history buffs, with World War II bunkers strewn about the hillsides. its cascades of waterfalls lining your entire walk. 3. Alamere Falls, Pt. Reyes National Seashore Alamere Falls is perhaps the most popular trail along the Pt. Reyes National Seashore for its rare 40-foot tall tidefall, a waterfall which flows directly out into the ocean. However the trail now has a new starting point due to COVID-19 and Woodward fire restrictions. Instead of the usual Palomarin Trailhead, hikers are required to park at the Olema Valley trailhead. You then hike to the falls over six miles, making a long 12-mile day with over 2,500 feet in elevation gain. 4. Marin Headlands, Marin County Just north of San Francisco is one of my favorite local treasures – the Marin Headlands and its collection of military bunkers which date to before World War II. Here, you can bunker hop up the headlands all the way to the peak of Hill 88, a former radar and landing zone. 5. Wildcat Peak, Tilden Park Perhaps the most underrated view in the entire Bay Area, Tilden Park’s Wildcat Peak provides a sweeping view of Oakland, San Francisco, and the Carquinez Straight through Contra Costa County. 6. Purisima Creek, Midpeninsula Regional Open Space Purisima Creek in the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space Preserve has views of the rolling hills of San Mateo County where you’ll walk beneath groves of redwood trees on the way down to Purisima Creek—which has remnants of the Bay Area’s old logging industry. 7. Burma Road Trail, Mt. Diablo The Burma Road Trail on Mt. Diablo is a grueling six-mile hike with over 2,000 feet in elevation gain, with stretches of steep gradients. At the top are views of the Bay Area and Mt. Diablo. You’ll also pass a small pond of koi fish with an inscription: “Burma Springs, 1968.” 8. Donner Pass, Donner Lake A definite hidden treasure of California, the Donner Pass Trail is an abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867. Perhaps the most unique of all these, the trek takes you through carved out tunnels and snow sheds through the granit mountains above Donner Lake. Locals call the area a unique gem in the winter. as the sheds enable hikers to take in the mystical sight of the snow covered mountains. 9. Sibley Regional, Oakland Hills A local favorite, Sibley Regional in the springtime is a sight to see with its fields of California poppies. Although the stone labyrinths within the park are its claim to fame, nothing beats Sibley’s wildflowers in the spring. 10. Garden of Eden, Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park This is not a trail, per se. The Garden of Eden is a swimming hole in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park in the Santa Cruz mountains. With a trail alongside the San Lorenzo River, you can hike for miles. 5. Wildcat Peak in Tilden Park is our top trail for the East Bay given its commanding view of the Bay Area. 6. Purisima Creek is a haven for redwood tree lovers. 7. Mt. Diablo’s Burma Road Trail is a challenging hike, but has a unique pond filled with koi fish. Inscribed on the concrete is “Burma Springs, 1968.” 8. Donner Pass is a trail alongside Donner Lake, created from the former Union Pacific railway that was created in 1867. You can venture through snow sheds and hollowed out mountain tunnels. 9. Sibley Regional is our top Oakland park for its geological history and rolling hills of poppies during springtime. 10. Garden of Eden is a swimming hole in the Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park in the Santa Cruz mountains.

articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Gardens, located in Walnut Creek, will be dressed up in festive lights for the holiday season. “Garden of d’Lights” at the Ruth Bancroft Gardens is a safe outdoor holiday lights experience that is suitable for all ages. Thousands of lights and lasers transform the Garden’s cacti, succulents and trees into magical, multicolored botanical sculptures, unlike anything else in the East Bay. The event will be open Friday through Sunday nights for one month, from this Friday, November 20 through December 20. Due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic, there will be limited capacity this year, and advanced tickets are required. There are three admission times each night, at 5:30, 6:30 and 7:30 p.m. Masks are required at Garden of d’Lights at the Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek. all times for guests aged 3 and older. Tickets are $20 for adults, and $10 for children age 6 through 16. Children under 5 can visit for free. Ruth Bancroft Garden members receive 20 percent discounts on tickets. To obtain tickets, visit https:// sf.funcheap.com/garden-dlightssafe-outdoor-holiday-lights-ruthbancroft-garden-nov-20-dec-20/.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Brian Copeland’s The Jewelry Box online from November 28 through December 25. The comedy is a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show, Not a Genuine Black Man, and follows young protagonist Brian as he heads to the “mean streets” of Oakland to buy his mom a Christmas present. When he finds the perfect gift – a jewelry box in the White Front store – six-year-old Brian sets out to earn the required $11.97 by Christmas Eve. The play follows Brian’s adventures as he scours the “help wanted” ads, applies for jobs, and collects bottles, inching his way toward the perfect Christmas gift. Copeland debuted his first one-man play, Not a Genuine Black Man at The Marsh in San Francisco. The play explored his childhood experiences as a member of one of the only African American families living in San Leandro, then a predominately white suburb. Not a Genuine Black Man went on to become the longest-running solo show Bay Area actor and comedian Brian Copeland. in San Francisco theatrical history with over 800 performances. The show has been performed in over 30 cities, including a critically acclaimed run Off-Broadway in New York City. The play is currently in television series development. To watch The Jewelry Box, visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sf ph /2020-2021-season / the-jewelry-box/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents The Jewelry Box Nov. 28–Dec. 25

articles.text: World-renowned mezzo-soprano Susan Graham leads the cast of Opera San Jose’s first fully-staged digital production, Three Decembers. The chamber opera is by Bay Area opera composer Jake Heggie, with libretto by Gene Scheer. It is based on playwright Terrence McNally’s unpublished play, “Some Christmas Letters.” Music will be conducted by Resident Conductor Christopher James Ray, and Directed by Resident Director Tara Branham. The opera was first presented under the working title “Last Acts” at the world premiere by the Houston Grand Opera. A chamber orchestra of 10 instruments included two pianos played by Heggie and Patrick Summers. 1996, and 2006. The opera follows the story of a famous actress, Madeline Mitchell, in a role that will be sung by Graham. The two adult children, Beatrice and Charlie, are portrayed by Opera San Jose Resident Artists Maya Kherani and Efrain Solis. Graham makes her company debut, reuniting with composer Heggie, who created the role of Sister Helen in Dead Man Walking specifically for Graham. Three Decembers will begin streaming on December 3 at 10 a.m., and will feature a virtual post-show conversation with Graham, Heggie, and the full artistic team. To see the opera, click on https://operasj.secure.force.com/ ticket/#/instances/a0Ff400000 Mezzo soprano Susan Graham makes her debut with Opera San Jose on December 3. articles.text: SF Jazz, the Jazz music venue located in the Hayes Valley neighborhood of San Francisco, has been offering an online concert series every Friday during shelter-in-place restrictions. Entitled Fridays at Five, the concert series features weekly pre-recorded concerts that aspire to connect audience members directly with musicians. This Friday, November 20, will feature the Anat Cohen Tentet from Israel. At the leading edge of a wave of brilliant Israeli improvisers who have energized the New York jazz scene over the past twenty years, Cohen is one of the most acclaimed clarinetists of her generation, as well as a commanding tenor saxophonist. The ensemble includes some of the most up-and-coming young musicians in New York, including Maria Schneider Orchestra trumpeter Nadje Noordhuis, Brazilian pianist and accordionist Vitor Gonçalves, vibraphonist James Shipp, and guitarist Sheryl Bailey. Another member, music director/arranger Oded Lev-Ari, is a protégé of the legendary trombonist and arranger Bob Jazz clarinetist Anat Cohen brings her tentet to SF Jazz on Friday, November 20. Brookmeyer. The Tentet’s songbook is ripe with Cohen’s love of Brazilian music. The concert was originally filmed on December 3, 2017 and was the West Coast debut of her recent Tentet project. To watch this weekend’s episode of Fridays at Five, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ fridaysatfive/. Maestro Michael Morgan introduced the archival performance and said that Dvorak’s setting of the Stabat Mater is a masterpiece dating from 1876 and 1877. articles.text: French composer Camille Saiant-Saens. There are many famous pieces of music which everyone knows. But not everyone knows from whence they came. Here are some of the stories that nobody knows due to ghost writers behind the fame. Everybody knows Carnival of the Animals by French composer Saint-Saens. It is his most famous piece. But it is not original. As you will see, excepting for Einstein’s famous theory, nothing comes out of the blue. Carnival was so popular that Saint-Saens forbade publication except for “The Swan“. But his idea for Carnival was not exactly original. Nine years before he wrote it, a friend named Hubert Leonard composed “Five Humerus Pieces”. History and the public has long forgotten Leonard’s work. But Saint-Saens reaped fame and fortune. Niccolo Paganini is considered the most famous violinist of all time. His fourth violin Concerto wowed Paris in the 1830s. It is a dramatic showpiece displaying incredible virtuosity. But its opening salvo is entirely derived from a student concerto by Vivaldi. The important German-American conductor and educator Walter Damrosch wrote a popular song entitled “Danny Deaver”. The song gives every hint of genius. But there has never been a mention that Damrosch drew as his inspiration a funeral march from a Beethoven piano Sonata. One of the greatest violin sonatas was written by the Belgian composer Caesar Franck. But cellists insist that Franck conceived the work as a cello piece. This, may I say, is absolutely incorrect. Franck wrote his great sonata as a wedding present for violinist Eugene Ysaye in 1886. But the impetus for his monumental work actually derives from a sonata by a friend of Franck, the Hungarian violinist Hubay. He wrote his sonata in 1871, a full 15 years before Franck wrote his sonata. Sometimes fate goes the other way. Sometimes composers write music which is assumed to be folk music. Dvorak’s New World Symphony acquired folk music status when it became the popular song, “Goin’ home.” The great American songwriter Stephen Foster contributed a host of songs which suffered the same fate. History can often be selective. How often does the public celebrate the works of composers like Saint-Saens, Paganini, Beethoven, and Franck? Lost in the shuffle is their inspiration. So when you listen to Carnival of the Animals, or Paganini’s 4th Violin Concerto, or the Franck Sonata, please give a thought to those “other composers” who received no credit - the ghost writers. A holiday recipe The case of the vanishing duck Duck is a festive dish, especially when the weather turns cold. The one I made was special, and it vanished before I could take its picture. Preparation is easy, despite numerous ingredients. Preheat the oven to 450°. Take a large skillet and put some oil in it; brown the duck lightly. Be sure to prick the skin in a few places. Place the duck in a covered roasting pan, add salt and pepper, and squeeze three or four tangerines over the duck. Add the rind along with two minced trumpet mushrooms, one onion and two cloves of garlic. Around the duck scatter some of your favorite dried fruit. I use cranberries and apricots, but you can add any fruit you want including a fresh apple or guava. To keep the duck moist, pour at least 3 tablespoons of wine vinegar over the duck. This is a very important ingredient Finally, top the duck with a generous amount of fresh rosemary. Cover and roast for an hour and a half, then remove it from the oven, carve it and serve with wild rice and a bitter vegetable like brussels sprouts or broccoli. Skimming the fat is optional. For dessert, serve an Italian Panettone. The last time I made this, it was so popular it vanished before I could photograph it.

articles.text: The California Society of Printmakers’ 106th Exhibition will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from November 15 to December 5. As part of the wide range of art offered at the Center throughout the year, the Society of Printmakers exhibition is an annual show. It highlights a variety of printmaking techniques and the ways its member artists use many techniques to create unique and meaningful works of art. The Society’s mission is to support the integrity of traditional printmaking while providing a community for artists exploring new directions in contemporary print methods. To that end, the Society organizes exhibitions, artist talks, demonstrations, lectures, residencies, and produces a journal publication. Gallery viewing will be by reservation this year, within a safe and socially distanced setting. Gallery dates are Saturday and Sunday, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. on November 21-22, 28-29, and from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Saturday, December: 5. Timed entry will be in 45-minute time periods. With a maximum of 10 visitors per period. Masks are required. Check back here soon for a link to make your reservation.

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. The exhibition Awaken: A Tibetan Buddhist Journey Toward Enlightenment, will be ending at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco on November 30. The exhibition features more than 100 Himalayan Buddhist paintings, sculptures, and textiles designed to bring about enlightenment, or awakening. Awaken: A Tibetan Buddhist Journey Toward Enlightenment brings together Buddhist artworks from the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts and the Asian Art Museum, home of two of the country’s most significant collections of Himalayan art. Sculptures, paintings, textiles and book arts made between 800 A.D. and 2016 will be on display. The SF Asian Art Museum is following the San Francisco Health Department’s strict guidelines to ensure all visitors feel safe and comfortable in a clean environment. Because the museum is open at 25 percent capacity only, obtaining tickets in advance is strongly encouraged. The museum is offering timed ticketing only. Face coverings are required, and visitors are asked to observe directional signage. The Asian Art Museum is offering free admission to essential workers, and San Francisco public school students, children 12 and under, and active duty military personnel. To reserve tickets, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/awaken-a-tibetan-buddhist-journey-toward-enlightenment/.
articles.title: Last chance to see Awaken exhibition at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) announced yesterday, November 17, that it needs to postpone its recently announced plans to reopen due to a surge in COVID cases in Alameda County. The museum announced last week that it was preparing to reopen to the public on Friday, November 27, with three free community access days over that weekend through Sunday, November 29. Gov. Gavin Newsom issued a statement on Tuesday indicating that several California counties, including Alameda County, have moved to the most restrictive “purple” tier. These restrictions explicitly exclude the opening of indoor museums, and OMCA will no longer move forward with its scheduled plans. Oakland Museum has remained closed to the public for eight months following the impacts of the ongoing health pandemic.
articles.title: Oakland Museum told to delay reopening due to spike in COVID cases

articles.text: Richard Gere and Hilary Swank in Amelia. Movie review by Chris Honoré Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific Ocean on July 2, 1937. She was attempting to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, something that had never been done before. Her success depended not only on her flying skills but on the ability of Fred Noonan, her navigator. On the Pacific leg of the flight, he would have to find a mere speck of land, Howland Island, in a body of water so vast that there would be no second chance. Told that it was dangerous, perhaps reckless in the extreme – there was a good Hilary Swank as Amelia Earhart in Amelia. chance she would run out of fuel – Earhart was committed to trying. She left Miami on June 1 and began what would be her final journey. Earhart was driven to fly, consumed with an unrelenting passion to be in the air, no matter the craft no matter the challenge. She broke records, flew solo across the Atlantic in a gorgeous, red Lockeed Vega 58, landing to her delight and surprise in Ireland. Her passion for flight was unequivocal. What the film is unable to do is capture that bright, burning need to be aloft. Had the movie focused on flight, her desire since childhood to pilot airplanes, and explored the serenity she found aloft with the discomfort she found on land, then this would have been an examination of her as a person and not just a quickly glimpse into the life of this highly commercialized heroine. Hillary Swank, portraying Earhart, is a dead ringer for the fresh-faced, tossle-hair, androgynous flier. But for reasons known only to the screenwriters, Swank, an accomplished Oscar-winning actress, is never asked to stretch in the role. Earhart was controversial, she was self-absorbed, single-minded and independent in a time when women were more typically seen and not heard. In the years leading up to World War II, most women were still home. articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Cat Returns Movie review by Chris Honoré The Cat Returns, directed by Hiroyuki Murita (his only feature for Studio Ghibli), is based on a manga story written by Aoi Hiragi. The narrative has at its center Haru (Anne Hathaway), a shy, insecure Tokyo schoolgirl who has a repressed affinity for cats (she can talk to them). One day, when she is out and about, she saves a cat from being run over by a truck. As it turns out, the cat, called Lune (Andrew Bevis), is the son of the Cat King (Tim Curry). Wanting to reward Haru’s heroism, the King insists that she come to the Cat Kingdom and there he creates a plan to have Haru marry Lune. But in order for this to take place, Haru must begin her transformation into a cat. Soon Haru grows ears, whiskers and a tail. Distressed by what is happening, she realizes that she must escape the Cat Kingdom before it is too late for her to be able to return to her human world. It’s at this point in the story that the story drops down an Alice in Wonderland rabbit hole and becomes a mix of characters and silly plans focused on Haru finding a portal that will return her to her previous life. She hears a soft feminine voice telling her to find a chunky cat named Muta (Peter Boyle). Muta leads her to the Baron (Gary Elwes), a statuette brought to life with the help of Toto (Elliot Gould), a stone raven. And so on. They plan and connive to rescue Haru, all while trying to avoid the King. When Lune discovers Haru’s wish to escape, he reveals he wants to marry another, Yuki (Judy Greer), a servant working in the kingdom. I would judge that The Cat Returns is best suited for young viewers. Unlike the work produced by Studio Ghibli, its story is slight, definitely cartoony, and just hectic fun. However, the quality of the animation, as always, is superb with a strong color palette with a cast of characters that will engage. The Cat Returns (2002). Directed by Hiroyuki Murita. Animé by Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Anne Hathaway, Gary Elwes, Peter Boyle and Elliot Gould. 1 hr., 15 min. Rated G.

Movie review by Chris Honoré Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific Ocean on July 2, 1937. She was attempting to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, something that had never been done before. Her success depended not only on her flying skills but on the ability of Fred Noonan, her navigator. On the Pacific leg of the flight, he would have to find a mere speck of land, Howland Island, in a body of water so vast that there would be no second chance. Told that it was dangerous, perhaps reckless in the extreme – there was a good Hilary Swank as Amelia Earhart in Amelia. chance she would run out of fuel – Earhart was committed to trying. She left Miami on June 1 and began what would be her final journey. Earhart was driven to fly, consumed with an unrelenting passion to be in the air, no matter the craft no matter the challenge. She broke records, flew solo across the Atlantic in a gorgeous, red Lockeed Vega 58, landing to her delight and surprise in Ireland. Her passion for flight was unequivocal. What the film is unable to do is capture that bright, burning need to be aloft. Had the movie focused on flight, her desire since childhood to pilot airplanes, and explored the serenity she found aloft with the discomfort she found on land, then this would have been an examination of her as a person and not just a quickly glimpse into the life of this highly commercialized heroine. Hillary Swank, portraying Earhart, is a dead ringer for the fresh-faced, tossle-hair, androgynous flier. But for reasons known only to the screenwriters, Swank, an accomplished Oscar-winning actress, is never asked to stretch in the role. Earhart was controversial, she was self-absorbed, single-minded and independent in a time when women were more typically seen and not heard. In the years leading up to World War II, most women were still home. The war changed everything and women in pants and leather jackets, building airplanes and then flying them, become far more common. articles.text: Front-runners in the 2017 Piedmont Turkey Trot bolt from the starting line on Thanksgiving morning in the 16th annual event. The Smegal family won the award for the most family trotters in 2017. Pictured are (front) Leann Foster (left) Lucy the Dog, Cory Smegal; (middle) Kelly Moyer, Allison Moyer, Tommy Smegal; (top) family patriarch Tom Smegal, son Tom Smegal, Anna Smegal, Allison Foster, Katie Foster, Marlene Schneider, Jack Texeira, Ryan Moyer and Tom Moyer. horns, the precursor of French horns. Kay Ling, a new member of the Piedmont Turkey Trot board that year, hailed the Trot as one of Piedmont’s greatest annual events. “Students, residents, and city officials volunteer their time to bring this charming small-town event every year,” she observed. “Where else can you see family members of all ages and pups alike trotting all together?” The 16th annual Trot brought participants from all over the Bay Area. That year’s winner was 18-year-old Nicholas Kleibar of Oakland, with an impressive time of 15:54. The overall female winner was Carolyn Jaeger of San Francisco, who ran the course in 18:39. For most participants, though, the trot is a social event – a time to sip coffee and cocoa with your neighbors, courtesy of Highland Partners. Racers also enjoyed bananas, Clif bars, yogurt, and other snacks provided by sponsors. For several years, the Smegal family easily captured the coveted award for Most Participants by a Family. That year was no exception, as family patriarch Tom Smegal gathered 16 family members and animals to help burnish his reputation as a person who has competed in every Trot since its inception. Mission Gold jazz band returned that year to play Dixieland music starting at 8 a.m. in front of the Exedra. The 2017 Turkey Trot continued to enjoy great support from many community sponsors, including Piedmont Grocery, Transports, Piedmont Post, McCutcheon Construction, MB Jessee, Village Market, Highland Partners, Dr. Gregory Young and Dr. Frank Helm, J. Miller Flowers and Ocho Candy. Next: Last year’s Trot had 2,200 runners, despite cold temperatures at 42 degrees. articles.text: Kids gather by one of 49 Turkey Trot signs placed throughout the city for a virtual scavenger hunt. Given local health directives, the Piedmont Turkey Trot will not be held live this year. However, The Trot is putting its best shank forward, and will carry on the spirit of the Piedmont Turkey Trot – virtually. The Piedmont Turkey Trot Challenge will be a virtual scavenger hunt and/or run. Register online at piedmontturkeytrot.com and then run or walk the streets of Piedmont to find the PTT Sponsored Lawn signs in various gardens or businesses around town. Snap a selfie with the sign, upload to our Instagram account #piedmontturkeytrot and be entered into a drawing for prizes. Each Instagram posting from a registered participant is an entry into the drawing. Find all 49 sponsored signs and increase your chances to win. Prizes include gift certificates from Piedmont Grocery, Transports, Piedmont Post and more. Or win a free registration to next year’s Trot. If you are looking to move your feet a little faster, participants may also upload their 5K time for bragging rights at their (smaller, yet mighty) Thanksgiving table. Prizes will be awarded to the top finisher (male/female) in each age category. Lawn signs will be up through November 28, the Saturday after Thanksgiving. Registration is $10. articles.text: The Piedmont Turkey Trot is designed for residents to unleash a preemptive strike on Thanksgiving Day calories. The event draws everyone from avid runners to leisurely joggers, and by its 16th year, the event grew into the second largest public event in Piedmont – second only to the 4th of July Parade. In 2017, a total of 2,800 runners and joggers filled the streets for the event, an early morning 5-kilometer run on Piedmont streets. It marked the largest turnout in the history of the race, abetted by mild, clear weather that year. The trot began in the middle of town outside the police station and continued along Highland Avenue, Wildwood Avenue and La Salle Avenue, before looping back along Sea View and Mountain Avenues. Participants finished at the intersection of Highland Avenue and Magnolia Avenue, a few feet from where they began. Winners in each age division received a pumpkin pie from Piedmont Grocery, a cap, flowers from J. Miller Flowers and a gift certificate from Transports. Many trotters wore turkey-themed hats, autumnal floral garlands, or full turkey body suits. A particularly popular trend that year was pumpkin pie hats. observing more “green” practices and encouraged racers to bring reusable water bottles and carpool or bike to the event. Another new addition that year was the offer of two symphony musicians, both French horn players, who played a fanfare at the start of the race – but on authentic hunting Avenue.

articles.text: On a chilly Friday morning, October 30th, about 20 dogs of all sizes and furs celebrated Halloween by dressing up in costumes and trick-or-treating under the redwoods in Dracena Park. Heidi Kistler, owner of Positively Pampered Pets invited her Piedmont clients to join her on a wild romp as costumed dogs celebrated Howl-O-Ween, while nearby small children giggled as they watched from the play structure. It was the first year the dogs had their costume party away from Bushy Dell Creek, the traditional meeting and sniffing Hazel the Golden Retriever wore a lovely Snow White ensemble, and the small but mighty 15-pound Agnes, a black pug, was transformed into a healthy Pug Taco. Woody from Toy Story was there, as well as a ladybug, an ostrich and a sizeable muscle man hound that appeared determined to sniff all canines and humans. Many girl dogs wore beautiful gowns imitating the Disney Princesses, while the boy dogs seemed to favor various Premier League soccer stars. Amazingly, nary a dog growl was heard. Even without handing out treats, a good time was had by all. The dogs were not required to observe social distancing, but the owners did their best. All owners wore masks, but they weren’t anywhere near as funny as their four-legged friends. Dogs and owners gather at Dracena park on Halloween eve, Friday, October 30. articles.text: Walking through town it is impossible not to notice the aesthetic impact of different ancillary structures that are an integral part of the design of many homes. Falling somewhere between architecture and landscape architecture, fences, walls, and their associated gates are chief among these. They can enhance (or unfortunately sometimes compromise) the building, landscape and/or site design. So…what constitutes nice retaining walls, appealing fences or beautiful gates? Like all of the discussions in this column, I point out different ideas or considerations that hopefully help to answer this ongoing question. But there are usually many good answers as well as exceptions to every general rule. What is ultimately important is just what looks and feels right – what appeals to us. That being said, here are some thoughts. The first thing that comes to mind is that these secondary structures need as much study and consideration as the main building(s) or landscape treatment of which they are a part. It is unfortunately obvious when they are designed as simply an afterthought. Fences, walls and gates certainly must be in the same architectural “family” as the home, though this doesn’t mean they have to be exactly the same form, color or even the same material. They do need to relate most appropriately. They are indeed an opportunity to aesthetically deviate to some degree and add interest to both the building(s) and property. Fences or walls can be used to provide privacy, add security, or merely to demarcate the edge of private or semi-private spaces between adjacent properties, or between a property and the street. After adherence to the architectural style of the buildings, the intended use or function of the barrier will be the primary consideration in determining its type, shape and character, i.e., solid (wall) vs, airy (spaced boards), height, extent, and access or gate placements. Gates are, of course, a promPhotos and sketch by Will Adams Photos above and below: Two well designed variations of the traditional white picket fence, both stepping to nicely accommodate the slope of the sidewalk and site, as well as adding interest and texture to the street.

articles.text: SUNROOM BEDROOM WIC LIVING ROOM KITCHEN BATH DINING LAUNDRY GARAGE GARAGE WIC BEDROOM BEDROOM FOYER BEDROOM PORCH Many older adults prefer living in their homes as long as possible in order to maintain their daily lifestyle in a familiar environment. However, aging typically brings challenges with it, including reduced vision and hearing, decreased mobility, and the increased risk of falls. Here are some practical and easy design solutions to consider to make your home safer and easier to live in as you age. Foyers Install an outdoor motion light sensor to ensure good visibility when unlocking your door and trying to find the light switch in the foyer. When it comes to door handles, lever type handles are easier to grip and operate than door knobs. Make sure your entry foyer is free of obstructions and well-lit as well. Living Rooms Finishes and layout of living areas have a big impact on a person’s ability to move around safely and be independent. Make sure you have a clear path with no clutter when moving from one room to another. Transitions between different floor finishes should be smooth to prevent falls. If you have area rugs, make sure to install non-slip pads or double-sided carpet tape to reduce the risk of tripping. Short pile carpets are safer than large loop carpets as they help increase mobility. Kitchens Kitchens are typically one of the busiest rooms in our homes. Drawers and pull out base cabinets are much easier to use than cabinet doors and fixed shelves. If you do not have the budget to replace existing cabinet doors you can simply add roll out trays or a lazy susan inside the cabinets. Another easy retrofit is to replace cabinet door knobs with curved edge handles that have enough surface area for an easy grasp. Be careful not to choose handles with sharp edges that can snag clothes or be painful to bump into. Also, lever style faucets are much easier to operate than faucets with turn handles. Bathrooms Most falls happen in the bathroom, so special attention should be paid to safety in your bathrooms. Nightlights are extremely helpful to locate a bathroom easily in the middle of the night. Grab bars are life savers in many situations. Common areas for grab bars are inside your showers or tubs and adjacent to the toilet for ease of mobility and safety. Towel bars may not support your weight, so they are not safe to rely on as a grab bar. Consider adding textured strips on the bottom of your tub or shower to prevent slips and falls while bathing. Similarly, secure your bath mats with nonslip pads or choose non-slip mats. Bedrooms As we age, our eyes lose the ability to differentiate between shades of colors. Use light switch covers that contrast with wall colors so they are easy to see. Choose solid colored low pile carpet for your bedrooms in lieu of patterned carpet that may be confusing and distracting as aging brings declining vision. Laundry areas Raising your washer and dryer off the floor makes it easier to load and unload without bending for long periods. General It is essential to have a welllit house with a consistent level of ambient lighting. Make sure stairways are well-lit and have handrails at least on one side. Replacing toggle style light switches with lever style switches will make the operation easier and faster. These simple upgrades will increase your quality of life and help you enjoy your home for many years to come. Yildiz Duransoy is Project Manager at BDE Architecture in San Francisco and is a member of the Piedmont Planning Commission. For information, contact yduransoy@gmail.com.
articles.title: Living longer – and safer – in your home

articles.text: Roland Marzolf (left) and brother Wayne, founders of Drawbridge Cellars. In 2008, Piedmont resident Wayne Marzolf teamed up with his brother Roland for a little experiment: let’s try to make a couple of barrels of wine in the garage. The Malbec wine – all 50 cases of it – was a huge hit. Not being bonded, he gave it away to friends and family. (Full disclosure. I am a longtime friend of Wayne and Roland.) “I really didn’t know what I was doing,” Wayne said later. “I just threw the grapes and yeast in the barrel and hoped for the best. Beginners luck I guess.” Over the ensuing years Wayne and Roland, who ran a successful East Bay construction company, began to ramp up their wine production. They opened up a makeshift winery in the Oakland building that housed their construction offices. Over the years they bought more and more barrels and acquired more equipment. In 2017 the winery was bonded and production rose to 350 cases. They both have retired from the construction business, and now the winery takes up most of their time. They named the winery Drawbridge in honor of its home, the city of Alameda which is an island serviced by multiple drawbridges. Today Drawbridge Cellars produces 10 different bottlings with an emphasis on Rhone varietals. They source from many different varied vineyards around the state, sometimes even picking the grapes themselves. As a friend, I have had a ringside seat watching the wines and the winery grow and improve. Wayne and Roland have gone from a couple of guys with good luck to skilled winemakers whose chemical and technical skills have improved greatly. What I like about their wines is that they still feel homemade and down to earth, not commercially manipulated like so many modern California wines. The wines are just beginning to be available in the East Bay. You can find them at Mulberry’s Market in Piedmont and a few restaurants in Alameda. But the best thing to do is call Wayne and Roland and make an appointment to meet at the winery tasting room in Oakland. They are happy to pour their current releases and even better, there is no tasting fee. Drawbridge Cellars wine label.
articles.title: Delightful Drawbridge Cellars

pages.text: Wednesday, November 18, 2020 23 The Wine Corner Delightful Drawbridge Cellars SUNROOM BEDROOM WIC LIVING ROOM KITCHEN BATH DINING LAUNDRY GARAGE GARAGE WIC BEDROOM BEDROOM FOYER BEDROOM PORCH Living longer – and safer – in your home By Yildiz Duransoy, AIA Many older adults prefer living in their homes as long as possible in order to maintain their daily lifestyle in a familiar environment. However, aging typically brings challenges with it, including reduced vision and hearing, decreased mobility, and the increased risk of falls. Here are some practical and easy design solutions to consider to make your home safer and easier to live in as you age. Foyers Install an outdoor motion light sensor to ensure good visibility when unlocking your door and trying to find the light switch in the foyer. When it comes to door handles, lever type handles are easier to grip and operate than door knobs. Make sure your entry foyer is free of obstructions and well-lit as well. Living Rooms Finishes and layout of living areas have a big impact on a person’s ability to move around safely and be independent. Make sure you have a clear path with no clutter when moving from one room to another. Transitions between different floor finishes should be smooth to prevent falls. If you have area rugs, make sure to install non-slip pads or double-sided carpet tape to reduce the risk of tripping. Short pile carpets are safer than large loop carpets as they help increase mobility. Kitchens Kitchens are typically one of the busiest rooms in our homes. Drawers and pull out base cabinets are much easier to use than cabinet doors and fixed shelves. If you do not have the budget to replace existing cabinet doors you can simply add roll out trays or a lazy susan inside the cabinets. Another easy retrofit is to replace cabinet door knobs with curved edge handles that have enough surface area for an easy grasp. Be careful not to choose handles with sharp edges that can snag clothes or be painful to bump into. Also, lever style faucets are much easier to operate than faucets with turn handles. Bathrooms Most falls happen in the bathroom, so special attention should be paid to safety in your bathrooms. Nightlights are extremely helpful to locate a bathroom easily in the middle of the night. Grab bars are life savers in many situations. Common areas for grab bars are inside your showers or tubs and adjacent to the toilet for ease of mobility and safety. Towel bars may not support your weight, so they are not safe to rely on as a grab bar. Consider adding textured strips on the bottom of your tub or shower to prevent slips and falls while bathing. Similarly, secure your bath mats with nonslip pads or choose non-slip mats. Bedrooms As we age, our eyes lose the ability to differentiate between shades of colors. Use light switch covers that contrast with wall colors so they are easy to see. Choose solid colored low pile carpet for your bedrooms in lieu of patterned carpet that may be confusing and distracting as aging brings declining vision. Laundry areas Raising your washer and dryer off the floor makes it easier to load and unload without bending for long periods. General It is essential to have a welllit house with a consistent level of ambient lighting. Make sure stairways are well-lit and have handrails at least on one side. Replacing toggle style light switches with lever style switches will make the operation easier and faster. These simple upgrades will increase your quality of life and help you enjoy your home for many years to come. Yildiz Duransoy is Project Manager at BDE Architecture in San Francisco and is a member of the Piedmont Planning Commission. For information, contact yduransoy@gmail.com. Roland Marzolf (left) and brother Wayne, founders of Drawbridge Cellars. By Pierre DuMont In 2008, Piedmont resident Wayne Marzolf teamed up with his brother Roland for a little experiment: let’s try to make a couple of barrels of wine in the garage. The Malbec wine – all 50 cases of it – was a huge hit. Not being bonded, he gave it away to friends and family. (Full disclosure. I am a longtime friend of Wayne and Roland.) “I really didn’t know what I was doing,” Wayne said later. “I just threw the grapes and yeast in the barrel and hoped for the best. Beginners luck I guess.” Over the ensuing years Wayne and Roland, who ran a successful East Bay construction company, began to ramp up their wine production. They opened up a makeshift winery in the Oakland building that housed their construction offices. Over the years they bought more and more barrels and acquired more equipment. In 2017 the winery was bonded and production rose to 350 cases. They both have retired from the construction business, and now the winery takes up most of their time. They named the winery Drawbridge in honor of its home, the city of Alameda which is an island serviced by multiple drawbridges. Today Drawbridge Cellars produces 10 different bottlings with an emphasis on Rhone varietals. They source from many different varied vineyards around the state, sometimes even picking the grapes themselves. As a friend, I have had a ringside seat watching the wines and the winery grow and improve. Wayne and Roland have gone from a couple of guys with good luck to skilled winemakers whose chemical and technical skills have improved greatly. What I like about their wines is that they still feel homemade and down to earth, not commercially manipulated like so many modern California wines. The wines are just beginning to be available in the East Bay. You can find them at Mulberry’s Market in Piedmont and a few restaurants in Alameda. But the best thing to do is call Wayne and Roland and make an appointment to meet at the winery tasting room in Oakland. They are happy to pour their current releases and even better, there is no tasting fee. See Wine Corner on page 29 Drawbridge Cellars wine label. The community is invited to Boren, the Executive Director of Sustainable Conservation, speak about the climate and environmental challenges in California. The event will take place on zoom on Sunday, December 6, from 4:00–5:00 p.m. For access, the zoom link is: https://us02web.zoom. us/j/82722017449?pwd=dlUzMXR1WlBFenl5U2U5UXlzMzAydz09. Sustainable Conservation brings together business, landowners, government and other non-profit organizations to steward the resources people depend on. Boren Ashley serves on the California State Board of Food and Agriculture and the UC California President’s Advisory Commission for the Agriculture and Natural Resources Division. She earned a BA in human biology, MA in applied economics and MBA from Stanford University.

articles.text: Like it or not, it looks like we’ll be celebrating this holiday season mostly at home, shelving our plans for festive meals and parties out in favor of more cooking and eating in. Even more than usual, this means our choices about what we eat and how we prepare it matters more than ever. Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan and yearly greenhouse gas inventories tell us that our homes and cars create the bulk of our collective emissions within the boundaries of our fair town. But you might be surprised to learn that the impact of our food choices dwarfs that of our energy usage in the grand scheme of things. “Plant-rich diets,” which basically means eating less red meat and dairy, pencils out as one of the biggest solutions according to Project Drawdown, a group that models the point when levels of greenhouse gases stop climbing and start to steadily decline. A study this month in Science magazine concludes that we cannot possibly reach urgent climate goals, in the US or globally, without reforming how we eat and the way we farm. The real biggie is food waste According to multiple sources, 30-40% of food goes to waste, which means land and resources used and greenhouse gases emitted in producing it were unnecessary. On top of that, food we discard into the trash (rather than our green compost bins) creates methane, a greenhouse gas much more potent than carbon dioxide, as it decomposes in landfills. Stop and think about that: we don’t eat 30-40% of the food we grow, process, distribute and buy! We’ve all had the experience of finding wilted produce in our crisper and “vintage” leftovers on a forgotten shelf. But with some vigilance and motivation, it’s possible to battle food waste in our homes. I’m a fan of using grocery delivery services (Good Eggs is my favorite) to schedule multiple deliveries per week and avoid overbuying. It can also help to master a few dishes like frittatas, soups, stir fries, and fried rice, that readily accept bits of leftover vegetables or meats. And definitely compost rather than trashing food scraps, but try not to let compost be an excuse to waste food. Reducing food waste is the single most impactful Drawdown solution, with a much bigger impact than solar or electric cars. But, when it comes to reversing climate change, we don’t have the luxury of either/or solutions. We need to eat down the food chain, and reduce food waste, and add solar, and switch to electric cars – and do it all soon. StopWaste and the NRDC’s Save the Food campaign provide a range of practical tips and tools, like food storage reference guides and meal-planning “guestimators” that help you to buy and serve accurate quantities. So, let’s make the most of this mostly at-home holiday season to cultivate some planet-friendly food practices, and carry them with us post-pandemic and beyond. Susan Miller-Davis is a member of Piedmont Connect.
articles.title: Recipe for climate action at the holiday table

articles.text: The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held on December 4 but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,” she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to-go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.
articles.title: Cancer League Holly Ball to be virtual on December 4

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: It is with great sorrow that we inform all of you that our dear Mother, Alpha Mae Beamer, passed away on October 13, 2020. She was born at home on February 11, 1920 during the Spanish Flu Epidemic, and she died at home during the Covid epidemic in 2020. She lived to be 100 years and 8 months. Alpha Mae lived her early years in Berkeley. Her family moved to Lindsay, California during the Great Depression. She attended Lindsay High School and learned to play the piano, something she enjoyed all of her life. While in high school, she was the accompanist for the Boy’s Glee Club. Upon graduation she entered the University of California at Berkeley in 1938, joined Sigma Kappa Sorority; and remained an active alumna throughout her life. In her freshman year at Cal, she met Scott Beamer and married him in the fall of 1939 when she was 19. They moved to Piedmont in 1948 and raised a family of five children. “We were all blessed to town. Throughout her life she supported the schools, the Piedmont Community Church, the Boy Scouts, Children’s Hospital, Merritt Hospital, Lincoln Child Center, The Oakland Museum of California and its White Elephant Sale; and all of the many causes and charities in the East Bay. She served on the Piedmont Board of Education and was President of most all of the organizations to which she belonged. “She really loved her community,” said Metcalf. Alpha Mae Beamer is survived by her five children, Joan Metcalf, Scott Beamer Jr., Ron Beamer, Alex Beamer, and Debbie Taylor. She is also survived by 11 grandchildren and 14 great grandchildren, all of whom she adored. Due to Covid restrictions, a private family burial was scheduled. “What she did was for everyone else; nothing was for her,” said grandson Jonathan Metcalf. To honor her life and good works, memorial donations may be made to the charity of your choice. Alpha Mae Beamer, a resident of Piedmont for 72 years, passed away on October 13 at age 100 grow up in a large and loving family,” said daughter Joan Metcalf. articles.text: Piedmont resident Stuart Schneck passed away on Sunday, October 11, 2020. He was 77. Born on October 12, 1942 in New York City, NY, he was the son of Murray and Sybil Schneck. He was raised in New York and after high school he headed to Ohio for his undergraduate studies at Miami University and later to obtain a law degree from Ohio State University. Following law school, the inner hippie in Stuart came calling and he made his way to California as an entrepreneur where he met his wife, Christina Schneck. Stuart and Christina were married in the Berkeley Rose Garden on March 20, 1976. Later in the 1970s, Stuart founded a company that was at one point the largest US-based manufacturer of macrame. As international competition heated up, Stuart pivoted and invented a hydroponic garden product, used to grow plants without soil. In typical Stuart fashion, when Kransco Group Companies inquired about purchasing his company, he leveraged that conversation to get himself a job as General Counsel at Kransco, where he stayed for many years and made lifelong Stuart Schneck, a resident of Piedmont for many years, died on October 11, 2020 of complications from Leukemia and kidney diseasse. He was 77. friends. After Kransco, he served as General Counsel at a number of other companies before retiring about 10 years ago. In retirement he developed a passion for cooking, bridge, golf, naps and filing cases in Small Claims Court, no matter how small the dollar amount. He battled leukemia and kidney disease for the past few years and his time with us was unfortunately cut short. Stuart is survived by his wife Christina, his son Stephan and daughter-in-law Danielle, his sister Robin, and several cousins, nieces and nephews. His ashes are at the Mountain View Cemetery in Oakland. Memorial donations in his honor may be made to the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03
articles.title: Stuart Schneck dies on October 11

This year’s ceremony will take place on Wednesday, December 2, at 7 p.m. Every year, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation kicks off the holiday season with the Annual Tree Lighting ceremony, traditionally held on the first Wednesday of December at the Piedmont Community Hall. The Foundation maintains, installs and removes the colorful LED lights each year. This also offers community members the opportunity of donating to the Holiday Tree Lighting Fund as a way of extending holiday wishes to their friends and neighbors. “We’ve never had a virtual tree-lighting before. As a result of social distancing precautions due to the coronavirus, this year’s ceremony will take place virtually,” Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap said. On Tuesday morning, December 1, the Public Works Department, assisted by members of the Piedmont Garden Club will install lights on the large Redwood tree above the Community Hall. Dunlap pointed out that the tree that will be dressed this year is the very first tree to receive the Piedmont Heritage Tree designation. The tree-lighting will be taped on December 1 and broadcast on KCOM (Channel 27) the next day, December 2 at 7 p.m. Mayor Bob McBain, City Administrator Sara Lillevand, Piedmont Beautification Foundation president Gayle Lambert, and former Foundation president Patty Siskind will offer remarks. Music will be The large, Redwood tree in front of Community Hall will be dressed with festive lights this year, but the ceremony will be held virtually. performed by the Piedmont High School Troubadours. A youth representative from Make-a-Wish Foundation will assist with the tree-lighting. Due to shelter-in-place restrictions, all speeches will be pre-recorded and then edited together in one final package. Residents are asked not to gather in person for this year’s tree-lighting. Additionally, new social distancing guidelines released by Gov. Gavin Newsom limits large gatherings to only three families or households. Santa Claus, who is everyone’s favorite guest at the tree lighting ceremony each year, will also observe shelter-in-place regulations. In his place, a special mailbox will be installed next to the tree for notes destined for the North Pole. The tree-lighting ceremony also will be available to stream on the city’s website. “We hope that lots of people will enjoy this happy, long-standing tradition for residents of every age,” Dunlap said.
