articles.text: Piedmont will receive a large new truck to flush its sewer system after City Council unanimously approved the purchase at a meeting on Monday, November 2. The truck, described as a flusher/jetter, is a custom Vactor Ramjet built by Owens Equipment and will cost $336,000. The money will be appropriated from the City’s Sewer Fund. The truck is used for cleaning Piedmont’s sewers when they become clogged with debris. “The flusher truck is an essential piece of specialized equipment that cleans our sanitary sewer system,” Director of Public Works Chester Nakahara told the Post. “Basically, it is a very powerful pressure washer that we insert and pull through our pipes to clear any blockages and flush out any debris that has accumulated in the pipes.” Currently, the City owns an International 4400 Flusher/Jetter that was purchased in 2006. “It has served the City well and has been through rigorous use for 14 years as a vital component in our quest to meet compliance requirements of the Environmental Protection Agency Consent Decree,” Nakahara said in a staff report, mentioning the Consent Decree regarding wastewater collection that involves the East Bay Municipal Utility District, Piedmont and the EPA. The EPA Consent Decree requires that Piedmont cleans its A new flusher truck will replace the city’s current vehicle which was purchased 14 years ago. sewer pipes regularly. The current truck will not meet California Air Resources Board standards in the future. “Staff carefully considered the truck make, model, and options for the replacement,” Nakahara continued in the report, noting that staff even test drove various options around the Corporation Yard. Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich and vehicle fleet manager Bill Higgins researched various vendors. “Owens Equipment was able to provide a vehicle that would respond to the rigors of working in Piedmont and submitted a competitive price that included the desired features,” Nakahara said. The new flusher/jetter is built on a 2020 Freightliner 108SD chassis powered by a diesel 270 horsepower engine. In the front, it is outfitted with a Ramjet hose reel while a 2,000-gallon water tank is saddled on the back of the truck. The approved budget for the fiscal year 2020-2021 appropriated $300,000 in the Sewer Fund to buy a new flusher truck, and Council this month approved an additional appropriation of $36,000 from the Sewer Fund to cover the remaining cost of the truck. An extended warranty of 60 months or 100,000 miles was included at no extra cost. The City expects the new truck to be delivered within six months. Like other vehicles used by the City, the old truck will be auctioned off and proceeds will go back into the Sewer Fund.
articles.title: New flusher truck replaces one bought in 2006

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department recently received a $100,000 grant from the California Citizens Option for Public Safety (COPS). The funds will be used for “frontline” uses that benefit public safety in Piedmont. The spending plan was approved by the City Council at its November 2 meeting. The COPS funds must be used for frontline municipal police services and must supplement and not supplant existing funding. By law, the City Council is required to hold a public hearing, apart from its usual budget hearings, to consider the written request of Police Chief Jeremy Bowers for use of the funds. In addition, funds in the amount of $505,713 are being carried forward from prior years, resulting in total funds available of $605,713. These funds will need to be spent or encumbered by June 20, 2021. Approximately $10,000 will be used toward police safety gear and field supplies. The largest amount will go toward technology and software, including public safety cameras in the amount of $300,000. Public safety cameras were installed in the city three years ago at the intersection of Oakland and Grand Avenue. Another $225,000 will be earmarked for police department facility updates, to include updating the briefing room, A/V equipment for the public safety camera system, and training. Twenty thousand dollars will be allotted for crime prevention and community engagement and will be used for social media consulting and information on the web page.
articles.title: Police Dept. receives $100,000 state grant

pages.text: Wednesday, November 11, 2020 29 Challenge in November: reducing energy use at home By Nate Redinbo Somehow 2020 is almost over and November is finally upon us. Thanksgiving, the sun setting earlier, beautiful leaves swirling, oversleeping because your alarm clock doesn’t register daylight savings – who doesn’t enjoy fall? The thing that is most exciting about November for me is the Piedmont Climate Challenge. You can sign up at www.PiedmontClimateChallenge.org at any time, earn points, and make a difference in Piedmont’s climate effort. This month’s challenge focuses on how we can reduce energy usage in households, so I’d like to discuss energy and how it is related to climate change. As we head into the colder months of the year, this topic becomes more and more important. The average Piedmont household uses three times more natural gas than the average household in PG&E’s service area. Natural gas is an emitter of methane, an emission that traps about 84 times as much heat as carbon dioxide over its lifetime. Natural gas powers appliances throughout our homes, and switching those appliances from natural gas to electric can radically decrease your household’s impact. Some of the appliances you can electrify include gas furnaces, water heaters, cooktops, and clothes dryers. Piedmont is a “built out” city – there is very little new construction, and most building is renovations of existing homes. The majority of its housing stock is older, and older homes are far less energy efficient than newer homes. Seventy percent of Piedmont households were constructed before 1940, a percentage that is higher than any other city in the Bay Area. Additionally, many of these older homes are larger than the average Bay Area home, meaning there are more nooks and crannies for heat to leak out. All of this means that focusing on energy efficiency is a very important part of Piedmont’s climate action plan. While the words “energy efficiency” might not sound like the most exciting response to climate change, it can make a very real difference. It can also make a huge difference to homeowners’ bills. According to the Department of Energy, proper energy efficiency efforts can save households 25 percent on their utility bills – hardly an amount to sneeze at. Energy efficiency is an umbrella that covers a variety of projects. Something as simple as changing out light bulbs to improving insulation counts as an energy efficiency effort. Projects like these can also help the community as a whole, and there are often rebates that can offset the cost. To get more information look at the City’s website or e-mail me at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov. Learning more about your home’s energy usage and taking action can make a very real difference to your carbon footprint and our community’s emissions. It may not sound as exciting as electric vehicles or planting trees, but energy efficiency is a very real solution to a very real problem we are facing in Piedmont. Improving your home’s energy efficiency and switching your gas appliances to electric ones are some of the most impactful steps you can take as a resident. Contact me if you have questions or comments and if you would like to see a certain topic covered in the newspaper. Nate Redinbo is working in the Planning and Building Department for one year as Piedmont’s Civic Spark fellow. He will be publishing a monthly article on environmental topics that affect Piedmonters. City replaces sewer flusher truck for $336.000 New flusher truck replaces one bought in 2006 By Barry Eitel Piedmont will receive a large new truck to flush its sewer system after City Council unanimously approved the purchase at a meeting on Monday, November 2. The truck, described as a flusher/jetter, is a custom Vactor Ramjet built by Owens Equipment and will cost $336,000. The money will be appropriated from the City’s Sewer Fund. The truck is used for cleaning Piedmont’s sewers when they become clogged with debris. “The flusher truck is an essential piece of specialized equipment that cleans our sanitary sewer system,” Director of Public Works Chester Nakahara told the Post. “Basically, it is a very powerful pressure washer that we insert and pull through our pipes to clear any blockages and flush out any debris that has accumulated in the pipes.” Currently, the City owns an International 4400 Flusher/Jetter that was purchased in 2006. “It has served the City well and has been through rigorous use for 14 years as a vital component in our quest to meet compliance requirements of the Environmental Protection Agency Consent Decree,” Nakahara said in a staff report, mentioning the Consent Decree regarding wastewater collection that involves the East Bay Municipal Utility District, Piedmont and the EPA. The EPA Consent Decree requires that Piedmont cleans its A new flusher truck will replace the city’s current vehicle which was purchased 14 years ago. sewer pipes regularly. The current truck will not meet California Air Resources Board standards in the future. “Staff carefully considered the truck make, model, and options for the replacement,” Nakahara continued in the report, noting that staff even test drove various options around the Corporation Yard. Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich and vehicle fleet manager Bill Higgins researched various vendors. “Owens Equipment was able to provide a vehicle that would respond to the rigors of working in Piedmont and submitted a competitive price that included the desired features,” Nakahara said. The new flusher/jetter is built on a 2020 Freightliner 108SD chassis powered by a diesel 270 horsepower engine. In the front, it is outfitted with a Ramjet hose reel while a 2,000-gallon water tank is saddled on the back of the truck. The approved budget for the fiscal year 2020-2021 appropriated $300,000 in the Sewer Fund to buy a new flusher truck, and Council this month approved an additional appropriation of $36,000 from the Sewer Fund to cover the remaining cost of the truck. An extended warranty of 60 months or 100,000 miles was included at no extra cost. The City expects the new truck to be delivered within six months. Like other vehicles used by the City, the old truck will be auctioned off and proceeds will go back into the Sewer Fund. Piedmont COVID-19 cases now over 50 Daily new cases in Alameda County rising again By Barry Eitel Six more cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Piedmont in the past week according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department released on Tuesday, November 10. This comes after four new cases were reported last week. The increase brings the total number of cases reported in Piedmont to 53 since the pandemic began in March. Across Alameda County, new cases have been ticking up in recent days after trending downward since August 28. On Monday, November 9, 93 new cases were reported, compared to 35 reported on October 15. On August 13, the worst day yet for the county, there were 419 new cases. Overall in Alameda County, the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 2.3 percent, a notable increase compared to recent weeks. The caseload in Alameda County is now 25,110, an increase of over 900 cases from one week ago. Alameda County has recorded 474 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 9,513. In Hayward, 3,737 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,812 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,440 and Livermore reported 1,083. Alameda County updated its shelter in place order on October 23 that reflects the county’s status as an Orange Tier county according to the state of California. The Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, is the second-least restrictive tier for reopening the economy and allows for activities such as indoor dining with capacity restrictions. The state placed Alameda County into the Orange Tier on October 13. Holiday health concerns Health officials nationwide have warned about potential spikes in COVID-19 due to holiday traveling and family gatherings. On Monday, November 9, Bay Area health officers released some guidelines for celebrating Thanksgiving safely. “The risk of spreading COVID-19 goes up when we gather with people we don’t live with, and that means the holidays will be different for all of us this year,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Alameda County residents can help ensure the holiday season doesn’t lead to a wave of new cases by celebrating safely and taking the right steps to protect themselves and loved ones from this highly contagious virus.” First, the health officers recommend that holidays should be celebrated with only the people who live in a household. They said that any gathering in person should be small, brief, stable and outside. Any nonessential travel is not recommended. Alameda County new cases per day remains too high to meet benchmarks for the Yellow Tier, or Minimal Tier. The county now is counting 3.4 cases per 100,000 people, while a county must have 1 case per 100,000 or fewer to be in the Yellow Tier. If the number of new cases per 100,000 hits 4 or more, the county would move back into the Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, according to state metrics. As of press time, 977,218 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded in California. Cases have trended upward since October 18 in the state. There have been 18,001 deaths due to the disease statewide. Police Dept. receives $100,000 state grant By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Police Department recently received a $100,000 grant from the California Citizens Option for Public Safety (COPS). The funds will be used for “frontline” uses that benefit public safety in Piedmont. The spending plan was approved by the City Council at its November 2 meeting. The COPS funds must be used for frontline municipal police services and must supplement and not supplant existing funding. By law, the City Council is required to hold a public hearing, apart from its usual budget hearings, to consider the written request of Police Chief Jeremy Bowers for use of the funds. In addition, funds in the amount of $505,713 are being carried forward from prior years, resulting in total funds available of $605,713. These funds will need to be spent or encumbered by June 20, 2021. Approximately $10,000 will be used toward police safety gear and field supplies. The largest amount will go toward technology and software, including public safety cameras in the amount of $300,000. Public safety cameras were installed in the city three years ago at the intersection of Oakland and Grand Avenue. Another $225,000 will be earmarked for police department facility updates, to include updating the briefing room, A/V equipment for the public safety camera system, and training. Twenty thousand dollars will be allotted for crime prevention and community engagement and will be used for social media consulting and information on the web page. ADVERTISE IN THE POST

articles.text: On Monday morning, November 9, President-elect Joe Biden and Vice President-elect Kamala Harris announced the establishment of a Coronavirus Advisory Board, the first step in their commitment to developing a national strategy to bring the COVID-19 pandemic under control. The Transition COVID-19 Advisory Board will provide public health and scientific advice to Biden, Harris, and the transition team’s COVID-19 staff. “Dealing with the coronavirus pandemic is one of the most important battles our administration will face, and I will be informed by science and by experts,” said Biden in a statement. “The Advisory Board will help shape my approach to managing the surge in reported infections; ensuring vaccines are safe, effective, and distributed efficiently, equitably, and free; and protecting at-risk populations.” The three co-chairs are Vivek Murthy, MD, the surgeon general under former President Barack Obama; Marcella Nunez-Smith, MD, associate professor of internal medicine, public health, and management at Yale School of Medicine; and UCSF’s David Kessler, MD, JD, professor of pediatrics, and of epidemiology and biostatistics, and former dean of the School of Medicine and vice chancellor of UCSF. Kessler served as commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration under the administrations of Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton. Two other members of the UCSF faculty have also been named to the 13-person Advisory Board: Eric Goosby, MD, and Robert M. Rodriguez, MD. Goosby, a UCSF professor of medicine, served as the interim Director of the White House’s Office of National AIDS Policy in the Clinton Administration and implemented the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) in the Obama administration, among other senior leadership roles. Rodriguez, a UCSF professor of emergency medicine, works in the Emergency Department of Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital and Trauma Center and in the Intensive Care Unit at Highland Hospital in Oakland. He has led national research teams examining a range of topics in medicine, including the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health of frontline providers. They will serve on the Advisory Board alongside Luciana Borio, MD; Rick Bright, PhD; Ezekiel Emanuel, MD, PhD; Atul Gawande, MD, MPH; Celine Gounder, MD, ScM; Julie Morita, MD; Michael Osterholm, PhD, MPH; and Loyce Pace, MPH. “I wish Drs. Kessler, Goosby and Rodriguez the best as they assume these critical leadership roles,” said UCSF Chancellor Sam Hawgood, MBBS, in a letter to the UCSF community. “They represent the extraordinary and relentless dedication the UCSF community has shown in meeting the challenge of the coronavirus across our patient care, research, and education efforts. Our public health mission has never been clearer nor pursued with greater determination. “UCSF looks forward to working with President-elect Biden’s administration,” he said. “We remain committed as ever to our partnership with public health officials at the national, state, and local levels.” The University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) is exclusively focused on the health sciences and is dedicated to promoting health worldwide through advanced biomedical research, graduate-level education in the life sciences and health professions, and excellence in patient care. UCSF Health, which serves as UCSF’s primary academic medical center, includes topranked specialty hospitals and other clinical programs, and has affiliations throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: The following letter was sent to School Supt. Randy Booker on November 10. Editor: While the COVID-19 pandemic has affected the delivery of a quality education to all of Piedmont’s students, one group is especially adversely affected by the switch to distance learning – students with special needs. While other school districts are delivering in-person services and instruction to their special education students, Piedmont School District has failed for eight months to take action to restore the needed on-site instruction for all special education students. These students desperately need onsite instruction; they are falling behind academically and losing critical skills. Nor can the existence of the pandemic be used as an excuse for inaction. As early as August 18, 2020, California approved onsite instruction for children with disabilities. Education Code section 43504, enacted as part of the 2020-21 Budget, specifies that schools should “offer in-person instruction to the greatest extent possible,” and the State has made clear over and over again that “students with disabilities should be prioritized by the LEA and school for receiving targeted supports and services.” Indeed, the California Department of Public Health issued specific guidance on September 4, permitting cohorts of multiple high-needs students to begin meeting in person, as long as students and teachers met strict safety protocols. The current school reopening plan, announced November 8, is inadequate: it does not address the needs of special education students as a group, focusing instead on bringing the elementary school cohort back to school. While Principal Littlefield’s November 8 update does indicate that a small group of students will be allowed on campus at Piedmont High School in December, there is no indication that all the PHS special education students will be included. They should be. Bringing middle and high school special education students, not just elementary school students, back to school would present few, if any, of the health, safety, and logistical challenges inherent in a return to school by the larger student population, as class sizes in the former group are much smaller and teacher/ student ratios are higher. For this reason, delivery of special education classes and services to all K-12 special education students should take place as soon as possible. These services are needed immediately to provide critical support for these students who are at higher risk of falling behind. The District’s failure to serve its special needs children is shameful. Students with special needs are suffering both as a result of having been denied the support they need to access their education, and from the very real anguish and depression that accompanies this deprivation. The distance learning model has failed the District’s most vulnerable students, denying them the appropriate public education that is the right of every child in California. Piedmont looks to you to exercise leadership on behalf of our community’s high-needs students. –Author’s name withheld by request A special thanks goes out to her for her kindness and camaraderie during the campaign. As our newest Council member, Conna McCarthy will continue her dedication and hard work for our City. I would like to extend my deepest, most heartfelt thanks to all of my diehard supporters. So many of you gave me good advice, good ideas, and kept my spirits high. I can’t thank you enough for getting me through my first campaign. A big, loving thank-you to my wonderful husband Mark for his help, support and encouragement. He was my campaign committee of one and I wouldn’t have it any other way. And last, a thank you to Kapo, our loyal 4-legged family member. She logged a lot of miles carrying my “Vote Herrick” sign and brought a smile to many people’s faces. She’ll miss the campaign trail. I wish you all good health, a lot less stress and lots of hope as we go forward into 2021. In community and with joyful gratitude, –Connie Herrick

articles.text: Piedmont voters re-elected Jen Cavenaugh to a four-year term on the City Council, and elected Conna McCarthy to her first term based on partial voting results late last night. Two seats were available with a total of four candidates running – Cavenaugh, McCarthy, Connie Herrick, and Nancy Bostrom As of 11:30 p.m. Tuesday night, November 3, Cavenaugh received 3,197 votes, and McCarthy received 2,660. Herrick received 765 votes, Bostrom received 192 votes, and there were 44 write-in votes. Due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic, polling locations were limited in Piedmont. In 2016, there were polling locations for the city’s six precincts. This year, the six precincts were compressed into a single voting location, the Piedmont Veterans Jennifer Cavenaugh was well on her way to be re-elected to the City Council in partial voting returns last night. Conna McCarthy was the second leading vote getter in the race for City Council.
articles.title: Cavenaugh, McCarthy on way to seats on City Council

articles.text: Measure TT (Transfer Tax) trailing as of midnight Measure UU, the $19 million bond that will fund a redesigned Community Pool in Piedmont, was passing with nearly 69 percent of the vote as of midnight, Monday, November 3. The measure needs 66.6 percent, or two-thirds to pass. Shortly before midnight last night, Measure UU received 2,883 yes votes (68.89%) and 1,302 no votes (31.11%). Based upon data on the Alameda County Registrar of Voters website, before election day over 7100 ballots had been cast. The total ballots counted last night represented approximately 4200 of the city’s 9000 voter total, indicating that it could take until late today for all ballots to be tabulated. Cou ncil member Betsey Andersen, who campaigned for Yes on Measure UU, recognized that it might be too early to celebrate a victory, even at the heels of midnight on election day. “Regardless of the outcome, I’m grateful to the campaign Co-chairs - Amy Aubrecht, Anne Callahan, and Vince Saunders - and the amazing campaign committee behind this effort. At the end of the day, Measure UU is about building community, and I appreciate all the many volunteers who have worked so hard under challenging circumstances for the future of the Piedmont Pool and the success of Measure UU,” she said. Friends of the Piedmont Pool, Yes on UU campaign received over $26,000 in contributions, and spent over $17,000 in expenditures. Supporters also participated in several forums leading up to the election; most recently, councilmember Betsy Andersen, Mayor Bob McBain and school board member Sarah Pearson answered questions from residents about Measure UU in a virtual forum on October 20. Measure TT In contrast, Measure TT, the real estate transfer tax, was losing, albeit by less than 100 votes. At 10:30 p.m. last night the vote total showed Measure TT losing, 2092 (No) to 2063 (Yes), a margin of 29 votes. Measure TT, requires only a simple majority to pass. The National and California Realtors Associations both committed expenditures in a campaign against Measure TT.

articles.text: Voter’s Edge nonpartisan guide ready in time for Nov. 3 election The League of Women Voters of California has produced a comprehensive, nonpartisan online guide to elections, covering federal, state, and local races. The online document, called Voter’s Edge, aims to provide all Californians with reliable voter resources to counter the surge of misinformation in the news. The League describes Voter’s Edge as the “Gold Standard in voter information”, and the only one that offers campaign finance data. It also helps you find your polling location or where to drop off your ballot. This past week, the website garnered over 4 million views. When you visit the page, you will be asked to enter your street address and zip code. From that information, you can view ballots by county, see measures and races within the state, and see a list of past elections in the election archive. Voter’s Edge is a joint project of MapLight and the League of Women Voters of California. The League of Women Voters of California Education Fund produced one of the nation’s first election information websites, SmartVoter.org. Since 1996, the Smart Voter project has been California’s premier online source for authoritative, nonpartisan coverage of election contests, candidates, and ballot measures. MapLight’s Voter’s Edge tool was first designed to help voters understand the sources of funding behind ballot measures in California. In some years, the project has also covered candidates and elections in states beyond California. In 2014, the League and MapLight joined forces to create a successful pilot project. The result is Voter’s Edge California. articles.text: Dear Community of Piedmont: As we write this, we do not know the outcome of the November 3 election. Of course, we hope Measure UU passes, and we can come together as a community to rebuild the Piedmont Pool. But regardless of the outcome, we want to express our appreciation to all the volunteers who helped with the campaign. Hundreds of friends and neighbors stepped up to spend thousands of hours to pass Measure UU for the future of Piedmont. It was inspiring to see citizens of all ages and backgrounds reaching out to one another to talk about the need to replace the failing Piedmont Pool. When the three of us decided to lead this campaign, we had no idea that we would be supported by such a diverse and talented team, including community leaders, neighborhood advocates, students -- athletes and non-athletes, and over 600 community endorsers. Like us, they were motivated by the fact that the Piedmont Pool has been an integral part of our community and our schools for 56 years. Their enthusiasm and efforts to bring people together and strengthen our community reflect the very best of Piedmont. With our sincere thanks and gratitude, –Amy Aubrecht, Anne Callahan & Vince Saunders Co-Chairs, Community Pool for Piedmont - Yes on Measure UU For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Otherwise we are left to ask, “Where in the World Are They?” Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
articles.title: Letter of thanks for Piedmont Community

articles.text: The headline in the East Bay Times read; “Relax, Oakland… Gerald the turkey has been captured.” It was big news. Gerald, a wild turkey had taken up residence in Oakland’s Morcom Rose Garden and because of his aggressive, bullying behavior toward garden visitors, had forced its closure. Agencies like the Oakland Parks Department, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and Oakland Animal Services debated what to do. Some thought he should be trapped, although he proved adept at avoiding capture. Some thought he should be killed, although that seemed a punishment more extreme than the crime. Finally, in late October, Rebecca Dmytryk, director of Wildlife Emergency Services, got Gerald’s attention with some of his favorite food, sunflower seeds and blueberries, and pretended to be an older woman. Predictably, Gerald, notorious for his aggressive behavior toward those he perceived to be weak and fearful, came closer. Dmytryk grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and wrapped her arms around him. With the assistance of her husband they got him into a large carrier. Fish and Wildlife officials then came and took Gerald to the hills of Orinda where wild turkeys thrive, tagged him and released him. Dmytrk said the whole episode could have been avoided if human beings would have refrained from feeding wildlife, in this case Gerald. That is a good lesson. Perhaps there is another lesson. For those of us who spend our time in religious communities like churches, the behaviors exhibited by Gerald – aggressive, bullying, demanding, targeting those perceived to be weak – are far from unfamiliar. Let’s commit to stop rewarding Geraldish behavior. If you act like Gerald, you don’t get attention. If you act like Gerald, you don’t get to be chair of the committee. If you act like Gerald, you don’t get to share your opinion. If you act like Gerald, you don’t deserve to be the pastor. Perhaps there is still one more

pages.text: 2 Wednesday, November 4, 2020 Opinion Letter of thanks for Piedmont Community Dear Community of Piedmont: As we write this, we do not know the outcome of the November 3 election. Of course, we hope Measure UU passes, and we can come together as a community to rebuild the Piedmont Pool. But regardless of the outcome, we want to express our appreciation to all the volunteers who helped with the campaign. Hundreds of friends and neighbors stepped up to spend thousands of hours to pass Measure UU for the future of Piedmont. It was inspiring to see citizens of all ages and backgrounds reaching out to one another to talk about the need to replace the failing Piedmont Pool. When the three of us decided to lead this campaign, we had no idea that we would be supported by such a diverse and talented team, including community leaders, neighborhood advocates, students -- athletes and non-athletes, and over 600 community endorsers. Like us, they were motivated by the fact that the Piedmont Pool has been an integral part of our community and our schools for 56 years. Their enthusiasm and efforts to bring people together and strengthen our community reflect the very best of Piedmont. With our sincere thanks and gratitude, –Amy Aubrecht, Anne Callahan & Vince Saunders Co-Chairs, Community Pool for Piedmont - Yes on Measure UU Sheltering in place? Where in the World are You? For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send us photos still on your camera or in a scrapbook for publication in the Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. articles.text: The following article was originally sent prior to the November The upcoming Piedmont elections will have important measures and candidates on the ballot that will lead Piedmont to becoming more environmentally conscious. Learn what your vote means for Piedmont, the difference it will make in the years to come, and what your City Council Candidates have to say about it. Measure UU – the Pool Bond The objective is to prevent permanent closure of the Piedmont community pool. Our current pool is 56 years old and is far overdue for some fixing up. Conna McCarthy notes, “We either have to rebuild it, or we have to close it.” Moreover, the current state of the pool is unsustainable for the environment. Council member Jen Cavenaugh says the community pool leaks more than 3,000 gallons of water a day, or over 1 million gallons Since there is only one pool in Piedmont, it is often used by many. Parents bring their kids to learn how to swim, high school teams practice sports, and it is even used for rehabilitating injuries. According to council candidate Connie Herrick, a longtime Piedmont Pool member, “It is really important that we pass [measure UU] next month; each time we delay, we push out several years. At this point, in the best-case scenario, we’re going to be open maybe in 2024, so we really can’t delay anymore.” Measure TT – The Transfer Tax The transfer tax funds can be used for various purposes which is why voting for environmentally friendly council members is crucial. They can help ensure the general fund is used for more environmentally concious decision-making. For example, ecofriendly equipment replacement, solar energy options, and sustainable landscaping. Opponents argue that when Measure TT was written, there were no safeguards that ensure the money will be spent the way voters would like. In this case, money from transfer taxes can be used for any means such as salaries, pensions, project over-runs, etc. Voting for candidates that are sure of using funds for pressing issues and eco-friendly spending is key. How are our City Council candidates adressing climate action? Jen Cavenaugh, a City Council member completing her first four-year term, has a history of community service related to the environment. Cavenaugh is a member of Piedmont Connect, an organization that supports city efforts to become a more sustainable city. She is also involved with The Imperfect Food customer buying program, which ships imperfect products with eco-friendly packaging, minimizing waste. “No plastic, no extra packaging,” Cavenaugh says. On the environmental quality committee, she advocated for a bill focused on product consumption and making sure residents “push the burden on the manufacturers. When you do that, suddenly they are accountable, and now they have an incentive to do better.” Connie Herrick is participating in the Piedmont Climate Challenge, which prompts its participants to reduce food waste, eat less meat, shop local, recycle, turn off lights, and change their means of transportation to be more environmentally friendly. She supports the current Climate Action Plan and is in favor of implementing a climate committee. “We need a climate action committee. As you know, our city has all these committees. We’ve got public safety, recreation, parks, we even have one for the pedestrian bikeway. But we don’t have one for climate action. And if it’s that important to us, which it is, then we need to have that commitment.” Conna McCarthy fully supports Piedmont doing its part to protect the earth’s climate. Working off the climate action plan, she speaks fondly of the reach proposal. “We are asking people to go beyond to help mitigate climate change by lowering their carbon footprint,” she said. The proposal leans towards becoming more dependant on electric, renewable energy. “There’s a menu with about seven energy efficient items. When someone does a construction project over a certain value, it triggers that homeowner to choose from the menu,” she said. The reach will allow our city to make the switch from unsustainable items that contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, to more eco-friendly options. My takeaway Piedmont has many environmentally friendly candidates, giving voters multiple options for how they want the city to be run. This election is about more than whether or not our candidates are environmentally friendly, it’s about how they are environmentally friendly. And no time is better than the present to take part in determining the future of our city. Ed. Note: Emily Ballati and her family have recently moved to Piedmont from Oakland. She is a junior at Bishop O’Dowd High School.

articles.text: Wildfire season continues; August Complex Fire burns over 1 million acres October was markedly warm and dry in the Bay Area, the National Weather Service said November 1, although cooler weather is expected to move into the region this weekend. Across the Bay Area and Central Coast, average temperatures during October 2020 were 4 to 7 degrees hotter than normal. Additionally, most areas received no rain for the entire month. After hot, gusty conditions blew across the region last week, officials were concerned that more wildfires would break out and a Red Flag Warning was issued for the entire Bay Area. Although Cal Fire responded to several fires in Northern California the past week, the new blazes were quickly contained. The Red Flag Warning expired on Tuesday, October 27. “A big pattern change is still being forecast on Friday and over the weekend,” NWS Bay Area said this week, adding that the region might see scattered showers this weekend. “We are moving into a typical fall weather pattern, with cool and moist evenings,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black. “The biggest wildfire threat for the fall occurs when we see wind and humidity interplay creating significant potential for wildfire.” Black noted that wildfire risk will only be reduced with heavy and consistent rain. “Until we see significant and sustained rain, we will continue to see exceptionally low fuel moistures and high ‘Probability of Ignition,’” he added. Air quality in Piedmont has remained moderate or better for the past few days, and this outlook is expected to continue. Some smokey haze drifted over the area last weekend due to fires that are burning along the Sierra Nevada mountain range to the east. Both Cal Fire and Black noted that “wildfire season” will last through November. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. “The Camp Fire started on November 8 in conditions similar to our current weather,” Black continued. “Piedmont residents traveling for Thanksgiving are reminded to stay vigilant and informed for wildfire threats.” Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history have occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which continues to burn in and around Mendocino National Forest, is the largest wildfire in California history and is the first fire to burn over 1 million acres in the state. The fire, which was caused by lightning back in August, is now 91 percent contained. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org.
articles.title: Cooler weather expected in November

articles.text: Council shifts $500,000 from General fund to facilities maintenance City finances are in good shape, despite negative fiscal impacts related to COVID-19. Such was the message from the Piedmont City Council as it reviewed year-end fund transfers, appropriations, and adjustments at an October 19 meeting. The Council unanimously approved a year-end transfer of $500,000 from the general fund to the facilities maintenance fund. In fiscal year 2019-20 (July 1, 2019 to June 30, 2020), favorable revenue trends and lower than anticipated expenses resulted in a net income of approximately $804,000 in the general fund. The city’s general funds can be used for any discretionary spending and finances many of the basic municipal services such as public safety or public works. The transfer of $500,000 to the city’s facilities maintenance fund would result in a General Fund ending balance of $5.6 million, representing 21 percent of operating expenditures, consistent with prior years. The council took similar action in October 2019 to distribute excess net revenue. Facilities maintenance funds go toward any and all city facilities, except for the community pool. This includes annual repairs for each facility (including parks and walkways), scheduled maintenance, and capital projects. All operating city department expenditures were lower than budgeted except for the Public Works Department, according to the staff report authored by City Finance Director Michael Szczech. Public Works expenses exceeded budget due to overages in city engineering, tree pruning, janitorial (due to COVID-19), and utilities expense. These costs were partially offset by savings in personnel and equipment related costs. The Finance Department recommended that the FY 2019-20 appropriation be increased by $56,574, which was approved by city council. Non-Departmental expenses exceeded budget due to higher than expected workers compensation claims. Workers compensation costs exceeded budget by $23,254. At that meeting, property transfer taxes, business and sales taxes and recreational revenues were all projected to be down. pages.text: Wednesday, November 4, 2020 5 Cooler weather expected in November Wildfire season continues; August Complex Fire burns over 1 million acres By Barry Eitel October was markedly warm and dry in the Bay Area, the National Weather Service said November 1, although cooler weather is expected to move into the region this weekend. Across the Bay Area and Central Coast, average temperatures during October 2020 were 4 to 7 degrees hotter than normal. Additionally, most areas received no rain for the entire month. After hot, gusty conditions blew across the region last week, officials were concerned that more wildfires would break out and a Red Flag Warning was issued for the entire Bay Area. Although Cal Fire responded to several fires in Northern California the past week, the new blazes were quickly contained. The Red Flag Warning expired on Tuesday, October 27. “A big pattern change is still being forecast on Friday and over the weekend,” NWS Bay Area said this week, adding that the region might see scattered showers this weekend. “We are moving into a typical fall weather pattern, with cool and moist evenings,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black. “The biggest wildfire threat for the fall occurs when we see wind and humidity interplay creating significant potential for wildfire.” Black noted that wildfire risk will only be reduced with heavy and consistent rain. “Until we see significant and sustained rain, we will continue to see exceptionally low fuel moistures and high ‘Probability of Ignition,’” he added. Air quality in Piedmont has remained moderate or better for the past few days, and this outlook is expected to continue. Some smokey haze drifted over the area last weekend due to fires that are burning along the Sierra Nevada mountain range to the east. Both Cal Fire and Black noted that “wildfire season” will last through November. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. “The Camp Fire started on November 8 in conditions similar to our current weather,” Black continued. “Piedmont residents traveling for Thanksgiving are reminded to stay vigilant and informed for wildfire threats.” Five of the top 20 largest wildfires in state history have occurred this year. The August Complex Fire, which continues to burn in and around Mendocino National Forest, is the largest wildfire in California history and is the first fire to burn over 1 million acres in the state. The fire, which was caused by lightning back in August, is now 91 percent contained. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Standing at the top of his front stairs on the porch, he could put pieces of wrapped candy in a long tube, allowing kids to place their bag at the bottom of the tube. A simple solution to a complex issue. articles.text: One of the most important tenets of the Scout Law is “a Scout is helpful”. For 36 years the Piedmont Scouts BSA has collected food and funds to help feed families in Alameda County. Last year Piedmont residents were especially generous, donating 8,095 pounds of food and $6,215 in cash to the Food Bank. This year’s event is moving to online donations, and the Scouts have set an ambitious goal of raising $7,500. Instead of a one-day annual food collection drive, this year’s campaign will last for five weeks, from November 1 through December 6. In addition, every Tuesday is Giving Back Tuesday. “We hope that those who have so generously donated food in the past will give online this year to help us combat food insecurity,” said Katy Kobal, Scouting for Food Chair. Every dollar donated allows the Food Bank to purchase $7 worth of food. We estimate that our need has doubled in Alameda county,” said Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. “October was our biggest month in food distribution ever. We anticipated distributing five million pounds of food. That is record-breaking, stunning.” Pre-COVID, Alameda County had one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. One in five residents of the county live below the poverty line. Of those Piedmont Troop 6 Scouts John Cumbelich (left) and Jack GrossWhitaker present a check in the amount of $3395.90 for the Alameda County Food Bank to newscasters from KPIX in November 2018 at the conclusion of the annual Scouting for Food campaign. receiving assistance from the Alameda County Food Bank, two-thirds are children and the elderly. How the food bank helps Yvonne and her family are just one example of the many families that are struggling during this pandemic. Yvonne is a mom who enjoys spending time with her two children: 11-year-old Elliott and 10-year-old Jordan. She owns a day care facility but had to close it at the beginning of March due to the pandemic. Her husband still works at an insurance company; however, scaling down to one income has been challenging. “Things are a lot tighter. For the first time, we’re using programs like the Food Bank to save money,” Yvonne said. She said she loves the fresh fruits and veggies she gets from the school pantry in Oakland. While things are different and money is tight, Yvonne said she’s thankful she’s able to spend more time with her children. Setting up a daily schedule has helped them stay on track with school. “The food pantry has been a blessing,” she said. About Piedmont Council BSA The Piedmont Council has proudly served our community since 1910 when the first troop overnight event was held in Redwood Canyon in Oakland. The council was chartered eleven years later, in 1921. Although it is one of the smallest councils in the nation, it is widely recognized for its excellence and traditions of service and quality programs. Year after year more than 50% of the eligible youth in Piedmont participate in the council’s many programs. Currently more than 1000 young people and 300 adult volunteers actively participate in Scouting in Piedont.

articles.text: More than half of the world’s population is bilingual, and the number of bilingual speakers in the U.S. is growing. So too is the body of research looking at the effects of bilingualism, which shows many cognitive advantages compared to monolingualism. Those include increased vocabulary, listening and reading skills, advanced problem solving, flexible thinking, and multi-tasking. In some cases, the bilingualism is forced, such as when a family moves to a country with a different language. In other instances, the bilingualism is optional, such as when a family decides to enroll their child in an immersion program in preschool or kindergarten. Simultaneous bilinguals learn two languages from birth, while sequential bilinguals learn a first language, and later introduce a second. Regardless of the specific circumstance, children have an enormous capacity for developing more than one language. With regard to supporting bilingual learners, the goal is simple: provide a high quantity of high-quality exposure to each language. The exact manner in which to accomplish this seems to be causing some confusion and conflicting advice to parents. For example, some parents are advised to take a structured approach based on a person, with one parent speaking one language and the other parent speaking the other. (In this situation, preference should be given to the language proficiency of each family member.) Some parents are advised to take a structured approach based on place, with one language spoken in the home and the other at school. And other families find a flexible use of both languages, without fixed rules, leads to balanced exposure and positive results. Some of the developmental guidelines for bilingual children also seem to be causing some confusion. Most bilingual children speak their first words by the time they are 1 year old, as is the case for monolingual children. Most bilingual children combine words into short phrases by the time they are 2 years old, as is the case with monolingual children. These early vocabulary words can be in one or both languages. As language develops, bilingual children may mix grammar rules, and/or use words from both languages within the same sentence. This is an entirely normal part of becoming a bilingual speaker. Some bilingual children, particularly sequential bilinguals, may not talk very much when they begin using their second language. This silent period may last several weeks or months and is also a normal part of becoming a bilingual speaker. I have regular conversations with parents regarding children who are exposed to multiple language, and are thinking that their children are “confused” or “delayed” due to multiple language exposure, or bilingualism. Bilingual children are not more likely than monolingual children to have difficulties with language, show delays in learning, or be diagnosed with a language disorder. But parent perceptions are often otherwise, revealing a disconnect from scientific findings. If a bilingual child is exhibiting symptoms of a speech, language and/or reading delay or difficulty, it will be evident in both languages, and should be evaluated by a professional. And if the child is not, parents should continue to provide a high quantity of high-quality exposure to each language. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. articles.text: When it became clear that Halloween activities would be curtailed this year, Piedmont parent Liz Mosbaugh went to work. She combined two of her passions -- creativity and fundraising for Piedmont schools -- to launch Piedmont BOO!, a socially-distanced, reverse trick-or-treat game. Starting on Saturday, October 17, Liz invited everyone in the community to sign up and purchase either a starter BOO! kit of a lawn sign, three BOO! count stickers, and access to the address list of other participants in the game, or the full BOO! kit which included the same supplies plus three complete BOO! bags filled with treats. Liz safely distributed the kits from her front yard with the help of her husband, Scott, and son, Chris. Participants would then “give a BOO!” by dropping a treat bag at the door of a participating home. When you received a surprise BOO!, you would place a round pumpkin sticker provided by Liz onto your colorful lawn sign. Once you received three BOO!s, you were done! Liz kept track of which homes still needed BOO!s on a handy map. Piedmont BOO! was a hit and Liz sold out of the lawn signs by October 28. All told, she put together 144 treat bags for 87 participating families, which raised more than $2,300 for the Piedmont Education Foundation and Piedmont schools. She

articles.text: Members of Piedmont Boy Scout Troop 1 had a great hike on October 24 in Briones Regional Park. All in all, it was a nearly 10-mile hike in an area that many had not been to before. Highlights of the trip included a sighting of a large coyote. articles.text: Last week, Cub Scouts and other elementary-aged youth engaged in a fun virtual Twilight Camp. This annual camp, typically held in person over three days at Dracena Park, was done virtually this year. Kids enjoyed Halloween-themed crafts and snacks, they carved pumpkins, created mummy bookmarks, and participated in other fun activities. This threeday camp, traditionaly held in October prior to Halloween, was introduced in Piedmont by Deborah Aracic and quickly became a part of the Cub Scout program nationwide. For informtion about Cub Scouts or to find other fun activities and local hikes, see: www. piedmontbsa.org.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Continuing with COVIDsafe activities, Piedmont Scouts and leaders in Troop 4 recently went white-water rafting on the American River. To ensure health safety, the trip was organized around family “pods” rather than the normal scout patrols. Scouts cooked, camped and rafted with members of their families. The first afternoon was spent tubing and setting up camp. Later, the families made dinner and rested up for the big rafting day. “This is one of the Troop 4 scouts’ favorite annual trips. I’m glad we figured out a way to go safely this year,” said Scoutmaster Rob Rachwald. “Scouting has taken on special importance during quarantine by getting Troop 4 Scouts Jerry Yu (left) and Chris Li cook dinner for their families. The Rachwald family pod floating down the American River in October. The adventure brought many a smile to the scouts’ faces. Pictured are Troop 4 Scouts Jerry Yu (left) and Chris Li. scouts and adults into the great outdoors safely while showing you don’t need to be contained to your house.” His family pod included Scouts Lizzy and Peter Rachwald as well as his sister Inga and niece Maddie. Minfen Ding, the mother of Scout Jerry Yu, exclaimed, “This was the most fun trip ever for our group of eight since the pandemic. We all enjoyed the rafting, tubing and even jumping into the cold water.” For some families, part of the fun was going into the cold water, which the Frontiera-Dupree family got to experience when they tried to “surf” a rapid. Despite their involuntary swim, everyone was okay and back on their way in no time. “This was a very special weekend for the Scouts because they got to enjoy an outdoor adventure that was COVID-safe. They are still talking about it. My goal for Troop 4 is to make sure we can keep active and safe,” said Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. Troop 4 is recruiting. Families with sons and daughters who are looking for adventure are encouraged to contact Sarah King (sarahdmertz@yahoo.com) for details. The Stokes family was all smiles amidst the white water and rapids in the American River. Pictured on the left side are Ryan, Julia and Peter Stokes, and on right side Scoutmaster Walter Stokes and Christine Schooley Stokes. Jonah Dupree (left) and Zach Dupree get partially dunked on the American River.

articles.text: “The Sky’s the Limit” exhibition includes 72 paintings At a time when beauty has never been more important, come be a part of the resilience of the arts. The one element in a painting that can have the greatest impact on the perception of atmosphere is sky. The types of colors used, the cloud composition, the quality of brush stroke....these are some of the details that can effect a viewer’s perception of sky. But this was not always the case. In the world of French classical painting, for instance, the landscape was a mere backdrop for some tale from antiquity or a scene from the Bible. It wasn’t until the late 1700’s that we see greater emphasis on sky: horizon lines dropped as artists began to explore greater variations in the rendering of sky. Indeed, in some art, sky was no longer a backdrop, but rather became the subject. Join artist and art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a zoom lecture to lead us on an examination of sky in painting. This lecture will also serve to open his current exhibition, “The Sky’s the Limit!” Michael will also describe his own approach to rendering variable skies. articles.text: Piedmont native Mackenzie McDonald has powered his way to the quarterfinals of two recent tournaments, the Istanbul Challenger Open from October 18-23, and the Astana Open in Khazakstan from October 28-October 30. This comes after being knocked out in the second round of the French Open on September 30 by No. 1 ranked Rafael Nadal in three sets, 6-1, 6-0, 6-3, and a first-round loss to Alexander Bublik in the St. Petersburg Open on October 12. McDonald has been a man on a mission since those losses, jumping in the ranking from No. 236 to No. 191. McDonald’s highest ATP ranking was No. 57 in April 2019, but a hamstring injury and subsequent surgery caused him to miss the entire 2019 season and training as well. “It took a really serious team and a lot of hard work. The surgery was pretty big. I have a masPhotos courtesy of ATPTour.com Piedmont native Mackenzie McDonald reached the quarterfinals of his last two ATP tour competitions. sive scar underneath my butt and I wasn’t able to walk for the first month-and-a-half, two months. Time was going by really slowly,” McDonald said, via ATPTour. com. Mackenzie McDonald defeated No. 49 ranked Alexander Bublik in the Astana Open in Khazakstan, marking a turnaround from a loss to him in St. Petersburg. At the Istanbul ATP Challenger he competed in five matches, entering as the topranked entrant of the qualifiers. He defeated Felipe Meligini Rodrigues Alves (3-6, 6-1, 6-3) and Viktor Galovic (6-2, 6-4) to reach the Round of 32. In the first round of the knockout stages, McDonald took down Teymuraz Gabashvili in straight sets, 6-4, 6-1. In the Round of 16, the Pride of Piedmont won again in straight sets over Nino Serdausic 7-6 (9), 6-3. The first set finished in a heated 10-point superbreaker which went backand-forth to an extra 11th point. In the quarterfinals, McDonald lost to No. 149 ranked Martin Klizan 4-6, 6-4, 6-3. At the Astana Open in Khazakstan, McDonald won in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2, in a rematch with Bublik, who entered as the sixth seed in the ladder in the Round of 32 and ranked No. 49 among ATP players. It was McDonald’s biggest win since returning from injury. In th ematch, McDonald powered his first serve into play on 37 of 49 attempts for a sparkling 76 percent conversion rate. He won points on 27 of them despite making only gaining one ace. He also did well on returns, converting 36 of 69 points (52 percent). He went on to take down No. 103 ranked Andreas Seppi in the Round of 16 in similar fashion, winning 36 of 55 first-serve points, a stellar 65 percent, while getting the ball into play on 55 of 87 first serves – notching seven aces this time. McDonald finished the tourament after losing 6-1, 6-4 to No. 36 ranked Adrian Mannarino in the quarterfinals.
articles.title: McDonald reaches quarterfinals of last 2 tournaments

articles.text: As Piedmont begins to get its high school sports programs back (at least online), hope trickles its way back into town. The hope is that fraternity, exercise, socialization and above all, distraction, will bring some pep to the steps of the city’s young athletes and their fans. The revival of professional sports in the last few months made for some soap opera-worthy drama. The NBA moved for an extended stay in a “bubble” at Disney World. Major League Baseball changed its rules: extra innings saw a runner start the inning on base, and double-headers turned into seven-inning games. Baseball’s postseason took place at empty neutral sites littered with teddy bears, and cardboard cutoffs of fans, dogs and even Bernie from the movie Weekend at Bernie’s. It turned out that Los Angeles won both the NBA and MLB championships. Although this reporter does not ever brandish the black and orange of the S.F. Giants, seeing Los Angeles succeed at anything is terribly upsetting. Nobody outside of L.A. can tolerate L.A., right? Or am I projecting? On the bright side, the Los Angeles Angels and Los Angeles Clippers did not win their leagues. So, think about this – in one way, L.A. loses every year by having multiple teams. At any rate, the opening of sports did bring back a modicum of distraction to fans across the globe. Having something to watch and something on a calendar brings much needed familiarity, tradition and relief. In-person attendance has all but been nixed – except for limited capacity at 13 games in the MLB postseason, and limited attendance at some NFL stadiums. The joy of going to a pro sporting event in person was acutely absent this summer. The Coliseum, Oracle stadium, the new Chase Center, and the Raider’s brand-new Death Star stadium in Vegas have been oh, so lonely. No mustard loaded hot dogs have rolled downstairs, nor have any tragic beer spills hit the bleachers. No seats have been played like drums, and the decibels from crowd noise have not hit triple digits. Things could have been much worse, though. If a pro athlete were to get deathly ill with COVID-19 with permanent damage, what was to happen? Season canceled, right? That contingency was not explicitly disseminated to the public. Luckily that did not happen, even in the NFL where maybe one third of the league’s players are over 300 pounds. Obesity increases the chance of serious COVID cases. But so far, so good in the world of pro sports. At least the cheating Houston Astros did not make the World Series. A championship by the Asterisks of Houston would have left a foul taste in the mouths of many. It would have been a taste that not even the “loss of taste” COVID-19 symptom could have altered. Back home, equipped with a new and spirited Athletic Director, youthful, energetic Bradley Smet, Piedmont is preparing to bring back some masked, in-person, distanced and outdoor workouts for its sports teams. Tennis, as a naturally socially-distance sport, has already been practicing in the afternoons. Other teams will expand their digital workouts through Zoom and Google Meet. Water polo players have enjoyed collectively working out as a team for some weeks, though without water – the basis of their existence. Sure, there is increased risk by bringing athletes back in person, but people need something, and sports can certainly be that something. As we collectively but unsuccessfully have been trying to say “goodbye COVID” for more than seven months, now at least we can say “Go Highlanders!”
articles.title: And the crowd goes silent

articles.text: Before traveling out of town to enjoy the California wilderness, it remains important to stay updated. On October 28, California State Parks officials announced that 13 of its parks remain fully closed due to the wildfires throughout the state, while four parks have partially opened, some of which are in the Bay Area. Of the LNU Complex Fire which affected Sonoma County, the Armstrong Redwoods and Austin Creek remain fully closed. The Armstrong Redwoods’ 1,400 year old giant redwood, Colonel Armstrong, was not damaged by the blaze. Also fully closed in Sonoma County are Sugarloaf Ridge and Trione-Annadel state parks due to the Glass Fire, which has also closed Napa County’s Bale Grist Mills State Historic, Bothe-Napa Valley State Park, and Robert Although a popular destination, Julia Pfeiffer Burns State Park in Big Sur is still fully closed. Photos courtesy of California State Parks The Armstrong Redwoods State Reserve of Sonoma County is still closed due to damage from the LNU Complex Fire. Louis Stevenson State Park. Henry W. Coe State Park in Santa Clara County is still fully closed, a victim of fire damage in the SCU Complex Fire. Also, several East Bay Regional parks remain closed due to the SCU Complex fire, including Castle Rock, the Morgan Territory, Ohlone Wilderness, Round Valley, and the Sunol Regional Wilderness. Sunol includes the popular Little Yosemite area. The CZU Complex Fire caused the closure of Big Basin Redwoods State Park near Santa Cruz, a closure that could last for one year. Butano State Park in San Mateo County is also fully closed. Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park is partially closed. South of Santa Cruz, the Dolan Fire affected Julia Pfeiffer Burns State Park I Big Sur and Limekiln State Park in Monterey County. Outside the Bay Area, the Jones Fire has forced th eclosure of South Yuba River State Park outside Yuba City and Sacramento. Lake Oroville is also closed due to the Northern Complex West Zone. The Mono Lake Tufa State Natural Reserve in in Mono County, East of Yosemite, is fully closed due to the Beach Fire.
articles.title: A list of what’s open and parks still closed

articles.text: Pac-12 Conference fans, we’re back! Football returns this Saturday, November 7 for a slate of seven games. Could this be the year for the California Golden Bears or Stanford Cardinal to take control of the Northern Conference? The defending champion Oregon Ducks, are looking a bit vulnerable after replacing five starters from last year, including the quarterback, while replacing their offensive coordinator despite being ranked No. 12 in the country. Meanwhile, Washington finds itself in a similar situation with new head coach Jimmy Lake. Oregon State’s defense is solid, but they are working on the shortend on offense. Here’s taking a look at both the University of California Golden Bears and the Stanford Cardinal. California Golden Bears The Golden Bears are back with a wealth of returning starters, including quarterback Chase Garbers, running back Chris Brown, along with their entire starting offensive line. Coach Justin Wilcox is entering his fourth year and isknown for defensive prowess.Cal has returning starters defensive backs Elijah Hicks, Cam Bynum, and linebackers Cameron Goode and Kuony Deng. Gee, you’d think that if Oregon, Stanford, or even Washington had as few of question marks, pundits would call it a title contender. California clearly has the leadership to get it done. But it all hinges on Garbers’ ability to stay healthy – something he’s struggled with throughout his college career. The Bears went 7-0 last season when Garbers played at least half the game and completed over 60 percent of his passes. The Bears currently have the Axe, and if they can stay healthy it will be difficult for Stanford to reclaim it. Cal hosts the Washington Huskies on Saturday but the visitors are the early favorites. It will be a good measuring stick to determine whether the Golden Bears are, in fact, contenders for the Pac-12 title. Stanford Cardinal Stanford tarts the season afterfimishing a surpriisng 4-8 last season. Like Oregon, it had a talented recruiting class. Quarterback Davis Mills enters his senior season and it seems their success hinges largely on his progress. Mills, like Garbers, must be able to stay healthy after multiple knee injuries throughout his college career. He has the complete package for the prototypical Stanford pro-style quarterback – arm strength, accuracy, mobility, amd decision making. Last year he completed 65.6 percent of his passes for 1,960 yards, with 11 touchdowns and six interceptions. But Stanford had two major players opt out. They will be without left tackle Walker Little and cornerback Paulson Adebo. However, they return three talented receivers who could become the team’s X-factor, Michael Wilson, Simi Fehoko and Connor Weddington. Their defense also has defensive end Thomas Booker, among the top-rated prospects in football entering his junior season. The Cardinal travel to No. 12 Oregon for the season opener this Saturday Photo courtesy of CalBears Twitter The California Bears and head coach Justin Wilcox look to a big 2021 season. They hope to retain the Stanford Axe and contend in the Pac-12 North. Photo courtesy of Stanford Athletics Stanford quarterback Davis Mills enters his senior season.
articles.title: Pac-12 Football returns to action this Saturday

articles.text: Photo courtesy of NFL.com The Raiders are 4-3 after defeating the Browns last Sunday, 16-6. They will play the Los Angeles Chargers this week, and we’re predicting a Vegas win. Ah, it’s nice when my predictions come true. The Raiders’ defense got the job done against a hampered Cleveland Browns’ squad and won 16-6 last weekend. On the other hand, the 49ers were handed a convincing loss by the Seahawks, 37-27. Don’t look now, but the Raiders are putting together a season that could land them a Wild Card berth. They have a 4-3 record midway through the season and have a semi-favorable schedule over the next five weeks. They face a challenge this weekend in a game with division foe, the Los Angeles Chargers, a team with a stout defense and talented playmakers on offense. The team includes rookie QB Justin Herbert and former Cal WR Keenan Allen L.A. dropped a 21 point lead against the Broncos in Week 8 and traded starting CB Desmond King on Monday, meaning the Chargers are ripe for the picking. The 49ers are 4-4 and in last place in the NFC West. They recently traded LB Kwon Alexander in exchange for veteran LB Kiko Alonso and a 2021 fifthrounder ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, so it seems the front office is already looking to next year. But never say die for this roster: The LA Rams were upset by the Dolphins in Week 8, meaning the Niners are only a 1.5 games back of the Cardinals in second and a potential Wild Card spot. San Francisco has a critical game against the Green Bay Packers tomorrow night, Thursday. The Packs are coming off a 28-22 loss to the Vikings, a game in which Dalvin Cook ran wild for 226 total yards and four touchdowns. Beating the Packers will be tough, but perhaps Kyle Shanahan can dial up an attack with his elusive Runnikc backs Tevin Coleman and JaMycal Hasty. They’ll have to lean on the running game die to All-League tight end George Kittle possibly missing the rest of the season, and WB Jimmy Garoppolo expected to be out some time. The 49ers’ list of injuries may prove to be too costly for them to succeed. SOCCER Premier League Match Day 7 review How fun is the first quarter of the season, with 13 teams within six points of first place. Who would have guessed that mighty Photo courtesy of Mirror.co.uk After seven games, Manchester United shockingly has slid to 15th place. Could manager Ole Gunnar Solskjær be on the move? Photo courtesy of Mercury News The 49ers are coming off a 37-27 loss to the division-leading Seahawks. They face the Aaron Rodgers and the Packers this week, a game which favors Green Bay. Manchester United might be just four points out of relegation and in 15th place with a 2-1-3 record. United is certainly becoming a team to watch regarding its inconsistency after losing 1-0 to Arsenal on a penalty relinquished by the $88 million-man Paul Pogba last weekend But ManU demolished RB Leipzig 5-0 in the Champions League Group Stage on October 28. The Red Devils have a tough match with Everton (3rd, 13 points) this Saturday, and if they continue this bad run of form, Man. U could be on the hunt for a new manager, which is ironically a similar situation to Tottenham Hotspur around the same time in 2019. Why is that ironic? Because if Manchester United sacks manager Ole Gunnar Solskjær, the leading man for the job appears to be former Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino. Pochettino was fired by Tottenham on November 19 of last year when his team was sitting in 14th place. It made way for José Mourinho, who was sacked by Man U in 2018. Under Mourinho, the Hotspurs are now in 3rd with 14 points after a 2-1 win over Brighton, albeit a nervy and narrow victory. The microscope will undoubtedly be focused on Solskjær over the next month given their slate of winnable contests. Should United struggle against Everton, West Brom on November 21, Southampton on Nov. 29, or their remaining Champs. League Group Stage matches—Manchester United could be the big managerial change of 2020. Now, finally looking ahead to the Match Day 8 schedule, Sunday’s meeting of Liverpool and Manchester City is the match of the week—a rematch of last year’s No.1 and No. 2 teams. The Reds of Liverpool are back in 1st with 16 points, but a City win could catapult Leicester City or Tottenham to first place of Premier League. The Foxes of Leicester have a tough game against the Wolves (6th, 13 points), but LCFC are coming off a big 4-1 win over Leeds and striker Jaime Vardy is in top form. Hotspurs will have to beat West Brom (18th, 3 points)— which they should. For Manchester City (10th, 11 points), some reported confrontations in their own locker room, plus a narrow 1-0 win over Sheffield isn’t a good look when going into a game against the defending champions, Liverpool. However, the Reds’ Virgil Van Dyke (knee) is out, meaning the possibility for Man. City goals is high, while manager Pep Guardiola is well aware a win puts them back into the top-four. The game suits up to be a thriller.
articles.title: Raiders in the hunt; 49ers’ schedule gets tougher; Premier League Match Day 7 review
