They recently traded LB Kwon Alexander in exchange for veteran LB Kiko Alonso and a 2021 fifthrounder ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, so it seems the front office is already looking to next year. But never say die for this roster: The LA Rams were upset by the Dolphins in Week 8, meaning the Niners are only a 1.5 games back of the Cardinals in second and a potential Wild Card spot. San Francisco has a critical game against the Green Bay Packers tomorrow night, Thursday. The Packs are coming off a 28-22 loss to the Vikings, a game in which Dalvin Cook ran wild for 226 total yards and four touchdowns. Beating the Packers will be tough, but perhaps Kyle Shanahan can dial up an attack with his elusive Runnikc backs Tevin Coleman and JaMycal Hasty. They’ll have to lean on the running game die to All-League tight end George Kittle possibly missing the rest of the season, and WB Jimmy Garoppolo expected to be out some time. The 49ers’ list of injuries may prove to be too costly for them to succeed. SOCCER Premier League Match Day 7 review How fun is the first quarter of the season, with 13 teams within six points of first place. Who would have guessed that mighty Photo courtesy of Mirror.co.uk After seven games, Manchester United shockingly has slid to 15th place. Could manager Ole Gunnar Solskjær be on the move? Photo courtesy of Mercury News The 49ers are coming off a 37-27 loss to the division-leading Seahawks. They face the Aaron Rodgers and the Packers this week, a game which favors Green Bay. Manchester United might be just four points out of relegation and in 15th place with a 2-1-3 record. United is certainly becoming a team to watch regarding its inconsistency after losing 1-0 to Arsenal on a penalty relinquished by the $88 million-man Paul Pogba last weekend But ManU demolished RB Leipzig 5-0 in the Champions League Group Stage on October 28. The Red Devils have a tough match with Everton (3rd, 13 points) this Saturday, and if they continue this bad run of form, Man. U could be on the hunt for a new manager, which is ironically a similar situation to Tottenham Hotspur around the same time in 2019. Why is that ironic? Because if Manchester United sacks manager Ole Gunnar Solskjær, the leading man for the job appears to be former Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino. Pochettino was fired by Tottenham on November 19 of last year when his team was sitting in 14th place. It made way for José Mourinho, who was sacked by Man U in 2018. Under Mourinho, the Hotspurs are now in 3rd with 14 points after a 2-1 win over Brighton, albeit a nervy and narrow victory. The microscope will undoubtedly be focused on Solskjær over the next month given their slate of winnable contests. Should United struggle against Everton, West Brom on November 21, Southampton on Nov. 29, or their remaining Champs. League Group Stage matches—Manchester United could be the big managerial change of 2020. Now, finally looking ahead to the Match Day 8 schedule, Sunday’s meeting of Liverpool and Manchester City is the match of the week—a rematch of last year’s No.1 and No. 2 teams. The Reds of Liverpool are back in 1st with 16 points, but a City win could catapult Leicester City or Tottenham to first place of Premier League. The Foxes of Leicester have a tough game against the Wolves (6th, 13 points), but LCFC are coming off a big 4-1 win over Leeds and striker Jaime Vardy is in top form. Hotspurs will have to beat West Brom (18th, 3 points)— which they should. For Manchester City (10th, 11 points), some reported confrontations in their own locker room, plus a narrow 1-0 win over Sheffield isn’t a good look when going into a game against the defending champions, Liverpool. However, the Reds’ Virgil Van Dyke (knee) is out, meaning the possibility for Man. City goals is high, while manager Pep Guardiola is well aware a win puts them back into the top-four. The game suits up to be a thriller. Pac-12 Football returns to action this Saturday By Jonathan Comeaux Pac-12 Conference fans, we’re back! Football returns this Saturday, November 7 for a slate of seven games. Could this be the year for the California Golden Bears or Stanford Cardinal to take control of the Northern Conference? The defending champion Oregon Ducks, are looking a bit vulnerable after replacing five starters from last year, including the quarterback, while replacing their offensive coordinator despite being ranked No. 12 in the country. Meanwhile, Washington finds itself in a similar situation with new head coach Jimmy Lake. Oregon State’s defense is solid, but they are working on the shortend on offense. Here’s taking a look at both the University of California Golden Bears and the Stanford Cardinal. California Golden Bears The Golden Bears are back with a wealth of returning starters, including quarterback Chase Garbers, running back Chris Brown, along with their entire starting offensive line. Coach Justin Wilcox is entering his fourth year and isknown for defensive prowess.Cal has returning starters defensive backs Elijah Hicks, Cam Bynum, and linebackers Cameron Goode and Kuony Deng. Gee, you’d think that if Oregon, Stanford, or even Washington had as few of question marks, pundits would call it a title contender. California clearly has the leadership to get it done. But it all hinges on Garbers’ ability to stay healthy – something he’s struggled with throughout his college career. The Bears went 7-0 last season when Garbers played at least half the game and completed over 60 percent of his passes. The Bears currently have the Axe, and if they can stay healthy it will be difficult for Stanford to reclaim it. Cal hosts the Washington Huskies on Saturday but the visitors are the early favorites. It will be a good measuring stick to determine whether the Golden Bears are, in fact, contenders for the Pac-12 title. Stanford Cardinal Stanford tarts the season afterfimishing a surpriisng 4-8 last season. Like Oregon, it had a talented recruiting class. Quarterback Davis Mills enters his senior season and it seems their success hinges largely on his progress. Mills, like Garbers, must be able to stay healthy after multiple knee injuries throughout his college career. He has the complete package for the prototypical Stanford pro-style quarterback – arm strength, accuracy, mobility, amd decision making. Last year he completed 65.6 percent of his passes for 1,960 yards, with 11 touchdowns and six interceptions. But Stanford had two major players opt out. They will be without left tackle Walker Little and cornerback Paulson Adebo. However, they return three talented receivers who could become the team’s X-factor, Michael Wilson, Simi Fehoko and Connor Weddington. Their defense also has defensive end Thomas Booker, among the top-rated prospects in football entering his junior season. The Cardinal travel to No. 12 Oregon for the season opener this Saturday Photo courtesy of CalBears Twitter The California Bears and head coach Justin Wilcox look to a big 2021 season. They hope to retain the Stanford Axe and contend in the Pac-12 North. Photo courtesy of Stanford Athletics Stanford quarterback Davis Mills enters his senior season.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 4, 2020 15 HIKING WITH JON Wandering along the California Coastal Trail By Jonathan Comeaux The California Coastal Trail, or CCT, is a system of trails that, upon its full completion, will connect 1,200 miles of the California coast from the Mexico border to Oregon. The trail allows hikers, bikers, joggers, and equestrians to travel alongside the Pacific Ocean on a combination of paved surfaces, gravel paths and some narrow pathways down to beaches. For this week’s venture, we traveled about five miles along the coast starting at Half Moon Bay’s Poplar Beach parking lot, past the Ritz Carlton Hotel and its beautifual golf course, thenn beach hopping our way toward farmlands and untouched nature preserves. Alltogether it was an 11-mile day. It’s worth mentioning that this tirp takes you through some busy intersections. We counted 188 people throughout the day on the hike. However, over half of them were peope passing through the Ritz Carlton outdoor restaurant and golf course. The area is popular for offroad bikers given the width of trails, flat surface, level elevation gain, and length of time you can spend riding. With a bike, one could easily make a day of it, starting from San Francisco and ending at our final destination Staff Photos The California Coastal Trail in San Mateo County starts along Poplar Beach and the Wavecrest Open Space Preserve. The Wavecrest Open Space Preserve is an area thriving with wildlife. Under the brush are critters that make the area popular for birds of prey. You can travel down to Redondo Beach, but watch your footing. This writer was lucky enough to spot a great horned owl along the Wavecrest Open Space Preserve. A red-tailed hawk perched on a tree branch. The view from the 16th tee of Half Moon Bay Golf Course and the Ritz Carlton, overlooking Manhattan Beach. point, Seal Rock Overlook in San Mateo County. Starting at the Poplar Beach parking lot, you’ll walk next to the ocean and Wavecrest Open Space until reaching Redondo Beach, continuing on the paved path toward the Ritz Make sure you have your mask handy. The walk along the golf course is pretty, and there is a stairwell available down to Manhattan Beach. When reaching the 16th hole, you’ve reached the end of the golf course portion of the Coastal Trail. Keep an eye out for the small opening to the right, the start of the dirt trail. The dirt path will take you toward another landmark, Cowell Ranch Beach, the most secluded of the beaches thus far. But past the beach, continuing on the Cowell-Purisima portion of the Coastal Trail is a 3-mile stretch of untouched beachfront and nature preserves After you pass the golf course you will see vast acres of farmland where Brussels sprouts and artichokes are grown. A 3-mile stretch of untouched beachfront along the Cowell-Purisima portion of the Coastal Trail. alongside coastline and farmlands. You won’t spot a footprint in the sand. The walk gives you a glimpse of a marine preserve, Eel Rock, toward the end of the Cowell-Purisima trail at the Seal Rock overlook. The farmlands are currently lush with Brussels sprouts and a large field of pumpkins next to it. For bird watchers, the entire hike will be profuse with birds. You’ll spot red-tailed hawks, northern harriers, pelicans from the ocean, and if you’re lucky, a barn owl or great horned owl. This writer was fortunate enough to spot one each on a tree line of the Wavecrest Open Space portion of the trail. For a shorter walk, you can cut the distance in half by parking at the Cowell Ranch Beach lot, bypassing the the golf course and Wavecrest Open Space. To be safe, bring an extra layer of clothing; the fog can quickly overtake the land.

articles.text: Holiday theme nights at Filoli Gardens in Woodside begin on November 23. Starting Monday, November 23, Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside will host “theme nights.” Guests may visit the gardens each Monday for a fun and festive theme – from a pajama party to a winter solstice night – to make the start of the week merry and bright. If you match the theme, you will receive a special gift from Filoli. Admission for each theme night begins at 4 p.m. The theme nights are: • November 23 – “Night Lights” • November 30 – “Festive Face Masks” • December 7 – “Holiday Hats” • December 14 – “Holiday Pajama Party” • December 21 – “Solstice Night” • December 28 – “Vintage Christmas” To reserve a ticket for a Monday theme nights, visit https:// filoli.org/event/themenights/?instance_id=9467.

articles.text: San Francisco Conservatory of Music will celebrate Beethoven’s birthday with a mini-concert on Saturday, November 14. The concert, to be performed in Sol Joseph Recital Hall, will be available online and can be viewed from home. The mini-festival will feature Beethoven’s rarely performed, but still magnificent vocal works. The celebration of the 250th anniversary of Beethoven’s birth is presented by the San Francisco Conservatory of Music’s Historical Performance department. Included will be rarely heard vocal works, including solo songs, vocal duet and trios from Eight Songs, Op. 52 (1790-96), Six Songs, Op. 75 (1809), Four Ariettas and a Duet (1809), Three Songs, Op. 83 (1810), and arrangements of Scottish and Irish folk songs for voice, violin, cello and piano (1810-1818). The event is curated by Corey Jamason, Chair of the conservatory’s Historical Performances department. Sign up to receive a livestream link the day of the concert. Visit https://sfcm.edu/ performance-calendar/event/fallbaroque-voice-concert to sign up.
articles.title: SF Conservatory celebrates Beethoven’s birthday with mini-festival Nov. 14

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young hosts a series of free online musical gatherings entitled “Joseph Young and Friends,” which will conclude on November 19 with a look to the future. The final episode of the series offers a look into Berkeley Symphony’s future programs, by showcasing composers Brian Raphael Nabors and Jimmy Lopez. New Music USA recently announced a new commissioning project with Nabors and Berkeley Symphony. “This collaboration is important to me on so many levels and brings to life a vision that I have had since entering this industry,” Young said. “It has always been a goal of mine to champion composers that look like me, that speak to the range of today’s experiences, and that can offer diverse perspectives for our audiences. It is essential to provide a platform for composers to create openly and freely with limited parameters so that they can bring unique color and life to the ever-growing musical canon. Berkeley Symphony has a rich history of commissioning new works, and this collaboration with New Music USA will continue to shape the discovery of emerging composers through long term relationships between the composer, the orchestra, and our beloved community.” Nabors, originally from Birmingham, Alabama, is a composer of emotionally enriching music that tells exciting narratives with its vibrant themes and colorful harmonic language. Nabors draws from combinations of Jazz Funk, R&B, and Gospel. His music has been performed by the Cincinnati, Atlanta, Nashville, and Detroit Symphony Orchestras. He is a 2020 Fulbright scholarship University of Cincinnati Conservatory of Music. “This project is impactful in so many ways. I am beyond honored and elated to share and serve as a voice for so many who look like me and share my experience,” Nabors said. “Along with my wonderful colleagues, I believe this ground breaking work will help to lay the foundation for barriers to be broken and the eradication of stigmas that have plagued our field for many years. To be a part of that change is an affirmation of everything I’ve worked for and continue to work for. Watch the final episode at https://www.berkeleysymphony. org/joseph-young-friends/. Composer Brian Raphael Nabors recipient to Sydney, Australia, studying with composer Carl Vine at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music. He earned both a Doctor of Musical Arts and Master of Music degree in Composition from the
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony’s Joseph Young & Friends series concludes Nov. 19

articles.text: Meryl Streep and Amy Adams star in Julie and Julia. Movie review by Chris Honoré What is there to say to those who have not seen Julie and Julia but bon appetit! This film. Made in 2009, is a joy to watch, a celebration of Julia (Meryl Streep) and Julie (Amy Adams), two women who embrace life and manage to square the compass and find in cooking, in the preparation of sauces and chicken and lobster, a happiness that up to that point proved elusive. The film blends two books, My Life in France, a memoir by Julia Child, and Julie and Julia, a book by Julie Powell. Through seamless editing th film offers a glimpse into the live of both women as they struggle to master the art of French cooking. In the opening scene Julia and her husband Paul (Stanley Tucci) arrive in post-war France where he is posted as an American Cultural Attache’. Julia, feeling at a loss, enrolls in a French cooking school and unexpectedly, surprisingly, discovers she has a talent as well as a passion for cooking. The film then jumps ahead to 2002, and introduces Julie Powell, a frustrated writer, stuck in a confining office job, who decides to cook all the recipes in Child’s cookbook, Mastering the Art of French Cooking, and keep a daily blog of her experiences. Writrer Nora Ephron masterfully weaves the two parallel lives together, separated by 50 years, and directs a wonderful recipe for one of her best films to date. Of the many wonderful performances in Julie and Julia, we must begin with the role of Maryl Streep, who simply inhabits the character of Child. It is a stunning transformation. Child was a large and generous personality, effusive and expressive, hooting and laughing to the point of caricature. But never, not for a moment does Streep allow her character to become any more or less than deeply human and transfixing and completely Julia. It’s an unparalleled performance, subtle, nuanced and comic, one that is breathtaking in its craftsmanship. Ditto for the incomparable Tucci. He is masterful, nurturing constantly the chemistry between Julia and himself, able to speak volumes with one expression, capable of being absolutely still as a scene develops around him (recall his sterling performance in The Devil Wore Prada, where he was first teamed with Streep). As well, Amy Adams, playing against Streep, though they never meet, is perfect as the neophyte who bubbles with passion for the art of a recipe and reacts to every obstacle with emotion that is authentic and spot on. She is a consummate actress. If there is undiluted joy to be found in film, Nora Ephron has captured it in this very special movie. Julie and Julia. Starring Meryl Streep, Amy Adams, Stanley Tucci, Jane Lynch and Chris Messina. Written and Directed by Nora Ephron. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Julie and Julia a masterful film about cooking – and Julia Child

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Before you see Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story and the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is in two stories. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin). Both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. Newly arrived in Tahiti, she meets New Zealander Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), who has just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, with lives that share a world view that embraces an existence far off the grid. Of course, Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. Unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45-footer, from Tahiti to San Diego, Tami’s hometown. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two firstclass airplane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, the most intense part of the film. This is a compellingly entertaining film, and is especially well-acted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing. As full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing this on San Francisco Bay out by Alcatraz and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But blue water sailing is profoundly more difficult – something Adrift graphically conveys. Know that you don’t ever need to have stepped topside on a teak deck to become lost in Adrift. It’s an amazing film. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp star in Adrift.

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Grave of Fireflies. Movie review by Chris Honoré Grave of Fireflies is a must-see if you have been captured by the extraordinary animation and storytelling that has come to define Studio Ghibli. It is, without hesitation, an achingly beautiful film that transcends all expectations. Know, however, that the story is profoundly sad and emotive. Because it is animated, and its two main characters are children, it is easy to assume that its subject matter will reflect the fanciful innocence associated with the animé genre. But while the film is an allegory of sorts, it also challenges our assumptions about animation. Grave of Fireflies is set in Kobe, Japan. The year is 1945, and World War II is coming to a close, despite the unwillingness of the Japanese to stand down. Told in a long flashback, the tale focuses on a 14-year-old boy named Seita (J. Robert Spencer) and his 5-year-old sister, Setsuko (Rhoda Chrosite). Orphaned by allied fire-bombings, their mother killed, they go to live with their aunt (Amy Jones) whose initial charitable response to the children turns surprisingly bitter. Seita finally decides that they must leave. The two find a cave in the hills and for a brief time all is well. But before long malnutrition stalks them. Seita is beaten while looking for food and Setsuko falls ill. Their struggle is the struggle of the vulnerable who must confront events not of their making and the arc of the story is wrenchingly inevitable. There is no one they can turn to, no adults step forward to aid them. Kindness and generosity are casualties of war. They are profoundly alone. As is customary from Studio Ghibli, Grave of Fireflies is a masterpiece, based on the semi-biographical story by Akiyuki Nosaka. Hand-drawn, an art form that many studios have discarded, it is breathtaking, and a remarkable achievement. I would suggest that perhaps mature tweens, teens and adults are the intended viewers, and even so, they will find the film difficult, though never melodramatic. Of course, there are scenes of star-filled skies and stretching glades woven into this harrowing tragedy. However Grave of Fireflies is ultimately a lyrical meditation about the inherent nihilism of war and those who suffer. Grave of Fireflies. Directed by Isao Takahata. Animé by Studio Ghibli. With the voices of J. Robert Spencer, Rhoda Chrosite and Amy Jones. 1 hr., 28 min. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Grave of Fireflies.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Grave of Fireflies an achingly beautiful film

articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Inside Out. Film review by Chris Honoré The idea comprising the essence of Pixar’s Inside Out is inspired. The filmmakers, who have a long and solid resume of animated films (Up, Wall-E, Toy Story, Finding Nemo), are able to confront the third dimension in movies because they can. This is, after all, a world in which animators can take a step that otherwise would be impossible in a photographed feature. Here’s what they did: knowing that a filmed narrative cannot penetrate a character’s mind (except, perhaps, using voice over), they tell a familiar story of an 11-year-old girl named Riley (Kaitlyn Dias). She lives happily in the embrace of her parents in Minnesota, has loads of friends and plays on a hockey team. For Riley life is better than good. That is until her father takes a new job and they must relocate to San Francisco. Up until this point, Riley’s default setting is contentment and joy – school, friends, sports all fit into a much-enjoyed spectrum of childhood on the cusp of being a teenager (Riley defines the word tween). With the impending move, Riley’s world is rocked. She is confronted with challenges that are new to her. Her new house is a bit grim, as is her neighborhood. She tries out for hockey and it doesn’t go well. Suddenly Riley begins to slide into a funk. And though her parents ask her if everything is all right (of course, Riley grumbles that all is fine), the emotions taking place inside are a different story. Here is where the Pixar storytellers create another world. They craft a kind of emotional wheelhouse (in Riley’s head) that includes all of Riley’s emotions. It’s wonderful. There’s Joy (Amy Poehler), Fear (Bill Hader), Anger (Lewis Black), Disgust (Mindy Kaling) and Sadness (Phyllis Smith). Each is a unique and funny and engaging character, and all are coping with Riley’s new world and a bevy of feelings that are at first decidedly unsettling. Riley has always been encouraged to be happy. To smile. But then she has been grounded in a spiffy life. Hence Joy, vivacious and energetic, has always had her hand on the tiller, suddenly Anger and Fear and Sadness (most especially) find that their roles in Riley’s emotions are growing. Meanwhile, Joy, becomes lost in a labyrinth of Riley’s mind and must struggle to find its way back to emotion central before things get really awful for Riley. You have to see this crew in action – Anger is a squat, redfaced, short-fused guy – to have a complete understanding of what Pixar has accomplished. It tells a compelling story, one that kids will relate to and one that adults will quickly recognize . . Growth is dealing with the internal dialogue that takes place all of our lives. This may be Riley’s first experience with an unfamiliar spectrum of emotions, but it won’t be her last. And beginning on the journey of dealing with the crew up in the wheelhouse, to include Sadness and Fear and Anger, as well as Joy, she must make choices and sort out some stuff. Of course, it’s all a central if imperfect part of life. It’s also the meaning of that lifelong process called “growing up”, something that Riley eventually comes to realize. Watch for the credits. They’re terrific. As is Inside Out. Inside Out. Animated from Pixar Animation Studios and Walt Disney Pictures. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG. Released in 2015.
articles.title: Inside Out a marvel of animated moviemaking

articles.text: The California Society of Printmakers’ 106th Exhibition will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from November 15 to December 5. As part of the wide range of art offered at the Center throughout the year, the Society of Printmakers exhibition is an annual show. It highlights a variety of printmaking techniques and the ways its member artists use many techniques to create unique and meaningful works of art. The Society’s mission is to support the integrity of traditional printmaking while providing a community for artists exploring new directions in contemporary print methods. To that end, the Society organizes exhibitions, artist talks, demonstrations, lectures, residencies, and produces a journal publication. Gallery viewing will be by reservation this year, within a safe and socially distanced setting. Gallery dates are Saturday and Sunday, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. on November 15, 21-22, 28-29, and from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Saturday, December 5. Timed entry will be in 45-minute time periods. With a maximum of 10 visitors per period. Masks are required. Check back here soon for a link to make your reservation.
articles.title: Large California Printmakers exhibit returns to PCA

articles.text: Josef Haydn portrait by Ludwig Guttenbrunn Very few composers changed the course of music. The list is short. In chronological order they were Haydn, Beethoven, Paganini, Berlioz, Wagner, and Stravinsky. That’s about it. The main reason is that music is the most conservative of all the arts, and thus is the last to change directions. The graphic arts innovate first. They are happy flinging paint on a canvas. But music continues like the meandering of an old river. The rapids are few. In many ways, music is reactive. It is the last of the arts to change. Josef Haydn is the first composer to figure prominently as an innovator. It is interesting to consider the similarities between Haydn and Beethoven. People often think of Ludwig von Beethoven as the stupendous creator. To this, musicologists counter that Haydn did it long before Beethoven. Haydn established the tradition. He invented the string quartet and the symphony. Beethoven then took it to the iconoclast level – and in this he was perfect. We must keep in mind that Beethoven always lamented that the public never really understood him. They saw him as strange and eccentric. He was, however, the epitome of humanity, both personally and musically. All of the composers on this list were sensitive and generous. You might ask, what about Wagner? Yes, he fits the definition, but only in his own way. The next innovator was the French composer Hector Berlioz. His cataclysmic Symphonie Fantastique came only five years after the death of Beethoven. Berlioz painted his musical canvases with a completely new palette. Richard Wagner’s contributions to music are often considered the greatest of all. He unified all elements of music with drama and stage production. The most recent innovator was the Russian-born Igor Stravinsky. Like Beethoven, Stravinsky threw tradition out the window, then retrieved what society viewed as reprehensible and flung it in the face of tradition. He was a master of that… Like no one before. But the most sensational by far was Niccolò Paganini. In fact, he was the most sensational entertainer of all time. This is no exaggeration. Music is delineated by Paganini. When he arrived, the entire musical world changed. Paganini’s genius drew on all those violinists who came before him. He assimilated everything and then blazed a trail that no one had ever taken. He was, in every way, the embodiment of the modern performer – absolutely a trail-blazing virtuoso. He was also the prototype of the media-wise public figure. It was Paganini, in fact, who was the inventor of the publicity machine. Every entertainer since Paganini has modeled the media blitz after him. Last week, October 27, was Paganini’s birthday. It is interesting to note that Jascha Heifetz’s earth-shattering debut in Carnegie Hall was also on October 27 (1917). Historical recordings can be a revealing time machine. A recent release enabled me to relive a memorable concert of September 1, 1963. It was a gala concert in the Hollywood Bowl featuring Jascha Heifetz on violin, Gregor Piatigorsky on cello, and Leonard Bernstein conducting the New York Philharmonic. They performed the Brahms double concerto. What a different musical world it was back then. Those musicians were titans – so elevated from the terrestrial which passes as genius today. Standing ovations were earned back then, and Heifetz and Piatigorsky got a standing ovation at that September concert. I left the performance imagining myself in heaven. How wonderful it is to relive that experience.
articles.title: Timeless innovation

articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, will end on November 8 with a performance by Robert Howard. Howard, a cellist from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonic Baroque Orchestra, will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. He will also perform select movements from Suites #1, 2, and 3. Bach Connections is the final piece of three performances in the Bach Shorts series. Bach Shorts are one hour, live-streamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of The Six Cello Suites by J.S. Bach. The series showcased performances by two prominent Bay Area cellists, Christopher Costanza and Jennifer Kloetzel, and will conclude next month with Howard. The performance will stream live via YouTube on Sunday, November 8, at 4 p.m. To obtain tickets in advance, visit https:// app.ar ts-people.com /index. php?show=116151.
articles.title: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ Bach Shorts finale on November 8

articles.text: Gowns from the Die Fledermaus show will be available to purchase at this year’s San Francisco Opera costume sale. San Francisco Opera will have its first costume sale online from Friday to Sunday, November 13-15. The annual costume sale, which was moved to online this year due to the coronavirus, features individually designed outfits direct from the opera stage. Each costume carries a piece of San Francisco Opera history and was made locally in the Bay Area by a team of talented artists, craftspeople and costume designers. Unleash your inner warrior with costumes designed for fantasy dramas like Tannhäuser; or party like there’s no tomorrow with the ornate jackets and gowns of Die Fledermaus and The Merry Widow. Make sure to peruse through the size chart, available on the opera’s website, because costumes are often custom-made and are not traditionally sized. In the past, the opera’s costume shop sale has been one of the most anticipated events by patrons and the general public. As part of the wide range of art offered at the Center throughout the year, the Society of Printmakers exhibition is an annual show. It highlights a variety of printmaking techniques and the ways its member artists use many techniques to create unique and meaningful works of art. The Society’s mission is to support the integrity of traditional printmaking while providing a community for artists exploring new directions in contemporary print methods. Gallery viewing will be by reservation this year, within a safe and socially distanced setting. Timeless innovation Josef Haydn portrait by Ludwig Guttenbrunn By Joseph Gold Very few composers changed the course of music. The list is short. In chronological order they were Haydn, Beethoven, Paganini, Berlioz, Wagner, and Stravinsky. That’s about it. The main reason is that music is the most conservative of all the arts, and thus is the last to change directions. The graphic arts innovate first. They are happy flinging paint on a canvas. But music continues like the meandering of an old river. The rapids are few. In many ways, music is reactive. It is the last of the arts to change. Josef Haydn is the first composer to figure prominently as an innovator. It is interesting to consider the similarities between Haydn and Beethoven. People often think of Ludwig von Beethoven as the stupendous creator. To this, musicologists counter that Haydn did it long before Beethoven. Haydn established the tradition. He invented the string quartet and the symphony. Beethoven then took it to the iconoclast level – and in this he was perfect. We must keep in mind that Beethoven always lamented that the public never really understood him. They saw him as strange and eccentric. He was, however, the epitome of humanity, both personally and musically. All of the composers on this list were sensitive and generous. You might ask, what about Wagner? Yes, he fits the definition, but only in his own way. The next innovator was the French composer Hector Berlioz. His cataclysmic Symphonie Fantastique came only five years after the death of Beethoven. Berlioz painted his musical canvases with a completely new palette. Richard Wagner’s contributions to music are often considered the greatest of all. He unified all elements of music with drama and stage production. The most recent innovator was the Russian-born Igor Stravinsky. Like Beethoven, Stravinsky threw tradition out the window, then retrieved what society viewed as reprehensible and flung it in the face of tradition. He was a master of that… Like no one before. But the most sensational by far was Niccolò Paganini. In fact, he was the most sensational entertainer of all time. This is no exaggeration. Music is delineated by Paganini. When he arrived, the entire musical world changed. Paganini’s genius drew on all those violinists who came before him. He assimilated everything and then blazed a trail that no one had ever taken. He was, in every way, the embodiment of the modern performer – absolutely a trail-blazing virtuoso. He was also the prototype of the media-wise public figure. It was Paganini, in fact, who was the inventor of the publicity machine. Every entertainer since Paganini has modeled the media blitz after him. Last week, October 27, was Paganini’s birthday. It is interesting to note that Jascha Heifetz’s earth-shattering debut in Carnegie Hall was also on October 27 (1917). Historical recordings can be a revealing time machine. A recent release enabled me to relive a memorable concert of September 1, 1963. It was a gala concert in the Hollywood Bowl featuring Jascha Heifetz on violin, Gregor Piatigorsky on cello, and Leonard Bernstein conducting the New York Philharmonic. They performed the Brahms double concerto. What a different musical world it was back then. Those musicians were titans – so elevated from the terrestrial which passes as genius today. Standing ovations were earned back then, and Heifetz and Piatigorsky got a standing ovation at that September concert. I left the performance imagining myself in heaven. How wonderful it is to relive that experience. Gold Coast Chamber Players’ Bach Shorts finale on November 8 By Allyson Aleksey Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, will end on November 8 with a performance by Robert Howard. Howard, a cellist from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonic Baroque Orchestra, will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. He will also perform select movements from Suites #1, 2, and 3. Bach Connections is the final piece of three performances in the Bach Shorts series. Bach Shorts are one hour, live-streamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of The Six Cello Suites by J.S. Bach. The annual costume sale, which was moved to online this year due to the coronavirus, features individually designed outfits direct from the opera stage. articles.text: Piedmont, like much of California, is blessed with what is considered a temperate Mediterranean climate – often perfect for outdoor activities. To take advantage of this we create different kinds of outdoor spaces, everything from nature parks to improved sports fields to smaller contained areas for dining, socializing, or just relaxing. These latter spaces are often referred to as “outdoor rooms” in architectural jargon. While the exact description of an outdoor room is a little vague, there are a number of characteristics that help define this type of space, examples of which become recognizable when walking through town. I think the chief characteristic of an outdoor room is often referred to as a sense of enclosure, resembling in a certain way a “room” without a roof. Why a feeling of enclosure makes an outdoor space appealing and comfortable is difficult to define. Maybe it is a mixture of privacy, security, a feeling of boundary to a more developed space or simply the designation of a definitive area for a certain use, like the BBQ terrace or the dining patio. This enclosure is often made up of the exterior walls of an adjoining building. Higher planting, shrubbery, landscape walls or even trees can also form or contribute to these “walls” that form enclosure. Beautiful outdoor spaces in the category of outdoor rooms are most often next to and strongly connected to an adjacent common use interior space (like a Photos by Will Adams This convenient and comfortable outdoor sitting area next to the city hall entrance is a wonderful “outdoor room”: defined and enclosed by part of the exterior building wall of the council chambers, by the concrete planters with shrubbery, and the new scalloped-topped wall to the west (out of picture). The courtyard at Piedmont Community Church is certainly an “outdoor room”. Enclosed by building facades on three sides, the mature oak trees on the east, and the large redwoods to the south, it forms a part of the “entry experience” we spoke of last week as well as a popular function space where various kinds of events are held.

articles.text: You may have assumed from my name that I am French. That is half true but the other half of me hails from Scotland. I spend most of my time in the land of wine but once in a while my Scottish heart yearns for a wee dram of whisky. Since I drink it rarely, I tend to stay away from the popular blended whiskies like Johnnie Walker or Dewars and head straight for the king of whisky – Single Malt Scotch. For those of you unfamiliar with the ways of Scotch let me explain the two types of Scotch whisky. Single malt whiskies are made from malt and are produced at a single distillery. Blended whiskies are. as the name suggests. made from a blend of two or more single malt whiskies along with the addition of neutral grain whisky. It is the addition of the latter that allows blended whisky to be sold at a lower price. There is also the matter of volume - the production of single malt whiskies is miniscule compared with the millions of bottles of the major blends like Johnnie Walker, Cutty Sark, Famous Grouse. (By the way I am not a single malt snob. Some of the better blends like Grouse make a fine drink too.) Up until the 70’s, single malts were not sold by themselves as luxury items; they just went into the major blends. But in the 70’s two single malts were released that rocked the whisky world – Glenfiddich and Glenlivet. They were light and smooth and fine textured. What made them successful was that they were not too different from the blends that everyone was familiar with. Today I consider them the least distinctive of the single malts. Over these subsequent decades the world of single malts has exploded. There are now hundreds available on the market. Where there used to be only one Glenmorangie, now there are 15 different bottlings based on the number of years aged and the type of barrel it has been aged in. All the major producers are doing this, and frankly it has gotten a little out of hand. Still, I am always open to finding new and interesting single malts. I love my old standbys (Macallan, Lagavulin, Talisker) but it is really exciting to discover a new outstanding whisky that really rings your bells. So, I am pleased to share with you four recent discoveries that are worth seeking out and exploring. (All are whiskies imported by 375park.com.) anCnoc This new whisky (pronounced “a-nock”) is an outgrowth of the famous Knockdhu distillery in Aberdeenshire. The Knockdhu distillery (1894) is a small, charming distillery that draws its clear, pure water from a spring that in Gaelic is called anCnoc. The whisky is like a cross between a Speyside whisky and a Highland whisky and is light and refreshing. The nose is bright with freshly squeezed orange and lemon juices, and honey. The early palate mirrors the fresh fruit-laden nose, with developing ginger, peach and malt notes. Slowly drying in the finish ending it offers a smooth satisfaction. A lovely pre-dinner dram. Balblair 2005 Established in 1790, Balblair is the oldest working distillery in the Highlands. Unlike most distilleries they do not have a “current “product. They are the only distillery in in Scotland to solely release vintage whiskies. Each bottle is marked with the year that the whisky was “laid down” (put in barrel). They are released only when the distillery manager believes the moment has come. In other words, they treat each year as unique, as do vintners of fine wine. articles.text: Working from home for eight months at this point, and into the foreseeable future, has meant preparing lunch at home too. Most days I cobble together a plate of leftovers, but sometimes making lunch from scratch is the way to go. Eating out for lunch was my previous norm, and a San Francisco FiDi office meant there was no shortage of variety and options. Since I do WFH, any lunch I prepare from scratch has to be fast, and with ingredients on hand. Variety is a small pleasure too. The short start-to-finish of this satisfying bowl of noodle soup also means you can have it in your rotation for whenever you need a quick and easy meal – lunch or dinner. This recipe puts together a handful of pantry and ‘fridge staples, with endless substitutions for variety. Any noodle will work: soba, ramen, udon, rice sticks or spaghetti. Similarly, to “doctor” the broth, try flavor profiles from Central and Southeast Asia using curry powders or prepared pastes. These days there are many options in broths and flavors. You may find ones that require little to no “doctoring” for an easier means to a delicious end. I am already thinking of a Thai-style version by adding a splash of coconut milk and a spoonful of prepared curry paste, red or green; and adding shrimp for protein. The recipe below is a guide based on one serving, but it scales easily according to the number of servings desired, and heft of the appetites involved. It’s perfect for a quick dinner too. Soba Noodle Soup with Salmon and Broccoli Makes one hearty bowl INGREDIENTS For each serving: • 2 cups chicken broth, or preferred substitute • 1-1/2 ounces dried soba noodles • 3 ounces cooked salmon • 1/2 cup broccoli flowerets • 1/4 cup fresh mushrooms, sliced, optional • 1 green onion, sliced thin • 1/2 teaspoon soy sauce, to taste • 1/4 teaspoon toasted sesame seed oil • Pinch of powdered ginger, or a few of freshly grated • Pinch of granulated garlic, or a few of freshly grated • Pinch of ground white pepper • Sprinkle of shichimi togarashi, Japanese chili spice mix, to taste INSTRUCTIONS In a medium saucepan, boil the soba noodles according to package directions, except stop cooking just shy of done. They will continue cooking a bit while you prepare the broth. The brand I use calls for four minutes’ cooking time, I stop at about three minutes. Drain the soba noodles in a strainer and transfer to a prewarmed serving bowl. Make sure to use a generously sized bowl to assure everything fits. In the same saucepan, combine the broth, soy sauce, toasted sesame oil, ginger, garlic and white pepper to taste; and bring to a low boil. Add the broccoli and mushrooms (if using) and cook until just tender. Add the cooked salmon to reheat it. Add the salmon, broccoli and mushrooms to the soba noodles and then pour the hot broth over. Garnish with green onions and add shichimi togarashi, or other chili seasoning to taste. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com

articles.text: Barbara Jean Borsuk, a resident of Piedmont for more than 60 years, passed away peacefully surrounded by her family on September 19, 2020. She was 97. Born Barbara Jean Bacharach on October 28, 1922 in Oakland, she was the daughter of Percy and Etta Bacharach. She graduated from Lowell High School in San Francisco. and married Sidney Borsuk after World War II. A short while later they moved to Piedmont. Barbara firmly believed in education, and at age 63 she earned a bachelor’s degree in art at Holy Names University. Besides being active in her family’s real estate business, Barbara owned and managed a toy shop on Piedmont Avenue in the 1980s, which piqued her interest in designing dollhouses and miniatures. Barbara and Sidney had terrific adventures together, traveling the world, entertaining, and going on family vacations. They especially loved treating their family to annual vacations in Maui over the holidays. articles.text: David Maglaty, FAIA, 70, died at home in Piedmont with his family by his side on October 16, 2020. He spent the last year of his life with his family and friends, biking, walking and visiting in between treatments for prostate cancer. Born on June 29, 1950 in Hartford, Connecticut, David Cook Maglaty was the son of Esther Lila (Cook) Maglaty and Mario Louis Maglaty. David and his siblings Lois and Mark were raised in West Hartford where he attended school until college. In 1977 he graduated with a Bachelor of Architecture from the University of Oregon in Eugene. David met his wife, Jean Hansen, at Ratcliff Architects in Berkeley in July 1979. A lifelong runner, David’s days began with coffee, followed most days by a 5-7 mile run. He ran his first marathon shortly after his daughter’s birth, followed by some triathlons, and many 5K races, often competing with his neighbor and fellow runner, Steve Sidney. David was a consummate architect. Ever investigating the context and site for each project, working closely with the communities and clients where his projects were built, he explored design options with a skilled pencil or pen. He brought to life sketches that are today considered accomplished works in themselves, inspirations for many projects that were built, and some not. David is remembered for many projects, often on college campuses and the communities they serve. Close to home, his design of student infill housing for UC Berkeley, Units 1 and 2, on College Avenue and Durant Street, illustrates his idea that social space plays an important role and ultimately fosters a safer community environment. David’s work received numerous awards over the years, including the prestigious AIA National Honor Award in 2008 for the Units 1 and 2, Infill Student Housing at UC Berkeley (EHDD), as well as the AIA Santa Clara in 2012 and San Francisco Honor Award in 2013 David Maglaty, an architect and athlete, died at home on October 16. He was 70. for the Orchard School Library in San Jose (HMC). David was named a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 2014. David and Jean raised their children, Alissa and Peter, in Piedmont and he cherished them, appreciating every moment shared. He coached soccer for both kids’ teams and was a pack leader for Peter’s Cub Scout and Boy Scout troops. Father and son enjoyed high Sierra backpacking trips every year through high school with Troop 15. David is survived by his best friend and wife of 39 years, Jean Hansen, daughter, Alissa Maglaty and son, Peter Maglaty. He will be greatly missed by his sister, Lois McCabe and brother, Mark Maglaty; and his many beloved in-laws, walking buddies, fellow runners, colleagues and friends. The family is indebted to the staff at Kaiser Permanente, Oakland, especially their oncology department, palliative and hospice staff. They became a part of the family, and we so appreciate their regimens that kept David comfortable this past year. To attend a celebration/memorial, please contact the family at remembering.david.maglaty@ gmail.com. To make a contribution in memory of David that supports cancer research for Bay Area fire fighters and families, go to San Francisco Firefighters Cancer Prevention Foundation, https:// www.sffcpf.org/

articles.text: Jim Adams, a Piedmont native, passed away far too early of natural causes on October 23, 2020 at his home in San Francisco. He spent his last few days at his beloved family home in Glenbrook, Nevada, with beautiful, sunny Fall weather and sunsets that were “epic”. He was 58. Born James Thomas Adams on Groundhog Day, February 2, 1962, he was the son of Thomas and Sally Adams. He spent a happy childhood in Piedmont, with his older siblings, Julie and Mike. He attended Piedmont High School where he made lifelong friends through football, rugby, Rigma Lions and the Hagglund’s Hackers Championship basketball team. He graduated in 1980 and attended Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. He graduated from San Francisco State with a bachelor’s degree in Journalism. He settled in San Francisco and began a career as a stock brofamily. He even checked Punxatawney, PA off of his bucket list and saw the Groundhog at dawn on his birthday. Jim enjoyed all things outdoors – from fly fishing to duck hunting and especially scuba diving. He loved to simply watch the ocean and look for whales. He was a devoted member of the Bohemian Club and his beloved Camp, Meyerling. He was also a member of the St. Francis Yacht Club and had many friends in both clubs. Jim Adams is survived by his wife Christina, his mother Sally Adams, sister Julie Bradner and Randy, brother Mike Adams and Lori, and six nephews: Doug and Greg Bradner, and Tommy (Julia), Jake, Ted and Brent Adams. He leaves behind too many good friends to count. At Jim’s request, due to Covid there will be no public service. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: Pictured are Piedmont Walkers Barry Dubin, Jane and Dick Cohen, Helen and Lowell Dittmer and Barbara and Bob Morrison. On Saturday, October 24, a group of Piedmonters gathered for the 2020 East Bay Alzheimer’s Walk. Usually held in San Ramon, this year it was held in various neighborhoods throughout the East Bay to avoid gathering in large numbers due to current health restrictions imposed by Alameda County Public Health Department during the pandemic. Barbara Morrison formed the Beemorr Team about 10 years ago when she walked with her San Jose friend whose sister developed early Alzheimer’s in her 40’s. Four years ago, that same friend developed Alzheimer’s at age 70 - so Barbara now walks to honor her struggle with the disease. Other team members joined the Morrisons to honor their own family members and friends who have suffered from Alzheimer’s. This year, Beemorr’s team raised over $8,000 for the Alzheimer’s Association.
articles.title: Piedmonters turn out for annual Alzheimer’s Walk

Top Piedmont style-makers share their thoughts on Christmas By Sara Cumbelich Getting together with the designing women – and men – from Piedmont is always interesting, and especially as we begin to plan for the Holidays. Overall, the sense is that 2021 is an opportunity for a fresh start beginning with decorating for Christmas. Contributing to this segment on “What’s your Holiday Vibe?” are Laura Martin Bovard from LMB Interiors, Rachelle Sessions from RKS Interiors, and Nathan Walden of Nathan & Co. Interestingly, all three designers share strong preferences for white lights, Silvertip trees and ceiling-high trees filled with ornaments. And they all agree that the secret to keeping a tree fresh is to obsess – be obsessive about the water level. So, you’re saying, ‘It’s only November 1st, why are we talking about Christmas décor?’ It took a pandemic to change the way we think about our Christmas preparations. And because “a Scout is prepared”, the Piedmont Scout BSA Council is offering online Christmas tree shopping now – in November. They are scheduling deliveries and pickups for after Thanksgiving, but by ordering early, you’ll be sure to have the type and size of tree that you’ve always had. How to do it? Simply visit www. scouttreelot.org to purchase your trees, tree stands, wreaths and garlands. It culdn’t be easier. Some of us begin to prepare just after Halloween and some Rachelle Sessions makes glitter, clear glass, white lights, red and greenery work in a very stylish and Christmas tree at Nathan Walden’s country house. warm way. traditionalists don’t think about Christmas until Thanksgiving is a memory. Retailers know they don’t have that luxury. “We literally start ordering ornaments in January of each year. Imagine picking out ornaments after surviving the holiday rush?” opined Nathan Walden. Rachelle Sessions advises a thousand points of light! “You can’t have too many white lights on a tree, and when the tree is full add 50 more ornaments” she offered. It’s yes to glitter, toppers and white lights, but no food on the tree. It has something to do with homemade gingerbread ornaments and ants, needless to say, the ornaments were off-limits to the children. She doesn’t mix it up as much as she did in the past, finding herself going back to her favorite, and very elegant motif: red, silver and clear on a beautiful Silvertip. Like Rachelle, Laura Bovard said, “the saving grace of the hodgepodge collection of whimsical, sentimental, not-so-attractive decorations is my use of high-quality lights and hanging them on a very beautiful Silvertip tree.” She recommends white lights, an irreverent topper, and nothing too traditional, more on the vintage-modern vibe. She always buys a real tree but imagines an aluminum 1950s tinsel tree for a change. “I find that we all, especially the kids, like the predictability and comfort of our traditions.” “The quest for the perfect tree is always a daunting endeavor,” added Walden. “Each year the perfect tree has a different aesthetic goal to me,” he said. Some years, he loves the starkness of a Silvertip, other years he craves the happiness of a Noble Fir. Expanding on tree care, he said, “It also helps to keep the tree away from heating vents, fireplaces or any heat source. I love trees that can be lit and seen from the street, but a little less obviously placed. Direct sunlight on warmer December days can really dry out a tree.” When Walden was askd about using a topper, he answered “never.” He loves glitter and warm white lights. Color lights are great but stick to one color – never mix colors. He loves modern, vintage and sophisticated styles and tends to mix all three together for a look that is unique. “I love the beauty of nature and the organic feel of something not being absolutely perfect”, so I always buy a real tree. All agree that you should invest in a good waterproof tree stand. Pay attention to getting the right stand for the size of tree. The weight of tree and the weight of the ornaments in the wrong stand can cause a disaster. It’s 2020, so plan accordingly. The Piedmont Scout Tree Lot is open online now and for scheduled delivery or pickup after Thanksgiving. This year’s inventory will be high quality – like always – with beautiful Silvertips, Noble and Douglas Firs from Oregon, along with wreaths, garlands and quality tree stands available for purchase at scouttreelot.org. articles.text: Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning will have a distinctly different look this year. Covid-19 has thrown the world into a sticky mess - not unlike a kitchen sink after Thanksgiving dinner. Given Alameda County health directives, the Piedmont Turkey Trot will not be held live this year. However, the Trot is putting its best shank forward and will carry on the spirit of the Trot – virtually in 2020. While we can’t physically gather as usual to celebrate what would be the 19th Annual Trot amidst the beautiful fall colors on the lovely roads of Piedmont, we can still trot amongst ourselves this Thanksgiving – physically-distanced, but virtually-united. The Piedmont Turkey Trot Challenge will be a virtual scavenger hunt. Register online at piedmontturkeytrot.com and then run or walk the streets of Piedmont to find the PTT lawn signs in various gardens around town. Snap a selfie with the sign, upload to our Instagram account @piedmontturkeytrot, and be automatically entered into a drawing for prizes. Each Instagram posting from a registered participant is an official entry. The more signs you find, the more opportunities you will have to win. If you are looking to move your feet a little faster, participants may also choose to run their favorite 5K route on their own or in family pods, then upload their 5K time for bragging rights at their (smaller, yet mighty) Thanksgiving table. Lawn signs will be up from November 15 to November 29. Registration is $10. See you on Instagram!
articles.title: Piedmont Turkey Trot shifts to a Challenge

articles.text: Alameda County remains in Orange Tier for reopening of businesses Four more cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont during the past seven days, according to information from the Alameda County Public Health Department yesterday, Tuesday, November 3. In total, 47 cases now have been reported in the City since the coronavirus pandemic began in March. Overall in Alameda County, the weekly positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 1.6 percent, a slight uptick compared to recent weeks. The number of new cases countywide has crept upward in recent days, although figures are well below numbers in August. Yesterday, there were 55 new cases in the county. On August 13, the worst day yet for the county, there were 421 new cases. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 24,162, an increase of over 500 cases from one week ago. The county has recorded 466 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 9,273. In Hayward, 3,565 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,700 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,359 and Livermore reported 1,028. Alameda County updated its shelter-in-place order on Friday, October 23 that reflect the county’s status as an Orange Tier county. According to California’s reopening system, the Orange Tier is the second-least restrictive tier for reopening the economy. The state placed Alameda County into the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, on October 13. Indoor dining is now allowed, but capacity must be restricted to 25 percent or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Restaurant owners are not rushing to reopen indoors, many choosing to continue with outdoor dining. Bowling alleys, indoor worship services, movie theaters and gyms can reopen, all with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions for indoor retail and malls have been increased to 50 percent. Alameda County’s new cases per day remains too high for the county to meet benchmarks for the Yellow Tier, or Minimal Tier. The county is recording an average of 3.2 cases per 100,000 people. A county must have 1 case per 100,000 or fewer to be in the Yellow Tier. San Francisco is the only county in the Bay Area currently in the Yellow Tier. As of press time, 934,672 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded in California. There have been 17,686 deaths due to the disease statewide.

articles.text: Piedmont police arrested a man sleeping in his car at 6:34 a.m. one day before Halloween when he was found to have an outstanding $10,000 warrant out of Alameda County for a parole violation of Grand Theft. After receiving a call about a suspicious vehicle, the police interviewed and arrested Anthony Smith, 31, a transient, who was in a silver Mercedes parked on Oakland Avenue. Smith was on probation for grand theft and carrying a loaded firearm in public. Officers arrested Smith and transported him to Santa Rita jail without incident. The vehicle was left parked at the location of arrest. It was Piedmont’s first transport to jail of arrested individuals in weeks. Many suspects have been arrested and cited but have not gone to jail because of COVID-19 limitations on jail capacity.

articles.text: Piedmont elementary schools will not reopen November 3rd; the return of kids to in-person learning has been rescheduled for Tuesday, December 1st for TK-2 grade and December 8th for grades 3-5. According to School Superintendent Randy Booker, the delay was due to the district’s inability to create a master school schedule for the three elementary schools. Teachers opting out of in-person teaching or resigning has left the district short on teachers. A total of 74 percent of parents chose in-person learning for their elementary school students, while 26 percent preferred to stay with distance learning. Parent surveys were sent on October 9 and received back by October 14. In an email sent to parents on October 23, Booker stated, “Based on criteria spelled-out in our agreements with staff, teacher assignment has become even more complicated... especially with a desire to minimize involuntary transfers of our educators from one site to another, or even from grade level to grade level.” In the school board meeting Booker said the number of teachers that need to be hired is “less than a handful.” The exact number of teachers that need to be hired has not been publicly disclosed. A job opening on EdJoin was preemptively posted for an elementary school teacher on October 23 (https://www.edjoin.org/Home/ DistrictJobPosting/1339138) School staff members can qualify for leave and opt out of in-person teaching if they are at increased risk of severe illness to COVID-19 based upon criteria on the CDCs list: www.cdc.gov/ coronavirus/2019-ncov/need-extra-precautions/people-with-medical-conditions.html. The list includes conditions such as being over 65, obesity, cancer and heart conditions. Booker stated that “not a huge number” of teachers qualify for this leave at the elementary schools. Staff members can also qualify for the leave if they are the primary caretaker of someone at increased risk. restrictive purple tier of COVID
articles.title: Elementary school reopening delayed 1 month

articles.text: A record number of voters are expected to participate in the 2020 General Election in Piedmont and in Alameda County on November 3. The county has a total of 966,465 registered voters, nearly 77,000 more voters than during the last General Election in 2016. according to the Alameda County Registrar of Voters. Of that total, 59 percent are registered as Democrats, 11 percent as Republicans and 25 percent registered with no party preference. Approximately three weeks ago, the Registrar’s office sent absentee (vote-by-mail) ballots to residents. The state of California took an unprecedented step of mailing a ballot to every active registered voter this fall, after lawmakers approved a bill that required county officials to send A Piedmont voter puts his ballot in the drop box outside the Wells Fargo building. ballots to voters in response to the coronavirus outbreak. Ballot drop-boxes have been placed throughout the Bay Area to assist with the high volume of mail-in ballots this year. In order to accommodate the large turnout, the Registrar has increased the number of official ballot

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black has announced his intention to leave his position with the City in late November, after just two years with the City. He will become Chief of East Jefferson Fire and Rescue in Townsend, Washington. “I have valued my time in Piedmont as part of this team,” said Black. “My fondest memories will be from the relationships and friendships among fellow employees and the community. I feel privileged to have served the residents of Piedmont.” “The Piedmont community Jo Hazelett retires............... 1 Letters................. 2, 3, 10, 29 Question Man..................... 4 Schools . ........................... 6 Crystal Vacker column.......... 8 PPD Blue. .......................... 9 Letters – Measure UU.......... 10 Halloween Scarecrows. ........ 11 Sports............................. 12 Hiking with Jon.................. 15 Stehr art exhibit................. 16 Berkeley Symphony ............ 17 Musical Gourmet ............... 18 Restaurants reopen. ............ 19 Hazelett retirement............. 20 Obituary. .......................... 23 Underwriter List................. 24 Real Estate....................... 26 Piedmont firefighters........... 32 Where in the World?. ........... 32 Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black leaves the city after two years. has benefitted from Chief Black’s time in Piedmont,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “His knowledge of the fire service, particularly in the area of wildland fire has helped focus the Fire Department and organization as a whole on this important topic. We will miss his team spirit, sense of humor, and dedication to his profession.” Chief Black’s professional firefighting career began with Skywalker Ranch Fire Department in Marin County in 1997. A few years later, he relocated to the Clovis Fire Department in the Central Valley. In Clovis, Black rose through the ranks from firefighter, engineer, captain, training officer, to battalion chief. He began work as Piedmont’s Fire Chief on October 1, 2018. Black will remain with the City until November 30. The city will begin a search for his successor.

articles.text: Mayor Bob McBain, Councilmember Betsy Andersen, and School Board member Sarah Pearson answered questions from residents about Measure UU during a virtual forum on October 20. City Administrator Sara Lillevand was also available to provide additional facts, as requested. Resident Dion Lim served as a webinar host and moderator for the event. Measure UU is a $19.5 million bond that would create a new aquatics facility and swimming pool complex. The existing pool is 50 years old, is undersized for the needs of the community, and is in poor condition. Supporters of Measure UU say that, if the measure does not pass, the facilAndersen responded that she and McBain and Pearson were participating as Piedmont residents and not speaking on behalf of or representing any government entities. “The current Piedmont pool is crumbling, and Measure UU is about whether we want to invest in the needs of our residents for the next 50 years,” Andersen said. She then offered some anecdotal reasons for her interest in saving the pool. “My affiliation with the pool began when I was five years old, when I proudly owned my ‘white patch’ and the ability to swim in the big pool. I went on to compete with the Piedmont Swim Team for the next 13 years, and I had my first job as a lifeCouncilmember Betsy Andersen ity is up for permanent closure. Lim began the forum by asking each participant what the community pool means to them and what role it played in their lives as Piedmont residents.
articles.title: McBain, Andersen, Pearson answer questions about Measure UU in live forum

Can you imagine if we made our high school football team do that? Or our basketball or tennis teams? Without our local pool, there will be no summer jobs for our young adults to teach swim classes or lifeguard. articles.text: Cooper’s proven commitment to schools Editor: Based on my experiences working closely with Hilary Cooper on several campaigns for the Piedmont schools, I believe that Hilary would be an excellent school board member. Hilary has proven her commitment to our schools by volunteering for important roles over the past 11 years, including parent club president at PMS and PHS, Spring Fling co-chair, Giving Campaign co-chair (twice), and co-chair of the campaign to pass Measures G&H. I can vouch for Hilary’s capabilities because I worked alongside her, and former school board member Doug Ireland, last fall to co-chair the successful campaign to pass Measures G&H, our very important school parcel taxes. Hilary is one of those rare leaders who is good at both the big picture of strategy and the heavy lifting of day-to-day volunteering. During the campaign, Hilary had great ideas about how to promote and explain the parcel taxes, and she was willing and able to do the work behind the scenes, including endless emails, phone calls and spreadsheets. When Hilary decided to run for school board, I happily volunteered to be her campaign manager. I believe that one of the most important things we can do to support our schools this fall (in addition to donating to the Giving Campaign) is to elect a capable school board. articles.text: Editor: I am writing in full support of Jen Cavenaugh’s campaign for re-election to the Piedmont City Council. We met in 2011 when I was new to the city and our children attended Beach Elementary together. Over the past three years, I have gotten to know Jen better, both professionally and personally, through PADC (Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee). She is a strong advocate for inclusivity and truly listens to the perspectives of all stakeholders. Her ability to build rapport, make strong connections, skillfully collaborate, and take action make her an ideal thought partner between the city and community members. Her experience and background in management and business has proven to be an asset to the city and her deep understanding of fiduciary and fiscal responsibilities benefit both the city and the residents of Piedmont. Her track record as an active volunteer and as a current City Council member speaks to her level of dedication and commitment to public service. She will continue to serve the city well as a leader with integrity. I urge you to vote for Jen for re-election to the Piedmont City Council.
articles.title: Cavenaugh listens to perspectives of all stakeholders

articles.text: Editor: I met Cory Smegal in 2009 when we were co-presidents of our respective elementary school parent clubs. Since those early days, I’ve watched as Cory has consistently taken on new and increasingly significant roles to support our students and district. In addition, now I’m privileged to call her my friend. I again worked closely with Cory last year when I was president of PHS Parents’ Club. Cory was always a supportive and active School Board member, even before COVID turned things upside-down. One attribute I respect about Cory is that she always anchors her positions and efforts on what’s best for students. During her term she has led our district’s efforts to advocate for children across the state. In this way, she helps Piedmont take a leadership role in ensuring quality education for all. The traits that make Cory a great friend also make her a great community leader. She listens, is responsive, and works hard. She’s thoughtful, balanced and researches her positions before she reaches conclusions. And Cory is pragmatic, with a strong sense of fiduciary responsibility. Mostly, Cory cares deeply for our town and its children. Please join me in re-electing Cory Smegal for School Board. –Laura Katter the community. articles.text: Sales from vendors on Piedmont’s public sidewalks and in parks will be allowed as of Wednesday, November 4. Interested vendors will have to apply for a permit with the Piedmont Police Department. Vending in parks will only be permitted on paved areas and pedestrian movement cannot be impeded. The second reading of the ordinance was approved by City Council on Monday, October 5. After some discussion, a first reading was unanimously approved by Council on September 21. The ordinance brings Piedmont’s laws into compliance with new state legislation. On January 1, 2019, Senate Bill 946 established statewide rules for permitting vending on sidewalks and parks. The goal of the bill, signed by former Governor Jerry Brown in 2018, was to make the process less onerous for vendors. “The bill states that its purpose is to promote entrepreneurship and support immigrant and low-income communities, by decriminalizing the selling of food and merchandise on public sidewalks and in parks statewide,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, who has spearheaded the new sidewalk vending permitting process in the City, told the Post. The City defines a sidewalk vendor as a vendor selling food, beverages or merchandise by hand or from a non-motorized cart, wagon or rack. A vendor can be either roaming or stationary, although a stationary vendor cannot set up shop in a residential zone. “[SB 946] requires that cities allow sidewalk vending, and restrictions may only be imposed when directly related to objective public health, safety or welfare concerns,” Bowers continued. “Local jurisdictions that wish to regulate sidewalk vending are required to first adopt a compliant program with rules and regulations consistent with SB 946.” To receive a permit applicants need to provide personal identification, list the items intended for sale and undergo criminal background checks. Applicants must also submit evidence of health permits for food vending and state seller’s permits, as required. Bowers said that approval of applications will likely take 3-5 days, so applicants won’t be able to submit a permit and begin selling the same day. PPD will send notification to applicants regarding the decisions. SB 946 says there can be no limit to the number of sidewalk vendor permits issued. Approval or denial will hinge “on the basis of the ordinance requirements for the application and after an assessment of the individual’s criminal history, if one exists,” Bowers explained. Historically, the City has not allowed vendors on sidewalks or parks. The City Code does not explicitly regulate sidewalk vending, Bowers said. The City Attorney and PPD worked alongside the Planning Department and Recreation Department in crafting the new regulations. Vending may be prohibited under certain circumstances, such as if a vendor impedes movement on a sidewalk or if a special event is taking place. The City still does not allow food trucks. More information can be found on the City’s website.
