articles.text: Energy Reach Codes have the potential to change how the city functions in the future. As an employee with the City’s Planning Department, I would like to explain how they function and how they started. The California Energy Commission is a government organization that wants to ensure that California energy is clean and efficient now and in the future. The commission determines every three years to make sure cities have standards for energy efficiency. The subject may sound dry, but these energy code updates can change how we create buildings and infrastructure throughout the entire state. Once the state agency dictates standards, it is up to local municipalities to enact them and make sure that buildings are code compliant. Sometimes municipalities choose to go beyond what is currently required. This is when “reach codes” come into play. These proposals “reach” further than the existing energy codes, and help municipalities become more efficient than the state mandates. But Reach codes can be a tricky policy to pass. Because the state has new guidelines every three years, municipalities run the risk of having their reach codes become redundant when the next code cycle comes around. For example, the new set of statewide codes will become standard in 2023. However, municipalities don’t want to go too far, as this would leave both residents and contractors frustrated with changes that could feel too heavy-handed. When passing Reach codes, it’s critical to achieve balance: something that residents feel is reasonable and will be approved by City Council, and something that is still valid in three years. Piedmont is in the midst of a Reach code effort. The City is attempting to create a revised Reach code that will drastically cut greenhouse gas emissions from residences. If you are interested in learning about the different perspectives on this Reach code, there are numerous articles in the local papers, as well as on the City website. The City webpage has a FAQ section designed to answer many of the more common questions. Reach codes are common throughout the state, and a pretty good way to bring about changes. It’s an interesting experiment that other cities can look at to determine if a particular code is worth pursuing or not. It allows cities with more resources to attempt more solutions to their energy issues, while cities with fewer resources can pass codes that other cities have adopted, or wait for the three-year state cycle to come around again. For example, Piedmont’s Reach code was partially inspired by Berkeley’s first-in-the-nation ban on gas in new buildings. This kind of “observation before adoption” can make Reach codes a unique way to attempt new ordinances and be environmentally friendly pioneers. Piedmont’s attempts to pass Reach codes showcase some of the leadership for which this community is known. Piedmont is #1 in median family income, #6 in median household income, and #14 in per capita income in the state, so it makes sense for us to be at the forefront of environmental work. The proposed Reach codes is a way for equitable changes to be made in the building sector. Nate Redinbo is an Americorps fellow working this year in the City of Piedmont’s Planning and Building Department. Contact him at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov with any opinions and questions on reach codes, jogging, or bread baking. He will be publishing a monthly article on environmental topics that affect Piedmonters.
articles.title: What exactly are Reach Codes?

articles.text: Piedmont will kick off its second annual citywide Climate Challenge next month, following the success of its first challenge in 2019-2020. Last year, over 250 Piedmont households answered the call to be more environmentally-conscience through different challenges that aimed to reduce the city’s collective greenhouse gas emissions by over 200 tons. The city has announced an intention to double the number of participant households from 250 to 500 sign-ups by Earth Day, April 22, 2021. In addition, a goal has been set to reduce Piedmont’s carbon emissions by 500 tons. The Climate Challenge gives residents the chance to participate in teams and community organizations and to engage in some friendly competition to see which household can reduce their carbon footprint the most. Residents can use the platform to learn more about their household’s emissions and to plan lifestyle changes that will positively affect their impact on the environment. The challenge divides actionbased difficulty, from installing solar panels on houses, to switching to an electric vehicle, to turning off the water while brushing teeth. A new category, “Hanging out at home,” has been added given the number of people sheltering in place. Actions in this category are geared toward those who are telecommuting to work and spending most of their time in their home due to Covid- 19 health restrictions. The city is encouraging residents who signed up for the challenge last year to continue to participate. New challenges have been added. The Climate Challenge will go from November 2020 to May 2021. Sign up for the challenge at https://www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org/. There, you will create a profile for your household, and pledge to commit to adopt sustainable actions that help reduce your carbon footprint. Those actions will be added to your dashboard, and the platform will help with next steps, costs, and questions. “This is a fun, meaningful way to work towards a shared decrease in Piedmont emissions. Households, household transit and household consumption are responsible for more emissions than municipal or commercial activities combined. Using this website brings attention to this fact. It helps us all be more sustainable,” said Climate Fellow Nate Redinbo.
articles.title: Piedmont doubles its goals for this year’s Climate Challenge

articles.text: What do you see in this Rorschach image? I am the Head of a small independent high school and, to be honest, the last seven months have been brutal. And there’s no end in sight. We might go back to school at some point, in some form, but nothing’s going to feel normal, at least not anytime soon. Here’s how I deal with it. Every day I write an email to my school community. It’s called Sue’s Spew. I compose it in the dialect of adolescence, which is sarcasm, and so the thing pretty much writes itself. All I need is a little input from the community and I have my fodder for the day. For instance, last week I gave them a Rorschach image (I’m teaching Psychology and we are studying projective tests). I asked the community to tell me what they saw in the image. I may make this a regular feature of the Spew because I got mountains of stuff, which I then wrote about in my next Spew. People were seeing gnomes, and rhinos, and rhinos on acid . . . it was great. Another time I asked people to share their most recent rabbit hole experiences (mine was aliens) and I got a wealth of material. From the origin of language to Magyarization to Schitt’s Creek, you wouldn’t believe the stuff they came up with. Now this is parents, too – no kid is researching Magyarization, I can tell you. But this is what makes the Spew great – it’s a family affair. I also try to get serious (because, well, I’m the Head of School), and so I have features such as Wise Words Wednesdays. I can’t go too deep otherwise I’ll lose my audience. Teenagers have about a 90-second tolerance for sincerity before they tune out, and actually that’s being generous. So, I Spew away, and I try to get as many people involved as possible. I have my regular readers, such as Alessandro (his real name), who proposed last week – in response to the Rorschach image – that I should let him run the school. Believe me, I’m tempted. I started the Spew on March 12, the day we went online, but back then I didn’t call it the Spew. I sure as heck didn’t think it would last this long. But here we are. Trying to stay connected as a community. Trying to stay positive. Trying ... just to survive. And so, I spew. I highly recommend it. In non-pandemic time an AQI of 151-199 (unhealthy) will result in all PUSD employees being offered and encouraged to use respirator masks when working outdoors. In non-pandemic time if the AQI surpasses 200 (very unhealthy), “the Superintendent shall confer with the Board of Education and the Superintendent for the Alameda County Office of Education to determine if a school closure is warranted,” the policy states. AQI measures six air pollutants: PM2.5 (particulate matter with a diameter less than 2.5 micrometers), PM10, ozone, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide. Piedmont School District will use the Bay Area Air Quality Index Management District (BAAQMD) as the source of its AQI readings. To read the board policy, see: www.agendaonline.net/public/ Meeting/Attachments/DisplayAtt ach ment.aspx?At t ach mentID=1236435&IsArchive=0 In light of the number of days of poor air quality in Piedmont this year due to wildfires in Northern California, the Piedmont School Board voted at its October 14 meeting to enact an Environment Safety policy, which defines actions to take based upon Air Quality Index (AQI) readings. During the COVID-19 pandemic the cut off limit will be 101 AQI (unhealthy for sensitive groups). All classes will be canceled ahead of time if the forecast is for 101 AQI or above. In-person learning is predicated upon having a high level of air circulation. Running school ventilation systems during days with large amounts of particulate in the air would rapidly clog the newly installed MERV-13 filters. The MERV-13 filters are a requirement for schools to be able to open. Superintendent Randy Booker explained that the filters are not only expensive, but difficult to procure at this time. During COVID-19, if the AQI gets to 101 or higher unexpectedly during the school day, and if the ventilation is shut off, school will be canceled for the day. articles.text: Ever since Disney princesses have been created, everyone around the world has loved them. There have been Disney-themed birthdays, millions of people have packed Disneyland parks, and even more continue to buy Disney Princess merchandise. But recently some people have decided to “cancel” them, claiming that something is offensive and therefore the Disney Princess products should not be sold. So, what’s the trouble with Disney princesses – Belle, Rapunzel or Aurora? People are saying that they’re too unrealistic, that their body types and their beauty is not something that children should strive to emulate. I agree, but Disney characters by definition are fantasy and never meant to be something people should strive to achieve. Nor are they the world’s standard of beauty. They’re entertainment, just like fairy tales they represent. Entertainment follows some simple rules: it has to give people joy, make them laugh, make them have a good time. A Disney Princess technically isn’t even a real princess. In their fantasy world, being a princess is just doing what they want without any duties. But being a real royal is much harder. Take the Queen of England for example. She doesn’t spend all her time planning parties and hanging out with her friends. She actually has to run a whole country. She has to discuss policies with her parliament, implement new rules, meet dignitaries. When the creators of Disney Princesses were brainstorming what their characters would represent, I’m quite sure it wasn’t real royalty. People are also saying that the Disney Princesses lack diversity. This is wrong on many levels and shows ignorance. There are many different cultures, ethnicities and backgrounds among Disney princesses. For example, there is Princess Jasmine of Saudi Arabia, Princess Anastasia of Russia, Princess Tiana of New Orleans, who is African-American, Merida of Scotland, and Pocahontas, a Native American. And then there’s Ariel, who is half-fish. Yes, the Disney organization has had its problems with diversity, but they are demonstrating that any culture or ethnicity can be a princess. Not that everything is flawless in the Disney universe. Disney recently released the live action Mulan on the Disney Plus channel. Mulan is a Chinese princess, so Disney filmed parts of it in China. Some scenes were shot in the province where Uigher Muslims, a local oppressed minority, had been forced into internment camps. (China continues to deny the existence of these camps). That caused rightful criticism from human rights advocates around the world. The lead actress Liu Yifei spoke out in support of the police in Hong Kong, despite the fact the police were using excessive force and violence against the pro-democracy protesters. So, Disney could have done a better job. And it doesn’t help the Disney image to see some poor production decisions. Mushu, the beloved small red dragon from the Mulan animation, is missing in the live action version. And there is no singing and no love interest. But does a problem with one particular movie mean we should “cancel” the entire franchise? I don’t think so. Cancel culture, of course, isn’t just the Disney Princess problem. People are “canceling” movies, other people, songs, basically anything that they deem unfit or offensive for today’s world. Anybody can get “cancelled” at any moment. It got so bad that former President Barack Obama recently called attention to the cancel culture. In a video, he said, “That’s not activism. If all you’re doing is casting stones, then that’s probably not going to get you very far.” I agree: if you tell everyone what they are doing is wrong, that’s not going to create change. Instead, we should openly discuss important issues. We should learn to listen, not just to shut down. I grew up with the Disney Princesses. When I was a kid I would watch princess movies and I wanted to be just like them, which for me meant running through the forest, meeting Prince Charming, and having flawless hair in the morning, I did want all that, but I never thought that I had to look like them, or that I had to be perfect in every way. What the princesses taught me was that it’s the inner beauty that counts, that kindness is

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: The time is Now for Measure UU Our kids are grown, we don’t swim often, and we are 100% in support of Measure UU. Twenty-three years ago, when we moved to Piedmont with two young boys and a daughter on the way, there was a pool for us because caring people decades earlier had built it. Like most young families we couldn’t afford a private club and we didn’t have enough hours in the day to drive to other towns. The Piedmont pool taught our kids to swim, introduced us to our neighbors and lifelong friends, and provided cool relief on hot nights. It was a gift that Piedmonters whose kids were long grown had given to us. Now we’re thankful for the chance to pay it forward. The time is right for Measure UU. Our 56-year-old pool is no longer viable. It is no longer functional, and it is decades out of date for competitive swimming, water polo, and recreational sports. If we leave it empty, we deprive today’s families and athletes of an asset we’ve all had the opportunity to enjoy. And if there were ever a moment to take a pool off-line and rebuild it with minimal disruption, it is right now when a global pandemic restricts most swimming anyway. We can build something for the next 50 years now and give everyone in Piedmont a better place to gather when this sad and lonely time ends. So whether you ever expect to use the Piedmont pool or not, please vote for Measure UU. A community is more than just people who live in the same space; it’s a space where people look out for one another. Today, our home is literally surrounded by families with young children. They’ve settled here because generations of Piedmonters before them invested in families yet to come. These families make our lives richer (and our homes more valuable). It’s one of the strange joys of living in a place like this that whenever you do something good for others, you somehow find it does something good for you, too. A new pool helps all of us. Please join us in voting Yes on Measure UU to invest in a healthy Piedmont. get, and then hire the appropriate designers, contractors and other experts to bring your ideas to reality. If the community can first agree on the need for a new pool to replace the now defunct facility, then Measure UU authorizes up to $19.5 million which will be overseen by a committee and issued based on the final design. Setting a bond limit now and having each household pay for the bond issue is appropriate. I would submit that construction of a beautiful, new, public pool facility in Piedmont in return for a bond issue that costs less than the price of a Starbucks Venti Latte per week, per household, is an affordable and not unreasonable price for Piedmont residents to bear. Please join me in support of Measure UU. We can come together as a community and replace this deteriorated aquatics facility with a new pool facility for future generations to enjoy.

articles.text: What is Measure UU? Measure UU is a local Bond Measure which will provide funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable community pool for Piedmont families, students, and adults of all ages. Why is Measure UU needed? Built in 1964, the Piedmont Community Pool is well past the end of its useful life and needs to be replaced. Not only are there serious safety issues (on more than one occasion the concrete deck has failed and crumbled into the pool), the locker room facilities are outdated and restrooms do not comply with the Americans with Disability Act (ADA) requirements, the decades-old plumbing is failing and the pool leaks approximately 3,000 gallons of water daily – over a million gallons a year. Without the Piedmont Community Pool, Piedmont would be the only city (and only public school district) in Alameda County without access to a local pool. What will Measure UU funds do? The successful passage of Measure UU ensures that the Piedmont community will continue to have its own local pool facility for school sports/PE programs, lessons, and recreation, for the next 50 years. The cost includes planning, architectural fees, legal fees, demolition and construction for two new pools, restrooms, locker rooms, and community space. The three existing pools will be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. How much will Measure UU cost? Measure UU would allow the City to issue up to $19.5M in 30-year fixed rate bonds. Measure UU will cost 2.6 cents per $100 of assessed home value (NOT market rate value). For the median Piedmont home, this works out to less than 75 cents a day. To look up your assessed value, use this link to the Alameda County Assessor’s Office and enter your address: http://acgov. org/MS/prop/index.aspx What happens if Measure UU does not pass? When the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool is permanently closed, there will be no local swimming pool for residents or for Piedmont students. Piedmonters will have to travel and pay to use other communities’ pools, or pay initiation fees and annual dues for private swim clubs. With an empty padlocked pool facility in the center of town, the City will then have to decide what to do with that space. It is important to note that while the City decides, there is a cost to securing the site from blight and vandalism, as well as a significant cost associated with any future use of that space, whether it be for a pool or for some other use. If Measure UU passes, will there be a membership fee to use the pool? No, there is no membership fee. The Piedmont Community Pool has been a public pool since 2011. If Measure UU passes, the municipal bonds will be used to rebuild the pool facility. When the new facility opens, pool users will pay daily use fees, camp and lesson fees, annual and seasonal passes, and facility rentals, to offset operating costs. Pools are different from tennis courts and playing fields (which the City pays to maintain) in that pools are required to have trained staff present on-site during hours of operation (e.g. lifeguards, janitorial services). Like all programs run through the Recreation Department, Piedmont residents will have priority and will pay lower use fees than non-residents. For additional information visit the City of Piedmont’s website and FAQ page: https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___ departments/city_clerk/elections/november_3_2020_general_municipal_election/transfer_tax__pool_bond_measures/ pool_bond_frequently_asked_questions More information is also available at: www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com community life for many; a place where they see friends, meet neighbors, and hold celebrations. The project would include restrooms accessible to users of the adjacent Corey Reich Tennis Center, which currently has no restroom access. This would be a significant improvement to another popular community recreational facility. The pool isn’t the only infrastructure in Piedmont that will need attention in the coming years, and it might be more convenient if we didn’t need to address the pool now. However, it will not get less expensive with time, and, with the extraordinarily low interest rates expected to be in place for the next few years, this is actually the most opportune time to build it. Besides, the state of the current pool is such that it is unlikely to be reopened, as the rates of breakdown, mechanical failures, and leakage have made it no longer feasible to operate. The alternative scenario of a facility chained and closed for an indefinite duration is not, in our opinion, acceptable for a community the caliber of Piedmont. There will likely be more bond measures for other community facilities on the ballot in the coming years. Like all of us, we wish these things were less expensive. But we also think that we have all benefitted from capital investments made by generations past, and we think it is upon us now to make capital

articles.text: The November 2016 pool study on which Measure UU is based did not take into account the City Climate Action Plan. It called for a pool three times larger than the existing one. I believe that a larger pool could meet the CAB goal if about 150 households committed to installing solar panels on their houses and to assign the energy generated to the City. The current pool energy bill per year is $60,000. At $1.61 per therm it uses 37,267 therms per year. One therm equals 29.3 kWh. Hence 37,267 therms equals 1,091,925 kWh. Let us assume that because of a better design, the proposed pool would need twice rather than three times as much heat energy. One house with 8 panels produces 4,800 kWh. Therefore 454 houses would generate enough electricity to heat the new pool. Given the efficiency factor of three between electric energy and natural gas to generate heat , 454/3 or about 150 houses would be enough (this holds whether the pool uses a natural gas heat exchanger or heat pumps, as natural gas power plants are about 33% efficient to convert natural gas into electricity due to Carnot). The City would be ahead by 37,267 therms per year, thereby also making progress towards the long term 2050 CAB goal. As far as I understand in this forum and others, the proponents of Measure UU have committed to constrain the size of the pool so that it meets the City CAB, and to only issue the proportion of the Measure UU bond adjusted to the pool size compatible with the CAB. Under these conditions, I support Measure UU. I do think that the calculations are correct as the proposed number of houses is certainly in the right order of magnitude.

articles.text: Editor: As Piedmont homeowners, our family advocates in favor of Measure UU even though we: 1) have never visited the pool 2) may not use the new pool and 3) are generally opposed to regressive taxes. Why then am I in favor of UU? It’s not because the pool is leaking 3,000 gallons per day and needs to be fixed, or because the increased tax will have a limited impact on our finances at only $30/month (which is well above the average amount for homeowners since we recently purchased our house). Nor is it because I think the initiative is infallibly written. Rather, it is because of the decision we made to live in Piedmont when we relocated from the East Coast four years ago. We seriously considered all of the more affordable surrounding cities, but Piedmont prevailed because of the quality of its schools and, equally as important, its real sense of community. I’ve built my community by taking leadership roles on the boards of the Havens Dads Club and Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation, and by coaching the many sports teams that both my elementary school boys are on. So, even though we’re not a “swimming family,” I still believe that Piedmont families who seek community at the pool should have a great facility. Piedmont has invested significantly in the many sports fields and parks that all children and adults in the community enjoy. Those fields are part of the reason that Piedmont is as amazing as it is, and it would be even more so with an updated pool and facility to bring the community together. The ballot initiative isn’t perfect, nor is the timing of raising taxes during a pandemic, but rarely are plans in life perfect. Perfect should not be the enemy of the good. Vote Yes on UU to bring our neighborhoods even closer together at a time when our strong community is more important than ever.
articles.title: Former East Coast residents say Yes to a new pool

articles.text: In this country and in this city, in particular, there is a significant discrepancy between the amount of money spent on private vs. public improvements. The current situation – crumbling public infrastructure – is the result of years of the community’s inability to fully commit to supporting our public facilities. I see Measure UU to rebuild the Piedmont Community Pool first and foremost as a simple question: whether we, as a community, value a pool or not? City public improvements such as pools, parks, courts, tracks, and trails are the last remaining vestiges of what can be considered the commons – outdoor places that play a central role in both creating community and providing for the simple, nearby enjoyment of the outdoors. In an urban context, we would do well to not let our lives be limited to the experience of individual spaces, such as our cars or our homes. If we let our lives be connected only virtually by digital technologies, we lose out in the richness of experience that our world has to offer. It is important to note that while the City decides, there is a cost to securing the site from blight and vandalism, as well as a significant cost associated with any future use of that space, whether it be for a pool or for some other use. If Measure UU passes, will there be a membership fee to use the pool? No, there is no membership fee. The Piedmont Community Pool has been a public pool since 2011. If Measure UU passes, the municipal bonds will be used to rebuild the pool facility. When the new facility opens, pool users will pay daily use fees, camp and lesson fees, annual and seasonal passes, and facility rentals, to offset operating costs. Pools are different from tennis courts and playing fields (which the City pays to maintain) in that pools are required to have trained staff present on-site during hours of operation (e.g. lifeguards, janitorial services). Like all programs run through the Recreation Department, Piedmont residents will have priority and will pay lower use fees than non-residents. For additional information visit the City of Piedmont’s website and FAQ page: https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___ departments/city_clerk/elections/november_3_2020_general_municipal_election/transfer_tax__pool_bond_measures/ pool_bond_frequently_asked_questions More information is also available at: www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com community life for many; a place where they see friends, meet neighbors, and hold celebrations. The project would include restrooms accessible to users of the adjacent Corey Reich Tennis Center, which currently has no restroom access. This would be a significant improvement to another popular community recreational facility. The pool isn’t the only infrastructure in Piedmont that will need attention in the coming years, and it might be more convenient if we didn’t need to address the pool now. However, it will not get less expensive with time, and, with the extraordinarily low interest rates expected to be in place for the next few years, this is actually the most opportune time to build it. Besides, the state of the current pool is such that it is unlikely to be reopened, as the rates of breakdown, mechanical failures, and leakage have made it no longer feasible to operate. The alternative scenario of a facility chained and closed for an indefinite duration is not, in our opinion, acceptable for a community the caliber of Piedmont. There will likely be more bond measures for other community facilities on the ballot in the coming years. Like all of us, we wish these things were less expensive. But we also think that we have all benefitted from capital investments made by generations past, and we think it is upon us now to make capital See Pool Letters on page 29

articles.text: Piedmont High School principal Adam Littlefield announced recently that the school has hired Bradley Smet of San Luis Obispo as its new Athletic Director Smet, 29, was recently with Templeton High School in San Luis Obispo as their assistant athletic director until stepping in as their interim A.D. He will complete a Master’s Degree in Coaching and Athletic Administration in May. “I’m in the process of moving and looking to stay as close to Piedmont as possible. It’s a beautiful town and I love the area. We have a couple of places on the shortlist now,” said Smet. His experience in managing teams, coaches, and students in the midst of the Coronavirus pandemic undoubtedly played a factor in the hiring process for Piedmont. “I took on the interim (A.D.) role to finish up last year while I was finishing up my Master’s at Concordia University. I was the athletic director (at Templeton) when COVID started, so I got a first-hand look at what was happening, how it affected our kids, and what it meant for high school athletics,” said Smet. The Templeton School District returned to practice ahead of the CIF’s proposed December start for sports, meaning he comes with experience with al school bringing back sports safely and responsibly. “For the lack of a better term, I was fortunate enough to be there at the beginning instead of later on in the process. I know it is different for other counties, but I’ve got to see first-hand how other schools are going about bringing back athletics,” he added. “Everything comes down to what the State (CIF) is allowing, on down to the Alameda County Department of Public Health. We have to manage those two main pieces when putting our plan together,” he said of creating a master sports scheduled for Piedmont High. Smet comes with a background in education as a substitute teacher in the Atascadero Bradley Smet, 29, was hired as Piedmont High’s new Athletic Director. and Templeton Unified School Districts since December 2018; a special education teacher at Atascadero from 2016-2017; and as an elementary school teacher in 2013-2014. A former quarterback for Sterling College in Sterling, Kansas in 2012, Smet began his coaching career as Atascadero High as the JV offensive coordinator from 2013-2015 and in the spring was an assistant varsity baseball coach. He became the baseball team’s JV head coach for 2016. Smet became Atascadero’s varsity football offensive coordinator in 2016 and 2017, and in 2019 he joined Templeton High School’s varsity staff as its quarterbacks and receivers coach. The team finished with a 10-2 record with a league championship, but was upset in the Division 4 Central Coast Quarterfinals as the No. 3 seeded team. His position in Piedmont will be a .6 fulltime equivalent. He takes over after the unexpected departure of Alphonso Powell who spent one year at Piedmont with mixed reviews. Smet will be Piedmont’s fourth athletic director since 2016.
articles.title: Piedmont High hires Bradley Smet as new A.D.

articles.text: With the November ballot looming and Measure UU, the bond that would finance a new pool in Piedmont, we are taking a look at some recent success of the Piedmont High School swim team from 2014-2019. It was led by the Liu sisters, both now swimming for Division 1 Ivy League teams. Skyler Liu, PHS Class of 2017, is at Princeton and younger sister Sasha Liu, Class of 2019, is at Brown U. Starting in 2014, Skyler finished her freshman season at PHS with a record in the Western Alameda County Conference record in the 100 butterfly with a time of 58.09 and went on to improve her time in the North Coast Section trials with a 57.75. The WACC also named her the league’s Swimmer of the Year. She returned to the WACC Finals as a sophomore to drop her 100 fly PR time by over a second to 56.15, then followed up with her first visit to the NCS 100 fly Finals to clock a 55.51, placing 7th of 16. Then as a junior in 2016, Skyler made it a three-peat at the WACC Finals in the 100 butterfly with a 56.40 but also set a league record in the 200 Individual Medley with a time of 2:06.18—her first league title in another event after finishing second in the 200 IM as a freshman and sophomore. She won her second WACC Swimmer of the Year award, earning the honor alongside Bishop O’Dowd’s Catherine Boles Sasha made her first appearance with PHS that year as a freshman as well. She won the WACC’s 500 freestyle in 5:15.02, six seconds ahead of the second-place swimmer. At NCS, Skyler scored some major points for Piedmont in two events. She placed sixth of 16 in the 200 IM with a 2:04.95, then finished fifth of 16 in the 100 Sasha went on to swim for Brown University, and now is in her sophomore year. Staff Photos The Liu sisters helped Piedmont finish 10th out of 43 schools at the North Coast Section swimming championships. Pictured are Sasha Liu (left), Skyler Liu and former PHS coach Victoria Fernandez. fly in 55.20. Her sister, Sasha, reached the NCS Finals in the 500 freestyle, clocking 5:06.18 personal record. Skyler’s senior campaign at the school in 2017 provided her third Swimmer of the Year award after winning every meet she competed in at 200 IM, 100 fly, 100 stroke, and 100 free. She set the WACC’s 200 IM record at 2:05.33, 100 butterfly record at 55.40, and led the relay team to a 2:04.35 victory. As for Sasha, she won her second consecutive WACC 500 freestyle title with a time of 5:04.97 and also set the 100 breaststroke record with a winning time of 1:03.05. Then to North Coast Section, Skyler accounted for 51 of Piedmont’s 81 points. She set her 200 medley record in 2:04.35, finishing fourth of 16. She also placed fifth of 16 in the 100 fly in 56.09. As members of the relay team, the Highlanders won the WACC title and placed eighth of 38 participants in 1:50.08. Though Piedmont only entered six swimmers at NCS, the team finished 10th in a field of 43 schools. Skyler was named our 2017 Piedmont Post Athlete of the Year. Sasha placed second in the 200 IM at North Coast Section, two spots ahead of Skyler, clocking a 2:0281 as a sophomore. Her 2018 junior year would wind up being her final year of competition for Piedmont High after Sasha underwent surgery ahead of her freshman season at Brown. Sasha won her third consecutive WACC 500 freestyle finals by setting the league’s record with a time of 5:02.77 and winning her second consecutive 100 meter breast in 1:03.88. She placed second of 16 in the NCS Finals’ 200 IM with a time of 2:02.63, and also finished fourth in the 100 breast in 1:03.60. Skyler is now entering her senior year at Princeton, prior to the COVID-19 shutdown of sports, she logged times of 27.36 in the 50 freestyle, 33.44 in the 50 breast, 26.76 in the 50 fly, and 1:06.52 in the 100 IM. Sasha competed in seven events as a freshman prior to the shutdown and set a personal record in the 100 breast with a time of 1:03.33, a 2:21.10 in the 200 breast, and a 2:04.37 in the 200 IM. With Measure UU looming, strongly supported by all the competetive swimmers in Piedmont, it seems fitting to give a tip of the cap to the Liu Sisteres, who helped put Piedmont’s aquatics program on the map. Skyler Liu went on to swim for Princeton University in the Ivy League. Sasha Liu won three consecutive WACC 500 freestyle championships, setting the league record as a junior. She also won two league championships in the 100 breast.
articles.title: A look back: Skyler and Sasha Liu’s record setting swim years

articles.text: Piedmont Park Tennis Courts Piedmont Park Tennis Courts reopened on Monday, October 19, after being resurfaced. The City Council approved an agreement with Vintage Contractors for refurbishment of the Park Tennis Courts in the amount of $97,000. The unanimous approval was made at an August 17 meeting. Recreation Director Chelle Putzer provided an update on the renovations to the Recreation Commission at their October 21 meeting. The city’s four tennis court facilities are resurfaced and repaired on a rotational schedule set by the Facilities Maintenance Plan. Based on condition assessments and discussions with the Recreation Director, the scheduled repair of tennis courts began with Linda Beach Park adjacent to Beach School. Repairs to the Linda Beach courts were completed in 2016. Hampton Park required more substantial repair and was completed in 2017 as part of the comprehensive Hampton Park Improvement Plan. The Recreation Center Tennis Courts was completed in 2019 with overwhelming support from Staff photo the community and is now known as the Corey Reich Tennis Center. The Piedmont Main Park courts were the last to be refurbished. “We are getting rave reviews on how [the courts] play,” Putzer said. The scope of the project in Piedmont Park included resurfacing the two tennis courts with a slipsheet overlay system, similar to the Corey Reich Tennis Center, and the installation of new net posts and nets also, similar to the Corey Reich Tennis Center. All Piedmont tennis courts reopened on May 18 after a twomonth closure due to COVID-19 and shelter-inplace restrictions. Doubles tennis is still not allowed under current state and county regulations. Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King, an avid tennis player, said it is absolutely the right time to move forward in fixing the courts. “Hats off to Sara [Lillevand] for placing this item on the agenda. Everyone loves those courts and [the refurbishment] is the right thing to do with city resources,” King said at the August 17 city council meeting.
articles.title: Park Tennis Courts get a makeover

articles.text: 49ers back on track, Raiders look to rebound; Dodgers win World Series; Premier League update The season is at the halfway point of the 2020 season and subsequent trade deadline. The 49ers got back on track against the New England Patriots in a monumental 33-6 win with some the help of four interceptions, and a 112 yard, three touchdown performance by running back Jeffery Wilson. San Francisco faces NFC West leaders, the Seahawks, for a critical matchup this Sunday, November 1, and going to be difficult for the Red and Gold to come out with a win. SF will have to limit Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson’s productivity and his ability to escapabe on third-downs if thye hope to pull off an upset. They’ll also have to prevent Seattle receiver Tyler Lockett from beating them over the top. Lockett had a monster 15-reception, 200-yard, three-touchdown performance against Arizona. I previously mentioned the 49ers as being possible buyers at the trade deadline for a quarterback, which seems highly unlikely after a two-game winning streak under Jimmy Garoppolo, The 49ers are grasping for cap space with $3 million available this season, so a flashy trade won’t be coming. They have a need for an edge rusher, perhaps a veteran at a discount price would fit. As for the Raiders, they go into Week 8 coming off a 45-20 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers but are looking ahead to a slightly favorable matchup with the Cleveland Browns. The Browns are a tough team at 5-2 record, but are without WR Odell Beckham Jr. The Silver and Black will be focusing on stopping the league’s No. 1 rushing attack, the Browns’ Nick Chubb and Kareem Hunt. Although Cleveland is favored to win, their bottom ranked pass defense bodes well for Derek Carr and the Raiders’ efficient passing attack. It could come down to which offense is more consistent, something that should favor Vegas. As for the trade deadline, it doesn’t seem likely that Jon Gruden will do much. They are in a bad cap situation next season. Perhaps a defensive lineman with a rookie contract could fit into their scheme. Dodgers win World Series The Dodgers finally got it done, winning the World Series with a 3-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 6. A seeming choke-move by the Rays manager was the catalyst for L.A. after Tampa Bay removed starting pitcher Blake Snell in the bottom of the sixth inning when leading 1-0 with a runner on base. It was reminiscent of former Giants manager Dusty Baker removing Russ Ortiz in the 2002 World Series after six and a third innings when up 5-0. Snell was taken after relinquishing his second hit of the game, similar to Ortiz in ‘02. articles.text: Photos courtesy of EBRPD East Bay Regional officially opened the Sutter Regional Shoreline Park at the base of the Bay Bridge and alongside the new bridge segment. East Bay Regional Park District announced on Monday that it will continue its closure of 11 of its parks in the East Bay Hills through today, Wednesday, October 28 due to increased fire activity and safety. “The East Bay Regional Park District is following the NWS issuance of the Red Flag Warnings to be extra cautious, especially in the East Bay hills during these wind events,” said Park District Fire Chief Aileen Theile. “We want to protect people from falling trees or limbs. We apologize for the inconvenience to those who want to access these hill area parks, but the public’s safety is our priority.” Parks that will remain temporarily closed to the public include Wildcat Canyon, Tilden, Reinhardt Redwood, Roberts, Huckleberry, Sibley, Claremont Canyon, Leona Canyon, Anthony Chabot, Lake Chabot and Kennedy Grove. If closures in the East Bay hills continue, these are parks to make note of going forward. The District said that the recent high winds during the weekend caused 14 downed powerlines within or nearby each of the 11 hill area parks. “PGE’s de-energization of these power lines was critical in maintaining safety and not sparking fires from the downed lines. Additional damage to the parks included many fallen trees or tree limbs which park staff are removing to clear roads and trails,” said District spokesman Dave Mason. Mount Diablo State Park experienced winds up to 94 mph at the 1900-foot elevation. Sutter Regional Shoreline Park opens East Bay Regional Park District announced on Wednesday, October 21 that it has opened a new park, Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline, located at the eastern base of the Bay Bridge. They are calling it the “Gateway to the East Bay” with its visibility to eastbound bridge drivers coming from San Francisco. The new park includes a 600-foot long, 40-foot wide observation deck, built on top the old Bay Bridge. Nearby, East Bay Regional announced the opening of a new event center, the Bridge Yard, which is a renovated 1930s-era electric train maintenance building, now newly minted for concerts, events, and other public concessions. The park also connects with the Bay Bridge Bicycle-Pedestrian Trail that brings hikers and bikers over to Treasure Island. The new park is expected to be a popular tourist destination with sweeping views of the Bay and easy access to Bay Bridge Trail. Judge John Sutter was an East Bay civic and environmental leader and former Park District board member. The new park was part of Sutter’s long-range vision. He saw the potential for a future waterfront park in the 1960s while the area was still active as the Oakland Army Base. He first proposed the park in a 1967 letter to the Association of Bay Area Governments.
articles.title: Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline Park officially opened

The 49ers got back on track against the New England Patriots in a monumental 33-6 win with some the help of four interceptions, and a 112 yard, three touchdown performance by running back Jeffery Wilson. San Francisco faces NFC West leaders, the Seahawks, for a critical matchup this Sunday, November 1, and going to be difficult for the Red and Gold to come out with a win. SF will have to limit Seahawks quarterback Russell Wilson’s productivity and his ability to escapabe on third-downs if thye hope to pull off an upset. They’ll also have to prevent Seattle receiver Tyler Lockett from beating them over the top. Lockett had a monster 15-reception, 200-yard, three-touchdown performance against Arizona. I previously mentioned the 49ers as being possible buyers at the trade deadline for a quarterback, which seems highly unlikely after a two-game winning streak under Jimmy Garoppolo, The 49ers are grasping for cap space with $3 million available this season, so a flashy trade won’t be coming. As for the Raiders, they go into Week 8 coming off a 45-20 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers but are looking ahead to a slightly favorable matchup with the Cleveland Browns. articles.text: More than 6 miles on Hayward Plunge, Greenbelt trails Staff Photos A spillway along Ward Creek on the Hayward Plunge Trail, which is a notoriously haunted park in the East Bay. The trail is popular for mountain bikers with its quick ascents and declines. Eucalyptus trees tower overhead. Travel up the stairs next to Ward Creek to continue on the Hayward Plunge Trail. The hilly trail provides over 1,100 feet in elevation gain over six miles. It’s the week of Halloween, and what better time to delve into all things spooky and haunted? Growing up in the Hayward area, as kids we all heard the gruesome story of the Hayward Plunge Trail at Green Belt Park. The well-known story provided an eerie ghost hunt for teenagers at night. For those easily spooked, be advised that the story isn’t for the faint of heart. Allegedly, a swimming instructor back in the 1960s at the Hayward Plunge indoor pool led his entire class of children up the trail and left them in Ward Creek, telling them to wait until he returned. The children stayed there until the night; the coach returned and murdered them, leaving each of them in the creek. That is the unverified story, which has become a legend. Many locals claim strange sightings, like voices of children around them – sometimes laughter or cries, sounds of footsteps, cold spots, and dark shadows. This writer even had a strange sighting of children all in white garb during the day as a teenager. Spooky stuff, huh? Now that we’re past those horrors, the trail itself is gorgeous. You’ll be hiking under acanopy of California Bay Laurels, Oak trees, and towering Eucalyptus trees. It is known as a premier mountain biking destination in the inner East Bay with its variations of uphill ascents and steep descents. It is considered a technical course, but also possesses a wide, flat surface without any roots or jagged rocks protruding. Starting at Memorial Park, the initial portion of the Hayward Plunge Trail starts in the back of the park past the bandstand. It travels for 1.3 miles slightly uphill alongside Ward Creek until intersecting with Campus Drive and Oaks Drive. Continue up Oaks Drive to the Hayward Plunge Trail. From there, the trail goes for another 1.6 miles to Durham Way and gains 600 feet in elvation through the hills of Green Belt Park. You’ll top out above the tree-line, where you’ll have the option to do a 180 and head back down, or turn right and walk straight down Durham Way to continue the loop onto the Greenbelt Hiking and Riding trail. It reunites you with Ward Creek until reaching Campus Drive. In the six miles of hiking areound noon on a Sunday, we passed only 29 people, so fewer than five people per mile on a popular day for hikers and bikers. The trail is a great spot for a lower leg workout, with over 1,100 feet in elevation gain. No ghost sightings were made, but perhaps my own paranoia brought the feeling that eyes were always following. Punch in “Hayward Plunge” or “Memorial Park Hayward” into your GPS device to access this trail’s parking lot. To cut off the first 1.3 miles, park on Campus Drive.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON The haunted Hayward Plunge Trail

articles.text: The Sky’s the Limit – Exhibition Opening Lecture At a time when beauty has never been more important, come be a part of the resilience of the arts. The one element in a painting that can have the greatest impact on the perception of atmosphere is sky. The types of colors used, the cloud composition, the quality of brush stroke....these are some of the details that can effect a viewer’s perception of sky. But this was not always the case. In the world of French classical painting, for instance, the landscape was a mere backdrop for some tale from antiquity or a scene from the Bible. It wasn’t until the late 1700’s that we see greater emphasis on sky: horizon lines dropped as artists began to explore greater variations in the rendering of sky. Indeed, in some art, sky was no longer a backdrop, but rather became the subject. Join artist an art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a zoom lecture to lead us on an examination of sky in painting. This lecture will also serve to open his current exhibition “The Sky’s the Limit!” Michael will also describe his own approach to rendering variable skies.
articles.title: Stehr art exhibit opens Friday at PCA

articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, will end on November 8 with a performance by Robert Howard. Howard, a cellist from American Bach Soloists and Philharmonic Baroque Orchestra, will perform Bach’s Fourth Cello Suite and explore Bach’s universal appeal as he collaborates with cellists from Kenya and Colombia. He will also perform select movements from Bach’s Cello Suites #1, 2, and 3. Bach Connections is the final piece of three performances in the Bach Shorts series. Bach Shorts are one hour, live-streamed performances that seek to connect us through an intimate exploration of The Six Cello Suites by J.S. Bach. The series showcased performances by two prominent Bay Area cellists, Christopher Costanza and Jennifer Kloetzel, and Cellist Robert Howard will conclude next month with Howard. The performance will stream live via YouTube on Sunday, November 8, at 4 p.m. To obtain tickets in advance, visit https:// app.ar ts-people.com /index. php?show=116151.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young will celebrate the vibrancy of Berkeley in an evening of music dedicated exclusively to local composers. Berkeley-based composers Samuel Adams, Gabriela Lena Frank, and Myra Melford will join Young in an engrossing program of locally crafted contemporary music. Recently named a Guggenheim Fellow, Adams is a composer of acoustic and electroacoustic music. His work has been hailed as “mesmerizing” and the “music of a composer with a personal voice and keen imagination” by the New York Times, “canny and assured” by the Chicago Tribune, and “wondrously alluring” by the San Francisco Chronicle. He is the son of operatic composer John Adams. Frank, of Lithuanian, Jewish, Peruvian, and Chinese descent, ardently explores her multicultural heritage in her compositions. Her pieces also reflect her studies in Latin American folklore. Jazz pianist Myra Melford. Melford is a pianist and keyboardist with a strong background in Jazz, blues and global folk music. She is also known for her classical, yet avant-garde styles. This week’s episode will air live-stream this Friday, October 30, at 5 p.m. on: https://www. berkeleysymphony.org/josephyoung-friends/. You can also watch the episode later by following the same link. The episode is part of the “Joseph Young and Friends” series presented by Berkeley Symphony, connecting industry leaders in the Bay Area for a virtual discussion on a wide range of topics in classical and contemporary music. The series will conclude on November 19, and will offer a look into the Symphony’s future by showcasing composers Jimmy Lopez and Brian Raphael Nabors.
articles.title: Next episode of Berkeley Symphony’s “Joseph Young and Friends” airs this Friday

articles.text: Michael Tilson Thomas meets his idol, James Brown, in a new documentary made available through PBS. Michael Tilson Thomas: Where Now Is, a full-length documentary exploring the life and career of the renowned conductor, premiered on October 23 is now available to stream. It is part of the American Masters series. The documentary follows Michael Tilson Thomas from his childhood in California to the world stage and his leadership roles with the San Francisco Symphony and New World Symphony. The film features original interviews with Tilson Thomas and other classical music luminaries, including composer Steve Reich, Los Angeles Philharmonic CEO Chad Smith, pianist Ralph Grierson, Boston Symphony Orchestra CEO Mark Volpe, San Francisco Chronicle music critic Joshua Kosman, and many more. The film incorporates concert footage from Tilson Thomas’ youth through the present, performing with the San Francisco, New World, Boston and London Symphonies. In addition, Where Now Is also showcases a conversation between Tilson Thomas and his idol, legendary rhythm and blues vocalist James Brown, whose song “Cold Sweat” inspired Tilson Thomas’ concept of timing. The documentary is made available through PBS as part of its American Masters series. It can be viewed through the PBS video application, or pbs.org/ americanmasters. Visit https:// www.pbs.org/wnet/americanmasters/michael-tilson-thomas-documentary/15245/ for more information. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet has announced its 2021 repertory season, to run from January 19 to June 27, 2021. The seven-program season features four world premieres and one West Coast premiere over the first three programs between January 19 and February 22, followed by Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream to run from March 5 through March 31, and Jewels to run from March 25 through March 31. The 2021 repertory season will conclude with ballet artistic director Helgi Tomasson’s Swan Lake, May 28 through June 6, and Romeo and Juliet from June 18 through June 27. Commissions include works by Bay Area choreographer Danielle Rowe, San Francisco Ballet soloist Myles Thatcher, and Mark Morris, as well as two new works previously scheduled for the 2020 San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 repertory season will conclude with Romeo and Juliet. Michael Tilson Thomas documentary streaming now Michael Tilson Thomas meets his idol, James Brown, in a new documentary made available through PBS. By Allyson Aleksey Michael Tilson Thomas: Where Now Is, a full-length documentary exploring the life and career of the renowned conductor, premiered on October 23 is now available to stream. It is part of the American Masters series. The documentary follows Michael Tilson Thomas from his childhood in California to the world stage and his leadership roles with the San Francisco Symphony and New World Symphony. The film features original interviews with Tilson Thomas and other classical music luminaries, including composer Steve Reich, Los Angeles Philharmonic CEO Chad Smith, pianist Ralph Grierson, Boston Symphony Orchestra CEO Mark Volpe, San Francisco Chronicle music critic Joshua Kosman, and many more. The film incorporates concert footage from Tilson Thomas’ youth through the present, performing with the San Francisco, New World, Boston and London Symphonies. In addition, Where Now Is also showcases a conversation between Tilson Thomas and his idol, legendary rhythm and blues vocalist James Brown, whose song “Cold Sweat” inspired Tilson Thomas’ concept of timing. The documentary is made available through PBS as part of its American Masters series. It can be viewed through the PBS video application, or pbs.org/ americanmasters. articles.text: Celebrate Halloween with Cal Performances by watching a special, live-stream of Manual Cinema’s Frankenstein. For Cal Performances’ “Cal at Home” series, Manual Cinema has created a new iteration of its acclaimed Frankenstein production, made specifically for home viewing. The performance will premiere tomorrow, Thursday, October 29, at 7 p.m., and will be available on demand through January 27, 2021. The production, which was co-commissioned by Cal Performances, weaves together the plot of Mary Shelley’s gothic tale with themes of desire, birth, and loss from the author’s own biography – asking us to consider our responsibility to our modern-day creations. The company’s performers manipulate hundreds of paper puppets to create a silent animated film in real time, featuring live actors and an immersive score performed onstage by four Sarah Fornance in Manual Cinema’s Frankenstein. musicians. The production was devised by Drew Dir, Sarah Fornance, and Julia Miller, with puppet design by Dir and Lizi Breit, and original music and sound design by Ben Kauffman and Kyle Vegter. Court Theatre presented the world premiere of Frankenstein in Chicago in late 2018, and Frankenstein has its New York premiere at the Public Theatre’s Under the Radar Festival in January 2019. Its international debut occurred at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in Scotland in August 2019. To watch tomorrow’s stream, visit https://calperformances.org/ events/2020-21/theater/manual-cinema-frankenstein/#cal-performances-suggested-pricing.
articles.title: Cal Performances hosts Frankenstein, streaming tomorrow

articles.text: World famous boxer Joe Louis pursued a career in boxing rather than as a violinist. Joseph Louis Barrow. You probably don’t recognize the name, even though he was very famous. He was the grandson of slaves, born in Alabama. The family moved to Detroit to get away from the violent racism. Times were tough in the Great Depression. To make matters even worse, Joseph’s father was abusive. He deserted the family and died in a mental institution. Joseph’s mother was gentle and loving, and she wanted her son to become a violinist. She knew about other violinists of African descent. France had the flamboyant Chevalier de St-George, and in England there was a composer, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor. In Vienna there was Beethoven’s friend, George Bridgetower. It was for Bridgetower that Beethoven wrote his brilliant “Kreutzer sonata”. They all had African parents. America had Clarence Cameron White and William Grant Still. I knew maestro Still. But back to Barrow. Mrs. Barrow envisioned greatness for her son. She believed he would be world famous. He was but in a different art far removed from the violin. Joseph did have an aptitude for the violin, but, as I said, times were tough. A career in music was especially hard. Orchestras were out of work and musicians often played in restaurants and in cafeterias. Joseph wanted a better life for himself and for his family, but he had no education. While he loved the violin, he was forced to make other plans. He was big and strong, but football and baseball were segregated. That left only boxing. So, it was boxing that was his passport to fame and fortune. (I use the last word for effect only. The IRS treated Joseph horribly.) Joseph became a success as a boxer. Joseph never used his last name professionally, and he shortened his first name to Joe. And thus, the aspiring violinist Joseph Louis Barrow became boxing legend Joe Louis. Next week: The story of two violinists who changed history.
articles.title: Fame and success

articles.text: The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive hosted an “artist talk” with New Delhi-based photographer Gauri Gill. In this recorded talk in conjunction with the exhibition When All That Is Solid Melts into Air, Gill addresses her practice and how it has evolved over the recent past, as well as its formative roots. She speaks about various collaborative projects, including Fields of Sight –represented in the exhibition by the work A Seed’s Journey (2019) – and her ongoing engagement with the so-called “other,” including her work in rural India since 1999. Gill’s projects highlight her belief in collaboration and in using photography as a memory Photographer Gauri Gill practice. Her work addresses the twinned Indian identity marks of caste, class, and community as determinants of mobility and social behavior; it is marked by empathy, surprise, and concern over issues of survival. Visit https://bampfa.org/event/ artists-talk-gauri-gill to watch the discussion.
articles.title: Berkeley Art Museum hosts Artist Talk with photographer Gauri Gill

articles.text: As of Friday, October 23, restaurants were given the green light by the Alameda County Public Health Department to reopen for indoor dining, subject to 25 percent capacity or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Indoor dining was not allowed as of March 17 due to the coronavirus epidemic. Many restaurants adapted by creating outdoor dining spaces, which eventually became permissible by the county. It hasn’t been a seamless transition; in July the County suspended outdoor dining because it had not obtained variance from the state, causing confusion for restaurant owners who already moved outdoors. Despite the recent approval for indoor dining by the county, many restaurants are opting to remain outdoors for the time being. There is a similar trend in San Francisco, where indoor dining was permitted on September 30, but many are choosing to keep their tables outdoors. On October 13, the state an nou nced that Alameda County entered the less-restrictive orange tier, allowing for some business sectors to begin reopening. COVID-19 case rates, testing positivity and hospitalizations are stable, allowing Alameda County to continue moving at a measured pace to open or expand activities permitted under the Red Tier and some activities that are permitted under the orange tier. “Case rates are rising across the country and we continue to monitor the impact of activities that were previously permitted locally. With flu season nearly here, we must be vigilant and not move so quickly as to initiate a surge in cases that could result in hospitalizations and deaths,” Alameda County Public Health Officer Neetu Balram said. She added that Alameda County moves at a more measured pace than the State in order to avoid a sharp rise in cases. “It’s important for every resident to consider the potential risk of getting or spreading COVID- 19 and how they can participate in these newly opened activities safely,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Outdoor activities with fewer people are safer. It is increasingly less safe if more people are in attendance, if the activities are indoors, or if people are frequently removing their face coverings.”
articles.title: Restaurants in county OK’d for indoor dining

articles.text: Piedmont COVID-19 caseload increases to 43 Alameda County updated its shelter in place order on Friday, October 23 and the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in the county is currently 1.4 percent. This positivity rate has stayed below 2 percent throughout October. The new health orders reflect the county’s position as an Orange Tier county, the second-least restrictive tier for reopening the economy, according to state metrics. The state placed Alameda County into the Orange Tier (Moderate Tier) on October 13, although county officials have said it would take time to determine how to reopen. Indoor dining is now allowed according to the revised order, but capacity must be restricted to 25 percent or 100 people, whichever is fewer. Some indoor family entertainment centers, like bowling alleys and climbing walls, can reopen, as well as indoor worship services, movie theaters and gyms, all with capacity restrictions. Capacity restrictions for indoor retail and malls have been increased to 50 percent. “It’s important for every resident to consider the potential risk of getting or spreading COVID-19 and how they can participate in these newly opened activities safely,” Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer, said in a statement. “Outdoor activities with fewer people are safer. It is increasingly less safe if more people are in attendance, if the activities are indoors, or if people are frequently removing their face coverings.” Two new cases of COVID- 19 were recorded in Piedmont in the past week, according to Alameda County Health Public Health Department data released yesterday, Tuesday, October 27. In total, 43 cases have been reported in the City since the coronavirus pandemic began in March. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 23,471, an increase of over 650 cases from one week ago. The county has recorded 462 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 9,064. In Hayward, 3,475 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,633 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,291 and Livermore reported 1,004. More Bay Area counties moved into the Orange Tier, the second-least restrictive tier out of four according to California’s color-coded system, this week. Marin, Contra Costa, Santa Clara and San Mateo counties are all in the Orange Tier. San Francisco was moved into the Yellow Tier, the least restrictive “Minimal” tier, last week. Alameda County is close to meeting benchmarks for the Yellow Tier, except that the county’s cases per day per 100,000 remains too high. The county is counting 3.2 cases per 100,000 people, while a county must have 1 case per 100,000 or fewer to be in the Yellow Tier. As of press time, 904,198 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded in California. There have been 17,400 deaths due to the disease statewide. While California had the most cases in the United States for several months, Texas now has a higher caseload of 916,562, according to New York Times analysis. Gov. Gavin Newsom said Monday, October 26 that the state will independently review vaccines approved by the Food and Drug Administration before distribution can occur in California. One day later, western states Washington, Oregon and Nevada announced they would join California’s vaccine review group. “This vaccine plan will move at the speed of trust,” Newsom said in a press conference this week. “You have to have confidence in the efficacy of the vaccine, confidence that we’re not rushing to judgement in terms of its distribution and its accessibility.” The City of Piedmont last week echoed guidance from the county noting that trick-or-treating on Saturday, Halloween, is considered a high-risk activity and is not recommended. articles.text: Biologist Audra Barrios brings a live reptile and amphibian demonstration to the San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers. The San Francisco Conservatory of Flowers will host a “creepy, crawly” live animal demo this Friday, October 30, just in time for Halloween. The class will take place over teleconference application Zoom, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. Audra Barrios, Executive Director of Things That Creep, will introduce viewers to herpetology, the study of reptiles and amphibians. Barrios is a biologist and educator in the San Francisco Bay Area for over 12 years. Through her travels to Madagascar and Mexico, she saw a need for a conservation organization focused on underrepresented critters such as reptiles and amphibians. During the class, you will meet three unique species of geckos, including the Caledonian Giant Gecko, the largest gecko in the world. This event is recommended for children but is suitable for all ages. Class will include a virtual tour and scavenger hunt. General admission tickets are $18. There is also an option to purchase a $30 admission ticket, which includes a “Conservatory at Home” kit. The kit will include an “Air Plant,” hands-on activities, a hand lens, and a Conservatory pin. To purchase tickets, visit htt ps://conser vator yoff lowe r s . o r g / e x h i b i t s - e v e n t s / creepycrittersofthetropics/.
articles.title: October 30 event features amphibians, reptiles

articles.text: The Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) has announced the retirement of Executive Director Jo Hazelett, after 22 years of service in the position. Hazelett will officially end her two-decade long tenure on Saturday, October 31 (also known as Halloween). Hazlett began her career with the Piedmont Scout Council in November 1998. Before coming to Piedmont, she worked with the American Red Cross as a Disaster Services Director in Phoenix, Arizona for approximately 3 years. Before she joined the Piedmont BSA, she worked with the East Bay Conservation Corps, now known as the Civicorps Schools. The Civicorps Academy serves young adults ages 18 to 26 through a combination of on-thejob training in environmental improvement projects. “Through these experiences I became interested in how nonprofits sustain themselves,” she said. “Nonprofits needed money to survive; without money, there would be no program.” Hazelett came to the position in an unusual way, explained Dale Radcliff, a former Piedmont Council president and now Western Region BSA Vice President. “Twenty-two years ago, Wes Smith, Bob Lambing Sr. and I were designated a subcommittee of the Piedmont Council board to find a new Executive Director. At the time, our small Boy Scout council was not allowed to have a conforming Scout Executive and our subcommittee was forced to look for candidates outside the professional Scouting community. To our good fortune we and Jo Hazelett found each other and the rest is history,” Radcliff said. Hazelett recalled that she applied for the position because she was interested in running an organization after years of experience in development in the nonprofit sector. She noted that at the time of her hiring there were very few female directors in the Boy Scouts organization. “I may have been the second or third [female director] in the country,” she explained. Under Hazelett’s leadership, the Piedmont Council has been ranked first among the nation’s 253 councils on the Journey to Excellence (JTE) metric for the last four years. It is also the BSA. At the time, Boy Scouts of America spokesman Gregg Shields said if the Piedmont Council flouted the ban, it would be the first council in the country to do so. “All of a sudden it became a national story,” Hazelett said. “We just said that we didn’t find anything in the oath and law that would appear to sanction discrimination of any kind.” The ban on openly gay scouts was eventually lifted in 2013, in part with the leadership for 10 years of a few Piedmont Scout leaders. Piedmont’s inclusive council proved to be seminal. articles.text: Election Day is little more than a week away. As a citizen, you may feel the results will affect many aspects of life in this country. But as an investor, your situation probably won’t change after the votes are counted. No matter who wins, the financial markets may well show some politically driven volatility, but that often happens around elections, and it typically doesn’t last long. But what about the longer term? How might changes in policy and new legislation affect your investment outlook? To begin, keep in mind that many campaign promises remain just that – promises. And even when some of them are enacted, any ultimate legislation may be quite different from what was proposed on the campaign trail. Still, sometime in the future, we could see election-related changes that could affect your investment strategy. For example, over the years, we’ve seen many adjustments in the tax rates of capital gains and stock dividends, and it’s likely these rates will change again one day. When that happens, you may need to look at the equities portion of your portfolio to see if you want to make some adjustments. Many other changes, though, are hard to predict. It’s possible that future legislation could affect specific industries, either positively or negatively. Such moves could also influence the way you look at certain investments, but if you have a diversified portfolio that contains a broad mix of stocks, bonds and other securities, any actions affecting one particular industry probably won’t cause you to significantly adjust holdings invested in other sectors. In any case, while it may be a good idea to keep an eye open for things like tax rate changes or how new policies may affect different market segments, your main emphasis, in terms of your investment decisions, should remain on your goals and what you need to do to achieve them. At least once each year, review your portfolio carefully to make sure your investments are aligned with your goals, whether they are short-term (a new car, a long vacation and so on) or long-term (such as college for your children or a comfortable retirement). Periodically, depending on what’s happening in your life and the progress of your investment portfolio, you may need to evaluate your goals to ensure they’re prioritized appropriately to help keep you on track toward achieving what’s most important to you. Over time, your goals may change, too. Perhaps you’ve decided that instead of retiring early and traveling around the world, you now want to turn your hobby into a business. Changing this goal may require a different investment strategy. Or you might change your mind about where you want to live – instead of staying in your home, as originally planned, you might downsize and move to a different area. Your goals may change in many ways, all of which may warrant updating your investment strategies. Here’s the key point: You’re the one electing to make these changes. No matter what happens in this or any other election, be sure to “vote” for the strategies that have the potential for a winning outcome.
