articles.text: Jeanie Menke, the mother of Mark Menke of Piedmont, passed away on October 4, 2020 in Austin, Texas after a courageous 16-year battle with Parkinson’s Disease. She was 89. Born Jeanie Fay Rosenbaum on January 14, 1931 in rural Calhoun County, Texas, she was the daughter of Melvin Rosenbaum, Sr. and Alma Jaster Rosenbaum. Jeanie was a warm and loving wife, mother, grandmother and friend who faced Parkinson’s with grace, and did not let the disease keep her from living a rich and varied life. Under a soft exterior, Jeanie was intelligent and determined, qualities appreciated by those who knew her. Her faith was a strength and comfort to her always. She grew up on a farm outside of Port Lavaca, Texas, where she was Port Lavaca High School Valedictorian in 1948. After attending Southwestern Business School in Houston, Jeanie returned to Port Lavaca and became one of the early employees at Alcoa’s Point Comfort Works, where she worked as a secretary starting in 1950. At Point Comfort Works, Jeanie met Allen Menke of Victoria, Texas, and the two were married in 1952. The Menkes transferred to Rockdale, Texas with the 1952 opening of the Rockdale Alcoa plant. There, Allen began a 37-year career as a human resources manager, while Jeanie worked as a secretary until the birth of their first child in 1954. Jeanie and Allen had four children: Mark, James, Mary and Laura. She raised four successful children and nurtured a strong family culture that continues to this day. As her children married, Jeanie embraced her children’s spouses and became a loving grandmother and great grandmother to successive generations. Together, theme including live music and dancing. After Allen passed away in 1995, Jeanie held down the family farm until her Parkinson’s Disease required her to move into assisted living in 2014. She lived her last five years in Brookdale Northwest Hills in Austin. There she made friends with other residents and staff and was always looking for a bridge game. She even kept up her secretarial skills, using her computer to follow friends and family on email and Facebook. The family thanks the staff at Brookdale Northwest Hills for their many years of loving care. Jeanie is survived by son, Mark Menke and wife, Anne-Marie Lamarche of Piedmont, California, and their children Elise (Evan Stuller), Claire (Daniel Priestley) and Alexander, and a great granddaughter Emilie-Marie Faye Stuller; by son James Menke and wife, Beth of Austin, Texas and their four children Andrew (Nicole), Bryan (Rachel), Audrey, and Joseph (Emma) and two great grandsons Cameron and Lucas Menke (Andrew); by daughter Mary Strickland and husband Gary of Coleman, Texas and their two children Matt and Erin (Isla Cameron); and daughter Laura Arroyo and husband, Charles of Round Rock, Texas, and their three sons Brandon (Maureen Naval), Wesley (Natalie) and Connor. She is predeceased by her husband, Allen Menke, and brother Melvin Rosenbaum. A memorial service will be held at Peace Lutheran Church in Rockdale, Texas, on November 28 at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Peace Lutheran Church, P. O. Box 308, Rockdale, TX 76567 or The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research (www.michaeljfox.org). Jeanie Menke, the mother of Piedmont resident Mark Menke, died on October 4 in Austin, Texas. She was 89. Jeanie and Allen invested countless hours of labor and love to build their Rockdale farm, home and gardens from native Texas woodlands. The farm has become a living legacy and family gathering space for their children and grandchildren. Jeanie was an active member of Peace Lutheran Church in Rockdale for over 60 years, serving as church secretary for 23 years, assisting Pastors Waldemar Wendell and Herbert Lammert. She was an avid bridge player and a member of several bridge groups, including a couples’ bridge group with her husband. Jeanie had a closeknit group of friends in Rockdale who loved taking day trips around Central Texas, as well as extended travel and cruises around the U.S. Jeanie also traveled regularly to California to visit her son and his family, and to Europe to visit grandchildren who were studying abroad. pages.text: Wednesday, October 28, 2020 23 Jeanie Menke dies at age 89 Jeanie Menke, the mother of Mark Menke of Piedmont, passed away on October 4, 2020 in Austin, Texas after a courageous 16-year battle with Parkinson’s Disease. She was 89. Born Jeanie Fay Rosenbaum on January 14, 1931 in rural Calhoun County, Texas, she was the daughter of Melvin Rosenbaum, Sr. and Alma Jaster Rosenbaum. Jeanie was a warm and loving wife, mother, grandmother and friend who faced Parkinson’s with grace, and did not let the disease keep her from living a rich and varied life. Under a soft exterior, Jeanie was intelligent and determined, qualities appreciated by those who knew her. Her faith was a strength and comfort to her always. She grew up on a farm outside of Port Lavaca, Texas, where she was Port Lavaca High School Valedictorian in 1948. After attending Southwestern Business School in Houston, Jeanie returned to Port Lavaca and became one of the early employees at Alcoa’s Point Comfort Works, where she worked as a secretary starting in 1950. At Point Comfort Works, Jeanie met Allen Menke of Victoria, Texas, and the two were married in 1952. The Menkes transferred to Rockdale, Texas with the 1952 opening of the Rockdale Alcoa plant. There, Allen began a 37-year career as a human resources manager, while Jeanie worked as a secretary until the birth of their first child in 1954. Jeanie and Allen had four children: Mark, James, Mary and Laura. She raised four successful children and nurtured a strong family culture that continues to this day. As her children married, Jeanie embraced her children’s spouses and became a loving grandmother and great grandmother to successive generations. Together, theme including live music and dancing. After Allen passed away in 1995, Jeanie held down the family farm until her Parkinson’s Disease required her to move into assisted living in 2014. She lived her last five years in Brookdale Northwest Hills in Austin. There she made friends with other residents and staff and was always looking for a bridge game. She even kept up her secretarial skills, using her computer to follow friends and family on email and Facebook. The family thanks the staff at Brookdale Northwest Hills for their many years of loving care. Jeanie is survived by son, Mark Menke and wife, Anne-Marie Lamarche of Piedmont, California, and their children Elise (Evan Stuller), Claire (Daniel Priestley) and Alexander, and a great granddaughter Emilie-Marie Faye Stuller; by son James Menke and wife, Beth of Austin, Texas and their four children Andrew (Nicole), Bryan (Rachel), Audrey, and Joseph (Emma) and two great grandsons Cameron and Lucas Menke (Andrew); by daughter Mary Strickland and husband Gary of Coleman, Texas and their two children Matt and Erin (Isla Cameron); and daughter Laura Arroyo and husband, Charles of Round Rock, Texas, and their three sons Brandon (Maureen Naval), Wesley (Natalie) and Connor. She is predeceased by her husband, Allen Menke, and brother Melvin Rosenbaum. A memorial service will be held at Peace Lutheran Church in Rockdale, Texas, on November 28 at 11 a.m. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to Peace Lutheran Church, P. O. Box 308, Rockdale, TX 76567 or The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research (www.michaeljfox.org). Jeanie Menke, the mother of Piedmont resident Mark Menke, died on October 4 in Austin, Texas. She was 89. Jeanie and Allen invested countless hours of labor and love to build their Rockdale farm, home and gardens from native Texas woodlands. The farm has become a living legacy and family gathering space for their children and grandchildren. Jeanie was an active member of Peace Lutheran Church in Rockdale for over 60 years, serving as church secretary for 23 years, assisting Pastors Waldemar Wendell and Herbert Lammert. She was an avid bridge player and a member of several bridge groups, including a couples’ bridge group with her husband. Jeanie had a closeknit group of friends in Rockdale who loved taking day trips around Central Texas, as well as extended travel and cruises around the U.S. Jeanie also traveled regularly to California to visit her son and his family, and to Europe to visit grandchildren who were studying abroad. articles.text: work that she did, from organizing silent auction items for Spring Fling to creating agendas and lining up guest speakers for parent club meetings. Later, she would become even more involved for our schools by co-chairing the Giving Campaign and Measures G&H. Her commitment to making her community better inspired me and when I was in high school, I created a blog. My goal was to help keep politics, and current events in general, relevant, interesting and understandable for teenagers and all young people. I also worked on Senator Tammy Baldwin’s campaign in 2018 and I interned for Congressman Eric Swalwell this summer in Washington, DC. I am not sure what path my career will take me in, but because of my mom, I know I will always be committed to serving and supporting my community. the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and in her capacity as co-President of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC). When I first spoke to Veronica several months ago about my desire to work on anti-racism initiatives in Piedmont, I was immediately struck by her extraordinary knowledge. She has a deep background and understanding of diversity and equity issues, particularly as they pertain to public schools, through her work with PADC and her years of professional work in education policy and journalism. But even more than her knowledge, I was blown away by her warmth, her empathy, her ability to listen openly, and willingness to engage new perspectives and even critiques. Conversations about racial justice and diversity can be fraught and difficult. Veronica brings a notable grace and a positive, can-do attitude that are demonstrated in the programming that she has spearheaded through PADC, for example in organizing Martin Luther King, Jr. Day celebrations and helping launch a Black Students Union. Over the last few months, the members of our School Board have done a heroic job listening to parents, teachers, and students with diverse opinions. I’m convinced that Veronica will take up this work with exceptional openness, intelligence, balance, and care. She has demonstrated a commitment to lifting up every child in our community, including those who historically have been underserved and marginalized by the system. I believe that a School Board with Veronica on it will be one that works towards educational equity and that advances the values of diversity and excellence that all Piedmonters share.

articles.text: Editor: Our home values are linked to Piedmont’s historical reputation for excellent schools. That reputation is starting to falter as evidenced by the unexpected loss of 81 students from our school district this year. Once lost, it will take years to recover our reputation. Hari Titan is the School Board candidate who will add thoughtful management and responsible oversight to the School Board. Since 2013 he’s contributed over 500 hours of time which produced well-conceived recommendations that saved our schools and taxpayers millions of dollars. Our current school board is disproportionately influenced by the unions and our country-club society. Board decisions are too often unanimous with little public deliberation and are often dismissive of thoughtful public input. Titan will return transparent governance to the school board. My decision to vote for Hari is based on the content of his character and intellect. His experience as a businessman, mathematician, scientist, and STEM college professor brings valuable diversity and professional acumen to the board. Membership on the school board should not be a popularity contest. Titan is the responsible candidate we need.
articles.title: Titan: 7 years of valuable aid to schools

articles.text: Donald Chandler AIA Comprehensive immigration reform. Comprehensive Covid relief. Goals to which to aspire. Doesn’t Piedmont deserve a comprehensive solution to our known physical planning issues and a financial response to those issues? Those issues include (but are not limited to): • Our Essential Services Buildings – Fire and Police Buildings and City Hall; • Our Recreational facilities including the Community Pool; • The State Mandated Affordable Housing requirement. ( possibly several hundred units) We need a Land Use Plan and a Comprehensive Financing Plan for all these projects. How can we be asked to vote for only one project, the Community Pool, without a comprehensive plan? A No vote on UU gives the City a ‘break in the action’ and the time to address the investigations, planning, estimates required to present credible financing options to the voters -- and also time to implement a Plan B – a repair/ rehab of the pool at a cost of $3-5 million that could take as little as 6 months to complete. Plan B for the Community Pool has already been outlined in a study completed for the City Council in 2018. There has been a lot of rhetoric about Measure UU. Let’s look at some direct quotes from the Alameda County Voter Guide. 1. “Therefore, the City Council cannot guarantee that the bonds will provide sufficient funds to allow completion of all the needed improvements.” Is this prudent fiscal planning? Would you start a project on your home if you didn’t have sufficient funds? We say No. 2. “If Measure UU does not pass, the Piedmont Community Pool is on track to be closed permanently.” Is this proper civic behavior or just a scare tactic? Any prudent City action must have a backup plan and not just state that residents will be faced with “an empty padlocked pool”. 3. “The pool leaks approximately 3000 gallons of water a day.” The City has a study that states the leak can be repaired for $ 50-60,000 (while the leak costs the City over $10,000 per year). Why hasn’t that been done instead of using the leak as a major talking point in the campaign?
articles.title: Measure UU and some comprehensive solutions

articles.text: Prior to Covid I swam 3-5 days per week, so I like pools. But I am voting No on Measure UU. I don’t like being duped. The bond for replacing the pool was rushed on to this year’s ballot because the City feared that if they asked for what was really needed, $70 million to upgrade the police and fire buildings, which includes the pool, that voters would reject it. It was too much money to ask at one time and the City knew this. So instead, it was decided to slip Measure UU in knowing the psychology of asking for a smaller amount now, knowing that voters would vote later on the estimated $50 million needed to upgrade the fire and police buildings, which I support. What galls me is that the true cost of building a new pool is not known. The City Council passed a $23 million ordinance for improvements yet approved a $19.5 million bond measure for the ballot. I am advocating to vote No on Measure UU and have the City to do the job right, which is to get the proper cost estimates. We are entitled to know how our money will be spent. Use logic and don’t be persuaded by fear tactics.
articles.title: Was Measure UU rushed?

articles.text: Editor: In the 20 years I have known Hilary Cooper, I have been repeatedly impressed with her abilities to consider all angles, make the hard choices and complete the work. The projects she has taken on, including bond measures and essential fundraisers, require an ear for multiple constituents and an eye for detailed execution. I have seen Hilary’s to do lists and her calendars. I have seen her map out a project understanding every interdependency. She is exceptionally organized and reliable. In other words, no matter how complex or short-staffed the project is, she never fails to pull it off. I also know her to be deeply committed to the well being of students of all kinds. She has shown an active interest in how our schools meet (and could better meet) the needs of kids who excel, kids who need more and kids who feel lost or disenfranchised. articles.text: Editor: I have been swimming basically all my life. I can’t remember a time before I learned to swim. I really hope the pool gets redone so that other children can learn how to swim. Last year I won the attendance award for the Piedmont swim team. Now that the pool is closed I won’t be able to go to nearly as many practices. I think it is essential that we have a pool in our community. Swimming was always a wonderful experience for me and I know other kids love the pools as much as me. Children like me can’t vote so I hope people that can will vote yes for the pool!

Titan: 7 years of valuable aid to schools By Dai Meagher Editor: Our home values are linked to Piedmont’s historical reputation for excellent schools. That reputation is starting to falter as evidenced by the unexpected loss of 81 students from our school district this year. Once lost, it will take years to recover our reputation. Hari Titan is the School Board candidate who will add thoughtful management and responsible oversight to the School Board. Since 2013 he’s contributed over 500 hours of time which produced well-conceived recommendations that saved our schools and taxpayers millions of dollars. Our current school board is disproportionately influenced by the unions and our country-club society. Board decisions are too often unanimous with little public deliberation and are often dismissive of thoughtful public input. Titan will return transparent governance to the school board. My decision to vote for Hari is based on the content of his character and intellect. His experience as a businessman, mathematician, scientist, and STEM college professor brings valuable diversity and professional acumen to the board. Membership on the school board should not be a popularity contest. Titan is the responsible candidate we need. Helping kids excel is Cooper’s life’s work By Kelly Corrigan Editor: In the 20 years I have known Hilary Cooper, I have been repeatedly impressed with her abilities to consider all angles, make the hard choices and complete the work. The projects she has taken on, including bond measures and essential fundraisers, require an ear for multiple constituents and an eye for detailed execution. I have seen Hilary’s to do lists and her calendars. I have seen her map out a project understanding every interdependency. She is exceptionally organized and reliable. In other words, no matter how complex or short-staffed the project is, she never fails to pull it off. I also know her to be deeply committed to the well being of students of all kinds. She has shown an active interest in how our schools meet (and could better meet) the needs of kids who excel, kids who need more and kids who feel lost or disenfranchised. Thank you for your vote in support of Measure UU. I love swimming – Vote Yes on UU By Connor Carnazzo, 4th grade Editor: I’ve been on piedmont swim team for four years – since I was in kindergarten. I love swimming because it feels mellow on my joints and I like being part of a team. I hope the city rebuilds the pool in Piedmont so we will have a pool for us that won’t be far from home and that will represent our team. Was Measure UU rushed? By Karen Bixby Prior to Covid I swam 3-5 days per week, so I like pools. But I am voting No on Measure UU. I don’t like being duped. The bond for replacing the pool was rushed on to this year’s ballot because the City feared that if they asked for what was really needed, $70 million to upgrade the police and fire buildings, which includes the pool, that voters would reject it. It was too much money to ask at one time and the City knew this. So instead, it was decided to slip Measure UU in knowing the psychology of asking for a smaller amount now, knowing that voters would vote later on the estimated $50 million needed to upgrade the fire and police buildings, which I support. What galls me is that the true cost of building a new pool is not known. The City Council passed a $23 million ordinance for improvements yet approved a $19.5 million bond measure for the ballot. I am advocating to vote No on Measure UU and have the City to do the job right, which is to get the proper cost estimates. We are entitled to know how our money will be spent. Use logic and don’t be persuaded by fear tactics. Hoping adults will vote Yes on Measure UU By Vivie Oesterer, age 11 Editor: I have been swimming basically all my life. I can’t remember a time before I learned to swim. I really hope the pool gets redone so that other children can learn how to swim. Last year I won the attendance award for the Piedmont swim team. Now that the pool is closed I won’t be able to go to nearly as many practices. I think it is essential that we have a pool in our community. Swimming was always a wonderful experience for me and I know other kids love the pools as much as me. Children like me can’t vote so I hope people that can will vote yes for the pool! No for now on UU By Sam Smith Editor: I think without question we need a new pool facility in the center of Piedmont. There have been pleas from parents, grandparents, water polo team members and realtors stating that it is an important amenity to have in this town. As Alan Rudy, an experienced architect and longstanding resident said, this needs more study. We need to prioritize with police and fire safety, and the general upkeep of our town. Not so fast, Piedmont. Nobody is against a pool. Every town needs a local swimming hole. However, these are the reasons why we are voting No on UU at this time: Overdone ask: The analysis shows that the current facility can be replaced for approximately $10 million. The committee wants a blank check with flexibility to build the Hearst Castle of pools. Replace what we have with new and safe facilities, but don’t ask to develop additional buildings and a facility that goes beyond what we need. The UU committee says that non-residents will help pay the operational bill with entrance fees. Why aren’t we building something that can be self-sustained vs. something that only works with outside revenue dependence? Unfair taxing approach: The independent tax report done earlier this year said taxes for such amenities should be done using the parcel tax approach, not the ad valorem methodology. The marketing campaign for UU quotes average taxes on a daily basis. This is highly misleading. In fact, the tax report shows that 20% of the homes would pay 50% of the tax. The 20% are our newer homeowners, many with young families and dual-working parents. This just isn’t fair to them. Too quick: The whole plan has been rushed and put together too fast under the guise that the pool is not functional. There just hasn’t been enough study. Sure, the pool is leaking. Close it down, get a more concrete plan in place and come to the voters in a special election when ready and have us decide. Piedmont, please, No on UU. This is too much too quick. Ensuring that memories of pool continue By Ryan Stokes, 10th grade Editor: I’m a member of the Piedmont Swim Team and have been using the Piedmont pool my entire life. I hope that the next generations of Piedmont kids can have the same memories that I have – earning your white patch, lining up for the diving board, and playing on the innertubes. I started spending more time at the pool when I joined the swim team, and I saw our whole community there. It’s a gathering space for many. The pool has been a special place for me and I’ve made lifelong friends and lasting relationships on its hot, concrete deck and the its chlorinated water. By voting yes on measure UU, you can ensure that the future kids of Piedmont can have their own memories of playing at the pool. Andersen wants us to be thoughtful By Andy Wasserman In the recent LWV Forum on Measure UU reported on by the Post, Betsy Andersen was asked why the Council is prioritizing the pool over public services buildings. She replied that she does not see Measure UU as a choice between the two, but that “our community can and should thoughtfully do both”. Seriously? Of course it is a choice. By rushing through UU before it asks for even more money for essential services, the council is clearly prioritizing the pool. Stop and think – what are your priorities? Having Police and Fire Services that comply with state law and having facilities that do not collapse in an earthquake, or a swimming pool? Does anyone really think there is a choice? The total cost to repay $19.5 million in 30-year bonds at 3% interest is $29.6 million. The total cost to repay the $51 million of bonds it will take to rebuild the Police and Fire Stations with the same assumptions is $77.4 million. That’s a total of $107 million for the two projects. The City Council has admitted that it needs to do the essential services upgrade, both to comply with current law and to be able to provide services in case of a natural disaster. Let’s be “thoughtful”, as Ms. Andersen suggests, and put the pool on hold until the City’s essential services problems have been fixed. Then see if people still have the appetite and the financial resources for a pool. Measure UU and some comprehensive solutions By Alan Rudy AIA and Donald Chandler AIA Comprehensive immigration reform. Comprehensive Covid relief. Goals to which to aspire. Doesn’t Piedmont deserve a comprehensive solution to our known physical planning issues and a financial response to those issues? Those issues include (but are not limited to): • Our Essential Services Buildings – Fire and Police Buildings and City Hall; • Our Recreational facilities including the Community Pool; • The State Mandated Affordable Housing requirement. ( possibly several hundred units) We need a Land Use Plan and a Comprehensive Financing Plan for all these projects. How can we be asked to vote for only one project, the Community Pool, without a comprehensive plan? A No vote on UU gives the City a ‘break in the action’ and the time to address the investigations, planning, estimates required to present credible financing options to the voters -- and also time to implement a Plan B – a repair/ rehab of the pool at a cost of $3-5 million that could take as little as 6 months to complete. Plan B for the Community Pool has already been outlined in a study completed for the City Council in 2018. There has been a lot of rhetoric about Measure UU. Let’s look at some direct quotes from the Alameda County Voter Guide. 1. “Therefore, the City Council cannot guarantee that the bonds will provide sufficient funds to allow completion of all the needed improvements.” Is this prudent fiscal planning? Would you start a project on your home if you didn’t have sufficient funds? We say No. 2. “If Measure UU does not pass, the Piedmont Community Pool is on track to be closed permanently.” Is this proper civic behavior or just a scare tactic? Any prudent City action must have a backup plan and not just state that residents will be faced with “an empty padlocked pool”. 3. “The pool leaks approximately 3000 gallons of water a day.” The City has a study that states the leak can be repaired for $ 50-60,000 (while the leak costs the City over $10,000 per year). Why hasn’t that been done instead of using the leak as a major talking point in the campaign?

articles.text: The updated schedule for the revised reopening of elementary schools, approved by the school board on Monday night this week, October 26. restrictions Alameda County has permission from the state to open all schools. Alameda County’s Public Health Office enacted tighter restrictions which allowed for only elementary schools to open starting October 13 with a public reopening plan. Piedmont was slated to be the first public school in the county to reopen. Many private schools in the county already opened up this month. Middle schools in Alameda County do not have the green light to open now, and mid-November is expected to be the earliest date for them. High schools are not expected to be given the opportunity to open until next year, possibly in January 2021. While older students are more likely to be able to follow distancing and mask wearing rules, they are thought to transmit SARSCOV-2 more easily than the youngest learners. Many frustrated parents called into the three-hour special meeting on Monday night to voice their grievances, offer suggestions and query school board members. In an emotionally charged call to the board, Piedmont parent Laura Maestrelli read off nearly 10 anonymous responses from PHS and PMS students negatively affected by Distance Learning. “Every day feels the exact the same. I get headaches because of class and homework on screens. I have lost all motivation. It feels like we have whittled it down to the most depressing and worst parts of school – and that’s all we are doing,” said a PHS freshman. Many parents calling in expressed helplessness. Booker suggested some options for them. “The number one way [to help] is pay attention to the social contract. It only works if we all [follow those safety requirements]. Families have to do the health screening every morning, that is really important. We will be asking for help to grab some materials, like clorox wipes, and hand sanitizer,” Booker said. The reopening plan for TK-K still consists of only 2-hours, 15-minutes of in-person instruction four days a week, Tuesday through Friday. All elementary students have distance learning on Mondays. Grades 1-5 will have an additional 45 minutes of instruction. Classes have been split into AM and PM cohorts, with a maximum of 15 students per cohort. The schedules for distance learning and in-person learning are the same as they have been all year. Specialist instruction (P.E, art, computers) will be taught digitally, 45 minutes per day for TK - K and an hour for grades 1-5. Expanding the duration of instruction and giving parents the option to switch to in-person learning will take place later in the year, after scheduled breaks from instruction. An idea floated around the meeting about a rolling reopening to start sooner than December 1 for classes that do have teacher assignments lined up. Booker worried that parents would be upset if in-person school started for some kids, but not for others. Board member Cory Smegal recommended reflecting these parent’s desire. The board approved the motion to “Direct the superintendent to explore having a trial to bring a small number of general education students back prior to Thanksgiving break.” The most acute special education learners will return to campus November 3 at elementary schools as planned. Bringing back all special education students at all sites is allowable by the state and county. The board will examine the logistics of this possibility. The October 28 regular school board meeting originally had school reopening on the agenda, but it now will be taken off. articles.text: Residents advised to prepare for wildfire and power outages – again Hurricane force gusts blew through the North Bay this past weekend, and the entire Bay Area, including Piedmont, was put under a Red Flag Warning on Sunday, October 25. While the warning was lifted for Piedmont earlier this week, the Red Flag Warning persisted until 5 p.m. yesterday, Tuesday, October 27 for the East Bay Hills and North Bay Mountains. Dangerous wildfire weather is expected in the near term, so vigilance amongst the public is paramount, Fire Chief Bret Black explained. High winds and low humidity in the forecast are behind the concerns. “We are under extreme weather conditions ripe for a significant wildfire,” Black noted. On Monday, October 26, the National Weather Service measured peak wind gusts of 89 miles per hour, which counts as hurricane force, in the Mayacmas Mountains in the North Bay. That day at Mt. Diablo to the east of Piedmont, 70 miles per hour gusts were recorded. The NWS measured gusts over 50 miles per hour in Piedmont, where winds knocked down tree branches. But the temperatures remained cool, not the hot winds associated with fire-inducing winds from the East. “The low humidity and wind are posing a significant risk to all Californians,” Black said. A 2-alarm fire in Montclair yesterday, October 27, caused damage to two homes. PFD Fire Crew sent to So. Calif. The Piedmont Fire Department sent an engine down this week to fight devastating fires burning in Southern California. The PFD engine was sent along with 10 engines from other local agencies to battle the Silverado Fire near Irvine. Yesterday, Black noted that a fire in the Oakland neighborhood of Montclair ignited two homes and some vegetation. The Oakland Fire Department said no one was hurt but eight people were displaced. “Luckily, we have additional engines staged in the vicinity and the fire was quickly brought under control,” said Black, adding that it took several hours to extinguish all the small hot spots in the area. Tens of thousands of PG&E customers in the Bay Area were without power during a portion of the weekend due to a Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) due to the high fire danger. Some homes on the eastern edge of Piedmont were impacted on Sunday, October 25, and as of yesterday, several dozen customers in the City reported a loss of power. CalFire notes that “wildfire season” will last for several more weeks. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org.

A 24-hour accessible ballot drop-box is located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue in Piedmont. “We’ve been preparing for this,” Alameda County Registrar of Voters Information Officer Tim Dupuis said, adding that his department has doubled availability to match the record number of voters this year. Piedmont, a city already noted as producing the highest percentage of voters per capita in Alameda County, is also expected to show a record number of votes cast this year. Piedmont set a new county record in 2016 with an 86-percent voter turnout based upon 8,634 registered voters. The city’s current number of registered voters has increased to 9,035. The city’s population is 11,400. A nationwide “Walk the Vote” event, a grassroots effort aimed on promoting the importance of voting, was originally planned for Piedmont this weekend. It was then cancelled because of the high number of votes already placed. “After much back and forth with the [organizers] and Walk A Vote by Mail drop box is located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue outside the Wells Fargo building. the Vote team, we have found that there may not be a need for a walk in Piedmont, as an overwhelming majority of the residents have already voted – which is great,” Walk the Vote organizer Michael Stouber said. Yesterday was the last day to request a Vote by Mail Ballot for the November 3 General Election, but you can still vote early in person. “If anyone wants to vote early right now, even if they don’t have their ballot, they can come to our main office in downtown Oakland in the courthouse, and they can come and get their ballot and vote it,” Dupuis said.

articles.text: Led by Lt. Justin McNulty, a four-man strike team from Piedmont Fire Department left Tuesday morning, October 27, for Orange County in Southern California to assist in containing the Silverado Fire near Irvine. The crew that departed yesterday at 8:30 a.m. includes Engineer Alan Grace, Firefighter Sandor Lengyel, and Firefighter-Paramedic Brian Gidney. Piedmont Fire Chief Bret Black said that he expects the crew to be there through the weekend. The Silverado Fire began on Monday, October 26, in eastern Orange County and quickly spread west, forcing evacuations in Irvine. About 91,000 residents have been evacuated as of Tuesday afternoon. The fire is situated around Santiago Canyon Road and Silverado Canyon Road, southwest of Silverado. The fire may have been caused by Southern California Edison equipment, the utility company said late Monday. Edison officials in a letter to the California Public Utilities Commission said, “Preliminary information reflects SCE (Southern California Edison) overhead electrical facilities are located in the origin area of the Silverado Fire. We have no indication of any circuit activity prior to the reported time of the fire, nor downed overhead primary conductors in the origin area. However, it appears that a lashing wire that was attached to an underbuilt telecommunication line may have contacted SCE’s overhead primary conductor which may have resulted in the ignition of the fire. The investigation is ongoing.” Historically, October is one of the most destructive months of the year for wildfires in California, due in large part to months of dry conditions and strong winds. That has shifted in recent years, though, and especially in 2020. This year, the largest and most destructive wildfires in Northern California have occurred in August and September.

pages.text: YES on Measure UU Dear Piedmont Community, With the election less than a week away, we want to express our appreciation for the thousands of hours spent by hundreds of volunteers working hard to pass Measure UU for the future of Piedmont. It’s inspiring to see citizens of all ages and backgrounds reaching out to friends and neighbors to talk about the need to replace the failing Piedmont Pool. When the three of us stepped up to lead this campaign, we had no idea that we would be supported by such a diverse and talented team, including community leaders, neighborhood advocates, students -- athletes and non-athletes, and over 600 community endorsers. Like us, they are motivated by the fact that the Piedmont Pool has been an integral part of our community and our schools for 56 years. Their enthusiasm and efforts to bring people together and strengthen our community reflect the very best of Piedmont. Please join all of us and vote Yes on Measure UU! articles.text: The new three-story building at Piedmont High School, also known as the STEAM building, finally received its certificate of occupancy from the Division of State Architect on Friday, October 16. After a delay of 2-1/2 months, teachers will be able to occupy their classrooms and use them for broadcasting their distance learning lessons starting October 26. The combined amount for Overaa, the General Contractor for the STEAM building and its companion, the building that will house the Alan Harvey Theater, is $50 million. Roughly $30 million goes toward the STEAM building and $20 million for the adjacent theater building – to be completed by August 2021. Expenses for architects, project managers and other subcontractors are not included in this price, according to Facilities director Pete Palmer. During the October 14 school board meeting Palmer shared his optimism on the budget. Delivery some materials for the STEAM building was delayed due to COVID-19, but they are now arriving on campus. The list includes epoxy countertops and sinks for all science and prep rooms, and operable windows and actuators.
articles.title: STEAM building scheduled to open October 26

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a public forum, streamed live on October 15, to discuss ballot Measure UU, which authorizes the city to issue bonds in the amount of $19.5 million to reconstruct the community pool. The forum was moderated by LWV co-president Nancy Beninati. City Councilmember Betsy Andersen, a proponent of the measure, and resident Andy Wasserman, an opponent of the measure, were both given two minutes to provide an introduction on their stance. They were then given time to respond to questions from the public, which were collected from the audience and summarized by the league. Questions were also submitted through the YouTube chat feature. Andersen noted the pool’s age in her introductory statement. “The pool opened in 1964, when girls were not allowed to swim on the high school swim team, and the Beatles had just made their American debut on the Ed Sullivan show,” she said. “Certainly a lot has changed in 56 years, and after getting the most possible use out of our one and only pool, we have a decision to make.” Andersen added that her fellow councilmembers unanimously supported the measure. “The five of us could not in good conscience vote to close the pool permanently, without giving you, the voters, the chance to invest in Piedmont’s future,” she said. Wasserman, a resident of Piedmont for 40 years, pointed out that City Council has known for a number of months that the Police and Fire Departments have had serious deficiencies, and questioned the council’s priorities when placing the bond on the ballot. Measure UU will appear alongside Measure TT, a proposed increase in real estate transfer taxes, on next month’s ballot. “People don’t move to Piedmont because of a pool. articles.text: Measure TT, the real property transfer tax, will appear on the November 3 municipal ballot alongside Measure UU. Unlike Measure UU, Measure TT only requires a simple majority vote. If adopted by voters, Measure TT would increase the existing real property conveyance tax from the existing rate of $13 per $1,000 of transfer price, to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price. Like the current Real Property Transfer Tax, the increase being put before the voters in Measure TT, would be a general tax. “The council has stated its intention to put increased revenues from this tax, if approved, towards facilities maintenance,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand explained. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that the city devote increased funding to facilities maintenance, which was included in their report to city council on June 15, 2020. The committee recommended an increase in the Real Property Transfer Tax to fund facilities maintenance. Funds garnered from the general tax and its proceeds are deposited in the city’s general fund. This fund is used for the general operations of Piedmont. “To catch up on the City’s facilities maintenance backlog, the council generally makes a transfer from the General fund to the Facilities Maintenance Fund each budget year,” Lillevand said. articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Pumpkin Patch, a tradition for 40 years, has adapted well to its new location this year. articles.text: My husband and I have been exploring Piedmont streets on foot as much as possible while the COVID-19 travel restrictions are in force. We’ve enjoyed acquainting ourselves with streets we’d previously only traversed by car. This morning we walked along Highland to Blair, where we turned left to continue on our way. As we crossed Oakland Ave., we were startled by a white van traveling down Oakland Avenue from above Blair. We’d been watching for traffic, so we weren’t in any danger, but as we continued up Blair, we saw two girls on a bike (a young teenager on the seat and a slightly younger girl behind her) coasting down Blair toward Oakland and picking up speed on the steep decline. They shrieked as they approached the corner of Blair and Oakland, then blew through the stop sign and turned left (uphill) to slow down. It terrified me to imagine what might have happened if the girls had reached the corner a minute or two earlier, at the same time that the van arrived. Visibility is poor, and it’s unlikely that they or the van could have avoided a collision. My older son and his friends used to ride their skateboards down some of Piedmont’s steepest streets, looking for a thrill and feeling invincible. They survived to terrify us years later with tales of their exploits. I can only hope today’s bike riders are equally as lucky. –Karen Mead

articles.text: Mayor All Piedmont households recently received a letter from me asking for a Yes vote on Measure TT; the proposal to increase the Real Property Transfer Tax (“Transfer Tax”). It is on the ballot in the November 3 election. I want to highlight several important points. For almost a decade, the City Council has taken constructive steps to improve the City’s financial position by controlling costs and addressing long-term liabilities. The City Council and staff have been disciplined in managing resources to ensure that our high-quality services can be sustained and that a strategy is in place to address long-term financial challenges. The Council has a strong record of cautious financial management and will continue to carefully manage the City’s resources. The City’s aging infrastructure is the next challenge. The proposed increase in the Transfer Tax is focused on that issue. This increase will provide vital funding and help take on that challenge: The City can pave more streets, repair more sidewalks, improve park maintenance, and better address our aging city facilities. Piedmont voters first approved the Transfer Tax in 1968. In 1993, voters approved an increase to $13.00 per $1,000 of the sales price of homes when sold. articles.text: Editor: The day after I mailed my ballot home from Paris, I learned something that I had not noticed from my too-casual reading of Prop. 19. Voters need to read it carefully all the way through, as deep within it is a stowaway provision. Most voters won’t notice or understand its impact. It is a provision that should have been presented as a stand-alone proposition. Under present law a person may inherit a residence from his or her parents, including a rental residence, and the transfer of title does not have any tax consequences. The transfer of title does not trigger a reassessment of the property’s value to present market value. Prop. 19 changes this and provides that the transfer of title does trigger a reassessment of the property to present market value. This means that a house bought in 1978 for $60,000 and now taxed at $1600 a year will, when inherited, be taxed based on its present value, say $800,000, and the annual tax will increase to something well over $8000. This provision deserves to be considered on its own merits and not smuggled in with the other, more wholesome, provisions of Prop 19. –Michael A. Mathews, Piedmont resident on sabbatical 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 922-8711 • email: news@piedmontpost.org REVIEWERS
articles.title: Prop. 19 – beware of its stowaway provision

articles.text: Editor: Like many Piedmonters, we know there are so many good reasons to re-elect Jennifer Cavenaugh to City Council. We’ve been lucky enough to see Jen in action as a leader, a mentor and a friend. Jen has the experience, intelligence and heart to lead our city in making smart choices that bring us all closer together. She takes an inclusive and datadriven approach to ensure Piedmont serves the needs of the entire community. In addition to her four years on the Piedmont City Council, Jen led the Rec. Department Community Outreach Program, served as President of the Piedmont Language School and on the Parent Club Boards for Beach, PMS and PHS. In all of these roles, she has reached out to a wide range of stakeholders to develop programs and solutions that meet the needs of the entire community. Jen’s leadership has resulted in the launch of new Rec. Department programs for adults and teens, including the innovative Healthy Relationships program. She has helped the community tackle complex issues like upgrading our pool facilities through Measure UU and engage in important conversations about race by organizing the Let’s Talk program. She’s also encouraged countless other Piedmonters to join a committee, advocate for an idea or run for office. In each of these instances, Jen has taken the time to inform and educate herself, reach out to a wide range of people for input and lead in a way that encourages others to rally around a common goal. We trust Jen to serve our community with integrity, smarts, passion and good judgment. We hope all Piedmonters vote and will join us in supporting Jen Cavenaugh for another term. –Rani and Nick Batra
articles.title: Many reasons to re-elect Jen Cavenaugh

articles.text: Editor: The teachers of Piedmont Unified School District are excited to share their support for Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen for School Board. After interviews with each candidate, deliberations, and considerations about the current needs of our students, we believe that Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are the best candidates to meet the needs of our school community. Substantial changes to the educational and social landscape mean that we need candidates who will guide us into the future. These changes include renewed recognition of issues concerning equity, commitment to differences in learning, and an understanding that the students of today will need to navigate new terrain regarding technology, social interactions, environment, career, and more. Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen are candidates for positive change; they will bring important new perspectives to our School Board leadership. We are grateful that the current School Board has taken many important steps in terms of social justice and equity, and we believe these candidates will help take this work to the next level. Veronica Anderson Thigpen brings a wealth of experience as a journalist writing about educational policy and as an educational consultant on issues of equity in education. Jason Kelley brings a background in law, as well as broad experience and knowledge of Piedmont schools and issues concerning Special Education. Through their work on local committees, volunteerism, and experience as Piedmont parents, each has demonstrated a commitment and love for Piedmont schools. Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen will build bridges between teachers, students, and families that will form the basis for strong productive partnerships. Most importantly, as educational professionals, we are confident that they will be a positive force in the lives of our students. Support our students. Vote for Jason Kelley and Veronica Anderson Thigpen. Gabe Kessler is President of the Association of Piedmont Teachers.
articles.title: Teachers union in support of Kelley, Thigpen

articles.text: Editor: When Veronica Anderson Thigpen told me she was running for Piedmont School Board, I cried with joy. Since the first time I met her, she has taken an interest in my thoughts and opinions. Talking with her, I truly felt seen and heard. And speaking with other students in Piedmont, I’ve come to learn I am not an exception. Veronica values all student voices. While she brings a great resume as an educator, journalist, scholar, parent and community leader, what I love most about her is how she makes young people feel included and valued. That is critical to our school board’s mission to be more inclusive. I am reaching out to parents, grandparents and the entire Piedmont community on her behalf. Some of us are too young to vote. Keep us in your heart when you complete your ballot. Vote for the candidate who sees and listens to us — Veronica Anderson Thigpen for school board. –Casey Hidekawa PHS Class of 2019 Stanford Class of 2023
articles.title: Thigpen – paying attention to voices of students

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to enthusiastically support Jen Cavenaugh’s re-election to City Council. I have had the privilege of getting to know Jen through my work as co-chair of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) Housing/Zoning committee and other community causes. Jen is exactly the kind of intelligent, committed, progressive leader our city needs. In the time I’ve known Jen, I have consistently been impressed by her combination of knowledge, diplomatic skill, perseverance, attention to detail, and responsiveness to constituents. When taking on complex issues such as state and local housing policy, policing, and physical and financial planning for our city’s future, Jen consistently does her research, asks smart and well-informed questions, communicates effectively, and follows through with concrete actions.
articles.title: Cavenaugh a supporter of progressive causes

articles.text: In the summer of 1998, a small group of Piedmont high school parents frustrated by the lack of local coverage after the local paper had been sold got together with a plan. Meeting in a neighbor’s house with a large map of the city tacked onto the wall, they laid out the front page of what would become the Piedmont Post. Gray Cathrall, then a part-time sports writer, sent a letter to some 300 people – pretty much everyone he knew in town – inviting them to become subscribers and underwriters of a new paper, the Piedmont Post. Within four weeks, he raised three times what he needed to launch and sustain the paper for a half year. The first issue was delivered to homes through the city on October 20. It was an instant hit: when Gray, the Post’s publisher and editor, came by the high school office to drop off some copies, he saw scores of high schoolers reading the paper in the courtyard. “Any time we can get kids to sit down and read the newspaper, we’ve done something right,” he said later. This week, the Piedmont Post celebrates its 22nd anniversary, a stunning achievement in the world where not a day goes by without the news of another publication in the U.S. folding. No longer a shoestring operation, the paper has a vibrant staff of reporters, photographers, graphic designers, production specialists, columnists, and reviewers. Piedmont residents still make up a healthy portion of financial support along with advertising, which, in a small community with very little commerce, remains remarkable “This is a town that is passionate about having a paper,” said Cathrall. In its early days, the Post made a few decisions by which it abides today. The paper is content-heavy, with prominent space given to residents’ opinions, local news and politics, school matters and sports. It also features PPD Blue, an unedited log from the Piedmont Police Department whose hilarious entries make siblings fight for the right to read the paper first. Unusual for most local papers, it maintains a wide-ranging performing arts section, with live reviews of Bay Area theaters, symphony, opera and regional music organizations. Delivered every Wednesday by an army of primarily middle school-aged students, the Post provides as close to real-time news coverage as is possible with a weekly newspaper. Over the years it has shone the spotlight on countless important, sometimes controversial town matters, challenging city and school administration on staffing, budget, bond issue decisions. The paper consistently provided space for debate on topics from cellphone tower installations to community pool repairs, bringing forth a diversity of voices. It also has made a point of encouraging students to express themselves in print. Some are seen in print early. The current high school senior class president made her writing debut as a fourth grader when the paper published her petition to the City Council to reverse the candy throwing ban at the town’s Fourth of July Parade. The Post is also a chronicler of our lives in this hilly town by the bay. At home, many families have thick scrapbooks with Post’s cutouts that track the lives of their children, through sports teams, school activities and rallies, and even graduation speeches. Some of the lucky ones even show up in the popular where in the World Are We? photo feature (when they remember to send a photo from their latest vacation destination). For many, reading the paper on Wednesday nights has become a ritual. In the world that’s increasingly slipping into a myriad of disjointed silos, the Post, with its wall-to-wall coverage of the town and its inhabitants, reminds us we’re members of the community, not just residents. The Post’s value has come into an even sharper relief now, when the COVID pandemic has ruptured connections through shelter-in-place orders, school closures and cancellations of the activities that make the fabric of this town: sports tournaments, school dances, festivals, concerts. In these difficult times, the Post has lent its pages to support for local businesses fighting for survival, to Piedmonters away from home journaling their experience, as well as to throwbacks of past sports events as points of reference. It continues to be a paragon of non-politicized free speech, of important information about all things local, and a vehicle for all of us to stay together. Reflecting on the paper’s success, Gray, the Post’s towering 6’2” presence, is humble. “We were not really trying to do anything clever or catchy, but answering the question: Does this make sense for the residents of the community? It’s their paper. We just publish it.” Lic. No. 702138 Request a Virtual or On-Site Quote

articles.text: For over 50 years, Piedmont Scouts have offered a Scout Tree Lot for the local community. Run by community volunteers, the Tree Lot also serves as a major fundraiser to support the Piedmont Scout Council, a youth program with over 1000 young participants. Given the social distancing restrictions this year due to COVID-19, the Tree Lot will operate differently and has movd its operations to Online Sales. It’s sustainable; it’s tradition; it’s relaxing, it’s community... and, most of all, it’s easy. off Moraga Road. Please note that the tree lot cannot accept returns or refunds unless there is a specified damage to your items. For more details on COVID safety policies, please visit: www. scouttreelot.org/covid-policy. The goal of all Piedmont BSA Scout programs is to “Prepare for Life” – to prepare Piedmont youth for whatever life brings. By reorganizing to early online sales and contactless pick up and delivery, the Scouts allow customers to plan early for the holidays and relaxing in the spirit of family and home. For more information, contact Genevieve Bandrowski at the Scout office at 510-547-4493 (bsa42trees@gmail.com). We don’t look our age, but we are 110 years old! www.piedmontbsa.org and www.facebook. com/PiedmontBSA.

articles.text: The Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee, under the auspices of Piedmont City Council, held its first public meeting on October 13. The newly formed committee is tasked with implementing a safe streets master plan, and immediately dug in with an initial meeting lasting three hours. Six years ago, on November 3, 2014, the city council unanimously adopted the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan, with the intent of improving conditions for pedestrians and cyclists throughout the city. The master plan pays special attention to the needs of school children, because much of the walking and biking activity in Piedmont consists of children going to and from school. For these reasons the process was planned from the beginning to include a “Safe Routes to School” component. Its objective was to incorporate final recommendations in the master plan for improvements that will encourage more young residents to walk and bike to school, rather than drive or be taken in a carpool. The plan builds on other local planning efforts, particularly the city’s general plan, the American with Disabilities Act Rightof-Way Transition Plan, Climate Action Plan and Complete Streets policy. One example of this type of project is the Craig Avenue and Highland Avenue Crosswalk Enhancement (bulb-out) that was completed as part of the 2019 Paving Project and was identified in the master plan. There are many residual projects that will fall under the guidance of the committee. These include crosswalk enhancements at Oakland and Grand Avenue, Moraga and Highland Avenue, Oakland and Hillside Avenue, and Hampton Road and La Salle Avenue. The committee will also consider reconfiguration of the intersection at the corporation yard at Moraga Avenue and Red Rock Road, and various improvements to Magnolia Avenue and Highland Avenue. Enhanced street crossings are considered a high-priority project for the committee. To address safety concerns, the aforementioned intersections would feature a range of improvements, including striped crosswalks, sidewalk bulb-outs or extensions, advanced yield or stop lines, flashing crossing signs, pedestrian islands, and signage. It is estimated that the safer streets project will last less than a year, concluding in July 2021. The project will include public outreach. The committee includes Hugh Louch, Katie DeWitt, Sofia Barandiaran, Eugene Brown, Jr., Brett Hondorp, Tom Reicher, Kristin Robrock and students Audrey Edel, Piedmont senior class president, and Siddarth Bhatia, a freshman. Gopika Nair from the city staff will be the liaison. At the first meeting committee members chose Louch as Chair and DeWitt as Vice Chair. The committee is conducting a community needs assessment to determine what changes need to be made to the 2014 master plan. The committee will then present the report to the Planning Commission and City Council in the near future. Here are the simple steps for purchasing a beautiful tree: 1. The newly formed committee is tasked with implementing a safe streets master plan, and immediately dug in with an initial meeting lasting three hours. Six years ago, on November 3, 2014, the city council unanimously adopted the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan, with the intent of improving conditions for pedestrians and cyclists throughout the city. The master plan pays special attention to the needs of school children, because much of the walking and biking activity in Piedmont consists of children going to and from school. For these reasons the process was planned from the beginning to include a “Safe Routes to School” component. Its objective was to incorporate final recommendations in the master plan for improvements that will encourage more young residents to walk and bike to school, rather than drive or be taken in a carpool. The plan builds on other local planning efforts, particularly the city’s general plan, the American with Disabilities Act Rightof-Way Transition Plan, Climate Action Plan and Complete Streets policy. One example of this type of project is the Craig Avenue and Highland Avenue Crosswalk Enhancement (bulb-out) that was completed as part of the 2019 Paving Project and was identified in the master plan. There are many residual projects that will fall under the guidance of the committee. These include crosswalk enhancements at Oakland and Grand Avenue, Moraga and Highland Avenue, Oakland and Hillside Avenue, and Hampton Road and La Salle Avenue. The committee will also consider reconfiguration of the intersection at the corporation yard at Moraga Avenue and Red Rock Road, and various improvements to Magnolia Avenue and Highland Avenue. Enhanced street crossings are considered a high-priority project for the committee. To address safety concerns, the aforementioned intersections would feature a range of improvements, including striped crosswalks, sidewalk bulb-outs or extensions, advanced yield or stop lines, flashing crossing signs, pedestrian islands, and signage. It is estimated that the safer streets project will last less than a year, concluding in July 2021. The project will include public outreach. The committee includes Hugh Louch, Katie DeWitt, Sofia Barandiaran, Eugene Brown, Jr., Brett Hondorp, Tom Reicher, Kristin Robrock and students Audrey Edel, Piedmont senior class president, and Siddarth Bhatia, a freshman. Gopika Nair from the city staff will be the liaison. At the first meeting committee members chose Louch as Chair and DeWitt as Vice Chair. The committee is conducting a community needs assessment to determine what changes need to be made to the 2014 master plan. The committee will then present the report to the Planning Commission and City Council in the near future. articles.text: The Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign will host a discussion tonight on how race and segregation have impacted Piedmont schools. It will explore ways that educational equity can be rebalanced in Piedmont. The event is co-sponsored by Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and the Piedmont Education Speaker Series. Panelists will include Stefan Lallinger, Rebecca Sibilia, and Dorothy Lazard. Lallinger is Director of Bridges Collaborative, a group specializing in education policy and housing focused on integrated schools and neighborhoods. Previously, he was Special Assistant to the Chancellor of the New York Department of Education, a principal, teacher, and grade open-enrollment school in New Orleans after Katrina. Sibilia is the founder of EdBuild, a national organization focused on rethinking state funding for public schools. EdBuild has generated national headlines and was referenced in numerous presidential candidates’ platforms. Lazard manages the Oakland History Room of the Oakland Public Library. She has hosted popular history programs, curated exhibits, and written articles with a focus on making the East Bay’s history accessible to a broader audience. Fighting uncertainty: What parents can do By Nina Meehan Uncertainty. Will the kids actually go back to school? Once they are back, will they be able to stay in school? What will flu season look like? Will working from home become our new normal? These questions and so many more have become a drumbeat in our lives – a constant thump that never really leaves us. We adults have all learned to live with it, perhaps normalizing or quieting it with the hectic balance of home-school, work, household and community obligations. But, for our small people, whose ears are more sensitive than ours, this drumbeat of uncertainty may feel like the whole percussion section. So what’s a parent to do? There really is no end in sight right now, and our kids need to silence those cymbals so that they can learn, grow and thrive. I know for my family, when the pandemic hit we suddenly had more screen time enter our lives than ever before. I’m pretty sure we’re not alone in that. And now, eight months into this crisis, I’d really like to return to a more normal balance, but my energy is fast becoming depleted. I don’t know any parent right now who has the bandwidth for a multi-day project recreating the Jurassic period by turning our bedroom into a prehistoric jungles cape using all recycled and eco-friendly materials. But we can focus on what I like to think of as micro-moments of creativity – small engagements, maybe just once a day, that give us all a moment of connection and joy. Maybe we can sit with our kids for five minutes to glue some colored tissue paper into a lively collage. Maybe we can use breakfast time to make up a story together based on one of our favorite animals. Perhaps we can grab flashlights and have a mini-living room dance party for just one song per evening. If we shift our focus from over whelmed to just one micro-moment per day, how will that change our perspective? Our kids will have that moment of connection that grounds them. We will escape from the anxious buzz in our brains by focusing entirely on something different. And, hopefully, we will all fight uncertainty by bringing a tiny bit more laughter and imagination into our daily lives. articles.text: PMS Principal Ryan Fletcher (left) and Technology Coordinator Adam Saville (right) accept the donation of LEGO Mindstorms robotics from VP Fundraising Sally Aldridge (back left) and Makers President David Ragones. Piedmont Makers donated over 30 LEGO Mindstorms Robotics sets to Piedmont Middle School in a brief ceremony at the Piedmont Middle School Makerspace on October 16. The sets were used by members of Piedmont robotic teams from 2017-2019 as part of the FIRST LEGO League program. PMS Principal Ryan Fletcher and Technology Coordinator Adam Saville were on hand to receive the donated LEGO Mindstorms. The LEGO kits are far more than toys; they include the EV3 Intelligent Brick, a compact programmable computer that can control motors and collect sensor feedback. Students can build any sort of locomotive creation from the kits, from robots, to cranes or assembly line machines. Fletcher and Saville were excited and visibly pleased to receive the LEGOs. “Both Adam and I had toured different middle schools in the area, and one component that we have continued to be interested in is exploring a robotics unit for the middle school,” said Fletcher. “With your donation, that day may be sooner rather than later, and for that I thank you,” he said nodding to Ragones and Aldridge. “It opens up a lot of flexibility for us,” he continued. “They could be used in some of our computer arts and science classes or we could include it as a unit in our makers class. There is even an opportunity with all these sets to develop a whole robotics course,” said Saville. In the last four years the Piedmont Makers robotics program has grown from one team with 10 high school students to 34 teams and 220 students from kindergarten through 12th grade. FIRST LEGO League is for students in grades 4-8. In prior years, teams have competed in local qualifier tournaments and regional championships against other regional teams. This year, the teams will compete virtually. “As the FIRST LEGO League has transitioned to a new technology platform LEGO SPIKE Prime this season, Piedmont Makers is happy to give these LEGO Mindstorms sets a future home at Piedmont Middle School,” said Ragones. “We see these as a potential fit for the 6th grade wheel or 7th-8th grade elective courses for the Fab Lab. We recognize the extraordinary work that is being done in the schools virtually and look forward to students taking advantage of this donation when they are back in the classroom.” To learn more about Piedmont robotics see: www.piedmontmakers.org or email robotics@piedmontmakers.org Photo by Joshua Posamentier 2 Piedmont Middle School students Cora Chun (left), Cassandra Colby, and Jasper Schuetz align their LEGO Mindstorms robot during a 2019 Piedmont scrimmage.
articles.title: Piedmont Makers donate robotic kits to Middle School

articles.text: In late August a group of Piedmont High School students created a club, Teens4Biden, as a way to engage students – and the entire community – in the national election November 3 to help the Biden-Harris campaign. Since then, they have been helping the campaign with phone bank work and letter writing. The organizers believe this election is incredibly important, and they want to encourage people of all ages – not just students, to help get out the vote on November 3. The club has about 30 active members, with 200 followers on Instagram. As the election nears, a Grassroots event has been planned for this Sunday, October 25. After submitting a form to the Joe Biden event portal, Teens4Biden received approval as an official campaign organization, and now is listed on the Biden-Harris website. The students will be gathering virtually on October 25 to listen to individuals, including local politicians and activists, on the importance of this election. “We want to create an environment of unity among our friends, family, neighbors and community partners,” said co-founder Audrey Edel. “We are encouraging everyone in the community to attend and support Joe Biden and Kamala Harris with us. We are in this together!” Join Teens4Biden for a virtual event this Sunday, October 25th at 5 p.m. The conferencing link to join is: h t t p s: // w w w. m o b i l i z e . u s / 2020victory/event/351889/
articles.title: Organization to host virtual rally on Sunday

articles.text: Selwyn Kumar joined the Piedmont High School faculty on September 14 as a Biology teacher. Piedmont High School started this year off without a teacher for four periods of the course, so Principal Adam Littlefield stepped up to instruct the distance learning Biology classes himself. Kumar comes to Piedmont from San Mateo High where he taught biology. Coming to a new school mid-year and teaching virtually are not new experiences for him. At San Mateo he began his teaching position in the second semester. Two months later, in March 2020 he had to adapt to distance learning even before he was fully familiar with his students, the campus and staff. “There are challenges starting during the school year. It really requires you to hit the ground running. You haven’t had the opportunity to set up curriculum or learn what you need to teach, or figure out the system of how the school works, especially when you are new. This is not the first time this has happened to me actually.” Kumar will complete his master’s degree in Education and his teaching credentials at San Jose State in March 2021. Before San Mateo High he spent a year at charter school teaching 7th grade science. Prior to that he was a substitute teacher in San Jose and Milpitas for five years. Kumar said his favorite section is science is evolution and genetics. “I find it amazing how all the diverse life we have on our planet came from one common ancestor, even if that was hundreds of millions of years ago.” He will be teaching four periods of freshman Biology in Piedmont. “It is nice to have a full staff of teachers. It allows us to have a dedicated teacher rather than having Mr. Littlefield be so stretched across multiple roles,” said science teacher John Savage. Other new faculty PHS also welcomed Dean Covalt to the science department at the start of the school year. He will teach Honors Chemistry with Savage and teach freshman Selwyn Kumar joins Piedmont High School’s faculty as a Biology teacher. Earth Science and Biology. In the middle of the last school year, Sid Quinsaat, the acapella and AP Music Theory teacher, abandoned his teaching post and eventually quit. Retired teacher Joe Piazza eventually filled in through online teaching to help the students through the end of the school year. Other new teachers at PHS include: Ian Burns (math), Josh Ardis (social psychology) and new social studies teachers Hayley Adams and Hillary Freeman.

Cub Scout Twilight Camp returns Oct. 27-29 The Piedmont Scout Council is moving forward with Twilight Camp this year, but like many other events, they are conducting festivities over Zoom. The camp will be held from 7:00 – 8:00 p.m. each night. Girls and boys of all ages are welcome to join in the fun, which will include craft and snack activities with a Halloween theme. Interested families are asked to sign up online at: https:// www.piedmontbsa.org/events/ twilight-camp-2/. articles.text: The playground in Piedmont Park reopened last Friday, October 16. City-owned park playgrounds were given the green-light last Friday, October 16, by the state and county to reopen. The four city-operated playgrounds are located at Hampton Park, Piedmont Park, Dracena Park, and by Linda Beach Field and are now open to the public. The California Department of Public Health announced the reopening on September 28 and laid out extensive rules and guidance for playground visitors. Many counties in the Bay Area, including Alameda County, chose to open later than the state allowance. Piedmont announced the reopening in its COVID-19 newsletter update and stressed that the city is relying on all residents to follow the rules and use the playground safely. Parents and caregivers will need to closely monitor children to ensure the rules are followed. The city will not have monitors at playground sites. If rules are not followed, these areas may need to be closed again for noncompliance. The City staff made the decision in the past to close Linda Beach Field due to noncompliance with county health orders. The state’s health directives for playgrounds include: • Everyone over two years of age should wear a mask covering their nose and mouth. • Maintain physical distance of six feet between individuals from different households, and prevent the crowding of children. • Do not eat or drink in public playgrounds to ensure that masks are worn at all time. • Wash or sanitize hands before and after your visit. • Visit the park at different times or days to avoid crowds; limit your visit to 30 minutes when others are waiting. • Elderly residents and people with medical conditions should avoid playgrounds when others are present. Alameda County entered the less-restrictive “orange tier” of COVID health guidance on October 13, which permitted additional outdoor activities to resume. The Alameda County Health Care Services Agency will use the coming weeks to monitor the impact of students returning to school and the additional activities opened in the county to determine which, if any, additional activities may be considered for opening. “We are glad to see improving case rates and decreasing test positivity, including among our communities of color, but we caution residents that cases can rise very quickly, as we saw during the summer surge,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Interim Health Officer. “Especially with flu season coming, if we see spikes in COVID-19 cases and a rise in hospitalizations, we will take action to limit the spread and protect public health including resuming restrictions if needed.”

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. This led to my interest in examining college entrances (matriculation) for Piedmont graduates from records published each year in the local newspaper. We should always try to understand how our school district can help all students achieve. We need board members who promote best practices and find ways to improve the school district.
