articles.text: Measure UU is the result of thoughtful preparation and widespread community effort over many years. In 2016, the City Council formed an Aquatics Master Plan Steering Committee and hired pool experts Counsilman-Hunsaker, and LEED certified architects, Harley Ellis Devereaux (HED), to work with City staff and over 100 members of the community to develop a conceptual plan for the inevitable replacement of the Piedmont Pool. The conceptual plan that arose from that public process is reflected in Measure UU. There are over 350 pages of review, study, and discussion, including a 2018 report on the pool’s deteriorating condition, all of which is available to the public on the City’s website. The fact is that outdoor concrete pools do not last forever, and the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool has reached the end of its viability. There are no more lowcost fixes or patches that can save the disintegrating decks, fix the massive leaks, or address the chronically failing mechanical equipment. There is no Plan B. articles.text: Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (“PRFO”) mission statement reads: ”PRFO works collaboratively with the City of Piedmont to identify, advocate for, and bring private financial support to assist in the funding of projects that invest in healthy spaces within the city.” The tagline for PRFO is “Working Together so we can Play Together.” Never have these words been more relevant than in the City’s commitment to rebuild the Piedmont Pool complex through the passage of Measure UU. The Piedmont Pool is an iconic part of the community where generations of Piedmont residents have enjoyed the outdoors. Our one and only public pool is also an essential facility providing a safe and healthy place for families to enjoy aquatics. In addition to the community usage, it also provides Piedmont students the opportunity to compete in swimming and water polo which promotes teamwork, commitment, discipline, and drive. All important qualities as they embark on their life journeys. In support of its mission, PRFO has partnered with the City in the renovation of Hampton Park and the conversion of the City’s Vista tennis courts into the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Community enthusiasm and support have made these projects a reality through private financial contributions of over $1,300,000. The catalyst for the success of these fundraising initiatives has been the City’s willingness to take the lead and commit funding first. Then PRFO, in partnership with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (“PBF”) and other community groups, has been able to rally private donations to support the success of these improvements. The boards of PRFO and PBF have both endorsed Measure UU. Should Measure UU pass, and if asked by the City, PRFO would be willing and ready to rally community financial support for the Piedmont Pool. But first things first, the voters of Piedmont need to decide if they want the City to rebuild a pool for the next 50 years. For the sake of the health of our community, I hope the answer is yes. Steve Collins is President of Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization

articles.text: Below are answers to frequently asked questions regarding Measure UU, which, if approved, would authorize the issuance of general obligation bonds to replace the Piedmont Community Pool. 1. The City proposes to issue $19.5 Million in bonds. What is the actual expected borrowing interest rate assuming the bond passes this year? Municipal bonds can be issued in stages as the funds are needed, and the applicable interest rate is determined at the time the bonds are issued. As a frame of reference, the interest rate as of September 16, 2020 is 2.8%. 2. What is the City’s current total outstanding general obligation debt? The City currently has no outstanding general obligation debt. 3. What is the term of the bond repayment? Measure UU provides that the term of the bond repayment is 30 years with a fixed interest rate. 4. How long will the tax be imposed on properties, and will the amount of the tax ever decrease? Measure UU, if adopted, would impose a tax on properties for 30 years. articles.text: Members of the girl’s water polo team voiced their support of Measure UU, including PHS senior Grace Davies in an open letter. Measure UU is undoubtedly the marquee items on Piedmont’s November ballot. One flip through the Post the last month makes you aware. For athletes at Piedmont High, the measure means a legitimate future worth planning for and looking forward to. UU has undertaken a giant community effort, which had a student-led rally on Wednesday, October 14 at the corner of Highland and Oakland Avenue. Around 25 current and former student-athletes from Piedmont High attended the rally, organized by Piedmont Swim Team captain and PHS student Noah Kwong. Students and alumni are also taking a big role in social media outreach, in addition to helping manage the Measure UU campaign website: https://www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com/ Current Piedmont High senior Grace Davies wrote an official letter to help urge eligible voters in town to supply their “Yes” on the ballot, noting her experience on the water polo team and her time working as a lifeguard. “Being a part of the pool community through water polo opened my eyes to another great skill and opportunity for me — lifeguarding and teaching swim lessons. The pool provided the training and certifications for me to have a flexible work experience that was also very fulfilling. I can’t imagine a more convenient job for a PHS student — I could walk to work after school and schedule my hours around my other activities. Not only did I earn a paycheck, but I had an impact on others and got to work with a great community of staff at the pool,” she wrote. “Please remember the students when you consider your vote — and how much we all benefit from this project. We need to continue the tradition of a community pool and swimming program in Piedmont. Please vote YES on Measure UU for the future of swimming in Piedmont,” Davies continued. For mer Piedmont High All-American water polo athlete Henry Saunders (Class of 2019), now at USC, talked about the need of a new pool in town. Saunders set school records in the Piedmont pool and is now a member of perennial powerhouse USC. He has described the Piedmont Pool the “worst” he’s ever played in, and a place that precluded having a home-crowd atmosphere similar to other sports. “As a 2015-2019 PHS Water Polo and Swim athlete, I am a strong supporter of Yes on UU. I am very proud to have been raised in Piedmont, attended Piedmont schools K-12 and swam my first strokes in the Piedmont pool with my Grandfather,” wrote Saunders. “While I have fond memories of the Piedmont Pool, it is not the competitive pool Piedmont swimmers and water polo players deserve. I am very fortunate to have played regional and national water polo tournaments over the past 10 years and truthfully, the Piedmont Pool is unfortunately the worst pool I have competed in,” he continued. Saunders reiterated the sentiments of his former Piedmont High head coach John Savage, that the water polo program will not survive without the funding toward a new pool. “The Piedmont water polo program has great coaches and is growing as well, but it may die altogether if the Piedmont pool isn’t rebuilt. Every other city in Alameda County provides a pool for its students. Piedmont students deserve the same,” he wrote. For more information, visit the campaign site of Measure UU: https://www.communitypoolforpiedmont.com/. Former Piedmont High All-American Henry Saunders, now at USC, is in strong support of Measure UU which would create a new pool in town.

articles.text: East Bay Regional Parks re-opened their hill-based parks on Friday, October 16, after high winds threatened the area with possible extreme fire activity. Of parks re-opened, all are within miles of Piedmont: Anthony Chabot Regional Park, Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve, Kennedy Grove Regional Recreation Area, Leona Canyon Open Space Regional Preserve, Reinhardt Redwood Regional Park, Roberts Regional Recreation Area, Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve, Tilden Regional Park, Wildcat Canyon Regional Park Figuring out which parks to visit during fire season can be a confusing task. Aside from checking our weekly outdoors information in this section of the Piedmont Post, East Bay Regional lists the status of all parks at: ebparks.org. Although the SCU Complez Fire was contained in 44 days as of October 1, parks within the East Bay Regional Park District remain closed, including Castle Rock of the Diablo Foothills, the Morgan Territory Regional Preserve of Contra Costa County, Alameda Count y’s Sunol Regional Wilderness near Sunol and Hayward and the Ohlone Wilderness near Fremont. Earlier this month the park district announced that dogs are again, permitted to be off-leash in designated areas. “We thank dog owners for their understanding during COVID-19 and their cooperation with the temporary leash restrictions,” said East Bay Regional’s general manager Robert Doyle. “The restrictions have helped keep parks and trails open and safe. Regional Parks, now more than ever, play an important role in maintaining mental health and providing places where people and their pets can exercise in a safe, socially distant manner.” This does not mean that dogs are totally allowed to roam free, EBRP reminds. Dogs must still be leashed in parking lots, trailheads, and paved bike paths. “The return of normal dog rules is a reminder that dog owners need to be responsible and share the parks with others,” added Doyle. “Dog owners need to bag and bin their dog’s poop, leash their dogs in designated areas, including parking lots, trailheads, and paved trails, and keep their dogs on-leash around cattle and horses. Cattle play an important role in reducing vegetation and fire risks.” A closed East Bay Regional Park. Staff Photo

articles.text: It’s never too early to start examining the United States Men’s National Team, which should have no problem qualifying for the 2022 World Cup, right? Well, it’s not that simple. Not qualifying for the 2018 World Cup was a huge disappointment; and with the squad not appearing again until 2021, the U.S, seemingly has a much tighter time frame to get into form and determine its best 23 players. The United States isn’t scheduled for matches until the 2022 World Cup Qualifiers, which will take place between June 2021 and March 2022. The World Cup qualifier overlaps with the 2021 CONCACAF Gold Cup in July 2021. U.S. manager Gregg Berhalter announced the team would focus on arranging two European friendlies in November and some domestic matches this fall, however nothing is set at this point. Luckily for the U.S., the team automatically qualified for the final round of the World Cup qualifier along with Mexico, Costa Rica, Jamaica, and Honduras based on FIFA world rankings. The final round of World Cup Qualifiers will be an eightteam, single group round-robin of matches, with the top three teams automatically qualifying for the World Cup. A fourth CONCACAF team will qualify for FIFA’s Inter-Confederation playoffs to determine the last two teams in the World Cup. Inter-Confederation matches will be made up of one team from CONCACAF (North America), CONMEBOL (South America), OFC (Oceanic), and AFC (Asian). As for the U.S. roster, this writer wastes no time calling their future 2022 World Cup roster the start of its Golden Generation of players. It makes the possibility of not qualifying a terrifying thought. The U.S. will have nearly an entire roster of players under age 30, many of who play overseas in England, Germany, Spain, and France. Though matches will be limited for the next year, here is our look at the possible 23-man roster for the 2022 World Cup. CDM Kellyn Acosta (Colorado Rapids), CDM Jackson Yueill (San Jose Earthquakes), CAM Brenden Aaronson (RB Salzburg), CAM Richie Ledezma (PSV Einhoven) Weston McKennie, Tyler Adams, and Giovanni Reyna are three headliners overseas in Italy’s Serie A and Germany’s Bundesliga – each gaining valuable Champions League experience. Reyna is only 17-years old and could be a star in the making. Behind them it gets a little tougher and is visibly the weakest area of the roster. In need of defensive mids, Kellyn Acosta of the Colorado Rapids and Jackson Yueill from the San Jose Earthquakes could certainly be of use. But, attacking options with experience are bleak. Brenden Aaronson, 19, is joining Bundesliga’s RB Salzburg after making 45 appearances with the Philadelphia Union. Richie Ledezma, 20, plays for the Netherlands’ PSV Einhoven. However, Aaronson has one USMNT appearance and Ledezma has only three for the U23 team. The lack of experience on the backend could result in former captain Michael Bradley appearing as a veteran backup. Fellow veteran CM Paul Arriola also seems logical but also less than ideal. Defense: LB Sergino Dest (Barcelona), LB Antonee Robinson (Fulham), RB DeAndre Yedlin (Newcastle), RB Reggie Cannon (FC Dallas), CB John Brooks (Wolfsburg), CB Matt Miazga (Reading), CB Miles Robinson (Atlanta Utd) Sergino Dest, the 19-year old phenom made headlines when signing with Barcelona. He’s a major upgrade at wingback and is likely to suit up on the left. DeAndre Yedlin is among the Forward: LW Christian Pulisic (Chelsea), RW Tim Weah (Lille), FW Tyler Boyd (Beksitas), FW Jordan Morris (Seattle Sounders), ST Josh Sargent (Wolfsburg), ST Jozy Altidore (Toronto FC) The United States will have lots of speed and attacking options in 2022 like Tim Weah, who must prove he can stay healthy with Lille in France, and Chelsea’s Christian Pulisic, who will be the talisman and could line up at wing or central attacking midfield. The interesting subject of this group will be Jozy Altidore, who at age 32 should be the veteran leader in the locker room. But he’s sure to face competition for playing time from Josh Sargent and Jordan Morris – both younger and faster options. Another name to keep an eye on is Wolfsburg’s 19-year old Ulysses Llanez. However, it’s hard to see Llanez pushing for a spot with limited time due to COVID. Midfield: CM Weston McKennie (Juventus), CDM Tyler Adams (RB Leipzig), CAM Giovanni Reyna (Dortmund), Men’s soccer team manager Gregg Berhalter. most experienced and should start on the opposite side if he’s healthy. The United States is deepest at center back, meaning some talented players could miss out. John Brooks is the unquestioned captain and a regular starter for Germany’s Wolfsburg. Next to him could be Matt Miazga, who has been playing well in England, while Miles Robinson is considered a surging talent in the MLS. If Miazga and Robinson crack the 23-man roster, that means they will have unseated veterans Aaron Long and Tim Ream. Given that Ream can double as a left back and center back, he could be someone to keep an eye on despite being 35 when the World Cup starts. Goalkeeper: Zac Steffen (Fortuna Dusseldorf), Ethan Horvath (Club Brugge), Brad Guzan (Atlanta Utd) Zac Steffen, on loan to Dusseldorf from Manchester City, is the unquestioned leader at keeper. Behind him is a mere formality; Ethan Horvath plays for Club Brugge and is gaining Champions League experience this season. Brad Guzan could be a farfetched thought at 38-years old in 2022, but opting for experience could prove useful from a leadership standpoint. American soccer fans should get to know 17-year Gio Reyna of Borussia.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of LA Times 49ers cornerback Jason Verrett snatched a critical interception in a 24-16 win over the Rams last Sunday, October 18. Here we go again. The 49ers have yet again proven my predictions wrong after upsetting the Los Angeles Rams 24-16 last Sunday. Although San Francisco didn’t get any sacks, they rushed Rams QB Jared Goff into completing just 19 of 38 passes for 198 yards, two touchdowns, but a critical interception for Jason Verrett in the end zone. San Francisco QB Jimmy Garoppolo had a bounce-back game with three touchdowns and 268 yards passing. And when looking ahead to Week 7’s matchup with the Patriots, he’ll need to be as efficient. New England has among the best pass defenses in the league, but they are vulnerable without many weapons aside from quarterback Cam Newton. In the end, if Garoppolo and 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan are in sync, San Francisco could walk away with a big victory. If it becomes a defensive battle, the edge has to go toward the Patriots and its coach Bill Belichick. Raiders update The Raiders return from their bye week with a visit from Tom Brady and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Jon Gruden and Las Vegas have proven to do well in critical games this season, but this writer expects it will be a tough defensive battle. Tampa Bay has the 2nd best run defense in the league, meaning if Vegas can’t get Josh Jacobs going and become one-dimensional, it’s going to get tough. If the Raiders come out with a win, it will be becauseQB Derrick Carr is efficient with his throws and maybe lands a bomb or two with rookie WR Henry Ruggs. Premier League review Crossing the pond to England, Premier League returned from the international break for its fifth of 38 match days. Everton and Liverpool’s Merseyside Derby had the game of the week in a 2-2 draw, meaning Everton continues undefeated at 4-1-0 and first place of the league table. The match was highlighted in what would’ve been the game winning goal by Liverpool’s Jordan Henderson after VAR ruled Sadio Mane offside, while Liverpool defender Virgil Van Dijk sustained a season-ending knee injury. Aston Villa continues its unexpected winstreak to four games after defeating Leicester 1-0 when recent acquisition Ross Barkley scored the game-winner in the first of five minutes of stoppage time. The Lions are 4-0-0 and in second, a point behind the Toffees. Looking ahead to Matchday 6, some big games are happening with large implications on the table. Aston Villa square off with recently promoted Leeds on Friday, and Leeds are surprisingly listed as the favorite. Villa will surely face an uphill battle each week and, at some point, will dip down the table. But saying it will start against Leeds could be a bit of a stretch. Manchester United is currently in 15th of 20 with six points at 2-0-2, they’ll play Chelsea on Saturday—who are in 8th at 2-2-1. United are coming off a big 2-1 victory over PSG in their Champions League meeting on Tuesday, while Chelsea drew 3-3 with Southampton and are allowing a lot of goals. This could be time for the Reds to pounce. Everton and Southampton meet on Sunday, this writer could see a draw with Southampton’s Danny Ings in a great run of form. Arsenal and Leceister are another key match with the Gunners in fifth (3-0-2) and Foxes in fourth (3-0-2). Photo courtesy of The Guardian Aston Villa is still undefeated at 4-0-0. Can they continue their impressive run against Leeds this week?

Aston Villa continues its unexpected winstreak to four games after defeating Leicester 1-0 when recent acquisition Ross Barkley scored the game-winner in the first of five minutes of stoppage time. Arsenal and Leceister are another key match with the Gunners in fifth (3-0-2) and Foxes in fourth (3-0-2). A look at U.S. Men’s Soccer Team By Jonathan Comeaux It’s never too early to start examining the United States Men’s National Team, which should have no problem qualifying for the 2022 World Cup, right? Well, it’s not that simple. Not qualifying for the 2018 World Cup was a huge disappointment; and with the squad not appearing again until 2021, the U.S, seemingly has a much tighter time frame to get into form and determine its best 23 players. The United States isn’t scheduled for matches until the 2022 World Cup Qualifiers, which will take place between June 2021 and March 2022. The World Cup qualifier overlaps with the 2021 CONCACAF Gold Cup in July 2021. U.S. manager Gregg Berhalter announced the team would focus on arranging two European friendlies in November and some domestic matches this fall, however nothing is set at this point. Luckily for the U.S., the team automatically qualified for the final round of the World Cup qualifier along with Mexico, Costa Rica, Jamaica, and Honduras based on FIFA world rankings. The final round of World Cup Qualifiers will be an eightteam, single group round-robin of matches, with the top three teams automatically qualifying for the World Cup. A fourth CONCACAF team will qualify for FIFA’s Inter-Confederation playoffs to determine the last two teams in the World Cup. Inter-Confederation matches will be made up of one team from CONCACAF (North America), CONMEBOL (South America), OFC (Oceanic), and AFC (Asian). As for the U.S. roster, this writer wastes no time calling their future 2022 World Cup roster the start of its Golden Generation of players. It makes the possibility of not qualifying a terrifying thought. The U.S. will have nearly an entire roster of players under age 30, many of who play overseas in England, Germany, Spain, and France. Though matches will be limited for the next year, here is our look at the possible 23-man roster for the 2022 World Cup. CDM Kellyn Acosta (Colorado Rapids), CDM Jackson Yueill (San Jose Earthquakes), CAM Brenden Aaronson (RB Salzburg), CAM Richie Ledezma (PSV Einhoven) Weston McKennie, Tyler Adams, and Giovanni Reyna are three headliners overseas in Italy’s Serie A and Germany’s Bundesliga – each gaining valuable Champions League experience. Reyna is only 17-years old and could be a star in the making. Behind them it gets a little tougher and is visibly the weakest area of the roster. In need of defensive mids, Kellyn Acosta of the Colorado Rapids and Jackson Yueill from the San Jose Earthquakes could certainly be of use. But, attacking options with experience are bleak. Brenden Aaronson, 19, is joining Bundesliga’s RB Salzburg after making 45 appearances with the Philadelphia Union. Richie Ledezma, 20, plays for the Netherlands’ PSV Einhoven. However, Aaronson has one USMNT appearance and Ledezma has only three for the U23 team. The lack of experience on the backend could result in former captain Michael Bradley appearing as a veteran backup. Fellow veteran CM Paul Arriola also seems logical but also less than ideal. Defense: LB Sergino Dest (Barcelona), LB Antonee Robinson (Fulham), RB DeAndre Yedlin (Newcastle), RB Reggie Cannon (FC Dallas), CB John Brooks (Wolfsburg), CB Matt Miazga (Reading), CB Miles Robinson (Atlanta Utd) Sergino Dest, the 19-year old phenom made headlines when signing with Barcelona. He’s a major upgrade at wingback and is likely to suit up on the left. DeAndre Yedlin is among the Forward: LW Christian Pulisic (Chelsea), RW Tim Weah (Lille), FW Tyler Boyd (Beksitas), FW Jordan Morris (Seattle Sounders), ST Josh Sargent (Wolfsburg), ST Jozy Altidore (Toronto FC) The United States will have lots of speed and attacking options in 2022 like Tim Weah, who must prove he can stay healthy with Lille in France, and Chelsea’s Christian Pulisic, who will be the talisman and could line up at wing or central attacking midfield. The interesting subject of this group will be Jozy Altidore, who at age 32 should be the veteran leader in the locker room. But he’s sure to face competition for playing time from Josh Sargent and Jordan Morris – both younger and faster options. Another name to keep an eye on is Wolfsburg’s 19-year old Ulysses Llanez. However, it’s hard to see Llanez pushing for a spot with limited time due to COVID. Midfield: CM Weston McKennie (Juventus), CDM Tyler Adams (RB Leipzig), CAM Giovanni Reyna (Dortmund), Men’s soccer team manager Gregg Berhalter. most experienced and should start on the opposite side if he’s healthy. The United States is deepest at center back, meaning some talented players could miss out. John Brooks is the unquestioned captain and a regular starter for Germany’s Wolfsburg. Next to him could be Matt Miazga, who has been playing well in England, while Miles Robinson is considered a surging talent in the MLS. If Miazga and Robinson crack the 23-man roster, that means they will have unseated veterans Aaron Long and Tim Ream. Given that Ream can double as a left back and center back, he could be someone to keep an eye on despite being 35 when the World Cup starts. Goalkeeper: Zac Steffen (Fortuna Dusseldorf), Ethan Horvath (Club Brugge), Brad Guzan (Atlanta Utd) Zac Steffen, on loan to Dusseldorf from Manchester City, is the unquestioned leader at keeper. Behind him is a mere formality; Ethan Horvath plays for Club Brugge and is gaining Champions League experience this season. Brad Guzan could be a farfetched thought at 38-years old in 2022, but opting for experience could prove useful from a leadership standpoint. articles.text: It’s no surprise Piedmont kids are the number one supporters and advocates to rebuild the failing Piedmont Pool. It is children who will most benefit from a new facility. The kids will undoubtedly be harmed if Piedmont voters don’t pass Measure UU on November 3. Even though over 90% of them can’t vote, hundreds of Piedmont kids of all ages are walking the streets, writing letters, waving signs, posting on social media, creating a video and website, and making calls – all urging adult voters in town to think about the future of young people without any pool in the city. Nearly all Piedmont children use the pool for swim lessons, recreation, summer camps, PE, and athletics. If Piedmont doesn’t rebuild its pool, it will be the only city in Alameda County that doesn’t provide a pool for its families and students. “To many adults in town, Measure UU is just another line on their ballot. Some could even flip a coin on rebuilding the pool. But to Piedmont youth, the outcome of Measure UU will completely change our lives,” said Noah Kwong, captain of the Piedmont Swim Team. On Wednesday, October 14 during the afternoon rush hour, Piedmont youth ranging from first grade to recent Piedmont High School graduates rallied together at the intersection of Highland and Oakland Avenues, waving signs and placards in support of Measure UU. Supporters honked, gave the thumbs up, and cheered on the student athletes. In addition to the omnipresent blue Yes on UU signs, kids created homemade signs with words straight from their heart, including: “I don’t want to have to carpool to Orinda or Alameda just to swim!” “We have courts and fields. Where’s our Pool ” “I’m a basketball player, not a swimmer, but I’m out here in Sonja ten Grotenhuis (left), Madeline Payne, and Daniela Acevedo-Schiesel. solidarity with my fellow PHS athletes. A pool is just as important to our athletic program as a gym,” said Luke Harris, a recent recruit to play basketball at Carleton College. “Water Polo has changed our lives and those of our teammates. Without a pool in Piedmont, there are many who will have to quit the sport because of the high cost to rent space in another community’s pool, and the time it will take to commute to practice,” said Ella Wright and Spencer Stein, PHS water polo players. For the next few weeks, youth across town will continue to juggle online class work and campaign for Measure UU. For many, the campaign for a Piedmont Community Pool has been their first foray into politics. “As a swimmer, my heart is in this fight, and as a student, it’s been interesting to learn the political side of things,” said Gwenyth Jones, a PHS swimmer. “There’s so much at stake in this election from the top of the ballot down to Measure UU.” Piedmont’s youth will be watching the election returns on November 3rd, just like the adults in town. Piedmont Middle School seventh grader, Tai March-Cunningham summed up the kids’ perspective. “Adults had a pool when they were growing up. Why wouldn’t they vote for us to have one, too?” Water polo players Ella Wright (left), Hannah Mooney, Grace Davies, and Gwenyth Jones. Deniz Radzik (left), Kate Aubrecht, Josie Oesterer, Miles the dog, and Noah Kwong attend a rally in favor of a bond to build a new pool in Piedmont. Piedmont Swim team members encourage motorists to support Measure UU. Pictured are Farris Saffouri (left), Charlie White, Aaron Wu, Simon Lins, Brian Wu and Ryan Stokes.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse has announced its revised 2020–21 season, presented in a series of acts. Each act will be comprised of three shows for a total of nine productions. Act I will put talent back onstage again for a series of on-demand video streams. Act I: Taking the Leap will run from October 24 through December 31. It will consist of three video on-demand offerings from some of the Bay Area’s greatest artists as well as playwrights from across the globe. All three productions will be available for on-demand video streaming. The first work in Taking the Leap features a play by Yasmina Reza, directed by Bill English and starring Bobak Cyrus Bakhtiari, Johnny Moreno, and Jomar Tagatac. The play, entitled Art, explores how an upcoming election creates division between opposing camps. Although it is a comedy, it explores and addresses the complex layers of friendship. The show will stream from October 24 to November 7. The Jewelry Box, written and performed by Brian Copeland, will follow in Act I. In this story, a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show Not a Genuine Black Man, a young Brian heads to the mean streets of Oakland to buy his mother a Christmas gift. When he finds the perfect present – a jewelry box in the White Front store – six-year-old Brian sets out to earn the required $11.97 by Christmas Eve. The Jewelry Box will stream from November 28 to December 25. The entrance to San Francisco Playhouse at 450 Post Street. The final work scheduled for the holidays is From Blues to Broadway. It was created in collaboration with and performed by John Paul Gonzalez, Cate Hayman, Rodney Earl Jackson, Jr., and Katrina Lauren McGraw, with music direction by Dave Dobrusky. In this piece, Dobrusky directs a who’s who of San Francisco musical talent. Hayman, McGraw, Jackson, and Gonzalez will perform a medley of holiday songs. The piece will stream from December 12 through December 31. Act II and Act III will be announced in the near future. Subscribe to Act I plays at https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/2020-2021-season/.
articles.title: SF Playhouse season to begin October 24

articles.text: Violinist Lisa Lee will appear in a concert with Musaics of the Bay. Musaics of the Bay will present a Shubert concert performed by five Bay Area musicians on November 8. Schubert’s Cello Quintet in C Major, D. 956 will be performed by violinists Lisa Lee (one fifth of The Lee Trio) and Francisco Fullana, Jonathan Vinocour on viola, and cellists Peter Myers and Tanya Tomkins. Lee is a Fulbright Scholar and top prizewinner in the Tadeusz Wronski International Violin Competition, Pacific Symphony Orchestra Young Artists, and San Francisco Symphony Concerto competitions. She and her two sisters perform internationally as The Lee Trio and have appeared at the Piedmont Center of the Arts. She has been on the faculty at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music since 2017. Fullana, winner of the 2018 Avery Fisher Career Grant, is a native of Mallorca in Spain. He has soloed with the City of Birmingham, Vancouver, Pacific, and Madrid Symphonies as well as the Saint Paul Chamber Orchestra and the Spanish Radio Television Orchestra. Vinocour was appointed Principal Viola of the San Francisco Symphony in 2009. He previously was Principal Viola of the Saint Louis Symphony and Guest Principal of the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig. Myers has served as an assistant Principal Cellist of the San Francisco Opera since 2017 and is internationally known as a chamber musician. Cellist Tomkins is renowned in particular for her interpretation of the Bach Cello Suites, which she has performed many times at venues including New York’s Le Poisson Rouge and the Seattle Early Music Guild. articles.text: Oakland Symphony, as part of its “rePAST” archival concert streaming series, is celebrating Indigenous Peoples’ Day with a performance of John Christopher Wineglass’ Big Sur: The Night Sun. “The natural beauty of Big Sur is sacred to many. This feeling of sanctity was shared by Wineglass, who formed many of the themes of his tone poem Big Sur: The Night Sun while in residence on the grounds of the Glen Deven Ranch and other areas such as Pfeiffer Beach,” Music Director Michael Morgan explained. “The beautiful impressions and warm enlightenments that affected him while on the retreat become the root and soul of this magnificent work.” The performance features Emiliano Campobello on native flute, Marcie Chapa and Jayson Fann as world percussionists, and Kanyon Sayers-Roods, Native-American singer from the Costanoan Ohlone and Chumash Tribes. “This mesmerizing work features the haunting voice of Kanyon Sayers-Roods, her art is a sincere expression of her native heritage,” Morgan said. The piece was originally performed by the symphony at the Paramount Theatre on February 24, 2017, and is available online at https://www.oaklandsymphony. org/repast/.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony celebrates Indigenous Peoples’ Day

articles.text: Barns in Ferndale Local artist Michael Stehr will present his latest collection of paintings at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from October 30 through November 8. The exhibition, entitled “The Sky’s the Limit,” will focus on skies in landscape and cityscape work, and will show how the nature of sky affects mood and atmosphere. The exhibit marks the first opportunity to show his paintings since the pandemic limited public events seven months ago. Because his series of art lectures at the Center was interrupted due to COVID, he has had several free virtual art history lectures to stay connected with his audience. The Zoom lectures were very well attended, confirming Piedmont’s desire to connect to the arts during the pandemic. On Friday, October 30, Stehr will host a virtual opening of the art exhibit via Zoom starting at 6 p.m. During the presentation he will discuss details of his construction of skies: how the sky is rendered, the effect of using certain values, the forms of cloud composition, and the utilization of certain color harmonies as a way of achieving a particular feel for the painting. Stehr will also preview 36 new paintings, along with other previously exhibited work, to complete the robust exhibit. Reservations are required to visit the gallery in person. The exhibit will be open on Saturday and Sunday, October 31 and November 1, and Saturday and Sunday, November 7 and 8, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Visits will be at 30-minute intervals. A link to the reservation sign-up sheet can be found on the PCA website (www. piedmontcenterforthearts.org) or by visiting michaelstehr.com. Coastline at Normandy
articles.title: For artist Michael Stehr, the Sky’s The Limit

articles.text: American pop and jazz singer Frank Sinatra. The name Frank Sinatra conjures up deep feelings. Some say that he was the greatest pop singer of them all. Others assert, with equal fervor, that his fame was ill-deserved. No matter which side you were on, everyone had to agree that Sinatra had a distinctive style. I’m not talking about the way he dressed...which was the epitome of high fashion. I am speaking of the way he sang. No one sang a song like Sinatra. He was so stylish that he remained popular long after his voice had deserted him. It might shock you to know that he did not invent his style of singing. Critics, in their effort to analyze Sinatra’s success, claim that he patterned his singing after crooners like Bing Crosby. But if you really listen to Sinatra’s singing technique, perhaps you will understand and agree with me that Sinatra was actually inspired by the popular operatic baritone John Charles Thomas. Sinatra famously sang on consonants, a technique he got from John Charles Thomas. Sometimes Sinatra sang a combination of talking through a song and actually singing. He got this technique from John Charles Thomas. Sinatra caressed a phrase like no one else – also something he learned from John Charles Thomas. So, dear readers, listen to some recordings of Sinatra in his prime. And then listen to some of the songs that made John Charles Thomas so popular. First listen to some of his serious operatic arias. Then listen to his wisecracking rendition of Largo al factotum by Rossini. Follow this with a western song such as “Home on the Range,” and finally listen to his rendition of a kid’s song, “The Green Eyed Dragon with the 13 Tails.” It’s hard to believe that two singers who were 180° apart in type of music being sung could approach a song the same way. But they did. And each one was a phenomenal success. Now we will take a quick segue from vintage Sinatra to vintage wines. A friend who is in the communications business sent me a short piece on wine. Back in prehistoric times, our predecessors discovered that wine and other alcoholic beverages were actually safer to drink than water. Wine was quite easy to make. Grape juice and sugar-consuming yeast transform into wine. Actually, I think that the grapes come with their own yeast. Our predecessors tried different types of grapes and different types of yeast. And that’s where the arguments and the fun began. It was red versus white, dry versus sweet, fresh wine versus aged. Let’s not forget vintage versus vintage and finally the presentation. There is evidence of fermented drinks in ancient China around 7000 BC. Around 6000 BC wine was made in Georgia and then more recently in Sicily in 4000 BC. The Spanish tried to introduce wine in California. Success came much later. We put our trust in wine connoisseurs. These experts take themselves seriously. Once, while on a concert tour in Italy, I was invited to a prize-winning winery near Florence. We went to the tasting room and the famous vintner regaled us with his expertise. All the appropriate vocabulary was used while he swirled his wine around in an elegant glass. I didn’t know if I should take the man seriously, but the famous vintner knew exactly what he was doing. With a twinkle in his eye, he concluded his discourse on winemaking by saying, “It’s all <*<>\?!” And with that, he gave us a few bottles of his famous wine and sent us on our way. American operatic baritone John Charles Thomas.
articles.title: Vintage Frank Sinatra and vintage wines

articles.text: The University of California, Berkeley Botanical Garden will host a Zoom program exploring the many species of butterflies that have taken residence in the gardens. Join the garden’s resident propagator Sal Levinson and garden volunteer Sarab Seth for an illustrated slideshow of butterflies found among the flowers this time of year. Those who tune in will learn about the butterflies’ life cycle, host plants, and more. Some notable species that are Monarch butterflies are a common sight in the gardens. Sal Levinson commonly seen in the gardens are Cabbage White, West Coast Lady, Painted Lady, Common Buckeye, Fiery Skipper, California Ringlet, and Red Admiral. This Zoom event is suitable for all ages and includes live viewings of caterpillars. It will take place this Sunday, October 25, from 11 a.m. to 12 p.m. The event is free and open to the public. To register online, visit https://41780.blackbaudhosting. com/41780/Zoom-Program-Butterf lies-of-the-UC-BotanicalGarden-25Oct2020.
articles.title: See Monarchs up close in zoom program on Sunday

articles.text: A scene from JoJo Rabbit. Moview review by Chris Honoré The Oscar nominated film JoJo Rabbit is a high risk, high gain satire, using humor, irony and ridicule to comment on the Nazi regime during a period when Germany and Austria were fully committed to a pathological leader, millions enthusiastically raising their arms in euphoric, sieg heil approbation. So the question begged is whether it’s possible to use satire effectively when telling a story about a regime that is defined as evil. How to bring to bear even a hint of humor or exaggeration or ridicule while examining what is profoundly grim and awful? But that is what JoJo Rabbit attempts to do, choosing as its narrative vehicle a 10-year-old boy, JoJo Betzler (Roman Griffin Davis), a wide-eyed, newbie Nazi, dressed in a Hitler Youth uniform, ready to die for der Fuhrer, who also happens to be his imaginary friend. The mustachioed, strutting companion is always nearby (portrayed by writer/director Taiki Waititi), reminding JoJo that a good Nazi is a loyal Nazi, occasionally asking for a seig heil, just to keep in practice. What JoJo Rabbit serves up is a comical exaggeration with uniform-clad caricatures created to elicit a laugh, their strutting reminiscent of Charlie Chaplin’s slapstick performance in The Great Dictator. Actually, given the prism through which JoJo views his world, it’s evident that he is poorly equipped to even begin to critically evaluate the horror that surrounds him. His indoctrination has been complete, and the walls of his room are covered in fanboy Nazi propaganda. So, when JoJo discovers that his mother, Rosie (Scarlett Johansson), has been hiding a young Jewish girl, Elsa (Thomasin McKenzie), in an attic hideaway, he is instantly conflicted. He feels he should report this betrayal, reinforced vociferously by his Fuhrer; however, to do so would implicate his mother. As well, it is clear that this young boy, who simply wants to join a club of his peers and have an adventure, is completely unaware of the horror visited on the Jewish people by his swastika-wearing compatriots. His experience and understanding is far too limited. And yet, curious, taken with her, he sets out to know Elsa better, hoping to comprehend what being Jewish means. He writes her letters in the voice of her boyfriend, now missing. He asks about stereotypes, absent any understanding of the consequences of such prejudices and their entrenched racism. And so as Waititi uses satire; in the aggregate is seems no more then cute but pointless. JoJo’s point of view is framed by his naiveté and childlike innocence and so he is insulated from the awful truths that surround him. In one scene when he is passing through the town square he sees condemned Germans who have been hanged, their still bodies, hands bound, turning slowly in a light wind. He, of course, is incapable of making a connection between what he sees before him and his love of Nazism or the red swastika armband he proudly wears, or the meaning of his imaginary friend. For JoJo this hideous image of the hanged, filled with a remorseless finality, is devoid of implication and to connect what he sees to all that he dearly wants to be is a bridge too far. He’s just a kid. And therein is the flaw in the film. Its use of satire has no edge, no restrained rage, limited even in its final scenes by JoJo’s obliviousness. Humor, sarcasm, ridicule or exaggeration cannot save this story from a darkness that is beyond comprehension even by those much older. JoJo Rabbit. Written and directed by Taika Waititi. Starring Roman Griffin Davis, Thomasin McKenzie and Scarlett Johansson. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. This review originally appeared in the Post on January 19, 2020 Roman Griffin Davis stars as JoJo and Taiki Waititi as Adolf Hitler.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS JoJo Rabbit a satire on youth deceived during wartime

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Only Yesterday. Movie reeview by Chris Honoré Only Yesterday was written and directed by Isao Takahata who cofounded the iconic Studio Ghibli with Hayao Miyazaki. When released in Japan in 1991 it was a box office sensation, yet, surprisingly, failed to reach the U.S. until 2016. If the works of Miyazaki and Takahata have captured the imaginations of your youngsters, then Only Yesterday is a must see. It’s extraordinary, an example, once again, of the stunning artistry and storytelling that has become the brand of Ghibli. The film’s narrative touches on adult themes while focusing on hybrid protagonists: a 27-year-old woman and a 10-year-old girl. The story begins with Taeko Okajima, a kind of Japanese everywoman, an office worker and life-long resident of Tokyo. She departs by train for a vacation trip in the country to visit relatives, intending to help with the seasonal harvest of safflowers. On her journey while travelling through the night on a sleeper car, headed for the rural town of Yamagata, she begins to reminisce about her childhood: a strict father, puberty, bad grades, first crushes, insecurities, the mockery of mean girls, all told from the point of view of a 10-year-old who is negotiating the 5th grade. These images, beautifully animated and lyrical, are blended seamlessly with the reactions of the older, increasingly reflective Taeko. At one point she says, “I didn’t expect to bring my fifthgrade self along for the trip.” She is met at the Yamagata train station by a young man, Toshio (Dev Patel), a friend of the family, with whom she strikes up a friendship and it’s with him that she begins to share her very personal and conflicted memories. During her stay in this bucolic setting, walking the fields of flowers, enveloped by the soft hillsides, she grows ever more wistful about her past. She reflects on her dreams from childhood, and wonders if the life she is living in Tokyo is truly one she wishes to continue. There is, of course, her growing fondness for Toshio. Only Yesterday is a work of art, wonderfully told, absent intensely imagined, suspend-your-disbelief characters. Instead, the fable moves gently, at times sadly, from the present to the past and back with calm tenderness. Only Yesterday (1991). Written and directed by Isao Takahata. Animé by Studio Ghibli. Voices of Daisey Ridley, Dev Patel and Ashley Eckstein. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG
articles.title: Only Yesterday a must see for kids

articles.text: In search of something novel to do on a recent anniversary, we came across an exhibition of J. M. W. Turner, one of Michael’s favorite painters, born Joseph Mallord William Turner. The Turner exhibit is at the Jacquemart-André Musée, a small gem of a museum among the 130 or so in Paris. This retrospective of Turner’s art comprises 60 watercolors and 10 oil paintings. We spent an enjoyable hour and a half perusing them all, but, “These weren’t Turner’s A-list works,” Michael proclaimed. Drawn entirely from Clore Gallery, the London Tate is the treasure house of Turner’s massive bequest in 1856 to the National Gallery, comprising 300 oils, 30,000 watercolors, and Turner’s 300 sketchbooks. Anyone seeing the film Mr. Turner (2014) starring Timothy Spall, may recall the scenes portraying the artist’s final days amid sprawling stacks of canvases in his enormous day-lit workroom. The Turner exhibit at the Jacquemart-André, on view through late January, is worth a tour of this exquisite Italianate mansion, now a public museum. Serial displays of temporary art collections are open for viewing in the upperfloor gallery. Built under the vast urban project to rid Paris of slums, diseases, and crime, Georges-Eugène Haussmann, or Baron Haussmann as he’s referred to — was Napoleon III’s French official who accomplished, depending on one’s point of view, annihilation of the old city by bulldozing entire districts; or the genius who modernized Paris. “Rectilinear axes were traced out from the périphérique to the city’s center,” which means that streets became linear and boulevards were broadened into throughways. The Jacquemart mansion rose from the razed slums in the brand-new sparkling 8th arrondissement, appropriately near to luxury shopping at Galleries de Lafayette. We exited at the metro, unintentionally one station short of the musée, so we hoofed the extra mile. In clear evidence of Parisians’ love of art, culture, and history, we joined a queue of about a one-hour wait for museum entry. As is typical of city estates, from the street, you don’t have a clue as to how extraordinary and lavish the home behind the arched carriage doors really is. Finally, our turn in line, we walked up a cobbled stone driveway that circled the mansion; and beheld the home’s entry, a showstopper of grandeur with marble carvings and limestone glittering in the sunlight. Children in party dress were engaged in playful banter, and we slowed to linger with other guests as I dreamily envisioned that we had just disembarked from a carriage upon an afternoon garden party. The rooms inside the imposing structure are original, all decked out in 19th Century upper-caste décor. The walls are somberly The Field of Waterloo, oil painting, 1818. The 19th C. influential art critic John Ruskin elevated Turner above his contemporaries for his late in life mastery of watercolor in depicting light, atmosphere, and weather. painted in dense hues; rugs are finely hand-stitched; and every furnishing is ornately fitted with silken fabrics threaded in gold. The weight of its unrelenting richness feels oppressive. I thereby sought to find out who these fine people were. Edouard André was heir to the richest banking family in France. He graduated from Saint Cyr as an officer in the elite corps in protection of Napoleon III. At age 31, he left the military and assumed his father’s seat in the National Assembly and began building his mansion, a project that lasted nearly 10 years. He also enjoyed Parisian life, and the mansion’s 1876 debut was a society phenomenon attracting rave reviews. Turner (1775 – 1851), the art protégé exhibited from 1790 at the Royal Academy. A Londoner his entire life, he never lost the Cockney accent. One of Turner’s last oil paintings in 1850, La Visite de la Tombe. articles.text: One of the most important parts of the architecture of any building is the entry, the thing that first orients users and is very important in establishing an overall aesthetic impression. As I walk through Piedmont looking at the homes as well as the civic and commercial buildings, some entries are obvious, welcoming and the focal point of the street architecture. Unfortunately, a few are not so nice – sometimes abrupt and/or even difficult to find. The whole character of the building seems to be set by the entry. What then are some of the things that make for a nice entry? I think the first thing, most importantly, is the location. While certainly not necessary to be formally centered on the home or public building, it should be located in an obvious and primary position, reinforced by the massing and architectural punctuation of the entire entry façade. There should be no confusion as to where to enter. As much as possible the garage and car parking areas should be separate from and architecturally subordinate to the main pedestrian entry – the front door. articles.text: Supervisor Tom Wilhite and a team of four from Terra Landscape plant a new Southern Magnolia at the Piedmont Center for Arts. The Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia recently received a tree that helps identify its location. On October 15, a new Southern Magnolia was planted at the Center. The new tree replaces a magnolia that had been standing since the early 1930s when the building was constructed by the Wetmore family. The original had begun failing a half-dozen years ago. “That [tree] was one of the crown jewels of the city,” said Sue Malick, president of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “The city did a great job and showed sensitivity in the choice of this new tree. The Center is so grateful to be working with them in such a productive way,” added Sue Malick. Dave Frankel, an arborist, resident, and recently retired from the City as Public Works Supervisor had observed the slow decline of the former magnolia over the last decade. The tips of the branches were experiencing “dieback” - the progressive death of twigs, shoots, and branches from the tip downward. “I thought the city’s decision to take down the tree was very appropriate,” Frankel affirmed. Tom Wilhite, Construction Manager for Terra Landscape, the firm with a contract to maintain all the city’s parks and public spaces, explained the attributes of Piedmont’s newest tree, “That felty texture and rust color on The previous magnolia at the Center for the Arts was on its last legs, with roughly one-third of the tree dying. The new tree magnolia likes rich, moist, well-drained soil and could reach full size in 20 years. It is fast-growing and has begun to bloom at a young age. the underside of the leaves is highly desirable. This is a 36” box tree, which is a large tree to transplant.” This tree came from Boething Treeland in Portola Valley, not far from Palo Alto, so one might consider it a Stanford tree. “This South Magnolia’s particular cultivar is called ‘Samuel Sommer.’ Its beautiful white flowers are the largest of any Southern Magnolia cultivar; they can reach 14 inches across,” Wilhite said with a smile. Samuel Sommers types are half the size of other Southern Magnolias, growing 30-40 feet tall with a 30-foot wide canopy. They can live for up to 150 years. This tree (not yet named) has an excellent chance to thrive, Wilhite noted that the location was ideal because of its “sunny but somewhat protected place.” He and his team from Terra amended the soil with organic and mineral components and starter fertilizer. A berm was installed by the base as were two “bubblers” to ensure deep irrigation.

articles.text: Several years ago, I had the opportunity to visit the sherry producing region at the southern tip of Spain. My knowledge before the trip was somewhat limited – all I knew was that I loved a cold glass of fino sherry as an aperitif. When I got there, I discovered there was huge range of sherries that go from bone dry to immensely sweet. Sherry starts life as wine until someone dramatically interrupts it with a heaping serving of high-ABV neutral grain spirit. Not only does the spirit lift sherry’s alcohol level, it kills off any remaining yeast, stopping fermentation. But for sherry, that’s just the beginning. What really defines sherry is the way it’s aged: the different types are basically expressions of the science (and some slightly frustrating magic) of aging. mend a stop in the freezer for 15 minutes. It has a nose of lemony citrus and is clean and refreshing on the palate. The driest liquid you will ever taste. Serve with a hard Spanish cheese, like Manchego. • Gonzalez Byass Vina AB Amontillado, $25 Amontillado Sherries are a step up in intensity and weight from Fino Sherry. This one was aged 12 years in the solera and has a complex nose with strong aromatics, rosemary and thyme covering the roasted nuts, bitter oranges and curry. The medium-to-full-bodied palate shows a very spicy smoky wine with hints of coffee, layered, intense and subtle. All Sherry is aged with the Solera system – basically a cask-rotation system where the final product is a blend of younger and older sherries. But while some sherries are oxidized—meaning allowed exposure to oxygen, which impacts the flavor—some are intentionally deprived, kept under a naturally occurring (and systematically encouraged) layer of yeast called a “flor,” basically a club bouncer for oxygen trying to get into the party. Because the flor comes from ambient yeast in the winery, where sherry is aged becomes part of its expression. When the flor disappears, on purpose or by accident (see below), oxidation occurs and darker, richer flavors arise. That is one reason why sherry can achieve the incredible hoodwink of having a sweet, fruity, nutty aroma and a bone-dry mouthfeel. It also makes it great for food pairing and in cocktails. One of the regrets after my trip to Spain was that I did not have time to visit some important producers, one of which was Gonzales Byass. So, I was delighted to recently have the opportunity to taste the range of Gonzalez Byass Sherries. This outstanding producer was founded in 1835 and is one of the most venerated producers in Spain. Lucky for us, the wines are well distributed in the U.S. and are available in many Bay Area stores. For further information contact Donna White Communications. • Tio Pepe Fino Sherry, $20 This is probably the most famous dry sherry in America. Technically it is a fortified wine but at 15% alcohol it is not much stronger than a regular wine. The trick with this wine is to serve it extremely cold, I recom- • Gonzalez Byass Leonor Palo Cortado, $25 Palo Cortado is a super rare sherry that kind of exemplifies the mystery of it all: it starts life as a Fino or Amontillado (under the flor yeast), only to randomly (not by design) lose its flor, and continue aging as an Oloroso (with exposure to oxidation). The resulting Sherry combines the crisp, dry, delicate flavors of a Fino or Amontillado with the richness of Oloroso. This one is mostly dry and nutty with just a touch of sweetness. A very satisfying dram. • Gonzalez Byass Alfonso Oloroso Seco, $25 Olorosos come in both sweet and dry styles and this one is definitely dry. articles.text: Shopping by appointment starts October 25th The Bookmark Bookstore, operated by the nonprofit Friends of the Oakland Public Library, recently announced another way to shop for quality used books. The Bookmark is now accepting reservations for in-store shopping. Customers can make a reservation on the store website. “We are thrilled to welcome our customers back for live shopping using our new reservation system,” exclaimed Friends volunteer. With a $10 deposit, customers get to browse the store for 45 minutes. The deposit will be applied to purchases made at the Bookmark. Each 45-minute reservation may be used for one or two adults, plus children under 18. Safety is the Bookmark’s highest priority and customers are required to follow a few simple rules for the safety of customers, volunteers, and staff. Safety measures include wearing a mask, observing social distancing protocols, and use of hand sanitizer before entering the store. All the details of in-store shopping and the link to make a reservation are available on the website at https://www.fopl. org/bookmark-reservations. For customers who are not comfortable shopping in person or can’t find a time that work for their schedule, the Virtual Bookstore is a great option for shopping anytime: https://www.fopl.org/ virtual-bookstore. Books waiting to be purchased at the Bookmark Bookstore in Old Town Oakland await knowing buyers. The Bookmark Bookstore is located in Old Oakland, at 721 Washington Street. Modified store hours for in-store shopping reservations and curbside pickup are Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. All purchases support the Oakland Public Library.

articles.text: Lake Merritt at night. I am pleased to announce that The Lake Merritt has secured a very coveted speaker for our Topics of Merritt program on Tuesday, November 10, 2020 at 1:00 p.m. Damon Tighe, a Naturalist at the California Center for Natural History and Biotechnology, and Educator at Bio-Rad Laboratories, will present a free Zoom program for residents at The Lake Merritt. The event is open to all. Based in Oakland, Tighe has become acclaimed for his work documenting the spectacular marine organisms thriving beneath the surface of Lake Merritt. His dramatic underwater photographs and compelling stories reveal the history of these stunning life forms, many from around the world, who have found a home in Lake Merritt. Did you know that Lake Merritt is not a man-made lake, but a tidal lagoon that formed 10,000 years ago in the Neolithic era? At that time, rising sea levels carried water from the Pacific Ocean inland and a tidal lagoon formed in what is now Downtown Oakland. The lagoon was connected to the Bay by a large rivulet that carried a steady stream of saltwater and wildlife inland from the ocean. Fresh water from winter rains runs down our hills through many creeks and into the lake, creating a mixed brackish environment suitable for many marine creatures then and now. Over the decades Tighe has kept a watchful eye on the creatures living in the lake. After getting reports over several years in a row from boaters on the lake concerning a beautiful soft blue glow around their oars at night, Tighe investigated. His research resulted in a very compelling article in Bay Nature magazine. “Why Is Lake Merritt Turning Photo by Chris Hitchcock Blue at Night?” explains the phenomenon. Tighe’s research discovered that during the summer months when the creeks run dry, the salinity of the lake’s water rises to become much more like that of the Bay. Coinciding with this change in salinity, a bloom in marine organisms begins in the shallow warm waters. By late summer and early fall, the microscopic organisms responsible for the blue glow, a plankton called dinoflagellates, erupt and multiply. After reading an article about Tighe in The Oaklandside this past July, I was intrigued by some of his other discoveries. The citizen scientist knows the lake and its environs well. He steps around picnickers, turns over rocks on the shore, and even wades through the water, his eyes alert for the smallest marine critters. To date, more than 600 species have been identified at Lake Merritt, including non-native life forms and some that are so unique that they have not been found anywhere else on Earth. The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Community sits directly across from the lake. I have spent many an hour walking along the lake noticing the plants and wildlife, but never imagined what was under the water. To hear more, the public is invited to a webinar on Tuesday, November 10 at 1:00 p.m. Admission to this Zoom presentation is free, but reservations are required. To obtain a link for this webinar, email rsvp@thelakemerrittsenior. com or call 510-903-3600. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. For further information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com. pages.text: Wednesday, October 21, 2020 25 Seniors How to know you are being scammed By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I am a photographer. I just got an email from someone who wants to hire me for an outdoor wedding here in Oakland. He told me the date and asked for my fee. I told him that it depends on what he wants me to shoot, how many prints he wants, etc. , and suggested that we speak by phone. He asked for a ballpark figure which I gave him, and then I suggested again that he give me his phone number so we could speak on the phone. He emailed me back and said that his friend had offered to pay for my services as a wedding present. He never gave me his phone number, and then yesterday, I got a check for way over the fee that I gave him from some flooring company in Oklahoma. He then emailed me and asked if I received the check. This seems fishy! Is this a scam? Bart G.., Oakland Dear Bart: You are absolutely right. This is a kind of scam called a “fake check” scam. There are many ways that this can take form, but this request for your services, and then an overpayment is one that has been going around lately. As a matter of fact, some of you know that I am a professional musician as well as the MacMama. I received a very similar email last month, from somebody who wanted me to play violin at a wedding in Berkeley and asked about my fee. It’s almost exactly the same as the email you received. This person must have seen my website and reached out to me with details that would make me less likely to suspect his behavior. When I told him my fee, and said we should speak on the phone, he ignored me. And last week, I received a check for $1900, on a very flimsy piece of paper that looked fake. But these checks often get through the bank, according to the FTC “… because fake checks generally look just like real checks, even to bank employees. They are often printed with the names and addresses of legitimate financial institutions. They may even be real checks written on bank accounts that belong to identity theft victims. It can take weeks for a bank to figure out that the check is a fake. By law, banks have to make deposited funds available quickly, usually within two days. When the funds are made available in your account, the bank may say the check has “cleared,” but that doesn’t mean it’s a good check. Fake checks can take weeks to be discovered and untangled. By that time, the scammer has any money you sent, and you’re stuck paying the money back to the bank. Your best bet: Don’t rely on money from a check unless you know and trust the person you’re dealing with.” Since you are a photographer, with a website that probably has contact information, and even your office address (I have since removed my address from my websites), the scammer does not even need to pry that information out of you. And the fact that they did not ask the usual questions someone asks when hiring a photographer (or in my case a musician) for a wedding is a tip off. The use of an overpayment with a fake check is one of the most common tools. Often times, they claim that they sent the wrong check and want you to pay it back, sometimes even threatening you. But there are other ways that scammers trick folks out of thousands of dollars, sometimes contacting victims by phone, but more and more by email. I have heard from several self-employed contractors this month who have received emails like the one you received, with almost identical wording. Often times, these are folks who get a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, and then disappear. These days, credit card companies are getting savvy to fraudulent charges, so the scammers are finding other ways to steal from unsuspecting victims. You can read more on the subject on the FTC’s site here: https:// www.consumer.ftc.gov/articles/ how-spot-avoid-and-report-fakecheck-scams Lake Merritt – beneath the surface Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: In an all-Piedmont wedding, Elizabeth Chapple Faughnan (PHS ’08) and Daniel Scott Davis (PHS ’06) were married on September 12, 2020. The ceremony and reception were held among the redwoods at the Sonoma County property that has been in Libby’s family for over 50 years. The Honorable Kathleen A. Kelly, Judge for the Superior Court of San Francisco County and a close friend of the bride’s family, acted as officiant. Although Libby and Dan grew up less than a mile apart, they did not formally meet until attending college at UC Davis. Both are graduates of Piedmont High School, UC Davis and Samuel Merritt University, where they completed the Accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing. Libby also earned her Master of Science in Nursing—Family Nurse Practitioner degree at Samuel Merritt. Dan is an RN in the Intensive Care Unit at the Alta Bates Summit Medical Center, and Libby is an RN in the Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital Family Birth Center. Libby is the daughter of Vincent and Claire Faughnan and the granddaughter of James and Suzanne Soper, all of Piedmont, and the granddaughter of Vincent and Catherine Faughnan of New York. Dan is the son of Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado of Piedmont and the grandson of Herbert and Viella Jean Davis of Denver, Colorado, and the grandson of Juan de Jesus Alvarado and Ana Paula Sanchez de Alvarado of Caracas, Venezuela. Libby and Dan became engaged in October 2019 and started planning a large wedding to be held on September 12, 2020. Libby Faughnan and Dan Davis, both of Piedmont, were married on September 12 in Sonoma County. They did not let the coronavirus or California wildfires cancel their plans. They reduced their wedding guest list to an immediate family group of 12. The week they got married included days of dark, smoky skies and a day when the sun appeared blood-orange all day. articles.text: Lucretia Crandall Wieking, a longtime former Piedmont resident, passed away at home in Chico surrounded by her family on October 14, 2020. She was 87. Born on January 20, 1933 in Berkeley, California, she was the daughter of Giles and Lucile Crandall. She lived most of her life in Piedmont and the East Bay before moving to Chico in recent years to be closer to her family. She attended school at Havens Elementary in Piedmont, and Anna Head School in Oakland before enrolling at UC Berkeley. While at Cal she was a member of the Alpha Phi Sorority. She cherished her many beloved friends from her school days and continued those friendships throughout her life. She married James Potter Wieking on October 15, 1954. A stay-at-home mother and wife, she was her family’s rock and championed their lives. She felt her family was her greatest accomplishment. Her favorites in life were here family, her dear friends, sports, playing bridge, and her many treasured pets. She took joy in visiting the Oakland Zoo. She was a sports fan of the Cal Bears and Raiders football teams, and she frequently watched golf and mored way. She was known to say, “a little dirt won’t hurt”. Most recently she summed up her life in simple terms: “She came, she lived, she left”. Lucretia was a member of the Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland, the Junior Center of Arts and Science, and was a sustaining member of the Junior League of Oakland. She is survived by Jim Wieking, her husband of 66 years, and her brother, and sister-in-law Sheldon and Janet Crandall of Piedmont. She is also survived by daughter Linda Catalano and husband Tony, and son Edward Wieking. She is additionally survived by two grandchildren, Daniel James McDonald and Kinsey McDonald Gilbert (Danny Ray), by great-granddaughter Marie Gilbert, as well as numerous nieces and nephews. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations be made to the Oakland Zoo, Guide Dogs for the Blind in San Rafael, or any other animal welfare organization or charity of your choice. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, October 21, 2020 Wedding Announcement Libby Faughnan marries Dan Davis on September 12 In an all-Piedmont wedding, Elizabeth Chapple Faughnan (PHS ’08) and Daniel Scott Davis (PHS ’06) were married on September 12, 2020. The ceremony and reception were held among the redwoods at the Sonoma County property that has been in Libby’s family for over 50 years. The Honorable Kathleen A. Kelly, Judge for the Superior Court of San Francisco County and a close friend of the bride’s family, acted as officiant. Although Libby and Dan grew up less than a mile apart, they did not formally meet until attending college at UC Davis. Both are graduates of Piedmont High School, UC Davis and Samuel Merritt University, where they completed the Accelerated Bachelor of Science in Nursing. Libby also earned her Master of Science in Nursing—Family Nurse Practitioner degree at Samuel Merritt. Dan is an RN in the Intensive Care Unit at the Alta Bates Summit Medical Center, and Libby is an RN in the Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital Family Birth Center. Libby is the daughter of Vincent and Claire Faughnan and the granddaughter of James and Suzanne Soper, all of Piedmont, and the granddaughter of Vincent and Catherine Faughnan of New York. Dan is the son of Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado of Piedmont and the grandson of Herbert and Viella Jean Davis of Denver, Colorado, and the grandson of Juan de Jesus Alvarado and Ana Paula Sanchez de Alvarado of Caracas, Venezuela. Libby and Dan became engaged in October 2019 and started planning a large wedding to be held on September 12, 2020. Libby Faughnan and Dan Davis, both of Piedmont, were married on September 12 in Sonoma County. They did not let the coronavirus or California wildfires cancel their plans. They reduced their wedding guest list to an immediate family group of 12. The week they got married included days of dark, smoky skies and a day when the sun appeared blood-orange all day. Their wedding day was hazy but happy and the entire group was grateful to celebrate together. The bride and groom are planning a honeymoon in Hawaii in 2021. articles.text: Editor: Jen Cavenaugh will be getting my vote for Piedmont City Council this November 3. Jen is a dynamic leader who cares deeply about the issues facing our City. She listens closely to residents and takes action to develop solutions. She is not afraid to address challenging and complicated issues facing our community such as racial bias and sexual harassment. Jen was responsible for partnering with the Piedmont Recreation Department to bring much-needed classes on healthy relationships to kids in Piedmont. She works hard to address racial equity, inclusiveness, and cares about the social-emotional development of our kids. She brings community partners together to have hard conversations, develop a deeper understanding of the issues, and implement plans and policies to engage and improve our community. I urge you to join me in supporting Jen Cavenaugh for Piedmont City Council. –Sarah Puckett

articles.text: Editor: I met Veronica Thigpen several years ago, shortly after she moved to Piedmont from Chicago with her husband David and daughter August. It was when she attended her first PADC (Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee) meeting. It impressed me that she could enter a group of complete strangers with warmth and confidence, as well as offer substantive comments during the meeting. Veronica has since taken on the leadership role of co-president of the group. She helped guide the creation of a Black Student Union at the high school and chaired and emceed a successful MLK event in the city. Veronica’s expertise and knowledge in education research and policy, and experience working with school systems in Chicago and in Oakland, would bring to Piedmont a valuable perspective from beyond our borders. Through her collaborations with the district, she has proven to be a thoughtful and respectful, and a person who understands the importance of making connections and building bridges within our small community. Please join me in voting for Veronica Anderson Thigpen for Piedmont Board of Education. –Megan Pillsbury Member, Piedmont Board of Education

What are the estimated costs of the project compared to bond revenues and what steps will the City take to limit project costs to available bond revenues? The measure would authorize the City to issue bonds with a principal value that does not exceed $19.5 million. In the event the City receives an AA+ bond rating, it is conceivable the bonds would be sold at a premium and Measure UU would provide revenues in excess of the face value of the bonds. The City determined that the $19.5 million figure was appropriate based on rough “hard cost” estimates as follows: $8 million for the two pools to replace the current “medium” and “big” pools, $3.5 million for site preparation, and $6 million for a building to house the pool equipment, restrooms, offices, and community space. If necessary, the concept can be value-engineered during final design development to meet the budget parameters. 9. Can the City repair the existing pool? The City has determined that repairing the existing pool is not a feasible option. The City has been continuously repairing the existing pool since it took over operations in 2011. The repairs required to keep the facility safe and operational have become increasingly expensive every year, and the facility is now at the point where pool decks need to be removed in order to address structural issues. A renovation of the existing facility would require not only major structural repair and equipment replacement, but would also trigger significant site work required to meet current health, safety, and accessibility regulations. 10. What oversight is in place to ensure that the bond funds are used properly? Measure UU provides that a bond oversight committee be appointed to make sure the bonds are issued and spent in accordance with the terms of Measure UU. As with any project, staff and the City Council will also work to ensure proper use of public funds. The project will also be subject to the City’s project risk management policy.
