articles.text: We all know there comes a time when it no longer makes economic sense to spend money on something too broken to fix. For the Piedmont Pool, that time has come. Our old pool leaks over one million gallons of water a year from somewhere underneath the deck. The only way to fix the leaking is to rip out and replace the concrete, which would cost millions of tax dollars. Even if the City had funds to replace the deck, which it doesn’t, the unreliable and inefficient 56-year-old pool mechanics would remain. Replacing the deck would be like replacing an old car’s exterior, and hoping the unreliable gas guzzling engine can keep going a few more miles. When we’re spending millions of tax dollars, this makes no sense. If Piedmont is going to have a community pool, it’s time to build a new one. It has been apparent for decades that the city didn’t have a big enough pool to accommodate the many residents who would like to use it for sports, recreation, and exercise. In addition to better meeting resident needs, a new pool will provide a better community gathering place. It will be a place where we can have teen lifeguards supervising toddlers taking swimming lessons, have our high school chemistry teacher coaching the HS water polo team, have adults rehabbing from an injury, and have seniors lap swimming, all at the same time. There is no other facility that brings all members of our community together in such a way from the dead of winter to the hottest summer days. Sure, rebuilding a pool the same size as the current pool would be less expensive, but it would continue to exclude many families and it would still require the schools to spend tens of thousands of dollars to rent pool space elsewhere. When the School District rebuilt Havens and other school buildings, the community saw this as an opportunity to make these shared spaces materially better and strengthen our sense of community. Our contemplated investment in the Piedmont community pool is no different. Piedmonters do their homework, are well-informed about the issues, and are generous in their commitment to maintaining what’s great about our city. Investing in a new community pool for everyone to enjoy is the right decision for our community, our property values, and our stewardship for future generations. Let’s show our kids what it means to take care of the community we love, by rebuilding the community pool. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. Jen Cavenaugh is a member of Piedmont City Council
articles.title: Piedmont Pool too broken to be fixed

articles.text: Editor: I am a full-time working mom of three kids aged 6, 4, and 1.5. The amazing resources for working parents in this town — walkable neighborhood schools, easy access to great after-school activities — are a significant reason my family bought our house here in 2015. The pool factored into this calculation as well. Water safety is crucial, and it would be hard for my family to find time to drive kids to Alameda or Lafayette on a regular basis for swim lessons. My family, and many similarly situated families, place a high value on the ease of a nearby community pool for both lessons and just plain fun. I have no idea at this point if any of my children will be interested in competitive swimming, but I also very much hope they will at least have the opportunity to participate in local club and school swim teams without the potentially complicated logistics of practicing in rented space in other towns. We are an aff luent, kidfriendly suburban California community. It would be senseless to shutter our pool for good. Fundamentally, I also believe that investment in facilities for the common good of the community is worthy and important. The current pool has lasted for 56 years. Piedmont residents now have the opportunity to invest in a new facility that will support the schools and benefit the entire community for decades to come. I hope others will join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. –Amanda Straub
articles.title: Investment for common good of community is worthy

articles.text: Measure UU is not about me, and it’s not about today. I’m voting Yes on UU because it’s in the best long-term interests of our city, our community, and our neighbors – present and future. It’s for my friends next door, whose two young boys will learn to swim there. It’s for the young kids who will have fond memories of their birthday parties there like my family did. It’s for my elderly neighbor across the street; he can’t run, but he can still swim. It’s for the teenager who finds solace and belonging in water polo. It’s for the future homebuyers who see this facility as the centerpiece of our vibrant and verdant community. The time is now. We cannot wait. I hope you join me in improving our community today, and for generations to come, by voting Yes on UU. –Aaron J. Aubrecht

articles.text: About 55 years ago my parents joined the Piedmont Swim Club. My mother loved swimming and wanted to make sure all seven of her children could swim. My siblings and I participated on the swim team; became lifeguards, swim instructors and water polo coaches. I was also the pool manager after college and, last year, a swim instructor again. The pool wasn’t just the place where we learned to swim; we became part of the larger Piedmont aquatic community. It helped foster a love for swimming and water polo that we passed on to our children. We found our passion. During summers the Piedmont pool lifeguard staff was primarily Piedmont high school students and the swim program instructors were PHS graduates home from college. It became a reunion of swim team and swim club friends and classmates. It was fun to see the progress in students from one year to the next. Parents knew the colleges the guards and instuctors attended, even giving some good-natured ribbing about rival schools. We were a large family. Over the years working at the pool I saw firsthand the importance of having a pool in the center of town. People needed the pool for a variety of reasons: recovering from surgery, dealing with back issues, fighting through MS. My own mother needed the pool as she fought her cancer. The staff and other swimmers knew each of them by name; encouraged them during their workout and missed them when they were gone. When I started swimming back at the pool again with a masters team, I met Christine, Bev and others. We pushed each other through workouts and complained about the parts we didn’t like. We were friends through swimming. Having a pool in Piedmont is so important. It is a place where a child can gain self-esteem through swimming or water polo. It is a place where you find new friends who have a shared passion for swimming. It is a place where our youth can get their first job. It is a place where our high school and college students can be role models as teachers. It is a place where you find passion for aquatics; you can foster friendships. It is a place where you find our true community. Please support Measure UU. Megan Finney Hernandez is a former member of the U.S. Water Polo team.
articles.title: Measure UU is all about community

articles.text: No easing of restrictions by County after moving to Orange Tier Three new cases of COVID- 19 were recorded in Piedmont in the past week, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department yesterday, Tuesday, October 20. In total, 41 cases have been reported in Piedmont since the coronavirus outbreak in March. Overall, the caseload in Alameda County is 22,807 as of yesterday. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for tests in the county is 1.4 percent, slightly lower than earlier in the month. One person in Piedmont died since last Tuesday, October 13. The county has now recorded 432 total COVID-19 fatalities. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 8,888. In Hayward, 3,364 cases have been recorded and there have been 1,562 reported in Fremont. San Leandro has reported 1,242. Last week, state health officials proclaimed that Alameda County has been placed in a less-restrictive Orange Tier for reopening its economy amid the ongoing coronavirus pandemic. The Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, is the second-least restrictive tier of the state’s four-tiered color-coded system. However, county officials are proceeding with caution and keeping restrictions tighter than required by the state. The county said it will update current health orders next week. On Thursday, October 15, the county provided guidance for how to reopen some performing arts and fine arts sectors. San Francisco County was moved into the least restrictive Yellow Tier, or Minimal Tier, this week. It is the only Bay Area county to achieve that. Alameda County was in the most restrictive Purple Tier when the system was launched in August, then moved into the second-most restrictive Red Tier last month. Due to decreasing case and positivity rates, Alameda County is now one of 23 counties in the two least restrictive tiers, Orange and Yellow. According to the state, Orange Tier counties can allow for indoor dining, indoor religious services and indoor theaters, but with strict capacity limits. Capacity limits for indoor retail and shopping malls can be increased to 50 percent in Orange Tier counties. In California, 874,077 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded, and there have been 16,992 deaths due to the disease. The City of Piedmont last week echoed guidance from the county noting that trick-or-treating this Halloween is considered a high-risk activity and is not recommended. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host its citywide Climate Challenge next month, following the success of last year’s Climate Challenge. In 2019, more than 250 Piedmont households answered the call to be more environmentally-conscience through different challenges that aimed to reduce the city’s collective greenhouse gas emissions by over 200 tons. This year, the goals will be set even higher. The City has announced its intention to double the number of participating households, from 250 to 500 sign-ups, by Earth Day, April 22, 2021. In addition, a goal has been set to reduce Piedmont’s carbon emissions by 500 tons. The Climate Challenge gives residents the chance to participate in teams and community organizations, and to engage in some friendly competition to see which household can reduce their carbon footprint the most. Residents can use the platform to learn more about their household’s emissions, and to plan lifestyle changes that will positively affect their impact on the environment. The City is encouraging residents who signed up for the challenge last year to continue to engage with it this year. New actions and challenges have been added for this year’s challenge. The challenge will run from November 2020 to May 2021. Residents can sign up for the challenge at: https://www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org/. On that website residents can create a profile for their household and pledge to commit to adopt sustainable actions that help reduce their carbon footprint. Those actions will be added to your dashboard, and the platform will help with next steps, costs, and questions. “This is a fun, meaningful way to work towards a shared decrease in Piedmont emissions. The vast majority of emissions in Piedmont stem from households, and using this website brings attention to this fact and helps us all be more sustainable,” said Nate Redinbo, the Planning Department’s new Climate Fellow. However, county officials are proceeding with caution and keeping restrictions tighter than required by the state. The county said it will update current health orders next week. On Thursday, October 15, the county provided guidance for how to reopen some performing arts and fine arts sectors. San Francisco County was moved into the least restrictive Yellow Tier, or Minimal Tier, this week. It is the only Bay Area county to achieve that. Alameda County was in the most restrictive Purple Tier when the system was launched in August, then moved into the second-most restrictive Red Tier last month. Due to decreasing case and positivity rates, Alameda County is now one of 23 counties in the two least restrictive tiers, Orange and Yellow. According to the state, Orange Tier counties can allow for indoor dining, indoor religious services and indoor theaters, but with strict capacity limits. Capacity limits for indoor retail and shopping malls can be increased to 50 percent in Orange Tier counties. In California, 874,077 cases of COVID-19 have been recorded, and there have been 16,992 deaths due to the disease. The City of Piedmont last week echoed guidance from the county noting that trick-or-treating this Halloween is considered a high-risk activity and is not recommended. Furnishings for the lab were not included in the $30 million budget for the building The STEAM building has spent an additional three percent of its budget on change orders, the costs of which have been offset by “value engineering” cuts. “Considering everything that has gone on, the combination of the [Division of the State Architect] being a little bit crazy with some of their requirements and then COVID hitting, it is kind of a miracle that we are this far and the STEAM building will be opening shortly,” said school board member Andrea Swenson. The project is not over budget now, in part due to items like solar panels on the roof being taken off the job installation. The school district has said some of the deleted items could be easily added on at a later time if funds become available. The rooftop photovoltaic solar panels on both buildings were cut from the budget to save $1.2 million. The school district can buy solar panels for the STEAM building from the general contractor at a deep discount right now. “A subcontractor mistakenly ordered a portion of the deferred panels for the STEAM building. The subcontractor has offered to deliver and install these at cost. This would be a substantial discount — roughly $65,000 for 13 panels that would have cost $200,000 under the terms of the District’s contract with Overaa,” the Bond Program website reads. By Allyson Aleksey The City of Piedmont will host its citywide Climate Challenge next month, following the success of last year’s Climate Challenge. In 2019, more than 250 Piedmont households answered the call to be more environmentally-conscience through different challenges that aimed to reduce the city’s collective greenhouse gas emissions by over 200 tons. This year, the goals will be set even higher. The City has announced its intention to double the number of participating households, from 250 to 500 sign-ups, by Earth Day, April 22, 2021. In addition, a goal has been set to reduce Piedmont’s carbon emissions by 500 tons. The Climate Challenge gives residents the chance to participate in teams and community organizations, and to engage in some friendly competition to see which household can reduce their carbon footprint the most. Residents can use the platform to learn more about their household’s emissions, and to plan lifestyle changes that will positively affect their impact on the environment. The City is encouraging residents who signed up for the challenge last year to continue to engage with it this year. New actions and challenges have been added for this year’s challenge. The challenge will run from November 2020 to May 2021. Residents can sign up for the challenge at: https://www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org/. On that website residents can create a profile for their household and pledge to commit to adopt sustainable actions that help reduce their carbon footprint. Those actions will be added to your dashboard, and the platform will help with next steps, costs, and questions. “This is a fun, meaningful way to work towards a shared decrease in Piedmont emissions. The vast majority of emissions in Piedmont stem from households, and using this website brings attention to this fact and helps us all be more sustainable,” said Nate Redinbo, the Planning Department’s new Climate Fellow. articles.text: Just like everything in 2020, Halloween is going to look a little different, too. But before you give up on the fun of running to and from your neighbors’ doors, check out the new Halloween game in town! For two weeks, from October 17 to Halloween, Saturday, October 31, Piedmont BOO will allow kids to celebrate Halloween. It’s a fun, socially distanced, reverse trick or treat game for kids of all ages. Instead of ringing doorbells for candy, you choose a location from a map provided to participants, gather a few tricks and treats to share. and leave them on your neighbor’s doorstep, sneaking off unseen just like a ghost. That’s why it’s called a BOO! It’s also a fundraiser for schools with all proceeds going directly to the Piedmont Education Foundation. When you sign up to join the fun at www. piedmontstore.org, you’ll add your address to the Piedmont BOO participation list. Pick up your yard sign and BOO Count stickers from one of the drive-by pickup locations, gather some $25 for Piedmont BOO! Kit. It includes a lawn sign, three BOO count stickers and access to the address list for the game $50 for the WHOLE BOO Kit. This includes a lawn sign, three BOO count stickers, access to the address list, plus 3 complete BOO bags filled with treats and ready for giving. Fundraising for Piedmont schools has never been so much fun. Proceeds from this “reverse trick-or-treating” game will go to the Piedmont Education Foundation. Halloween goodies to share and choose three locations to deliver your spooky offerings to from the participant list or from Piedmont BOO signs in your neighborhood. Then slip over and leave an anonymous gift or treat on their doorstep. They’ve now been BOOed (distinctly different from ball games), and after adding a sticker to their yard sign to let everyone know they’ve gotten one of their three Halloween surprises, they’re off to choose their three houses to treat. Kids of all ages are welcome to play, whether age two or 80. To limit risk factors, you need to sign up to play so there’s a record of participants for safety. Piedmont BOO wants to see the whole town enjoying themselves by sharing their Halloween spirit with each other in a safe, socially-distanced way. Treats don’t need to be big. Grab a spooky bag or basket and fill it with your choice of Halloween surprises. Halloween crafts, small toys or games and packaged treats are always fun! Slime, small decorations and gift cards are also great options. Candy, of course, but be allergy aware in your choices by bagging chocolate and/or nut candies in separate Ziploc bags. To participate without putting a BOO basket together, choose “The Whole BOO!” option at piedmontstore.org and you can pick up three pre-filled BOO bags ready for gifting when you get your yard sign and BOO count stickers.
articles.title: Piedmont BOO: a socially-distanced, spooky celebration for kids

articles.text: To make autumn a little more festive, the Piedmont Arts Fund and Piedmont Makers are putting on a socially-distanced scarecrow community art and maker event. Families and pods are invited to make scarecrows for their front yards. This year’s theme is California Dreaming, because we could all use a little optimism and creative cheer. To participate, make a scarecrow with your family or pod and have it in your front yard by Saturday, October 24. Post a picture of your scarecrow on your Facebook or Instagram page and tag #PiedmontScarecrowWalk2020. The Piedmont Arts Fund and Piedmont Makers will be posting scarecrows on their Instagram and Facebook pages. Play Scarecrow Bingo with your family Print out the Scarecrow Bingo card that will be posted on Sunday, October 26. Then take a Scarecrow Walk through Piedmont and fill out your card. Bring your completed card to Mulberry’s Market between October 26 and October 31 to receive a Scarecrow treat (limit one per person). How to make a Scarecrow Piedmont Makers can help. Need some inspiration on design? The Piedmont Arts Fund has some scarecrow inspiration on their website: https://piedmontartsfund.org/upcoming-events/ scarecrowwalk. Have an old Scarecrow in the basement? If you have an old scarecrow in your garage or basement, pull it out, dust it off, and give it a little California spirit. Everyone is welcome to participate. Scarecrows are popping up everywhere this year.
articles.title: Community invited to make scarecrows for Halloween

articles.text: Waldo Avenue, one of Piedmont’s shortest streets and located in the middle of town, has a reputation for being one of the most popular streets for trick or treating on Halloween. Due to concerns about the coronavirus, the Waldonians decided this year to keep the lights off and not host trick or treating – “a sad but safe decision for all,” commented resident Mary Margaret Sinnema. For the past few years Waldo Avenue has had nearly 900 kids come through. The best advice is for families to put Waldo on their list of Halloween activities for October 2021, but not this year.
articles.title: No trick or treating on Waldo this year

articles.text: Dear Piedmonters, Before you vote on Measure UU, we thought there were a few things we needed to tell you. We did tell you that the City has no outstanding General Obligation Bonds, but we didn’t mention that we have LOTS of debts - $7 million in sewer loans, $13 million in Post Employment Benefits Payable, and $26 million in Pension Benefits Payable. Oh, and if our pension portfolio returns only 6.15% instead of the estimated 7.15% (you can get 7.15% on your investments in today’s crazy market with bonds yielding close to zero, can’t you?), our Pension Benefit Liability alone increases to over $43 million. Speaking of deficits, did we mention that our General Fund – that is, unrestricted money that the City can spend on anything – has a deficit of about $9 million? We also glossed over the fact that the ordinance we passed estimates that the total cost of the “improvements” is $23 million, but that it allows us to issue $19.5 million in bonds. Guess who is paying for the difference? We also haven’t mentioned it, but by reading the City Council minutes for the last six months, you can see that we know about the major deficiencies in our ability to deliver essential public services – the Police Chief, Fire Chief, and City Administrator are all on the record as saying that we do not comply with the Essential Services Act, that the fire station may sustain major damage in an earthquake, and that it may cost up to $51 million to fix these problems. That’s why we are looking at creating a Community Facilities District (aka Mello-Roos) to make it easier to issue bonds backed by another special tax on Piedmont homeowners in the near future. And because we generally ask for the maximum amount, it will probably be for the full $51 million. Finally, we haven’t mentioned that 100% of Piedmont citizens rely on our Police and Fire Departments, while an estimated 25% of citizens use the pool. So, if we had placed two bond measures on the November ballot - $50 million for Police and Fire, and $20 million for a new pool, we knew what would happen. Citizens would vote to maintain essential services, but they would turn down the pool. After spending $56 million in 2006 and another $66 million in 2016 on School District Bonds (all that money is gone, and they still haven’t finished their projects), $10 million per year on Measure G, $2.6 million per year on Measure H, and $2.4 million per year on Measure T, citizens are getting a little tax weary. After all, aren’t our property tax rates some of the highest in California? So, think carefully before you vote on measure UU. We’ll see you soon with our new $51 million bond request. You will HAVE to vote yes to maintain city services, but you can vote NO on Measure UU.
articles.title: The Measure UU Letter From the City Council That We Should Have Received

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont has confirmed that it will host a virtual “Pros and Cons” forum for a public discussion of ballot Measure UU on Wednesday, October 14, at 6:00 p.m. The measure is a proposed bond for $19.5 million to rebuild the City’s swimming pool at the existing location. The forum will feature a question and answer period for representatives in favor of and in opposition to the ballot measure and will be broadcast live on The Piedmont LWV YouTube Channel. Speaking in favor of the measure will be Betsy Andersen, a member of the City Council. Speaking in opposition will be resident Andy Wasserman, whose statement in opposition is in the voter handbook as part of the official ballot arguments. The public is invited to submit questions to be answered during the forum by emailing lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The forum will begin with each side giving a two minute to opening statement, followed by a question and answer session. Each side will have one minute to answer each question. Each side will then be permitted to present a two-minute closing statement This will be the only ballot measure addressed during this forum. The opponents to Measure TT, increasing the Real Property Transfer Tax on home sales, declined to participate. According to LWV’s rules, both sides must agree to participate for the League to host a public forum. articles.text: Editor: Unfortunately, I missed the first Zoom discussion by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. We moved to the City 52 years ago, and I researched its history as much as possible. Our home was built in 1919. But I found no more information in the City or County offices. I know the area around the spa was developed by wealthy San Franciscans as a summer resort. By many it was called a Millionaire’s Enclave. Segregation was caused by money. [The city] was always expensive, not only for blacks but whites also. I came from Europe 60 some years ago and was unfamiliar with racial differences or maltreatment of people different from me. But I learned it while living here. Ten or 15 years ago the black maintenance man of our office building occasionally came up to help me in our home. Every time coming or going, he was stopped by the Piedmont Police with some lousy excuse. No more. The City has changed a lot during this half century, particularly after the Oakland fire when a lot of younger people moved here. The past is past. Piedmont was segregated and the present sky-high property values, mostly in several millions in my opinion, does not make it a good prospect for the development of affordable housing. –Nicholas D. Molnar
articles.title: Piedmont may not be a good target for affordable housing

articles.text: Over the last few weeks the topic of housing equity in Piedmont has been the subject of community conversations, most notably via the information forum entitled, “Racial Segregation and Housing in Piedmont: How Did We Get Here? What Can We Do About It?”. In my review of recent articles, the discussion of the current housing realities included links and references to the history of Sidney Dearing, dubbed the first Black man to live in Piedmont. I first learned of Sidney Dearing on June 12th during a gathering in Piedmont Park when a number of people marched from the Wildwood Avenue area to the park to hear from a few speakers, most notably, young student speakers. It was at that event, I happened to be standing next to a woman who had material and signage with Sidney Dearing’s name and information. I was curious so I introduced myself and asked the woman to tell me about Sidney Dearing. The woman was Meghan Bennett and the history she recounted that day intrigued me and led to further review of her informative website that is dedicated to the Dearing/Piedmont history. I learned that the Department I lead had been on the wrong side of history. Others in the community have recently written about this history and I encourage people to read about it and visit the website. As a person of African descent, the information unfortunately was not surprising to me. As the Chief of Police of the Piedmont Police Department, it was ironic. As a professional law enforcement organization, it is this current-day Piedmont Police Department’s duty to understand this history, own it, and ensure we demonstrate an aptitude to be on the right side of history as we move forward. After learning of Ms. Bennett’s website, each member of the Piedmont Police Department had a conversation with me to review the site and discuss it. The conversations were interesting, introspective and cathartic. The power of the history of Sidney Dearing, from my perspective, is the specificity and tangible nature it attaches to what can sometimes seem abstract to some. This City, this police department, and members of this community did specific reprehensible things to this man to run him out of town because he was Black. To sit with current-day staff from the police department and for us to look at each other and talk about this history was impactful. This begs the questions, “So what?” and “What is the Department going to do that is different or impactful?” A number of years ago, President Barack Obama established the President’s Task Force on 21st Century Policing which developed guidance pertaining to progressive policing practices focused on building trust and legitimacy with the public, training, technology, policy formation, and officer wellness. articles.text: Editor: Three renowned infectious disease epidemiologists and public health scientists, Dr. Martin Kulldorff, professor of medicine at Harvard University, Dr. Sunetra Gupta, professor at Oxford University, and Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, professor at Stanford University Medical School, have authored an opinion about the best policy to control COVID, called “Focused Protection” dated October 20, 2020. The text is at: https://gbdeclaration.org/. “Current lockdown policies are producing devastating effects on short and long-term public health. The results (to name a few) include lower childhood vaccination rates, worsening cardiovascular disease outcomes, fewer cancer screenings and deteriorating mental health – leading to greater excess mortality in years to come, with the working class and younger members of society carrying the heaviest burden. Keeping students out of school is a grave injustice.” Keeping these measures in place until a vaccine is available will cause irreparable damage, with the underprivileged disproportionately harmed. “The most compassionate approach that balances the risks and benefits of reaching herd immunity, is to allow those who are at minimal risk of death to live their lives normally to build up immunity to the virus through natural infection, while better protecting those who are at highest risk. We call this Focused Protection.” Over 6000 medical and public health scientists and over 12,000 medical practitioners have signed this declaration. Please read the dcument, and if you support it, sign it as a member of the general public. With enough support, it could influence the current Bay Area COVID policies. –Bernard Pech Piedmont resident 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 922-8711 • email: news@piedmontpost.org REVIEWERS
articles.title: “Focused Protection” as a new policy to control COVID

What Can We Do About It?”. In my review of recent articles, the discussion of the current housing realities included links and references to the history of Sidney Dearing, dubbed the first Black man to live in Piedmont. I first learned of Sidney Dearing on June 12th during a gathering in Piedmont Park when a number of people marched from the Wildwood Avenue area to the park to hear from a few speakers, most notably, young student speakers. It was at that event, I happened to be standing next to a woman who had material and signage with Sidney Dearing’s name and information. I was curious so I introduced myself and asked the woman to tell me about Sidney Dearing. The woman was Meghan Bennett and the history she recounted that day intrigued me and led to further review of her informative website that is dedicated to the Dearing/Piedmont history. I learned that the Department I lead had been on the wrong side of history. Others in the community have recently written about this history and I encourage people to read about it and visit the website. As a person of African descent, the information unfortunately was not surprising to me. As the Chief of Police of the Piedmont Police Department, it was ironic. As a professional law enforcement organization, it is this current-day Piedmont Police Department’s duty to understand this history, own it, and ensure we demonstrate an aptitude to be on the right side of history as we move forward. After learning of Ms. Bennett’s website, each member of the Piedmont Police Department had a conversation with me to review the site and discuss it. The conversations were interesting, introspective and cathartic. The power of the history of Sidney Dearing, from my perspective, is the specificity and tangible nature it attaches to what can sometimes seem abstract to some. This City, this police department, and members of this community did specific reprehensible things to this man to run him out of town because he was Black. To sit with current-day staff from the police department and for us to look at each other and talk about this history was impactful. This begs the questions, “So what?” and “What is the Department going to do that is different or impactful?” A number of years ago, President Barack Obama established the President’s Task Force on 21st Century Policing which developed guidance pertaining to progressive policing practices focused on building trust and legitimacy with the public, training, technology, policy formation, and officer wellness. articles.text: What is Measure UU? Measure UU is a local Bond Measure which will provide funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable community pool for Piedmont families, students, and adults of all ages. Why is Measure UU needed? Built in 1964, the Piedmont Community Pool is well past the end of its useful life and needs to be replaced. Not only are there serious safety issues (on more than one occasion the concrete deck has failed and crumbled into the pool), the locker room facilities are outdated and restrooms do not comply with the Americans with Disability Act (ADA) requirements, the decades-old plumbing is failing and the pool leaks approximately 3,000 gallons of water daily – over a million gallons a year. Without the Piedmont Community Pool, Piedmont would be the only city (and only public school district) in Alameda County without access to a local pool. What will Measure UU funds do? The successful passage of Measure UU ensures that the Piedmont community will continue to have its own local pool facility for school sports/PE programs, lessons, and recreation, for the next 50 years. The cost includes planning, architectural fees, legal fees, demolition and construction for two new pools, restrooms, locker rooms, and community space. The three existing pools will be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. How much will Measure UU cost? Measure UU would allow the City to issue up to $19.5M in 30-year fixed rate bonds. Measure UU will cost 2.6 cents per $100 of assessed home value (NOT market rate value). For the median Piedmont home, this works out to less than 75 cents a day. To look up your assessed value, use this link to the Alameda County Assessor’s Office and enter your address: http://acgov.org/MS/ prop/index.aspx What happens if Measure UU does not pass? When the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool is permanently closed, there will be no local swimming pool for residents or for Piedmont students. Piedmonters will have to travel and pay to use other communities’ pools, or pay initiation fees and annual dues for private swim clubs. With an empty padlocked pool facility in the center of town, the City will then have to decide what to do with that space. It is important to note that while the City decides, there is a cost to securing the site from blight and vandalism, as well as a significant cost associated with any future use of that space, whether it be for a pool or for some other use. If Measure UU passes, will there be a membership fee to use the pool? No, there is no membership fee. The Piedmont Community Pool has been a public pool since 2011. If Measure UU passes, the municipal bonds will be used to rebuild the pool facility. When the new facility opens, pool users will pay daily use fees, camp and lesson fees, annual and seasonal passes, and facility rentals, to offset operating costs. articles.text: Editor: We all know that public services will be under tremendous pressure during this pandemic and its aftermath, and we need professionals with judgment, deep understanding of the hard tradeoffs local governments face, and compassion to meet this moment. We’ve closely watched the work of the Piedmont City Council during our over two decades as residents, and this is a time when we need our very best. Jen Cavanaugh has earned our trust and deserves re-election. There is no public servant better qualified to join her on the Council than Conna McCarthy. Conna understands how government works, and especially how Piedmont works, and has proved her commitment through her service on everything from the Municipal Tax Review Committee, the Recreation Commission, parcel tax campaigns, and her deep roots in this community. She will be an extraordinary Council member at a critical time. We are voting for Conna McCarthy and Jen Cavanaugh, and we urge others to join us. –Jeff and Becky Bleich

articles.text: Ordinance becomes effective on Nov. 4 At its meeting on Monday, October 5, Piedmont’s City Council approved a comprehensive sidewalk vending program. The city’s staff recommended the approval of a second reading of Ordinance 757, which allows sidewalk vending in compliance with California’s Senate Bill 946. It amends Piedmont’s current provisions that regulate sidewalk sales and other forms of mobile vending within the city. At its September 21 meeting, the council approved the first reading of the ordinance. Since then the ordinance has been available on the city’s website. No public comments have been received by the City Clerk’s office since the first reading. The ordinance goes into effect on Wednesday, November 4, 2020. The new ordinance allows sidewalk vending subject to the vendor obtaining a vending permit issued by the Piedmont Police Department. The city for many years has required all people selling door-to-door to first obtain a sales permit from the police department. Under the new ordinance, a sidewalk vendor must provide valid identification, proposed hours and days of operation, proposed location, type of merchandise to be sold, a valid seller’s permit, proof of a valid Piedmont business tax certificate, and any other information as may be required by the police department. The ordinance does not include guidance on food truck vendors.
articles.title: City Council approves street vending plan

articles.text: Piedmont must have its Measure A1 base allocation housing application approved by Alameda County in roughly 14 months, by December 31, 2021. The Alameda County bond, passed in 2016, allotted Piedmont $2,188,170 to create affordable housing. In the four years since its passage, Piedmont has not committed any of those funds toward affordable housing, but is currently exploring options. The measure was discussed during the newly formed Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign’s (PREC) first forum. Panelist Gloria Bruce, Executive Director of East Bay Housing Organizations, detailed the effect of the Measure A1 Housing Bond in Piedmont. It passed with 73 percent of the vote countywide, but only 52 percent of Piedmonters voted yes on the measure. The forum, which focused on housing equity in Piedmont in an ongoing series that explored a charge of systemic racism, prompted some residents to wonder why these funds are still untouched. Piedmont has made insufficient progress toward creating low-income housing, according to the California Department of Housing and Community Development. The city has a built-out quality with minimal space for new development, unlike neighboring cities that have quickly utilized the bond funds. Piedmont’s status triggers Senate Bill 35 (SB 35), which encourages cities to create housing on their own or be forced to accept housing developments. SB 35 aims to address the state’s housing shortage by increasing supply, and was signed into law in 2017 by former Gov. Jerry Brown as part of California’s 2017 Housing Package. The city’s housing element goals are to produce 38 affordable units by the end of 2022. On August 17, 2020, the City entered into a contract with Lisa Wise Consulting (LWC) to research incentives for the construction of accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, that are rent-restricted or otherwise affordable to very low and low-income residents. LWC is tasked with identifying potential sources of funding to support local incentives for the construction of income-restricted ADUs, and Measure A1 could be a potential source for funding. There may be other uses for funding identified through public engagement for the Senate Bill 2 housing programs or public engagement for the Piedmont housing element update. Senate Bill 2 provides up to $160,000 to plan projects that would streamline development of new affordable housing. “These funds must be used for projects which are affordable to very low and low-income residents for 55 years or more, as well as other restrictions and terms. The City has been discussing the options for using the Measure A1 funds with County staff, staff in other jurisdictions, as well as Habitat for Humanity,” said Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell . “The City would like to find ways to help fund the construction of ADUs, using Measure A1 or other sources.” In addition to the base allocation funding, City of Piedmont residents and employees are eligible for countywide Measure A1 programs, such as the AC Boost programs offered through the county for first-time homebuyer assistance for emergency responders and educators, as well as the AC Renew home repair program for eligible residents. The AC Boost brochures are posted on the city’s website and can be found by visiting https:// piedmont.ca.gov/cms/one.aspx ?portalId=13659823&pageId =16745183.
articles.title: City received allocation from County bond in 2016

City still sitting on $2.2 million for affordable housing City received allocation from County bond in 2016 By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont must have its Measure A1 base allocation housing application approved by Alameda County in roughly 14 months, by December 31, 2021. The Alameda County bond, passed in 2016, allotted Piedmont $2,188,170 to create affordable housing. In the four years since its passage, Piedmont has not committed any of those funds toward affordable housing, but is currently exploring options. The measure was discussed during the newly formed Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign’s (PREC) first forum. Panelist Gloria Bruce, Executive Director of East Bay Housing Organizations, detailed the effect of the Measure A1 Housing Bond in Piedmont. It passed with 73 percent of the vote countywide, but only 52 percent of Piedmonters voted yes on the measure. The forum, which focused on housing equity in Piedmont in an ongoing series that explored a charge of systemic racism, prompted some residents to wonder why these funds are still untouched. Piedmont has made insufficient progress toward creating low-income housing, according to the California Department of Housing and Community Development. The city has a built-out quality with minimal space for new development, unlike neighboring cities that have quickly utilized the bond funds. Piedmont’s status triggers Senate Bill 35 (SB 35), which encourages cities to create housing on their own or be forced to accept housing developments. SB 35 aims to address the state’s housing shortage by increasing supply, and was signed into law in 2017 by former Gov. Jerry Brown as part of California’s 2017 Housing Package. The city’s housing element goals are to produce 38 affordable units by the end of 2022. On August 17, 2020, the City entered into a contract with Lisa Wise Consulting (LWC) to research incentives for the construction of accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, that are rent-restricted or otherwise affordable to very low and low-income residents. LWC is tasked with identifying potential sources of funding to support local incentives for the construction of income-restricted ADUs, and Measure A1 could be a potential source for funding. There may be other uses for funding identified through public engagement for the Senate Bill 2 housing programs or public engagement for the Piedmont housing element update. Senate Bill 2 provides up to $160,000 to plan projects that would streamline development of new affordable housing. “These funds must be used for projects which are affordable to very low and low-income residents for 55 years or more, as well as other restrictions and terms. The City has been discussing the options for using the Measure A1 funds with County staff, staff in other jurisdictions, as well as Habitat for Humanity,” said Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell . “The City would like to find ways to help fund the construction of ADUs, using Measure A1 or other sources.” In addition to the base allocation funding, City of Piedmont residents and employees are eligible for countywide Measure A1 programs, such as the AC Boost programs offered through the county for first-time homebuyer assistance for emergency responders and educators, as well as the AC Renew home repair program for eligible residents. The AC Boost brochures are posted on the city’s website and can be found by visiting https:// piedmont.ca.gov/cms/one.aspx ?portalId=13659823&pageId =16745183. articles.text: Authorizes the City to Issue Bonds to Reconstruct the Piedmont Community Pool 2/3 vote needed to pass THE QUESTION Should the City of Piedmont be authorized to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of improvements for the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas? THE SITUATION The existing Piedmont Community Pool opened in 1964 and is now in its 56th year. The usual lifespan of most outdoor pools is 50 years. Prior to closure due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place orders, the City was spending approximately $1,000 a day to keep the pool safe and operational. The City believes that residents rely upon the Piedmont Community Pool as a resource to learn to swim, exercise, compete, play, and socialize. It has also been a steady source of employment for local youth. Based on a July, 2020 Concept Study, the estimated cost for replacement of the Piedmont Community Pool including bath house, pools and surrounding site work is $18.8 million. THE PROPOSAL If adopted, Measure UU would authorize the City of Piedmont to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of replacing the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas. It is proposed that the three existing pools be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. The new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas would conserve energy and water, comply with state and federal disability and safety standards, and provide restroom access for those using the tennis courts. FISCAL EFFECTS: If all of the bonds were issued and sold, the best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest is $37,446,788. A “YES” vote on Measure UU would be in favor of authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool . A “NO” vote on Measure UU would be against authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool Supporters Say: The pool needs to be replaced or it will be permanently closed. Measure UU provides necessary funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility to serve Piedmont families, students, and seniors for the next 50 years. Passing this bond measure this year means taking advantage of historically low interest rates and avoiding continued escalation of construction costs in the future. Neuroscience research shows that deep, lasting learning is achieved through productive struggle. To tap into this learning phenomenon, we need to emphasize the effort over the correct answer. Smart brains are efficient brains. When a student learns a skill or concept, myelin is produced, making brain signals faster and stronger. articles.text: This year’s Piedmont Education Foundation Giving Campaign has been overwhelmed with the positive response to the Giving Challenge that was announced last week. The Co-Chairs and the Foundation Board together have pledged to match, dollar for dollar, all new contributions to the Giving Campaign made between October 5 and October 19, up to $200,000. “We received such an amazing response after the match was announced. Gifts and pledges started coming in right away, and people were so happy to be able to double the impact of their gift,” said co-chair Colleen Allen. Some Giving Campaign donors are just learning that there are many ways to give. According to Foundation Executive Director Heather Frank, the Giving Campaign works to provide as many options as possible for families. It accepts checks, credits cards, and stock transfers, and gifts may be made through payroll deduction or donor advised funds. Pledges can be made now and paid off over time. “An increasingly popular option is to set up an automatic bill pay with your bank to send checks made out to PEF on a monthly or quarterly basis,” says Frank. “This allows our donors to pay off a pledge over several months and has the added benefit of eliminating credit card fees.” Frank also encourages everyone to learn more about their company’s matching program. Each year thousands of dollars are donated from companies that provide matching grants to their employees. Individuals are encouraged to check with their company’s HR department to learn more about the program. To help Piedmonters maximize their Giving Campaign donations and to better understand charitable deductions, Ludo Thomasson, a CFP and Wealth Manager and PUSD parent, is offering a short question and answer session on Friday, October 16 at 12:30pm. Registration is free and available at https://bit.ly/33Hh8CL. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, October 14, 2020 SchOOLs S P E E C H , I N C . “Productive Struggle” makes better learners By Katie Pengilly In the education literature, the term “productive struggle” refers to the process of effortful learning that develops grit and creative problem-solving. Neuroscience research shows that deep, lasting learning is achieved through productive struggle. To tap into this learning phenomenon, we need to emphasize the effort over the correct answer. Smart brains are efficient brains. When a student learns a skill or concept, myelin is produced, making brain signals faster and stronger. Challenging tasks which require cognitive struggle increase the production of myelin. Although challenge and struggle may make the learning feel more difficult in the moment, it is a difficulty that pays off in the long run. We can think about learning as a continuum, with surface learning at one end, and deep learning at the other. An example of surface learning would be a fact that is memorized for a test the next day. This can create an illusion of knowledge, yet this surface learning tends to dissipate, and may not be able to be retrieved for a future application to a new situation. On the other end of the continuum, we have deep learning, or mastery. Deep learning is enhanced by productive struggle, and results in conceptual understanding and procedural fluency with the new skill that is transferrable across situations and persists over time. For example, by adding some heavy lifting such as “show/discuss/ explain your work”, rather than simply produce a correct answer, the element of struggle and effort required can led to more durable learning. Both educators and parents can respond to incorrect answers by asking back questions which narrow the area of struggle, but do not entirely remove the struggle by giving the correct answer. Techniques to enhance productive struggle can be included in the classroom as well as at home. In the class setting, students called on who may not have the correct answer. Within a safe and supportive environment, students can be given time to explore and tinker with their ideas, alone or in a pair or group. Assessments can include expression and discussion of ideas and reasoning, the challenge/struggle of which will contribute to enhanced knowledge and retrieval, as opposed to a more passive multiple-choice format which tests a student’s ability to simply recognize a correct answer. At home, praise can be given for perseverance, or being able to express, discuss or explain a concept. Parents can encourage the child to apply curricular items to personal, meaningful experiences. Mixed practice can be encouraged at home, which may seem counterproductive, but due to the productive struggle which it creates, significantly improves long term performance. Simply highlighting and modeling our own reasoning process can also be educational. By making learning environments which value the “productive struggle”, in additional to enhancing specific learning, we are also teaching our children the life skill of embracing, rather than being made uncomfortable by, a challenge. We are teaching our children to enjoy the effort, starting with being intrigued by and learning from our mistakes. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. articles.text: City recommends to avoid trick-or-treating this year The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) declared traditional trick-or-treating to be a “high-risk” activity for COVID-19 transmission, even with precautionary measures such as sanitizing and social distancing. Although trick-or-treating is primarily an outdoor activity, a statement issued by ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram said that it would be difficult to maintain a safe distance on porches and doorsteps. Instead, the health officer is encouraging community members to focus on decorations, and to limit activities to household members only. Parties are high-risk, because mixing among people who don’t live in the same home introduces more opportunities for the virus to pass from one person to another,” Balram said. The department is still encouraging the use of masks, frequent sanitizing, and social distancing. Costume masks are not a substitute for protective cloth masks, but “avoid wearing a costume mask over a protective cloth mask because it can be dangerous if the costume mask makes it hard to breathe,” Balram added. Low-risk activities are recommended by the county, to include visiting an outdoor pumpkin patch, carving and decorating pumpkins outside, and preparing traditional family recipes with members of your household. The risk of traditional trickor-treating can be mitigated from high-risk to moderate-risk, if children participate in one-way trickor-treating where individually wrapped goodie bags are lined up for families to pick up and go while continuing to socially distance. The County also recommends that everyone participating should bring a hand sanitizer, use it frequently, and wash hands immediately after coming home. The Piedmont Police Department echoed the Alameda County recommendations. “The bottom line is that the city is recommending that people do not engage in high-risk behavior such as trick-or-treating,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said.

No in-person classes will be held on Mondays, when everyone will participate in distance learning. All specialist instruction (art, P.E., music, and computers) will be done through distance learning online to limit contact between students and multiple teachers. As recommended by the state and county, Piedmont’s School Reopening Plan requires all school employees returning to campus to receive a COVID test the week before school resumes. 50 percent of the employees will receive additional COVID tests every two weeks on a rotating schedule. Students are not required to receive tests according to the plan. This was a point of concern for a few parents and staff who called into the school board meeting on October 6. The county and state’s position is that tests need to be saved for individuals who have been exposed or have symptoms. Piedmont mom Christine Schooley offered her observations as a teacher in Oakland. “I teach at a school in the flats that has the highest rate of COVID in the county for students and families. I ask that Piedmont, as a group, for the greater, save testing for those who really need it and who don’t have access. We can do this without our families rushing to require testing that gives a false sense of security for our students.” Each day before going to school, all students and staff must fill out a screening form for COVID symptoms. Checking off any item on the screening form requires at least 48 hours of quarantine at home. Items include: new or worsening cough, fever over 100 degrees, chills, diarrhea, nausea, and runny nose. Anyone on campus with a cough (even with asthma, allergies, etc.) needs medical clearance to stay. The county has directed PUSD to set the bar low for sending staff and students home. Additionally, if anyone reports yes to “close contact” (defined as: contact with another within six feet for 15 minutes or more, regardless of mask wearing) with anyone that has tested positive or has COVID symptoms, they must quarantine for 14 days while the rest of the class continues in person. The screening form is available here: www.docs.google.com/ forms/d/1avflS7rFbPGC7Vfrhu 9H0ue9xA5T3LIEYnYQMcCk7Io/viewform?edit_requested=true&gxids=7757 “I believe screening is incredibly important. By filling out the screening form every morning, everyone who comes to our school sites will be reminded of the importance of staying home if they are symptomatic or have been in close contact with someone who is symptomatic or who tested positive,” said school board member Dr. Sarah Pearson, a pediatrician.

articles.text: trigger a return to distance learning for everyone. “School closure may be appropriate when there are multiple cases in multiple cohorts at a school or when at least 5 percent of the total number of teachers/student/staff are [positive] cases within a 14-day period,” the document states. At all times, everyone on campus must keep six feet from others, wear a mask, and wash their hands before entering a new room. There will not be on-campus lunch; hallways and entrances will be one way when possible. Plexiglass has been installed for teachers in classrooms. Teachers will have the right to dismiss any student not following safety requirements. Extensive cleaning will take place in all rooms and electrostatic sprayers will be used. Electrostatic spray is positively charged, allowing the appropriate sanitizers, mold preventatives and disinfectants to wrap around and evenly coat all types of surfaces for a more complete clean. All classrooms have been equipped with new MERV-13 filters on the heating and air conditioning units. Doors and windows will be open as indoor and outdoor conditions safely permit. “The idea is to use a variety of prevention techniques with the recognition that they won’t be able to be implemented perfectly all of the time by everyone, but in combination they should be very protective,” said Pearson. Children’s Fairyland Outdoor Park - Now Open Fairyland opened its Fairy Gates on Saturday, October 3. To ensure safety, puppet shows, Toddler Storytimes, live performances and rides have been put on pause. All tickets are reduced to $8. The slides are open, along with most Storybook sets. Kids can run up and roll down the Jack and Jill Hill, and Gideon, Pixie, and all their other animals are ready to see the return of families. The cafe will be open for snacks. Picnickers are invited and social bubbles are marked with circular chalked areas throughout the park. The park is open Wednesday to Sunday. Get off the screen and get instruction from a professional with 20 years teaching experience in Maui, and Huntington Beach. Mornings or afternoon lessons available. 1-1/2 to 2-hour sessions are available and a surfboard is provided. Wetsuits can be rented at a nearby surf shop. Meet at the beach or carpool from Piedmont available. Museum of Children’s Arts (MOCHA) Daycare and Distance Learning MOCHA has started an “Equitable Pod” program at the museum for parents that need daycare and want their kids to be in a creative environment during distance learning. Staff members will assist kids in logging into their virtual classes and answering questions. Classes consist of 10-12 per stable pod for kids aged 5-12, masks and social distancing are required throughout. An hour lunch time and two break times will let kids have a chance to run around and play games outside. The class runs from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. and additional after-care is available until 5:30 p.m. Winchester Mystery Museum Self-Guided Mansion Tour and Halloween Flashlight Tour The mansion has one-way tour paths and features the larger rooms in the mansion. Guests will be able to experience the house like never before, with ample space and time in each room. Tour the 160 rooms at your own pace in your space. The Mansion Tour ticket also includes access to the Victorian Gardens. A nighttime flashlight tour is also open this month for Halloween. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

A Citizen Bond Oversight Committee will be selected to monitor the use of bond proceeds and to share their perspective with the community. If Measure UU does not pass, the city will likely begin a process to permanently close the pool and determine alternate uses for that site. 2 – Budgets are a reflection of a community’s values. Public Safety, including crime prevention, wildfire prevention and disaster preparedness, is a top priority for Piedmonters. Over two-thirds of Piedmont’s General Fund budget is spent on personnel costs and two-thirds of the city’s personnel are police and fire personnel, consistent with our community’s values. We ensure efficient use of public funds and budget oversight with support of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee (BAFPC), a tremendous asset to City Council and residents. As a former member, I found my colleagues on the committee to be smart, hard-working, dedicated financial professionals who offer comprehensive, detailed analysis and recommendations. The work of this committee has provided independent budget oversight, transparency and in-depth understanding of city finances. By implementing recommendations of this committee the city consistently strengthens its financial position. The BAFPC has consistently identified insufficient funds available to support the years of deferred maintenance the city has accrued which cannot be funded through existing General Fund revenue sources. Current ballot Measure TT will provide the necessary funds to begin to address this shortage. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – I’ve talked with several hundred residents during this campaign. The one issue that is on everyone’s mind is our community pool. I strongly believe we need to replace our pool. It is over 20 years past its usable life and beyond repair. We now have a tremendous opportunity to build a state-of-the-art eco-conscious aquatic facility, at a time when interest rates are in our favor. Once the project is funded through Measure UU, a citizen’s committee will be formed to determine the best design. Our pool is a midtown jewel that is critical for our schools and strengthens all our property values. Potential home buyers find our community amenity extremely attractive. I hope for an energy-efficient facility that can easily accommodate all our sports, fitness, recreation and community gathering needs. I believe we will always reap significant returns on an investment we make in our health, wellbeing and community. 2 – Yes. Piedmont’s reputation for good schools and as a beautiful place to live is due to the efficient management of our tax dollars. Our schools are excellent thanks to PUSD, students and parents. We have gorgeous parks and a large variety of trees, carefully chosen and placed by our Parks Commission. Our streets, sewers and sidewalks are all extraordinarily well maintained. There is no emergency our Public Works Department can’t handle. Our Recreation Department provides a wonderful selection of community activities to support our health and well-being. Thanks to our Police Department, we enjoy a higher level of safety compared with our neighboring cities. Our Fire Department arrives within minutes to aid with emergency health or property issues. City staff and the volunteer efforts from all our other commissions/committees keep our City running smoothly. Given all the diverse challenges our City faces, we are doing a good job maximizing public funds. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – Public safety and emergency preparedness are primary, overlapping, compelling issues. We must evaluate Piedmont’s essential services buildings to bring them up to current codes and standards. We must engage the community to measure interest, support and understanding of financial implications. Residents should sleep at night secure in knowing police and fire professionals will show up with all necessary equipment to provide essential services during a personal crisis, as well as, during and after a public disaster. Piedmont police are housed in a 70 y/o facility. Among many inadequacies, our existing police facility prevents Piedmont from meeting the national effort to update the 911 system. Piedmont Fire professionals are housed in the City Hall building, originally constructed 110 years ago. On the list of many inadequacies, our existing fire facility is too small to accommodate current fire apparatus and equipment. Piedmont’s climate action plan serves as a framework for all infrastructure planning 2 – Overall, yes. Surveys conducted in early summer reveal a majority of Piedmonters have a positive opinion of our City’s financial management. Transparency is critical to oversight. Oversight is critical to efficiency. Piedmont residents have access to budget information and can critique or applaud what their decision-making bodies are doing. I served on the Municipal Tax Review Committee, (now Budget Advisory and Financial Planning). It is tasked with reviewing financial projections, funding and expenditures. Following the June 2020 review of the City’s annual budget proposal, proposed funding and expenditures from several long-term funds, and proposed midyear budget adjustments, the BAFP committee concluded: “Piedmont’s Finance Director was very thorough dealing with potential revenue risk, projected pension costs, OPEB funding, equipment replacement, and facilities maintenance. Overall we believe the assumptions used in results presented to be reasonable and consistent with past practices which have proven to be appropriately conservative.” NANCY BOSTROM No response received.

The Post asks each candidate two questions every week. Responses are listed below. JEN CAVENAUGH, Incumbent 1 – As a City Council Member for the last four years, my top priority has been to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. If Measure TT passes, the city will have the necessary funds so we can begin to address decadeslong deferred maintenance of our over 20 municipal buildings that are each 60-100 years old. I would also work to make sure that we have a strong communication plan that would push messages to parents in three ways -- text, email and PUSD application notification. I would consult with [health] experts to make sure our numbers remain low and that tracing is completed when there are positive cases. I would also like to see a weekly dashboard of numbers and information available to parents and families JASON KELLEY 1 – Regarding schools, the single most compelling issue facing Piedmont right now is how and when we reopen in-person learning. The three groups of experts whose knowledge will guide us as we make decisions on this issue are: public health professionals, educators, and parents. Listening to these experts and finding consensus is the way forward. The plan now in place to open elementary schools incrementally is the result of much hard work and is a good beginning. As Alameda County hopefully begins to allow upper grades to return to school over the coming months, we should continue to listen to the concerns of both parents and teachers find the best way forward. 2 – In addition to the points outlined in my answer to the previous question, I think we also need to be working on instilling a sense of community responsibility among residents. Once schools have opened for in-person learning again, it will be everyone’s responsibility to make personal behavior decisions that will maximize the chances that the schools can stay open. That includes wearing masks and maintaining social distancing, not sending kids to school who have any symptoms are who are likely to have been exposed to anyone with the virus, and taking all the other steps recommended by public health experts to keep ourselves and our community safe. HARI TITAN 1 – I feel the most compelling issue facing Piedmont is continuing to earn the City’s reputation as an excellent place to educate our pre-K-12 kids. The median home value in Piedmont has risen to $2.2 million. Our additional school property taxes are still significantly lower than private school tuition. However, over the summer our response to Covid led some parents to temporarily move to areas that had in-classroom instruction. After a long back- and-forth and conflicting advice, this issue was recently resolved by the school board for elementary school. If I am elected, I will work to expand the parental choice of in-classroom instruction for middle school and high school as soon as we are allowed by county health officials and are prepared to move forward. As long as more families want to move here than leave, our home values will keep rising over the long term and all Piedmonters, including empty-nesters, will benefit. 2 – With in-classroom instruction resuming shortly, my biggest school safety concern is compliance with the school district’s mandates for wearing masks and social distancing as well as truthful reporting of health status at the beginning of each school day. This social contract needs 100% compliance for access to school grounds. I would offer to conduct school safety summits with parents to answer questions live and focus my risk assessment presentation to convince as many parents as possible of the importance of this compliance. Another idea is to utilize a School Resource Officer (SRO) in a proactive strategy designed to prevent compliance violations and also to intervene when non-compliant persons need to be removed from school grounds. This is totally in the scope of the SRO program which was developed to address juvenile crime and safety concerns in our local schools. SROs are typically tasked with maintaining a safe, secure, and orderly learning environment for students, teachers, and staff. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – Of course, coping with the pandemic is the most challenging current issue. And while this will likely further impact school funding, our constant constraint, Piedmont has the opportunity to be a leader in addressing student well-being. Every year the District works to understand how our students are doing -- not just academically, but also from a social-emotional perspective. We survey our students once a year and not surprisingly, they are feeling stressed, they aren’t getting enough sleep, and many are just “doing school.” I am sure this hasn’t improved during the pandemic. The Board has recognized that this is a major issue. We held a Board workshop on student stress. We also purposefully updated one of our strategic goals to change the emphasis from achievement to engagement. We want our students to participate in relevant learning experiences that will foster life-long curiosity and that will spark creativity and promote collaboration. 2 – On October 6th, the School Board unanimously approved an approach for reopening that will phase in hybrid learning for our students, starting with our students with special needs and continuing with our youngest learners on November 3rd. Our plan covers the important aspects under the school’s control such as cleaning, disinfection and ventilation, cohorting, PPE, health screenings for students and staff, and testing, as well as rules for physical distancing and movement within the schools. As a Board member who helped shape these plans, I believe my role is to evaluate performance regularly and communicate clearly with the community. Everyone needs to understand the safeguards that have been put in place. Just as important are the measures families can take to ensure we are successful -- wear masks at all times when not at home, and be vigilant about washing hands, social distancing, and limiting the number of contacts. VERONICA ANDERSON THIGPEN 1 – Our schools are a microcosm of the most compelling issues we face as a community. PUSD faces challenges with school climate and culture that need to be addressed. Narrow definitions around performance and what it means to be a successful student lead to stress or disengagement. Reliance on traditional historical narratives combined with little to no diversity create a feeding ground for misguided beliefs and bias. Likewise, for Piedmont. Historically defined as a closed community, Piedmont today should use its social and economic capital to stimulate inclusion. Despite the abundant diversity in Oakland and other nearby communities, diversity here remains elusive. Community advocates are working intentionally to create policies and raise awareness through public discourse. This longterm work must be supported if we are ever to realize the community of belonging that we envision. 2 – I would support efforts to communicate to families the protocols for operating schools safely. Families also need details about their options if they have concerns or health risks. I would want to ensure that communications with parents are consistent, clear and transparent, and I’d suggest the district create easy-to-read materials to help parents have conversations with their young children about how to be safe when they go back to school. I’d want to be clear that, depending on COVID risk, it may be necessary to revert to distance learning at some point. I would also want to have confidence in county protocols for testing and contact tracing to contain exposure if someone gets sick. We must clearly communicate these protocols to families so that they know what to expect.

I’d want to be clear that, depending on COVID risk, it may be necessary to revert to distance learning at some point. I would also want to have confidence in county protocols for testing and contact tracing to contain exposure if someone gets sick. We must clearly communicate these protocols to families so that they know what to expect.
