articles.text: We are swimmers and non-swimmers; people whose families have lived here for generations and people who are newer to the neighborhood; we are former mayors, school board members, Piedmont school teachers, city commissioners, and every day residents; people with experience in real estate and project development and people who understand city finance; people with young kids and retirees whose kids have long since flown the coop. We volunteered to be on the Community Pool for Piedmont Advisory Committee for one reason: we love Piedmont and believe a public pool is vital to what makes the town of Piedmont a great place to live. We believe rebuilding the community pool is a priority that Piedmont should commit to now because of these facts: 1. The current pool can no longer function. Keeping the existing pool open is not a realistic option. The pool is crumbling, unsafe, and leaks thousands of gallons of water daily. It has frequent breakdowns taking it out of service. The significant maintenance costs throw the City’s good money after bad. The pool is now closed, and, unfortunately, its permanent closure is inevitable. 4. The existing pool doesn’t meet the needs of the community. Built in 1964, when LBJ was President, the current pool doesn’t meet modern needs or homebuyer expectations. The existing pool isn’t big enough for all the residents who want to use it – team practices, lap swimming, recreational play, and swim lessons. Our kids have to leave town just to practice their sport, and adults can’t get their exercise in after a long day at work. The proposed design better serves the community with an attractive, functional civic amenity at an important location in the center of town. 2. The existing pool has been used by a broad cross-section of Piedmont residents for the last 56 years. Virtually every Piedmont kid has used the pool – at swim lessons, summer camps, PE classes, birthday parties, lifeguard training, school celebrations, Piedmont Swim Team, or in high school as student athletes on the PHS/MHS swim and water polo teams. Adults have enjoyed the pool with their families or used it for exercise, rehabilitation, or recreation. 5. This is the right economic time to build the pool. Despite global economic uncertainty, it is actually an advantageous time for municipal construction projects. Interest rates are at historic lows and borrowing money will probably never be cheaper. Construction costs may even be lower, depending on the economic environment. Our tax payments don’t start when we authorize the bonds, but only when the bonds are issued as needed for the project. 3. Without a functioning and safe pool, Piedmont will be the only city in Alameda County that doesn’t provide a pool for its community and schools. Piedmont realtors are emphatic that a public pool for school and community use is one of the municipal features most highly valued by families making a move. Like the other characteristics that make Piedmont such a desirable place to live, a safe and accessible pool for our residents and our schools will translate into higher property values. 6. This project has been carefully evaluated and considered by City staff and the City Council for over five years. There have been hundreds of hours of meetings with consultants, hearings before the Recreation Commission and City Council, and numerous staff reports. There are 18 documents on the City’s projects/community pool web page chronicling the City Council action and analysis since 2015. These include the master plan and the aquatics feasibility study led by the leading aquatics consultants, Counsilman-Hunsaker, who have completed more than 1,000 aquatics projects across the country of every size and complexity. Piedmonters who came before us invested in the infrastructure that helps make Piedmont the wonderful town that it is. We’ve all been the beneficiaries of that generosity and foresight. It’s now our time to make an investment in our community that will last for generations of Piedmonters to come. It’s time to rebuild a community pool that meets the needs of the whole community. Join us, the unanimous Piedmont City Council and School Board, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Piedmont Recreational Facilitates Organization, the Beach Parents’ Organization, the Havens Parents’ Club, the Wildwood Parents’ Club, the PMS Parents’ Club, the PHS Parents’ Club, and the Piedmont High School Boosters Club, in supporting Measure UU. Abe Friedman Cathy Glazier Sue Herrick Wayne Jordan Community Pool for Piedmont Advisory Committee Valerie Matzger Nancy McHugh Sarah Meyjes Chad Olcott Sarah Pearson Neil Ruthven Jon Sakol Tom Sullivan Ken Taylor Cameron Wolfe, Jr.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 14, 2020 11 POOL LETTERS MAIN Why I support the Pool and Measure UU By Jon Sakol When the City took over operation of the pool in 2011, I was asked to help design how the pool would operate. The system we came up with generated twice as much revenue as other public pools and saved the City a lot of money. I spent over a thousand hours in that effort. I was motivated to do so for two reasons: I wanted to be sure the City’s operation of the pool was a success, and I was concerned that if the pool got too expensive, the City might lose interest in it. I brought those same concerns to the discussions that led to the current pool proposal. We need to build a pool that meets the needs of the schools as well as the rest of the community. Under the facilities sharing arrangement between the City and the schools, the schools get to use the pool just as the City gets to use the schools’ gyms and sports fields. We are the same taxpayers who would be called on to fund a school pool. It’s time to have one facility that works for everyone – a pool designed so the Piedmont Swim Team doesn’t have to rent additional space in other communities and spend hours a week commuting to practice; designed so the high school water polo and swim teams don’t have to practice at night or commute to other pools; designed so kids can both play and have swim lessons after school; designed so lap swimmers have room to swim their laps when they get home from work at night. It’s not too expensive. The bond measure is about financing, not cost. You can’t bid the project until you have detailed construction drawings and no one would pay to have those drawings done until they knew they had the financing and the project would proceed. The increased cost estimate from 2016, when the conceptual design was initially approved, simply reflects that it will be built at least six years later. You don’t have to issue or spend all the bonds that are authorized. The City Council didn’t prioritize the pool over public safety, by putting the pool on the ballot. The fact is our infrastructure is old and needs to be addressed. The pool is on the ballot because there already was a plan to deal with the pool. The public safety issues just came up, there isn’t a plan to deal with them yet. The question is simple: does Piedmont want a pool or not? If we do, it makes no sense to build an inadequate pool. It’s time to have a community pool that finally meets the needs of the whole community. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. articles.text: Richey recounts the time when he was ranked No. 1 in the U.S. A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s monumental sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. With the French Open now concluded, it’s a fiiting time to look back to a former top tennis tournament in the Bay Area: The Pacific Coast Championships. In the late 60s and early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world would gather in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the Berkeley Tennis Club and compete in the Pacific Coast Championship. One of the oldest sports events in the U.S., it was a top draw for major players from 1889 to 2013, it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States, predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of the Open era in professional tennis beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championship, 1969-1971, meant the best players in the world were close by. Many influential matches were taking place for the end-of-year rankings. An October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. Back in 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States in the semifinals of the PCC. It was one of the most memorable matches in the history of the sport. Their match lasyed more than “All the players, officials, or anybody who was close to the game knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an active spokesman for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. In his book, Acing Depression, Richey describes his challenges with the disease in the years following his tennis career. “It’s been a good book from the standpoint of what I wrote it for – to be able to help just one person. Clinical depression has 10 or 12 criteria that lasts various amounts of time. It is a bonafide medical illness. In America we’re allowed to be sick from the Adam’s Apple down but not the Adam;s Apple up. It can happen to anybody,” Richey said. In the book he recounts some of his experiences with depression and what led to him write the book. “I had episodes throughout my life. In tennis on my last six years of the tour, I had lost my game; I couldn’t get my backhand back. That’s why I got depressed; I had lost what was most valuable to me: my skill. I had a three year breakdown at my worst,” said Richey, describing some situations from his book. “I’ve spoken at 60 or so events over the last 10 years and hosted some golf events. I wrote the book as a mental-health book, with as desire to help others who Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey suffered like I did. It just so happened that my daughter had a year off from being a professor at Texas A&M. She did a wonderful job of putting [the book] together It’s my tennis career and depression running on parallel tracks, meeting at the end,” he explained. . Pacific Coast Championship history In 1971,the final yearof the Pacific Coast Championship at Berkeley Tennis Club, Australian legends Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall squared off in what became Laver’s sixth singles title of the year. The doubles’ title in ‘71 was another all-Australian performance with Laver and Roy Emerson defeating Rosewall and Fred Stolle. It was held in multiple venues, starting at the Old Del Monte Lodge in Monterey in 1889, moving to the Hotel Rafael in San Rafael from 1890 to 1899, and then to Berkeley from 1900 to 1930 for its initial stay. From there, the PCC played in Alamo from 1931-1933, returned to Berkeley from 1934-1941, went to San Francisco in ’42-’48, then back to Berkeley from 1949 through 1971. The Cow Palace and SF Civic Auditorium then hosted from 1973 to 1993 before it moved oto its final destination, the SAP Center in San Jose,; During its time it was in San Francisco, John McEnroe dominated the event with 14 combined singles and doubles titles – five in singles. four hours and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point as the end-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner to upset Smith, the favorite. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey, now 73 and living in San Angelo, Texas. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey about the match. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals in London. I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my butt was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals,in Berkeley in another epic match, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified the previous round. Photo courtesy of Berkeley Tennis Club Berkeley Tennis Club hosted the Pacific Coast Championships until 1971, featuring some of the world’s best tennis players. Photo courtesy of World Tennis Magazine Cliff Richey talks with the Post about his tennis career and mentalhealth activism.

articles.text: Piedmont High senior Makenna Thiel won the NorCal Excellence tennis tournament in Manteca on September 2 against a group of highly rated players. Piedmont High senior Makenna Thiel, a ramked tennis player who has committed to the California Golden Bears next year, finished off the summer by winning the NorCal Excellence championship in the U-18 bracket. Competing from August 29 to September 2 in Manteca, she defeated some highly rated tennis players. Thiel opened with a 7-5, 6-4 victory over Esther Vrylan, a five-star rated freshman from Sacramento, then nearly double-bageled her next two opponents: Kate Sexton, 6-0, 6-0 and five-star recruit Gayathri Krishnan of Cupertino, 6-1, 6-1. “Excellence tournaments are the second highest level tournament. It was my second tournament since the start of quarantine,” said Thiel. “First round matches are always a little shaky, especially after not playing for a few months. I had to warm up in the first round, get a feel for the ball, and get back in match-mode,” said Thiel, a nationally rated prospect by the Tennis Recruiting Network. As an added incentive to her quick victories, it was her dad’s birthday on August 30. “The second day was my dad’s birthday and my sister said, ‘Get it done quickly so we can go home!’ I went out and probably played one of my best matches [against Krishnan]. My dad hasn’t been to one of my matches in some time, so it was nice to play well while he was there.” She defeated a familiar competitor, Tomi Main of R.L. Stevenson School in Pebble beach, 7-5, 3-6, 6-4 to win the tournament with th etemperaaature over 100 degrees. “I’ve been playing her (Main) quite a bit and we’ve always had competitive matches. It was very, very hot; our matches got delayed during the hottest part of the day. It was a battle,” she explained. Although the match was in the semifinal rounds, Maribella Zamarippa of St. Helena dropped out of the finals due to illness, elevating Thiel and Main to the championship round. The pair has squared off time and again, including in the semifinals of the 2019 NorCal Sectional Championships, which Thiel also won in three sets. “I didn’t feel necessarily fatigued at the end of it but I was so happy to be done with the match,” said Thiel with a laugh. “Maybe the adrenaline helped me out but I’ve been doing a lot of fitness to get through matches like those. It got me through.” With COVID causing changes in tournameen schedules, the match in Manteca was hher first since this summer. “It was my first tournament since June. I’ve just been focusing on practice because there are only so many tournaments in the area and I’m not really comfortable enough to get on a plane yet. There’s no need to rush around right now,” she said. A year from now, Thie will be among the headliners in Cal’s 2021 recruiting class after having committing to Cal in July. California’s 2020 recruiting class this summer included fellow five-star recruits Cami Brown of Irvine, Canadian champion Jada Bui, and Hannah Viller Moller of Denmark, meaning Cal could become the Pac 12 school y to keep an eye on in the coming years. Thiel is the Post’s 2019 Athlete of the Year after she won the North Coast Section Div. I doubles championship with Lauren Young. pages.text: Wednesday, October 14, 2020 13 PHS senior Makenna Thiel wins NorCal Excellence tournament in Manteca Piedmont High senior Makenna Thiel won the NorCal Excellence tennis tournament in Manteca on September 2 against a group of highly rated players. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High senior Makenna Thiel, a ramked tennis player who has committed to the California Golden Bears next year, finished off the summer by winning the NorCal Excellence championship in the U-18 bracket. Competing from August 29 to September 2 in Manteca, she defeated some highly rated tennis players. Thiel opened with a 7-5, 6-4 victory over Esther Vrylan, a five-star rated freshman from Sacramento, then nearly double-bageled her next two opponents: Kate Sexton, 6-0, 6-0 and five-star recruit Gayathri Krishnan of Cupertino, 6-1, 6-1. “Excellence tournaments are the second highest level tournament. It was my second tournament since the start of quarantine,” said Thiel. “First round matches are always a little shaky, especially after not playing for a few months. I had to warm up in the first round, get a feel for the ball, and get back in match-mode,” said Thiel, a nationally rated prospect by the Tennis Recruiting Network. As an added incentive to her quick victories, it was her dad’s birthday on August 30. “The second day was my dad’s birthday and my sister said, ‘Get it done quickly so we can go home!’ I went out and probably played one of my best matches [against Krishnan]. My dad hasn’t been to one of my matches in some time, so it was nice to play well while he was there.” She defeated a familiar competitor, Tomi Main of R.L. Stevenson School in Pebble beach, 7-5, 3-6, 6-4 to win the tournament with th etemperaaature over 100 degrees. “I’ve been playing her (Main) quite a bit and we’ve always had competitive matches. It was very, very hot; our matches got delayed during the hottest part of the day. It was a battle,” she explained. Although the match was in the semifinal rounds, Maribella Zamarippa of St. Helena dropped out of the finals due to illness, elevating Thiel and Main to the championship round. The pair has squared off time and again, including in the semifinals of the 2019 NorCal Sectional Championships, which Thiel also won in three sets. “I didn’t feel necessarily fatigued at the end of it but I was so happy to be done with the match,” said Thiel with a laugh. “Maybe the adrenaline helped me out but I’ve been doing a lot of fitness to get through matches like those. It got me through.” With COVID causing changes in tournameen schedules, the match in Manteca was hher first since this summer. “It was my first tournament since June. I’ve just been focusing on practice because there are only so many tournaments in the area and I’m not really comfortable enough to get on a plane yet. There’s no need to rush around right now,” she said. A year from now, Thie will be among the headliners in Cal’s 2021 recruiting class after having committing to Cal in July. California’s 2020 recruiting class this summer included fellow five-star recruits Cami Brown of Irvine, Canadian champion Jada Bui, and Hannah Viller Moller of Denmark, meaning Cal could become the Pac 12 school y to keep an eye on in the coming years. Thiel is the Post’s 2019 Athlete of the Year after she won the North Coast Section Div. I doubles championship with Lauren Young. She was also the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2018 after helping Piedmont;s tennis team win its fifth straight North Coast Section team championship. articles.text: The CZU Complex Fire that waged in Big Basin Redwoods State Park of San Mateo and Santa Cruz Counties was contained in 37 days with an estimated 40 percent of its redwoods charred and 86,000 acres of the Along with the historic redwoods, the park’s headquarters building, constructed in 1936 as a WPA project, was destroyed. Additionally, the visitor center and campgrounds were burned. Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating to 1902. It contains and preserves some Redwood trees that date back more than 2,000 years. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 of old-growth redwoods. The Peninsula Open Space Trust, a conservation organization, announced that a 9,000-acre preserve called the San Vicente Redwoods were destroyed. “For me, these were more than just ‘structures,’” said Walter T. Moore, president of the Open Space Trust. “They were places where we gathered for generations with our friends and families, places where we made memories and found ourselves surrounded by the splendor of the redwood forest.” He indicated that officials may not be able to fully assess the fire damage d for “months, if not years. But fire in this landscape can be healthy and beneficial for the redwood forest, which is very well adapted to survive fire. Fire is an integral part of this environment and helps to maintain the health of the ecosystem. Redwood trees, especially old growth, can withstand fire — and early indications are that many have survived,” he said. Last month, park officials said it could take a full year before Big Basin reopens. That sentiment was reiterated by Noelle Chambers Thurlow, Vice President of Peninsula Open Space. “It’s hard to answer when (the forest) will come back. We can only speculate. One year from now we’ll have a much better idea,” said Thurlow. “The fire was also a huge threat to farms in and around Pescadero and more broadly along the San Mateo County coast. Many of these farms operate on protected land and were evacuated with little warning. Forced from their operations for several weeks, their businesses suffered as they lost their ability to harvest and distribute their products,” added Moore. After a brief closure of the parking lot near Rodeo Beach, park officials re-opened the area for hikers and beach goers. pages.text: Wednesday, October 14, 2020 15 HIKING WITH JON Bunker hopping in the Marin Headlands Post sports writer runs into a bobcat By Jonathan Comeaux It’s been a couple of years since our last visit to the Marin Headlands and Rodeo Beach, that bucolic, untamed stretch of land just past the Golden Gate Bridge. Last week we traveled far past Battery Townsley, bouncing around in and out of former military bunkers that date back to the 1930s. One of our destinations was Hill 88, a former military radar control station. The hike was 6.4 miles round trip and over 1,300 feet of elevation gain. After a brief closure of the parking lot near Rodeo Beach, park officials re-opened the area for hikers and beach goers. Given the popularity of the beach and first and last stopping point of Battery Townsley, you can expect to pass a lot of people at the start and end of your day. I passed 112 people on the day. One way to avoid lots of hikers would be to use the Coastal Trail bike path on the way up to Battery Townsley. Once you pass Townsley, keep an eye out for the trail sign that reads: “Wolf Ridge and Hill 88,” then continue up the Coastal Trail toward Hill 88. A smaller hillside bunker sits in the Marin Headlands. Keep an eye out for this trail sign after Battery Townsley. You can hop bunker to bunker up the hillside in the Marin Headlands. A view of Tennessee Valley Beach from a platform in the headlands. Ascending Hill 88, an abandoned military base on the other side of the Golden Gate Bridge. Hill 88 is an old radar control station. You can spot areas where aircraft used to land. The structures are open to explore. Photos by Jonathan Comeaux The view above Battery Townsley, the first of many former military bunkers around the Marin Headlands. From this point, you can easily venture around the headlands to separate yourself from other trail-goers. The Coastal Trail diverts in many directions; traveling northwest can take you to Tennessee Valley Beach – another trail we previously covered – or to a hilltop platform I sat on to take in the view of the headlands toward Mt. Tamalpais and the beach resting below. From that platform continuing west back on the Coastal Trail for a mile is Hill 88, which now is a graffiti-covered former military base where you can observe the peaks of the Golden Gate Bridge and San Francisco in the distance. It’s a good spot to rest and take in your surroundings after the ascent up after gaining over 1,000 feet in elevation gain in the time it takes you to get to Hill 88. You’ll pass a collection of two other former military bunkers on your way there, some with old sandbags that have hardened over time. The headlands are characterized by its open space with large fields of California poppies, coast rock cress, lupine, and monkey flowers. No matter where you are, you’ll see red tailed hawks soaring far overhead as they scan the ground for their next meal, often gophers. It was here that I had a shocking encounter with a fully-grown bobcat. Bobcat encounter Roughly 100 feet past the initial entrance of Battery Townsley is a second “gunner station,” which is directly across from the Wolf Ridge and Hill 88 trail marker. When exploring the open area on my own, a fully-grown bobcat ran away from the space I had just entered. Instead of snapping photos, I instinctively made my arms wide and shouted toward the wildcat. He ran without threatening me, but the sight was jarring given the amount of young children and dogs just hundreds of yards away. Local park rangers said that the sighting was considerably rare given that bobcats are nocturnal hunters. “To see a fully-grown cat at this time of day at that area is very rare. There have been some bobcat sightings in the past, but very seldom,” said a park ranger. Here are some guidelines for wildcat sightings: • Refrain from turning around and running. It shows fear, and an animal’s instinct is to chase its prey (that’s you). Back away slowly and deliberately get big. Spread your arms and be loud to scare the animal away. Inside the second gunnery station of Battery Townsley. Moments later, this writer had an unexpected encounter with a bobcat. Photo courtesy of Mercury News An encounter with a wild, fully-grown bobcat at Battery Townsley in the Marin Headlands.

articles.text: SF Ballet’s Jahna Frantziskonis is featured in Sequentia. San Francisco Ballet presents Sequentia, a choreographic chain letter to keep dancers and patrons connected during the global pandemic. Ten San Francisco Ballet dancers are connected through their movement in this choreographic chain letter. The film originated with a dancer who improvised a six-second solo to the music, and this choreography was passed along to the next dancer who picked up where the previous one left off. From the San Francisco Ballet, to New York City Ballet, to American Ballet Theatre, the “digital letter” started at the beginning of shelter-in-place restrictions and continues more than six months later through October in Seattle. In the video, patrons can view Pacific Northwest Ballet’s take on Seattle’s cityscape, working around and in-between the wildfires that have plagued the West Coast this year. San Francisco Ballet dancers who are featured include Tiit Helimets, Misa Kuranaga, Cavan Conley, Jahna Frantziskonis, Daniel Deivison-Oliveira, Myles Thatcher, Yuan Yuan Tan, Diego Cruz, Dores André, and Joshua Jack Price. The featured video for San Francisco is produced by Helimets and edited by Ben Estabrook. You can view the film on Youtube at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=zhFuJEaVBtQ. In the performing department, singers are given more creative liberty and reach new heights of personal expression, deepening their relationship with music. Singers now understand the complexities of their vocal range, and are able to practice with this in mind. Beyond the music, students also begin to form their own “musical personalities and identities,” and often make lifelong bonds with like-minded friends within the choir. The majority of students in the senior department began the program in the kinder or training department, and have likely joined their peers at sleepaway camps, in recitals and on tours. All singers are required to participate in a number of performances throughout the year. All performing department choirs perform in the Candlelight Concert in December, the Winter Concert and/or New Music Concert in mid-spring, the Spring Sing! Concert in late Spring, and the Bon Voyage Concert in June when the touring vocal groups have their final concert before leaving for international choral competitions. Singers are also likely to participate in supplementary opportunities, like Jazz and Beyond, and the Ancora Recital. In the past, some students have opted to work with a current composer on a new work. There is a big emphasis on touring in this department. International choral competition has been a centerpiece of the choir’s program since 1984. Since its founding, Piedmont Children’s Choir has performed in 26 countries and 13 states in the U.S. It has been an invited choir in 19 choral competitions in Europe, Asia, and North America, and has a display case filled with gold and silver medals from the most prestigious choral competitions in the world. The final part of the series will explore international touring and competition.

articles.text: Bobak Cyrus Bakitiari (left) Johnny Moreno, and Jomar Tagatac star in the San Francisco Playouse production of Art. San Francisco Playhouse will premiere Art by Yasmina Reza on Saturday, October 24. The premiere will be streamed live and will be available to view for two weeks. The play explores how colleagues and friends can turn on each other when divided into opposing camps. There is a special focus on the complex layers of friendship, while at the same time maintaining a comedic tone. The play asks the question: Are we who we think we are, or are we who our friends think we are? Directed by Bill English, Art is translated by Christopher Hampton. It casts Bobak Cyrus Bakhtiari as Yvan, Johnny Moreno as Serge, and Jomar Tagatac as Marc. Reza is a French playwright and novelist based in Paris whose works have won many awards and received critical and popular international success. Art received the 1998 Tony Award and the New York Drama Critics Circle Award for Best Play. The London production of Art received the Olivier Award as Best Play in 1996. The original National Theatre production of Life x 3 also earned a 2001 Olivier Award nomination for Best Play. Her other noteworthy plays include After a Burial, The Passage of Winter, and The Unexpected Man. Theater fans can watch the video stream anytime between October 24 and November 7. History of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Performing Dept. a rigorous music education for young singers By Allyson Aleksey Part 5 in a series The most advanced program in the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, the Performing Department, is comprised of students in grades 5 through 12. In this program, choral teachers challenge the students further through advanced music theory, ear training, and sight singing, along with foreign language diction, healthy vocal technique, resonance, breathing, vowel formation, performance, and storytelling. Students will expand on the basic building blocks of choral singing that were instilled in both the kinder and training department. Its four choral groups – Concert Choir, Ensemble, Ecco, and Ancora – represent the pinnacle of children’s choral training and performance. Singers in these groups have studied music for several years. The students are admitted into the groups following a vocal placement. In the performing department, singers are given more creative liberty and reach new heights of personal expression, deepening their relationship with music. Singers now understand the complexities of their vocal range, and are able to practice with this in mind. Beyond the music, students also begin to form their own “musical personalities and identities,” and often make lifelong bonds with like-minded friends within the choir. The majority of students in the senior department began the program in the kinder or training department, and have likely joined their peers at sleepaway camps, in recitals and on tours. All singers are required to participate in a number of performances throughout the year. All performing department choirs perform in the Candlelight Concert in December, the Winter Concert and/or New Music Concert in mid-spring, the Spring Sing! Concert in late Spring, and the Bon Voyage Concert in June when the touring vocal groups have their final concert before leaving for international choral competitions. Singers are also likely to participate in supplementary opportunities, like Jazz and Beyond, and the Ancora Recital. In the past, some students have opted to work with a current composer on a new work. There is a big emphasis on touring in this department. International choral competition has been a centerpiece of the choir’s program since 1984. Since its founding, Piedmont Children’s Choir has performed in 26 countries and 13 states in the U.S. It has been an invited choir in 19 choral competitions in Europe, Asia, and North America, and has a display case filled with gold and silver medals from the most prestigious choral competitions in the world. The final part of the series will explore international touring and competition. SF Ballet’s Jahna Frantziskonis is featured in Sequentia. By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet presents Sequentia, a choreographic chain letter to keep dancers and patrons connected during the global pandemic. Ten San Francisco Ballet dancers are connected through their movement in this choreographic chain letter. The film originated with a dancer who improvised a six-second solo to the music, and this choreography was passed along to the next dancer who picked up where the previous one left off. From the San Francisco Ballet, to New York City Ballet, to American Ballet Theatre, the “digital letter” started at the beginning of shelter-in-place restrictions and continues more than six months later through October in Seattle. In the video, patrons can view Pacific Northwest Ballet’s take on Seattle’s cityscape, working around and in-between the wildfires that have plagued the West Coast this year. San Francisco Ballet dancers who are featured include Tiit Helimets, Misa Kuranaga, Cavan Conley, Jahna Frantziskonis, Daniel Deivison-Oliveira, Myles Thatcher, Yuan Yuan Tan, Diego Cruz, Dores André, and Joshua Jack Price. The featured video for San Francisco is produced by Helimets and edited by Ben Estabrook. You can view the film on Youtube at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=zhFuJEaVBtQ. articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside has reopened to the public and will be hosting its seasonal “Orchard Days” every weekend in October. Every year, fruit trees at the Filoli gardens produce pears, apples, grapes, persimmons and more. You can visit the orchard on Saturdays and Sundays through Sunday, November 1. During Orchard Days visitors can gain special access to the Orchard where hundreds of heritage fruit trees grow. There are many other fun fall features, including fall sweet treats from The Town Kitchen in the Orchard including hand pies, donuts, pumpkin bread, and caramel apples. Visitors can take fall-inspired photo vignettes, created by the Filoli horticulture department, and kids will enjoy exploring the mini-hay maze. Local Bay Area artists will be selling their unique work. This weekend, October 17-18, will feature artwork from Carry On Designs, Soni Bergman Designs, Black Sheep Handweavers Guild, Earth Sisters Bags, and The entrance to Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside. Luca Angeli. For admission, purchase online tickets at: https://filoli.org/event/ orchard-days/. Orchard Days are included with general admission or member reservations. The gardens and the estate trail, a 1-mile loop through the property’s nature preserve, has been open since May. “We have a desire to be a place of respite and beauty and relaxation for our community in a time that we feel everyone really needs it,” said Susan O’Sullivan, Filoli’s chief external relations officer. O’Sullivan emphasized the importance of all visitors getting their tickets in advance, or members making reservations, ensures a contactless experience. Filoli can accept 800 visitors per day. Visitors must wear face coverings, practice social distancing, and wash and sanitize hands frequently. Admission is free to members and $20 for adults; $15 for seniors (65+); $15 for students, teachers and military; $10 for children (5-17 years old); and free for children under 5 years old. For more information, call 650-364-8300 or visit filoli.org.

articles.text: Writer and artist Chanel Miller will make her first museum debut, hosted by the San Francisco Asian Art Museum. Her exhibit, I was, I am, I will be, can be seen from the Hyde Street exterior of the museum. Miller was first known publicly as Emily Doe, the victim of sexual assault by Brock Allen Turner at Stanford University in 2015. The victim impact statement she wrote and read at her assailant’s sentencing hearing the following year went viral. It was read 11 million times within four days. The case gained international recognition because Turner, a 19-year old student athlete who raped Miller while she was unconscious, received only three months in jail. The case influenced the California legislature to require prison terms for rapists whose victims were unconscious. Judge Persky, who handed down the light sentence, was recalled from office by county voters in 2018. Miller’s memoir detailing the tragic event caught the attention of the Asian Art Museum’s head of Contemporary Art, Abby Chen. “Not only is she an amazing writer, she’s also this visual artist. But of course, she’s incredibly young,” Chen said. Chen and the museum staff began the process of collaborating with Miller. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum but never dreamed that one day she would be featured. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said, pointing to her art. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to shelterin-place orders, Miller’s exhibit was visible without even setting foot into the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. “The whole journey of healing is never linear,” Miller said, adding that she hopes the piece will be seen as universal and not confined to her particular experience. articles.text: Eugene Rodriguez (left), Fabiola Trujillo, Lucina Rodriguez, and Emiliano Rodreiguez of Los Cenzontles San Francisco Symphony continues its digital programming curated and hosted by Oakland Symphony conductor Michael Morgan in collaboration with San Francisco Symphony musicians and guest artists from the Bay Area. The Currents video series and companion podcast series is released every two weeks, and explores the intersection of classical music with four musical cultures, illuminating the connections and ways that cultures influence each other and evolve together. The last in the series of four, is Viva Mexico!, exploring Mexico’s multi-generational musical culture, and feature the music group Los Cenzontles (guitar, vocals, percussion). Maestro Morgan will introduce Eugene Rodriquez from Los Cenzontles, Bay Area musician and teacher Martha Rodriguez-Salazar, and San Francisco Symphony cellist Jill Rachuy Brindel, who describe how Mexican culture connects and transforms traditions while building community. “I am thrilled to be helping the San Francisco Symphony share all the wonderful things they do with a wider and more diverse audience. Within the symphony we have musicians with almost every musical interest. We just want to share our broad interests with our audience, old and new,” Morgan said. The episode will be released in conjunction with a podcast series, which aims to further elaborate on and personalize the conversations and themes introduced to its accompanying video episodes. Released the week following each video episode, the audio episodes provide additional opportunities to tie in current events, personal stories and perspectives. The Currents series includes performances and candid, personal reflections by members of the San Francisco Symphony. The complimentary podcast is hosted and curated by conductor Daniel Bartholomew-Poyser, who will explain the interactive activities at the end of each video. “We don’t want you just to listen. We want you to engage and respond to what you’re hearing in our Currents series,” he said. To view the performance, see: sfsymphony.org/currents. Free Delivery to Piedmont

articles.text: The first time I became fully aware of Ruth Bader Ginsberg was when I saw the Betsy West/ Julie Cohen documentary, RBG. It was revelatory. Here was a woman, an octogenarian, a justice of the Supreme Court, a progressive icon who has been for all of her professional life a frontline champion of women’s rights. Popularly known as the “Notorious RBG,” in recent years she had become diminutive, even fragile in appearance. She was often seen on an interview stage wearing her signature gloves, her mind resolutely incisive and keen, a figure embraced by the public’s imagination during a time fraught with divisive politics. In recent years she had health scares; cancerous nodules were excised from her lung. For the first time she was absent from the high court while following arguments at home. It is no exaggeration to say that her health challenges sent a shudder through the center-left political milieu; clearly her voice would be dearly missed. Made in 2018 the feature film On the Basis of Sex is a broad biopic that opens with RBG, played by Felicity Jones, as one of nine women in a class of 500 admitted to Harvard Law School. The year was 1954. At a dinner party the women are asked to explain to all gathered why they have chosen to “occupy a place at Harvard that could have gone to a man.” This question is proffered by Harvard’s Law School Dean (Sam Waterston) and proves to be startlingly tone deaf, though in keeping with the attitudes of the time. Still, Ruth perseveres. She is married to Marty Ginsberg (Armie Hammer) and the mother of a babe in arms. When Marty, a class ahead of Ruth at Harvard, is stricken with a serious illness, it is Ruth who attends his classes and her own, while keeping the home afloat. The film skips five years ahead to 1959. Now graduated, she is frustrated when work is all but impossible to find for a woman. It’s a male dominion. She ends up teaching law instead of practicing law, which was her closely held intention. In 1972 Ruth takes on what will eventually become a landmark legal case regarding sex discrimination. Ironically, the plaintiff is a man. As it turns out, Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsberg who passed away on September 18, 2020 is the subject of the film On the Basis of Sex. Ruth prevails and the outcome impacts sex discrimination law nationwide and launches her in a direction that neither she nor Marty could have anticipated. On the Basis of Sex is a nicely done tribute film, extolling the career of a woman of extraordinary talent and resilience. It is also a window into her life outside of the classroom and courtroom, unabashedly showing that RBG was fortunate to have had a caring, confident and generous man standing by her side. articles.text: Rose Byrne and Hugh Dancy in Adam. Moview review by Chris Honoré Call it a staple of Hollywood screenwriting: girl meets damaged boy. She is moved to reach out and care for him, perhaps rescue him in some fashion. Ditto for boy meets damaged girl. Incrementally and inextricably, both scenarios become matters of the heart and love is soon entangled with the impulse to help. As stories go, it’s instantly familiar but also ripe with new and interesting permutations. Adam, written and directed by Max Mayer in 2009 and nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival, is such a narrative. Beth (Rose Byrne), twenty-something, an aspiring writer of children’s books, having just escaped a disastrous love affair, moves into an Upper West Side brownstone. Living in the building is Adam (Hugh Dancy), an electrical engineer who designs toys and is also consumed with origins of the universe. When they first meet, in the laundry room, it is inescapable that Adam’s affect and responses are different. He doesn’t respond to the normal cues of conversation. Beth is intrigued for Adam is also bright and direct and sincere. What she soon learns is that his quirkiness is caused by Asperger’s Syndrome, a form of high functioning autism. Though she comes to understand how Adam’s Asperger’s presents itself, she also recognizes a lovely human being. In slow motion she falls in love with him and he with her. Beth also comes to understand that an aspect of the syndrome (at least in Adam’s case) is an inability to feel empathy, or make straightforward contact, such as looking her in the eyes. Adam hears what others say, but he is unable to feel the subtext behind the words or detect humor or irony. What is said, he takes at face value, even if a sentence ends with a question mark. Still, Beth moves forward, slowly involving Adam in her life, introducing him to her parents and to her friends. It’s not easy for her or for Adam. Adam is a small, sweet movie, wonderfully acted, and, to Mayer’s credit, explores both characters. Clearly, it was tempting to make this Adam’s story, but Mayer resisted. Hence, Beth’s ambivalence and personal qualities are nicely balanced with Adam’s struggles. As well, there’s a tangential story concerning Beth’s affluent parents (Amy Irving and Peter Gallagher): her father is on trial for embezzlement, the family uncertain if he will go to prison. Adam is a small nugget. Mayer has created a touching film that’s worth seeing. Adam. Starring Hugh Dancy, Rose Byrne, Frankie Felson, Peter Gallagher and Amy Irving. Directed by Max Mayer. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Adam a small gem from director Max Mayer

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Tale of Princess Kaguya. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Tale of Princess Kaguya is based on a 10th century Japanese folk tale called The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter. The film was written, directed and animated by the co-founder of Ghibli Studios, Isao Takahata. Though less known worldwide to his colleague Hayao Miyazaki, he is an equally gifted storyteller and animator, his talents made manifest with this Oscar nominated film. Princess Kaguya is, however, a departure from the vibrant hand-drawn animé that made the Studio Ghibli films coveted not only in Japan, but globally. The images of Princess Kaguya are soft, using a pale palate that is absent the full-frame insistence of primary colors. Instead, the animation is a blend of pencil, ink, and watercolor washes with restrained splashes of color. As well, its narrative tone is calm, subtle, telling the wonderfully imagined story of a middle-aged bamboo cutter (James Caan) who comes upon a strange stalk and finds enveloped inside a fully formed, elegantly dressed little girl (Chloe Grace Moretz), no bigger than a small sparrow. In amazement, he stands holding this small mystery-miracle cupped in his hands. He brings the tiny child home to his wife (Mary Steenburgen). Childless, they are overjoyed and embrace the foundling. What they soon find miraculous is that within weeks the tiny girl, who they regard as a heaven-sent blessing, grows into a beautiful young woman who finds joy in the natural beauty that surrounds her bucolic home. She plays with the neighboring children (a bit feral) and is drawn to a handsome farm boy (Darren Criss). Her parents, however, become convinced that this special daughter they call Princess is of noble blood and so take her to live in a mansion just outside the city, hoping a high society suitor will appear. And indeed, she is soon courted by five handsome Princes, who, as it turns out, cause her continued displeasure. She tells her parents that it is her wish to not marry. It soon is evident that the life she desires is in the countryside. Before long we see Princess Kayguya escape, running through the forest – a montage of rushing streams, enveloping flora and fauns – gripped by an anguished need to return to the life she had before and that special farm boy who only showed her kindness. The Tale of Princess Kaguya is whimsical, magical, while possessing a thread of melancholy throughout. Its story is one that is slow to emerge and may test the patience of a young American audience. But typical of the Studio Ghibli brand, it is lovely to behold. The Tale of Princess Kaguya (2014). Directed by Isao Takahata. Animé from Studio Ghibli. Voices of Chloe Grace Moretz, James Caan, Mary Steenburgen and Darren Criss. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s UP. Film Review by Chris Honoré Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E – Up delights and entertains audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail breathtaking. It’s the story a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, squarefaced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer, Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed: years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. The only thing missing in his life is that one magnificent adventure he has dreamed of for years. Having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning he and the house imply float away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well-equipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of liftoff. And so the journey begins, with a most unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. Pete Docter and his team at Pixar used unbridled imagination and an enchanting story that captivates and entertains. Made in 2009, it won an Oscar as Best Animated Feature. The film even manages to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell. Carl’s uses that poignant aphorism that life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). UP. Animated with the voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Written and Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Petersen. Pixar films. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: UP – the finest from Pixar

articles.text: One Fair Wage founder Saru Jayaraman, will speak and answer questions with Waging Change filmmaker Abby Ginzberg on Zoom October 14. Waging Change, a film by Abby Ginzberg, is a powerful, uplifting documentary about the long-shot campaign of Saru Jayaraman and her restaurant worker colleagues to oppose the powerful National Restaurant Association and its lobbyists in order to achieve a livable income for their work and to end the unfair tip-based system of payment. The Federal minimum wage for tipped workers is $2.13 an hour. For our screening of Waging Change, we’re trying a new format: Stream the film between October 9-18 at your convenience. Join the filmmaker and One Fair Wage founder in an exclusive Q & A on Zoom on October 14. It is free. To register for the film and discussion, click on www.diversityfilmseries.org.

articles.text: Music has had more than its share of comedians. Some, like Victor Borge, were just plain funny. Mozart’s humor was scatological. French composer Erik Satie was slyly societal. Richard Wagner was completely humorous. At the opposite end of the spectrum, was American composer Benjamin Franklin. Yes, you read that correctly… American composer Benjamin Franklin. While he was on diplomatic service in Paris, Franklin embedded himself into every manner of Parisian society. He was popular with the ladies even when he couldn’t even speak proper French. His scientific mind encouraged him to go to the violin shops and see the greatest bow maker of the time. This resulted in Franklin‘s invention of a most controversial musical instrument. The glass armonica became immensely popular for a while. It disappeared almost as fast as it appeared when it acquired the reputation that playing it could cause insanity. I know…it sounds crazy. Undeterred, Franklin investigated other areas. Chamber music was very popular among amateur musicians. Seeing a ready market, Franklin decided to become a composer. Readers should be aware that the string quartet medium is probably the most difficult medium in all of composition. But Ben was undeterred. He set about writing a string quartet. After all, he knew most of the great composers of the time. The first thing that he did was to invent a special tuning system for the four instruments. Once he did that, he knew success was his. Virtually anyone could play the Benjamin Franklin String Quartet. All the players needed to do was to tune their instruments the Franklin way. That was all. You see, with the Franklin system, you didn’t even need to put your fingers on the instruments. Calabrian-inspired fish I haven’t given a recipe lately, so here is one of my favorites. It’s easy to make and can be ready to serve in less than 10 minutes. Ingredients Opah (moonfish), tuna or trout Salt, Italian seasonings, red pepper flakes Avocado, marinated artichoke hearts, either roasted red peppers or dried tomatoes Starch - potatoes, polenta or bread Season the fish liberally with some salt, and Italian seasoning fortified with red pepper flakes. The fish should have some bite. Sauté the fish gently in butter. Top the fish with some slices of avocado. Serve on the same plate with marinated artichoke hearts, roasted red pepper or dried tomatoes, and potatoes, polenta or bread. Total cooking time from preparation to table is about eight minutes. Beverage: a light beer or an effervescent red wine complements the spice of the fish. For those who avoid alcohol, try some peach iced tea. Dessert is equally easy: iced coffee and vanilla ice cream. Piedmont Center for the Arts looks into the future While the Piedmont Center for the Arts has been treading water during the COVID crisis, I have good news. Piedmont’s cultural gem is making plans for an exciting future. Its history has been one of tremendous artistic diversity. It has welcomed art shows and art lectures. History has become enlivened by those who actually lived it. And music has set the pace. Some of the most important European concert artists are ready to set concert dates in the city’s lovely performing venue. They will be here at the first opportunity. I feel like I am back on the track team. The runners are at their mark… anticipating... Calabrian fish: Bright colors and lively flavors make Calabrian fish a winner. It’s very easy to make and takes obly about eight minutes.
articles.title: The last laugh

articles.text: The Oakland Tribune printed this sketch in 1967 with an article on the historic hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park. ating Coaches Field. Throughout the years, parts of Blair Park have been sold. Mountain View Cemetery purchased the land between the middle lake and the homes on Moraga. Blair’s stone dam is still visible between the lower and middle lakes in the cemetery. In the 1920s the City of Piedmont bought the eastern portion of the park for its Corporation Yard. (A side note: During World War II Piedmont sold rock from the quarry in its Corporation Yard to Bethlehem Steel, enlarging the yard and nursery to almost its present size.) You may wonder, as I did, how all the Blair Park attractions could fit in the narrow strip of land between Moraga Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery. For one thing, the lots along Moraga Avenue are very deep, up to 300 feet deep. They slope steeply from the street and are relatively level out to the cemetery land. They form a large, relatively flat area for the Bandstand, Venetian Canal, Japanese Tea House and all of Blair Park’s amusements. Fragments of the paved paths still exist in some of the backyards on Blair Park closed in 1905. This photo shows the bandstand (left) and the 28-foot bronze fountain (right). The
articles.title: History of Piedmont

articles.text: To attract more riders on their cable car line to Piedmont, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company built a Bandstand for concerts, a Tea House, Maze, Venetian Canal and small amusements for children. As the Cable Company failed to make a profit and was going into receivership in 1893, they added balloon ascensions to attract more riders on their cable cars. Hot Air Balloon Ascensions There was always an element of excitement and danger with the hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park, and they drew many visitors. By 1896, there were balloon ascensions every Sunday and on the 4th of July. Balloonists were considered daredevils, and for 25 cents visitors could ride up with the balloonist. Most of the balloon ascensions at Blair Park were aerial gymnasts, “dressed in spangles and tights” and doing “hair raising” stunts on a trapeze suspended from a captive balloon. It was exciting to watch the balloon fill with hot air. Young boys were allowed to hold the anchor lines as the balloon filled. As the aerialist climbed into the balloon basket, the balloon handler ordered the boys to “Let Go!” Visitors watched in awe as the balloon rose over their heads. One particularly daring aerialist hung upside down from the trapeze bar as it ascended. After several acrobatic stunts on the bar, the aerialist finished with a parachute drop from a height of 1000 feet. The balloon was on a long tether, and the balloon manager pulled it back to earth at the end of the show. One Sunday a balloon ascension ended fatally. Little Bertram Hills was visiting Blair Park with his aunt in July 1897. He had been holding onto one of the sand bag anchor lines when the balloon began to rise. He failed to let go of the line and rose with the balloon - 300, 600, 900 feet up in the air. The tether failed. It was a terrible sight to see little Bertram dangling from the line and holding on for his life while balloonist Charles Conlon attempted to return the balloon to earth. Unfortunately, Bertram’s strength gave out before the balloon could descend, and he fell to his death. His body was found a half mile away on farmland in the Montclair hills. The public lost its taste for balloon ascensions in Blair Park after little Bertram’s death, and the ascensions in Blair Park ended shortly thereafter. What Became of Blair Park? As fine as the intentions of the park operators were, Blair Park seems to have encountered problems almost immediately. In 1892, the Oakland Tribune reported that “gamblers had things their own way up at Blair Park” and described prospering shell games. Citizens were also concerned that the planned casino would attract “scum and hoodlum.” In 1896 the Board of Directors of Mountain View Cemetery complained that “the balloon ascensions on Sundays from Blair Park is [sic] becoming a great nuisance, attracting a great crowd of the hoodlum element and causing a disturbance in the Cemetery Grounds.” They called on the Sheriff to protect the cemetery grounds and arrest trespassers. The fate of Blair Park was tied to the fiscal success of the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company. In 1892, electric trolleys were replacing the cable cars and competing for ridership. Due to the great expense of building the cable line, the Piedmont Cable Company went into receivership in 1893, and the assets were sold at auction in 1895. Walter Blair’s heirs continued to own the park land, but it was heavily mortgaged. In 1897 all of Blair’s 235 acres, including Blair Park, were for sale. Mountain View Cemetery bought 1-1/2 acres on the northern edge of the park. In 1901, the Cable Company announced that it was abandoning the park and that it would not reopen that spring. the Realty Syndicate owned the park land. The park was set for development. Throughout these last years, Blair Park continued to operate. Park, because the Blair family no longer owned the land. Charles Vosmer, one of the park’s balloonists, managed the park up to 1905 when its listing disappeared from city directories. The Blair Park land was still vacant in 1913 when the City of Piedmont, then six years old, voted to acquire land for parks. Voters approved the purchase of Dracena and Linda Parks, but not Blair Park. In 1917, new homes began to appear on the Blair Park site. Builder Guy Taylor built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue, both shingled and stucco styles. He returned in 1922 to build at least 6 more bungalows. As you drive along Moraga Avenue today, you can see the similarities that many of these homes share. Blair Park Today The early sketches show Blair Park in a grove of eucalyptus trees. Walter Blair thinned some of these trees to make paths and picnic areas. The Cable Company thinned more trees to make room for their attractions. Finally, more eucalyptus were thinned when the houses were built along Moraga Avenue. Today, the former grove of eucalyptus is just a narrow row of trees along the cemetery border. There were cascading waterfalls in Blair Park in the 1880s. The stream that ran down Moraga Canyon is now in a conduit under Moraga Avenue. The canyon was filled for decades ultimately creballoon shaped sign is a reminder of the ascensions in the 1890s.
articles.title: The end of Blair Park

Finally, more eucalyptus were thinned when the houses were built along Moraga Avenue. Today, the former grove of eucalyptus is just a narrow row of trees along the cemetery border. There were cascading waterfalls in Blair Park in the 1880s. The stream that ran down Moraga Canyon is now in a conduit under Moraga Avenue. The canyon was filled for decades ultimately creThe Oakland Tribune printed this sketch in 1967 with an article on the historic hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park. ating Coaches Field. Throughout the years, parts of Blair Park have been sold. Mountain View Cemetery purchased the land between the middle lake and the homes on Moraga. Blair’s stone dam is still visible between the lower and middle lakes in the cemetery. In the 1920s the City of Piedmont bought the eastern portion of the park for its Corporation Yard. (A side note: During World War II Piedmont sold rock from the quarry in its Corporation Yard to Bethlehem Steel, enlarging the yard and nursery to almost its present size.) You may wonder, as I did, how all the Blair Park attractions could fit in the narrow strip of land between Moraga Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery. For one thing, the lots along Moraga Avenue are very deep, up to 300 feet deep. They slope steeply from the street and are relatively level out to the cemetery land. They form a large, relatively flat area for the Bandstand, Venetian Canal, Japanese Tea House and all of Blair Park’s amusements. Fragments of the paved paths still exist in some of the backyards on Moraga. The name “Blair Park” continues to live on current maps of Piedmont. Today the City calls the land opposite Maxwelton Road, “Blair Park.” This is a portion of Walter Blair’s greater 235 acres, but the Blair Park of history was at the end of Highland Avenue. Continuing the Tradition Blair Park began as an amusement park where visitors came to enjoy being outdoors. It is fitting that today the tradition has come full circle with Coaches Play Field and the William F Kennelly Skate Park. If you enjoy reading these biweekly columns on the history of Piedmont, please consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving our annual newsletter. More information on Piedmont’s history and membership is on our website, Piedmonthistorical.org or contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@pacbell.net. The balloon shaped sign is a reminder of the ascensions in the 1890s.

articles.text: Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn is currently at the helm of the Piedmont Community Church following the retirement of Rev. Dr. Bill McNabb on September 20. Ashburn, the Associate Pastor, will serve as Acting Head of Staff until January 1, when the new Transitional Minister, Rev. Dr. Steve Schibsted, begins. Ashburn, who lives in Piedmont with wife Margaret and two children, has been with the church since 2003, Ashburn graduated from San Francisco Theological Seminary in 1997 and later earned a Doctorate of Ministry degree there in 2015. He now preaches on Sundays, teaches a Wednesday morning Bible Study by Zoom and leads a Friday morning Prayer Service. If filling in for McNabb after a celebrated 19-year career isn’t hard enough, Ashburn must do so via recorded video, audio and Zoom meetings. His first sermon was a week ago on October 4. Hampered by the invisible coronavirus, Ashburn has had to rely on the internet and Wi-Fi, to reach the church’s congregation of approximately 1000 people. “It is harder to preach in front of a camera than it is to preach in front of people,” Ashburn acknowledged. “I get my energy to preach from the people there in person. So now I have to generate it all for the camera. I have gotten better at it, and it is really good to be able to reach more people than just those in church on Sunday morning.” he said. Ashburn counts the work of the church’s Communications Director, Michael Barber, as a blessing. Barber puts together the digital audio and visual content on the PCC website. PCC’s sermons are recorded through Soundcloud at www.piedmontchurch.org/worship-podcasts/. The church is cautiously optimistic that in-person services may return in November. Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn is the Acting Head of Staff until Transitional Minister Steve Schibsted starts on January 1. “We have a task force that is working very actively on [reopening]. We have done as much preparation as we can. I think we can be ready when the time comes. Our top priority is making sure people are healthy and safe,” Ashburn confirmed. Ashburn expressed deep veneration for the work of McNabb. “[Bill] has gone off to this new horizon of retirement and left behind a good, solid basis on which we can do ministry. We will miss his gifts in preaching and commitment to the church’s involvement in its local outreach and mission.” Ashburn has known Schibsted for a few years and feels confident the church will be in good hands under his direction starting next year. “Steve has a good sense of humor and is very centered in his faith. I think he will make a really great difference at PCC. He is a really good guy,” Ashburn added. For now the church is focused on continuing its outreach to a community facing today’s unique coronavirus challenges. “I’m really optimistic. I think it is a really good time to try a bunch of new things to make the changes we need to make, while keeping the things we need to keep with integrity and faithfulness.” Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: At an August 5 meeting the Piedmont Park Commission considered three types of trees as the official street tree for residents on Olive Avenue. After a lively discussion a winner was declared: the Purple-Leaf Plum. It beat out the others – Chinese Pistache, and the White Flowering Crepe Myrtle, currently on view in front of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Commissioners noted that Purple-Leaf Plums already on Olive Avenue were some of the best examples of the species in Piedmont. There are currently eight existing Purple-Leaf Plum trees on the same block. Purple-Leaf Plum trees, also called cherry plum trees or flowering plum trees, are small deciduous trees known for their dark red to purple foliage. The species is noted to be fast-growing, with low maintenance and little pruning. The commission was asked to choose a designated street tree at an October 7 meeting, and decide if the neighborhood would benefit from the uniform look of one species. Chair Patty Dunlap said that she would like the commission to explore the idea of a single species tree designation for the entire street. “The Plums are doing really well [in this location], and the neighbors had asked about a faster-growing tree. The plums fit that [request] to a pretty good extent,” she said. Commissioner Betsy Goodman wondered if there was a lighter colored Purple-Leaf Plum option. Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent responded that another type was lighter – bronze in color – but was rejected as an option. “I don’t think we can suggest a different variety of the Purple-Leaf,” Kent said. Dunlap supported the choice of Purple-Leaf Plums. “What I love is the elegance it adds, the rich color, and the continuity would really elevate that street and make it look pretty majestic,” she said. “It was a great process. We had a chance to go out into the community and make this selection. The city did their due diligence and their homework,” she added. The new trees could be planted before the end of the year. “Our Public Works team will take the lead on that. I think we’ll have them planted in about a month or so,” Kent said. Purple-Leaf Plum tree

articles.text: An orphaned mountain lion cub was rescued by Cal Fire firefighters on September 27 in the destructive Zogg Fire in southwestern Shasta County. The male cub was brought to Oakland Zoo to begin recovery and rehabilitation. Upon discovering the lone cub, Cal Fire notified the Shasta County Sherriff’s Department, who asked for guidance from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife [CDFW]. CDFW Veterinarians contacted Oakland Zoo for help in treating the young mountain lion. The young cub has been nicknamed “Captain Cal” as an homage to the fictitious Cal Fire mascot. The two share a strikingly similar story: mascot Cal also survived a wildfire and found a home with the firefighters who led the community to safety. Captain Cal is only four to six months old, “a small victim of climate change,” Veterinary Hospital Director Dr. Alex Herman said. He arrived at the Zoo at about 7 p.m. on September 30, driven from Redding by Pete Figura, Supervising Wildlife Biologist for the CDFW. Removal of the dead skin allows for the antibiotics to work on infected areas, Herman explained. She noted that the cub is hyper, feisty, and “always ready for food.” Captain Cal is fed a mix of milk and meat. On Monday, Dr. Herman reported that Captain Cal was eating well and does not need an anesthetic procedure or bandage change for the first time since arriving at the Zoo. He is continuing to gain weight. “We’re grateful to be part of this amazing little cub’s rescue and rehabilitation. In the past two years, this marks our 13th mountain lion cub rescue for Oakland Zoo in partnership with CDFW,” Dr. Herman said. Yesterday, Tuesday, Captain Cal was introduced to two female cubs, also victims of the destructive wildfire season. The females are in better condition than Captain Cal, but have also been orphaned due to the Zogg Fire. Captain Cal will be living at Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital temporarily as he continues his rehabilitation. Without a mother, he cannot return to the wild at this age, even once healthy. Instead, he will move to a permanent home at another facility. “We are so grateful for the Oakland Zoo’s expertise, worldclass facilities and willingness to step up – on extremely short notice – to help wildlife in need,” said Dr. Deana Clifford, CDFW’s senior wildlife veterinarian. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: William V Hassenzahl Jr, the father of three children, passed away on October 10, 2019. He was 53. He was born on January 21, 1964 in Urbana, Illinois, the son of Jeanne and Bill Hassenzahl Sr. He attended Piedmont schools and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1983. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had another engaging book discussion on Zoom is October 5th. A strong turnout of 16 members of the group were on the call to discuss their October read, The Dutch House by Ann Patchett. The group was pleased to welcome Maya Rath, a first-time participant. City Councilmember Jen Cavenaugh was on the call, too. Regular members participating included Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Jeri Lockhart, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Margie Blodgett, Bella Almanzan, Karin Featherston, Albert Chen, Margie Blodgett, Sally Arney, Sweeling Chen, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The Dutch House is the eighth novel by Patchett, who has also written three non-fiction books. The readers agreed that she is a gifted writer. It was also noted that the book has been described as a modern fairy tale with elements of Cinderella, The Little Princess, and Hansel and Gretel. The book describes the life story two siblings, Maeve and Danny Conroy, and their family in “The Dutch House,” a 1922 mansion outside Philadelphia. Their father, Cyril, a successful real estate businessman, bought it at a 1946 estate sale as a surprise for his wife, Elna. The house was built by a wealthy Dutch couple and thus was given its name. However, Elna hates the house, both aesthetically and ethically. It is just too wasteful for her when the world has so many other needs. She flees the house and her family when the children are ten and three, ostensibly to go to India to devote herself to serving the poor. Mauve and Danny bond tightly after their mother leaves, but they and the family suffer; as if “they had all become characters in the worst part of a fairy tale,” as Patchett writes. Andrea, a pretty young widow 18 years younger than Cyril, falls in love with his house and manages to get Cyril to marry her. She and her two small daughters move into the house and the troubles for Maeve and Danny begin. After Cyril dies, their wicked stepmother forces Mauve and Danny out of the house in classic fairy tale fashion. The rest of the novel is their complicated life story, their relationship with the house, and their long journey back to it. The Dutch House was well received by most of the readers, but some had issues with the book, and thus made it an excellent book group selection. Some readers thoroughly enjoyed the novel. For them it was beautiful, charming, and entertaining. Mauve and Danny’s strong, supportive, sibling relationship was appreciated. Patchett’s character development of them and others made the story personal and enjoyable for the readers. The Dutch House is written in the first person from Danny’s adult point of view. Some readers felt Danny and his father were clueless about what the family was experiencing. Some members listened to an audio version of the book read by Tom Hanks, and loved his presentation and the emotions he conveyed in his reading. Some readers were not as satisfied with the book, saying that the story fell apart in Part III and at the book’s ending. They found many elements of the story unbelievable. Everyone seemed to agree that The Dutch House is a well-written fairy tale. The group previously selected Caste by Isabel Wilkerson for their November read and Jane Austen’s classic, Pride and Prejudice, for December. Some readers said they want to read Longbourn by Jo Baker, a story from the Pride and Prejudice servants’ perspectives. The First Monday Reading Group next meets on November 2, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration with the Recreation Department is required. For more information, contact John Wilk at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Thigpen can allow school board to finally walk the walk Editor: Veronica…Finally! When I first read Veronica Anderson Thigpen’s bio several months ago, I was blown away with excitement. I don’t remember knowing any past candidate with her qualifications in education, creating policy, and helping school districts achieve their goals. Plus, she so instantly spoke to the issues we so urgently need to address that I felt a newfound sense of hope for our city and our children at this critical time in our history. In Veronica’s outreach, she even wanted to know how we citizens felt about issues in Piedmont Unified School District – how refreshing. Upon meeting her, I was further impressed by her natural sense of inclusivity as she listened closely to our concerns and spoke to our group. Finally, a wise, calm, super-qualified person of color can hold a political office on our school board. This is her time, I believe. Having had the privilege of teaching art at Wildwood Elementary for 20 years has allowed me to see that reaching students is way more than getting the lesson done; it’s more than test standards and test scores. Students need a level playing field, safety, empowerment, and a voice in order to establish the confidence to grow, be curious, and to love learning. Let’s not let a gem like Veronica Anderson Thigpen slip by. With Veronica, we can and not just talk the talk of equity in our schools. –Suzie Skugstad
