articles.text: Editor: It’s time to vote for School Board seats and I recommend Hilary Cooper. I believe she has all the essential attributes of a successful, effective member of the board. She brings perspective, energy and commitment to our town and our schools. Over the last decade, she has: • Galvanized neighbors and community members to support our schools financially by spearheading two PEF Giving Campaigns • Led the Parent Boards of the Middle and High School • Partnered with administration and staff during leadership transitions, learning first-hand the players and the roles. • Been a liaison with the Wellness Center on the social/ emotional needs of our students • Succeeded in passing Measure G&H to secure critical local funding for our schools Her commitment to our schools and our kids is supported by her long record of success. Whether it’s funding, staffing, curriculum, student needs, parent concerns or community buy-in, she has the experience and drive to keep our schools great. I hope you’ll join me in voting for her for Piedmont School Board. –Doug Ireland
articles.title: Voting for Hilary Cooper to keep schools great

articles.text: Editor: We are writing in enthusiastic support of Conna McCarthy for Piedmont City Council. Conna’s life has been steeped in public service in every aspect of her life and, for years, she has volunteered her talents to Piedmont’s education and civic communities. She is intelligent, capable, direct, and deeply principled. Conna knows Piedmont and our city has benefitted time and again from her expertise, interest, energy, and time. The breadth of her knowledge and experience, her on-going commitment, and her candid approach will continue to serve us. Please join us in voting for Conna for City Council. –Amal & Rick Smith

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Veronica Anderson Thigpen for election to the Piedmont School Board. Veronica will bring a dynamic new perspective to the board. Her professional, volunteer and life experiences make her an excellent candidate. Veronica moved to Piedmont from Chicago where she earned degrees in Economics and Journalism from Northwestern University. Veronica has authored award winning writings on educational policy, and currently advises school systems and educational nonprofits on building equitable and effective organizations. Upon arrival in Piedmont, Veronica eagerly joined our enthusiastic volunteer community and has made several important contributions. We are fortunate to have a candidate with such broad understanding of educational policy, and a willingness to share her talents and knowledge.
articles.title: Thigpen to bring new, dynamic perspective to School Board

articles.text: Editor: Conna’s commitment to our community is obvious - through her participation on school parent boards, chairing of fundraising activities, service as Recreation Commissioner and spearheading of city campaigns. Conna thrives on creative problem solving and seeks out diverse opinions in order to find solutions. Her community interests range from school sports and civic programs to city beatification and the arts. And, I must add, her love for the Piedmont community is clearly evident in her vast purple and white wardrobe! Most inspiring, however, is the way Conna has prioritized service to others and instilled this value in her family. Whether serving our country, our community or vulnerable segments of the population, Conna, Peter and their children have all made career and volunteer choices that contribute to the greater good.
articles.title: McCarthy’s commitment to service and community

articles.text: Editor: Conna McCarthy has real leadership qualities. I have watched Conna in action in many volunteer situations. She listens, she is curious, she asks questions, she seeks many opinions. She understands there is a process and is not afraid to speak up and advocate for what she feels is right. She really knows how to build bridges and seeks the higher ground. She is a problem-solver and is the right woman for the job and future of Piedmont. Vote for Conna McCarthy for City Council. –Valerie Corvin

Piedmont’s City Council would be fortunate to benefit from Conna’s proven skills and lifelong commitment to service and giving back to her community. –Molly Waste Ashford

articles.text: Do buildings or pools have ‘life spans’? We say No. Most of the homes in Piedmont are much older than the Community Pool complex. Our homes are not obsolete. With proper maintenance, repair and updating of systems, our homes and the pool do not have ‘life spans’. Yet, the City Council has concluded that the community pool ‘life span’ is over. Even though the City Council has a Study, completed in 2018,* that concluded that the pool could be repaired and rehabilitated for a cost in the low millions and that the pool would be out of service for only about 6 months. Measure UU will require a 3-4 year shutdown and a $19.5 million price tag. There are several examples of this community’s ability to raise those sums for a project fairly quickly. The 2018 study concluded that “the pool vessels appear to be structurally sound”. Why then should we demolish every structure on the Pool site and start afresh at a site which is far from ideal with respect to parking, traffic congestion and impact on the neighborhood? In our opinion, the case for pool repair and rehab has not been fully explored or explained to the voters by Council or the proponents of UU. That is the major flaw in the logic for putting forth this Measure at this time. We consider it to be misplaced priorities. Is Measure UU the first and highest priority for the City? We have previously and continue to say No. The safety of our community should always be the highest priority. The structural upgrade of our Essential Police, Fire and City Hall Buildings should be the City’s highest priority at this time! In our opinion, this issue should preempt any decision about the scope, nature and the location of a community pool. Choosing repair and rehab of the pool complex now would give the City Council and staff the time – a breather if you will – to properly and prudently complete the extensive due diligence (schematic plans, environmental and traffic studies and good quality estimates, etc.) required on all of the major projects on the City Facilities Needs Summary. At that point an orderly and logical Capital Construction Plan could be implemented. We encourage voters to do some research on these very important issues, and we strongly urge a No vote on UU to create a timeout. That alone would allow for a proper planning and budgeting process. Respectfully submitted, Alan Rudy AIA, and Donald Chandler AIA in efforts to identify and organize much of this work in the development of our strategic plan update currently underway. Public participation and feedback has been an essential part of our planning process. As the Piedmont Police Department moves forward in this work, we will continue to seek opportunities to communicate with and involve the public in these efforts. This strategic plan will ultimately aid in our continued efforts to provide professional police services to all who live, visit and work in our community to ensure we stay on the right side of history. articles.text: Editor: Years have passed since our kids grew up. The splashing and playing are warm memories. The swim lessons are thankfully long past. There were the July 4th games for which the kids couldn’t wait. Looking ahead, we might occasionally swim laps in a new pool, which will provide a healthy outlet, and it will be wonderful to see a beautiful new facility, but our family is not likely to be a regular user. Rebuilding the pool facility will be expensive. So why support it? When we moved to Piedmont in 1996, the pool was there for us, as part of the City’s broad array of recreational facilities, and we made good use of it. It’s time to pay it forward. Like all Piedmont residents, we are proud of our town, and we want it to flourish in the future. We will be proud to do our share for the new pool. I have been on the Recreation Commission for almost six years, and its Chair for over half that time. Through the Commission’s broad dealings with recreation in Piedmont, there is one constant – the need for more and improved facilities. It would be incredibly unfortunate to reduce the facilities we have now. Please join us in supporting Measure UU. –Steve and Karen Roland
articles.title: UU and Piedmont’s pool. Time to pay it forward

articles.text: Editor: We are writing in support of Measure UU which will replace our decaying Piedmont pool infrastructure with two new pools – a larger pool for lap swimming and competitive sports and a much-improved recreation pool for shallow water play, swim lessons, and other water fitness programs. Located in the center of town, the pool is a part of what makes Piedmont such a special place and keeps our property values strong. The new competitive sports pool will: • Allow the 1,000 students currently involved in Piedmont Scouting to complete their mandatory BSA swimming merit badges. Over the past 10 years, many hundreds of students have earned this badge at the Piedmont Pool. • Provide a place for advanced swim lessons and opportunities for our youth to learn valuable lifesaving and water safety skills. • Host the Piedmont High School swim and water polo teams – allowing these teams to practice and play close to home rather than commute to neighboring communities. • Be a venue for lifelong exercise and social interaction for lap and Masters swimmers. • • • The new recreational pool will: Include improved space for beginner swim lessons and safe water play. Provide a place where Piedmonters of all ages and swimming abilities can swim and socialize together on warm summer days. Allow senior citizens and lessabled residents to benefit from water exercise and strengthening classes; getting into the water will be aided by the new zero depth entry feature. We urge all our citizens to support this measure to upgrade this vital and nurturing community resource. Please vote Yes on UU. –Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke
articles.title: Plenty of reasons to Vote Yes on Measure UU

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont pool is an important community resource and serves many groups within our town, including Scouting. Scouting BSA runs many different programs for both boys and girls from the ages of 6 to 18. An important part of these is water safety. Scouts use the pool for swim safety testing prior to going to summer camps. They earn merit badges including the Swimming Merit Badge and the Lifesaving Merit Badge. And many take lifeguard training and CPR at the pool. Learning to swim, learning about water safety, and generally having fun are all essential parts of scouting and life. Let’s rebuild the pool into something we can all be proud of for many generations to come just as Piedmonters did 50 years ago for us. Vote yes on Measure UU. –Glyn Burge

articles.text: Editor: First, I would like to thank the Piedmont Post for providing a forum for a lively but respectful exchange of views on Measure UU. However, I would like to disagree with the statement made by the Editor in last week’s paper that “the residents have spoken”. There are roughly 8,500 registered voters in Piedmont, and they will speak on November 3rd. On November 4th, we will know what they said. That is how the democratic process works. Until that time, any attempts to speak for them are purely opinions and should be treated as such. –Bob Morrison

One of the great advantages of Piedmont was that our children were able walk to school, to their friends’ homes, to sports team practices and to the pool. There was no need to be constantly in the car – carpooling and driving children from place to place as we did in Houston. Over the years, my children enjoyed recreational swim at the Piedmont pool, and I started my days with a 6 a.m. lap swim. When our first grandchild, Luke, was born, his first exposure to swimming was a parent-child swim class with me at the Piedmont pool. Luke continued using the pool at Piedmont High School where he was a member of the PHS water polo and swim teams. For the past six years, our 13-year-old granddaughter has been a member of the Piedmont Swim Team. With no pool to use in Piedmont, she and the team practice at pools in Emeryville, Alameda and Montclair. I’m now carpooling again! I know the important role that a swimming pool plays in the community and I am passionate about having a pool available to Piedmont residents and students attending Piedmont schools. I grew up spending my summers at the local public pool and eventually, during college summers, was employed as head lifeguard and director of the learn-to-swim program at the local public pool. articles.text: 2. Candidates were asked whether the council should consider an increase to the current utility tax to create a climate fund. Herrick said she would support investigating a tax, but that she was reluctant to say she supported a tax increase because she was already in favor of Measure UU and Measure TT, which would raise taxes. She added that there are other ways Piedmonters can be more energy-conscience. Bostrom commented that the pool would be an enormous drain on the city energy-wise. Cavenaugh said that climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and environment. She said that we “would have the greatest impact if we reduce our consumption, switch to 100 percent renewable energy sources, and walk, bike, take public transportation or drive an electric car.” McCarthy supported a conversation about a utility tax, but said it is not the right time to propose. “Piedmonters already pay a premium. I think it’s $6 a month for East Bay Community Energy for 100 percent renewable energy on our electrical appliances. I don’t see the necessity right now,” she said. 3. Beninati asked the candidates how Piedmont can add more affordable housing. Herrick started by saying she was a very strong advocate for affordable housing and said that she recognized Piedmont’s builtout characteristic. “We are basically horizontally-challenged. We’ve maxed out on the lots. Is there a way that for us to go up? And can we go up in areas that are more commercially oriented, like on Grand Avenue or in the center of town? That would preserve the residential flavor of the rest of our city,” she said. Cavenuagh said that, even though Piedmont is a small city, more needs to be done to provide affordable housing. “We are embarking on a process to reevaluate our plans for providing housing of all types, specifically meet our regional housing number allocation that comes from the state. This process is going to look at lot size minimums, (Accessory Dwelling Unit) guidelines, multi-family housing zoning and many other aspects of our housing element to identify options for new housing,” she said. McCarthy provided SOME statistics on Piedmont housing goals. “For 2007 to 2014, our number was 40 units, for 2015 to 2022, our [state] allocation is 60 units with 49 units already completed by the end of 2019. Most of those new units are Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU). It’s predicted in the next period our ask to Piedmont could be 180-600 units. We’re not going to get there with ADUs. We have to be creative, we have to look at multi-dwelling structures, maybe in commercial areas where there’s space,” she said. Bostrom said that it would have to be delicately decided. “It will change the look of this city forever,” she said. SUDOKU SOLUTION

articles.text: Because of the current health pandemic, and to mitigate potential gatherings, only one polling precinct will be open in Piedmont this upcoming election. Customarily Piedmont has six voting locations during an election The Veterans’ Memorial Building will serve as the only voting location for in-person voting this election. Any resident of Alameda County can come to the Veterans Hall and cast a ballot, and any county resident, including Piedmonters, may drop off their absentee ballot with a precinct worker. The building will be open four consecutive days, from Saturday, October 31, through Tuesday, November 4. Hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. the first three days, and 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on the official Election Day, November 3. Voters may also put their absentee ballots (Vote By Mail ballots) into the secure ballot box located on Highland Way near the two US. Post Office mailboxes. The deadline for ballots to be turned in is November 3 at 8 p.m. A complete list of voting locations in Alameda County is available online at: https://www. acgov.org/rov_app/pollinglist. The Alameda County Registrar of Voters began mailing Sample Ballot and Voter Information Guides to registered voters on September 24. Absentee ballots were mailed to Piedmont voters on Wednesday, October 7, and Sample Ballots were received at residences in Piedmont this past Saturday, October 10. Candidates were asked whether the council should consider an increase to the current utility tax to create a climate fund. Herrick said she would support investigating a tax, but that she was reluctant to say she supported a tax increase because she was already in favor of Measure UU and Measure TT, which would raise taxes. She added that there are other ways Piedmonters can be more energy-conscience. Bostrom commented that the pool would be an enormous drain on the city energy-wise. Cavenaugh said that climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and environment. She said that we “would have the greatest impact if we reduce our consumption, switch to 100 percent renewable energy sources, and walk, bike, take public transportation or drive an electric car.” McCarthy supported a conversation about a utility tax, but said it is not the right time to propose. “Piedmonters already pay a premium. I think it’s $6 a month for East Bay Community Energy for 100 percent renewable energy on our electrical appliances. I don’t see the necessity right now,” she said. 3. Beninati asked the candidates how Piedmont can add more affordable housing. Herrick started by saying she was a very strong advocate for affordable housing and said that she recognized Piedmont’s builtout characteristic. “We are basically horizontally-challenged. We’ve maxed out on the lots. Is there a way that for us to go up? And can we go up in areas that are more commercially oriented, like on Grand Avenue or in the center of town? That would preserve the residential flavor of the rest of our city,” she said. Cavenuagh said that, even though Piedmont is a small city, more needs to be done to provide affordable housing. “We are embarking on a process to reevaluate our plans for providing housing of all types, specifically meet our regional housing number allocation that comes from the state. This process is going to look at lot size minimums, (Accessory Dwelling Unit) guidelines, multi-family housing zoning and many other aspects of our housing element to identify options for new housing,” she said. McCarthy provided SOME statistics on Piedmont housing goals. “For 2007 to 2014, our number was 40 units, for 2015 to 2022, our [state] allocation is 60 units with 49 units already completed by the end of 2019. Most of those new units are Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU). It’s predicted in the next period our ask to Piedmont could be 180-600 units. We’re not going to get there with ADUs. We have to be creative, we have to look at multi-dwelling structures, maybe in commercial areas where there’s space,” she said. Bostrom said that it would have to be delicately decided. “It will change the look of this city forever,” she said. She added that faculty would receive training as well, and that the district can create safe spaces that “would feel inclusive and welcoming for students of color and where they could meet up and feel a sense of community.” Cooper said that it is imperative students have role models that they can lean on. “I also think the mentor program that the Black Student Union and the Asian American Association started at Havens is a really wonderful example of reaching out to our students to make sure that they have role models that look like them and share similar culture that they can feel like their voices are heard and have somebody to lean on,” Cooper said. Kelley provided an anecdote. “I know what it’s like to feel marginalized in Piedmont schools. As a gay kid in the 1980s, I felt very alone, and I really wish I had a teacher or other adult to connect with and talk with about that,” he said. Candidates were then asked if they supported the vote to reopen schools in phase with special education students and K-2 students returning to in person first. Titan praised the board’s decision to reopen. “It’s not the same risk for everyone, as teachers have been saying in their negotiations with the school district. articles.text: Akebono Cherries along Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park T he Park Com mission revealed the 2020 Heritage Tree designations at their October 7 meeting. The Heritage Tree program was created in 2018 under the leadership of commissioner Jim Horner. In 2019, the commission selected five trees from more than a dozen submissions. This year, 11 nominations were received: 6 for single trees, and 5 for groups of trees, Horner explained. Submitted nominations were evaluated on their aesthetic, education, or historical metrics. Nominations must be trees situated on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees are then forwarded to the commission for review and selection. “It’s a wonderful tradition, and a positive connection that the city makes with the residents all over Piedmont every spring,” Commission Chair Patty Dunlap said. Traditionally, winning trees are recognized on Arbor Day. Because of the current health pandemic, this year’s announcements were made six months later via teleconference application Zoom. Five trees were chosen this year. Commissioner Eileen Ruby nominated a multi-trunk Japanese Maple, prominently positioned at the entrance to the teahouse garden in Piedmont Park. Resident Tami Becker nominated a Coast Live Oak in Dracena Park. “It is a handsome, featured tree, and its prominence will become more dramatic and important as years go by,” Horner commented. Commissioner Brian Mahany nominated the Southern Magnolia in the Huntleigh/Hampton Triangle. A circle of Coast Redwoods at the Jerome Triangle. Resident Jennifer Marinelly nominated a grove of Coast Redwoods at the Jerome Triangle. “They’ve been growing strong since they were planted by [former Public Works Supervisor] Dave Frankel in 1991,” Horner explained. Resident Nancy McHugh nominated the Akebono Cherry trees along Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park. “We are excited for when we can all be together and have an appropriate celebration. These are beautiful selections,” Dunlap commented. Signage for the newly designated trees is underway, said Nancy Kent. A multi-trunk Japanese Maple in Piedmont Park. Everyone’s favorite Southern Magnolia, which is located in the Huntleigh/Hampton Triangle.

articles.text: PG&E may shut off power for some areas near Piedmont today Hot, dry and gusty weather is forecasted for later this week, leading to concerns of increased wildfire risks throughout Northern California over the next few days. Yesterday, Tuesday, October 13, the National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning, meaning wildfire risk is high through Friday morning, October 16 for higher elevation areas in the East Bay Hills. The Weather Service pointed to gusty winds moving from offshore paired with an extremely dry air mass moving from the south. Fire Chief Bret Black said earlier this week that the Red Flag Warning was expected considering weather patterns. “We are expecting dangerously low humidity and some significant winds for the rest of the week,” Black told the Post. PG&E said this week that some Alameda County residents were among 50,000 Northern California customers notified this week about a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) starting today, Wednesday, October 14 due to wildfire risk. According to the power utility’s website as of press time, impacted areas include Oakland neighborhoods directly to the east of Piedmont, including Montclair. “These types of weather events can trigger a PSPS event; residents should stay informed by visiting PG&E’s website where they can update their emergency contact information for PG&E’s alerting system,” Black continued. He advised Piedmonters to check PG&E’s website, pge.com, for PSPS information. On Saturday, October 10, the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) put a “Spare the Air” alert into place for the following four days, but the alert was lifted on Monday, October 12. BAAQMD said that increased containment of the Glass Fire in the North Bay has resulted in less smoke in the overall region, although it did cause hazy skies in the Bay Area last weekend. The Glass Fire began early on September 27 and has burned over 67,000 acres in Napa and Sonoma counties. An estimated 1,555 structures have been destroyed. The Heritage Tree program was created in 2018 under the leadership of commissioner Jim Horner. In 2019, the commission selected five trees from more than a dozen submissions. This year, 11 nominations were received: 6 for single trees, and 5 for groups of trees, Horner explained. Submitted nominations were evaluated on their aesthetic, education, or historical metrics. Nominations must be trees situated on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees are then forwarded to the commission for review and selection. “It’s a wonderful tradition, and a positive connection that the city makes with the residents all over Piedmont every spring,” Commission Chair Patty Dunlap said. Traditionally, winning trees are recognized on Arbor Day. Because of the current health pandemic, this year’s announcements were made six months later via teleconference application Zoom. Five trees were chosen this year. Commissioner Eileen Ruby nominated a multi-trunk Japanese Maple, prominently positioned at the entrance to the teahouse garden in Piedmont Park. Resident Tami Becker nominated a Coast Live Oak in Dracena Park. “It is a handsome, featured tree, and its prominence will become more dramatic and important as years go by,” Horner commented. Commissioner Brian Mahany nominated the Southern Magnolia in the Huntleigh/Hampton Triangle. A circle of Coast Redwoods at the Jerome Triangle. articles.text: The residents have spoken. The only swimming pool in this small town of 11,000 people is owned and operated by the city. There is no pool on the school campus, meaning the city bears the responsibiity to make its pool available to all. It also inherits the burden to make the pool safe and accessible for everyone. The timing for placing a $19.5 million bond on the ballot in less than a month is not ideal. But it is the first time in decades the city has asked voters to approve a bond for any physical stucture. When the City Council announced it was going to the votes for a bond to pay for a long needed pool that would accommodate the many needs of residents, we applauded the council. We chided them for showing admirable restraint in not routinely placing bonds on the ballot. The reality is here and it is now. Using a sports analogy, everyone’s beloved, cozy hometown pool has just finished regulation time, has gone into ovetime, and the whistle has blown. The game is over. Rather than list the many reasons a pool should not be built at this time, we are fully supporting Measure UU for a simple reason: it is based upon trust. The City Council and senior city management have demonstrated consistent integrity in their decisions. The city governmnt’s ethos is based upon transparency and honesty. We can thank people like former City Administrator Paul Benoit and former Police Chief Rikki Goede for creating a culture of openess. Mayor Bob McBain and others on the Council have inherited that ethos, and take it seriously. I fully trust that the Council will include the community in plans for a new pool, and will produce a pool ofwhich everyone will be proud.
articles.title: This is the time. A pool must be built

articles.text: No lost time due to Covid for creative Wildwood dads Piedmont’s traditional and time-honored pumpkin patch has a new home this year. Organized by the Wildwood Dads Club for more than 40 years, the famed pumpkin patch was moved from Coaches Field on Moraga Avenue to the enclosed lunch courtyard in front of Wildwood School. What could be more logical? The patch helps create Halloween spirit while raising funds for the elementary school. Knowing that everything is different this year due to the coronavirus epidemic, Wildwood Dads Club president Brian Learn began coordinating plans with city officials as early as July. “As we [Wildwood Dads] kicked off the year this was one of the first things we focused on,” he said. “We wanted to make sure we knew what we needed to do and how we needed to do it.” The dads will be monitoring social distancing, ensuring that everyone wears a mask, and limiting access to the patch to two small groups at a time. Due to COVID-19 they cannot offer the traditional walk and shop experience, but pumpkin hunters can still point out their favorite gourd to take home. Orders can be place online, and walk-ups are still welcome. The Dads Club followed the Alameda County Safety Protection outline, created a plan and submitted it to the city and county. “It was pretty easy actually.” Learn said. “The fire department came by the first morning and approved what we did.” One thing that won’t be different will be the quality of pumpkins. “I’ve worked really closely with our supplier, specifically because we are going to have a slightly reduced selection. We wanted to make sure we have the top picks of the stock, number ones of each variety,” Learn said. In addition to the traditional orange or white carving pumpkins, the patch has numerous specialty pumpkins. articles.text: Coinciding nicely with election day, the Piedmont School Board voted to begin getting students back in class as early as Tuesday, November 3. At a special school board meeting last night, October 6, the five-member board approved a school reopening plan presented by Superintendent Randy Booker. Students in transitional kindergarten through 2nd grade will return to their respective schools on November 3, followed one week later by 3rd, 4th and 5th graders being back in school on November 10. “This [proposal] feels smart and measured and it allows us to make adjustments after a few days to figure it out,” said board president Amal Smith. The board unanimously voted to: 1) Authorize allowable student contact and on-site participation for activities 2) Authorize staff to implement a hybrid/modified, staggered in-person return at the elementary level 3) Authorize elementary family choice between hybrid/modified return and full-year distance learning programs Alameda County moved into the Red Tier of COVID- 19 restriction on September 22. The state allows counties that have been in the Red Tier for two weeks to open their schools with approval from their county. The Alameda County Health Department set a date of October 13 as the earliest day for TK-6th grade students to return if COVID-19 health and safety plans are in place. Elementary schools are required to post their reopening plans to their school or school district website and submit their plan to the Alameda County Office of Education. Each side will then be permitted to present a two-minute closing statement This will be the only ballot measure addressed during this forum. The opponents to Measure TT, increasing the Real Property Transfer Tax on home sales, declined to participate. According to LWV’s rules, both sides must agree to participate for the League to host a public forum. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has aging infrastructure. Our buildings, facilities, streets, and sidewalks need upgrading. City Council and City staff are keenly aware of these needs and are taking steps to address them. In fact, that’s what Measures UU and TT are all about. At a June 29, 2020 Special Meeting, there were two items on the Council Agenda: (1) The Future of the Piedmont Pool and (2) Local Ballot Measures for November. The City Council could not, in good conscience, vote to permanently close the Piedmont Pool without giving voters a chance to decide whether to invest in a replacement. Measure UU is quite simple. Do Piedmonters want to continue to have a public pool for our residents and our schools? Or not? This is not a false choice or an idle threat. Our 56-year-old pool is on its last legs. No matter how well pools are maintained, they do not last forever. The concept behind Measure UU arose from a comprehensive public planning process begun in 2016. The popularity of water sports and exercise has grown enormously since 1964 when the pool was built. The goal of Measure UU is to build a pool facility that meets our community’s needs and can operate cost effectively. Young families and proud grandparents alike want a local pool where all generations can exercise, play, and spend time together. Please join me, the Piedmont City Council, the Piedmont Board of Education, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization, and many other community members, and Vote Yes on Measure UU. Let’s come together and build a pool facility we can be proud of for the next 50 years. A mostly white crowd of thousands gathered on the National Mall to pray for national unity, the well-being of President Trump, the Supreme Court, an end to abortion, an end to the pandemic, an end to racism and violence against “people who have suffered unjustly.” Convinced I would be supportive, a friend who had watched the event on Facebook emailed me afterward urging me to find a recording and watch it myself. articles.text: I applaud the Piedmont City Council for its unanimous decision to place Measure UU to rebuild the Piedmont pool on the November ballot. These decisions are never easy, but in this case there are no good alternatives. The pool is in desperate condition and Piedmont deserves better. After a long career in city government, I had the distinct honor and privilege of serving as Piedmont’s City Administrator from 2014 through 2019. During my tenure, I worked with the City Council to address significant deficiencies in Piedmont’s technology systems, civic buildings, and recreational facilities. Most are in need of attention. With limited funds and the benefit of public/private partnerships, the Council was able to vastly improve Hampton Park as well as the main tennis courts. On a relative basis, those projects were “low hanging fruit.” The Recreation Building, City Hall, and the Police and Fire facilities are all in need of attention. Only one facility, however, is in such poor condition that it should be closed permanently. That facility is the Piedmont Pool. Over my five plus years as City Administrator the pool had constant and often significant, costly maintenance issues. The need for the City to subsidize the operational costs grew each year. This could have been rationalized, to a point, as an investment in Piedmont’s youth and resident recreation, except the pool, with its limited size, deteriorating condition, and odd configuration did not meet the needs of the community or Piedmont schools. Over the course of the past four years, the City has made a significant investment to professionally analyze the pool’s condition and work with the community to determine exactly what type of aquatic facility would best serve Piedmont. In 2016, the City Council formed a citizens’ steering committee and held numerous public meetings. The result of this public process was a comprehensive report and conceptual design for a pool facility that fits the site, serves the community, meets the needs of youth for recreation and competitive play, and above all, is both safe and cost effective to operate. Out of deference to the School District’s timing for its bond measure, and subsequent parcel tax measures, the City did not put the Piedmont Pool on the ballot in 2016 or 2018. But a decision about the future of the Piedmont Pool can no longer be delayed. I now live in Astoria, Oregon, population 10,000— similar in size to Piedmont. Residents here overwhelmingly approved a bond measure to build a community pool some years ago. I know from experience that well-designed municipal pools are an amazing resource for a small community. Even though I now live in Oregon, I still want what is best for Piedmont, and I urge you to vote YES on Measure UU. Paul Benoit is the retired City Administrator of the City of Piedmont. “Are you sure we had the software package with us when we closed the Hilton bar?”

articles.text: Editor: It was my pleasure to get to know Jen Cavanaugh about two years ago when we met during discussions by the Park Commission about how to incorporate the sport of pickleball into the City’s recreation program. Jen attended the meetings of the Commission as an observer for the City Council. She did not play a role in the discussions, but I soon learned of her skill in listening to us players before and after the meetings, seeking our opinions, and providing questions and thoughts for us to consider as we worked with the Commission toward a clear plan for pickleball play. She was a quiet presence, sharing ideas but never intervening in the formal discussions that were taking place. Her engagement was instrumental, in a behind-the-scenes way, in helping the players come to an excellent accord with the Commission that has lasted to this day. Since that period of activism, I have had opportunities to get to know Jen even better. My initial impression that she is a dedicated, thoughtful and intelligent public servant has only been reinforced. Please join me in voting to keep her talent at work for our City. –Lester Ellis

articles.text: Editor: I’m writing to encourage my fellow Piedmont citizens to vote for Hilary Cooper for school board. As a parent of elementary and middle school students in Piedmont, I believe that Hilary would be a great addition to the school board. I worked with Hilary on the campaign to pass Measures G&H, our very important school parcel taxes last year, and I was impressed by her work ethic and her collaborative leadership. Rarely do you see a leader who has both the big picture vision for success, and the desire to work behind the scenes to make sure the details get done. During the G&H campaign, she tracked all of the data diligently to ensure accuracy and kept all milestones on schedule. Hilary was particularly passionate about supporting our teachers via the passage of Measure H. Hilary is committed to supporting all students. She is aware of the importance of differentiation in the classroom, so that each student’s needs are addressed. She listens and she takes feedback graciously. Hilary also has ideas to enhance our district’s efforts with regard to diversity and inclusion. She will ensure all students are heard and feel safe, both physically and socially/ emotionally. We are living in challenging times, and we need leaders who will bring our community together to achieve the best results for our children. Please join me from Chicago where she earned degrees in Economics and Journalism from Northwestern University. Veronica has authored award winning writings on educational policy, and currently advises school systems and educational nonprofits on building equitable and effective organizations. Upon arrival in Piedmont, Veronica eagerly joined our enthusiastic volunteer community and has made several important contributions. We are fortunate to have a candidate with such broad understanding of educational policy, and a willingness to share her talents and knowledge. Veronica is also a trained facilitator whose calm, thoughtful demeanor and sense of humor make her an effective collaborator. Veronica is articulate and is a skilled listener. Her positive attitude and willingness to address difficult issues are critical strengths in these challenging time. My association with the school district began in 1980 when I was hired to teach art at Piedmont Middle School. For many years both the school district and the city have expressed a desire to increase diversity within their staffs. In Veronica we have a competent, eminently qualified leader who is also a woman of color. Veronica will make a wonderful addition to our dedicated Board of Education. Please join me in voting for Veronica Anderson Thigpen for School Board. –Cathy Michelotti Glazier
articles.title: Hilary Cooper a community leader

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council upheld a Planning Commission decision to deny an application for a new accessory building and garage proposed at 212 Bonita Avenue. Seamus and Fernanda Meagher, owners of the property, appealed the July 13, 2020 Planning Commission decision to deny the application. Prior to that meeting, the Planning Commission held a public hearing on June 8 to consider an application to demolish an existing narrow one-car garage at the corner of the 14,245-square-foot property and in its place construct a two-story 1,257-squarefoot accessory building with garage. The plan was denied by the commission, and it went to the city council on an appeal. -Project architect Amy Nunes On a new application, the applicants proposed demolishing the existing garage, constructing a new two-story accessory building, and designing the garage so it could provide a turnaround area, up to two parking spaces, create a new trash and recycling enclosure, and install new exterior lighting. These changes were considered on July 13, and again denied The residence at 212 Bonita Avenue, with a garage at the rear of the property. by the commission. An appeal was heard by the city council on September 21 but was denied. The city council may uphold, modify, add to, or overrule the planning commission’s decision. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon noted that council cannot overturn the commission’s decision “simply because it does not agree with the decision. It must make findings regarding why the commission’s decision is faulty.” “The appeal contends that the Planning Commission’s decision is not supported by the weight of evidence of the city code,” City Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell said. Neighbors, Oscar and Betty Rojas, whose house is at the back of the Meagher property, wrote to the Planning Commission expressing their support of the proposed project. “The new structure will provide privacy for both parties. We can currently see into our neighbors’ entire back yard and rear home windows from our upstairs windows, and our neighbors can see into the windows of our upstairs rooms from their main home. The new structure will provide a barrier of privacy that we will both benefit from without blocking any natural light,” they wrote. articles.text: • Amends the Existing Real Property Transfer Tax Should the Piedmont City Code be amended to increase the existing real property transfer tax to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price? Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT) is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale. In the City of Piedmont, the tax is currently at the rate of $13.00 per $1,000 of the value of the property The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that minimum additional funding of approximately $850,000/ year for the next five to ten years is needed to maintain the condition of city buildings, parks, streets and sidewalks. Measure TT would generate around $948,462/ year. Funds generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used A “YES” vote on Measure TT would be in favor of increasing the real property conveyance tax to the new rate of $17.50 per $1,000. A “NO” vote on Measure TT would be against the increase in the real property conveyance tax and would maintain the current rate of Opponents Say: The proposed increase of the City’s Transfer Tax rate would make it the highest flat rate in the entire State of California and could cost homeowners tens of thousands of dollars when buying or selling their home. There are no safeguards to ensure that the money from this tax will be directed to repair and maintain city facilities and that means the tax can be used for anything including salaries, pensions or project over runs. Piedmont already has an extremely high transfer tax rate. Increasing it will set a bad precedent in the region and could adversely affect homeowners that wish to sell their home in order to move into a retirement community. Opposition – Signers of official arguments/ rebuttals: Eric Wong - President, Bridge Association of REA • •

articles.text: Authorizes the City to Issue Bonds to Reconstruct the Piedmont Community Pool 2/3 vote needed to pass THE QUESTION Should the City of Piedmont be authorized to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of improvements for the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas? THE SITUATION The existing Piedmont Community Pool opened in 1964 and is now in its 56th year. The usual lifespan of most outdoor pools is 50 years. Prior to closure due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place orders, the City was spending approximately $1,000 a day to keep the pool safe and operational. The City believes that residents rely upon the Piedmont Community Pool as a resource to learn to swim, exercise, compete, play, and socialize. It has also been a steady source of employment for local youth. Based on a July, 2020 Concept Study, the estimated cost for replacement of the Piedmont Community Pool including bath house, pools and surrounding site work is $18.8 million. THE PROPOSAL If adopted, Measure UU would authorize the City of Piedmont to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of replacing the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas. It is proposed that the three existing pools be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. The new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas would conserve energy and water, comply with state and federal disability and safety standards, and provide restroom access for those using the tennis courts. FISCAL EFFECTS: If all of the bonds were issued and sold, the best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest is $37,446,788. A “YES” vote on Measure UU would be in favor of authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool . A “NO” vote on Measure UU would be against authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool Supporters Say: The pool needs to be replaced or it will be permanently closed. Measure UU provides necessary funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility to serve Piedmont families, students, and seniors for the next 50 years. Passing this bond measure this year means taking advantage of historically low interest rates and avoiding continued escalation of construction costs in the future. Without the pool, Piedmont would be the only school district in Alameda County without a local pool for swim lessons, P.E, and water sports. Opponents Say: Piedmont should not be taking on $20 million of general obligation debt in the midst of fiscal uncertainty resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. Piedmont has other liabilities including pension liabilities and sewer loans and shouldn’t be adding general obligation debt to its liabilities. pages.text: Wednesday, October 7, 2020 5 • • • • League of Women Voters’ Guide of Pros and Cons for Piedmont measures Visit VotersEdge.org to see everything on your ballot, your polling place, and un-biased information on all of your voting choices. A longer more detailed version of this guide is available at https://www.lwvpiedmont.org/content.aspx?page_id=5&club_id=601389&item_id=57942 A forum on the Measure UU will be held by the LWV Wed. Oct. 14, 6:00 p.m. to - 6:30 p.m. at www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg Measure TT: Amends the Existing Real Property Transfer Tax Majority of votes required to pass THE QUESTION Should the Piedmont City Code be amended to increase the existing real property transfer tax to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price? THE SITUATION Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT) is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale. In the City of Piedmont, the tax is currently at the rate of $13.00 per $1,000 of the value of the property transferred. This rate was set in 1993. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that minimum additional funding of approximately $850,000/ year for the next five to ten years is needed to maintain the condition of city buildings, parks, streets and sidewalks. FISCAL EFFECTS: Measure TT would generate around $948,462/ year. Funds generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used for any City general revenue purpose. A “YES” vote on Measure TT would be in favor of increasing the real property conveyance tax to the new rate of $17.50 per $1,000. A “NO” vote on Measure TT would be against the increase in the real property conveyance tax and would maintain the current rate of $13.00 per $1,000. Supporters Say: The transfer tax is assessed only on property when it is sold, so it will affect relatively few residents each year. The proposed increase in the Transfer Tax rate will provide necessary funds for maintaining and improving city facilities, streets, sidewalks, and parks. The current transfer tax rate is significantly lower than Berkeley or Oakland and the increased rate would be lower than Berkeley and Oakland for some property sale values. Support – Signers of official arguments/ rebuttals: Robert S. McBain - Mayor Teddy Gray King - Vice Mayor Bill Hosler - Chair, Budget Advisory and Fin. Planning Committee John Y. Chiang - Former Mayor Chris Kwei - Member, Budget Advisory And Financial Planning Committee Opponents Say: The proposed increase of the City’s Transfer Tax rate would make it the highest flat rate in the entire State of California and could cost homeowners tens of thousands of dollars when buying or selling their home. There are no safeguards to ensure that the money from this tax will be directed to repair and maintain city facilities and that means the tax can be used for anything including salaries, pensions or project over runs. Piedmont already has an extremely high transfer tax rate. Increasing it will set a bad precedent in the region and could adversely affect homeowners that wish to sell their home in order to move into a retirement community. Opposition – Signers of official arguments/ rebuttals: Eric Wong - President, Bridge Association of REA Measure UU: Authorizes the City to Issue Bonds to Reconstruct the Piedmont Community Pool 2/3 vote needed to pass THE QUESTION Should the City of Piedmont be authorized to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of improvements for the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas? THE SITUATION The existing Piedmont Community Pool opened in 1964 and is now in its 56th year. The usual lifespan of most outdoor pools is 50 years. Prior to closure due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place orders, the City was spending approximately $1,000 a day to keep the pool safe and operational. The City believes that residents rely upon the Piedmont Community Pool as a resource to learn to swim, exercise, compete, play, and socialize. It has also been a steady source of employment for local youth. Based on a July, 2020 Concept Study, the estimated cost for replacement of the Piedmont Community Pool including bath house, pools and surrounding site work is $18.8 million. THE PROPOSAL If adopted, Measure UU would authorize the City of Piedmont to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of replacing the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas. It is proposed that the three existing pools be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. The new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas would conserve energy and water, comply with state and federal disability and safety standards, and provide restroom access for those using the tennis courts. FISCAL EFFECTS: If all of the bonds were issued and sold, the best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest is $37,446,788. A “YES” vote on Measure UU would be in favor of authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool . A “NO” vote on Measure UU would be against authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool Supporters Say: The pool needs to be replaced or it will be permanently closed. Measure UU provides necessary funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility to serve Piedmont families, students, and seniors for the next 50 years. Passing this bond measure this year means taking advantage of historically low interest rates and avoiding continued escalation of construction costs in the future. Without the pool, Piedmont would be the only school district in Alameda County without a local pool for swim lessons, P.E, and water sports. Opponents Say: Piedmont should not be taking on $20 million of general obligation debt in the midst of fiscal uncertainty resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. Piedmont has other liabilities including pension liabilities and sewer loans and shouldn’t be adding general obligation debt to its liabilities. Because of the pandemic, the pool will remain closed for the foreseeable future, so we should wait to see if things return to normal before passing this bond measure. articles.text: The Bay Area sky in September after wildfires 100 miles away. On September 9, the Bay Area woke up to a strange phenomenon. The skies were filled with smoke, filtering sunlight to a low-orange glow. Not only did this create a sense of unease, as if we were living on a Martian planet, but it also sparked curiosity over the unique phenomena we were collectively experiencing. While acknowledging the terrible devastation that wildfires are causing across the Pacific Northwest, there is also some interesting science that can be used to discuss what is going on at home. Use the simple demonstration below to show how light filters through our skies, and use it to better understand his historic event. MATERIALS • Flashlight • Colored cellophane: red, blue, and green. Other colors optional. • White paper PROCEDURE 1. Begin by asking some questions: a. What do you think light is? b. Do you think light is moving or staying still? c. What are some sources of light/what are some things that produce light? 2. Shine a flashlight on a piece of white paper. 3. Grab a piece of colored cellophane and predict: a. What do you think will happen if we shine the light through this [red, blue, or green] filter? 4. Place the cellophane over the flashlight and shine it on the paper. Discuss: a. What happened to the light? b. Did it change at all? How so? 5. Repeat this with the other colors. 6. After testing them all, discuss: a. Why do you think the color of the light changes to the color of the filter placed over it? 7. Now, try combining two cellophane colors at a time. Predict what will happen before testing each combination. Then, discuss: a. Why do you think the light changed to [insert color] when we use these two filters together? 8. Now, try combining all of the colors at once. Predict what will happen, then test them together. Make some observations: a. What did you notice? b. How was it different from the previous tests? c. Was this similar or different to your prediction? 9. Discuss some of the following questions with your learners: a. What new ideas do you have about light now? b. Do you think light travels or stays still now that we’ve experimented a bit more with it? c. Do you think sunlight travels through filters in nature? What would be a natural filter of sunlight? d. Is the light from the sun always the same in brightness, color, or direction? What are some of the different ways you’ve seen sunlight? How light changes colors The size of the tiny waves that light travels in determines what color of light we see. If the waves are long and wide (long wavelength), they make yellow, orange, or red light. If the waves are short and thin (short wavelength), they make green, blue, and purple light. If the wavelength ever changes, so does the light that we see! In this case, when the light from a flashlight passes through a colored filter, the waves change from making white light to making colored light… the same color as the filter. This happens because the filter acts like a screen, only allowing the waves of light that match its color to pass through. All of the other wavelengths (and colors) of light are absorbed by the filter and therefore, not allowed to pass. This leaves only the one color of light traveling beyond the filter. articles.text: Committee is already thinking about Walk for Wellness 2021. “There was so much enthusiasm for this year’s event. Even if we can hold a traditional in-person community walk next year, we plan to include the week-long mileage tracking piece,” explained event co-chair Nicki Gilbert. “We hope the combination of a large community gathering and a week-long celebration of physical and mental health will turn Walk for Wellness into a much-loved annual Piedmont tradition.” The Support Committee is grateful to the more than 30 Piedmont families who sponsored Walk for Wellness 2020, and to Bay Design & Build, The Cooper Group, East Bay Pediatrics, Harmless Harvest, Mulberry’s Market, Niantic and Xantrion for their generous corporate sponsorships. To donate to the Wellness Center, click on PiedmontStore. org. Funds are collected throughout the year. Want to help with next year’s Walk for Wellness? E-mail piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com. Terri Burge & Natalie Williamson Walk for Wellness 2020, Piedmont School District’s largest fundraiser for its Wellness Center, had more than 400 individuals who walked a combined 1,200 miles and raised more than $37,000 during the week of September 21. It was organized by the Wellness Center Support Committee, a group of parent volunteers, “We’re thrilled with the success of Walk for Wellness,” said event co-chair KeriAnne Hohener. “All aspects of the event – the number of participants, the miles logged, the money raised – exceeded our expectations.” The event was an inclusive, accessible and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont community. Participants received a Walk for Wellness visor and access to seven maps detailing various walks around town. During the week they were able to log mileage from their walks online, share their favorite walks with other participants, and post photos on social media. Dr. Alisa Crovetti, the Clinical Supervisor of the Wellness Center, expressed her gratitude to the Piedmont community for understanding the need for counseling services for middle and high school students, “It is absolutely crucial that we prioritize the mental health of our students, especially during distance learning,” she said. “I’m thrilled with the response to Walk for Wellness and very much appreciate the community’s support of the Wellness Center.” The Wellness Center Support Ethan & Jeremy Block

articles.text: City recommends to avoid trick-or-treating this year The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) declared traditional trick-or-treating to be a “high-risk” activity for COVID-19 transmission, even with precautionary measures such as sanitizing and social distancing. Although trick-or-treating is primarily an outdoor activity, a statement issued by ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram said that it would be difficult to maintain a safe distance on porches and doorsteps. Instead, the health officer is encouraging community members to focus on decorations, and to limit activities to household members only. ACPHD also encourages virtual costume parties in lieu of in-person socialization. “Trick-or-treating is a highrisk activity because it increases contact with people outside of your household who may not be as careful about COVID-19 prevention. Parties are high-risk, because mixing among people who don’t live in the same home introduces more opportunities for the virus to pass from one person to another,” Balram said. The department is still encouraging the use of masks, frequent sanitizing, and social distancing. Costume masks are not a substitute for protective cloth masks, but “avoid wearing a costume mask over a protective cloth mask because it can be dangerous if the costume mask makes it hard to breathe,” Balram added. Alameda County residents are reminded that local and state health officer orders are still in effect. Halloween gatherings, celebrations of Dia de los Muertos, and events or parties with non-household members are not permitted unless they are conducted in compliance with local and state health orders. Activities that are not permitted and are considered very high risk are crowded parties, haunted houses, and indoor mazes. Low-risk activities are recommended by the county, to include visiting an outdoor pumpkin patch, carving and decorating pumpkins outside, and preparing traditional family recipes with members of your household. The risk of traditional trickor-treating can be mitigated from high-risk to moderate-risk, if children participate in one-way trickor-treating where individually wrapped goodie bags are lined up for families to pick up and go while continuing to socially distance. The County also recommends that everyone participating should bring hand sanitizer, use it frequently, and wash hands immediately after coming home. The Piedmont Police Department echoed the Alameda County recommendations. “The bottom line is that the city is recommending that people do not engage in high-risk behavior such as trick-or-treating,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said.
articles.title: County says trick-or-treating is high-risk for COVID transmission

County says trick-or-treating is high-risk for COVID transmission City recommends to avoid trick-or-treating this year By Allyson Aleksey The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) declared traditional trick-or-treating to be a “high-risk” activity for COVID-19 transmission, even with precautionary measures such as sanitizing and social distancing. Although trick-or-treating is primarily an outdoor activity, a statement issued by ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram said that it would be difficult to maintain a safe distance on porches and doorsteps. Instead, the health officer is encouraging community members to focus on decorations, and to limit activities to household members only. ACPHD also encourages virtual costume parties in lieu of in-person socialization. “Trick-or-treating is a highrisk activity because it increases contact with people outside of your household who may not be as careful about COVID-19 prevention. Parties are high-risk, because mixing among people who don’t live in the same home introduces more opportunities for the virus to pass from one person to another,” Balram said. The department is still encouraging the use of masks, frequent sanitizing, and social distancing. Costume masks are not a substitute for protective cloth masks, but “avoid wearing a costume mask over a protective cloth mask because it can be dangerous if the costume mask makes it hard to breathe,” Balram added. Alameda County residents are reminded that local and state health officer orders are still in effect. Halloween gatherings, celebrations of Dia de los Muertos, and events or parties with non-household members are not permitted unless they are conducted in compliance with local and state health orders. Activities that are not permitted and are considered very high risk are crowded parties, haunted houses, and indoor mazes. Low-risk activities are recommended by the county, to include visiting an outdoor pumpkin patch, carving and decorating pumpkins outside, and preparing traditional family recipes with members of your household. The risk of traditional trickor-treating can be mitigated from high-risk to moderate-risk, if children participate in one-way trickor-treating where individually wrapped goodie bags are lined up for families to pick up and go while continuing to socially distance. The County also recommends that everyone participating should bring hand sanitizer, use it frequently, and wash hands immediately after coming home. The Piedmont Police Department echoed the Alameda County recommendations. “The bottom line is that the city is recommending that people do not engage in high-risk behavior such as trick-or-treating,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said. articles.text: Successor to Jo Hazelett as Council Executive starts Nov. 1 Kate Benson and daughter Kajsa are experienced hikers and campers. The Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America (BSA) announced that Kate Benson has been hired as its new Scout Executive, effective November 1, 2020. She succeeds Jo Hazelett, who is retiring after 22 years of distinguished service in that position. “We’re delighted to welcome Kate to the Piedmont community,” said Seth Hilton, president of the Executive Council. “She brings energy and new ideas that will build on the foundation laid by Jo Hazelett.” “In this succession, we wanted to maintain Jo’s connections throughout our community and across the BSA movement,” said Rob James, Selection Committee chair and past president. “Kate has made those same kinds of connections. We know she will communicate the spirit of our mission for a new era.” Kate comes to Piedmont Scouting from the Silicon Valley Monterey Bay Council, where she is Development Director overseeing large special events and annual fundraising activities. She has 17 years of experience as a Scouting professional, including work as a District Director and Senior District Executive in Portland and Spokane, responsible for fund development, endowment gifts, marketing, membership, and large district administration. Kate and her husband, Neil, have two daughters, Cub Scout Anna (8) and Scout BSA member Kajsa (11). Kate is currently Cubmaster of Pack 785 in Gilroy, is a member of the Order of the Arrow, and was a staff member at the 2017 National Jamboree at the Summit Bechtel Reserve. Kate is a past president of the Vancouver, Washington Rotary Club and an avid rower and musician. “I am excited to be joining the Piedmont Council – clearly an organization that invests in the development of young people,” she said. “My passion is communicating the value and values of Scouting to new audiences, including folks who might not have been associated with Scouts before. Our volunteers spend countless hours working with youth to develop character, fitness, citizenship, and leadership; and through that program, they provide service to the larger community. “Our programs are more inclusive than ever before and I want all families to know they are welcome. I look forward to participating, virtually and soon in person. Piedmont Scouting serves approximately 1,100 young men and women in its programs, ranging from Cub Scouts in grades 1-5; Scouts BSA (formerly Boy Scouts) in grades 6-12; coed Venturing (including the Piedmont Community Service Crew), Police Exploring and Sea Scouts for youth up to age 21, and through Learning for Life, the Piedmont Language School. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. It is not possible to always reach consensus in our decisions, but that’s how our representative government works -- for the people. 2 – My top priority is to balance fiscal responsibility with a commitment to improving Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and enhancing public services. If Measure UU passes, in two years we will have finished the design process and hopefully be into the construction phase for a new community pool for Piedmont. However, if Measure UU fails, if more than one third of voters decide that they do not want to have a community pool, then our old pool will likely have been closed, drained, and secured, and the city will have to begin a process to determine what to do with the space. Second, this current crisis has made it abundantly clear that wildfire prevention, disaster preparedness, community health and public safety must be priorities. Next, the city is embarking on a process to reevaluate our plans for providing housing of all types and income levels, specifically to meet our state-mandated Regional Housing Number Allocation in 2021. The current expectation is that our allocation could be as high as 600 units. We will look to creatively provide housing that integrates into our community while maintaining the essence of what makes Piedmont special. Lastly, climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and the environment. The implementation of the city’s Climate Action Plan is a high priority for the city, and we will continue to work with residents to ensure the plan is actionable and reasonable. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – Disagreeing can be productive. Opportunities to air concerns and share ideas lead to cooperation, compromise and the best decisions. We can disagree passionately and argue civilly at the same time. However, if we disagree and argue with the primary intention of “winning” or “being right,” then we shift to a negative space. Tempers flare and feelings are hurt with possible lasting damage to relationships. The Hawaiian word “laulima” means “many hands working together, and is a core principle within the Hawaiian Aloha culture. One set of hands can accomplish much. But many hands can accomplish infinitely more and tackle complex problems. When we embrace this concept, then disagreements become opportunities to listen, receive education and forge new ideas together. I always respect my colleagues and look forward to our “laulima.” 2 – My short list is •. Focus on current priority projects, keep them moving forward to completion and work tirelessly for our City. • Complete Piedmont City Council onboarding requirements. Understand all Council rules of conduct. Attend the League of California Cities New Mayor and Council Members Academy. Complete required California public service ethics laws and principles coursework. • Meet with every City department, Piedmont organization (including student organizations) and the PUSD Board of Education to discuss their priorities and find out where I can support their efforts. Meet as many Oakland, Berkeley, Emeryville City Councilmembers and Alameda County officials as possible to find shared opportunities and forge relationships. • Create a private Piedmont Resident Online Forum on my website for all residents to post their concerns and comments on City issues. Add survey software to my website so I can construct simple, straightforward questions and residents can quickly and anonymously share their opinions. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – Anyone who seeks a leadership position as an elected decision-maker should understand that robust discussions and disagreements are common. People who avoid conflict may miss opportunities to engage in productive problem-solving because disagreements often lead to positive outcomes. Nevertheless, while I believe colleagues should, when appropriate, challenge each other, it is important to verbalize disagreements without being personal. The world changed in 2016 revealing a deepening lack of civility. Trusted institutions no longer function in predictable ways. Conspiracy theories abound. Name calling is commonplace. Good leaders understand the importance of setting limits, practicing emotional control and establishing expectations. If I earn a seat on Piedmont City Council, I will begin my tenure by listening, observing and looking for opportunities to contribute. I have tremendous respect for currently serving members of council. I will work to nurture dynamic relationships with each of them as we work together for a better Piedmont. 2 – Public safety is a priority. Piedmont residents should go to sleep at night with the security of knowing police and fire professionals will show up with all necessary equipment to provide essential services for a personal crisis, as well as, during and after a public disaster. Our Police Department is housed in a 70-year-old facility. Inadequacies in our existing police facility prevent Piedmont from meeting the national effort to update the 911 system. Our Fire Department is housed in City Hall, originally constructed 110 years ago. Our existing fire facility is inadequate in size to accommodate current fire apparatus and equipment. It is imperative that we evaluate the state of Piedmont’s essential services buildings to bring them to current codes and standards. We must engage the community to gauge interest, support and understanding of the financial implications. Piedmont’s climate action plan serves as a framework for all infrastructure planning.
