I am also committed to an audit of our curriculum around racial justice and equity and to pursuing hiring more BIPOC teachers and administrators when openings occur. These are complex issues, but they are all critical to the success of our students. JASON KELLEY 1 – In our small community, the focus should be on consensus building. This process takes time and a commitment to good-will and respect for everyone’s viewpoints. When colleagues disagree, they must take the time to understand each other’s views by honestly expressing their own and carefully listening to the other’s. They should be seeking a way forward that meets the needs of both while not betraying the core values of either. There may well be times when a compromise cannot be found, and then in our system a vote is taken and all sides agree to abide by the result. This is why it is very important for the school board to be made up of people with a diverse set of interests, backgrounds, experiences, and skill sets. That way, the board represents the whole community and can reach consensus that benefits the most people. 2 – My short list is: • Ensure schools reopen safely and in a way that promotes stability and meets the needs of all stakeholders: students, teachers, families and the wider Piedmont community. Families and educators need as much stability as possible right now, so they are able to plan effectively. • Address the needs of the rapidly increasing population of special education students by adding more teachers and paraeducators. • Engage in planning for how education can best be delivered in the future in light of the lessons we’ve learned during distance learning. There may be place for some form of distance learning going forward for particular students who might benefit from it, including advanced placement students who may want to take classes our schools do not have the population to support. CORY SMEGAL 1 – During my four years on the School Board, there have been times when other Board members and I have disagreed on a decision. What I’ve found to be most important during those discussions is each member’s willingness to listen to other points of view and respectfully discuss differences of opinion. It’s not always easy -- those discussions are in public and can be challenging. My colleagues on the Board are all people that I hold in high esteem. They impress me all the time, not only with their intelligence and thoughtfulness, but also with their commitment to our District. We’ve worked hard over the last several years to develop relationships built on trust and a desire to do what is best for all the stakeholders of the Piedmont schools. During these challenging times, it will be critical for the new Board to work together to solve problems. 2 – My 3 priorities are: • Educational excellence, with engaging opportunities for all students • Fiscal responsibility • Focus on mental health and well being In the last six months, the Board and the District have been focused on how school can best work during a pandemic. Now that Alameda County has entered the red tier, we must focus our efforts on a safe return to school. The County has provided direction that calls for a phased return, which we agree will promote safety. Returning students to school can both improve students’ mental health and continue the District’s efforts on educational excellence. The Board has also recently approved a new policy on racial equity. In this policy, there are several specific actions to take and that work will begin this fall. Finally, in all of this, we must be fiscally responsible with the District’s resources. VERONICA ANDERSON THIGPEN 1 – If I disagree with a colleague, I see an opportunity to learn something. These situations call for deep listening, clarifying questions and reflection. When approached with a spirit of learning and an understanding of the need to reach consensus, then creative problem solving can occur. In the end, my colleague and I may not come to agreement, but if there is a decision to be made, the hope is that deliberations and decisions have benefited from a variety of perspectives. 2 – The first item on my short list is to ensure the continuity of education for our students through the uncertainties of this pandemic, however long it lasts. On my list for the first two years is implementing important elements of the district’s new racial equity policy, such as hiring diverse teachers and adoption of a K12 anti-racism curriculum. I also feel that it is essential for the culture throughout PUSD to be welcoming to all students, families and teachers, and that every learner would receive the scaffolding and differentiation they need. There would be recognition that student voices are a key ingredient of educational planning and decision-making. HARI TITAN 1 – The first thing is to find out if your colleague is thinking independently about the topic in question or is deferring to someone else who is the decision-maker for that topic. Often on the school board, board members defer to each other based on interest and experience on various topics under deliberation. The next thing to find out is if your colleague can argue their case with facts and evidence and likewise that you prepare your own arguments. It may not serve the stakeholders well if you simply agree to disagree. It would be better to debate the positions and find the optimal solution for all stakeholders. Getting partial agreement on what are the facts surrounding a situation is very helpful even if total agreement cannot be achieved. This partial agreement can help frame the issue for public participation in a public school board meeting. 2 – My short list is: • A safe return to the option of classroom instruction will likely happen sooner rather than later. If elected, I would ensure Piedmont Unified is not the reason for falling back into 100% Distance learning. This would require close monitoring and systems in place to help ensure compliance with all precautions. • Making activities on advisory committees fully transparent to the public to allow for public participation. I would institute a digital town hall with moderated wiki pages on every topic under deliberation in the school district. • Fiscal solvency of the school district. There is the chance we won’t get the funding we need to operate at the level we currently do. I would work to minimize the impact on student success post-graduation. • Improving the quality of experts and teachers hired by the school district. Instead of who you know, it should be based on what you know and how well you can explain difficult concepts. NANCY “SUNNY” BOSTROM Returned papers as candidate for School Board. articles.text: It is long past time for Piedmont to rebuild our one and only community pool. Current residents of Piedmont have benefitted from the generosity of prior residents who built, paid for, and in many cases donated our buildings, parks, playfields and of course, the pool. Their generosity toward future generations has allowed us, as taxpayers, to focus our collective resources on our excellent public schools. It is now our turn to step up to rebuild our failing infrastructure. The two measures on the ballot in November are about repairing and replacing what is broken. Measure UU will allow Piedmont to issue, for the first time ever, municipal bonds to rebuild the failing 56-year-old Piedmont Pool. Municipal bonds are like a 30-year fixed-rate community mortgage, repaid through property tax assessments. Measure TT will align the real property transfer tax – only paid when a home is bought or sold – to match those of Berkeley and Oakland, and use the funds to repair and maintain our city facilities and failing roads and sidewalks. To us, six former Piedmont Mayors, the focus on long-term planning is a sign of pragmatic and strategic thinking. The current City Council unanimously placed Measures UU and TT on the ballot because our failing infrastructure can’t wait. Spending more to repair a crumbling pool facility makes no fiscal sense. Borrowing money at low interest rates to rebuild a necessary civic asset is the prudent decision. Soon the City Council will be forced to make the decision that no one wants to make: to permanently close the Piedmont Pool. If Measure UU does not pass, Piedmont will then fail to provide a basic public amenity that every other city in Alameda County provides to its residents. Whether you swim or not, the lack of a municipal pool would be a profound loss for our community and our schools. Please join us in supporting the future of Piedmont and voting yes on Measures UU and TT. Former Piedmont Mayors: Dean Barbieri Michael Bruck John Chiang Abe Friedman Susan Hill Valerie Matzger
articles.title: Former Mayors make the case for community pool

articles.text: Editor: I am very happy to write in support of UU so that we can finally get a new aquatic center in Piedmont. As some may remember, I was involved in the last major effort to build a new pool (2000- 02. Predictably, the same tired opposition points are emerging this time – parking, traffic, noise, cost, “outsiders,” “now is not the time,” and (horrors!) the specter of swim meets. If we can finally build an aquatic center befitting Piedmont, every member of the community will benefit, from little babies learning to swim; to young children playing to their hearts’ content; to club team members; to high school athletes; to adult lap swimmers; to the disabled; to seniors looking for safe exercise. The aquatic center will also be a gathering place for community members to enjoy each other’s company in a casual atmosphere by the pool. If we don’t build a new aquatic center, Piedmont will be relegated to the ranks of those few California communities that have neither a community pool nor a high school pool, and this will affect the appeal of Piedmont as a place to live, not to mention the effect on property values. So, let’s finally get this done. A new aquatic center will be a highlight among everything that makes Piedmont such a great place to live! Please vote yes on UU! –Josh Bernstein, DDS
articles.title: After 20 years, let’s get the job done

The Piedmont Pool is an iconic part of the community where generations of Piedmont residents have enjoyed the outdoors. Our one and only public pool is also an essential facility providing a safe and healthy place for families to enjoy aquatics. articles.text: City’s answers to Frequently Asked Questions about Pool bond. 1. The City proposes to issue $19.5 Million in bonds. What is the actual expected borrowing interest rate assuming the bond passes this year? Municipal bonds can be issued in stages as the funds are needed, and the applicable interest rate is determined at the time the bonds are issued. As a frame of reference, the interest rate as of September 16, 2020 is 2.8%. 2. What is the City’s current total outstanding general obligation debt? The City currently has no outstanding general obligation debt. 3. What is the term of the bond repayment? Measure UU provides that the term of the bond repayment is 30 years with a fixed interest rate. 4. How long will the tax be imposed on properties, and will the amount of the tax ever decrease? Measure UU, if adopted, would impose a tax on properties for 30 years. In the event our property tax roll increases at 3.5% per year (10- year average is ~4.5%), the tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value will drop from $0.26 (if all bonds are issued) to approximately $0.10 in thirty years. The total tax assessed would still be the same but redistributed based on the individual property assessment. 5. How can a property owner ascertain the assessed value of property? pages.text: Wednesday, October 7, 2020 11 PRFO voices its support of Pool Bond, Measure UU By Steve Collins Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (“PRFO”) mission statement reads: ”PRFO works collaboratively with the City of Piedmont to identify, advocate for, and bring private financial support to assist in the funding of projects that invest in healthy spaces within the city.” The tagline for PRFO is “Working Together so we can Play Together.” Never have these words been more relevant than in the City’s commitment to rebuild the Piedmont Pool complex through the passage of Measure UU. The Piedmont Pool is an iconic part of the community where generations of Piedmont residents have enjoyed the outdoors. Our one and only public pool is also an essential facility providing a safe and healthy place for families to enjoy aquatics. In addition to the community usage, it also provides Piedmont students the opportunity to compete in swimming and water polo which promotes teamwork, commitment, discipline, and drive. All important qualities as they embark on their life journeys. In support of its mission, PRFO has partnered with the City in the renovation of Hampton Park and the conversion of the City’s Vista tennis courts into the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Community enthusiasm and support have made these projects a reality through private financial contributions of over $1,300,000. The catalyst for the success of these fundraising initiatives has been the City’s willingness to take the lead and commit funding first. Then PRFO, in partnership with the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (“PBF”) and other community groups, has been able to rally private donations to support the success of these improvements. The boards of PRFO and PBF have both endorsed Measure UU. Should Measure UU pass, and if asked by the City, PRFO would be willing and ready to rally community financial support for the Piedmont Pool. But first things first, the voters of Piedmont need to decide if they want the City to rebuild a pool for the next 50 years. For the sake of the health of our community, I hope the answer is yes. Steve Collins is President of Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization. Measure UU – F.A.Q. City’s answers to Frequently Asked Questions about Pool bond. 1. The City proposes to issue $19.5 Million in bonds. What is the actual expected borrowing interest rate assuming the bond passes this year? Municipal bonds can be issued in stages as the funds are needed, and the applicable interest rate is determined at the time the bonds are issued. As a frame of reference, the interest rate as of September 16, 2020 is 2.8%. 2. What is the City’s current total outstanding general obligation debt? The City currently has no outstanding general obligation debt. 3. What is the term of the bond repayment? Measure UU provides that the term of the bond repayment is 30 years with a fixed interest rate. 4. How long will the tax be imposed on properties, and will the amount of the tax ever decrease? Measure UU, if adopted, would impose a tax on properties for 30 years. In the event our property tax roll increases at 3.5% per year (10- year average is ~4.5%), the tax rate per $1,000 of assessed value will drop from $0.26 (if all bonds are issued) to approximately $0.10 in thirty years. The total tax assessed would still be the same but redistributed based on the individual property assessment. 5. How can a property owner ascertain the assessed value of property? Each year, the Alameda County Assessor’s Office notifies all property owners of the property’s annual assessed value. This number can also be found on a property owner’s property tax bill. Residents can ascertain the assessed value of their home on the Alameda County Assessor’s website. 6. How does Measure UU impact the City’s General Fund? Measure UU does not have an impact on the City’s General Fund. 7. What is the proposed concept for replacing the existing pool? In the event Measure UU is adopted, the exact design of the pool facility will be finalized through a public process. The current proposed concept to replace the existing pool is the establishment of two pools: (1) a warmer, shallower recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation, and (2) a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. Each pool would be larger than the current “medium” and “big” pools. 8. What are the estimated costs of the project compared to bond revenues and what steps will the City take to limit project costs to available bond revenues? The measure would authorize the City to issue bonds with a principal value that does not exceed $19.5 million. In the event the City receives an AA+ bond rating, it is conceivable the bonds would be sold at a premium and Measure UU would provide revenues in excess of the face value of the bonds. The City determined that the $19.5 million figure was appropriate based on rough “hard cost” estimates as follows: $8 million for the two pools to replace the current “medium” and “big” pools, $3.5 million for site preparation, and $6 million for a building to house the pool equipment, restrooms, offices, and community space. If necessary, the concept can be value-engineered during final design development to meet the budget parameters. 9. Can the City repair the existing pool? The City has determined that repairing the existing pool is not a feasible option. The City has been continuously repairing the existing pool since it took over operations in 2011. The repairs required to keep the facility safe and operational have become increasingly expensive every year, and the facility is now at the point where pool decks need to be removed in order to address structural issues. A renovation of the existing facility would require not only major structural repair and equipment replacement but would also trigger significant site work required to meet current health, safety, and accessibility regulations. 10. What oversight is in place to ensure that the bond funds are used properly? Measure UU provides that a bond oversight committee be appointed to make sure the bonds are issued and spent in accordance with the terms of Measure UU. As with any project, staff and the City Council will also work to ensure proper use of public funds. The project will also be subject to the City’s project risk management policy. For more information see the website: www. communitypoolforpiedmont.com. READ IT IN THE POST Former Mayors make the case for community pool It is long past time for Piedmont to rebuild our one and only community pool. Current residents of Piedmont have benefitted from the generosity of prior residents who built, paid for, and in many cases donated our buildings, parks, playfields and of course, the pool. Their generosity toward future generations has allowed us, as taxpayers, to focus our collective resources on our excellent public schools. It is now our turn to step up to rebuild our failing infrastructure. The two measures on the ballot in November are about repairing and replacing what is broken. Measure UU will allow Piedmont to issue, for the first time ever, municipal bonds to rebuild the failing 56-year-old Piedmont Pool. Municipal bonds are like a 30-year fixed-rate community mortgage, repaid through property tax assessments. Measure TT will align the real property transfer tax – only paid when a home is bought or sold – to match those of Berkeley and Oakland, and use the funds to repair and maintain our city facilities and failing roads and sidewalks. To us, six former Piedmont Mayors, the focus on long-term planning is a sign of pragmatic and strategic thinking. The current City Council unanimously placed Measures UU and TT on the ballot because our failing infrastructure can’t wait. Spending more to repair a crumbling pool facility makes no fiscal sense. Borrowing money at low interest rates to rebuild a necessary civic asset is the prudent decision. Soon the City Council will be forced to make the decision that no one wants to make: to permanently close the Piedmont Pool. If Measure UU does not pass, Piedmont will then fail to provide a basic public amenity that every other city in Alameda County provides to its residents. Whether you swim or not, the lack of a municipal pool would be a profound loss for our community and our schools. Please join us in supporting the future of Piedmont and voting yes on Measures UU and TT. Former Piedmont Mayors: Dean Barbieri Michael Bruck John Chiang Abe Friedman Susan Hill Valerie Matzger After 20 years, let’s get the job done Editor: I am very happy to write in support of UU so that we can finally get a new aquatic center in Piedmont. As some may remember, I was involved in the last major effort to build a new pool (2000- 02. Predictably, the same tired opposition points are emerging this time – parking, traffic, noise, cost, “outsiders,” “now is not the time,” and (horrors!) the specter of swim meets. If we can finally build an aquatic center befitting Piedmont, every member of the community will benefit, from little babies learning to swim; to young children playing to their hearts’ content; to club team members; to high school athletes; to adult lap swimmers; to the disabled; to seniors looking for safe exercise. The aquatic center will also be a gathering place for community members to enjoy each other’s company in a casual atmosphere by the pool. If we don’t build a new aquatic center, Piedmont will be relegated to the ranks of those few California communities that have neither a community pool nor a high school pool, and this will affect the appeal of Piedmont as a place to live, not to mention the effect on property values. So, let’s finally get this done. A new aquatic center will be a highlight among everything that makes Piedmont such a great place to live! Th team is inviting all interested Piedmonts to come on a practice ride. They even have bikes for students to use initially. “We’re committed to getting more kids on bikes. A residual impact of COVID- 19 on sports throughout the country has been the rise of biking. As example, the Piedmont Mountain Bike team has grown to 30 members, all Piedmont High School students. They hopel to become an official school activity at PHS with a season to run concurrently with other sports. “We’ve been doubling our members every year. We’re in conversation with the high school about whether we’d become a true Piedmont sport or we stay a club,” said coach Sally Aldridge. “The team is in the transitional phase. We’re looking for a home and ready for the next step.” Unike orevious years, Piedmont is no longer a member of the Oakland Composite Mountain Bike Team, which was a mix of kids from Piedmont, Oakland Tech, Bishop O’Dowd, HeadRoyce, and Skyline. With the unique circumstances of coronavirus, a separation from Oakland Composite was required in order to ride in smaller pods. But a the uncertainties of many sports, including when and where to play and how, has meant a boon for biking. “Fortunately we’re now large enough to stand alone, so this is an opportunity to put in the work to become our own program,” said Aldridge. “Our growth rate meant we were planning on eventually making the move. Now is a good time. Of note, its expansion has been without active recruiting. Even with 30 members, its large coaching staff says there’s plenty of room. The teams has 18 returning riders and 12 who are new. Team members will start recruiting this month. “We are open to expanding. We have 13 volunteer coaches and we feel that we can safely break up into pods. We have a relatively low COVID risk for a sport due to being non-contact and outdoors. We have a natural six-foot separation when riding on bikes. We’re outside in nature and we’re moving, creating a lot of wind flow,”said Aldridge Current plans are to have recruiting rides every Sunday at 10 a.m. until November 22, with the specific hopes of adding more girls to the team. It is an inclusive “no-cut” team, so everyone gets to ride. In addition to individual races there is team scoring, having plenty of boys and girls will help the team with competeive scoring. Piedmont is in the heart of some spectacular mountain bike courses, so it puts the team memebrs into some of the best trails in Joaquin Miller, Redwood Regional, and Anthony Chabot Regiona Parks. Their season is expected to start on December 1 with three practices per week; two outdoor and one indoor dependent on weather. The team is still waiting on official word from the governing body of the National Interscholastic Cycling Association regarding schedules and competitin, but time trials similar using Piedmont senior Nate Willson takes a turn. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team will be recruiting new members from October 18 to November 22.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Roots The Roots now prepare for their USL campaign in the fall of next year. The Oakland Roots soccer team suffered a 2-1 loss to Detroit City FC in the NISA Finals on October 2 ot end their season. It was a familiar feeling for the Roots after losing by the same score against the same team in the group stage of the tournament. Prior to the game, the Roots announced that the championship round would be their last appearance in NISA. Next year they will be playing in the United Soccer League, with an opening scheduled for fall of 2021. The game was played at Keyworth Stadium on the outskirts of Detroit. Oakland entered a bit shorthanded at the back without captain Nana Attakora and starting rightback Robert Hines, both out with leg injuries. The Roots have done well up to that point out of the back with David Abidor as their defensive leader at centerback, Daniel Navarro filling in for Attakora, while manager Jordan Ferrell rotated backup Niall Irwin and usual winger Diego Casillas at rightback. The Roots held a 1-0 advantage at halftime, with a goal in the 27th minute by Johnny Rodriguez who scored on a leaping header off a corner kick from Nelson Blanco – both recently acquired players. The Roots had another goal called off after veteran forward Matt Fondy was a couple of feet offside on the far-post. But, similar to their earlier loss to Detroit in the group stages, Oakland’ failure to capitalize on its scoring chances in the first half came back to haunt them. Detroit tied it at 1-1 on a goal in the 65th minute after its super sub, Shawn-Claud Lawson, entered three minutes earlier. Lawson has been Detroit’s sub in each game, scoring in the first 25 minutes. After a failed clearance attempt by Casillas, the ball went to Lawson’s feet like a magnet and he score with a shot to the bottom right corner of the net. The Roots had another chance moments later in the 69th after Blanco sent a nice ball over the top to Fondy, but he didn’t make solid contact on his first-touch Photo courtesy of SFGate The Oakland Roots soccer team lost in the NISA Finals 2-1 to Detroit City FC. shot attempt. The game-winner came in the 84th minute after Detroit sent a long ball down toward the Roots’ penalty area. Oakland keeper Christian Herrera was caught out of position after attempting to approach the ball, then backtracking toward net. The Detroit attacker quickly chipped the ball over Herrera off a volley from the top-left area of the box. The Roots nearly tied the game in stoppage time after gaining a corner opportunity. Striker Jack McInerney found a bouncing ball in the area, sending a shot toward the net. After a ricochet to Fondy in front of the goal line, the ball somehow skipped off Detroit defender Evans Frimpong’s chest sitting on the goal line, skipping it high into the crossbar and out of goal. Abidor had a shot in the 95th minute, but ti was headed off the line by a defender. The final whistle blew moments later and Detroit stormed the field. Good news for local soccer fans. United Soccer League games are scheduled to be shown on ESPN next yeaar.

articles.text: Another week in the NFL season has come and gone, and both the 49ers and Raiders proved me wrong in Week 4. The Niners lost 25-20 to the Eagles and Vegas (Raiders) lost to the Bills, 30-23 loss. KC is allowing 161 rushing yards per game, so it’s possible Raiders RB Josh Jacobs could be on track for his first 100-yard rushing performance of the season. Their use of him will depend on Vegas’ ability to keep the score close. A’s facing elimination The second-seeded A’s lost 5-2 yesterday in the playoffs against division rivals and defending AL champs, the Houston Astros. They dropped their first game 10-5 on Monday. Now down 2-0 in a best of five series, they play again tomorrow at 12:35 p.m. and face elimination in American League Division. It’s been a home runs fest between both teams with a combined six homers in Monday’s game followed by five on Tuesday. The A’s also faced elimination in the best of three AL Wildcard series after falling behind to the White Sox, but survived. For the perennial underdog Athletics, perhaps their backs being against the wall is what sparks its magic. Premier League With the Oakland Roots professiona soccer team concluding its season, we jump over the pond back to England and the Premier League, which just closed its summer transfer window. Teams will not be eligible to adjust their roster again until January. Now entering the International Break for Europe’s Nations League and other national-team matches, play will not resume for the Premier League for two weeks. But, boy, did the fourth of 38 Match Days provide some action. Far and away the biggest shock was Aston Villa – which finished just outside of relegation in 17th – pounce on defending Premier League champions Liverpool 7-2 on Sunday. It was the first time Liverpool FC ever conceded seven goals in a Premier League game and the first time they have allowed seven since facing Tottenham in 1963. Tottenham Hotspur, meanwhile, handed Manchester United a 6-1 defeat last Sunday as well. As things stand right now, Everton and Aston Villa are the only undefeated teams in Premier League. The Toffees of Everton are in first with a 4-0-0 record with Villa already having a third of their wins total from last year in second at 3-0-0. Photos courtesy of NBC Sports Kyle Shanahan’ 49eers were upset 25-20 by the Eagles. They face the Dolphins this weekend and are expected to win. The 49ers, expected to win, were unable to get anything going behind backup quarterback Nick Mullens. He threw an interception which was returned for a touchdown for what proved to eb th winning score. The Eagles only allowed three sacks against SF’s aggressive scheme. San Francisco is now 2-2 and coach Kyle Shanahan is unsure if QB Jimmy Garoppolo, with a high ankle sprain, will be ready for Week 5 against the Miami Dolphins this Sunday. Regardless, the 49ers should be favored, as they were last week. To win, the 49ers’ defense will have to continue playing well against a Dolphins’ offense that ranks in the bottom half of the league. Miami, meanwhile, has one of the worst defenses in the league. All in all, Niner fans should expect a win – or did we say that last week? Raiders The Raiders pushed to within a touchdown, 30-23, but the offense did itself no favors by losing a fumble with the game at 23-16 in the fourth quarter. It led to the Bills scoring their final touchdown. Vegas faces another tall task this week against the defending Super Bowl champions, Kansas City. If the Raiders want to pull off an upset, they will need to limit Chiefs’ quartrback Patrick Mahomes, a highly unlikely outcome. In recent years, swimmers were transported by boat to the south tower of the Golden Gate Bridge, then swam one mile to the north tower, where they were picked up and returned by boat. articles.text: There were few ways to connect safely with others during the pandemic, but Piedmont’s Scouts in Troop 4 kept busy this summer with public service and outdoor activities, all in a COVID-safe manner. Wearing masks and social distancing allowed them to participate in a number of adventures during a time when many activities were not allowed. “COVID-19 made it more difficult to enjoy our regular summer scouting activities, like Camp Marin Sierra,” confirmed Troop 4 Scoutmaster Walter Stokes. “But Troop 4 rose to the occasion and put together a variety of outdoor and public service activities that were COVID-safe. “The feedback from our Scouts is that they greatly enjoyed these in-person activities despite the restrictions. They helped us fulfill our scouting goals of physical fitness, character building, and community service,” he added. Some Scouts rode their bikes from Piedmont to Treasure Island and back. Other Scouts got up early to ride the biking trails in Briones and Redwood Regional Parks. They even created their own bicycle maintenance and repair workshop where each Scout, with a set of tools, learned important repair skills. Not only did Scouts have fun, but they earned merit badges as well. Troop 4 also did some backyard camping this summer. Scouts were able to connect with each other via Zoom and review valuable skills while enjoying the great outdoors. Scouts also enjoyed masked hikes in local regional parks. And some even went sailing. Scouts who went on the traditional 50-Mile backpacking trip maintained a “pod” for three weeks in advance to make sure they were all COVID-free when they embarked on the trip. Several of the Scouts even got tested in advance. Several Troop 4 Scouts managed to complete their Eagle projects over the summer. Newly minted Eagle Scout Tom Robinson led a group in painting a mural on a storage shed at Maya Angelou Academy in Oakland, adding color and beauty to the playground. Troop 4 is now welcoming new members. If your son or daughter is interested in exploring Scouts, contact Sarah King at sarahdmertz@yahoo.com. His brother Kevin Blodgett completed his Eagle project by building a fruit storage box for Piedmont Middle School’s Green Team.

articles.text: Summer choir camps are a balance of intensive instruction and peer interaction. trails, and students even get to try organic cuisine grown from the camp’s garden, made possible by restaurateur Alice Waters, known for her Berkeley restaurant Chez Panisse. “Choir camp is a balance of really intensive music training, a bunch of traditions that we’ve developed over 35 years, and being in a beautiful and natural environment,” explained Founding Artistic Director Robert Geary. Each camp runs for about one week, and includes rigorous music theory and choral instruction, balanced with socialization and downtime. Singers rehearse for four to five hours each day. “When young people get together out of their home and school environment, it’s a real growing experience,” Geary said. Given the current uncertainty surrounding the health safety of group singing, Piedmont Children’s Choir decided to offer camp as a virtual program this past summer. Artistic Director Eric Tuan confessed that the students were disappointed by the news due to their love of spending time at the camp. “When the students learned that they couldn’t go to Walker Creek this year, they cried. Camp is such an integral part of the experience,” Tuan said. But the choir faculty was able to craft an engaging experience through the digital medium, while providing something that was different from the online rehearsals that they had in the Spring semester. Maintaining engagement and ensuring students were out of their chairs were key factors when developing a digital camp. “I think it exemplified what the challenge is. We asked ourselves, ‘What is the core of our program? What keeps our students engaged with music. How do we transfer that to a completely different medium?’” Tuan said. Mornings at camp consisted of campfire songs or activities to start the day, followed by a 30-minute music theory class and rehearsal rotations. One advantage of the digital camp was that each student was given individualized choral instruction. “Which is no mean feat for a group of 46,” Tuan added with a smile. The camp faculty sent students home with “camp kits,” which included an electric candle, friendship bracelet material, arts and crafts and other sleepaway camp essentials. In an effort to keep students creatively engaged. As example, this year’s camp was based on a theme of Harry Potter. Students were part of a Potter-themed “house,” and competed against one another to win a prize at the end of camp. Working cohesively and building peer relations are pillars of the camp program, explained Tuan. Utilizing small group classes and one-on-one vocal training in combination with adapted camp traditions helped make it a smooth transition. For more information on choir camps, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/camps-and-tours. Next week: Performing Department

articles.text: Comedian Andy Samberg B e r k e l e y S y m p h o n y announced the launch of “Reading is Instrumental,” a new weekly musical storytime series for children and adults. The series is hosted by the symphony, in partnership with the Berkeley Public Library. It is co-produced by the symphony and the Berkeley Public Library Foundation. Weekly storytime readings began on Friday, September 25, with multi-awardwinning actress Rita Moreno, who read The Runaway Bunny by Margaret Wise Brown. The series continued last Friday with author and Professor Emerita at University of California, Berkeley Maxine Hong Kingston and husband Earl Kingston. The couple read Baby’s Got the Blues by Carol Diggory Shields, a humorous story about the trials of babyhood that tips its cap to legendary blues artist B.B. King. The event this Friday, October 9, will feature comedian and actor Andy Samberg, best known as a former Saturday Night Live cast member. He will read a new book by his friend Jorma Taccone titled Little Fox and the Wild Imagination. The read will begin at 11 a.m. “Berkeley Symphony is proud to partner with the Berkeley Public Library Foundation on this exciting new project that combines the art of story-telling with live music performance,” Music Director Joseph Young said. “The series encapsulates two of my lifelong passions: bringing music to young people and creating community enrichment through shared stories and experiences. There is no better time for our friends and family to come together virtually and see that arts are alive and well in Berkeley.” Berkeley Public Library Foundation Executive Director Kathy Huff echoed Young’s sentiments. “Music and words together are a magical combination,” she said. “We are incredibly grateful for all who have agreed to help make this fun program happen during these exceptional times. We all need stories and music to keep our spirits up, but our kids and families who are at home need them.” Earlier reads are available on the symphony’s Facebook page: ht t ps://w w w.facebook.com / berkeleypubliclibrary/.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young will be joined in a one-on-one conversation with pianist Conrad Tao tomorrow, October 8. He has captivated Berkeley audiences in his earlier performances with the symphony. Young sits down with Tao for a wide-ranging conversation, punctuated by piano performances featuring Tao’s vast catalogue of original works, classic favorites, and modern masterpieces. Tao has appeared worldwide as a pianist and composer, and is a recipient of an Avery Fisher Career Grant, and was named a Gilmore Young Artist, an honor highlighting the most promising American pianists of the new generation. His 2018-2019 season began with the New York Philharmonic’s world premiere of a commissioned work, Everything Must Go. He made his Los Angeles Philharmonic debut performHumboldt State University, and Oregon State. Tao’s evening-length collaboration with choreographer Caleb Teicher, More Forever, will be presented by Celebrity Series of Boston, and will make its West Coast premiere at Segerstrom Hall in Orange County. His ongoing electroacoustic collaboration with improviser and vocalist Charmaine Lee continues with an opening-night performance at the 2019 Resonant Bodies Festival in New York. Young’s interview with Tao is the third episode in the “Joseph Young & Friends” series, hosted by the symphony. The series is composed of free online music gatherings, where Young invites colleagues to share intimate musical experiences. The conversations are held via teleconference application Zoom. articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players’ virtual series, Bach Shorts, continues this Sunday, Octobr 11, with cellist Jennifer Kloetzel. A founding member of the San Francisco-based Cypress String Quartet (1996-2016), she has performed at such renowned venues as Lincoln Center, the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the Lobkowicz Palaces in both Vienna and Prague, as well as prominent colleges and conservatories worldwide. She is a graduate of the Julliard School and is a Fulbright Scholar. She has concertized throughout the United States, Europe, and Asia as a soloist and chamber musician. Kloetzel’s performance this Sunday is at 4 p.m. The event will be live-streamed via YouTube Live. She will perform Bach’s popular First Cello Suite, paired with a world premiere by composer Elena Ruehr called Cricket the Fiddler. Ruehr will be on hand to share how Bach’s First Suite inspired her composition. An after-party with the musicians will be held via teleconferencing application Zoom following the performance. articles.text: Reprise of 2016 production will be in advance of elections Berkeley Repertory Theatre will produce the Sinclair Lewis novel, It Can’t Happen Here, written in 1935 during the rise of fascism in Europe. It will be staged prior to America’s presidential election on November 3. Lewis’ darkly satirical novel follows the ascent of a demagogue who becomes president of the United States by promising to return the country to greatness. The novel describes the rise of Berzelius “Buzz” Windrip, a president who foments fear and promises drastic economic and social reforms while promoting traditional values. After his election, Windrip takes complete control of the government and imposes totalitarian rule with the help of a ruthless paramilitary force in the manner of European fascists such as Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. articles.text: Bay Area Children’s Theatre (BACT) has joined a nationwide letter writing effort, #ArtsAreMySuperpower, to promote relief funding for the arts during COVID-19. The campaign encourages kids, families and teachers to write letters to the Senate and members of Congress expressing the necessity and rewards of theater, music, visual arts and dance in any culture. The campaign advocates for Congress to support the DAWN Act (Defend Arts Workers Now), a comprehensive, non-partisan, arts relief package. The DAWN act would authorize $44 billion in grants for the operators, employees, and artists of live venues, recording venues, and cultural spaces. Letter-writing templates for young artists are available at www.BeAnArtsHero.com/artsare-my-superpower, or letters can be drafted from scratch. Young artists are asked to attach a piece of art (a poem, a scene, a song, or a drawing) and send them to their senator. Pictures of the letters and artists can also be shared on social media with the hashtags: #ArtsAreMySuperpower, #ArtsHero, and #DAWNAct. “This campaign hopes to reach hundreds of thousands of kids. Hundreds of organizations are already signed on to help promote it,” said Nina Meehan, CEO of Bay Area Children’s Theater, the largest children’s theater program in California and formerly based at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “It is not only about theater, it is about visual arts, dance, and music. We know that there are so many talented, wonderful young people that have found their voice through all sorts of different medium. We just want to 8th grade BACT participant, Dhruv, holds up his letter in support of funding the arts through #ArtsAreMySuperpower. make sure our politicians understand that arts are a vital part of a young person’s life,” Meehan emphasized. “Without massive, immediate Federal relief to the Arts & Culture sector, we will lose an entire generation who would have otherwise joined the labor force of the Creative economy, not to mention consumers of Arts and Culture,” said Jonathan Chapman, executive director of Theater for Young Audiences, a national organization. The arts and culture industry added $877 billion to America’s GDP last year and employed 5.1 million people. Fine art and performing arts have been hit the hardest by COVID, with an estimated 1.4 million jobs and $42.5 billion in lost revenue. “Without [relief], our youths may be forced to divert their dreams, our social fabric will tear, and our economy will suffer catastrophic results locally and nationally,” Chapman added. The Bay Area Children’s Theater is based in Oakland and has reached over 700,000 students thorough its productions and educational programs in its 16-year existence. The #ArtsAreMySuperpower letter writing campaign continues to the end of October.
articles.title: Bay Area Children’s Theater fights with the pen for survival of arts

articles.text: Everyone knows about Benjamin Franklin. He would be a fine subject for an opera. Richard Wagner could craft a profound melodrama - perhaps along the lines of Lohengrin. But Gilbert and Sullivan would do Franklin with equal aplomb. Rossini would zero in on Franklin‘s love life. After all, Franklin was the darling of Parisienne society, deluding himself on his fluent French. Can you imagine the soliloquy scene during the electric storm? That would surely test the skills of a stage manager. But we need a quick fade to the insanity scene. Those “mad scenes“ were popular in opera. Why insanity? Because Benjamin Franklin actually invented a musical instrument which caused insanity. Like a kid plunking his finger on water glasses, Franklin invented the glass armonica. It was very popular – for a time. But when insanity put the foremost armonica players into the crazy house, that was the end of the glass armonica. The instrument resurfaced more recently when the glass armonica claimed that its old reputation was a lie. Benjamin Franklin had a minor career as a composer. But that is a story in itself – and for another day. Organists come in two categories: church organists and concert organists. There are many of the first category and very few of the second. Supply and demand has a lot to do with it. Though there were many church organists, there was only one Johann Sebastian Bach. Conversely, just as there were many orchestrators, there was only one Beethoven. I discovered the artistry of an Italian organist on YouTube the other day, and he is awesome. Marco Cadario played locally in the Piedmont Center for the Arts a few years ago, but here he played the Center’s beautiful Marco Cadario a wizard of the organ. Steinway. That was awesome enough. But his organ playing is amazing. It’s worth searching on the internet for Cadario playing Rossini‘s overture to La Gazza Ladra. You will discover the very meaning of greatness. Like most people, organists have two hands and two feet. But the organ has as many as four keyboards, a wooden keyboard manipulated by the feet , and a warren of levers to color the sound. The levers are the spice cabinet of the gourmet. With hands flying in all directions, feet running akimbo, and levers opened and closed to color the sound, an organist needs to be many at one time. The ideal organist might look like the offspring of a stegosaurus and an octopus. Benjamin Franklin seated at the glass armonica.
articles.title: Water glasses and insanity (that’s crazy)

articles.text: One Fair Wage founder Saru Jayaraman, will speak and answer questions with Waging Change filmmaker Abby Ginzberg on Zoom October 14. Waging Change, a film by Abby Ginzberg, is a powerful, uplifting documentary about the long-shot campaign of Saru Jayaraman and her restaurant worker colleagues to oppose the powerful National Restaurant Association and its lobbyists in order to achieve a livable income for their work and to end the unfair tip-based system of payment. The Federal minimum wage for tipped workers is $2.13 an hour. For our screening of Waging Change, we’re trying a new format: Stream the film between October 9-18 at your convenience. Join the filmmaker and One Fair Wage founder in an exclusive Q & A on Zoom on October 14. It is free. To register for the film and discussion, click on www.diversityfilmseries.org.

articles.text: Jeng is no stranger to exhibiting her work. Home from college last spring because of the pandemic, she painted a still-life series using toilet paper rolls and take-out containers as part of the Art Walk on June 13 sponsored by the Piedmont Arts Fund. Her paintings sold within the first hour. “There is more to consider now; there are heavy events happening in the world,” Jeng said. “But I feel like art is my happy escape. The toilet-paper rolls and take-out containers were more a funny, comical nod to COVID than the difficult, hard aspects of it.” “Ever since I was kid, I’ve liked drawing,” said Jeng who created and helped lead the Art Jam Club at Piedmont High. “It’s a life-long and fundamental hobby of mine. Because I’ve been doing it for so long, my identity and how my life has gone, is because of art,” said Jeng. Discover local artists at the next Piedmont Arts Fund Art Walk on May 2, 2021. To nominate a visual or performing artist in Piedmont for a future article, please contact Kristen Hatcher at hatcherk10@gmail.com Natalie Jeng is currently enrolled at Chicago Art Institute. When Natalie Jeng finished the final painting of her Advanced Placement Art Class at Piedmont High before she graduated in 2019, she had no idea it would hang in a renowned San Francisco art museum the very next year. In August she was notified that she would be among 762 artists from nine Bay Area counties selected to be included in the deYoung Open. Her painting, “The Pale Man”, will be on display starting this weekend, October 10. Fewer than eight percent of submissions were accepted. Jeng plans to attend the artists’ viewing of the exhibit during the weekend. “It is really exciting and really unexpected,” said Jeng, now a sophomore at Chicago Art Institute. . “I’m so honored and I’m so happy to be part of the show,” she said. Artist Natalie Jeng at work in her home studio.

articles.text: A scene from Kin Dza Dza. My grandma is Russian. She is one of the greatest people in the world. When I have a problem – any problem – I always leave her apartment with a solution. She also finds a treat for me to give to my mom when I get home. But the one type of advice I do not go to her for is movies. The thing is that my grandma is not bilingual so we usually watch movies from Russia which she enjoys and can understand everything. Right now, I think I know what you’re thinking: it’s not that bad, it’s just American movies but translated to Russian, right? Wrong. This amazing woman will find movies that were made when Russia became the USSR. That means crazy plots, strange scripts, and bizarre costumes. The champion of those kinds of movies is Kin Dza Dza. This movie is about a man who goes to buy bread and sees a homeless man, so he and another man stop to help. The homeless man claims that he is an alien who is shapeshifted to fit in. The three of them are arguing and somehow the two strangers get transported to the alien’s world. If you aren’t confused yet, you will be. The two men are now on a new planet with nothing but a pack of cigarettes, matches and a violin. We find out later it is called Pluke and is desert as far as the eye can see. We learn that the inhabitants are human versions of moles because they live underground. As any rational human, they are very confused as to how they got there, and they try to figure out how to get back to earth. We see a flying apparatus approaching, something that looks like a rusted metal bucket with a propeller on top. I am still so confused as to how the thing didn’t fall apart, much less flying you somewhere. But these are locals and they seem to know what they are doing. communicate through one word, KU. This word may look simple but when you say it with different tones it can have different meanings. The two locals get out of there flying mobile, bend their knees, tap their cheeks twice, and extend their arms to their sides, and quizzically ask, ku? As if asking themselves what the heck they are doing there. After five cringe-worthy minutes of trying to talk to each other, the locals get back in their flying rust bucket and start flying away. In anger one of the stranded men takes out a pack of cigarettes and strikes a match to light it. The rust bucket that was flying quickly comes back and the locals start going crazy because of his matches. We learn that this world is deprived of fire, so it is their most prized possession. After trying, one of the locals adapts to their language which is Russian. Now able to properly communicate, the stranded man tells the locals that they need to get back to earth. The locals explain that they need a special kind of fuel to get them home. After flying around, they get to an outpost, which obviously is underground. And since they are visitors, they must wear bells around their noses for some absurd reason. I couldn’t figure that out for the life of me. Being a foolish person, the visitor traded away some of the matches for food, but the traders now with the matches, high-tailed it out of there. They are down by a couple of matches, so they try to find another outpost but with no success. One of the stranded men asks to use the restroom and he is shown the bathroom. After a suspicious amount of time in the bathroom, the second man looks, only to see that the bathroom is gone. The locals said that he was catapulted out. The second man demands that they search for him. While he was looking for him, the locals got back into their apparatus and flew away, leaving the two Russians stranded once more. Eventually they find each other. And that is it for the first of two episodes. I won’t explain the next episode to save you any further trauma. If I had to pick a movie to describe our current year, 2020, this would be the perfect one. It’s so crazy and confusing that it’s as if the Russians predicted the future. If you are into this kind of stuff and don’t mind subtitles, this movie would be perfect. A scene from Kin Dza Dza.
articles.title: Movie recommendations from Grandma

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) reopened on Sunday, October 4, after about six months of closure due to the current health crisis. There is still time to catch the “Dawoud Bey: An American Project” exhibition, which will close on October 12. Since the beginning of his career, Bey has used the camera to depict communities and histories that have largely remained underrepresented or even unseen. This full-scale retrospective highlights the artist’s commitment over the course of his four-decade career to portraying the Black subject and African-American history in a manner that is at once direct and poetic, and immediate and symbolic. The exhibition includes his tender and perceptive early portraits of Harlem residents, largescale color Polaroids, and a series of collaborative word and image portraits of high school students, among others. More recent projects have taken a historical turn: The Birmingham Project (2012) commemorates the 1963 bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama, in a series of deeply affective portrait diptychs. Lately, Bey has turned to landscapes: Night Coming TenArtist Dawoud Bey derly, Black (2018) depicts, in deep shades of black and gray, the imagined experience of a fugitive slave moving along the Underground Railroad, marking a formal departure from the artist’s earlier work but considering the same existential questions about race, history, and the possibility of bearing witness through contemporary photography. The exhibition is co-organized with the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York City. For more information, see: https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/dawoud-bey-an-americanproject/. SF MOMA is offering two weeks of free community days and free parking at the museum from now through October 18. Daily attendance will be limited to 25 percent capacity. Social distancing is required, and all visitors age 3 and older must wear masks while in the building. Entry will be through timed tickets. In response to COVID-19, the museum has temporarily paused all group tours. The museum opens at 10 a.m. Friday through Monday and opens at 1 p.m. on Thursdays.
articles.title: Dawoud Bey exhibition at SF MOMA closes Oct. 12

Social distancing is required, and all visitors age 3 and older must wear masks while in the building. Entry will be through timed tickets. In response to COVID-19, the museum has temporarily paused all group tours. The museum opens at 10 a.m. Friday through Monday and opens at 1 p.m. on Thursdays. Movie recommendations from Grandma A scene from Kin Dza Dza. By Larissa Edel My grandma is Russian. She is one of the greatest people in the world. When I have a problem – any problem – I always leave her apartment with a solution. She also finds a treat for me to give to my mom when I get home. But the one type of advice I do not go to her for is movies. The thing is that my grandma is not bilingual so we usually watch movies from Russia which she enjoys and can understand everything. Right now, I think I know what you’re thinking: it’s not that bad, it’s just American movies but translated to Russian, right? Wrong. This amazing woman will find movies that were made when Russia became the USSR. That means crazy plots, strange scripts, and bizarre costumes. The champion of those kinds of movies is Kin Dza Dza. This movie is about a man who goes to buy bread and sees a homeless man, so he and another man stop to help. The homeless man claims that he is an alien who is shapeshifted to fit in. The three of them are arguing and somehow the two strangers get transported to the alien’s world. If you aren’t confused yet, you will be. The two men are now on a new planet with nothing but a pack of cigarettes, matches and a violin. We find out later it is called Pluke and is desert as far as the eye can see. We learn that the inhabitants are human versions of moles because they live underground. As any rational human, they are very confused as to how they got there, and they try to figure out how to get back to earth. We see a flying apparatus approaching, something that looks like a rusted metal bucket with a propeller on top. I am still so confused as to how the thing didn’t fall apart, much less flying you somewhere. But these are locals and they seem to know what they are doing. By the way, the locals can only communicate through one word, KU. This word may look simple but when you say it with different tones it can have different meanings. The two locals get out of there flying mobile, bend their knees, tap their cheeks twice, and extend their arms to their sides, and quizzically ask, ku? As if asking themselves what the heck they are doing there. After five cringe-worthy minutes of trying to talk to each other, the locals get back in their flying rust bucket and start flying away. In anger one of the stranded men takes out a pack of cigarettes and strikes a match to light it. The rust bucket that was flying quickly comes back and the locals start going crazy because of his matches. We learn that this world is deprived of fire, so it is their most prized possession. After trying, one of the locals adapts to their language which is Russian. Now able to properly communicate, the stranded man tells the locals that they need to get back to earth. The locals explain that they need a special kind of fuel to get them home. After flying around, they get to an outpost, which obviously is underground. And since they are visitors, they must wear bells around their noses for some absurd reason. I couldn’t figure that out for the life of me. Being a foolish person, the visitor traded away some of the matches for food, but the traders now with the matches, high-tailed it out of there. They are down by a couple of matches, so they try to find another outpost but with no success. One of the stranded men asks to use the restroom and he is shown the bathroom. After a suspicious amount of time in the bathroom, the second man looks, only to see that the bathroom is gone. The locals said that he was catapulted out. The second man demands that they search for him. While he was looking for him, the locals got back into their apparatus and flew away, leaving the two Russians stranded once more. Eventually they find each other. And that is it for the first of two episodes. I won’t explain the next episode to save you any further trauma. If I had to pick a movie to describe our current year, 2020, this would be the perfect one. It’s so crazy and confusing that it’s as if the Russians predicted the future. If you are into this kind of stuff and don’t mind subtitles, this movie would be perfect. A scene from Kin Dza Dza.

articles.text: Tom Holland and Charlie Hunnam stars in The Lost City of Z. The Lost City of Z is based on the best-selling nonfiction book by David Grann, wherein he recounts the early 20th century expeditions of Major Percy Fawcett to the Amazon in search of a dream he called “Z.” The year is 1905, and, as the film soon reveals, Percy’s first expedition is at the behest of the Royal Geographic Society who wishes him to survey what is a questionable border between Brazil and Bolivia. Percy (Charlie Hunnam) agrees, hoping to redeem his family name (apparently his father was a dissolute rogue) in the hopes of being promoted among the ranks of both the army and society. He and his second in command, Henry Costin (Robert Pattison), carrying surveying gear and only a general idea of their destination, arrive at the Amazon River, hire local guides, procure a raft, and thus begin what will be a two-year trip into a jungle that is startlingly beautiful, oppressively hot and ominously dangerous, its gorgeous lethality ever present. England it is not. They encounter not only a hostile natural environment, but also hostile natives who attack them from the shore with spears and arrows. They also come across, in the dead of night, a most improbable and surreal opera performance, organized by a rubber baron who gives them a raft, supplies and local guides. Meanwhile, Fawcett and Costin persevere, traveling deep into the forest, mapping and diagraming the area. It is when they finally reach the headwaters of the Amazon that Percy comes upon carvings in trees and shards of refined pottery, all indicating that there had once been a sophisticated civilization there, something that was unexpected. It was a discovery that would engulf Fawcett’s imagination for the rest of his life. Having completed their assignment and running low on supplies, they make the arduous journey back down river, eventually arriving in England to a hero’s welcome. The Royal Society asks Fawcett to deliver a summary of his astonishing expedition; however, so rigid is the colonial viewpoint held in the England of 1905, the members insist that Fawcett’s claim of an advanced society deep in the jungle is nonsense, The tribes that inhabit the area were considered as “savages,” a practiced colonial point of view. Percy claims to differ and attempts to argue his findings, much to the Society’s disbelief that there could have been a civilization that predated their own. What makes this film compelling is Fawcett’s obsession with his conviction that what he found (and called the Lost City of “Z,” or “Zed,”) was real. Percy has a lovely family that he must leave behind for years each time he returns to the rain forest in search of what many believed to be a myth. His wife, Nina Fawcett (Sienna Miller), is at first supportive. But as their family grows, she argues that though their children who need them both, she insists on accompanying him on his next trip. But it is out of the question. And so, Nina stays behind, feeling the full weight of a patriarchal society. What receives little exposition in the film is the price that Fawcett is willing to pay in order to search for his dream. His willingness to abandon his family for repeated journeys into this unforgiving environment, seems irrational. And yet he returns and returns again until that moment arrives when he and his now grown son, Jack (Tom Holland), who pleads to go with him on one final expedition, are never seen again. What comes to mind is the unforgettable story of George Mallory as he and a guide trekked up the face of Everest, only to vanish in the mist (recently found, frozen and intact, Mallory’s body pointing upward). This impulse to explore is woven into the tapestry of the human condition, the unknown ever seductive, beckoning, harrowing, and often ultimately demanding a sacrifice that can become irrevocable. In The Lost City of Z it’s the Amazon. But it’s also Everest, the Arctic, the ocean’s horizon, all involving travels both outward and inward, just beyond the reach and just beyond the grasp. The Lost City of Z. Starring Robert Pattison, Charlie Hunnan and Sienna Miller. 140 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Lost City of Z a search for an ancient civilization

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré If you have been exploring the extraordinary works from Studio Ghibli, you have discovered that the lead character is often a young female who is simultaneously fragile and fearless. When Marnie Was There is based on the 1967 fantasy book by English author Joan G. Robinson. The protagonist is a lonely, androgynous 12-year-old girl named Anna (Kiernan Shipka) who lives in urban Sapporo, Japan. Because she is asthmatic, her foster mother, Mrs. Kadoya (Kathy Bates), sends her to live with relatives in the country – a windswept, marshy, seaside area that will, hopefully, restore Anna’s health. While exploring the marshes, Anna unexpectedly comes across a deserted mansion that seems eerily familiar. It’s there that she encounters a strange, mysterious girl of her own age, very western looking, with striking blonde hair and wearing outof-date clothes. Unexpectedly, the two develop a friendship and begin to share dreams and diaries which, for Anna, lead to moments of self-discovery and revelation. Gradually she begins to emerge from her reclusive shell, growing more and more captivated with the house and is inhabitant, a spectral girl named Marnie. The story, languid and almost wistful, gently pulls the audience into its inherent magic, while adding goosebump moments, especially when the girls wander through a seemingly haunted lighthouse during a rainstorm. When Marnie Was There is compelling in so many ways: softly sinister at times, enigmatic, and also a coming-of-age tale with tom-boyish Anna beginning to come to terms not only with her past but with her future. The artistry is breathtaking, always hand drawn, possessing a level of exceptional animé that is the Studio Ghibli’s brand. The images – a Monet-like forest, ocean waves cresting across an inlet bay, bucolic scenes with long, contrasting shadows in a dew-covered garden – add to the richness and enchantment of the remarkable fable. When Marnie Was There (2014). Animé from Studio Ghibli. Written and directed by Hiromasa Yonebayashi. With the voices of Hailee Seinfeld, Kiernan Shipka, and Kathy Bates. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: When Marnie Was There – more magic from Studio Ghibli

articles.text: And Bill does this in spades.” Barbara Thompson reflected on her move back to California in 2004, after 11 moves around the country, “and just as many churches.” “We thought we would try Piedmont Community Church first, but after hearing one sermon by Bill, we knew we had found the perfect minister,” she said. Rich Thompson, sharing his wife’s sentiments, added that he stands in awe of McNabb’s ability to conceive, create, and deliver wonderful high-impact messages Sunday after Sunday. “You are leaving us with a strong, vibrant, financially sound church community, and a foundation on which to build for the future,” Thompson said in a final message to McNabb. Though retired, McNabb and his wife Maureen remain busy and still living at home in Piedmont. For church member stories, see: https://www.youtube.com/ w a t c h? v =l JS nV YJQ t OE &- feature=youtu.be. For stories by church staff members, see: ht t p s://w w w.yout u b e.c om / watch?v=e7VephCfx_A&feature=youtu.be. Photos by Michael Barber Retiring Senior Minister Dr. William McNabb delivers a last video message for Piedmont Community Church. Piedmont Community Church members and staff reflected on Dr. William McNabb’s time as Senior Minister in a touching virtual celebration last Sunday, September 27. The church presented a final video tribute to McNabb following his last sermon as he retired after 19 years at the helm. Long-time Church Office Manager Jean Leahy said that she has seen a number of ministers come and go, but added that she has especially enjoyed the past 19 years with McNabb. Associate Minister Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn said that he and McNabb shared a great dynamic in the church. “I think it’s been a great strength of us as a team,” Ashburn said. Leslie Quantz, Director of Children’s Ministries, shared that she had no prior experience with youth ministries when she started with the church, but that McNabb became her mentor. “When he called and asked me to do the job on an interim basis, I was really shocked,” she recalled. “I took the job and asked to become permanent after a few months because I loved it so much. I think a lot of that has to do with Bill’s guidance and support.” Quantz has been with the church for over 13 years. “Life’s way too short to work with people you don’t like. I really appreciate how Bill nurtured the family aspect of our whole staff,” said Rev. Scott Kail, the youth minister. Music Director Dr. Steve Main gathered jazz violinist Mads Tolling, guitarist Mitch Polzak and vocalist Sylvia Sudat for a musical tribute celebrate McNabb’s retirement. Each performance was done separately and edited together in a digital format. The group performed “Livin’ in the Name of Love” by Jim Rushing and Marshall Chapman, with Main, the church organist and choir director, on bass. Reflecting on his first meeting with McNabb at the Claremont Hotel in Berkeley, Main said, “While we were waiting for our table, Bill stopped and talked about the extensive wines of the Bay Area that he loved, and he remarked on the local produce we were about to eat in the meal. What became clear to me was that he was a guy who experiences his spirituality through the full enjoyment and delight of what’s right in front of him,” he said. Church members also offered their well wishes to McNabb. “Bill was probably the reason that we joined Piedmont Community Church. I was so drawn to the sermons. We’ve always appreciated how thoughtful they are, how much perspective they bring to life,” said Gwedolyn Osburn. Her husband, Mike Osburn, was baptized by McNabb along with their three daughters. Bob Coleman, always wry, said, “The trick in preaching is coming up with the right message at the right time in the right way. Rich and Barbara Thompson Jean Leahy Bob Coleman Gwedolyn and Mike Osborn McNabb exits the church after his final sermon on September 27. EAST BAY AGENCY FOR CHILDREN AUXILIARY PRESENTS
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church in fond sendoff for Bill McNabb

articles.text: The other day I stepped outside and felt that “Fall feeling.” Right now, it can be hard to detect here in the Bay Area, given how the smoke keeps settling in. Many of us are experiencing anxiety about our beloved wine country being up in flames and the impact that the fires have on everyone’s lives. Last month in this column I described a recent trip Darshan and I took to tour the studio of our beloved glass-blowing vendors, Bel Vetro in Healdsburg. This month I worry about their wellbeing and the safety of their beautiful space. As of this writing, fires are still burning in Napa County and evacuation orders continue to be in effect. One of our favorite woodworker’s homes is threatened. Bel Vetro’s owners, who have put their hearts and souls into their company, have had to evacuate twice this year. And two of our clients’ homes are in peril. All of that hard work, the love, the time, and the living that’s gone into and gone on in their homes and studios. And the heartache of the iconic Meadowood Resort, now burned. How is this possible? We need to get serious about global warming. Since I’m on this tangent already, may I suggest that you watch Kiss the Ground on Netflix for ideas on how we can heal this planet. Fires, and the heartache of that first Presidential debate last week? Heartburn. So, in light of all of this, may I say that in spite of everything, I am having a really great day. I’m noticing lately how, if somebody is doing well, they are afraid to say they are. I am afraid to say I am because it might sound like I am not concerned about what is going on in politics, institutionalized racism, the fires, COVID, all the things. And frankly, these days, I have a similar feeling when I talk about creating beautiful spaces for people. If not everyone can live in a beautiful, thoughtfully curated home, then it’s not okay for me to be an interior designer. Period. How do I make sense of the Haves and the Have-Nots? This question takes me back to my time studying and meditating with the Center for Spiritual Living. There is a principle I first heard there, and that I am reminding myself of today. “My feeling bad for someone does not do anything to make their situation better.” What do guilt and sadness do for them? Nothing. However, if I feel great, if I am engaged in self-care. if I am resourced, I’m going to want to help other people. In light of the needs of the sick, the issues being fought for in the Black Lives Matter movement, the destruction of homes and businesses in the fires, how do we go on and feel okay about what we are doing as beauty-makers? I am taking a stand for creating beauty and having self-care and self-love — and not feeling Entry— Art Deco entry with sideboard and mirror: A place to pause for a moment, in reflection.
articles.title: Finding comfort, inspiration, and joy

articles.text: It’s that time of year when, if you work for a medium-to-large employer, you’ve got some decisions to make, because it’s open enrollment time. Depending on your situation you may have been working remotely for a while, but, even so, you will likely have the opportunity to review your benefits package and make changes. You’ll want to make the right moves because your choices can have a big financial impact on your life. Take a close look at these key areas of your benefits program: be enough for your needs. If you only had this group policy, but your family situation has recently changed through marriage or the addition of a new child, you may well need to add some private insurance. • Health insurance Think about your health care needs over the coming year – will you or someone in your family be coping with a chronic illness or facing a surgery? Will you need to at least consider testing and possible treatment for COVID- 19? In any case, make sure you’re choosing the right plan for your needs. And pay close attention to any changes in your health insurance, such as whether the plan’s provider networks have changed – you may want to make sure your own doctor is still in-network. Also, check to see if you can reduce your health care premiums by taking part in a wellness program or health-risk assessment. • Disability insurance In addition to offering group life insurance, your employer may provide short-term disability insurance as an employee benefit. Like group insurance, this disability coverage may not cost you anything, but it may not be adequate – typically, short-term disability only replaces part of your income for three to six months. And while you may never need to miss work for an extended period of time, you never can tell – after all, more than one in four 20-year-olds will become disabled before they retire, according to the U.S. Social Security Administration. You may want to consider purchasing your own long-term disability policy on top of the coverage offered by your employer. • Life insurance Your employer may offer a group life insurance policy for free, or for a small amount. It’s probably worth your while to take this coverage, but it may not • Retirement plan You can probably make changes to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan at any time, but why not look at it now, when you’re reviewing all your benefits? If you can afford to increase your contributions, you probably should, because a 401(k), with its tax advantages and ease of contribution through paycheck deductions, is a great way to save for retirement. At a minimum, put in enough to earn your employer’s match. You’ll also want to review your 401(k)’s investment mix. Is it still providing you with significant growth potential within the context of your individual risk tolerance? Over time, you may need to make some adjustments, either because an investment is underperforming or because you’re getting close to retirement and you need to reduce your risk exposure. In any case, it’s a good idea to check up on your 401(k)’s investments at least once a year. Your employee benefits are an important part of your overall financial picture – so do what you can to get the most from them.
