If you only had this group policy, but your family situation has recently changed through marriage or the addition of a new child, you may well need to add some private insurance. • Health insurance Think about your health care needs over the coming year – will you or someone in your family be coping with a chronic illness or facing a surgery? Will you need to at least consider testing and possible treatment for COVID- 19? In any case, make sure you’re choosing the right plan for your needs. And pay close attention to any changes in your health insurance, such as whether the plan’s provider networks have changed – you may want to make sure your own doctor is still in-network. Also, check to see if you can reduce your health care premiums by taking part in a wellness program or health-risk assessment. • Disability insurance In addition to offering group life insurance, your employer may provide short-term disability insurance as an employee benefit. Like group insurance, this disability coverage may not cost you anything, but it may not be adequate – typically, short-term disability only replaces part of your income for three to six months. And while you may never need to miss work for an extended period of time, you never can tell – after all, more than one in four 20-year-olds will become disabled before they retire, according to the U.S. Social Security Administration. You may want to consider purchasing your own long-term disability policy on top of the coverage offered by your employer. • Life insurance Your employer may offer a group life insurance policy for free, or for a small amount. It’s probably worth your while to take this coverage, but it may not • Retirement plan You can probably make changes to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan at any time, but why not look at it now, when you’re reviewing all your benefits? If you can afford to increase your contributions, you probably should, because a 401(k), with its tax advantages and ease of contribution through paycheck deductions, is a great way to save for retirement. At a minimum, put in enough to earn your employer’s match. You’ll also want to review your 401(k)’s investment mix. Is it still providing you with significant growth potential within the context of your individual risk tolerance? Over time, you may need to make some adjustments, either because an investment is underperforming or because you’re getting close to retirement and you need to reduce your risk exposure. In any case, it’s a good idea to check up on your 401(k)’s investments at least once a year. Your employee benefits are an important part of your overall financial picture – so do what you can to get the most from them. Many of us are experiencing anxiety about our beloved wine country being up in flames and the impact that the fires have on everyone’s lives. Last month in this column I described a recent trip Darshan and I took to tour the studio of our beloved glass-blowing vendors, Bel Vetro in Healdsburg. This month I worry about their wellbeing and the safety of their beautiful space. As of this writing, fires are still burning in Napa County and evacuation orders continue to be in effect. One of our favorite woodworker’s homes is threatened. Bel Vetro’s owners, who have put their hearts and souls into their company, have had to evacuate twice this year. And two of our clients’ homes are in peril. All of that hard work, the love, the time, and the living that’s gone into and gone on in their homes and studios. And the heartache of the iconic Meadowood Resort, now burned. How is this possible? We need to get serious about global warming. Since I’m on this tangent already, may I suggest that you watch Kiss the Ground on Netflix for ideas on how we can heal this planet. Fires, and the heartache of that first Presidential debate last week? Heartburn. So, in light of all of this, may I say that in spite of everything, I am having a really great day. I’m noticing lately how, if somebody is doing well, they are afraid to say they are. I am afraid to say I am because it might sound like I am not concerned about what is going on in politics, institutionalized racism, the fires, COVID, all the things. And frankly, these days, I have a similar feeling when I talk about creating beautiful spaces for people. If not everyone can live in a beautiful, thoughtfully curated home, then it’s not okay for me to be an interior designer. Period. How do I make sense of the Haves and the Have-Nots? This question takes me back to my time studying and meditating with the Center for Spiritual Living. There is a principle I first heard there, and that I am reminding myself of today. “My feeling bad for someone does not do anything to make their situation better.” What do guilt and sadness do for them? Nothing. However, if I feel great, if I am engaged in self-care. if I am resourced, I’m going to want to help other people. In light of the needs of the sick, the issues being fought for in the Black Lives Matter movement, the destruction of homes and businesses in the fires, how do we go on and feel okay about what we are doing as beauty-makers? I am taking a stand for creating beauty and having self-care and self-love — and not feeling shame and guilt about it. Because these can be acts that will fortify us to be a part of the change we want to see in the world. I can spend time, effort, and energy creating beauty because beauty is the thing that brings us in alignment with our souls, with being human. Beauty inspires us. If we feel good, we naturally want to do good for other people If we feel terrible, then the answer is “No.” Parents, you feel me on this one? articles.text: One of the unfortunate side effects of the excessive number of cars (and traffic) in our built environment is the overabundance of required parking that goes along with it. Walking through Piedmont, it is clear that one reason it is so nice is the absence of large paved public parking lots so common in other communities. Even in our town center with a church, community center, art center, city hall, market, banks, offices, high school, middle school, and alternative school, there are no large, often desolate parking lots that are so destructive to the desired pedestrian scaled character and fabric a city. We are fortunate that this city was founded and laid out in an era before the ubiquitous auto dominance in our culture. If this city were designed today, conforming to typical current required parking standards, the town center would look nothing like it does. It would look instead like The main town center public parking is wonderfully designed. A curved narrow aisle visually breaks up the lot, cars are screened by planting on two sides, the lot is softened by larger trees, and there is a clear, simple search pattern. Curbside parking is generally a good thing. It is convenient, slows street traffic, and provides a barrier between pedestrians and the traffic flow of the street. Although currently a necessity in our culture, most parking lots are simply not very nice. They take up an incredible amount of space and impermeable paving and make up a large no-man’s land between the users and the facilities they serve. Often, they sit sparsely used or empty on off hours.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 7, 2020 23 Part 4: Parking in Piedmont By Will Adams One of the unfortunate side effects of the excessive number of cars (and traffic) in our built environment is the overabundance of required parking that goes along with it. Walking through Piedmont, it is clear that one reason it is so nice is the absence of large paved public parking lots so common in other communities. Even in our town center with a church, community center, art center, city hall, market, banks, offices, high school, middle school, and alternative school, there are no large, often desolate parking lots that are so destructive to the desired pedestrian scaled character and fabric a city. We are fortunate that this city was founded and laid out in an era before the ubiquitous auto dominance in our culture. If this city were designed today, conforming to typical current required parking standards, the town center would look nothing like it does. It would look instead like The main town center public parking is wonderfully designed. A curved narrow aisle visually breaks up the lot, cars are screened by planting on two sides, the lot is softened by larger trees, and there is a clear, simple search pattern. Curbside parking is generally a good thing. It is convenient, slows street traffic, and provides a barrier between pedestrians and the traffic flow of the street. Although currently a necessity in our culture, most parking lots are simply not very nice. They take up an incredible amount of space and impermeable paving and make up a large no-man’s land between the users and the facilities they serve. Often, they sit sparsely used or empty on off hours. There are numerous nice small parking lots located throughout the central area of the city. many areas of the surrounding newer communities, often essentially parking lots with isolated buildings in them. The interesting thing is that the reasonable small parking lots we have somehow work. Everybody finds parking places for all the activities. How is this possible? Several things come to mind. First, all our parking lots are shared by the surrounding uses. The church for example doesn’t have its own lot separate from the community center nor does the city hall have a separate lot from the art center. Secondly, there is curbside parking everywhere. Newer communities often prohibit this in central areas in what I consider an ill-conceived effort to move traffic faster on the streets. Third, a fair amount of people walk to events – the church, the store, city hall and neighbors’ houses, reducing the traffic and also the need for parking. Residential private parking on individual lots is the other part of the parking equation. The nicest homes, and coincidentally the nicest residential streets, are those that have the car parking clearly subordinate in the architectural design. There are a number of ways this is accomplished. A number of streets in town have associated mid-block alleys that provide auto access to rear facing garages at the back of the lots. We also see many detached front accessed garages placed to the rear of the property, away from and not competing with the street facade. And finally, there are many homes with attached front facing garages that are recessed or cleverly located to the side so they are not dominant in the street-side architecture of the home. Once parked cars and/or garage doors are given equal or more visual importance than the pedestrian entrance of a home, the scale is destroyed and the whole character of the home is compromised. We will discuss more of this in a future column. Next: Entries and Porches Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for close to 30 years. He can be reached at Will@MakingDesignSense.com. articles.text: Oven-roasted Brussels sprouts and delicata squash are a clear signal we’re transitioning from summer to autumn meals. This is my third published recipe using delicata squash in as many years. We enjoy this seasonal favorite countless times throughout fall and winter. Creating dishes using minimal ingredients with maximal taste is the key in these days of home cooking. A spice blend will do the heavy lifting on seasoning this dish. It’s the key behind this five-ingredient recipe. In addition to a chile blend, I’ve prepared versions of roasted vegetables using curry blends, harissa, Ras el Hanout, and Chinese Five Spice. You get to take your pick. This recipe has endless adaptations with vegetables, aromatics, spices and herbs. I happen to have a favorite spicery where I’ve purchased freshly milled herbs, chiles, and spices for years, Local Spicery. It’s important to like the spice blends right out of the jar to minimize fussing and doctoring them to suit your taste buds. The idea is that they make things easy, so go with a brand that works for you. There is no shortage of local spice shops for that personal touch, and there is an abundant variety of spice blends at local markets. Any flavor profile you enjoy will work here. So will a simple dusting of sea salt and freshly ground pepper. Five ingredients deliver an outstanding result. F-I-V-E! • • • • deep green, sliced in half lengthwise 1 pound delicata squash, ends trimmed, halved and seeds removed; sliced into 1/2-inch thick pieces 1 tablespoon olive oil 1 tablespoon chile powder blend, or substitute any preferred spice blend 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste if your spice blend is salt-free INSTRUCTIONS Place an oven rack on the middle rack of the oven and preheat the oven to either 350° F on the “convection-roast” setting, or 400° F on the “bake” setting. Place the sliced Brussels sprouts and delicata squash on a sheet pan and drizzle with 1 tablespoons of olive oil. Stir the Brussels sprouts and squash pieces around to cover each with olive oil. Add more oil if needed. Arrange the slices into a single layer. Place the pan of Brussels sprouts and squash into the oven and roast for about 12 – 15 minutes, when you see some browning on them, remove the pan from the oven. Using a spatula, move the pieces close together and sprinkle with chile powder blend (or other spice blend) and salt to taste. Stir to mix, then spread out into an even layer and return the pan to the oven. Roast an additional 5 – 7 minutes until both the Brussels sprouts and squash are golden-brown. Test the vegetables with a fork to check they are tender but still provide slight resistance. You don’t want them mushy. Chile Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Delicata Squash Makes about four cups INGREDIENTS • 1 pound Brussels sprouts, For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com

articles.text: For the first time in its 22-year history, the annual Piedmont Harvest Festival was held online rather than in Piedmont Park due the current health pandemic. The Recreation Department asked residents to send in photographs of the items they otherwise would have brought to the Community Hall as part of the bounty of samples of home-grown foods. Mayor Bob McBain picked the winners in a random drawing. Rami Albert was the winner of the Edible Food Contest with a picture of cucumbers that were grown locally. The honor came with a $60 gift certificate from Ace Garden Center. Everyone who entered the contest received a participation ribbon and was entered into the random drawing. Piedmont Garden Club sponsored a youth art contest this year as well. Piedmont kids ages 14 and younger were asked to download a coloring poster, create their own vegetable drawing, or make a collage from a nature scavenger hunt page. The winner was 8th grader Sophie Glass, whose art work was chosen by a random draw. Glass received a $30 gift certificate from Village Market for her entry. Harvest Festival founder and former mayor Susan Hill noted that there were more entrants this year than ever before. The festival will return for its 23rd year in 2021. Rami Albert’s home-grown cucumbers won the Harvest Festival Edible Food Contest this year. A pastel by Sophie Glass won the youth art contest at the virtual Piedmont Harvest Festival in September.
articles.title: Harvest Festival announces winners of Edible Food Contest

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: In support of Hilary Cooper for school board I am writing in strong support for Hilary Cooper for the Piedmont School Board. I have a long history of advocacy for S.T.E.A.M. subjects in town including co-founding Piedmont Makers in 2014 and serving as President. I first met Hilary when she was the PMS parent club president and we were starting Makers. Hilary was very supportive of our start-up process including securing part of our “seed” funding from her parent club budget. She saw the value that Makers could bring to Piedmont. Since then it has grown to encompass many programs including School Maker Faires, Makerspaces, over 30 Robotics teams, and our $400,000 fundraising campaign to outfit the engineering lab in the new S.T.E.A.M. building. Based on my experiences with Hilary, I believe she would continue to be a strong supporter of innovation in our district. In order to meet the constantly evolving demands of distance learning, getting our kids back to school safely, and keeping our curriculum and technology up-to-date is important. We cannot think of our pre-COVID curriculum and teaching models as the world changes around us. I worked with Hilary when I was on the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) board of directors and Hilary was co-chair of the Giving Campaign. She deeply understands the role that PEF plays in our school budgeting process which will only get more important moving forward. Most recently she co-chaired the successful Measures G&H campaign, which provides approximately 30% of the district’s operating budget. Her ability to lead strategic campaigns to successful outcomes is proof of the impact she can bring on the school board. Hilary brings over 11 years of experience supporting our schools in various capacities as a volunteer. I know that she would put all of her skills and experience to work making our schools the best they can be for all learners. Please join me in voting for Hilary Cooper for the school board. We are within all zoning requirements, commissioners have complimented the design, and we have not asked for any variances,” Nunes said. “We have been denied approval for reasons that I just don’t think are justified.” The first denial came because of height and alleged neighborhood impact, and a tight automobile turnaround. Alice Creason, a neighbor at 408 Blair Avenue, stated that the proposed 90-degree turn in the driveway is a radical change from the existing condition. The property, she stated, is sufficiently large for the garage to be located elsewhere on the property. Nunes said those concerns were addressed and modified and brought back to the commission with a resulting denial. Commissioners claimed they could not support the project because of the impacts on light, views, and privacy for the neighbor at 412 Blair Avenue, the narrow driveway, and the difficulty of vehicles accessing the garage. Commissioners suggested relocating the garage. A row of tall, fully mature trees creates a visual barrier between the Meagher and Creason residences. From the garage and driveway, the Creason house is nearly invisible due to the foliage. “There is no significant impact on light. We explained that [this design] improves privacy, and there is no view in question as defined by the city,” Nunes said. “If we can’t get a project approved that is fully-compliant, then really we are encouraged to leave this substandard garage in place.” At the September 21 council meeting, Meagher offered her observations. “[The planning commission] discussed the easement, which they should not have; it is not part of this project. They discussed the driveway, which is not part of the project either. They [speculated] on a possible future owner at 412 Blair, which feels like a far, far reach and abuse of discretionary power,” she said. She concluded that denying the project would strip the city of two off-street parking spaces and an accessory-dwelling unit for the city. Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King said she supported the denial by Planning Commission. She said that she was not persuaded that the proposed garage and living unit above it would be used as affordable housing, and that the owners might use it as a “rumpus-room.” She noted the repeated concerns about the narrow driveway as well. “I continue to be extremely concerned about the width of emergency vehicles accessing the [narrow] garage,” King said. Councilmember Tim Rood noted that future inhabitants may choose to back out of the very long driveway, rather than perform the turn to drive off the property, creating a pedestrian safety risk. “To me, that is the crux of why we should deny the appeal,” he said. Councilmember Jen Cavenaugh said that if the denial was on the basis of an insufficient turnaround space, the applicant believes they have in fact provided evidence on an adequate driveway and turnaround. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon requested a consensus among the councilmembers present. articles.text: Editor: From the moment I met Veronica Thigpen at a community event, I immediately felt a connection with her. Her warmth, kindness and sincerity resonated with me. I’ve gotten to know Veronica very well, having worked with her closely on several projects. Juggling multiple tasks under the pressure of looming deadlines, she has demonstrated the ability to make quick, yet thoughtful decisions, while remaining calm and positive. Her receptivity to input from all team members created a supportive environment that encouraged the sharing of ideas. After living in Piedmont for over 16 years, it was Veronica, a relative newcomer to Piedmont, who made me feel, for the first time, a part of the Piedmont Community. Veronica’s decision to run for School Board excites me. In addition to the personal qualities she has demonstrated, Veronica has the experience and insight to bring our district into the light of current thought. Through her focus on equity, she will help the Board address the social issues of our time, and help our children gain the tools to face an ever-changing world while maintaining top level academics. Join me in voting. Veronica Thigpen for Piedmont School Board. –Suzanne Lane
articles.title: Veronica Thigpen well-suited to be on school board

articles.text: Editor: I am urging readers to vote for Jennifer Cavenaugh in her run for re-election to the Piedmont City Council. Probably most people know Jen and her contribution. But for the few who don’t, let me count the ways. • She has been an active contributor to the Piedmont City Council. • She was a member of the Piedmont Budget Advisory Committee. • She has organized events and programs with the Piedmont Recreation Dept. • She was an outstanding board member of the Parent Board at Beach, PMS, and PHS. • She was Piedmont Language School President and a Board Member. • She has led programs to include the Oakland Treasure Hunt Event Jen is a parent of a classmate of my daughter, so I have seen her in action; seen her commitment and passion to making Piedmont the wonderful and warm town that we all want it to be. Her enthusiasm has got me and other neighbors to volunteer with school programs, testifying at city hall meetings, and getting involved with the pool. Cory’s deep roots within our community and 16 years of experience raising children in our schools makes her a supremely relevant candidate for Piedmont families with kids of all ages. During these critical times when the District is facing unprecedented challenges, responsiveness by board members is critical. She was able to quickly identify the organizations, leaders and communities to highlight, as well as education experts in academia and philanthropy that were featured in panel discussions that provided important contextual background. I greatly appreciated how Veronica made sure that the site visits highlighted a diversity of Black, Latino and White parent leaders that represented a range of Chicago neighborhoods that were homogenous as well as diverse. articles.text: A “Spare the Air” alert was extended for the San Francisco Bay Area, including Piedmont, through tomorrow, Thursday, October 7, the Bay Area Air Quality Management District said yesterday, Tuesday, October 6. The region’s air quality is being negatively impacted by the destructive Glass Fire that continues to burn through Sonoma and Napa counties. “While most of the Bay Area has experienced cleaner air over the past few days, localized and intermittent smoke impacts will continue near the Glass Fire,”said Jack Broadbent of Bay Air Aire Quality District. “Bay Area residents should continue to be vigilant about air quality conditions over the next couple of days. As fire containment efforts progress and more favorable weather conditions move into the region, we expect more widespread relief from smoke starting this weekend.” When Spare the Air warnings are in effect, people are advised to limit their times outdoors, especially those with who are sensitive to air conditions. Additionally, the use of fireplaces, wood stoves, pellet stoves, outdoor fire pits or other wood-burning devices is prohibited. The Glass Fire began early on September 27. Thousands of people have been evacuated in and aroudn Calistoga, 66,840 acres have burned in the North Bay and 1,411 structures have been destroyed. The fire, which has burned through many vineyards and wineries, is 50 percent contained as of yesterday. The weather in the Bay Area is expected to improve from a wildfire risk standpoint throughout the week, and some precipitation is expected this weekend. However, Fire Chief Bret Black said that wildfire season is a long time from ending. “We are seeing some cooling in the Bay Area and the potential for a little moisture of Friday and Saturday,” Black told the Post. “It is important to note that a little bit of precipitation does not end the wildfire threat. A significant warming trend is forecasted toward the middle of next week.” Black noted that the Camp Fire, which decimated the California city of Paradise in 2018, began on November 8 of that year. “Expect significant wildfire potential through the end of November,” Black continued. “Some of California’s deadliest wildfires started in October and even November.” The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. He recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage of the City’s website and www.ReadyForWildfire.org. articles.text: There is an emotional tie to the Piedmont Swimming Pool. We were members for years. Our daughter played high school water polo and was on the Piedmont Swim Team from 2nd grade on. All our children learned to swim there and were so proud to display their white patches. It was an important piece of our lives and the lives of many Piedmonters. This is clearly an emotional issue, as evidenced by the pro-UU letters to the Post. However, as with many other situations we now face, I listen to the experts. I listen to our Chief of Police who stated in April that his “Police Department Facility was not complying with the Essential Services Act”. I listen to our Fire Chief who stated in April that an earthquake would cause “significant structural damage to the Fire Station.” I listen to the financial experts who estimate that the Police and Fire upgrades will cost anywhere from $23 million to $39 million, and who point to the drop in transfer tax revenue year over year. I listen to the financial analysts who wonder how we are going to pay our $7 million sewer system loans, our $13 million Post Employee Benefits Program and our $26 million Net Pension Liability. And I listen to the experienced architects who question the minimal amount of detail in the [Measure UU] plans and the cost estimates for the pool. Would I love to have a new pool? Absolutely. Is this the right time? Absolutely not. I am taking a step back from the emotional side of this issue and relying on the practical side of things. Vote no on UU and let us find a time in the future when we can do this the right way.

Please vote yes on UU –Kay and Bob Cheatham Piedmont pool for 21st century means zero-carbon By Tom Webster Last week’s Piedmont Post included a discussion about priorities for when to build new city facilities (a pool, fire and police buildings). To that topic, we would like to add a discussion on how new facilities should be built, in particular a new swimming pool. Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan, approved by City Council in 2018, recommends that municipal facilities and services be zero carbon by 2050. To achieve that objective, the city of Piedmont will have to install solar panels, switch to electric vehicles and stop using natural gas. All new facilities will have to be built for a future of zero carbon emissions. Swimming pools, heated year-round to 70 degrees, require enormous amounts of energy. We examined how to make the proposed pool carbon free. The proposed pool design calls for using green technology to produce 10% of the pool complex electricity from solar panels and 50% of pool heating from solar water heater. That means much of the remaining energy will come from non-renewable sources like natural gas. We explored a scenario that uses a larger on-site solar array to power heat pumps to evaluate designs that could plausibly achieve the zero-carbon standard for the lap pool alone. By directly using solar power collected at the pool and using it to power heat pumps, no natural gas is required to heat the water. The area of the solar array needed to heat a pool with heat pumps depends on the size of the pool and how much of the annual heating load is produced by heat pumps. To heat the pool 100% of the time with solar energy, the solar array would need to be about 70% of the pool size. (see chart from our analysis at the Connect Resources page, https://www.piedmontconnect.org/resources) By using on-site, solar-generated electricity to power heat pumps, and the traditional electricity grid as backup, the heating needs of the lap pool could be met without relying on natural gas. This all-electric pool design would significantly reduce the GHG emissions compared with the proposed design, which uses natural gas. Our analysis shows how different lap pool sizes can be made zero-carbon if sufficient area is available for solar arrays. Our analysis does not account for the energy needs of the fun pool and building, which also must be zero-carbon by 2050. Should Piedmont residents vote in November in favor of building a new pool complex, it behooves the City Council and city staff to ensure that the new facility be built to accommodate a large enough solar array along with heat pumps to eliminate the use of natural gas. By California law, all electricity must be carbon free by 2045, so by building an all-electric lap pool now and relying on the transition to an all-renewable energy grid, the pool complex may be zero-carbon by 2050. articles.text: Local residents Celine McTaggart and her husband, and piedmont resident Rick Arney, founded Californians for Consumer Privacy, the group that spearheaded the campaign for the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018. It passed unanimously in both the state assembly and senate, which gave Californians the strongest data privacy rights in the United States. This was a huge step forward for consumer privacy in the U.S., but an assault in the legislature the following year (2019) by Big Tech pushed to dilute the rights that would be given to consumers. It was then that a decision to put it on the ballot was made – to allow voters to decide its fate rather than the state legislature. Prop. 24 would allow any pro-privacy amendments with a simple majority of the LegislaNearly one million people signed the petition to put Prop 24 on the ballot. It currently is polling at 81%. Andrew Yang, a presidnetial candidate this year, is Chair of the Prop. 24 Advisory Board, along with Jim Steyer, founder of Common Sense Media. ture, while preventing amendments that hurt consumer privacy. What does Prop. 24 do? 1. Consumers can stop large corporations from using personal data based on race, ethnicity, union membership, sexual orientation, health, etc. 2. It triples fines for abuses of kids’ data, which is more important now since school is online. 3. It creates an enforcement arm to deal with data breaches and abuses of consumer data. The Prop. 24 campaign says, “It is a necessary step to protect California’s leading position in privacy law, to prevent privacy from being gutted in the legislature, and would without a doubt set a strong floor for privacy at the federal level.” For a short history and basis of it qualifying to be on the ballot, see: https://www. caprivacy.org/california-privacy-r ights-act-cpra-qualifies-for-the-november-2020-ballot/ “This is really also about democracy and giving people a choice about their own personal information, like that of their race, ethnicity, and health, and letting them decide who gets to use it – or not.” For more informtion contact Celine Mactaggart at cmactaggart@caprivacy.org. of all that we are facing, to care about surrounding ourselves with quality. What does it have to do with the orange sky? This activity, though simple, is a good representation of what happened on September 9th . You can think of the flashlight as representing the sun and its light, traveling all the way to Earth. As it reaches our planet, it must pass through our atmosphere and any other mediums in its path, such as clouds. These natural filters are similar to the cellophane filters we used in the activity. They slow down and change the light as it passes through, changing its wavelength and therefore, the way we see it. When there are thick clouds in the sky it can act like a filter and change the light passing through to appear dark and gray, like what we see on a gloomy day… something we are very familiar with here in the Bay Area.

articles.text: Piedmont firefighters have answered the call to assist in yet another large fire in Northern California as the state trudges through a catastrophic wildfire season. On the morning of September 28, Piedmont Fire Department was requested to the Glass Fire incident for several large spot fires. Engine 2841 left for Calistoga at about 1:30 a.m. The four-man crew assigned to the incident includes Captain Mike Carlisle, Engineer Alan Grace, Firefighter Sandor Lengyel, and Firefighter/Paramedic Brian Gidney. The firefighters went to work immediately in Calistoga, rescuing residents and performing structure protection where possible. Piedmont responded along with Fremont and Berkeley Fire Departments. “The crew is expected to be assigned to the Glass Fire for at least a few more days,” Fire Chief Bret Black confirmed. As of October 5 the Glass Fire had burned over 65,000 acres and was located near North Fork Crystal Springs Road in St. Helena. It has impacted Napa and Sonoma counties. Through Sunday night, the fire burned actively due to low humidity and high temperatures. Aggressive mop-up work continued in areas where the fire’s forward progress had stopped, according to Cal Fire. Crews were working aggressively on Monday to construct and reinforce existing control lines. As of Monday afternoon, 1,235 residential and commercial structures had been destroyed, including much of the famed Meadowood resort. A total of 27 crews have been assigned to assist in containing the fire. This year has marked a record fire season for the state, with a total of four million acres burned by October 2020. While many of California’s largest fires occur in late summer, the deadliest and most destructive blazes tend to occur at the end of the dry season, from September to December. Cal Fire noted that, while wildfires are a natural part of California’s landscape, the fire season in California and across the West is starting earlier and ending later each year. “Climate change is considered a key driver of this trend. Warmer spring and summer temperatures, reduced snowpack, and earlier spring snowmelt create longer and more intense dry seasons that increase moisture stress on vegetation and make forests more susceptible to severe wildfire,” Cal Fire stated. The length of California’s fire season is estimated to have increased by 75 days across the Sierras and seems to correspond with an increase in the extent of forest fires across the state. upgrades, or play structure improvements. “We work closely with Carol Cramer, the school principal, and try to support her with anything she needs,” said Learn. “Our main effort is trying to bring back a little bit of normal life so we can kind of forget about the rest of the chaos swirling around,” said Learn with a grin. articles.text: According to the Alameda County Registrar of Voter, to avoid large gatherings of people only one voting location will be open in Piedmont on election day, November 3. The Veterans’ Memorial Building at 401 Highland Avenue will serve as the city’s voting location for in-person voting this election, but it will be open three days instead of only on election day. Residents can vote at the Veterans’ Memorial Building on Saturday, October 31, and on Monday and Tuesday, November 2 - 3, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Any resident of Alameda County can come to the Veterans Hall and cast their ballot, or drop off their absentee ballot. They may also put their absentee ballot in the secure ballot box located on Highland Way near the two mailboxes. Ballots may be dropped off anytime up to 8 p.m. on November 4. A list of all polling locations in Alameda County is available online at https:// w w w.acgov.org /rov_ app/ pollinglist. The Registrar of Voters was scheduled to began mailing ballots to all voters this week, starting on Monday, October 5. Residents who have not received a sample ballot may contact the registrar’s office at (510) 272-6933. The local election will include names of candidates for two seats on the Piedmont City Council and three seats on the School Board. Other noteworthy elections include the President of the United States, United States Representative, and Assemblymember, as well as several statewide measures, special district measures, and two City of Piedmont measures: Measure TT and Measure UU.
